questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a UK-listed general insurer is preparing a report for the audit committee that summarizes the UK regulatory expectations on operational resilience. Which of the following statements should she include in the report?

options.text: The FCA, PRA, and Bank of England issued the first regulatory guidance on resilience in 2018, and the new requirements sit alongside existing operational risk requirements.
The FCA, PRA, and Bank of England issued the first regulatory guidance on resilience in 2018, and the new requirements will replace the existing operational risk requirements.
The FCA, PRA, and Bank of England issued their 2018 resilience paper mainly to address the risks of remote working that followed the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Basel Committee issued the first regulatory guidance on resilience, and the FCA, PRA, and Bank of England later adopted its seven principles in 2018.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: CCO of a UK-listed general insurer chooses the accurate summary of UK resilience expectations for the audit committee.

**Concept and theory**

Who and when. UK regulators were the first to publish regulatory guidance on resilience. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and the Bank of England (BoE) jointly issued a discussion paper in July 2018, Building the UK financial sector’s operational resilience, as the start of a comprehensive framework.

Context. GARP observes that the 2018 paper “reads very much like a response to the TSB Bank disruption” (a failed IT migration that cut millions of retail customers off their accounts). The industry at the time was mainly worried about IT disruptions and cyberattacks, and built much of its resilience capacity around the continuity of IT infrastructures and services. Then came COVID-19: remote working, call centers moved to living rooms, critical payments and market transactions run under conditions beyond any tested stress scenario.

Relation to existing rules. Regulators made clear that the new requirements “sit alongside existing ORM requirements as opposed to replacing them.” The BoE stated in 2018 that operational resilience is already a responsibility of firms and FMIs and an outcome supported by the existing regulatory framework, and that the authorities were considering how to supplement existing policies.

| Item | UK position |
|---|---|
| Issuers | FCA, PRA, and BoE jointly |
| First document | July 2018 discussion paper (first regulatory guidance on resilience) |
| Initial focus | IT disruption and cyberattacks; continuity of IT services |
| Later shock | COVID-19 and remote working (2020) |
| Relation to ORM rules | Sit alongside; supplement, do not replace |

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share the same frame, so find the one changed fact in each. Option A keeps every element right: joint issuers, first guidance, 2018, and “alongside.”

**Fragile fact.** Order of publication: UK 2018 first, then Fed 2020, then BCBS March 2021; and UK resilience rules supplement, not replace, ORM rules.

**Reference**

LO 42.d (wording as in Solution 1). GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6, “First Regulatory Guidance on Operational Resilience: The UK” and the BoE 2018 statement that follows. Schweser LO 42.d, “UK Regulations.” Version note: Schweser says “additional regulations were added in 2018,” whereas GARP describes the 2018 document as a joint discussion paper that initiated the framework; GARP’s description is used. Schweser also attributes the COVID-19 adjustments to the UK framework, while GARP says the later BCBS 2021 guidance integrates COVID-19 lessons; this question does not depend on that difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-1 d, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: Option A matches GARP: UK regulators were the first to publish guidance (2018 joint paper by FCA, PRA, and BoE), and the new requirements sit alongside existing ORM requirements rather than replacing them.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Identical to A except that “sit alongside” becomes “replace.” GARP and Schweser both say existing ORM requirements were not replaced. Option B would be correct only if the regulators had repealed the existing operational risk rules, which they explicitly said they would not do.

c.reason: (scope or condition error (timing)). The 2018 paper predates the pandemic; at the time the concern was IT disruption and cyberattacks. Remote-working risk became a theme only after COVID-19 in 2020. Option C would be correct for the 2021 MAS and ABS paper on remote working, or as a description of later adjustments, not for the 2018 UK paper.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The first-mover is wrong. The UK regulators published first (2018); the BCBS principles came in March 2021. Option D would be correct only if the sequence were reversed.

questions.question: A risk consultant is helping a US regional bank map its departments onto the building blocks of operational resilience that arrange the topics of the Federal Reserve’s 2020 sound practices paper into a single structure. Which of the following placements is the most accurate?

options.text: Governance forms the base, ORM is the central component, and third-party risk management and scenario analysis are the two supporting pillars.
ORM forms the base, governance is the central component, and business continuity management and IT systems resilience are the two supporting pillars.
Governance forms the base, ORM is the central component, and business continuity management and IT systems resilience are the two supporting pillars.
Governance forms the base, business continuity management is the central component, and ORM and IT systems resilience are the two supporting pillars.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant maps a US regional bank’s departments onto the building blocks of resilience arranged from the Fed’s 2020 paper.

**Concept and theory**

In 2020 the Federal Reserve issued Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience. GARP’s Figure 1.3 (source: Chapelle) rearranges the topics of the Fed document into a single picture, the “building blocks of operational resilience,” with operational resilience as the holistic result. Think of it as a building:

| Position | Component and reason |
|---|---|
| Base | Governance: roles and responsibilities to coordinate ORM and resilience; the required starting point |
| Central component | ORM: resilience is not possible without proper ORM |
| Two ORM specializations | Third-party risk management (resilience of supply chains); scenario analysis (preparedness for tail events) |
| Two supporting pillars | Business continuity management (BCM); IT systems resilience |
| Over everything | Monitoring and reporting of coordination and maintenance |
| Result (roof) | Operational resilience |

The traps are role swaps between levels: which is the base, which is the center, and which pair are pillars versus specializations of ORM.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each option’s three slots (base, center, pillars) against the table. Only option C has governance at the base, ORM at the center, and BCM plus IT systems resilience as the pillars.

**Fragile fact.** Base: governance. Center: ORM. Pillars: BCM and IT systems resilience. ORM specializations: third-party risk management and scenario analysis. Over all: monitoring and reporting.

**Reference**

LO 42.d (wording as in Solution 1). GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6, “US Regulation” and Figure 1.3 “Building blocks of operational resilience” (source: Chapelle). Schweser LO 42.d, “U.S. Regulations” and Figure 42.1. Note: GARP presents the figure as Chapelle’s rearrangement of the Fed document’s chapters, not as a figure the Fed itself published; Schweser’s text reads as if the Fed described it. Content of the placements is the same in both.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-1 d, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (sibling swap). Base and center are right, but the pillars are replaced by the two ORM specializations. Third-party risk management and scenario analysis are specializations of ORM, not the supporting pillars. Option A would be correct if the stem asked “Which two specializations of ORM support resilience?”

b.reason: (role misassignment). The pillars are right, but governance and ORM have swapped positions. Governance is the base (starting point of coordination); ORM is the center. Option B would be correct only if the figure placed ORM at the foundation, which it does not.

c.reason: GARP: “Governance forms the basis ... ORM is the central component of operational resilience ... The two critical supporting pillars of operational resilience are business continuity management (BCM) and IT systems resilience.” Option C states these three placements.

d.reason: (role misassignment). BCM is moved to the center and ORM is demoted to a pillar. In the figure BCM is a pillar and ORM is central. It would be correct only if the figure were built around continuity planning, which is the older view resilience moved beyond.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian bank with a US subsidiary is checking a slide that summarizes the Federal Reserve’s 2020 Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience. The slide contains these statements:

I. The guidance views operational resilience as a key outcome of an effective operational risk management framework.

II. The guidance stresses the need to place operational resilience within a holistic enterprise management framework.

III. Third-party risk management supports resilience mainly by preparing the firm for tail events, while scenario analysis protects the resilience of supply chains.

IV. Since resilience is the outcome, a firm with a strong business continuity plan may treat resilience as a substitute for an operational risk management framework.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II, and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Internal auditor checks four statements on a slide summarizing the Fed’s 2020 Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience.

**Concept and theory**

GARP summarizes the Fed’s 2020 paper as running along similar lines to the UK approach (important business services, impact tolerance) and adding two framing points:

(1) operational resilience is “a key outcome of an effective ORMF”; and

(2) there is a need to insert operational resilience into a holistic enterprise management framework.

Schweser puts it as: an effective ORM framework would have operational resilience as the major result.

In the building-blocks arrangement, ORM is central because “operational resilience is not possible without proper ORM,” and two ORM specializations each have a specific purpose:

| Specialization | Purpose (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Third-party risk management | Essential for the resilience of supply chains |
| Scenario analysis | Necessary preparedness for tail events (low-probability, high-severity) |

The logical direction matters: ORM is the cause, resilience is the outcome. An outcome cannot replace the process that produces it.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: “key outcome of an effective ORMF.” Accurate.
- II: “insert operational resilience in a holistic enterprise management framework.” Accurate.
- III: the purposes are swapped (third parties go with supply chains; scenario analysis with tail events). Inaccurate.
- IV: reverses the cause and effect; resilience is not possible without proper ORM, so it cannot substitute for it. Inaccurate.

I and II only: option B.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: ORM produces resilience (resilience is the outcome); third parties pair with supply chains, scenario analysis with tail events.

**Reference**

LO 42.d (wording as in Solution 1). GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6, “US Regulation” and the text accompanying Figure 1.3. Schweser LO 42.d, “U.S. Regulations.” The sources agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-1 d, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (scope error (rejects a true statement)). Option A accepts I but rejects II. The Fed guidance explicitly stresses placing resilience in a holistic enterprise framework. Option A would be correct only if Statement II had said resilience should be managed as a standalone program outside enterprise risk management.

b.reason: Statements I and II restate GARP’s summary of the Fed paper: resilience as a key outcome of an effective ORMF, inserted into a holistic enterprise framework.

c.reason: (role misassignment (via Statement III)). Option C accepts Statement III, which assigns each specialization the other’s purpose. Third-party risk management protects supply-chain resilience; scenario analysis prepares for tail events. Statement III would be correct if the two names were swapped back.

d.reason: (polarity flip (via Statement IV)). Option D accepts IV, which reverses the causal direction: it treats resilience (the outcome) as a substitute for ORM (the cause), and drops I. GARP says resilience is not possible without proper ORM. Statement IV would only be correct if resilience could be achieved through BCP alone, which the building-blocks view rules out.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a Shanghai-based commercial bank is preparing a gap analysis against the Basel Committee’s 2021 Principles for Operational Resilience. Which of the following correctly states what the named principle asks banks to do?

options.text: Principle 1 (governance): set up a new, dedicated governance structure for resilience that operates separately from the bank’s existing governance.
Principle 5 (third-party dependency management): eliminate all dependencies on third parties and intragroup entities for the delivery of critical operations.
Principle 3 (business continuity planning and testing): map the internal and external interconnections and interdependencies needed to deliver critical operations.
Principle 6 (incident management): develop and implement response and recovery plans to manage incidents that could disrupt the delivery of critical operations.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Shanghai bank analyst’s gap analysis: which option correctly states what a named BCBS 2021 resilience principle asks banks to do.

**Concept and theory**

In March 2021 the BCBS issued seven Principles for Operational Resilience. Each is phrased as “Banks should ...” (GARP Table 1.3):

| No. | Category | Banks should ... |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Governance | utilize their existing governance structure |
| 2 | Operational risk management | leverage their respective functions for the management of operational risk |
| 3 | Business continuity planning and testing | have business continuity plans in place |
| 4 | Mapping interconnections and | map the internal and external interconnections and |
|  | interdependencies | interdependencies necessary for the delivery of critical operations |
| 5 | Third-party dependency management | manage their dependencies on relationships to third parties or intragroup entities |
| 6 | Incident management | develop and implement response and recovery plans to manage incidents that could disrupt the delivery of critical operations |
| 7 | ICT including cybersecurity | ensure resilient ICT including cybersecurity |

The design idea behind Principles 1 and 2 is that resilience is built on top of what already exists (governance, ORM), not in a parallel structure.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option names a principle and attaches an action. Check whether the action belongs to that principle and is stated with the right verb (utilize, manage, map, develop). Only option D attaches the correct action to the correct principle.

**Fragile fact.** Principle 1 uses the existing governance; Principle 5 manages (not eliminates) third-party dependencies; mapping is Principle 4, response and recovery plans are Principle 6.

**Reference**

LO 42.d (wording as in Solution 1). GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6, “BCBS Principles on Operational Resilience” and Table 1.3. Schweser LO 42.d, “Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)” lists the same seven principles by name only; the “Banks should” content is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-1 d, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: (polarity flip). Principle 1 asks banks to utilize their existing governance structure; option A asks for a new, separate one. GARP stresses using the existing governance framework (Principles 1 and 2). Option A would be correct only if the principle said “establish a new governance structure,” which it does not.

b.reason: (absolute claim). Principle 5 asks banks to manage dependencies on third parties and intragroup entities; it does not ask them to eliminate them. Option B turns management into elimination. It would be correct only under a rule banning outsourcing of critical operations, which is not in the principles.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The action (mapping interconnections and interdependencies) is Principle 4’s, attached to Principle 3’s name. Principle 3 asks banks to have business continuity plans in place. Option C would be correct if the label were changed to Principle 4.

d.reason: Option D matches Principle 6 in Table 1.3: develop and implement response and recovery plans to manage incidents that could disrupt the delivery of critical operations.

questions.question: A supervisor at a national banking regulator is explaining to newly hired examiners how the Basel Committee’s 2021 Principles for Operational Resilience relate to operational risk management and to earlier national guidance. Which of the following statements is the most accurate?

options.text: Principles 3, 5, and 7 mirror the UK regulators’ approach, while Principles 4 and 6 mirror the elements highlighted in the Federal Reserve’s paper.
The principles were issued separately from the operational risk principles, to signal that the Committee sees resilience as independent of ORM.
The principles were issued together with the revised operational risk principles, because the Committee sees resilience as an outcome of effective ORM.
The Committee states that the robustness of a bank’s ICT framework, rather than of its ORM framework, is the first condition for good resilience.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Supervisor explains to new examiners how the BCBS 2021 resilience principles relate to ORM and to earlier UK and US guidance.

**Concept and theory**

Timing and link to ORM. The BCBS principles on operational resilience came out in March 2021, at the same time as the revisions to the Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk (RPSMOR). GARP says this was intentional: Basel links the two topics, stating that “operational resilience is an outcome that benefits from the effective management of operational risk.” In its opening statements the BCBS makes clear that the robustness of an ORM framework is the first condition for a good level of operational resilience.

Mapping to earlier guidance. The seven principles absorb both national approaches:

| Principles | Content | Echoes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 and 2 | Use existing governance; leverage ORM functions | Holistic integration into existing risk management |
| 3, 5, and 7 | BCP; third parties; ICT | The Fed document |
| 4 and 6 | Mapping interconnections for critical operations; incident response and recovery | The UK regulators’ approach |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes one claim about either the timing and rationale or the mapping. The decisive facts are: published together with RPSMOR, on purpose, because resilience is an outcome of effective ORM; 3, 5, and 7 echo the Fed; 4 and 6 echo the UK. Option C is the only one consistent with these facts.

**Fragile fact.** Attribution: 3, 5, 7 echo the US (Fed); 4 and 6 echo the UK. And the BCBS published resilience together with the revised ORM principles because resilience is an outcome of effective ORM.

**Reference**

LO 42.d (wording as in Solution 1). GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6, “BCBS Principles on Operational Resilience.” Schweser LO 42.d, “Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)” (Principles 1 and 2 use the existing governance; 3, 5, 7 similar to US guidance; 4 and 6 similar to UK guidance). Schweser does not mention the joint release with RPSMOR; that fact is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-1 d, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (role misassignment (attribution swap)). The mapping is reversed. GARP says Principles 3, 5, and 7 (BCP, third parties, ICT) are the elements highlighted in the Fed document, and Principles 4 and 6 (mapping, incident management) are in the same spirit as the UK approach. Option A would be correct if “UK” and “Federal Reserve” were swapped back.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Option B reverses both the timing (separately instead of together) and the rationale (independent instead of linked). Both facts come from one GARP sentence, so this is a single reversal of the link. It would be correct only if the Committee had chosen to treat resilience as a standalone topic.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP: the resilience principles were issued in March 2021 together with RPSMOR, intentionally, because the BCBS considers operational resilience “an outcome that benefits from the effective management of operational risk.”

d.reason: (sibling swap). The first condition named by the BCBS is the robustness of the ORM framework. ICT resilience is Principle 7, one element among seven. Option D substitutes a sibling principle for the foundation. It would be correct if the stem asked which principle deals with cybersecurity.

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Brazilian bank with branches in the European Union and Singapore is summarizing the regulatory material on operational resilience as it stood in May 2022. Which of the following statements is the most accurate?

options.text: The UK, US, and BCBS are the three main issuers of official resilience guidelines, while the ECB’s Digital Operational Resilience Act was published as a draft regulation.
The paper from the MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore mainly brings ICT-related requirements for financial entities in Singapore together into a single regulation.
The ECB’s Digital Operational Resilience Act mainly addresses the new risks from remote working, including staff misconduct and the effects on people and culture.
The ECB, through its Digital Operational Resilience Act, is one of the three main regulators to have issued official guidelines for operational resilience.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant to a Brazilian bank with EU and Singapore branches summarizes the resilience regulatory landscape as of May 2022.

**Concept and theory**

GARP (written as of May 2022) separates official guidelines from other publications:

| Issuer | Document | Content |
|---|---|---|
| UK (FCA, PRA, | 2018 discussion paper | Official guidance: important services, impact |
| BoE) | onward | tolerance |
| US (Fed) | 2020 Sound Practices | Official guidance: resilience as outcome of effective ORMF |
| BCBS | March 2021 Principles | Official guidance: seven principles |
| ECB | September 2020 draft regulation, DORA | Part of an EU digital-finance strategy; imposes ICT-related requirements on financial entities; brings EU initiatives together into one regulation |
| MAS with ABS | March 2021 paper on remote working | Risks from extensive remote working during COVID-19: operations, technology and information security, fraud and staff misconduct, legal and regulatory; people and culture; best-practice benchmark |

GARP: “The UK, US, and BCBS are the three main regulators having issued official guidelines for operational resilience.” Other regulators “have published consultation documents or guidelines of certain aspects of resilience.”

**Applying it to this question**

The options test two things: which bodies count as the three main official issuers, and which content belongs to DORA versus the MAS and ABS paper. Option A gets both right: the three main issuers are the UK, US, and BCBS, and DORA was a draft regulation.

**Fragile fact.** Three main official issuers as of May 2022: UK, US, BCBS. DORA (ECB) is about ICT and was a draft; MAS and ABS is about remote working.

**Reference**

LO 42.d (wording as in Solution 1). GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6, “Other Regulators on Other Aspects of Resilience: ECB and MAS.” Schweser LO 42.d, “Other Regulators.” Schweser says the ECB issued “proposed rules” in 2020; GARP calls it a draft regulation published in September 2020 as part of a European Commission strategy. No conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-1 d, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: Option A restates GARP: the UK, US, and BCBS are the three main regulators with official guidelines, and the ECB published DORA as a draft regulation (September 2020).

b.reason: (sibling swap). The content belongs to DORA (ICT-related requirements brought into one regulation), not to the MAS and ABS paper, which deals with risks from remote working. Option B would be correct if “the MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore” were replaced by “the ECB’s DORA.”

c.reason: (sibling swap). The reverse swap: remote-working risks, staff misconduct, and people and culture are the subject of the MAS and ABS paper, not DORA. Option C would be correct if the issuer were the MAS and ABS.

d.reason: (scope error). DORA was a draft regulation, and the ECB is not one of the three main official issuers; GARP places it among regulators that published documents on certain aspects of resilience. Option D would be correct only if DORA had been in force as official resilience guidance by May 2022, which the source does not say.

questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 b Q1
questions.question:
A risk consultant engaged by a Singapore-headquartered banking group is reviewing how the group’s Malaysia country operational risk committee works. The committee sits at the lowest level of the group’s committee pyramid, meets monthly, and has a predetermined escalation limit of SGD 1.0 million per event. Its March agenda contained the items below.

| Item | Description | Amount (SGD million) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Failed batch of retail payments, since corrected | 0.4 |
| 2 | Outage at an outsourced IT vendor affecting branches | 2.3 |
| 3 | Quarterly update of local risk indicator values | n/a |

Which of the following best describes how the committee should handle these items, consistent with its role in the committee structure?

options.text: Report the vendor outage directly to the full board with a recommendation on the resulting risk exposure, since the committee advises the board on risk-based decisions.
Resolve all three items locally and pass them upward only in an annual summary, since the committee holds full authority over operational risk within its scope.
Oversee the items within its scope, feed its information into the broader risk profile, and escalate the vendor outage to a firm-wide risk committee.
Escalate all three items to the board risk committee for a decision, since lowest-level committees collect risk information but do not oversee operational risk.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Malaysia country committee (lowest level) handling a SGD 0.4m loss, a SGD 2.3m vendor outage above its SGD 1.0m limit, and routine risk indicator data.

**Concept and theory**

Operational risk is the most decentralized of the regulated risk types: it arises in every process, system and team. Governance therefore cannot sit in one place. GARP explains that governance of operational risk is organized around committees taking collegial decisions, based on reporting and escalated information at different levels of the firm’s decision-making hierarchy. In larger and more complex firms this produces a pyramid of committees, each with responsibility for oversight, management, monitoring and reporting (or escalation).

| Level | Typical body | Role (GARP 2.3 a) |
|---|---|---|
| Lowest | Committees by business type or function (corporate banking, investment banking, support services) or by geography (country, region) | Oversee operational risk within their own scope; provide information to help determine the broader operational risk profile; escalate significant issues, or issues exceeding predetermined limits, to a firm-wide or second line of defense risk committee |
| Middle | Group (organization) operational risk committee | Oversees, manages, monitors and reports the consolidated picture to the executive/management committee and the board risk committee |
| Top | Board risk committee (board-created, enterprise level) | Oversees all operational risk; makes recommendations to the full board; reviews and monitors investigation of larger incidents |

The logic of the lowest level is a filter: local committees know the local business, so they deal with what is within their scope, but they must not sit on issues that are significant or that breach the limits set for them. Those travel upward, so the top of the pyramid sees what matters without being flooded.

**Applying it to this question**

The country committee is at the lowest level. Item 1 (SGD 0.4 million, already corrected) is within its SGD 1.0 million limit, so it is overseen locally. Item 3 is routine local information: its value is that it feeds the broader operational risk profile. Item 2 (SGD 2.3 million) exceeds the predetermined limit, which is exactly the trigger GARP gives for escalation to a firm-wide (or second line) risk committee. The monthly meeting frequency is irrelevant to the decision.

**Fragile fact.** Escalation from the lowest level is conditional (significant or above a predetermined limit) and goes to a firm-wide committee, not straight to the full board.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3 Operational Risk Governance, (a) Risk and Committee Structure, and Figure 2.3. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Risk Committee Structure (lowest level). No content conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (sibling swap). It gives the lowest-level committee the board risk committee’s property: making recommendations to the full board on risk exposure and risk-based decisions. A country committee escalates to a firm-wide committee; it does not advise the full board. This option would be correct if the stem described the board risk committee receiving an escalated incident.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It keeps the true part (the committee oversees operational risk within its scope) but drops the stated condition that significant issues and issues exceeding predetermined limits must be escalated, and overextends the committee’s authority to “full”. It would be correct only if every item were within the committee’s predetermined limits and none were significant, and even then periodic upward information flow, not an annual summary, is the expectation.

c.reason: Option C reproduces the three duties GARP assigns to lowest-level committees: oversee operational risk within their scope, provide information to help determine the broader profile, and escalate significant or limit-exceeding issues to a firm-wide committee. Schweser says the same: such committees provide valuable data for assessing firmwide risk and forward crucial issues to the middle or top level.

d.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses “these committees oversee operational risk within their respective scopes” into “do not oversee operational risk”. Escalating everything, including routine data and a corrected small loss, defeats the filtering purpose of the pyramid. It would be correct only for an item that is significant or above the limit, which applies to item 2 alone.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a large Canadian universal bank is preparing an induction session for newly hired analysts. She wants a slide that matches each governance body in the bank’s operational risk structure to the role it plays.

| Body | Governance body |
|---|---|
| 1 | Capital markets operational risk committee (one business line) |
| 2 | Group operational risk committee |
| 3 | Board risk committee |
| 4 | Full board of directors |
| Role | Description |
| P | Oversees, manages and monitors operational risk across the group and reports the consolidated picture to the management committee and the board risk committee |
| Q | Oversees all operational risk, makes recommendations on risk-based decisions and risk exposure, and reviews and monitors the investigation of larger incidents |
| R | Oversees operational risk within its own scope and provides information that helps determine the broader operational risk profile |
| S | Holds ultimate responsibility, sets the risk appetite, and validates the operational risk management framework |

Which matching is most accurate?
questions.solution:
Stem summary: Induction slide matching a business-line committee, the group operational risk committee, the board risk committee and the full board to four roles.

**Concept and theory**

The LO asks you to compare bodies, so the skill tested is to tell apart four verbs: oversee within scope and inform, consolidate and report, oversee all and recommend, and decide and hold ultimate responsibility.

| Body | What it does | What it does not do |
|---|---|---|
| Business-line, function or country committee | Oversees operational risk in its scope; supplies information to the broader profile; escalates significant or limit-breaching issues | Consolidate the group picture; advise the full board |
| Group operational risk committee (Schweser: organization risk committee) | Oversees, manages, monitors and reports the consolidated picture to the executive/management committee and the board risk committee | Make recommendations to the full board |
| Board risk committee | Board-created, enterprise level; oversees all operational risk; recommends to the full board on risk-based decisions, exposure and risk management; reviews and monitors investigation of larger incidents | Hold ultimate responsibility; set the risk appetite in place of the board |
| Full board of directors | Ultimately responsible for the general administration of the firm, including risk management; sets the risk appetite; validates the ORMF and ensures its periodic revision | Run committee-level monitoring |

The design principle is delegation upward of information and downward of authority: the board keeps responsibility, the board risk committee is its specialist adviser, and the committees below gather and consolidate.

**Applying it to this question**

Body 1 (one business line) oversees risk in its own scope and feeds information: role R. Body 2 (group committee) consolidates and reports to the management committee and the board risk committee: role P. Body 3 (board risk committee) oversees all operational risk, recommends and reviews larger incidents: role Q. Body 4 (full board) holds ultimate responsibility, sets appetite and validates the ORMF: role S.

**Fragile fact.** The board risk committee recommends; the full board decides and is ultimately responsible. The group committee reports to the board risk committee, not to the full board.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(a) Risk and Committee Structure (Figure 2.3) and Section 2.3(c) The Role of the Board for Operational Risk and Resilience. Naming note: GARP’s text calls the middle body the “group operational risk committee” while its Figure 2.3 and Schweser call it the “organization risk committee”; Schweser has it reporting to the executive risk committee and board risk committee, GARP to the executive/management committee and the board risk committee. Same body, no substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: Option A is the only matching that follows GARP 2.3(a) for bodies 1 to 3 and GARP 2.3(c) for the board (“the board of directors is ultimately responsible . . . responsible for setting the risk appetite”; “regulators require that the board of directors validate the operational risk management framework”).

b.reason: (sibling swap). It swaps the middle and top levels: the group committee is given the board risk committee’s recommending and incident-review role (Q), and the board risk committee is given the consolidation and reporting role (P). It would be correct only if the stem had listed the bodies in the order board risk committee, then group committee.

c.reason: (role misassignment). It gives the board risk committee the full board’s ultimate responsibility (S) and leaves the full board making recommendations (Q). The committee recommends to the full board; it never holds ultimate responsibility. This would be correct only if bodies 3 and 4 were listed the other way round.

d.reason: (sibling swap). It swaps the lowest and middle levels: the business-line committee is made to consolidate the group picture (P) and the group committee is confined to one scope (R). It would be correct only if body 1 were the group committee and body 2 a single business-line committee.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 b Q3
questions.question: The board risk committee of a Japanese trust bank is meeting after the group operational risk committee escalated a JPY 4.8 billion loss caused by a mis-keyed securities transfer. A newly appointed independent director asks what the committee itself should now do. Which action is most consistent with the role of the board risk committee?

options.text: Carry out the root-cause investigation itself and redesign the transfer controls, since the committee oversees all operational risk at the enterprise level.
Decide on the bank’s revised risk exposure in place of the full board and inform the board afterwards, since the committee sits at the top of the pyramid.
Return the incident to the business-line committee for resolution, since the committee reviews only incidents that breach the board-approved risk appetite.
Review and monitor the investigation of the incident, and make recommendations to the full board on the risk exposure and risk-based decisions it requires.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Board risk committee of a Japanese trust bank receiving an escalated JPY 4.8bn securities-transfer loss.

**Concept and theory**

The board risk committee is a committee created by the board at enterprise level. It sits at the top of the committee pyramid, directly below the full board, and receives what the group committee consolidates and escalates. GARP lists its role precisely:

- it oversees all operational risk;
- it makes recommendations to the full board with regard to risk-based decisions, risk exposure and risk management;
- together with the board, it receives regular risk reporting;
- it reviews and monitors the investigation of larger incidents;
- its meeting frequency should ensure consistent oversight and adequate escalation of issues to the board; its members must have recent and relevant experience.

Two boundaries matter. Upward, the committee recommends and the full board decides, because the board keeps ultimate responsibility. Downward, the committee reviews and monitors investigations; it does not perform them, because investigation and control redesign are management and first-line work.

**Applying it to this question**

The incident is large (JPY 4.8 billion) and has been escalated from the group committee, so it is a “larger incident” that the board risk committee should review and monitor. The decision on the bank’s risk exposure belongs to the full board, so the committee’s output is a recommendation to the board. The loss size is not a calculation input; it simply confirms the incident is large.

**Fragile fact.** Board risk committee: reviews and monitors investigations (does not run them) and recommends to the full board (does not decide for it).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(a) Risk and Committee Structure (board risk committee bullet). Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Risk Committee Structure (top level). Schweser says the board risk committee “manages both the middle and lowest levels”, while GARP says it “oversees all operational risk”; GARP’s wording is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: (role misassignment). The action (investigating the root cause and redesigning controls) is right, but the actor is wrong: management and the business carry out investigations and redesign controls, while the committee reviews and monitors that work. The option would be correct if the stem asked what the business line and senior management should do after the incident.

b.reason: (role misassignment). It moves the full board’s decision right to the committee. Sitting at the top of the committee pyramid does not make the committee the decision-maker: it recommends to the full board, which remains ultimately responsible. It would be correct only if the question asked about the full board of directors.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). It invents a narrowing condition (only appetite breaches) and sends a larger escalated incident back down. GARP says the committee reviews and monitors the investigation of larger incidents, and escalation flows upward, not back. It would be correct for a small, within-limit incident that the business-line committee should oversee in its own scope.

d.reason: Option D combines the two verbs GARP gives the committee for this situation: it “reviews and monitors the investigation of larger incidents” and “makes recommendations to the full board with regards to risk-based decisions, risk exposure, and risk management”. Schweser: it “oversees the evaluation of major operational risk incidents” and “provides recommendations to the board”.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 b Q4
questions.question:
A risk committee member at a Brazilian commercial bank is reviewing a briefing note on the bank’s board risk committee before the annual governance review. The note makes the following statements:

I. Membership of the board risk committee is subject to guidelines, and regulators require that its members have recent and relevant experience.

II. The committee’s meeting frequency should ensure consistent oversight of operational risk and adequate escalation of potential issues to the board.

III. Because the committee receives regular risk reporting, the full board no longer needs to receive regular risk reporting itself.

IV. The committee is created by the board, but it oversees operational risk only for the business lines whose issues are escalated to it.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Four-statement audit of a briefing note on a Brazilian bank’s board risk committee.

**Concept and theory**

Regulators care about the board risk committee because it is the board’s main lens on operational risk. GARP therefore sets out not only what it does but how it must be constituted and run:

- **Creation and scope:** it is “the board-created enterprise-level risk committee” and it “oversees all operational risk”.
- **Reporting:** “The board of directors and the board risk committee receive regular risk reporting.”
- **Meetings:** “The frequency of meetings should ensure consistent oversight of operational risk, and adequate representation and escalation of potential issues to the board.”
- **Membership:** it “is the subject of guidelines and regulators require that the members have recent and relevant experience”.

The reason for each rule: a committee created by the board answers to the board; it must see the whole risk profile, not a slice; meeting rhythm is set by the need for oversight and escalation, not by habit; and challenge is only credible if members know current risk practice.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches the membership rule: true. Statement II matches the meeting-frequency rule: true. Statement III contradicts “the board of directors and the board risk committee receive regular risk reporting”: false. Statement IV gets the creation right (board-created) but narrows the scope: the committee oversees all operational risk, not only escalated business lines: false. Only I and II survive.

**Fragile fact.** Board-created; oversees all operational risk, not only what is escalated; members need recent and relevant experience; the board itself still receives regular risk reporting.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(a) Risk and Committee Structure (board risk committee bullet). Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Risk Committee Structure (top level: “members must have risk management experience that is pertinent and current”). Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It drops statement II, treating meeting frequency as outside the regulatory expectations for the committee. GARP states the frequency should ensure consistent oversight and escalation. A would be correct only if statement II had been corrupted, for example to say that the committee should meet only when an incident is escalated.

b.reason: Option B (I and II only) is the only option that contains both true statements and neither false one.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). It accepts statement III, which drops the full board from the regular reporting line. Delegating to a committee does not remove the board’s need for information; both receive regular risk reporting. C would be correct only if statement III said that both the board and the committee receive regular risk reporting.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). It accepts statement IV, which narrows the committee’s scope to escalated business lines, and it rejects the true statement I. D would be correct only if statement IV read “created by the board, and it oversees all operational risk” and statement I were false.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a small Australian mutual bank is reviewing the bank’s operational risk committee structure ahead of a supervisory visit. The bank has the profile below and a single operational risk committee that oversees the activity and reports to the management committee and to the board risk committee.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Total assets (AUD million) | 3,200.0 |
| Number of staff | 410 |
| Business lines | 1 |
| Operational losses last year (AUD million) | 1.8 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The structure is deficient, because regulators require every bank to run a full pyramid of business-line, group and board-level operational risk committees.
The structure is deficient, because each operational risk category, such as fraud and information security, must have its own dedicated committee.
The structure can be acceptable only if the committee reports directly to the full board, because small banks are not expected to have a board risk committee.
The structure can be acceptable, because the structure and escalation process should be justified by the size, nature, scale and complexity of the firm.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Small single-business-line Australian mutual bank with one operational risk committee reporting to the management committee and board risk committee.

**Concept and theory**

Committee structures are a means, not an end. GARP states that “the size and complexity of the organization will influence the size and number of committees”, that “an individual firm’s risk committee structure and escalation process is usually determined by the size, nature, scale, and complexity of the firm”, and that “different structures can be fine, as long as they are justified by the size and the complexity of the business”. It gives the small-firm case directly: “a small firm is likely to have a single operational risk committee that oversees the activity and reports to the management committee and board risk committee.”

| Firm | Typical structure (GARP 2.3 a) |
|---|---|
| Large, complex | Pyramid: business-line or country committees, group operational risk committee, board risk committee; in many large organizations, separate committees for operational risk categories (for example information security, legal and compliance, fraud), subordinated either to the board or enterprise risk committee or to the operational risk committee (Figures 2.4 and 2.5) |
| Small | One operational risk committee reporting to the management committee and the board risk committee |

This is proportionality: the supervisor’s test is whether the structure is justified by the business, not whether it copies a large-bank template.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank has one business line, 410 staff and AUD 3.2 billion of assets: small and simple. Its single committee oversees the activity and reports to the management committee and to the board risk committee, which is GARP’s small-firm description almost word for word. The loss figure is irrelevant to the structural question.

**Fragile fact.** The small-firm single committee reports to both the management committee and the board risk committee; “different structures can be fine” only when justified by size and complexity.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(a) Risk and Committee Structure, including “ORM and ERM and Committee Structure” and Figures 2.4 and 2.5. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b (“A small bank will probably have one operational risk committee with both oversight and reporting duties”). Schweser describes only the “enterprise risk as umbrella” layout (GARP Figure 2.5) and omits GARP’s alternative in which operational risk frames all non-financial risks (Figure 2.4); GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: (absolute-claim trap). It turns the pyramid, which GARP presents as what larger and more complex firms “generally have”, into a universal requirement for “every bank”. It would be correct only if the stem described a large, complex group with many business lines and regions operating with a single committee.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It overextends a large-organization practice (“each category having its own committee in many large organizations”) to a small bank and makes it mandatory. It would be correct only as a description of a structure that is common in many large organizations, not as a requirement for a small firm.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). It adds a condition that contradicts the source: GARP’s small firm reports to the management committee and the board risk committee, so small firms are expected to have that reporting line. It would be correct only if the source said small firms report directly to the full board, which it does not.

d.reason: Option D states the proportionality rule: structure and escalation are determined by, and must be justified by, size, nature, scale and complexity. The bank’s set-up is therefore capable of being acceptable.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a Swiss private bank is drafting the Terms of Reference for a newly formed operational risk committee. The draft contains the items below.

| Item | Draft content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Role and purpose of the committee |
| 2 | Membership, listing the names or functions of the members |
| 3 | Step-by-step instructions for reconciling nostro accounts |
| 4 | Frequency of meetings |
| 5 | Record of amendments to the charter over time and the reasons for them |
| 6 | Roles and responsibilities of members |

Which item is least appropriate to include in the Terms of Reference, and why?

options.text: Item 3, because step-by-step task instructions belong in procedures, which guide task execution, not in the document setting the committee’s authority.
Item 5, because the charter records only the committee’s current authority, so past amendments and their reasons belong in the committee minutes instead.
Item 2, because membership must be described by function only, so naming individual members would conflict with the purpose of the committee charter.
Item 4, because meeting frequency is decided on each meeting’s agenda and recorded in the minutes rather than being fixed in the committee charter.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Swiss private bank’s draft Terms of Reference containing six items, one of them a nostro reconciliation procedure.

**Concept and theory**

A committee can only exercise authority that has been delegated to it, and supervisors want to see that delegation in writing. GARP defines the **Terms of Reference (TOR)**, or “committee charter”, as the document “that details the specific authority that a given committee holds to oversee a delegated area of responsibility”. Its contents are:

1. role and purpose;
2. membership (names or function of the members);
3. roles and responsibilities of members;
4. frequency of meetings;
5. amendments, modifications or variation in the charter over time, and the motivation for such.

Separately, **policies** describe the rules and principles by which a company runs its business, and **procedures and guidelines** “provide more specific guidance on how to execute certain tasks or processes”. Three documents, three jobs: the TOR says what the committee may do; minutes record what it discussed, decided and why; procedures tell staff how to perform tasks.

**Applying it to this question**

Items 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 each map to one of the five TOR contents. Item 3, step-by-step instructions for reconciling nostro accounts, is guidance on how to execute a task: that is a procedure, not part of a committee’s charter.

**Fragile fact.** TOR = authority, purpose, membership, roles, meeting frequency and amendment history with motivation; how-to steps belong in procedures.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(b) Governance and Risk Documentation. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Governance and Risk Documentation (“mission and objective, membership duties and functions, and meeting frequency”). Schweser’s list omits the amendment history and motivation that GARP includes; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: Option A identifies item 3 and gives the correct reason: detailed task instructions are procedures, which give guidance on executing tasks, while the TOR sets out the committee’s delegated authority.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It drops a listed TOR content: GARP expressly includes “amendments, modifications, or variation in the charter over time, and the motivation for such”. It also misplaces the history in the minutes, which record discussions and decisions of meetings. B would be correct only if the item were, for example, a record of each meeting’s debate, which belongs in minutes.

c.reason: (absolute-claim trap). It asserts membership must be by function only. GARP says membership is shown by “names or function” of members, so either is acceptable. C would be correct only under a rule that prohibited naming individuals, which the source does not contain.

d.reason: (sibling swap). It moves meeting frequency from the TOR (where GARP lists it) to agendas and minutes, the sibling documents. D would be correct if the item were “the discussions held and decisions taken at each meeting”, which belongs in minutes.

questions.question: A supervisor’s on-site team is assessing operational risk governance at a UK building society. The operational risk committee met 11 times last year, reviewed the operational risk reports produced for it, and validated a revised operational risk policy. Its minutes record attendance and each decision taken, but not the content of the discussions or the reasons for the decisions. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: The minutes are adequate, because supervisors judge governance on decisions taken, and reasons need to be recorded only for meetings of the full board itself.
The minutes are incomplete, but the gap is closed if the committee’s Terms of Reference are updated to record the reasons behind each decision taken in the year.
The minutes are incomplete, because the discussions held, the decisions taken and the motivation for them should be documented as evidence of good governance.
The minutes are adequate, because validating operational risk policy is a board duty, so the committee’s discussion of the policy did not need to be recorded.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Supervisor reviewing a UK building society’s operational risk committee whose minutes record decisions but not discussions or reasons.

**Concept and theory**

Supervisors cannot sit in on every committee meeting, so they judge governance from the written record. GARP describes what committees do and what must be documented: committees “review the risk information and risk reporting produced at the relevant level of the firm to support the decisions to be taken, and review and validate the policies that guide the management of operational risk”. Then: “The content of the discussions held, the decisions taken, and the motivation of these decisions must be captured and documented in committee minutes, that will provide the necessary evidence of good governance of operational risk requested by the supervisors as part of their evaluation.” These rules apply to other risks as well.

Three elements, not one: discussion (shows challenge took place), decision (shows an outcome), and motivation (shows the decision was reasoned and risk-informed). A record of decisions alone cannot show that risk was considered.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee did the right things (reviewed reports, validated policy), but its minutes capture only attendance and decisions. Two of the three required elements, the discussions and the motivation, are missing, so the minutes do not provide the evidence supervisors ask for. The 11 meetings are an irrelevant input: frequency does not cure a documentation gap.

**Fragile fact.** Minutes must hold three things: discussions, decisions and the motivation for decisions. Committees, not only the board, validate operational risk policies.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(b) Governance and Risk Documentation. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Governance and Risk Documentation. Consistent. Related context (LO 43.a, not tested here): GARP’s use-test passage notes that, to regulators, absence of evidence is evidence of absence.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It narrows the documentation rule to the full board’s meetings. GARP applies it to committees (“captured and documented in committee minutes”). A would be correct only if the question concerned what is sufficient for a body outside the governance structure, which the source does not discuss.

b.reason: (sibling swap). It assigns to the Terms of Reference a job that belongs to minutes. The TOR records the committee’s authority, membership, roles, meeting frequency and changes to the charter with their motivation, not the reasons for individual decisions. B would be correct if the gap were an undocumented change to the committee’s mandate, which does belong in the TOR.

c.reason: Option C restates GARP’s requirement that discussions, decisions and motivation be documented in committee minutes as evidence of good governance for supervisors. Schweser: documenting “the agenda, the actions taken, and the justification behind those actions” demonstrates the governance supervisors require.

d.reason: (role misassignment). It says validating operational risk policy is only a board duty. GARP says committees “review and validate the policies that guide the management of operational risk”. D would be correct only if the stem had concerned the board’s validation of the ORMF itself, which is a board duty.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Chinese joint-stock bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the place of policies and procedures in the bank’s operational risk governance. Which of the following statements should she include as most accurate?

options.text: Policies, procedures and guidelines are detective controls, and to be effective they must be publicized, regularly updated and embedded in daily operations.
Policies, procedures and guidelines are directive controls, and to be effective they must be publicized, regularly updated and embedded in daily operations.
Procedures set out the rules and principles by which the bank runs its business, while policies give more specific guidance on how to execute individual tasks.
Once a policy has been validated by the committee, it should be kept unchanged so that the training given to new employees at on-boarding stays consistent.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Presentation to new analysts at a Chinese bank on policies and procedures in operational risk governance.

**Concept and theory**

Policies and procedures are where governance meets daily work. GARP defines them in a hierarchy:

| Document | Purpose (GARP 2.3 b) |
|---|---|
| Policies | Describe the rules and principles according to which a company runs its business and organizes its processes |
| Procedures and guidelines | Provide more specific guidance on how to execute certain tasks or processes |

Both limit the risk of errors and provide training, “importantly at the on-boarding of new employees”. GARP classifies them as a form of internal control: **directive controls**, controls that direct people to act in the intended way. A document on a shelf directs no one, so GARP adds conditions for effectiveness: policies and procedures must be publicized, subject to regular updates and embedded in the operations; they should reflect business reality, apply in daily practice and be meaningful; and they must evolve with the business (new activities, revamped processes).

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the single accurate statement. Check each against the two facts: the control label (directive) and the effectiveness conditions (publicized, updated, embedded). Only option B states both correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Policies = rules and principles; procedures = how to execute tasks; both are directive controls and must be publicized, updated and embedded.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(b) Governance and Risk Documentation. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b (“Policies and procedures serve as internal controls” and remain useful only if actively used, updated and consistent with operations). Schweser does not use the term “directive controls”; that classification is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (sibling swap). It keeps the effectiveness conditions but gives the documents the label of a sibling control type, “detective”. Policies direct behavior before the event; they do not detect errors after it. A would be correct only if the stem had been about controls that identify errors after they occur, such as reconciliations.

b.reason: Option B matches GARP: “Policies, procedures, and other guidelines are a form of internal controls, known as directive controls” and “for policies and procedures to be effective they must be publicized, subject to regular updates, and be embedded in the operations of the organization.”

c.reason: (sibling swap). It swaps the definitions of the two documents: policies carry the rules and principles, procedures give task-level guidance. C would be correct if the words “procedures” and “policies” were exchanged.

d.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses “policies must evolve to reflect the changes in the business” into “kept unchanged”. It borrows a true point (training at on-boarding) to justify a false conclusion. D would be correct only in a business that never changed its activities or processes, a condition GARP does not grant.

questions.question:
The chair of an Italian bank’s board is running a board self-assessment. She has listed six activities and wants to confirm which of them regulators assign to the board of directors itself in operational risk governance.

| No. | Activity |
|---|---|
| 1 | Validating the operational risk management framework (ORMF) |
| 2 | Writing the business-unit procedures that put the ORMF into practice |
| 3 | Ensuring that the ORMF is revised periodically |
| 4 | Obtaining assurance that senior management implements the ORMF policies, processes and systems effectively at all decision levels |
| 5 | Running the day-to-day monitoring of risk indicator values in the payments division |
| 6 | Determining the nature and extent of the significant risks the bank is willing to take to achieve its strategic objectives |

Which activities are responsibilities of the board?

options.text: 1, 3, 4 and 6 only
1, 3 and 6 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Italian bank board self-assessment: which of six activities are board responsibilities.

**Concept and theory**

The board’s role is oversight with ultimate responsibility, not execution. GARP gives two layers:

- **General:** “The board of directors is ultimately responsible for the general administration of the firm, including risk management.” Corporate governance codes and BCBS express that the board “is responsible for determining the nature and extent of the significant risks the firm is willing to take to achieve its strategic objectives”; in other words, the board sets the risk appetite and makes sure the firm operates within it.
- **Principle 3 of RPSMOR (2021):** regulators require that the board (i) validate the ORMF; (ii) ensure a periodic revision of the ORMF; and (iii) get assurance that senior management implements the policies, processes and systems of the ORMF effectively at all decision levels (for example through the committee structure).

Implementation, including turning the framework into procedures and running day-to-day monitoring, sits with senior management and the business.

**Applying it to this question**

Item 1: validate the ORMF, board. Item 2: write business-unit procedures, implementation, not board. Item 3: ensure periodic revision, board. Item 4: obtain assurance on implementation at all decision levels, board. Item 5: day-to-day monitoring of risk indicators, implementation, not board. Item 6: determine the nature and extent of significant risks (risk appetite), board. Board set: 1, 3, 4 and 6.

**Fragile fact.** The board validates, ensures periodic revision and gets assurance; senior management implements. Assurance stays with the board even though implementation is delegated.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(c) The Role of the Board for Operational Risk and Resilience, “Regulatory Guidance on the Role of the Board for Operational Risk”. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Board of Directors Role (Operational Risk): approving the ORMF, establishing ongoing updates, ensuring senior management executes the policies and procedures. Schweser says “approving”; GARP says “validate”; same duty.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: Option A lists exactly the three Principle 3 duties (1, 3, 4) plus the appetite-setting duty (6), each stated in GARP 2.3(c).

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It drops item 4, treating assurance over implementation as delegated away with the implementation itself. GARP keeps it with the board: the board delegates the doing but must obtain assurance that it is done effectively. B would be correct if item 4 had read “implementing the ORMF policies and systems” rather than “obtaining assurance”.

c.reason: (role misassignment). It gives the board item 2 (writing business-unit procedures), which is senior management’s implementation work, and omits item 6, which GARP assigns to the board. C would be correct for a list of senior management and board tasks combined without item 6.

d.reason: (role misassignment). It adds item 5, day-to-day monitoring, which is a business and management activity. The board receives reporting and assurance; it does not run monitoring. D would be correct only if item 5 read “receiving regular risk reporting”, which GARP does assign to the board.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 b Q10
questions.question:
A risk consultant hired by a US regional bank’s nominating committee is preparing an induction pack for new directors on the board’s role in operational risk. The draft pack contains the following statements:

I. The board is ultimately responsible for the general administration of the firm, including risk management.

II. The board is responsible for establishing a risk management culture that is communicated effectively to the firm.

III. Because implementation is delegated to senior management, directors do not need operational risk training; training is needed only by staff in risk functions.

IV. The board is responsible for setting the firm’s risk appetite and for making sure that the firm operates within the limits of that appetite.

Which of the statements should be retained as accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Four-statement audit of a director induction pack on the board’s role in operational risk.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond approving the framework, GARP gives the board three further responsibilities that explain why it is “ultimately” responsible:

1. **Ultimate responsibility:** for the general administration of the firm, including risk management.
2. **Risk appetite:** determining the nature and extent of significant risks the firm will take, and making sure it operates within those limits.
3. **Culture and training:** establishing a risk management culture that is communicated effectively to the firm; and, to fulfill its oversight duty, the board itself “needs to receive adequate training” and must ensure all functions relating to operational risk management receive adequate training.

The training rule exists because oversight without understanding is rubber-stamping, which regulators explicitly reject: a board cannot challenge what it does not understand.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: GARP verbatim in substance, true. Statement II: the board is responsible for establishing a risk management culture communicated effectively, true. Statement III: contradicts GARP, since the board itself needs adequate training and must ensure that all functions relating to operational risk management are trained, false. Statement IV: setting the risk appetite and ensuring the firm operates within its limits, true. Accurate set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Training applies to the board itself and to all functions involved in operational risk management, not only to the risk department.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(c), “Regulatory Guidance on the Role of the Board for Operational Risk”. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Board of Directors Role (Operational Risk): “the board must create a culture of risk management . . . Training is central . . . both in terms of the training for board members and the relevant staff”. Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It omits statement IV, treating risk appetite as outside the board’s role. GARP states “the board is responsible for setting the risk appetite of the firm and for making sure that it operates within the limits”. A would be correct only if statement IV had been corrupted (for example, “senior management sets the risk appetite”).

b.reason: (role misassignment). It accepts statement III, which removes the training duty from the board and narrows it to risk staff, and it drops the true statement II. B would be correct only if statement II were false and statement III correctly described training.

c.reason: Option C (I, II and IV only) contains every true statement and excludes the false one.

d.reason: (absolute-claim trap). It accepts every statement, including III. Choosing “all of the above” ignores the explicit requirement that the board itself receive adequate training. D would be correct only if statement III read “the board needs adequate training and must ensure that all functions relating to operational risk management are adequately trained”.

questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 b Q11
questions.question: A non-executive director of a German savings bank is reviewing a draft operational resilience approach that senior management has submitted to the board. Which feature of the draft is most consistent with regulatory guidance on the board’s role in operational resilience?

options.text: The approach considers the bank’s appetite and tolerance for disruption to its critical operations, and its capabilities under the most extreme scenarios regardless of plausibility.
The approach considers the bank’s appetite and tolerance for disruption to its critical operations, and its capabilities under a broad range of severe but plausible scenarios.
The approach is run through a new governance structure set up apart from the existing committees, so that resilience is overseen separately from operational risk.
The approach assigns oversight of senior management’s implementation to the chief operating officer, who reports on its progress to the board risk committee.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German savings bank director reviewing a draft operational resilience approach.

**Concept and theory**

Operational resilience is the ability to keep delivering critical operations through disruption. GARP explains that new regulation extended the board’s responsibilities “to the supervision and assurance of the effective management of the firm on that matter”, with expectations “often similar to those for operational risk”. Under BCBS Principle 1 on operational resilience:

- directors “utilize their existing governance structure to establish, oversee and implement” an effective resilience approach;
- the board takes an active role in establishing a broad understanding of the approach through clear communication of its objectives (part of its responsibility for risk culture);
- the approach “must consider its risk appetite and tolerance for disruption to its critical operations as well as its operational capabilities given a broad range of severe but plausible scenarios”;
- the board oversees senior management’s implementation and ensures sufficient financial and technical resources;
- the board receives assurance through timely reporting from senior management.

“Severe but plausible” is the key calibration: scenarios harsh enough to test the firm, yet realistic enough to plan for.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks which feature of the draft matches the guidance. Check each option against three anchors: critical operations plus appetite and tolerance for disruption; a broad range of severe but plausible scenarios; existing governance structure overseen by the board.

**Fragile fact.** Scenarios must be severe but plausible, and resilience runs through the existing governance structure with the board overseeing management.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(c), “Regulatory Guidance on the Role of the Board for Operational Resilience” (BCBS Principles for Operational Resilience, Principle 1). Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Board of Directors Role (Operational Resilience). The “existing governance structure” point is in GARP only; Schweser does not mention it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It keeps everything except the condition “plausible”, replacing a broad range of severe but plausible scenarios with the most extreme scenarios regardless of plausibility. It would be correct only if the guidance asked for unconstrained worst-case analysis, which it does not.

b.reason: Option B reproduces GARP’s requirement on the content of the approach: appetite and tolerance for disruption to critical operations, and capabilities under a broad range of severe but plausible scenarios. Schweser: situations that are harsh, low probability, “and yet remain reasonably foreseen”.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses “utilize their existing governance structure” into “a new governance structure set up apart from existing committees”. Resilience is integrated into existing governance, not run in parallel. C would be correct only if the guidance required a stand-alone structure.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The action (overseeing senior management’s implementation) is right but the actor is wrong: GARP gives it to the board of directors. A chief operating officer, part of senior management, overseeing management’s own implementation would be self-review. D would be correct only if it said the board oversees implementation and receives reports from senior management.

questions.loText: Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.
