questions.question: An internal auditor at an Indian private-sector bank is testing whether the board can demonstrate that it meets regulatory expectations on operational resilience. She has gathered four findings. Which finding would NOT support the conclusion that the board meets those expectations?

options.text: Board minutes show timely reports from senior management on resilience, in particular where significant deficiencies could affect delivery of critical operations.
The board approved additional financial and technical resources for operational resilience after reviewing a gap analysis presented by senior management.
The directors’ skills matrix shows that board members have sufficient knowledge, skills and experience to meet their operational resilience responsibilities.
Directors and senior managers have had resilience training, but the board chose not to extend it to other staff because they take part in continuity drills.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Indian bank internal auditor testing four findings on the board’s operational resilience responsibilities; which does NOT support compliance.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes its board guidance on resilience with what firms must be able to demonstrate:

| Expectation | GARP 2.3(c) wording |
|---|---|
| Resources | The board ensures that sufficient financial and technical resources are allocated to operational resilience |
| Reporting | The board receives assurance through timely reporting from senior management, particularly when significant deficiencies could affect delivery of critical operations |
| Board capability | The board has received training in operational resilience and has sufficient knowledge, skills and experience |
| Staff training | That training is provided to all staff |

The training requirement has two halves. Training the board alone leaves the people who must actually keep critical operations running without the same understanding.

**Applying it to this question**

With a NOT qualifier, three findings match the guidance and one breaches it. Finding A matches reporting; finding B matches resources; finding C matches board capability. Finding D satisfies board training but deliberately excludes other staff, contradicting “that training is provided to all staff”. Participation in continuity drills is not the same as resilience training under the guidance.

**Fragile fact.** Resilience training must reach the board and all staff; reporting to the board must be timely, especially on deficiencies that threaten critical operations.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 43.b):** Describe and compare the roles of different committees and the board of directors in operational risk governance.

GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(c), “Regulatory Guidance on the Role of the Board for Operational Resilience”. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.b, Board of Directors Role (Operational Resilience) (“the board should request periodic reports”, “direct enough funds and other support”, training for “both the board and all relevant employees”). Schweser says “periodic” reports and “all relevant employees”; GARP says “timely” reporting and “all staff”. GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (qualifier trap: true statement). The finding matches GARP’s reporting expectation. A candidate who picks it may believe the board should hear only about disruptions after they occur (a polarity flip of “timely”). A would be the answer if the finding said the board received resilience reports only after an incident had disrupted critical operations.

b.reason: (qualifier trap: true statement). The finding matches the requirement that the board ensures sufficient financial and technical resources. A candidate may think resource allocation is a management decision (role misassignment). B would be the answer if the finding said the board left resourcing for resilience entirely to senior management without review.

c.reason: (qualifier trap: true statement). The finding matches the requirement that the board has sufficient knowledge, skills and experience. A candidate may think skills belong only to management. C would be the answer if the finding said board members lacked resilience expertise and relied wholly on management.

d.reason: Option D is the finding that does not support compliance: the board limited resilience training to directors and senior managers, whereas GARP requires firms to show that training is provided to all staff. Schweser: training “applies to both the board and all relevant employees”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q1
questions.question: The chief risk officer of a USD 85 billion US commercial bank is presenting the bank’s operational risk governance to newly hired analysts. One slide maps each line of defense to the term used for it in the Basel Committee’s Revisions to the Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk (RPSMOR) and to its core activity. Which of the following mappings is most accurate?

options.text: Line 1: “business unit management”, which provides independent oversight of the risk processes of the business.
Line 2: “an independent corporate operational risk management function”, which challenges business-line activities.
Line 3: “independent assurance”, provided by the bank’s external auditor over the general system of operational controls.
Line 2: “independent assurance”, provided by the risk function over the business lines’ controls and risk taking.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: CRO at a US bank mapping each line to its RPSMOR term and core activity.

**Concept and theory**

The three lines of defense (3LoD) model is the generally accepted way to organize controls and risk management in financial services. GARP notes it was originally developed, in a slightly different format, in the military sector, and over the last decade it became the recommended organizing principle for banks. Its logic is simple: the people who take a risk manage it, a separate group sets the framework and checks how well the risk takers apply it, and a third group, independent of both, gives assurance that the whole system works.

| Line | BCBS (RPSMOR) term | Who and what |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | “business unit management” | Risk owners: the front line of the business and any business or front-office staff responsible for managing risk. |
| 2 | “an independent corporate operational risk management function (CORF)” | Independent risk oversight over business processes and the implementation of risk policies and the framework; challenges the activities and behavior of the business lines. |
| 3 | “independent assurance” | The internal audit function. |

External audit is not one of the three internal lines. GARP states that independent assurance is provided by internal audit for the general system of operational controls, and by the external auditors for the organization’s financials and the controls around financial reporting.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must get two things right for one line: the RPSMOR label and the activity. Check each option against the table. Only option B pairs the second line with the RPSMOR label “an independent corporate operational risk management function” and with its signature activity, challenging the business lines. The deciding facts are the three labels and the fact that “independent assurance” belongs to internal audit.

**Fragile fact.** “Independent assurance” is Line 3 (internal audit); “independent CORF” is Line 2; external audit sits outside the three lines and opines on the financial statements.

**Reference**

LO 43.c: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense. GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(d) “Three Lines of Defense Model (3LoD)” and “Roles and Responsibilities of the Third Line of Defense”. Schweser describes Line 2 as “also known as the corporate operational risk function (CORF)” and does not quote the RPSMOR labels for Lines 1 and 3; no conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (role misassignment). The label “business unit management” is right for Line 1, but the activity attached to it, independent oversight, is the second line’s job. The first line manages the risk it generates; it does not oversee itself independently. The option would be correct if the activity read “which identifies, assesses and controls the risks it generates”.

b.reason: GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(d): Line 2 “comprises those who provide independent risk oversight over business processes” and “are responsible for challenging the activities and behavior of the business lines. The BCBS (RPSMOR) calls the second line of defense an independent corporate operational risk management function (CORF).” Option B states exactly this pairing.

c.reason: (scope error). “Independent assurance” is the RPSMOR term for Line 3, but Line 3 is the internal audit function, not the external auditor. GARP limits the external auditor’s role to an opinion on the financial statements and the system of controls around financial reporting. The option would be correct if it said “provided by the bank’s internal audit function”.

d.reason: (sibling swap). The option gives the second line the third line’s label. “Independent assurance” is how RPSMOR describes internal audit; the risk function’s label is the CORF. The option would be correct if it began “Line 3” and named internal audit as the provider.

questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q2
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing how a mid-sized Canadian bank (total assets CAD 48 billion) has mapped its functions to the three lines of defense. She drafts the following statements for her report:

I. What places a function in a particular line is the roles and responsibilities attributed to it, not the name of its department.

II. Because operational risk management is more centralized than credit or market risk management, delineating the three lines is easier for operational risk.

III. Control functions such as finance, legal or security do not always have a clearly defined attribution to a single line of defense.

IV. The degree of formality with which the three lines are implemented should be the same for every regulated entity, regardless of its size and complexity.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant auditing four statements on how the three lines are delineated.

**Concept and theory**

The 3LoD model is easy to state and hard to apply. GARP lists the reasons:

- Lines are defined by roles. What makes a function first, second or third line “is not so much the name of the department or division in a firm but the roles and responsibilities attributed to that department or division.”
- Operational risk is decentralized. ORM “tends to be less centralized than credit, market, or liquidity risks”, because operational risk is present in every process. This makes the lines harder, not easier, to delineate.
- Control functions straddle lines. Finance, legal or security “do not always have a clearly defined attribution to a single line of defense”.
- Formality is proportional. The degree of formality “may vary depending on the size, nature, and complexity of the regulated entity”.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against those four facts. I: matches the “roles, not names” principle. Accurate. II: reverses the centralization comparison and its consequence. Inaccurate. III: matches GARP on control functions. Accurate. IV: denies the proportionality GARP states. Inaccurate. The accurate set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Direction to remember: ORM is less centralized than credit or market risk, so the lines are harder to draw, and what places a function in a line is its role, not its department name.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.3(d) and “Lines of Defense Delineation and Hybrid Control Function in Operational Risk”. Schweser makes the same points (“given the decentralized nature of ORM, differentiating between the three lines is not always easy”; “It is actually the roles and duties performed in each group that best delineate the three lines”); no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: (absolute claim). Choosing “I only” means rejecting III, which implies that every control function can be attributed cleanly to one line. GARP says the opposite. This would be correct only if statement III claimed that control functions always sit in the second line, which would make III false.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Accepting II reverses GARP’s comparison: ORM is less centralized than credit, market or liquidity risk management, so delineation is more difficult. B would be the answer only if ORM really were more centralized than credit and market risk (making II true) and statement III were false.

c.reason: (absolute claim). Accepting IV imposes identical formality on all entities. GARP says formality varies with size, nature and complexity, which is also why small banks may secure CORF independence differently from large ones. The option would be correct if IV said formality “may vary with size, nature and complexity”.

d.reason: Option D (I and III only) is the only combination that contains both accurate statements and neither inaccurate one, in line with GARP Section 2.3(d) and “Lines of Defense Delineation and Hybrid Control Function in Operational Risk”.

questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q3
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing a draft mapping prepared by four departments that, because of limited staff, each perform both first-line and second-line activities. The draft assigns one activity per department to a line of defense:

| Department | Activity | Proposed line | Staff (FTE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legal | Drafting client contracts | Second | 14 |
| HR | Overseeing people management in the business lines | Second | 22 |
| IT Security | Encrypting data and monitoring network activity | First | 37 |
| Finance | Verifying whether business exposures remain under authorized limits | First | 29 |

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: The Legal and Finance rows are misclassified, and the bank must document and distinguish the two roles, emphasizing the independence of the second line.
The Legal and Finance rows are misclassified, and the bank must move each second-line activity into a separate department reporting to the CORF.
The HR and IT Security rows are misclassified, and the bank must document and distinguish the two roles, emphasizing the independence of the second line.
Only the Finance row is misclassified, and the bank must document and distinguish the two roles, emphasizing the independence of the second line.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Internal auditor checking a hybrid-function mapping across Legal, HR, IT Security and Finance.

**Concept and theory**

A hybrid function is a department that performs both first-line and second-line activities. GARP notes this is common in small and medium-sized institutions when a function lacks the staff to create separate first-line and second-line teams; the usual candidates are finance, HR, legal, ICT and information and physical security. BCBS does not ban hybrids. Instead it requires the bank to “document and distinguish the responsibilities of such functions in the first and second line of defense, emphasizing the independence of the second line of defense.”

GARP Table 2.4 gives examples. The rule of thumb: the first-line role is doing the work; the second-line role is overseeing or verifying the work done in the business lines.

| Department | First line role | Second line role |
|---|---|---|
| Legal | Drafting contracts | Overseeing legal activities in the business lines |
| HR | Administering pay, recording performance against objectives | Overseeing people management in the business lines |
| IT Security | Encrypting data, partitioning network, monitoring network activity | Verifying implementation of ICT controls, enforcing security policies |
| Finance | Managing treasury and accounting | Verifying whether business exposures remain under authorized limits |

**Applying it to this question**

Compare each proposed line with Table 2.4. The FTE column is irrelevant. Legal, drafting contracts: first line in GARP, proposed second. Misclassified. HR, overseeing people management: second line in GARP, proposed second. Correct. IT Security, encrypting and monitoring: first line in GARP, proposed first. Correct. Finance, verifying exposures against limits: second line in GARP, proposed first. Misclassified. So two rows (Legal and Finance) are wrong, and the remedy is documentation and separation of roles, with second-line independence emphasized.

**Fragile fact.** Doing the work is first line (drafting, encrypting, administering pay, treasury and accounting); overseeing or verifying it is second line. The BCBS fix for a hybrid is documentation of the two roles and independence of the second, not a forced split.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Lines of Defense Delineation and Hybrid Control Function in Operational Risk” and Table 2.4. Version note: Schweser illustrates the legal second-line role as “dealing with the legal issues (e.g., litigation)” arising from contracts and attributes hybrids to staffing shortages; GARP’s table uses “Overseeing legal activities that take place in the business lines”. The answer follows GARP; both agree that drafting contracts is first line.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: Option A names exactly the two misclassified rows and states the BCBS requirement as GARP quotes it: document and distinguish the first-line and second-line responsibilities, emphasizing the independence of the second line.

b.reason: (scope error). The classification is right but the remedy overreaches. BCBS accepts hybrid functions and requires documentation and distinction of roles, not relocation of each second-line activity into a new department. This would be correct only if the stem said the bank’s supervisor had already rejected the hybrid arrangement and ordered structural separation.

c.reason: (polarity flip). This inverts the classification: it calls the two correct rows wrong and the two wrong rows right. It would be correct if the table had proposed HR oversight as first line and IT encryption as second line, with Legal drafting as first line and Finance verification as second line.

d.reason: (sibling swap). This accepts contract drafting as second line, confusing Legal’s two roles: drafting is the first-line role, while overseeing legal activities in the business lines is the second-line role. It would be correct if the Legal row read “Overseeing legal activities in the business lines”.

questions.question:
A banking supervisor in Australia is reviewing how two banks secure the independence of their corporate operational risk function (CORF):

| Bank | Total assets (AUD bn) | Arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| X | 3.2 | The operational risk officer also works in the finance team; duties are separated so that he never reviews processes he runs, and his work is independently reviewed. |
| Y | 640.0 | The head of the CORF reports to the head of institutional markets; the CORF designs, maintains and develops the bank’s ORMF. |

Which of the following best describes the supervisor’s conclusion?

options.text: Both arrangements are acceptable, because separation of duties and independent review can secure CORF independence at any bank.
Neither arrangement is acceptable, because every bank’s CORF must have a reporting line separate from all business units.
Bank X’s arrangement can be acceptable, but Bank Y’s CORF should report independently of the risk-generating business units.
Bank Y’s arrangement can be acceptable, but Bank X’s CORF should report independently of the risk-generating business units.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Supervisor comparing CORF independence at a small bank (separation of duties) and a large bank (CORF reporting to markets).

**Concept and theory**

The second line’s value comes from being able to challenge the business objectively. If the CORF reports to the people who generate the risk, its challenge is compromised. GARP states that regulators recognize the degree of CORF independence may differ among banks:

| Bank type | How CORF independence is achieved |
|---|---|
| Small banks | Separation of duties and independent review of processes and functions |
| Larger banks | A reporting structure independent of the risk-generating business units; the CORF is responsible for the design, maintenance and ongoing development of the ORMF |

GARP adds that banks should have a policy that clearly defines the CORF’s roles and responsibilities, reflecting the size and complexity of the organization.

**Applying it to this question**

Bank X is small (AUD 3.2 billion). Its operational risk officer sits in finance, but duties are separated and his work is independently reviewed. That is exactly the small-bank route GARP describes, so it can be acceptable. Bank Y is large (AUD 640 billion). Its CORF correctly designs and maintains the ORMF, but its head reports to the head of institutional markets, a risk-generating business. GARP requires a larger bank’s CORF to have a reporting structure independent of the risk-generating units, so Bank Y fails.

**Fragile fact.** Size decides the route: small bank, separation of duties and independent review; large bank, an independent reporting structure plus responsibility for the ORMF.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Lines of Defense Delineation and Hybrid Control Function in Operational Risk”. Schweser agrees: smaller entities use “segregation of duties and independent review”, while for larger entities the CORF “would be wholly separate from the bank’s risk-generating (profit-generating) groups”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (scope error). The option extends the small-bank route to every bank. GARP limits separation of duties and independent review to small banks; larger banks need an independent reporting structure. It would be correct if Bank Y were also a small bank.

b.reason: (absolute claim). The option imposes one standard on every bank. GARP says regulators recognize that the degree of independence may differ, and that at small banks separation of duties can suffice. It would be correct only if Bank X were a large bank.

c.reason: Option C matches both halves: the small bank’s separation of duties and independent review can satisfy the requirement, and the large bank’s CORF must report independently of the risk-generating business units.

d.reason: (polarity flip). The option reverses which bank passes. Bank Y’s reporting line to a business head is the defect; Bank X’s arrangement is the accepted small-bank route. It would be correct if the arrangements in the table were swapped between the two banks.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q5
questions.question: The head of payments operations at a Japanese bank concludes that her unit lacks the tools and training needed to identify and assess its operational risks. In the same quarter the unit recorded a JPY 40 million loss event and two control deficiencies that its existing controls did not mitigate. Which action is most consistent with the responsibilities of the first line of defense?

options.text: Transfer ownership of the payment risks to the CORF until the unit’s tools and training have been brought up to standard.
Report the resource gap, the loss event and the control deficiencies to the CORF while retaining ownership of the risks.
Report the resource gap, the loss event and the control deficiencies to internal audit, which then remediates the weaknesses.
Report only the loss event to the CORF, since control deficiencies that have not yet caused a loss are not escalated.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese payments operations head with a resource gap, a JPY 40 million loss and two control deficiencies.

**Concept and theory**

“Risk is managed where it is generated.” The first line, the business, is the risk owner: it is responsible for the consequences of the risks it generates or supervises and therefore for assessing and mitigating them. GARP’s example: the head of IT owns IT risk. Ironically, risk is not owned by the risk management function.

GARP lists the responsibilities of an effective first line:

- identifying and assessing the materiality of operational risks inherent in the business;
- establishing appropriate controls;
- assessing the design and effectiveness of these controls;
- monitoring and reporting the business units’ operational risk profiles.

Two escalation duties follow. If the unit believes it lacks adequate resources, tools and training to identify and assess its operational risks, it reports that to the second line (the CORF). It also reports residual operational risks not mitigated by controls, including operational loss events, control deficiencies, process inadequacies and noncompliance with operational risk tolerances.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem contains both triggers: a resource and training gap, and residual risks (one loss event and two unmitigated control deficiencies). The first line must escalate both to the CORF. Escalating does not hand over ownership: the payments head still owns the risks.

**Fragile fact.** The first line escalates to the second line (CORF), not to internal audit, and escalation never transfers ownership: the business stays the risk owner.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Roles and Responsibilities of the First Line of Defense”. Schweser agrees (control weaknesses, process weaknesses and losses “need to be escalated to the second line”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (role misassignment). Ownership cannot move to the second line. GARP is explicit that risk is owned by the business, not the risk function; the CORF oversees and challenges. The option would be correct only for the escalation step, if it read “report the gap to the CORF” and dropped the transfer of ownership.

b.reason: Option B reports all three items to the correct recipient (the CORF) and keeps ownership in the first line, as GARP’s “Roles and Responsibilities of the First Line of Defense” requires.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The recipient is wrong. GARP directs first-line escalation to the second line, “i.e., to the corporate operational risk function”. Internal audit is independent of risk management and gives assurance; it does not remediate the business’s weaknesses. The option would be correct if “internal audit” were replaced by “the CORF” and the remediation stayed with the business.

d.reason: (scope error). The option narrows the escalation duty to losses. GARP lists control deficiencies, process inadequacies and noncompliance with tolerances alongside loss events, and the resource gap must be reported too. It would be correct only if the duty covered realized losses alone, which it does not.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q6
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German asset manager (assets under management EUR 210 billion) is preparing a report on the “risk correspondents” appointed in each investment department, sometimes called Line 1.5. He lists the following as their roles:

I. Acting as the main correspondent for risk issues within the department.

II. Collecting and recording the department’s risk events and losses.

III. Taking over ownership of the department’s operational risks so that its managers can focus on generating revenue.

IV. Developing the firm’s operational risk measurement policies and challenging the departments’ use of risk tools.

Which of the statements are consistent with the role of risk specialists in the three lines of defense model?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
II only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Analyst at a German asset manager listing the roles of risk correspondents (Line 1.5).

**Concept and theory**

ORM is decentralized: it is present in every process and operation. Yet not everyone in the business has the vocation to be a risk specialist or to master risk terminology. So many organizations designate risk specialists, also called “risk champions”, “stewards” or “risk correspondents”, in each business department to interact with the risk function. They are sometimes labeled Line “1.5” or “1.6” and are particularly common in larger organizations.

GARP lists their roles within the first line:

1. being the main correspondent for risk issues;
2. collecting and recording the risk events and losses;
3. mapping the risks and controls in line with the group definitions (when appropriate);
4. following up on the control rules defined, risk management action plans and audit tracking.

The crucial caveat: firms must ensure that “the ownership of operational risk in the first line of defense is not assumed by, or passed to, those providing first line operational specialist expertise and services.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: role 1 in GARP’s list. Consistent. II: role 2 in GARP’s list. Consistent. III: transfers ownership to the specialists, which GARP expressly rules out. Not consistent. IV: developing measurement policies and challenging the departments’ use of tools are second-line (CORF) duties. Not consistent. The consistent set is I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Line 1.5 sits inside the first line, and the label does not move risk ownership: the business managers still own the risk.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Roles and Responsibilities of the Risk Champions and Line 1.5”. Version note: Schweser paraphrases role 3 as “anticipate the key risks and controls within the group” and role 4 as ensuring “risk management plans are completed”; GARP’s wording (mapping risks and controls in line with group definitions; following up on control rules, action plans and audit tracking) is used here. Statements I and II match both sources.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: Option A contains the two statements that reproduce GARP’s listed roles and excludes the ownership transfer and the second-line duties.

b.reason: (role misassignment). Accepting III assumes risk ownership moves to the champion. GARP says ownership stays with the first line and is not passed to those providing specialist expertise. The option would be correct only if III read “helping managers own and manage the department’s operational risks”.

c.reason: (sibling swap). Accepting IV gives the champion the CORF’s role. Developing policies and challenging the business units’ use of tools are duties 1 and 3 of the second line. The option would be correct if IV read “following up on control rules, action plans and audit tracking”.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Rejecting I treats “main correspondent for risk issues” as a second-line role. GARP lists it first among the risk specialists’ roles within the first line. The option would be correct only if I described the CORF’s role, for example “acting as the bank’s independent challenger on risk issues”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q7
questions.question:
The newly appointed head of the corporate operational risk function at a UK bank drafts the function’s charter. The draft lists six activities with their planned budgets:

| No. | Activity | Budget (GBP 000) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Developing and maintaining operational risk management and measurement policies, standards and guidelines | 310 |
| 2 | Designing and delivering operational risk training to promote awareness and risk competency | 145 |
| 3 | Developing an independent view on the business units’ identification of material risks and on the design and effectiveness of key controls | 260 |
| 4 | Providing the final sign-off on each business unit’s risk and control assessment | 90 |
| 5 | Reviewing and contributing to the monitoring and reporting of the operational risk profile | 180 |
| 6 | Defining its own view of the organization’s key risks, around which it builds an audit universe | 120 |

How many of the listed activities are appropriate responsibilities of the second line of defense?
questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK CORF head’s draft charter: counting which of six activities are second-line duties.

**Concept and theory**

In the 3LoD model the second line develops the risk management framework and reviews and challenges its implementation by the first line. GARP lists four responsibilities of an effective second line:

1. developing and maintaining ORM and measurement policies, standards and guidelines, and designing and delivering operational risk training to promote awareness and risk competency;
2. developing an independent view on the business units’ identification of material operational risks, the design and effectiveness of key controls, and the respect of risk appetite and tolerance limits;
3. challenging the relevance and consistency of the business units’ implementation of ORM tools, measurement activities and reporting systems, and providing evidence of this effective challenge;
4. reviewing and contributing to the monitoring and reporting of the operational risk profile.

Two activities belong elsewhere. The first line “needs to own the final sign-off on their risks assessment and controls; this is not a role that the second line should take.” And defining an independent view of the organization’s key risks around which an audit universe is built is what internal audit does.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each row; the budget column is irrelevant.

| No. | Line | Basis in GARP |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Second | Duty 1: policies, standards and guidelines |
| 2 | Second | Duty 1: designing and delivering training |
| 3 | Second | Duty 2: independent view |
| 4 | First | First line owns the final sign-off |
| 5 | Second | Duty 4: monitoring and reporting the profile |
| 6 | Third | Internal audit defines its own audit universe |

Second-line activities = {1, 2, 3, 5}

Count = 4

The CORF charter should drop activity 4 (return the sign-off to the business) and activity 6 (leave it to internal audit).

**Fragile fact.** The second line owns the methodology; the first line owns the risks and the sign-off; the audit universe is internal audit’s own.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Roles and Responsibilities of the Second Line of Defense”, “Second Line of Defense: Between Guidance and Challenge” and “Roles and Responsibilities of the Third Line of Defense”. Schweser lists the same four second-line duties; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (sibling swap). The count of 3 comes from excluding activity 5 on the belief that monitoring and reporting the risk profile belongs only to the first line. The first line does monitor and report its own unit’s profile, but GARP also gives the second line the duty of reviewing and contributing to that monitoring and reporting. Count: {1, 2, 3} = 3. It would be correct if activity 5 read “monitoring and reporting the business unit’s own risk profile as its risk owner”.

b.reason: (role misassignment). The count of 5 comes from adding activity 4, the final sign-off, to the four correct items: 4 + 1 = 5. GARP gives the sign-off to the first line; the second line owns the methodology, not the risks. It would be correct if activity 4 read “providing evidence of its challenge of each unit’s assessment”.

c.reason: (scope error). The count of 6 counts every row because the CORF head proposed it, ignoring that lines are defined by role, not by who drafts the list: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6. It would be correct only if activities 4 and 6 were rewritten as second-line duties.

d.reason: Four activities (1, 2, 3 and 5) match the second-line responsibilities GARP lists, so option D is correct.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q8
questions.question: A commercial bank in China plans to acquire a payments fintech for CNY 1.2 billion. The CORF’s analysis shows that, as currently structured, the integration would push the business line’s projected operational losses above the operational risk appetite limit agreed by the board. The deal is commercially attractive and complies with all regulations. Which course of action by the CORF is most consistent with the role of the second line of defense?

options.text: Refrain from giving a view on the deal, since acquisitions are business decisions that lie outside the remit of the second line.
Veto the deal, and any other deal it judges commercially unattractive, since its challenge extends to all business matters.
Give its view of the risks and mitigation options, and use its delegated authority to veto the deal as currently structured.
Give its view of the risks and mitigation options, but leave any veto to internal audit, which holds that authority in the model.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank’s CNY 1.2 billion fintech acquisition breaching the board’s risk appetite limit.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond oversight and challenge, GARP gives the risk function another important role: supporting business decisions with an informed view of the possible risks and the mitigating options. It should act as a sounding board for decisions that would change the institution’s risk profile, such as new ventures, commercial agreements, acquisitions, new products or markets, investments and divestments.

To make the challenge effective, the risk function “needs to have enough delegated authority to veto some business decisions that may either contradict regulatory requirements or that exceed the risk appetite limits agreed by the board.” The veto has two triggers only. The IIA’s 2021 model adds the boundary: the second line’s challenge applies to risk-related matters, and it is not its role to interfere in business matters outside its area of competence.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem settles three facts. The deal changes the risk profile (an acquisition), so the CORF should give its view. It breaches the board-agreed risk appetite limit, which is one of the two veto triggers. It is compliant and commercially attractive, so the only legitimate ground for the veto is the risk appetite breach, not commercial judgment. The right action is to advise on risks and mitigation and veto the deal as currently structured.

**Fragile fact.** Veto triggers: contradicts regulation, or exceeds the board-agreed risk appetite limits. The actor is the second line, and commercial merit is not a trigger.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Roles and Responsibilities of the Second Line of Defense” and “The IIA’s Three Lines Model”. Schweser agrees: the second line’s effectiveness “is enhanced when it is given the power to overturn business decisions that do not comply with regulations and/or breach any board-authorized risk limits”. The risk appetite concept itself belongs to LO 43.d; here it appears only as the veto trigger.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip). The option reverses GARP: acquisitions are named among the decisions where the risk function should provide an informed view. It would be correct only if the decision had no effect on the institution’s risk profile, for example a purely commercial pricing choice within approved limits.

b.reason: (scope error). The veto is right for this deal but the stated scope is wrong. The veto is limited to decisions that contradict regulation or exceed board risk appetite limits, and the IIA model says the second line’s challenge applies to risk-related matters, not to commercial attractiveness. It would be correct if the second clause read “and any other deal that breaches regulation or the board’s risk appetite”.

c.reason: Option C combines the sounding-board role with the veto on the GARP trigger “exceed the risk appetite limits agreed by the board”.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The advice is right but the veto is given to the wrong line. GARP gives the delegated authority to veto to the risk function (second line); internal audit gives independent assurance and does not take business decisions. It would be correct if “internal audit” were replaced by “the CORF itself”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q9
questions.question: A small Brazilian bank (total assets BRL 9 billion) has just set up a CORF. The business-unit managers are new to operational risk management and have not yet implemented any of the risk tools. The head of the CORF proposes to launch intensive challenge reviews of every business unit next month. A risk consultant is asked to recommend how the second line should proceed. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Prioritize teaching staff what operational risk is, how incidents are recognized and reported, and the benefits of good ORM.
Prioritize intensive challenge of the business units, since the second line must establish its independence before it offers any education or guidance.
Prioritize challenge and leave ORM education to internal audit, since educating the first line would impair the independence of the second line.
Prioritize completing the business units’ risk assessments on their behalf, since the second line owns both the methodology and the risks.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: New CORF at a small Brazilian bank whose business managers are new to ORM.

**Concept and theory**

The relationship between the first and second lines is, in GARP’s words, probably the most debated aspect of the 3LoD model. Regulators require an “independent” second line providing “oversight and challenge”. But pure independence raises two problems: possible redundancy with internal audit, and the fact that “it can be very difficult to operate effective oversight and challenge on risk management activities in the business before these activities are properly implemented, understood, and maturing.”

GARP’s resolution: the first role of the ORM function is to educate all internal parties on the essentials of ORM, especially in younger or smaller organizations and in business units where management is new to the discipline. BCBS-recommended essential training covers:

1. What is operational risk?
2. How are operational incidents recognized and reported?
3. What are the benefits of good operational risk management?
4. What are the pitfalls of poor risk management?

Training can then move to risk tools: risk identification, assessment, root-cause analysis and scenario workshops.

**Applying it to this question**

Every condition GARP names is present: a small bank, a new CORF, managers new to ORM, and no tools implemented yet. Intensive challenge now would have nothing mature to challenge. The recommendation is education first, then challenge as the activities mature.

**Fragile fact.** For immature business units the order is education first, challenge later, and the training is delivered by the second line, not by internal audit.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Second Line of Defense: Between Guidance and Challenge”. Schweser agrees that the second line “should focus on guidance and informing all relevant staff about ORM” and that challenge “may be ineffective until the risk management work in Line 1 is fully executed”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: Option A states GARP’s prescription and its content (what operational risk is, how incidents are recognized and reported, the benefits of good ORM). “Prioritize” places this education before intensive challenge, which is GARP’s sequence.

b.reason: (polarity flip). The option reverses GARP’s sequence. GARP says education is the first role, and challenge is very difficult before activities are implemented and maturing. It would be correct only for a bank whose business units already run mature ORM tools.

c.reason: (role misassignment). Training is a second-line duty (designing and delivering operational risk training), not internal audit’s. GARP shows the second line keeps its independence while guiding, by asking questions without preempting answers. It would be correct if training were said to be delivered by the CORF.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The second line owns the methodology; the first line owns the risks and signs off its own assessments. Completing the assessments for the business would destroy independence and create a self-review threat. It would be correct if it read “helping the business units complete their own risk assessments using the CORF’s methodology”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q10
questions.question: A second-line operational risk manager at an Irish bank will run a risk and control self-assessment (RCSA) workshop with managers of the credit cards business, whose card fraud losses were EUR 3.4 million last year. Which approach is least likely to compromise the independence of the second line?

options.text: Pre-populating the workshop template with the risk ratings she expects, so that the business managers can confirm them efficiently.
Letting the business managers draft the assessment, then signing it off herself after amending any ratings she disagrees with.
Declining to run the workshop, since any facilitation of a first-line assessment by the second line creates a self-review threat.
Facilitating without influencing the answers, then collecting the responses and challenging the ratings and their justifications.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Second-line manager running an RCSA workshop with an Irish bank’s cards business.

**Concept and theory**

How can the second line guide the first line without losing independence? GARP’s answer is to provide guidance and ask questions, but “without preempting the answers”. A second-line risk manager may run a risk and control self-assessment (RCSA) workshop with business staff and managers, prompting reflection on risks and controls, while “avoiding exerting influence on the content of the answers and assessments made”. Afterwards she collects the responses and challenges the answers and their justifications.

Two ownership rules complete the picture: “The first line needs to own the final sign-off on their risks assessment and controls; this is not a role that the second line should take. The second line owns the methodology; the first line owns the risks.” Influencing the answers or signing them off would put the second line in the position of reviewing its own work, a self-review threat.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks which approach is least likely to compromise independence, so look for the one that matches GARP’s sequence: facilitate, do not influence, collect, then challenge. The EUR 3.4 million fraud figure is irrelevant. Option D follows that sequence; A, B and C each break a rule.

**Fragile fact.** The second line owns the methodology; the first line owns the risks and the final sign-off; the second line challenges after the answers come in, never before.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Second Line of Defense: Between Guidance and Challenge”. Version note: Schweser states that Line 2 “must not have any involvement in Line 1, or else there will be a self-review threat”, which reads more absolutely than GARP (“should not be directly involved in the risk management activities . . . but rather provide guidance, oversight, and challenge”). Both sources allow second-line training workshops followed by challenge; the answer follows GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: (role misassignment). Pre-populating the ratings preempts the answers, which GARP says the second line must avoid; the second line would then challenge its own ratings. It would be acceptable if the template carried the CORF’s methodology and rating scale but no pre-filled ratings.

b.reason: (role misassignment). The final sign-off belongs to the first line; GARP says it “is not a role that the second line should take”. Amending and signing off would make the second line the owner of the assessment. It would be acceptable if she challenged the ratings and the business managers decided on any changes and signed off.

c.reason: (absolute claim). GARP explicitly says a second-line risk manager “may very well run” an RCSA workshop while staying independent. Facilitation alone does not create a self-review threat; influencing the content does. It would be correct only if running the workshop meant supplying the answers.

d.reason: Option D is GARP’s description almost step by step: run the workshop without influencing the content, then collect the responses and challenge the ratings and their justifications.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q11
questions.question: A member of the audit committee of a Singapore bank (total assets SGD 120 billion) is reviewing four proposals from the head of internal audit for the coming year. Which of the following proposals is NOT consistent with the role of internal audit as the third line of defense?

options.text: Coordinating its agenda with the risk function, so that business-line managers are not overloaded with redundant visits and assessments.
Adopting the CORF’s risk register as its audit universe, so that the second and third lines assess an identical set of key risks.
Reporting in solid line to a non-executive director, such as the chair of the audit committee, rather than to the chief risk officer.
Including the risk function itself within the scope of its independent assessment of compliance with policies and procedures.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Audit committee member at a Singapore bank screening four internal audit proposals (NOT question).

**Concept and theory**

The third line of defense is internal audit, “probably the line with the clearest boundaries”. Its features in GARP:

- It is independent of the risk management process.
- It independently assesses the control system and compliance with the policies and procedures of the different departments and activities, “including that of the risk function”.
- It “typically defines its own view of the organization’s key risks around which it develops its audit universe”.
- In some firms audit and risk coordinate their agendas so as not to overload business-line managers with redundant visits and risk assessments, and the second and third lines exchange information and findings.
- It must be independent and should report in solid line to a non-executive director, for example the chair of the audit committee, the senior independent non-executive director, or the non-executive chairman.

Coordination is allowed; surrendering the independent view of risk is not.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT question: three proposals are consistent with GARP, one is not. A: coordination to avoid redundant visits is described by GARP. Consistent. B: adopting the CORF’s register as the audit universe abandons internal audit’s own view of key risks. Not consistent. C: solid-line reporting to a non-executive director. Consistent. D: the scope includes the risk function. Consistent.

**Fragile fact.** Internal audit reports in solid line to a non-executive director (not the CRO), keeps its own audit universe, and audits the risk function too.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Roles and Responsibilities of the Third Line of Defense”. Schweser agrees and adds that independence “could be achieved by having them report directly to one of the bank’s nonexecutive directors”; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: (true statement, absolute-claim trap). A candidate picks A by assuming that any coordination with the risk function compromises independence. GARP explicitly describes agenda coordination and the sharing of information and findings between the second and third lines. A would be the answer only if it said audit should adopt the risk function’s conclusions without its own testing.

b.reason: Option B contradicts GARP’s statement that internal audit defines its own view of the organization’s key risks around which it builds its audit universe. Schweser says the same: internal audit keeps its independence “partly by establishing its own list of significant risks”.

c.reason: (true statement, role-misassignment trap). A candidate picks C by believing internal audit should report to the CRO. GARP requires a solid line to a non-executive director precisely so that audit is independent of the risk function it assesses. C would be the answer if it read “reporting in solid line to the chief risk officer”.

d.reason: (true statement, scope-error trap). A candidate picks D by assuming the risk function, being already independent of the business, is outside audit’s scope. GARP says audit assesses compliance across departments “including that of the risk function”. D would be the answer if it proposed excluding the risk function from scope.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q12
questions.question:
An internal audit manager at an Australian bank is planning a review of trade surveillance. The compliance function has already tested the area this year, and the audit team proposes to rely on that work. The planning data are:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Trade alerts tested by compliance this year | 400 |
| Exceptions found by compliance | 6 |
| Trade alerts in the population (thousand) | 185 |
| Proposed internal audit sample | 0 |

Internal audit has not yet evaluated the effectiveness of the compliance function for this area. Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The plan is acceptable, because internal audit may rely exclusively on compliance’s testing provided compliance is independent of the business.
The plan must be replaced by one that disregards compliance’s work entirely, because any reliance on it compromises internal audit’s independence.
Internal audit may reduce its testing only after evaluating the effectiveness of compliance in this area, and must still examine a sample itself.
Internal audit may reduce its testing once the CORF has evaluated the effectiveness of compliance in this area, and must still examine a sample itself.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian internal audit plan relying fully on compliance’s trade surveillance testing.

**Concept and theory**

GARP cites the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA, 2017) on how internal audit should interact with risk management, compliance and finance:

- These functions are essential parts of corporate governance; internal audit should be independent of them and be “neither responsible for, nor part of, them”.
- Internal audit’s scope should include an assessment of the adequacy and effectiveness of these functions.
- “In no circumstances should internal audit rely exclusively on the work of risk management, compliance or finance. Internal audit should always examine, for itself, an appropriate sample of the activities under review.”
- Internal audit should use informed judgment on how far to take account of others’ work in its risk assessment or in deciding the level of testing. Any judgment that leads to less intense audit scrutiny “should only be made after an evaluation of the effectiveness of that function in relation to the area under review.”

So reliance is allowed, but it is partial, conditional on internal audit’s own evaluation, and never replaces its own sample.

**Applying it to this question**

Two facts in the stem decide the answer. The proposed audit sample is 0, which is exclusive reliance. Internal audit has not yet evaluated compliance’s effectiveness for the area, so even partial reduction is not yet justified. The figures 400, 6 and 185 thousand are irrelevant to the principle. The correct conclusion: evaluate compliance first, then reduce testing if justified, and always test a sample.

**Fragile fact.** Never rely exclusively; reduce scrutiny only after internal audit’s own evaluation of that function in that area; always test a sample yourself.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Roles and Responsibilities of the Third Line of Defense” (IIA, 2017 guidance). Schweser agrees: “There should not be full reliance” and reliance “is permissible only after internal audit has assessed the reliability of the work done”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (condition error). GARP says “in no circumstances” should internal audit rely exclusively on compliance’s work; compliance’s independence from the business does not change that. This would be correct only for partial reliance after audit’s own evaluation, never for exclusive reliance.

b.reason: (absolute claim). The IIA guidance allows internal audit to take account of others’ work, in its risk assessment and in setting the level of testing, after evaluating that function. Disregarding the work entirely is not required. It would be correct if compliance’s work had been evaluated and found ineffective for the area.

c.reason: Option C states both IIA conditions: reduction only after internal audit evaluates the effectiveness of the function in that area, and internal audit must always examine an appropriate sample itself.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The evaluation must be made by internal audit. Letting the CORF, a second-line function that audit itself assesses, decide how much audit can rely on compliance breaks audit’s independence. It would be correct if “the CORF” were replaced by “internal audit”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 c Q13
questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of a US bank asks a senior risk analyst to brief the committee on recent developments in the three lines of defense model. The analyst drafts the following statements:

I. Some institutions call the model the “three lines of accountability” to stress the delimitation and accountability of roles, but this is not a true departure from the original model.

II. Under the IIA’s 2021 Three Lines Model, the second line is independent of management and reports directly to the governing body.

III. The IIA’s 2021 model specifies that the second line’s challenge applies to risk-related matters rather than to business matters generally.

IV. The IIA’s 2021 model describes third line roles as independent and objective assurance and advice on all matters related to the achievement of objectives.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Briefing a US board risk committee on “three lines of accountability” and the IIA’s 2021 model.

**Concept and theory**

Two developments refine the original 3LoD model.

Three lines of accountability. Some institutions rename the model to insist on the delimitation of roles and responsibilities across the lines and to stress each actor’s accountability. GARP: “Besides a difference in name, the three lines of accountability is not, however, a true departure from the original model.”

The IIA’s Three Lines Model (2021). The Institute of Internal Auditors refined the model to reflect how risk management has evolved and to foster closer collaboration between business functions, including internal audit (GARP Figure 2.6):

| Role | IIA 2021 description |
|---|---|
| Governing body | Accountability to stakeholders for organizational oversight; integrity, leadership and transparency |
| First line | Provision of products and services to clients; managing risk |
| Second line | Expertise, support, monitoring and challenge on risk-related matters |
| Third line (internal audit) | Independent and objective assurance and advice on all matters related to the achievement of objectives |

The model reinforces the second line’s expertise and support, and specifies that its challenge applies to risk-related matters. GARP notes that some risk functions had become so independent that they stressed oversight and challenge at the expense of support and expertise, “confusing their role with that of internal audit”. The IIA reminds that “the second line is part of and reports to general management”. Risk is seen as a function that helps the firm create and protect value.

**Applying it to this question**

I: matches GARP on the renaming. Accurate. II: reverses the IIA position; the second line is part of and reports to management. Inaccurate. III: matches GARP. Accurate. IV: matches Figure 2.6. Accurate. The accurate set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Under the IIA 2021 model the second line is part of management and its challenge is limited to risk-related matters; only internal audit is independent of management.

**Reference**

LO 43.c (wording as above). GARP Chapter 2, “Three Lines of Accountability” and “The IIA’s Three Lines Model” (Figure 2.6). Content from GARP only: Schweser’s LO 43.c section does not discuss the renaming or the IIA 2021 update. This is treated as in scope because it is part of GARP’s description of the three lines model named in the LO.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 c, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: (scope error). Rejecting IV treats internal audit as giving assurance only. Figure 2.6 describes third line roles as “independent and objective assurance and advice”. The option would be correct if IV had described the third line as managing risk or giving assurance on financial statements only.

b.reason: Option B is the only combination that includes the three accurate statements and excludes II, consistent with GARP’s “Three Lines of Accountability” and “The IIA’s Three Lines Model”.

c.reason: (polarity flip). Rejecting I treats the renaming as a substantive change. GARP says it is not a true departure from the original model. The option would be correct if I claimed the renaming created a fourth line or reassigned roles.

d.reason: (polarity flip). Accepting II puts the second line outside management. The IIA reminds that the second line is part of and reports to general management; it is the third line that is independent. The option would be correct if II described internal audit rather than the second line.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices and regulatory expectations for the development of a risk appetite for operational risk and for a strong risk culture.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-2 d Q1
questions.question: A risk consultant is advising the board of a mid-sized Australian retail bank that is defining an operational risk appetite for the first time. One director suggests the exercise is a formality that can be completed in a single meeting by approving a firm-wide annual operational loss figure of AUD 40 million. Which of the following statements about defining a risk appetite for operational risk is most accurate?

options.text: Approving a single firm-wide loss figure completes the definition of risk appetite, and the bank’s control environment can then be designed separately, without reference to the appetite limits.
Defining appetite is generally easier for operational risk than for financial risks, because most operational incidents can be avoided, so the acceptable level of incidents is close to zero.

A thorough definition may expose contradictions between what the bank officially states and how operational risks are really managed, and the resulting limits drive the priorities of the control environment.
Defining the appetite is the responsibility of the chief risk officer, and the role of the board is limited to receiving the resulting limits for information once they have been set.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank board defining operational risk appetite for the first time; a director wants to approve one loss figure.

**Concept and theory**

Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Corporate governance codes name the board as responsible for determining the nature and extent of the significant risks the firm is willing to take, so directors naturally take an interest in it. GARP stresses that this is “easier said than done”: many firms struggle with both the concept and its practical use, especially for non-financial risks.

GARP describes what defining a risk appetite actually involves:

| Step | What it means |
|---|---|
| 1. Assess | Assess all the key risks facing the organisation |
| 2. Bound | Establish the boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable incidents |
| 3. Control | Create the controls that these limits require |

Two consequences follow. First, done thoroughly, the exercise “may lead to difficult conversations”: it can reveal internal contradictions between what the organisation officially states and what is really happening in the management of operational risk. Second, according to BCBS, the definition and limits of appetite and tolerance, when done consistently, drive the priorities of the entire control environment, which is also a board responsibility. Appetite is therefore not a number filed away; it is the steering input for controls.

**Applying it to this question**

The director proposes a single firm-wide loss figure approved in one meeting. Test each option against the three-step definition and the two consequences. A single figure skips step 2 (boundaries on incidents) and step 3 (controls the limits require), and it ignores the fact that appetite drives control priorities. The deciding fact is GARP’s statement that a thorough definition may expose contradictions and that appetite limits drive the priorities of the whole control environment.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: risk appetite is hardest, not easiest, to define for non-financial risks; and the flow is appetite → control priorities, not the reverse.

**Reference**

LO 43.d “Explain best practices and regulatory expectations for the development of a risk appetite for operational risk and for a strong risk culture.” GARP Chapter 2, end of Section 2.3 leading into Section 2.4 “Risk Appetite for Operational Risk” (defining a risk appetite). Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.d, “Risk Appetite (Regulatory Expectations)”. No conflict; GARP is richer.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 d, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). The option drops two of the three components of defining appetite (boundaries on incidents and the controls the limits require) and severs the link between appetite and the control environment. GARP says the opposite: appetite limits drive the priorities of the control environment. It would be correct only under a stem asking what the director’s (mistaken) proposal implies, not what best practice requires.

b.reason: (polarity flip). GARP says firms struggle with risk appetite “especially for non-financial risks”; the option reverses this into “easier”. It also implies near-zero tolerance is natural, whereas GARP’s own example accepts isolated unintentional incidents. It would be correct if the stem asked which statement a regulator would reject.

c.reason: Option C restates both consequences in GARP Section 2.3/2.4: thorough definition “may lead to difficult conversations and highlight painful truths, such as internal contradictions” between stated and actual risk management, and the limits “drive the priorities of the entire control environment”. Schweser says the same: a proper definition may expose inconsistencies between reported and actual ORM, and ideally sets the key objectives of the control system.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The right action (defining appetite) is attributed to the wrong actor. The board is responsible for determining the nature and extent of significant risks it is willing to take, that is, for setting the risk appetite; the CRO and risk function support implementation and reporting. The option would be correct if it described the risk function’s role in implementing and reporting on limits delegated through the board risk committee.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian cooperative bank is checking whether the draft operational risk appetite and tolerance statement meets the expectations of the BCBS principle dedicated to risk appetite and tolerance. She lists four features of the draft:

I. The statement is easy to communicate and understand, and it justifies the reasons for taking, limiting or avoiding particular types of operational risk.

II. The boundaries used to monitor the limits are restricted to quantitative indicators, because qualitative boundaries cannot be used to monitor operational risk.

III. The appetite is forward-looking, is subject to scenario analysis and stress testing, and takes a view of which events could push the bank outside its limits.

IV. The appetite is set independently of the bank’s strategy and business plans, so that it can act as an objective constraint on management’s growth ambitions.

Which of the features are consistent with the regulatory expectations for risk appetite and tolerance statements?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian cooperative bank: four features of a draft appetite statement audited against the BCBS principle.

**Concept and theory**

BCBS dedicates its fourth principle for the sound management of operational risk to risk appetite and tolerance: the board should approve and periodically review a risk appetite and tolerance statement for operational risk. GARP summarises what such statements need to be:

| Feature | GARP wording (paraphrased) |
|---|---|
| Clarity | Easy to communicate and understand |
| Justification | Justify the reasons for taking, limiting or avoiding certain types of operational risk |
| Alignment | In alignment with the bank’s strategy and business plans |
| Monitoring | Limits monitored through indicators of risk exposure, control environment and loss events |
| Forward-looking | Subject to scenario and stress testing, with a view of what events might push the bank outside its appetite and tolerance |

On the monitoring metrics, BCBS refers to “boundaries or indicators (which may be quantitative or not)”; banks call them monitoring KRIs. The reason for each feature is practical: a statement that nobody understands cannot guide decisions; one that does not explain why risks are taken cannot express the risk-return trade-off; one detached from strategy cannot steer the business; and one that only looks backwards cannot warn of events that would breach it.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement in turn. I combines clarity and justification: consistent. II restricts boundaries to quantitative indicators: inconsistent, because BCBS allows boundaries “quantitative or not”. III is the forward-looking and stress testing feature: consistent. IV sets appetite independently of strategy: inconsistent, because statements must be aligned with strategy and business plans. Consistent set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Boundaries for monitoring appetite “may be quantitative or not”; appetite is aligned with strategy, not independent of it.

**Reference**

LO 43.d “Explain best practices and regulatory expectations for the development of a risk appetite for operational risk and for a strong risk culture.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.4(a) “Regulatory Guidance on Risk Appetite for Operational Risk” and Section 2.4(b) “Risk Appetite Structure and Monitoring”. Schweser Reading 43, LO 43.d, “Risk Appetite (Regulatory Expectations)” and “Risk Appetite (Best Practices)”. Schweser compresses the monitoring indicators to “exposure limits, significant controls, and acceptable loss events”; GARP’s wording is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-2 d, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error, via statement II). Including II accepts a condition BCBS does not impose: boundaries may be quantitative or not. Box 2.1 in GARP shows qualitative elements (for example, failing agents dismissed if the breach was intentional) alongside numeric KRIs. A would be correct only if II read “the boundaries may be quantitative or qualitative”.

b.reason: Option B (I and III only) matches GARP Section 2.4(a): statements must be easy to communicate and understand, justify reasons for taking, limiting or avoiding risk, and be forward-looking and subject to scenario and stress testing.

c.reason: (polarity flip, via statement IV, and omission of I). IV reverses “aligned with the bank’s strategy and business plans” into “independent of” them, and C also drops the valid statement I. Appetite is meant to support strategy, not stand outside it. C would be correct only if IV said the appetite is aligned with strategy and I were false.

d.reason: (polarity flip, via statement IV). D contains both correct statements but adds IV. The single error is the reversal of the alignment requirement. D would be correct if IV read “the appetite is aligned with the bank’s strategy and business plans”.
