questions.question: A model validator at a UK bank is reviewing the GBP internal loss dataset used to model future operational losses. In 2026 the general ledger recorded a large settlement for a mis-selling event that began in 2015, under a product range and a management team that the bank has since replaced. Which view is most appropriate?

options.text: The loss’s relevance to future events should be questioned, as it reflects a past business context; multi-year lags to settlement are common for large losses.
The loss reflects the current risk profile because it settled recently, so it should be weighted as heavily as recent events in the modelling dataset.
The event should not have been reported before it settled, because material incidents are best reported only once their final amount is known.
The lag from occurrence to settlement is mainly explained by slow discovery-to-reporting in the business line, so tighter reporting deadlines would remove it.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK bank model validator reviews a 2026 settlement for a mis-selling event that began in 2015.

**Concept and theory**

The date of settlement is when all the effects of an incident have been accounted for in the general ledger. For events with regulatory and legal implications, settlement can take years. Box 4.1 (from Grimwade, 2021) analyses losses above USD 100 million at 31 G-SIBs before the Global Financial Crisis: these most commonly had three to five years between the reporting date and the settlement date, and average loss values peak around three to five years of duration.

This lag has two consequences.

- **Measurement.** Some losses hitting the accounts today took place years ago, in a different business context and under different management. Their relevance for modelling future events should be questioned.
- **Management.** The lessons from such past failures should likewise be questioned in light of how much the business has changed.

The lag does not mean reporting should wait: Table 4.1 records an “expected direct financial loss (may evolve until closure)”, and material incidents should be reported within a few working days.

**Applying it to this question**

The settlement arrives in 2026 for an event that began in 2015 under a product range and management team that no longer exist. That is exactly GARP’s case: the event belongs to a different business context, so its relevance to future losses should be questioned. The “recent” accounting date does not make it representative of the current profile.

**Fragile fact.** Recently settled does not mean recently occurred: old losses settled now may not represent today’s business.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.” (Schweser LO 45.a). Source: GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 4 “Risk Measurement and Assessment”, Section 4.1 “Operational Risk Events”, subsection “Dates of Incidents and Settlement Lags” and Box 4.1 “Examples of Gaps Between Settlement and Reporting”. Schweser states the same caution and the three-to-five-year range; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 a, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: Option A is correct because GARP states that “some of the events hitting the accounts took place years ago, in a different business context and under different management. The relevance of older losses for the modeling of future operational events . . . should therefore be questioned accordingly”, and that large losses most commonly take three to five years from reporting to settlement.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Option B treats the recent settlement date as evidence of current relevance. The source draws the opposite conclusion: a loss settled now may reflect a past context. Option B would be correct only if the event had also occurred recently under the current business model.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). Option C makes reporting wait for settlement. Best practice is risk-based: material incidents are reported within a few working days, and the expected direct loss may evolve until closure. Option C would be correct only for the accounting date, which by definition comes when the effects reach the general ledger.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Option D blames the discovery-to-reporting interval. GARP names time to discovery (occurrence to discovery) as the main factor in the occurrence-to-settlement gap, and legal and regulatory processes for the long reporting-to-settlement gap. Option D would be correct if it said “mainly explained by the time taken to discover the event”.

questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 a Q10
questions.question:
A regulatory reporting analyst at a Canadian bank is building the operational loss dataset for the year. The following events were identified:

| Event | Description | Loss (CAD million) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Loss on a defaulted commercial loan, worsened because collateral was recorded incorrectly; the loss is accounted for in credit risk RWAs | 2.4 |
| 2 | Loss on a retail loan caused by a documentation error; the loss is not accounted for in credit risk RWAs | 0.6 |
| 3 | Trading loss after a bond position was booked twice in error | 1.1 |
| 4 | Mark-to-market loss on the bond portfolio after a central bank rate rise | 3.0 |

Applying the BCBS guidance on boundary events, what total loss from these events should be included in the operational loss dataset?

options.text: CAD 0.6 million
CAD 1.1 million
CAD 1.7 million
CAD 4.1 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst applies boundary-event rules to four events to find the operational loss total.

**Concept and theory**

**Boundary events** materialise in a different risk class than their cause: for example a credit loss aggravated by incorrect recording of collateral, or a market loss due to an unintentional booking error. Without a rule, the same loss could be counted twice (once in credit or market risk, once in operational risk) or not at all. The BCBS gives this guidance:

| Type of event | Treatment in operational loss dataset |
|---|---|
| Operational loss related to credit risk, accounted for in credit risk RWAs | Excluded |
| Operational loss related to credit risk, not accounted for in credit risk RWAs | Included |
| Operational loss related to market risk | Included (treated as operational risk for minimum capital, subject to the SA) |

A pure market loss with no operational cause is not an operational event at all and is excluded.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each event, then sum the included losses (CAD million).

Event 1: credit-related, in credit RWAs ⇒ excluded

Event 2: credit-related, not in credit RWAs ⇒ included: 0.6

Event 3: market-related, operational cause ⇒ included: 1.1

Event 4: pure market risk, no operational cause ⇒ excluded

Total included = 0.6 + 1.1 = 1.7

Meaning: CAD 1.7 million enters the operational loss dataset; the CAD 2.4 million collateral case stays in credit risk, where it is already covered by credit capital.

**Fragile fact.** Credit-related: excluded only if already in credit RWAs. Market-related: always recorded as operational loss.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.” (Schweser LO 45.a). Source: GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 4 “Risk Measurement and Assessment”, Section 4.1 “Operational Risk Events”, subsection “Boundary Event Reporting”. Note: Schweser states that credit boundary events need not be included “to the extent they are already included in RWA” but does not spell out that those not in RWAs must be included; GARP (quoting BCBS points f and g) is explicit, and is followed here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 a, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: (polarity flip (market rule reversed)). CAD 0.6 million includes event 2 but excludes event 3, as if market-related operational losses stayed in market risk. GARP: boundary events “are not included in the models of market risk and need to be recorded as operational losses”. Option A would be correct if market-related boundary events were excluded.

b.reason: (scope error (credit rule overextended)). CAD 1.1 million excludes both credit-related events, applying the RWA exclusion to event 2 even though it is not in credit RWAs. Option B would be correct only if event 2 had also been accounted for in credit risk RWAs.

c.reason: Option C is correct because, per the BCBS points quoted by GARP, operational losses related to credit risk “that are accounted for in credit risk RWAs . . . should not be included”, those “not accounted for in credit risk RWAs should be included”, and operational losses related to market risk “are treated as operational risk”.

d.reason: (polarity flip (credit rule reversed)). CAD 4.1 million = 2.4 + 0.6 + 1.1 includes event 1, attributing the collateral-related credit loss back to its operational cause although it is already in credit RWAs. Option D would be correct only if event 1 had not been accounted for in credit RWAs.

questions.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.

questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 a Q11
questions.question:
A banking supervisor is preparing training on boundary events for newly hired examiners. Consider the following statements:

I. Boundary events are events that materialise in a different risk class than their cause, such as a market loss due to an unintentional booking error.

II. Leaving operational-caused credit losses where they materialise is justified because credit capital models are based on historical losses, so such losses are already covered by credit risk capital.

III. Operational-caused market losses should stay in the market risk class, because market risk models already include them.

IV. An operational-caused credit loss must always be excluded from the operational loss dataset, whatever its treatment in credit risk RWAs.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and IV only
II and III only
I and II only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Banking supervisor audits four statements on the definition and treatment of boundary events.

**Concept and theory**

A boundary event’s cause and its loss sit in different risk classes. The regulatory treatment differs by class, and GARP explains why.

- **Credit.** The pragmatic view adopted by international regulators is to leave credit events recorded where they materialise, without disentangling the cause. This is justified because credit loss models for regulatory capital are based on historical losses: even if past losses were due to operational risk, they are covered by regulatory capital in the credit risk class, “which is good enough from a prudential regulation perspective”. The exclusion applies to losses accounted for in credit RWAs; those not in credit RWAs are included in the operational dataset.
- **Market.** Boundary events are not included in market risk models, so they must be recorded as operational losses.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I gives the definition and GARP’s own example of a market boundary event. True.

Statement II gives the credit rationale. True. Statement III says market-related operational losses stay in market risk because market models include them. GARP says they are not in market risk models and must be recorded as operational losses. False. Statement IV says credit-related operational losses are always excluded. The exclusion holds only for losses accounted for in credit RWAs. False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** The credit exception rests on credit models being built on historical losses; market models are not, so market boundary events are operational.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.” (Schweser LO 45.a). Source: GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 4 “Risk Measurement and Assessment”, Section 4.1 “Operational Risk Events”, subsection “Boundary Event Reporting”. Schweser gives the definition and the two BCBS points in brief, without the rationale or the “not in RWAs” case; GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 a, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: (scope error (true statement omitted)). Option A accepts only I and leaves out II, which is GARP’s stated rationale for the credit treatment. Option A would be correct only if statement II had misstated the rationale, for example by saying credit models ignore historical losses.

b.reason: (absolute claim). Option B accepts statement IV, which turns a conditional rule into an absolute one with “always” and “whatever its treatment”. Losses not in credit RWAs must be included. Option B would be correct if statement IV had added “when it is accounted for in credit risk RWAs”.

c.reason: (polarity flip). Option C accepts statement III, which reverses the market treatment. Option C would be correct only if market risk models did capture these losses, which GARP explicitly denies.

d.reason: Option D is correct because GARP defines boundary events as “events that materialize in a different risk class than their cause”, and justifies the credit treatment “by the fact that credit loss models for regulatory capital are based on historical losses. So, even if past losses were due to operational risk, they are covered by regulatory capital in the credit risk class”.

questions.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 a Q12
questions.question: An operational risk manager at a Chinese commercial bank is testing the comprehensiveness of the incident database ahead of an internal audit review. During the year a pricing error meant that a corporate client was not charged CNY 2.3 million of fees that were due. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Reconciling the incident database to the general ledger will reveal the uncharged fees, since the ledger captures all cash inflows and outflows.
IT issues rated Priority 1 and Priority 2 can generally serve as proxies for operational incidents and be compared with the incident database.
The general ledger can replace a dedicated incident database, since it records direct losses together with the indirect effects of each event.
Customer complaints and provisions for pending lawsuits are unsuitable proxies, because they are not losses recorded in the general ledger.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank manager tests incident database comprehensiveness after an uncharged-fee error.

**Concept and theory**

The BCBS requires processes “to independently review the comprehensiveness and accuracy of loss data”. Comprehensiveness is the main quality question: how can a bank be sure that all material losses are recorded? The main answer is reconciliation with other sources.

- **General ledger (GL).** Captures all cash inflows and outflows, including unintentional losses and gains, so it is a good benchmark if entries are labelled so operational items can be identified. But it is no substitute for a dedicated event database: it captures only direct financial losses or accidental gains and does not link indirect effects. And an event that materialises as reduced revenue (for example under-charging or not charging a client) is invisible in the GL.
- **IT logs.** IT issues rated Priority 1 (P1) and Priority 2 (P2) can generally be considered proxies of operational incidents.
- **Other proxies (Figure 4.2).** Provisions for pending lawsuits, customer complaints and compensations, negative press and media reports, back-office issue logs.

Comparing the event database with these proxies is a good way to assess possible underreporting.

**Applying it to this question**

The uncharged fee is a loss of revenue: no cash left the bank, so nothing appears in the GL. Any statement claiming the GL will catch it, or can replace the database, fails. The correct statement must describe a valid proxy. Option B does: P1 and P2 IT issues. The CNY 2.3 million amount is not needed.

**Fragile fact.** Lost revenue is invisible in the GL; that is the GL’s blind spot, and why other proxies are needed.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.” (Schweser LO 45.a). Source: GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 4 “Risk Measurement and Assessment”, Section 4.1 “Operational Risk Events”, subsection “Data Quality Requirements” and Figure 4.2 “Other data sources as proxies for operational incidents”. Note: Schweser’s second GL limitation says items showing up as lower revenues “should actually be recorded as expenses or losses”; GARP’s point is that such items are invisible in the GL. Schweser also calls P1 and P2 issues “equivalent to” incidents where GARP says “proxies”. GARP is followed in both cases.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 a, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). The GL captures cash flows, but a fee never charged produces no flow. GARP: if an event “materializes as reduced revenue rather than a net loss (for instance, by accidently under-charging or not charging a client), it will be invisible in the GL”. Option A would be correct for an overpayment or a compensation payment, which do pass through the GL.

b.reason: Option B is correct because GARP states that “IT issues rated Priority 1 (P1) and Priority 2 (P2) can generally be considered as proxies of operational risk incidents” and that comparing them with the operational events recorded assesses the comprehensiveness of collection.

c.reason: (absolute claim). The GL captures only direct financial losses and accidental gains and “does not link the indirect effects”, so it “is no substitute for a dedicated operational event database”. Option C would be correct if it said the GL is a good benchmark for the database, not a replacement.

d.reason: (polarity flip). GARP lists provisions for pending lawsuits and customer complaints and compensations as proxies used to assess comprehensiveness. Not being in the GL is exactly why they are useful. Option D would be correct if it said these are suitable proxies.

questions.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a small German private bank suspects that operational incidents are underreported: the incident database shows far fewer events than the back-office issue log. Which pairing of likely cause and remedy is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: Cause: resistance to escalating errors. Remedy: risk metrics in managers’ balanced scorecards, and self-reporting with discipline if hidden events surface.
Cause: underreporting arises mainly at large firms. Remedy: raise the reporting threshold so that business units have fewer incidents to report.
Cause: unclear guidance on what to report. Remedy: drop self-reporting and rely only on general ledger extraction to find every incident.
Cause: cumbersome reporting processes. Remedy: let business lines assess their own loss collection processes in place of internal audit.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chief compliance officer at a small German private bank diagnoses and remedies underreporting.

**Concept and theory**

Despite detailed regulatory requirements, underreporting of operational incidents is still a challenge for many firms, especially smaller ones. GARP lists the causes and the incentives used to counter them:

| Causes of underreporting | Remedies and incentives |
|---|---|
| Lack of guidance on what and how to report | Incentives ranging from soft encouragement to stringent oversight |
| Resistance to escalate errors and failures | Required self-reporting, with the threat of disciplinary action if unreported events are later discovered |
| Unwillingness to engage in cumbersome reporting processes | Risk metrics in managers’ balanced scorecards (risk-based performance, encouraged by regulators); internal audit regularly assesses the collection processes |

Comparing the database with proxy sources, such as back-office issue logs, is how underreporting is detected in the first place.

**Applying it to this question**

The gap between the issue log and the incident database is a detection signal. The answer must pair a GARP cause with a GARP remedy. Option A pairs resistance to escalate with balanced-scorecard metrics and self-reporting under the threat of discipline: both halves come from the source.

**Fragile fact.** Underreporting is worst at smaller firms; internal audit, not the business, assesses the collection process.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.” (Schweser LO 45.a). Source: GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 4 “Risk Measurement and Assessment”, Section 4.1 “Operational Risk Events”, subsection “Data Quality Requirements”. Note: Schweser summarises the remedies as gentle reminders, risk metrics in managerial performance, and internal audit; GARP is broader (soft encouragement to stringent oversight, with disciplinary threat). GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 a, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: Option A is correct because GARP names “resistance to escalate errors and failures” as a cause, and states that “usually, self-reporting of incidents is required, with the threat of disciplinary action if unreported events are subsequently discovered” and that “most organizations include risk metrics in the balanced scorecard of their managers”.

b.reason: (polarity flip). GARP says underreporting is a challenge “especially” for smaller firms, not large ones. Raising the threshold to cut the number of reports would also reduce comprehensiveness. Option B would be correct only if the cause read “underreporting is a particular challenge at smaller firms” and the remedy were drawn from the incentive list.

c.reason: (scope error). The cause (lack of guidance) is genuine, but the remedy overreaches: the GL captures only direct losses, misses lost revenue, and “is no substitute for a dedicated operational event database”. Option C would be correct if the remedy were clearer reporting guidance, with the GL used as a benchmark for comprehensiveness.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The cause (cumbersome processes) is genuine, but GARP gives the assurance role to internal audit, which “regularly assess\[es\] the processes used in collecting operational loss data”. Having business lines assess themselves removes independence. Option D would be correct if internal audit carried out the assessment.

questions.question: A quantitative analyst at a Swiss asset manager is drafting a training note that compares operational risk data with market and credit risk data. Which statement is least accurate?

options.text: Operational risk data are specific to each firm and mostly unrelated to the behaviour of financial markets.
The frequency and impact distributions of operational risk data can have very wide tails.
Operational risk data are abundant, which makes them simpler to model than market and credit risk data.
Operational risk data can remain hidden for a long time, and their interpretation can be complex.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Swiss asset manager analyst identifies the least accurate statement about operational risk data features.

**Concept and theory**

Operational risk data differ from financial risk data in five ways, according to GARP:

1. They are specific to each firm and mostly unrelated to the behaviour of financial markets.
2. Their frequency and impact distributions can have very wide tails (extreme events).
3. They are scarce.
4. They can remain hidden for a long time.
5. Their interpretation can be complex, depending on the causes and downstream consequences.

These features have “profound consequences for the measurement and modelling of operational risk”: firm-specific, scarce, fat-tailed data are harder, not easier, to model than market prices or credit histories.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a “least accurate” question, so three options are true and one is false. A, B and D each restate one or two of GARP’s features. Option C says the data are abundant and simpler to model, which contradicts “they are scarce” and the stated modelling consequences.

**Fragile fact.** Operational risk data are scarce, firm-specific and fat-tailed, which makes them harder to model.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.” (Schweser LO 45.a). Source: GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 4 “Risk Measurement and Assessment”, Section 4.1 “Operational Risk Events”, subsection “Data Features of Operational Risk”. Schweser (under LO 45.a) gives the same features in condensed form; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 a, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: (true statement (not the answer)). This restates GARP’s first feature in substance. It would be the answer only if it had said operational data move closely with financial markets, a polarity flip of the source.

b.reason: (true statement (not the answer)). This restates the wide-tails feature. It would be the answer if it had said the distributions are thin-tailed or close to normal.

c.reason: Option C is the least accurate statement because GARP states that operational risk data “are scarce” and that their unique nature “has profound consequences for the measurement and modeling of operational risk”.

d.reason: (true statement (not the answer)). This combines the “hidden for a long time” and “complex interpretation” features. It would be the answer if it had said operational events are always identified promptly, which the date-gap discussion (salami frauds, rogue trading) contradicts.

questions.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 b Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian credit union is preparing the risk and control self-assessment (RCSA) file for the payments unit. For the risk “fraudulent payment instruction executed”, the workshop recorded the two assessments below. Testing evidence confirms that the dual-authorisation control and the call-back verification control both operate effectively.

| Assessment | Basis of the assessment | Likelihood | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dual authorisation and call-back verification assumed absent | Likely | Major |
| 2 | Dual authorisation and call-back verification taken into account | Unlikely | Major |

Which of the following statements about these assessments is most accurate?

options.text: Assessment 1 is the residual risk, since it shows the exposure that would remain if the two controls were removed.
Assessment 1 is the inherent risk, and it also indicates the possible impact if the two key controls were to fail.
The gap between the two assessments signals that the controls are failing, so the risk must be escalated above appetite.
Only Assessment 2 belongs in the RCSA, since an RCSA evaluates risk after controls and never assesses it before them.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Credit union payments unit: two assessments of the same fraud risk, one assuming controls absent, one taking them into account.

**Concept and theory**

An RCSA asks a business unit to evaluate the likelihood and impact of its operational risks twice. The first pass ignores the existing controls and gives the **inherent risk**: the exposure the activity would carry if nothing stood in the way. The second pass takes the existing controls and their effectiveness into account and gives the **residual risk**: what is left after the controls do their work. The difference between the two is, in effect, the contribution of the controls.

Why assess both? The residual rating tells management whether the unit is within risk appetite today. The inherent rating answers a different question: what happens if the key controls fail? GARP states that line managers and risk managers should get from an RCSA a view of their residual exposure to key risks and “a view of the possible impacts if the key controls fail (indicated by the level of inherent risk)”.

|  | Inherent risk | Residual risk |
|---|---|---|
| Controls considered? | No: assessed before the impact of existing controls | Yes: after evaluating the controls in place |
| Question it answers | How bad could it be if key controls fail? | Is the current exposure within appetite? |
| Compared with appetite? | No | Yes |

GARP also distinguishes control types: preventive controls reduce the likelihood of a risk, corrective controls reduce its impact.

**Applying it to this question**

Assessment 1 is built on the assumption that dual authorisation and call-back verification are absent, so by definition it is the inherent risk (Likely, Major). Assessment 2 takes the controls into account, so it is the residual risk (Unlikely, Major). Note that only the likelihood fell: both controls stop a fraudulent instruction from being executed, which is the behaviour GARP attributes to preventive controls. The impact rating stays Major, which is exactly what the unit would face if the two controls failed. That is the inherent-risk insight option B describes.

**Fragile fact.** Inherent = before controls; residual = after controls; it is the residual rating that is compared with appetite, while the inherent rating shows the impact if key controls fail.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2 Qualitative Risk Assessment: “RCSA Process” and the paragraph on what managers can expect from an RCSA (before “Outcome of RCSAs”). Schweser (LO 45.b) gives the same inherent and residual definitions and adds that “based on the assessment of inherent risk, the RCSA may also provide some clues as to what may happen in the event of failure of the main controls”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the before and after positions. The exposure that would exist if the controls were removed is the inherent risk, not the residual risk. Residual risk is what remains after the controls are considered. The option would be correct if it read: “Assessment 2 is the residual risk, since it shows the exposure that remains after the two controls are considered.”

b.reason: GARP defines inherent risk as the exposure “before the impact of existing controls has been assessed” and says the inherent level indicates “the possible impacts if the key controls fail”. Option B states both facts about Assessment 1.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). A residual rating below the inherent rating is the normal sign that controls work, not that they fail; the stem even says testing confirms both controls operate effectively. Appetite is judged by comparing the residual rating with the appetite set for that cell of the heatmap, which the stem does not give. The option would be correct if the stem said control testing found both controls ineffective and the residual rating fell in a band above appetite.

d.reason: (sibling swap). This describes the residual risk self-assessment (RRSA), a variation in which inherent risks are not specifically assessed. A standard RCSA covers both inherent and residual risk. The option would be correct if the stem said the credit union runs an RRSA rather than an RCSA.

questions.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 b Q2
questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a mid-sized Australian wealth manager is drafting the impact scales for the firm’s first RCSA. Each of the following design statements is consistent with the standard approach to RCSA impact scales EXCEPT:

options.text: Impact types commonly cover financial, regulatory, customer and reputation, with continuity of service a frequent addition given the focus on resilience.
Customer impacts are commonly expressed as a percentage of the client base, which makes the definitions usable by units of very different sizes.
Impacts are commonly rated on a four-point or five-point scale, running from “insignificant” or “low” up to “catastrophic” or “extreme”.
Regulatory and reputational damage cannot be measured precisely, so these impact types are left out of the scale and assessed outside the RCSA.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian wealth manager: which impact-scale design statement is NOT consistent with standard practice.

**Concept and theory**

An impact scale is the severity axis of the RCSA. It turns a judgement such as “this would hurt us badly” into one of a small number of defined levels, so that different people in different units rate severity the same way. GARP describes four design features.

**Impact types.** The most common scales cover four types of impact: financial, regulatory, customer and reputation. Since regulators began focusing on resilience, a common variation adds impact on continuity of service.

**Number of levels.** Impacts are commonly rated on a four-point or five-point scale, from “insignificant” or “low” up to “catastrophic” or “extreme”.

**Relative rather than absolute definitions.** Financial impact is expressed as a percentage of revenue or operating profit, and customer impact as a percentage of the client base. A fixed currency amount can be significant for a medium-sized department but minor for a large unit; percentages make the definitions scalable to all sizes.

**Qualitative types.** Regulatory, compliance and reputational impacts are usually defined qualitatively (for example “compliance breach resulting in regulatory fines”), although metrics such as the percentage of customers affected, the number of articles and negative press may complement the definitions.

**Applying it to this question**

The question is an EXCEPT question: three statements match GARP and one does not. A matches the four types plus continuity of service. B matches the client-base definition and its scalability rationale. C matches the four-point or five-point scale and its end labels. D claims that because regulatory and reputational damage cannot be measured precisely, those types are dropped from the scale. GARP says the opposite: they are standard impact types, defined qualitatively and supplemented with metrics where possible.

**Fragile fact.** Regulatory and reputational impacts stay on the scale: they are defined qualitatively, with metrics as a complement, never excluded.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Severity Assessment: Impact Scales” and Figure 4.3 (example of impact scale definitions and ratings). Schweser (LO 45.b, “Impact Scales”) matches, but labels its example ratings “low, medium, high, very high, extreme”; GARP’s end labels are “insignificant” or “low” to “catastrophic” or “extreme”. Wording difference only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: (true statement chosen in an EXCEPT question). GARP lists exactly these four types and notes continuity of service as a common variation driven by regulatory attention on resilience. Choosing A means treating the resilience addition as an error. It would be the answer only if the stem asked which statement adds an impact type not mentioned in older scales.

b.reason: (true statement chosen in an EXCEPT question). GARP states that customer impacts are expressed as a percentage of the client base and that relative definitions make the scales adaptable to departments of various sizes. B would be the answer only if it claimed customer impact must be a fixed number of customers.

c.reason: (true statement chosen in an EXCEPT question). GARP says impacts are commonly rated on a four-point or five-point scale, from “insignificant” or “low” to “catastrophic” or “extreme”. C would be the answer only if it claimed a continuous monetary scale is the norm.

d.reason: D is the statement that is not consistent with GARP. Lack of precise measurement is handled by qualitative definitions, not by exclusion. Regulatory and reputation are two of the four most common impact types in GARP’s list.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is recording likelihood ratings for the annual RCSA. The bank’s likelihood scale uses a one-year horizon:

| Rating | Probability of occurrence within one year |
|---|---|
| Remote | below 2.5% |
| Unlikely | 2.5% to below 10% |
| Possible | 10% to below 35% |
| Likely | 35% to below 60% |
| Highly likely | 60% or above |

The head of treasury operations describes a successful ransomware attack on the treasury platform as “roughly a 1-in-12-year event”. She adds that the platform is due to be replaced in three years and that such an attack would cost about AUD 45 million. Which probability and rating should the analyst record?

options.text: 8.3%, rated Unlikely
2.1%, rated Remote
23.0%, rated Possible
64.8%, rated Highly likely

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank treasury: convert a “1-in-12-year” ransomware estimate into a one-year probability and rating.

**Concept and theory**

A likelihood scale is the second axis of the RCSA. GARP says likelihood is expressed either as a percentage probability or as a frequency of occurrence (“once in $x$ years”). The two are linked by the RCSA’s time horizon, which is one year at most (sometimes a quarter or shorter). GARP is explicit that when risk managers speak of a 1-in-10-year event, they mean an event with a 10% chance of occurring within the next year, not once in a 10-year horizon. In general, with $N$ the stated return period in years and $p$ the probability of occurrence within the one-year RCSA horizon:

$p$ = $\frac{1}{N}$

The nuance matters most for rapidly evolving risks such as cyberattacks, technology change and regulatory sanctions, where it would be wrong to think “it will happen once in the next $N$ years, so not soon”.

**Applying it to this question**

$N$ = 12 years (the “1-in-12-year” estimate)

$p$ = $\frac{1}{N}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$ = 0.0833 = 8.33%

2.5% ≤ 8.33% \< 10% ⇒ Unlikely

The platform replacement date (three years) and the AUD 45 million impact are irrelevant to the likelihood rating: the first is a distraction, and the second belongs on the impact axis. The result means the bank judges there is roughly a one-in-twelve chance of a successful attack in the coming year.

**Fragile fact.** “1 in $N$ years” means a 1$/N$ probability within the next year (1 in 12 gives 8.3%), not “once over the next $N$ years”.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Likelihood Assessment Scales” and Figure 4.4 (example of likelihood scale). Schweser (LO 45.b, “Likelihood Assessment Scales”) makes the same point with a 1-in-25-year event (4%); GARP uses a 1-in-10-year event (10%). Schweser says the RCSA has a “maximum time horizon of 1 year”; GARP adds “sometimes a quarter or even shorter”. No conflict. The bank’s scale bands in the stem are illustrative and were set for this question.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: Option A applies GARP’s rule that a 1-in-$N$ -year event has a 1$/N$ chance of occurring within the next year, and places 8.3% in the bank’s 2.5% to below 10% band, which is Unlikely.

b.reason: (time-conversion slip). It converts the annual probability to a quarterly one: 8.33%/4 = 2.08% ≈ 2.1%, which is below 2.5% and so Remote. The bank’s scale uses a one-year horizon, so no division is needed. It would be correct if the bank ran quarterly RCSAs with a scale defined on a three-month horizon (and a constant hazard approximation were acceptable).

c.reason: (horizon slip using an irrelevant input). It computes the chance of at least one attack over the three years until replacement: 1 − (1 − $\text{1/12)}^{3}$ = 1 − 0.7703 = 22.97% ≈ 23.0%, which is Possible. The RCSA horizon is one year, not the remaining life of the platform. It would be correct only if the scale were defined as “probability of occurrence before the platform is replaced”. (The formula 1 − (1 $- p$)$^{n}$ is standard probability, used here only to reproduce the distractor; it is not part of the source.)

d.reason: (horizon slip: “once in $N$ years” read as a statement about the $N$ -year period). It treats the estimate as describing the coming 12 years and computes the chance of at least one event over that period: 1 − $\text{(11/12)}^{12}$ = 1 − 0.3520 = 64.80%, which is Highly likely. GARP specifically warns that a 1-in-$N$ -year event is a one-year probability, not a statement about an $N$ -year horizon. It would be correct only if the scale measured probability of occurrence over a 12-year horizon.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Japanese trust bank is presenting the bank’s four-colour operational risk heatmap to newly hired analysts. The colours reflect the bank’s risk appetite for each combination of likelihood and impact. Which of the following descriptions of a colour band is most accurate?

options.text: Yellow: exposure is beyond risk appetite and needs an urgent mitigation action plan, while regular monitoring of controls continues.
Green: exposure is within risk appetite, so no further action is needed and the controls no longer require any monitoring.
Amber: exposure is above acceptable levels and needs an action plan to cut residual likelihood or impact, or escalation and acceptance.
Red: exposure is much beyond risk appetite, but management may simply accept it through escalation instead of an action plan.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese trust bank: which description of a heatmap colour band is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The heatmap (or “RCSA matrix”) combines the two dimensions of risk quantification, likelihood and impact. Each combination is given a colour reflecting the intensity of the risk and, in many organisations, the firm’s risk appetite for that combination. GARP describes the bands as follows.

| Colour | Position against appetite | Required response |
|---|---|---|
| Green | Within risk appetite | No further action besides regular monitoring that activities and controls work as intended |
| Yellow | Within appetite but approaching excess levels | Active monitoring; further mitigation possibly required |
| Amber (GARP’s list says orange) | Above acceptable levels | Action plan to reduce residual exposure in likelihood or impact, or escalation and risk acceptance by management |
| Red | Much beyond risk appetite | Urgent risk mitigation action plan |

The logic is a ladder: the further the exposure sits from appetite, the more forceful and urgent the response. Only the amber band offers the alternative of escalation and acceptance by management. The colours themselves depend on how the likelihood and impact axes are defined in each firm.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each option’s colour against its position and response. Option C gives amber the position “above acceptable levels” and the two permitted responses: an action plan to reduce residual likelihood or impact, or escalation and acceptance. That is GARP’s description word for word in substance. Each other option attaches a feature of one band to another or overstates it.

**Fragile fact.** Escalation and acceptance by management is an amber (orange) option only; red always requires an urgent mitigation action plan.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Combining Likelihood and Impact: The Heatmap”. Colour naming differs: GARP’s bullet list uses green, yellow, orange, red (and mentions red-amber-yellow-green as a common scheme); Schweser uses green, yellow, amber, red and says amber risk “must be lowered in terms of likelihood or impact; otherwise, it must be escalated for approval”. Same content, different label.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (sibling swap). It gives yellow the description of red (beyond appetite, urgent mitigation). Yellow is still within appetite, only approaching excess levels, with active monitoring and possibly further mitigation. The option would be correct if the label were “Red”.

b.reason: (absolute claim). Green does require no further action, but GARP keeps “regular monitoring to ensure activities and controls take place as intended”. Saying the controls no longer need any monitoring overstates it. The option would be correct if it ended “beyond regular monitoring that the controls continue to work as intended”.

c.reason: GARP: “Orange: the current risk exposure is above acceptable levels, and it must be the object of an action plan to reduce residual exposure in likelihood or impact, or escalation and risk acceptance by management.” Option C restates this.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). It extends amber’s escalation-and-acceptance option to red. Red is much beyond appetite and must be subject to an urgent mitigation action plan; acceptance is not offered. The option would be correct if the label were “Amber” and the exposure “above acceptable levels”.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK banking group is rating the financial impact of one scenario for two business units. Last year the group retired its old absolute scale (under which Major meant a loss of GBP 1 million to GBP 10 million). It now rates financial impact as a percentage of the unit’s annual operating income: Low below 0.5%; Moderate 0.5% to below 5%; Major 5% to below 20%; Extreme 20% or above. The scenario is a GBP 3.0 million loss in each unit.

| Unit | Annual revenue (GBP m) | Annual operating income (GBP m) |
|---|---|---|
| X: Private banking | 95 | 40 |
| Y: Retail banking | 1,900 | 750 |
| Group total | 4,600 | 1,200 |

Which financial impact ratings should the analyst record?

options.text: Unit X: Moderate; Unit Y: Low
Unit X: Major; Unit Y: Low
Unit X: Low; Unit Y: Low
Unit X: Major; Unit Y: Major

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK banking group: rate a GBP 3.0 million loss in two units using a scale based on percentage of unit operating income.

**Concept and theory**

GARP recommends expressing financial impacts as percentages of revenues or of operating profit rather than as monetary amounts. The reason is scalability: a fixed amount (GARP’s example is USD 100,000) can be significant for a medium-sized department but minor for a larger business unit. A relative scale makes “Major” mean the same degree of pain everywhere in the organisation. The ratio must use the base the scale specifies for the unit being assessed:

Impact (%) = $\frac{\text{Loss in the scenario}}{\text{Unit’s annual operating income}} \times$ 100

**Applying it to this question**

Unit X: $\frac{3.0}{40}$ = 0.075 = 7.5% ⇒ 5% ≤ 7.5% \< 20% ⇒ Major

Unit Y: $\frac{3.0}{750}$ = 0.004 = 0.4% ⇒ 0.4% \< 0.5% ⇒ Low

The same GBP 3.0 million loss is Major for the small private bank and Low for the large retail bank. That asymmetry is the purpose of the relative scale. Revenue, the group total and the retired absolute scale are distractor inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Use the base the scale names (here unit operating income, not revenue or the group total); the same currency loss can carry different ratings in different units, by design.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Severity Assessment: Impact Scales” and Figure 4.3. Schweser (LO 45.b, “Impact Scales”) agrees that financial impacts are usually relative (percentage of revenue or operating income) “to allow flexibility to accommodate different sizes”. The band cut-offs in the stem follow the pattern of GARP’s Figure 4.3 (below 0.5%, 0.5% to 5%, 5% to 20%) and the top band was set for this question.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (wrong input twin (revenue for operating income)). It divides by revenue: X = 3.0/95 = 3.16% (Moderate); Y = 3.0/1,900 = 0.16% (Low). GARP allows either revenues or operating profit as the base, but this bank’s scale is defined on operating income. It would be correct if the scale were defined as a percentage of annual revenue.

b.reason: Option B applies the bank’s current scale with the specified base (each unit’s own operating income), as GARP’s relative-impact principle requires.

c.reason: (scope error (group base instead of unit base)). It divides by group operating income: 3.0/1,200 = 0.25% for both, so both Low. That ignores the size of the unit being assessed, which defeats the scalability GARP describes. It would be correct if the scenario were assessed at group level with a scale defined on group operating income.

d.reason: (sibling swap (retired absolute scale for the relative scale)). It uses the old rule that a loss of GBP 1 million to GBP 10 million is Major, which rates both units the same. This is exactly the problem relative scales were introduced to fix. It would be correct if the group still used the absolute scale.

questions.question:
A risk consultant reviewing a Shanghai-based bank’s operational risk framework finds that three business units use different assessment methods, described below.

| Unit | Method |
|---|---|
| 1 | Records documentation of control testing, examples of occasions when controls prevented an incident or reduced its impact, and comparisons of loss experience with similar activities internally or at peer firms. |
| 2 | Does not specifically assess inherent risks; evaluates only the level of risk after considering the controls in place. |
| 3 | Runs workshops in which staff self-assess the unit’s main inherent risks, the key controls and how effective they are, and the remaining residual risks. |

Which classification of the three methods is most accurate?

options.text: 1: risk and control assessment (RCA); 2: residual risk self-assessment (RRSA); 3: RCSA
1: residual risk self-assessment (RRSA); 2: risk and control assessment (RCA); 3: RCSA
1: risk and control assessment (RCA); 2: RCSA; 3: residual risk self-assessment (RRSA)
1: RCSA; 2: residual risk self-assessment (RRSA); 3: risk and control assessment (RCA)

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Shanghai bank: classify three units’ assessment methods as RCSA, RCA or RRSA.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes two variations on the standard RCSA. They differ in what they assess and in how much evidence they demand.

| Method | What is assessed | Distinguishing feature |
|---|---|---|
| RCSA | Inherent risks, key controls and their effectiveness, residual risks | Self-assessment, typically in workshops (or questionnaires in larger firms) |
| RCA (risk and control assessment) | Risks and controls | The assessment must be recorded: documentation of control testing, examples where controls prevented an incident or reduced its impact, or comparison with the loss experience of similar activities internally or at peer firms |
| RRSA (residual risk self-assessment) | Residual risk only | Inherent risks are not specifically assessed; the evaluation focuses on risk after the controls in place |

The RCA moves the exercise towards evidence; the RRSA narrows it to the residual view.

**Applying it to this question**

Unit 1 records documentation of control testing, examples of controls preventing incidents or reducing impact, and peer and internal loss comparisons: the RCA. Unit 2 does not assess inherent risk and looks only at risk after controls: the RRSA. Unit 3 runs workshops covering inherent risks, key controls, their effectiveness and residual risks: the standard RCSA.

**Fragile fact.** RRSA = no specific inherent assessment; RCA = assessment must be recorded with evidence (control testing, incidents prevented, loss comparisons).

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA)”: paragraph “Variations on the RCSA include the risk and control assessment (RCA) and the residual risk self-assessment (RRSA)”. Schweser (LO 45.b) describes the same two alternatives; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: Each description maps onto GARP’s definition: RCA for evidence-recorded assessment, RRSA for residual-only assessment, RCSA for the full self-assessment. Option A gives 1: RCA; 2: RRSA; 3: RCSA.

b.reason: (sibling swap (RCA and RRSA reversed)). It labels the evidence-based method as the RRSA and the residual-only method as the RCA. The RRSA is defined by skipping inherent risk, not by recording evidence. It would be correct if Unit 1’s description read “assesses only risk after controls” and Unit 2’s read “records control-testing evidence and peer loss comparisons”.

c.reason: (scope error (residual-only treated as a full RCSA)). It calls Unit 2 an RCSA, ignoring that an RCSA covers inherent as well as residual risk, and pushes the true RCSA into the RRSA label. It would be correct if Unit 2 also assessed inherent risks and Unit 3 assessed only residual risk.

d.reason: (sibling swap (evidence-based RCA treated as the RCSA)). It reads Unit 1’s control-testing documentation as the defining feature of an RCSA. Mature RCSAs may demand control-testing evidence, but recording that evidence (plus incident examples and loss comparisons) is what defines the RCA variation. It would be correct if Unit 1 ran inherent and residual self-assessment workshops and Unit 3 recorded control-testing documentation.

questions.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 b Q7
questions.question: The head of a newly formed risk assessment unit (RAU) at a Toronto investment dealer is briefing new analysts on how the firm will run its RCSAs. Which of the following statements about the RCSA process is most accurate?

options.text: Preventive controls mainly reduce the impact of a risk, whereas corrective controls mainly reduce the likelihood that it occurs.
An RAU must sit within the second-line risk function, since a business line cannot host the unit that conducts RCSAs.
Mature firms require evidence of control testing before a control is rated effective and inherent risk treated as within appetite.
RCSAs must now be run quarterly at all institutions, since an annual cycle cannot capture risks whose volatility has increased.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Toronto investment dealer: which statement about the RCSA process is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes the mechanics of the RCSA process as follows.

- **Frequency.** RCSAs are typically conducted annually; some institutions have moved to quarterly assessments to adapt to the increased volatility of some operational risks.
- **Who runs them.** Some organisations form a dedicated risk assessment unit (RAU), responsible for conducting RCSAs. An RAU can be part of a business line, a division or an organisational process.
- **How.** RCSAs are often workshop-style discussions in which the unit self-assesses its main inherent risks, the key controls and their effectiveness. Larger organisations may use questionnaires captured in risk software.
- **Control types.** Preventive controls reduce the likelihood of a risk; corrective controls reduce its impact.
- **Evidence.** RCSAs are qualitative and largely judgement-based, “although most mature firms demand evidence of control testing before controls can be rated as effective and inherent risks decreased to acceptable levels (i.e., within the limits of risk appetite)”.

The evidence requirement exists because a self-assessment can easily overrate the controls a unit owns. Testing turns “we think the control works” into “we have shown it works”.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is GARP’s statement on control-testing evidence in mature firms. Option C restates it. Each of the other options takes a correct element of the process (control types, RAU, frequency) and corrupts it.

**Fragile fact.** Preventive reduces likelihood, corrective reduces impact; the RAU can sit in a business line.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “RCSA Process” and “Impact and Likelihood Ratings and Assessments”. Schweser (LO 45.b) says RCSAs are annual and “a quarterly basis is possible if some operational risks are very significant”, where GARP links quarterly runs to increased volatility; Schweser likens control testing to a financial statement audit, and does not say where an RAU may sit (that detail is GARP only). No conflict on the deciding fact.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the control types. Preventive controls reduce likelihood (they stop the event happening); corrective controls reduce impact (they limit the damage once it has happened). The option would be correct if the words “impact” and “likelihood” were swapped.

b.reason: (role misassignment). GARP states that an RAU can be part of a business line, a division or an organisational process; nothing restricts it to the second line. The option would be correct if the stem said the firm’s own policy places the RAU in the risk function.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP: mature firms demand evidence of control testing before a control can be rated effective and the inherent risk regarded as reduced to within appetite.

d.reason: (absolute claim). RCSAs are typically annual; only some institutions have moved to quarterly assessments. “Must” and “at all institutions” overstate the source. The option would be correct if it read “Some institutions now run RCSAs quarterly to adapt to the increased volatility of some risks”.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is reviewing a backtest that compares the cards division’s last five annual RCSAs with its incident database.

| Risk | RCSA likelihood (one year, %) | Years with an event (of 5) | RCSA impact (BRL m) | Avg actual loss per event (BRL m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Card-not-present fraud spike | 10 | 3 | 60 | 14.0 |
| Authorisation system outage | 5 | 2 | 40 | 9.0 |
| Chargeback processing errors | 20 | 4 | 8 | 2.5 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: Participants overestimated likelihood and underestimated impact, which is the reverse of what such backtests usually show.
Participants underestimated both likelihood and impact, so the division’s exposure is understated in both dimensions.
The backtest is invalid, since qualitative RCSA ratings can never be meaningfully compared with past incident experience.
Participants underestimated likelihood and overestimated impact, which is the pattern such backtests usually show.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank cards division: read a backtest of RCSA likelihood and impact against incident history.

**Concept and theory**

Backtesting an RCSA means comparing what participants predicted with what actually happened. GARP notes that mature organisations back-test risk assessments against past incident experience, and that such exercises “often show a tendency for participants to underestimate the likelihood while over-estimating the impact of an operational risk event”. In plain terms, people tend to think bad things happen less often than they do, but imagine them as more severe than they turn out to be. GARP adds that the reliability of such exercises and their cost-benefit ratio are regularly questioned, yet RCSAs remain widely used and in Europe are frequently required by regulators. To compare, express the realised frequency in the same terms as the RCSA likelihood:

Realised annual frequency = $\frac{\text{Years with at least one event}}{\text{Years observed}}$

**Applying it to this question**

Card fraud: $\frac{3}{5}$ = 60% realised vs 10% assessed; 14.0 actual vs 60 assessed (BRL m)

System outage: $\frac{2}{5}$ = 40% realised vs 5% assessed; 9.0 actual vs 40 assessed

Chargebacks: $\frac{4}{5}$ = 80% realised vs 20% assessed; 2.5 actual vs 8 assessed

In every row the realised frequency exceeds the assessed likelihood (likelihood underestimated) and the realised severity is below the assessed impact (impact overestimated). This is the typical pattern GARP describes.

**Fragile fact.** Backtests: likelihood UNDER-estimated, impact OVER-estimated.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Impact and Likelihood Ratings and Assessments” (paragraph on back-testing). Schweser (LO 45.b) states the same: backtesting “often reveal\[s\] underestimates of the probability of occurrence of an incident, but overestimates of the severity”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip (both directions)). It reads both comparisons backwards. Assessed likelihoods (5% to 20%) are below realised frequencies (40% to 80%), and assessed impacts are above actual losses. It would be correct if the division had assessed, say, 60% likelihood for events seen in one year out of five, and impacts below actual losses.

b.reason: (polarity flip (impact only)). The likelihood half is right, but impact was overestimated (assessed BRL 60 m against BRL 14 m actual, and so on), not underestimated. It would be correct if average actual losses had exceeded the RCSA impact estimates.

c.reason: (absolute claim). GARP says mature organisations do back-test RCSA results against past incident experience; the qualitative nature of ratings makes interpretation careful, not impossible. It would be correct only if the RCSA had no likelihood or impact definitions that could be mapped to frequencies and amounts.

d.reason: Option D reads both columns in the right direction and links the result to the pattern GARP says backtests usually reveal.

questions.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 b Q9
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a German Landesbank is reviewing guidance notes for RCSA participants on rating likelihood. The notes contain four statements:

I. Likelihood may be expressed either as a percentage probability or as a frequency of occurrence, such as “once in $x$ years”.

II. A risk rated as a 1-in-20-year event is expected to occur once over the coming 20 years, so the rating says nothing about the next twelve months.

III. Historical event data are a natural input to likelihood, but the past is a weaker guide when the operating environment is unstable.

IV. A risk that has never materialised at the bank should receive the lowest likelihood rating, since no internal history supports a higher one.

Which of the statements should the analyst approve?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German Landesbank: audit four guidance statements on likelihood ratings.

**Concept and theory**

GARP makes four points about likelihood scales.

- **Form.** Likelihood is expressed either as a percentage or as a frequency of occurrence (“once in $x$ years”).
- **Horizon.** A 1-in-10-year event means a 10% chance within the next year, not once in a 10-year horizon. The RCSA horizon is one year at most. This matters for rapidly evolving risks (cyberattacks, technology change, regulatory sanctions).
- **Use of history.** Historical event data are naturally used to evaluate likelihood, especially (but not only) in stable environments. The past is not always a good predictor of the future, particularly in unstable environments.
- **Unmaterialised risks.** “The likelihood can be significant, even for risks that haven’t materialized yet.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: matches the form point. True.

II: reads “1 in 20 years” as once over 20 years and denies it says anything about the next year. GARP says the opposite: it is a 5% chance within the next year. False.

III: matches the use-of-history point. True.

IV: says no internal history means the lowest rating. GARP says likelihood can be significant even for risks that have not yet materialised. False.

Approved statements: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** A 1-in-20-year event is a 5% chance next year; no loss history does not mean low likelihood.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Likelihood Assessment Scales”. Schweser (LO 45.b) covers the form, the one-year horizon and the limits of history (“the past can be a poor indicator of the future”), but does not state the point on risks that have not yet materialised; that fact is from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (includes a polarity-flipped statement (II)). Statement II turns a one-year probability into a statement about a 20-year period. The combination would be correct if II read “A 1-in-20-year event has a 5% chance of occurring within the next year” and III were dropped.

b.reason: Option B is the only combination containing both true statements and neither false one.

c.reason: (includes an absolute-claim statement (IV)). Statement IV ties likelihood strictly to internal history, which GARP rejects. The combination would be correct if IV read “A risk that has never materialised at the bank can still be rated as having a significant likelihood”.

d.reason: (selects only the false statements). Both II and IV contradict GARP. This would be correct only if the stem asked which statements the analyst should reject.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a French bank is preparing a board report on the bank’s RCSA programme, which its supervisor expects it to run. Which of the following statements should the CRO include as the most accurate?

options.text: Standardised risk descriptions and precise definitions of rating levels are needed so that “high” means broadly the same in every unit.
The main purpose of the RCSA is to produce a precise measure of each unit’s risk exposure that can feed directly into capital.
Comparability of ratings across units matters little, since each unit’s RCSA results are used only by that unit’s own managers.
Subjectivity and behavioural biases in RCSA ratings can be removed fully by widening the pool of workshop participants.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French bank board report: purpose and limitations of the RCSA programme.

**Concept and theory**

An RCSA is a qualitative, simple and accessible tool, and that design shapes both its purpose and its weaknesses.

**Purpose.** GARP: “The main purpose of RCSA exercises is not, as some mistakenly believe, to produce a precise measure of risk exposures, which is impossible when using an approximative, qualitative rating scale and self-assessments.” It is to raise business awareness of risks and controls, to evaluate residual exposures given the current controls, and to decide whether more mitigation is needed and how to prioritise action plans. More broadly, “the main purpose of risk assessment is to prioritize risk management and mitigation responses”.

**Limitations.** Subjective judgements, behavioural biases and limited data input can quickly impede the quality and reliability of the output. A further challenge is comparability across assessment units, departments and businesses, which are often assessed by different people.

**Remedy for comparability.** Because prioritisation needs comparable results, “it is necessary to use standardized descriptions of risks and precise definitions of likelihood and impacts ratings to ensure that ‘high’, ‘medium’, or ‘low’ risk means broadly the same thing for everyone. Without comparable assessments, there is no ordering of risks and hence no proper prioritization of risk management actions.”

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO needs the one statement GARP supports. A restates the comparability remedy and its reason. B states the “mistaken belief”. C denies the need for comparability. D claims the biases can be removed completely. The regulatory context in the stem (the supervisor expects the RCSA) is consistent with GARP’s note that RCSAs are frequently required by regulators in Europe, but it does not change the purpose.

**Fragile fact.** The RCSA’s purpose is awareness and prioritisation, not precise measurement; comparability comes from standardised descriptions and precise rating definitions.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Impact and Likelihood Ratings and Assessments”. Schweser (LO 45.b) agrees that RCSAs “are not meant to quantify risk exposures” and that consistency needs “standardized risk descriptions and exact definitions of probability and severity”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: Option A matches GARP’s requirement for standardised risk descriptions and precise rating definitions so that “high” means broadly the same for everyone, which allows risks to be ordered and actions prioritised.

b.reason: (sibling swap (quantitative model purpose given to the RCSA)). Producing a precise measure of exposure for capital is the role of quantitative models, which GARP covers later in the chapter. GARP calls the belief that the RCSA does this a mistake. The option would be correct if the subject were a quantitative capital model rather than the RCSA.

c.reason: (scope error). RCSA results are used to rank risks across the firm and to prioritise mitigation, so comparability across units is “essential” in GARP’s words. The option would be correct only if each unit’s results were never aggregated or compared, which contradicts the purpose of risk assessment.

d.reason: (absolute claim). GARP lists subjectivity and behavioural biases as inherent limitations that impede reliability; it offers standardisation and back-testing to manage them, not a way to eliminate them. The option would be correct if it said these biases “can be reduced” by better-defined scales and cross-checking.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US regional bank is reviewing the governance of the bank’s RCSA programme. The draft policy contains four statements:

I. The results of each RCSA are documented and submitted to business line managers for approval and sign-off.

II. Mitigating action plans are owned by the second line (risk management), so that their delivery is independent of the business.

III. Progress on action plans is tracked and reported by the second or third line, in a similar way to audit recommendations.

IV. Line managers are responsible for the RCSA output and for implementing the mitigating action plans agreed in the exercise.

Which of the statements are consistent with good practice for RCSA outcomes?

options.text: I and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US regional bank: audit four governance statements on RCSA outcomes.

**Concept and theory**

An RCSA is only useful if its conclusions turn into action, so GARP assigns clear roles across the three lines of defence.

| Step | Who, per GARP |
|---|---|
| Approval and sign-off of RCSA results | Business line managers: results are documented and submitted to them |
| Responsibility for the output | Line managers |
| Ownership and implementation of action plans | First line (business-line managers), not the second line |
| Tracking and reporting of action plans | Second line or third line, in a similar way to audit recommendations |

GARP’s reasoning: buy-in from business-line managers creates the right incentives to achieve the plans. If the risk function owned them, the business would have less reason to deliver.

**Applying it to this question**

I: documentation and sign-off by business line managers. True.

II: action plans owned by the second line for independence. False: GARP says plans must be owned by the first line rather than the second.

III: tracking and reporting by the second or third line, like audit recommendations. True.

IV: line managers responsible for the output and for implementing action plans. True.

Consistent statements: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** First line owns and implements action plans; second or third line tracks them; business line managers sign off the results.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.2, “Outcome of RCSAs” and the paragraph on action plans. Schweser (LO 45.b) says output is “sent to unit managers for approval and sign-off” and that unit managers “must perform all mitigation actions”. It does not mention first-line ownership versus second-line ownership, or second or third-line tracking; statements II and III rest on GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 b, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: (scope error (true statement III omitted)). It drops statement III, as if tracking belonged to the first line along with ownership. GARP separates ownership (first line) from tracking (second or third line). The combination would be correct if III said the business itself tracks its own action plans.

b.reason: (includes a role-misassigned statement (II)). Statement II hands ownership to the second line. GARP says it is crucial for plans to be owned by the first line. The combination would be correct if II read “owned by the first line (business-line managers)”.

c.reason: Option C includes all three statements GARP supports and excludes the role-misassigned statement II.

d.reason: (includes a role-misassigned statement (II) and omits true statements I and IV). Statement II is false, and I and IV are true statements wrongly excluded. The combination would be correct only if the stem asked for statements about the roles of the second and third lines and II were reworded to say the second line tracks plans.
