questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the tail modelling work at a UK building society. Analyst 1 takes the largest loss in each calendar quarter for each unit of measure over 15 years and fits a distribution to these maxima. Analyst 2 keeps only losses above GBP 2 million, a level chosen to be sufficiently large, and models the excess amounts above that level. Which statement best describes the two approaches?

options.text: Analyst 1 applies peaks-over-threshold and Analyst 2 applies block maxima; the generalised Pareto distribution approximates the quarterly maxima.
Analyst 1 applies block maxima and Analyst 2 applies peaks-over-threshold; the excess distribution approaches a generalised Pareto for any threshold, however low.
Analyst 1 applies block maxima and Analyst 2 applies peaks-over-threshold; for a sufficiently high threshold the excess distribution is approximated by a generalised Pareto.
Analyst 1 applies block maxima and Analyst 2 applies peaks-over-threshold; block maxima should take each quarter’s largest loss across all units of measure combined.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK building society: quarterly maxima per UoM versus excesses above GBP 2 million; identify the EVT methods.

**Concept and theory**

LDA models are not sufficient on their own to capture the extreme skewness of operational losses. Modelling the tail requires completing the dataset with higher-value losses, extreme value theory (EVT), scenario data, or all of these. EVT is a mathematical theory giving asymptotic results about the maxima of datasets and about values beyond high thresholds. GARP describes two approaches:

|  | Block maxima (Fisher-Tippett) | Peaks-over-threshold (POT) |
|---|---|---|
| What is kept | The maximum loss in each equally spaced time block, per UoM | All observations above a high threshold $u$, defined to be “sufficiently large” |
| What is modelled | Distribution of these maxima | Distribution of the excess over $u$ |
| Limiting result | (Fisher-Tippett) | For sufficiently high $u$, the excess distribution $F_{u}$($y$) converges to the generalised Pareto distribution (GPD) as $u$ grows (Balkema and de Haan; Pickands) |

**Applying it to this question**

Analyst 1 keeps one maximum per calendar quarter per UoM: block maxima. Analyst 2 keeps every loss above GBP 2 million and models the excesses: POT. The decisive extra fact is the condition attached to the GPD result: it holds for a sufficiently high threshold. Option C names both methods correctly and states the condition correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Block maxima = one maximum per time block per UoM ; POT = excesses over a high threshold, and only POT is tied to the GPD.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsection “Extreme Value Theory” (Figure 4.11). Schweser Reading 45, “Extreme Value Theory (EVT)”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: (sibling swap). The method names are swapped, and the GPD is attached to block maxima instead of POT. A would be correct if Analyst 1 used a threshold and Analyst 2 used period maxima, and if it said the GPD approximates the excesses over the threshold.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). The GPD approximation is asymptotic: it holds only as the threshold becomes sufficiently high. Dropping that condition (“any threshold, however low”) makes the statement false. B would be correct with “for a sufficiently high threshold” in place of “for any threshold, however low”.

c.reason: GARP: block maxima “examines the behavior of the maxima equally spaced in time (e.g., the maximum operational loss per period of time and per UoM)”; for POT “for sufficiently high threshold $u$, the distribution function of the excess may be approximated by the Generalized Pareto Distribution”. Option C matches both.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). Block maxima takes the maximum loss per period and per UoM, not across all UoMs combined, so Analyst 1’s per-UoM approach is the right one. D would be correct if it said “block maxima takes each quarter’s largest loss within each unit of measure”.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Chinese commercial bank is reviewing a proposal from the modelling team. To estimate CNY operational risk capital, the team plans to pool the bank’s internal losses with external losses from many institutions, across all business lines and event types, fit one extreme value theory (EVT) model to the pooled tail, and extrapolate it to the 99.9th percentile. Which concern about the proposal is most valid?

options.text: EVT describes the body of the loss distribution, where internal data are already plentiful, so it adds little to the estimate of the tail of the distribution.
EVT’s asymptotic results hold for any heterogeneous dataset once enough losses are pooled, so the only real concern is the size of the external sample.
EVT is unnecessary here, because the LDA on its own fully captures the extreme skewness of operational losses without any extra tail data.
EVT is valid only if a single mechanism generates all observed losses and can produce future losses larger than those seen, which pooling is unlikely to meet.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Board risk committee reviewing a plan to fit one EVT model to pooled internal and external losses across all lines and event types.

**Concept and theory**

Why EVT at all? The LDA fits the body of the loss distribution well, because internal data are plentiful for frequent, moderate losses, but LDA models “are not quite sufficient to account for the extreme skewness of operational risk losses”. The tail must be completed with higher-value losses (for example external data), EVT, scenario data, or all of these.

EVT’s word of caution. EVT gives asymptotic results for maxima and for values above high thresholds, but only under certain regularity conditions. For operational losses coming from different institutions, business lines and risk types, it would be valid only if:

1. a single mechanism is responsible for all observed losses, and
2. that mechanism can be assumed to produce future losses that exceed the levels currently seen in the data.

Only then could one parametric model be fitted to all observed losses and used to extrapolate. These conditions are unlikely to hold, which raises concerns about applying EVT in operational risk. Alternatives include scenarios, causal modelling, fixed multipliers, and macro determinants of operational risk.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal pools losses from many institutions, all business lines and all event types, then fits one EVT model and extrapolates. That is precisely the setting in which GARP says the single-mechanism condition is unlikely to hold. The most valid concern therefore targets the regularity condition, which is option D.

**Fragile fact.** EVT needs one loss-generating mechanism that can produce losses larger than any seen; diverse operational losses rarely satisfy this, so scenarios and other alternatives are used.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsections “Interrelationships and Correlations of Operational Risk Events” (final paragraph) and “EVT: A Word of Caution”. Schweser Reading 45, “Extreme Value Theory (EVT)”. No conflict; Schweser phrases the condition as “one main underlying cause”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: (sibling swap). EVT is a tail technique; it is internal data that serve the body of the distribution. A would be correct if it described internal loss data and the LDA body fit rather than EVT.

b.reason: (absolute claim). EVT’s results hold only under regularity conditions; pooling more heterogeneous data makes a single generating mechanism less likely, not more. B would be correct only if all pooled losses came from one mechanism, in which case sample size would indeed become the main concern.

c.reason: (polarity flip). GARP says LDA models are not sufficient to capture the extreme skewness of operational losses; the tail must be completed with large losses, EVT or scenarios. C would be correct if it said “the LDA alone cannot capture the extreme skewness, so tail data or methods are needed”.

d.reason: GARP: with operational losses “coming from different institutions, business lines, and risk types, it would only be valid if a single mechanism is responsible for all observed losses and this mechanism can be assumed to produce future losses that exceed the levels currently seen in the data”. Option D states this condition and applies it to the pooling plan.

questions.question: The head of operational risk modelling at a mid-sized German bank is assessing external loss data sources to complement the bank’s internal EUR loss history before recalibrating its capital model. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Internal data mainly inform the tail of the distribution, because a single institution’s loss history reflects the full range of possible extreme outcomes.
Public-event databases identify the institution in each event, so relevance can be judged, but they are scarcer than members-only data, which may reduce model stability.
Members-only consortium databases identify each contributing institution and give rich event context, which makes judging the relevance of each peer straightforward.
External data should be drawn from the largest pool available, whatever the peers’ geography or reporting thresholds, since more data always improves the model.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German bank choosing external loss data sources; most accurate statement on internal and external data.

**Concept and theory**

**Internal loss data** are the backbone of the LDA. Beyond management information on risks and control failures, they give the modeller many data points, especially for the body of the distribution, where frequency is high and losses moderate. They are more relevant to the organisation than external data and contain more detail and context, which helps data cleaning, audit and model review. But a single institution’s loss history is not sufficient to reflect the full range of possible events and outcomes; it must be supplemented by external data from peers or related industries. **External data sources** compared:

| Source | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Public-event databases (press events, curated) | Full information on the institution in each event, so context and relevance can be judged | Scarcer than members-only data, which may reduce model stability |
| Members-only consortia (e.g. ORX, ORIC International) | Abundant data (ORX: 103 members, 800,000 events in 2022) | Anonymous, very little information about each event |

Firms choose external sources with criteria that ensure losses come from comparable peers: geographical distribution of activities, sector or business line concentration, length of data series by event type, data classification and certification rules, number, type and size of members, and the reporting threshold of the database.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank wants external data to complement its internal history. Option B is the only statement that correctly pairs a source with its strength and weakness. The others misplace internal data in the tail, give consortium data the properties of public data, or ignore the peer-comparability criteria.

**Fragile fact.** Public data: named but scarce; consortium data: abundant but anonymous. Internal data serve the body, not the tail.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsection “Using Internal and External Loss Data for Operational Risk Modeling”. Schweser Reading 45, “Internal and External Loss Data”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: (polarity flip). Internal data mainly inform the body of the distribution (high frequency, moderate losses), and a single institution’s history does not reflect the full range of outcomes. A would be correct if it said internal data mainly inform the body and must be supplemented for the tail.

b.reason: GARP: “Databases made of public operational risk events provide full information about the institution involved in each event, allowing the modeling organization to compare contexts and judge the relevance of each event to its risk profile. However, public data is scarcer than data available in members-only databases, which might reduce the stability of the model.” Option B condenses this.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The property of public databases (identified institutions, full context) has been given to members-only databases, which are anonymous with very little information per event. C would be correct if “members-only consortium” were replaced with “public-event”.

d.reason: (absolute claim). More data do not always improve the model: external losses must come from comparable peers, judged on criteria such as geography and the reporting threshold. D would be correct only under the condition that all candidate sources were already comparable peers with consistent thresholds.

questions.question: A model validation lead at a US regional bank finds that the risk function’s incident database holds 2,140 records for the past five years, while the modellers’ calculation dataset holds 1,870 records for the same period. The 270 missing records are near misses, accidental gains and rapidly recovered losses. Which treatment of these records would be the most conservative?

options.text: Include them in both frequency and severity, using their absolute value or their potential loss as the severity amount.
Include them in the frequency count but assign them no severity, so they raise the event count without adding loss amounts.
Exclude them from the calculation dataset entirely, because none of them produced a realised net loss for the bank.
Include them in severity at their potential loss amount, but leave them out of the frequency count to avoid double counting.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US regional bank: 270 near misses, accidental gains and rapidly recovered losses missing from the calculation dataset; most conservative treatment.

**Concept and theory**

There is typically a difference between the internal incident database kept by the risk management function and the calculation dataset used by modellers. Each institution must set rules and rationales for when incidents enter the calculation dataset, particularly special cases:

- near misses (an event happened but caused no loss),
- accidental (inadvertent) gains, and
- rapidly recovered losses.

GARP describes three practices, from most to least conservative:

| Practice | Frequency | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Most conservative | Included | Included, using the absolute value or the potential loss |
| Intermediate | Included | No severity recorded |
| Least conservative | Excluded | Excluded |

Why does this matter? Including events in frequency raises $\lambda$; including a severity amount fattens the severity distribution. Both push the 99.9th percentile, and so capital, upwards.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the most conservative treatment, the one that adds the most to modelled losses. That is inclusion in both frequency and severity, using absolute value or potential loss. The record counts (2,140 vs 1,870) just confirm that 270 such cases exist; they do not change the ranking.

**Fragile fact.** Most conservative = in both frequency and severity, at absolute or potential value; “frequency only, no severity” is the middle option.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsection “Using Internal and External Loss Data for Operational Risk Modeling”. Schweser Reading 45, “Internal and External Loss Data” (Schweser only says such amounts “are omitted when computing frequency and/or severity”; GARP gives the three practices). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: GARP: “The most conservative institutions will include those events both in frequency and in severity, considering the absolute value or potential loss as the severity.” Option A states exactly this.

b.reason: (sibling swap). This is GARP’s intermediate practice (frequency only, no severity), which is less conservative than A because it adds no loss amounts. B would be correct if the stem asked which treatment counts the events without affecting the severity distribution.

c.reason: (polarity flip). This is the least conservative practice: dropping the records lowers both frequency and severity. It would be correct if the stem asked for the least conservative treatment.

d.reason: (dropped term). This keeps the severity element of the conservative treatment but drops the frequency element, so it is less conservative than A and is not one of GARP’s three practices. It would only become correct if the stem asked for a treatment that leaves the frequency count unchanged while still recording loss amounts, which the source does not describe.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is documenting how a regional bank built the calculation dataset for its operational loss model by mixing internal and external loss data. Four decisions were recorded:

I. External losses enter the dataset only above the loss level at which the bank’s own observations become scarce.

II. A USD 400 million loss at a large international peer is reduced in proportion to the ratio of the bank’s size to the peer’s size.

III. Written criteria set in advance which external events are admitted, so that data cannot be cherry picked.

IV. Losses recorded in 2011 are restated in today’s money before they enter the dataset.

Which option correctly matches each decision to the data-mixing method it represents?

options.text: I scaling; II cut-off mix; III filtering; IV scaling
I cut-off mix; II scaling; III filtering; IV filtering
I filtering; II scaling; III cut-off mix; IV scaling
I cut-off mix; II scaling; III filtering; IV scaling

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Regional bank: match four dataset-building decisions to scaling, cut-off mix and filtering.

**Concept and theory**

Mixing internal and external loss data to create the calculation dataset requires methodological choices that can significantly influence results. Operational risk managers should understand the three core choices so they can challenge modellers:

| Method | What it does | Typical example |
|---|---|---|
| Scaling | Adjusts the size of external losses to the size of the institution, or to other dimensions | A large international bank’s loss scaled down proportionally to a smaller national bank’s size; correction for inflation when data span many years or the event occurred long ago |
| Cut-off mix | Sets the severity threshold at which external data are included | Threshold at the loss level where internal data become scarcer and more points are needed to estimate a distribution |
| Filtering | Sets criteria for losses to be filtered in or out of the calculation set | Clear rules required by regulators to avoid cherry picking and manipulation of results |

Note that inflation correction is a form of scaling, not a separate method.

**Applying it to this question**

I: external data enter above the level where internal data become scarce, so cut-off mix. II: proportional reduction to the bank’s size, so scaling. III: written inclusion rules set in advance to stop cherry picking, so filtering. IV: restating old losses in today’s money is inflation correction, a type of scaling. Mapping: cut-off mix, scaling, filtering, scaling.

**Fragile fact.** Scaling changes how big a loss is (size or inflation); cut-off mix decides above what level external data come in; filtering decides which losses come in at all.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsection “Mixing Internal and External Loss Data”. Schweser Reading 45, “Internal and External Loss Data” (methods 1 to 3). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: (sibling swap). Decisions I and II are swapped: the threshold rule is labelled scaling and the size adjustment cut-off mix. A would be correct if decision I described a size adjustment and decision II a threshold for admitting external data.

b.reason: (sibling swap). Decisions I to III are right, but inflation restatement (IV) is labelled filtering. Inflation correction changes loss amounts; filtering decides whether a loss enters the dataset. B would be correct if IV read “losses older than 2011 are excluded from the dataset”.

c.reason: (sibling swap). Decisions I and III are swapped: the threshold rule is labelled filtering and the written inclusion criteria cut-off mix. C would be correct if decision I were the written inclusion rules and decision III the severity threshold.

d.reason: Option D gives that mapping. Each element ties to GARP’s definitions in “Mixing Internal and External Loss Data”, including “Other types of scaling include the correction for inflation”.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian regional bank is adding one external loss to the calibration dataset of the bank’s operational risk model. Bank policy scales external losses in proportion to gross income and corrects them for inflation using a price index. The relevant data are shown below.

| Item | Unit | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Loss at a large international peer (recorded 2016) | CAD million | 360.0 |
| Peer’s annual gross income | CAD billion | 48.0 |
| Bank’s own annual gross income | CAD billion | 6.0 |
| Peer’s CET1 capital ratio | % | 14.2 |
| Price index, 2016 | index points | 100.0 |
| Price index, 2026 | index points | 128.0 |

What scaled loss amount should the analyst enter in the calibration dataset?

options.text: CAD 35.2 million
CAD 45.0 million
CAD 57.6 million
CAD 460.8 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank scaling a CAD 360 million 2016 peer loss by gross income and inflation.

**Concept and theory**

Scaling adjusts external losses so that they are consistent with the modelling institution. GARP gives two forms: (1) size, where a loss recorded by a large international bank is scaled down to fit a smaller national bank, for instance proportionally to the size of the institution; and (2) inflation, a correction applied when data span many years or the loss event occurred many years ago. With a proportional size measure $S$ and a price index $P$ :

$L_{\text{scaled}}$ = $L_{\text{peer}} \times\frac{S_{\text{own}}}{S_{\text{peer}}} \times\frac{P_{\text{today}}}{P_{\text{loss year}}}$

where $L_{\text{peer}}$ is the external loss as recorded, $S$ is the size measure set by policy (here gross income), and $P$ is the price index level. The size ratio is below 1 when the bank is smaller than the peer; the inflation ratio is above 1 when prices have risen since the loss year.

**Applying it to this question**

Size ratio = $\frac{S_{\text{own}}}{S_{\text{peer}}}$ = $\frac{6}{48}$ = 0.125

Size-scaled loss = 360 × 0.125 = 45.0 CAD million

Inflation factor = $\frac{P_{2026}}{P_{2016}}$ = $\frac{128}{100}$ = 1.28

$L_{\text{scaled}}$ = 45.0 × 1.28 = 57.6 CAD million

Meaning: the peer’s CAD 360 million loss is equivalent to about CAD 57.6 million for a bank one eighth of the peer’s size, expressed in 2026 money. The peer’s CET1 ratio is irrelevant: scaling uses the policy size measure, not capital strength.

**Fragile fact.** A smaller bank scales external losses down by size and up for inflation; the capital ratio is a distractor.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsection “Mixing Internal and External Loss Data” (Scaling). Schweser Reading 45, “Internal and External Loss Data”. The index-ratio arithmetic is standard; GARP and Schweser name the adjustments but give no formula.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: (sign or direction error). CAD 35.2 million is 45.0/1.28 = 35.16: the inflation correction is applied backwards, deflating a 2016 loss as if prices had fallen. It would be correct if the price index had been 128 in 2016 and 100 in 2026.

b.reason: (intermediate result). CAD 45.0 million is the size-scaled loss before the inflation correction. It would be correct if the loss had been recorded in 2026, or if bank policy did not correct for inflation.

c.reason: Option C applies both forms of scaling that GARP names, size (proportional) and inflation, in the correct direction.

d.reason: (dropped term). CAD 460.8 million is 360 × 1.28: inflation is applied but the size scaling is omitted. It would be correct if the peer were the same size as the bank (gross income ratio of 1).

questions.question: A supervisor at a European banking regulator is reviewing how a Tier-1 bank reuses its former Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA) model, built on internal loss data (ILD), external loss data (ELD), scenario data (SD), and business environment and internal control factors (BEICF), for its Pillar 2 capital assessment. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: ILD and ELD bring past observations into the model, while SD and BEICF bring prospective information on what could happen given the bank’s exposures and controls.
ILD and SD bring past observations into the model, while ELD and BEICF bring prospective information on what could happen given the bank’s exposures and controls.
Under the AMA, banks held capital to cover operational losses up to a 99% confidence level over a ten-day horizon, as validated by their home regulator.
Since the standardised approach took effect on 1 January 2023, banks must still model operational risk capital for Pillar 1, so AMA models cannot be reused.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Supervisor reviewing reuse of a former AMA model (ILD, ELD, SD, BEICF) for Pillar 2.

**Concept and theory**

**The old regime (AMA).** Under the Advanced Measurement Approaches for banks (and Internal Modeling Approaches for insurers), firms could assess their own capital needs, provided the regulator of each country of incorporation validated the model. Banks assessed the capital sufficient to cover all possible operational losses up to a 99.9% confidence level at a one-year horizon. The aim was regulatory capital that reflects the firm’s risk profile as closely as possible. A qualifying model needed four inputs:

| Input | Orientation | Content |
|---|---|---|
| ILD (internal loss data) | Past observations | The firm’s own loss history |
| ELD (external loss data) | Past observations | Peers’ losses |
| SD (scenario data) | Prospective | What could happen, given exposures and controls |
| BEICF | Prospective | Business environment and internal control factors |

AMA approval took on average three years and needed internal and external validation and about 30 qualitative and quantitative criteria.

**The new regime.** With the standardised approach effective 1 January 2023, there are no formal requirements to model operational risk capital. But large firms have over 20 years of modelling experience; the effort is moving to Pillar 2 and ICAAP, stress testing and operational resilience. The logic of the approach has not changed, and many AMA banks (as in GARP’s Box 4.4, a Tier-1 European bank with a hybrid LDA plus scenario model whose body and tail are calibrated with two different distributions) now use the model for Pillar 2 capital assessment.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem is about reusing an AMA model built on the four inputs. Option A correctly sorts the inputs into backward-looking (ILD, ELD) and prospective (SD, BEICF). The other options swap an input, change the confidence level and horizon, or reverse the post-2023 regime.

**Fragile fact.** ILD and ELD look back; SD and BEICF look forward; AMA capital was 99.9% over one year.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsections “Capital Modeling for Operational Risk” and “Operational Risk Regulatory Capital”, Box 4.4. Schweser Reading 45, “Capital Modeling” covers the 99.9% one-year standard and the move to Pillar 2 but does not list the four AMA inputs; that content is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: GARP: “ILD and ELD represent the input from past observations, whereas SD and BEICF insert prospective information on what could happen, given the risk exposure, and the control system of an organization.” Option A restates this.

b.reason: (sibling swap). ELD and SD have traded places. External loss data are past observations (other firms’ history); scenario data are prospective. B would be correct if “SD” and “ELD” were swapped back.

c.reason: (wrong percentile). The AMA standard was 99.9% at a one-year horizon; 99% over ten days is the market risk VaR convention. C would be correct if it read “99.9% confidence level over a one-year horizon”.

d.reason: (polarity flip). Since 1 January 2023 there are no formal requirements to model operational risk capital, and AMA models are being reused for Pillar 2, ICAAP and stress testing. D would be correct only under the pre-2023 AMA regime for a bank that had chosen the AMA.

questions.question: The newly appointed chief risk officer of a mid-sized UK bank is reviewing the draft of the bank’s operational risk internal capital adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) report before board sign-off. Which of the following statements in the draft is NOT correct?

options.text: The ICAAP sits in Pillar 2 and must cover all financial and non-financial risks to which the firm is exposed, not only operational risk.
Scenario identification, mitigation and assessment fall under Pillar 2a, while capital assessment, planning and stress testing fall under Pillar 2b.
The report to the regulator should justify how each scenario was selected and quantified, and explain why other scenarios were discarded.
Economic capital is the minimum capital the regulator sets for the firm, so its purpose differs from the ICAAP’s self-assessment of capital.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK CRO reviewing a draft operational risk ICAAP; identify the statement that is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

**ICAAP.** The internal capital adequacy assessment process is part of Pillar 2. It requires regulated firms to self-evaluate their level of capital in light of their specific risk profile. Pillar 2 capital must cover all financial and non-financial risks to which the firm is exposed; ICAAP applies to all risks, not only operational risk. It is regulator-mandated, used by firms of all sizes, and considers the business model and medium-term plan, the risk exposures given the nature and prospective evolution of the business, and the controls in place. It is present in the UK, continental Europe, Canada and Asia; the US focuses more on CCAR stress testing.

**Operational risk content.** Completing an operational risk ICAAP requires selecting relevant scenarios and quantifying them, considering business exposures, evidence of past events at the firm and at peers, and the control environment. In the UK regulator’s outline (Box 4.5), scenario identification, mitigation, assessment and stressed assessment sit under Pillar 2a; capital assessment, planning and ICAAP stress testing under Pillar 2b. The report sent to the regulator must give the rationale for selecting and quantifying scenarios, explain each scenario or capital component, and give the rationale for discarding scenarios that were not assessed.

**Economic capital.** “The amount of capital that a firm considers, internally, as necessary to cover its possible losses to either guarantee its survival or, often in practice, to maintain its current external credit rating.” The ICAAP can inform economic capital, and “to a large extent, economic capital and ICAAP have the same purpose”.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C match the ICAAP description, the Box 4.5 outline and the reporting requirement. D misattributes economic capital to the regulator and claims its purpose differs from the ICAAP. Since the question asks which statement is NOT correct, D is the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Economic capital is the firm’s own view of capital needed for survival or to keep its rating; Pillar 2a is scenarios, Pillar 2b is capital and stress testing.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, subsection “Operational Risk Regulatory Capital” (ICAAP discussion) and Box 4.5 “Operational ICAAP: Outline”. Schweser Reading 45, “Capital Modeling”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: (true statement (qualifier misread)). GARP: “Pillar 2 capital must cover all financial and non-financial risks to which the firm is exposed. ICAAP applies to all risks, not only operational risk.” Choosing A treats a correct statement as the false one. A would be the answer if it said the ICAAP covers operational risk only.

b.reason: (true statement (qualifier misread)). This matches the Box 4.5 split of Pillar 2a (scenarios: identification, mitigation, assessment) and Pillar 2b (capital assessment, planning, stress testing). B would be the answer if the two labels were reversed.

c.reason: (true statement (qualifier misread)). GARP requires a rationale for the selection and quantification of scenarios and for discarding scenarios that were not assessed. C would be the answer if it said discarded scenarios need not be mentioned.

d.reason: Economic capital is set internally by the firm, not by the regulator, and GARP says economic capital and the ICAAP largely share the same purpose. Option D contradicts both points.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a small Australian bank is testing whether its operational risk capital is sufficient using the simple multi-criteria scenario aggregation method used by many smaller firms. The bank holds AUD 65 million against operational risk and has annual gross income of AUD 900 million. Its scenario estimates and the clusters it judges could occur together are shown below. Treat the loss of a cluster as the sum of its scenario estimates.

| Scenario | Loss estimate (AUD m) | Clusters it belongs to |
|---|---|---|
| Cyberattack | 42 | 1, 2 |
| Loss of data centre | 30 | 2 |
| Pandemic | 18 | 1 |
| Key employee departure | 9 | 1, 3 |
| Internal fraud | 25 | 3 |
| Mis-selling of a product | 35 | none |

Which of the following correctly states the amount that capital must exceed and the conclusion?

options.text: Capital must exceed AUD 42 million, so the current AUD 65 million is sufficient.
Capital must exceed AUD 72 million, so the current AUD 65 million is not sufficient.
Capital must exceed AUD 114 million, so the current AUD 65 million is not sufficient.
Capital must exceed AUD 159 million, so the current AUD 65 million is not sufficient.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Small Australian bank applying the simple multi-criteria scenario aggregation rule to six scenarios and three clusters.

**Concept and theory**

To reach a capital estimate from scenarios (scenario aggregation), GARP describes two levels of sophistication:

- **Smaller organisations: a simple multi-criteria method.** Reserve an amount of capital that (1) exceeds at least the loss estimate of the largest scenario, and (2) exceeds the loss estimate of two to four scenarios that could happen as a cluster (examples: pandemic, key employee departure and cyberattack; cyberattack and loss of data centre; loss of key staff and internal fraud). If capital exceeds the amount of all these clusters, it is deemed sufficient and the estimation robust.
- **Larger Tier-1 banks and insurers:** more sophisticated correlation techniques, such as variance-covariance matrices or copulas, to estimate scenario aggregates.

The two criteria are tests that must both be passed, so the binding hurdle is the larger of the two amounts, not their sum:

$$K > \max\left(\max_{i} S_{i},\ \max_{j} C_{j}\right), \qquad C_{j} = \sum_{i \in \text{cluster } j} S_{i}$$

where $S_{i}$ is scenario $i$’s loss estimate, $C_{j}$ is cluster $j$’s combined loss and $K$ is the capital held.

**Applying it to this question**

Largest single scenario = max(42, 30, 18, 9, 25, 35) = 42

$C_{1}$ = 18 + 9 + 42 = 69 (pandemic, key employee, cyberattack)

$C_{2}$ = 42 + 30 = 72 (cyberattack, data centre)

$C_{3}$ = 9 + 25 = 34 (key employee, internal fraud)

Hurdle = max(42, 69, 72, 34) = 72 AUD million

Test = 65 \< 72 ⇒ not sufficient

Meaning: the bank needs more than AUD 72 million of operational risk capital; it is about AUD 7 million short. Gross income (AUD 900 million) plays no part in this method, and mis-selling (35) matters only for the single-scenario test, which it does not drive.

**Fragile fact.** Both tests must be passed, so the hurdle is the maximum of the largest scenario and the largest cluster, not their sum; copulas and variance-covariance matrices are for larger firms.

**Reference**

LO 45.f: “Describe approaches used to determine the level of operational risk capital for economic capital purposes, including their application and limitations.” GARP Chapter 4, section 4.4, ICAAP discussion following Box 4.5 (scenario aggregation). Schweser Reading 45, “Capital Modeling” (smaller banks provision capital greater than the largest scenario and greater than two to four clustered scenarios). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 f, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: (intermediate result). AUD 42 million applies only the first criterion (largest single scenario) and ignores the cluster test. It would be correct if no scenarios were judged able to occur together.

b.reason: Option B identifies the binding hurdle (the largest cluster, AUD 72 million, which exceeds the largest single scenario) and draws the right conclusion. This is GARP’s rule: capital must exceed the largest scenario and the two-to-four-scenario clusters.

c.reason: (calculation slip (criteria added)). AUD 114 million is 42 + 72: the two criteria are added instead of being applied as separate hurdles. It would be correct only if the rule required capital to cover the largest scenario on top of the largest cluster, which GARP does not say.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). AUD 159 million is the sum of all six scenarios, 42 + 30 + 18 + 9 + 25 + 35, which assumes every scenario happens together (perfect dependence). The method only asks about clusters of two to four scenarios judged able to occur together. D would be correct if a single cluster contained all six scenarios.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of an Australian retail bank is briefing newly appointed board members on how the bank’s operational resilience program relates to its existing operational risk management (ORM) framework, which already includes RCSAs, KRIs and a loss database. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Operational resilience is a separate discipline owned by business continuity, so ORM activities such as RCSAs and KRIs contribute to it only after a disruption has occurred.
Operational resilience is an input to the ORM framework, so the resilience self-assessment must be completed before risk identification and assessment can begin.
Operational resilience is an outcome that benefits from effective ORM, so identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring all work together to minimize disruptions.
Operational resilience is guaranteed by an effective ORM framework, so a bank with effective controls will maintain every service under every possible disruption.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank CRO explaining to the board how resilience relates to the ORM framework.

**Concept and theory**

Operational resilience is the ability of a firm to keep delivering its critical services through a severe disruption, and to recover them quickly. The GARP reading motivates it with scenarios of operational disasters (systems failures, cyberattacks, physical damage, compliance breaches) that could wipe out a large part of revenues, damage long-term earning capacity and reputation, and harm clients. Regulation asks firms to consider such plausible disasters even if they have never happened to them or to their peers, and to assess their own resilience if they did.

The key conceptual point is the direction of the relationship. Regulators, and the GARP reading, treat resilience as an outcome of sound operational risk management, not as a separate discipline or a prerequisite. The BIS (2021b) wording quoted in the reading is that operational resilience is an outcome that benefits from the effective management of operational risk: risk identification and assessment, risk mitigation (including controls) and the monitoring of risks and control effectiveness work together to minimize operational disruptions and their effects. The reading draws the consequence that every participant in the ORM framework also participates in improving the firm’s resilience.

| ORM activity | Contribution to resilience |
|---|---|
| Identification and assessment | reveals which services and resources are exposed |
| Mitigation and controls | reduces the chance and impact of disruption |
| Monitoring (KRIs, control effectiveness) | detects weaknesses before they become disruptions |

**Applying it to this question**

The bank already runs RCSAs, KRIs and a loss database. The question is how these relate to resilience. Per BIS, they feed resilience continuously: resilience is the outcome they produce. Any option that makes resilience a separate silo, an upstream input, or a guarantee contradicts that framing.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: resilience is the outcome of ORM (BIS), not an input to it; actor: every ORM participant contributes.

**Reference**

LO 45.g: “Describe and explain the steps to ensure a strong level of operational resilience, and to test the operational resilience of important business services.” GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5 “Quantification of Operational Resilience”, opening paragraphs (BIS 2021b quotation). Schweser Reading 45, “Operational Resilience”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: (role misassignment and scope error). It hands ownership to business continuity and confines ORM’s contribution to the post-event period. The reading says every ORM participant contributes to resilience, and identification, assessment and monitoring act before any disruption. It would be correct only for a stem asking about the recovery phase of BCM after an incident, not about resilience as a whole.

b.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the direction: resilience is presented as an input that must precede risk identification, whereas BIS calls it an outcome of ORM. The self-assessment is step 7 of the resilience steps, i.e. at the end. It would be correct only if the stem asked which ORM activities feed the resilience self-assessment (the reverse statement).

c.reason: Option C restates the BIS description in the reading: resilience is an outcome that benefits from effective ORM, with identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring working together to minimize disruptions and their effects (GARP 4.5, opening paragraphs; Schweser: “operational resilience should be the result of a strong ORM framework”).

d.reason: (absolute claim). “Guaranteed”, “every service” and “every possible disruption” overstate the outcome. BCBS defines resilience as maintaining critical services in all but the most extreme conditions, and intolerable impacts remain possible, though they must be truly exceptional. It would be correct only if “every possible disruption” were replaced by “all but the most extreme conditions” and “guaranteed” by “supported”.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing a memo, written by the business continuity team, that compares the bank’s traditional business continuity management (BCM) with its new operational resilience framework. The memo contains the following statements:

I. BCM is articulated by business process, whereas the resilience framework is articulated around important business services.

II. The impact tolerance set for an important business service plays a role equivalent to the recovery time objective used in BCM.

III. Because the resilience framework targets services rather than processes, it relies on risk management and mitigation methods that differ fundamentally from those of BCM.

IV. BCM aims to maintain important business services in all but the most extreme conditions, while resilience aims to recover each process within its recovery time objective.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese trust bank auditor reviewing a memo comparing BCM and the resilience framework.

**Concept and theory**

Business continuity management (BCM) is the older discipline. It works process by process: for each business process it sets a recovery time objective (RTO), the time within which the process must be restored after a disruption. The resilience framework moves the unit of analysis up to the important business service (IBS), such as a service to customers, and sets for each IBS an impact tolerance, which the reading describes as equivalent to an RTO. Resilience means maintaining critical business services in all but the most extreme conditions (BCBS 2021).

|  | BCM Operational resilience |
|---|---|
| Unit of analysis | Business process Important business service |
| Time limit | Recovery time objective (RTO) Impact tolerance (equivalent to RTO) |
| Goal | Continuity and recovery of each pro- Continuity and recovery of IBS in all cess but the most extreme conditions |
| Methods | Largely the same risk management and mitigation methods |

The reading stresses that although the two are articulated differently, both follow largely the same risk management and mitigation methods; impact tolerances themselves build on BCM data through the BIA.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: matches “BCM is articulated by business process, while resilience is articulated around IBS”. Accurate. Statement II: the reading says impact tolerances are “equivalent to RTOs”. Accurate. Statement III: the reading says both follow largely the same methods. Inaccurate. Statement IV: swaps the goals of the two frameworks. Inaccurate. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Impact tolerance is to an IBS what an RTO is to a process; the methods are largely the same, the unit of analysis differs.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, “Important Business Services and Impact Tolerance”. Schweser Reading 45 “Operational Resilience” (resilience vs BCM). Schweser does not mention the RTO equivalence or the shared methods; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: Option A (I and II only) is the only combination that contains both accurate statements and neither inaccurate one.

b.reason: (sibling swap (accepts statement III)). It includes III, which turns a difference in articulation (process vs service) into a difference in method. GARP says both frameworks follow largely the same risk management and mitigation methods. B would be correct only if III said the frameworks “use largely the same methods but are articulated differently”.

c.reason: (sibling swap (accepts statement IV) and omits I). Statement IV assigns resilience’s goal (IBS in all but the most extreme conditions) to BCM and BCM’s process RTO to resilience. C would be correct only if IV were written the right way round and I were false.

d.reason: (sibling swap (accepts statement III)). It adds III to the two true statements. D would be correct only if the reading said the frameworks used fundamentally different methods.

questions.question: A risk consultant is helping a UK wealth manager, which outsources its client reporting and payments processing to third parties, to draw up its first list of important business services. She wants the screening criterion to match the definition of the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) cited in the GARP reading. Which criterion should she use?

options.text: A service the firm provides directly, excluding services delivered on its behalf by third parties, which, if disrupted, could cause intolerable harm to clients or risk UK financial stability.
A service provided by the firm or on its behalf which, if disrupted, could cause intolerable harm to clients and, in addition, pose a risk to the soundness of the UK financial system.
A service provided by the firm or on its behalf which, if disrupted, could cause the largest loss in the firm’s operational risk capital model at the 99.9th percentile.
A service provided by the firm or on its behalf which, if disrupted, could cause intolerable harm to any one or more clients or pose a risk to UK financial stability or market order.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant choosing the FCA screening criterion for important business services at a UK wealth manager.

**Concept and theory**

The whole resilience framework is built on the list of IBS, so the definition used to screen services matters. GARP (Box 4.7) quotes the UK FCA: an important business service is a service provided by a firm, or by another person on behalf of the firm, which, if disrupted, could (1) cause intolerable levels of harm to any one or more of the firm’s clients; or (2) pose a risk to the soundness, stability or resilience of the UK financial system or the orderly operation of the financial markets.

Three features carry the definition: outsourced services are included; harm to a single client can suffice; and the two harm tests are alternatives (“or”), not cumulative. The test is about harm from disruption, not about the size of modeled capital losses.

**Applying it to this question**

The wealth manager outsources reporting and payments. Those services are delivered “on its behalf” and are still candidates. A service that could cause intolerable harm to clients qualifies even if it poses no systemic risk. Only option D keeps all three features.

**Fragile fact.** “Or”, not “and”; “any one or more clients”; and “on behalf of the firm” brings outsourced services in.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, Box 4.7 “Impact Tolerances for Important Business Services” (FCA Handbook). Schweser does not reproduce the FCA definition; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: (scope error). It drops “or by another person on behalf of the firm”. For a firm that outsources payments, this would wrongly remove a client-facing service from the list. A would be correct only if the definition covered in-house services alone.

b.reason: (condition error). It turns the disjunction into a conjunction (“and, in addition”), so a service harming clients but posing no systemic risk would fail. B would be correct for the stem: “which services meet both FCA harm tests?”

c.reason: (sibling swap). It substitutes a capital-modeling criterion (99.9th percentile loss, from LO 45.f) for the harm-based criterion. It would be correct only for a question about which scenario drives operational risk capital.

d.reason: D reproduces the FCA definition in Box 4.7: by the firm or on its behalf; intolerable harm to any one or more clients, or risk to UK financial stability or orderly markets.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is drafting the policy wording that defines an impact tolerance for the bank’s resilience framework. Which wording is most consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: The maximum tolerable level of disruption to an important business service, measured solely by the expected financial loss in SGD rather than by any length of time.
The maximum tolerable level of disruption to an important business service, measured by a length of time plus other relevant metrics, beyond which intolerable harm could arise.
The maximum tolerable level of disruption to each internal business process, measured by a length of time plus other relevant metrics, beyond which intolerable harm could arise.
The level of disruption to an important business service that the bank commits never to exceed, since resilience must cover even the most extreme conditions.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank analyst drafting the policy definition of an impact tolerance.

**Concept and theory**

Once IBS are identified, each receives an impact tolerance. The FCA definition in GARP Box 4.7: the maximum tolerable level of disruption to an important business service, as measured by a length of time in addition to any other relevant metrics, reflecting the point at which any further disruption could cause intolerable harm to clients or pose a risk to the soundness, stability or resilience of the UK financial system or orderly markets.

Three elements: (1) the object is the IBS, not a process (processes are BCM’s unit); (2) the primary measure is time, which is why the reading calls tolerances equivalent to RTOs, though other metrics may be added; (3) the threshold is the point of intolerable harm. Impacts beyond tolerance (“intolerable impacts”) must be truly exceptional: resilience is “the maintenance of critical business services in all but most extreme conditions” (BCBS 2021), though “most extreme conditions” is not formally defined. So a tolerance is not a promise that can never be breached.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each wording against the three elements and the “all but most extreme” qualifier. Only B has the right object (IBS), the right measure (time plus other metrics) and the right threshold (intolerable harm).

**Fragile fact.** Measured by time (plus other metrics), set per IBS; resilience covers all but the most extreme conditions.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, “Important Business Services and Impact Tolerance” and Box 4.7. Note: Schweser compresses this to “operational resilience only considers important business services in non-extreme situations”; GARP’s wording is “all but most extreme conditions”, with intolerable impacts truly exceptional and the notion not formally defined. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: (sibling swap of the metric). It replaces the time measure with expected financial loss alone. The FCA definition is anchored in a length of time; other metrics are additions, not substitutes. A would be correct only if the stem asked about a BIA’s financial impact estimate.

b.reason: B paraphrases the FCA definition reproduced in GARP Box 4.7.

c.reason: (scope error). Right measure, wrong object: tolerances are set per important business service, not per internal process (the BCM approach, where the equivalent concept is the RTO). C would be correct as a description of a process RTO in BCM.

d.reason: (absolute claim). Resilience covers critical services in all but the most extreme conditions; intolerable impacts beyond tolerance must be truly exceptional, not impossible. D would be correct only if “even the most extreme conditions” were replaced by “all but the most extreme conditions” and “commits never to exceed” by “aims to stay within”.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the important business service (IBS) lists prepared by three clients: an asset management firm, a large retail bank, and the corporate banking division of a universal bank. Which of the following statements in her review is NOT accurate?

options.text: For the asset management firm, order booking and trading is a natural candidate for an important business service.
For the corporate banking division, short-term funding and FX transaction execution are natural candidates for important business services.
Because every IBS must be fully covered by contingency planning, the large retail bank should give each service on its long list equal resilience resources.
For the large retail bank, retail cash and payments transactions are natural candidates for important business services.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant reviewing IBS lists at an asset manager, a retail bank and a corporate banking division.

**Concept and theory**

Step 1 of the resilience process is to identify important business services. GARP stresses that what counts as an IBS depends on the nature of the institution, its business provisions and its customers, and gives examples:

| Institution type | Example IBS in GARP |
|---|---|
| Banks (retail) | Retail cash and payments transactions |
| Asset management firms | Order booking and trading |
| Corporate banking | Short-term funding and FX transaction executions |
| General | Financial market transactions |

GARP adds that a firm, especially a large bank, can have many candidate IBS, but it must accept that not all of them are equally important and prioritize risk management resources and contingency planning accordingly. Schweser: larger banks may need to prioritize and narrow down the list.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D match GARP’s examples for each institution type. C rejects prioritization by requiring equal resources for every service on a long list.

**Fragile fact.** IBS are institution-specific, and the list must be prioritized: not every service is important.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5 text after Box 4.7 (what IBS is depends on the institution; prioritization). Schweser Reading 45 “Operational Resilience”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: (accurate statement (qualifier trap)). Order booking and trading is GARP’s example for asset managers. Choosing it misreads “NOT accurate”. It would be the answer only if the stem asked for an accurate statement.

b.reason: (accurate statement (qualifier trap)). Short-term funding and FX execution are GARP’s examples for corporate banking.

c.reason: C is the inaccurate statement, so it is the answer: GARP says not all services are important and resources and contingency planning must be prioritized.

d.reason: (accurate statement (qualifier trap)). Retail cash and payments are GARP’s examples for banks. D would be inaccurate only if it claimed these were IBS for every institution regardless of business model.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Brazilian bank is reviewing a draft operational resilience program prepared by a junior analyst. The draft lists the program’s steps in the following order:

| Draft step | Activity |
|---|---|
| 1 | Identify important business services |
| 2 | Map important business services end to end and identify the resources required |
| 3 | Set impact tolerances for important business services |
| 4 | Design severe but plausible scenarios to test the delivery of the services |
| 5 | Where an impact tolerance is exceeded, examine lessons learned and take action |
| 6 | Complete the annual self-assessment document for board sign-off |
| 7 | Ensure internal and external communication plans are in place |

Which change brings the draft into line with the seven-step sequence described in the reading?

options.text: Move impact tolerances ahead of mapping, and move communication plans ahead of the annual self-assessment.
Move impact tolerances ahead of mapping, and move scenario design after the lessons-learned step.
Move mapping ahead of service identification, and move communication plans ahead of the annual self-assessment.
Move impact tolerances ahead of mapping, and leave the self-assessment and communication plans as drafted.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank treasurer repairing the order of a draft seven-step resilience program.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s figure “Key steps for operational resilience” (Chapelle Consulting, 2021) sets out seven steps, which Schweser lists in the same order:

| Step | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Identify important business services |
| 2 | Set impact tolerances for important business services |
| 3 | Map important business services end to end and identify the resources required to deliver them |
| 4 | Design severe but plausible scenarios to test and identify vulnerabilities in the delivery of the IBS |
| 5 | Where an impact tolerance is exceeded, examine lessons learned from stress tests and take actions |
| 6 | Ensure internal and external communication plans are in place to be followed when an event occurs |
| 7 | Annual self-assessment document to be signed off by the Board |

The logic: you must know what matters (1) and how much disruption is tolerable (2) before mapping what delivers it (3); testing (4) needs a mapped service and a tolerance to test against; remediation (5) needs test results; communication readiness (6) is in place before the annual board-approved review closes the cycle (7).

**Applying it to this question**

Compare the draft with the reference sequence:

- Draft steps 2 and 3 are swapped: tolerances must come before mapping.
- Draft steps 6 and 7 are swapped: communication plans come before the annual self-assessment.
- Draft steps 1, 4 and 5 are already correct.

Both swaps must be undone, and nothing else moved.

**Fragile fact.** Tolerances (step 2) come before mapping (step 3); communication (6) before the board-signed annual self-assessment (7).

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, figure “Key steps for operational resilience”. Schweser Reading 45 “Operational Resilience”, Steps 1 to 7. No conflict on order. Note: Schweser words step 4 as “harsh, but realistic” scenarios; GARP says “severe but plausible”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: A fixes exactly the two inversions, which yields the reference sequence 1 to 7.

b.reason: (sequence (polarity) error on steps 4 and 5). It fixes the first inversion but moves scenario design after lessons learned. Lessons are drawn from stress test results, so scenarios must come first; and it leaves steps 6 and 7 inverted. B would be correct only if the draft had listed lessons learned before scenario design.

c.reason: (sequence error on steps 1 and 3). It fixes steps 6 and 7 but puts mapping before service identification; one cannot map IBS end to end before they are identified, and steps 2 and 3 stay inverted. C would be correct only if the draft had listed mapping before tolerances and the question asked only about the final two steps.

d.reason: (dropped correction (scope error)). It fixes only one of the two inversions. D would be correct if the draft had listed communication plans at step 6 and the self-assessment at step 7.

questions.question:
A junior analyst at a Canadian bank has drafted four statements for the chief compliance officer to include in the bank’s operational resilience testing policy:

I. Scenarios used to test important business services should be severe but plausible, and designed to identify vulnerabilities in the delivery of each service.

II. Scenarios should be limited to disruptions that the bank or its peers have actually experienced, so that the test results can be validated against history.

III. Where a scenario shows that an impact tolerance would be exceeded, the bank should examine the lessons learned from the test and take action.

IV. The annual resilience self-assessment document is signed off by the chief risk officer, with the board of directors informed afterwards.

Which statements should the chief compliance officer approve?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst drafting statements on resilience testing for the CCO.

**Concept and theory**

Testing the resilience of IBS is the heart of steps 4, 5 and 7:

- **Step 4: scenario design.** Scenarios must be severe but plausible and designed to identify vulnerabilities in the delivery of each IBS. GARP stresses that regulation requires firms to consider plausible disasters “which may never have happened to them before, or to their peers”. Restricting scenarios to history defeats the purpose.
- **Step 5: act on breaches.** Where an impact tolerance is exceeded, examine the lessons learned from the stress tests and take actions.
- **Step 7: governance.** An annual self-assessment document is signed off by the Board (Schweser: approved by the board of directors).

**Applying it to this question**

I: matches step 4. Accurate. II: contradicts GARP on unprecedented plausible disasters. Inaccurate. III: matches step 5. Accurate. IV: wrong actor; the Board signs off, not the CRO. Inaccurate. So approve I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the Board signs off the annual self-assessment; scenarios are severe but plausible, including events never experienced.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, opening paragraphs and figure “Key steps for operational resilience”. Schweser Reading 45, Steps 4, 5 and 7 (“harsh, but realistic”; “approved by the board of directors”). No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: (scope error (accepts II)). II restricts scenarios to experienced events; GARP explicitly extends them to plausible disasters never experienced by the firm or its peers. A would be correct only if II said scenarios should include, not be limited to, past events.

b.reason: (role misassignment (accepts IV) and scope error (accepts II)). It approves the two inaccurate statements. B would be correct only if the stem asked which statements the CCO should reject.

c.reason: (role misassignment (accepts IV)). The annual self-assessment is signed off by the Board. C would be correct only if IV read “signed off by the Board”.

d.reason: D (I and III only) contains both accurate statements and neither inaccurate one.

questions.question:
A resilience analyst at a German bank has run one severe but plausible scenario (a regional data center outage) against four important business services. The results are below.

| Important business service | Impact tolerance | Disruption in test (hours) | Annual revenue (EUR m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail payments | 24 hours | 30 | 410 |
| Card authorization | 4 hours | 3 | 265 |
| Securities settlement | 2 days | 40 | 120 |
| Mortgage origination | 3 days | 80 | 95 |

Which conclusion and next step are most appropriate?

options.text: Retail payments and mortgage origination exceed tolerance; the bank should raise these two tolerances to 30 hours and 80 hours so that future tests are passed.
Retail payments and mortgage origination exceed tolerance; the bank should examine the lessons learned from the test and take action to stay within tolerance.
Retail payments, securities settlement and mortgage origination exceed tolerance; the bank should examine the lessons learned and take action.
Retail payments and mortgage origination exceed tolerance; the bank should wait for an actual incident before acting, since lessons learned come from real events.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German bank analyst interpreting a data center outage test against four impact tolerances.

**Concept and theory**

Testing an IBS means running a severe but plausible scenario (step 4) and comparing the resulting disruption with the impact tolerance set in step 2. Because tolerances are measured primarily in time, the comparison is a duration check. Where the tolerance is exceeded, step 5 applies: examine the lessons learned from the stress test and take action, for instance to remove vulnerabilities on the mapped path. The tolerance reflects the point of intolerable harm to clients or markets, so it is not adjusted to fit the test result.

**Applying it to this question**

Convert every tolerance into hours, then compare:

Retail payments: 30 > 24 ⇒ exceeded by 6 hours

Card authorization: 3 \< 4 ⇒ within tolerance

Securities settlement: 2 days = 48 hours; 40 \< 48 ⇒ within tolerance

Mortgage origination: 3 days = 72 hours; 80 > 72 ⇒ exceeded by 8 hours

Annual revenue is irrelevant to whether a tolerance is breached. Two services breach, so step 5 is triggered for both.

**Fragile fact.** Convert days to clock hours before comparing; a breach triggers remediation, never a tolerance increase.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, figure “Key steps for operational resilience” (steps 2, 4, 5) and Box 4.7 (tolerance measured by time). Schweser Reading 45, Steps 2, 4, 5. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: (polarity flip of the remedy). The identification is right, but raising tolerances to match the test outcome reverses the logic: the tolerance marks the point of intolerable harm and the firm must adapt delivery, not the limit. A would be correct only if the stem showed the original tolerances had been mis-set relative to harm, which it does not.

b.reason: B identifies the two breaches and prescribes step 5: examine lessons learned from the test and take action.

c.reason: (unit slip). Treating a “day” as an 8-hour working day gives settlement 2 × 8 = 16 hours (40 > 16) and mortgages 3 × 8 = 24 hours (80 > 24), adding settlement as a false breach. C would be correct if settlement’s tolerance were 16 hours.

d.reason: (condition error). Step 5 is triggered by stress test results (“lessons learned from stress tests”), not only by real incidents. D would be correct only for a stem about post-incident reviews of an actual event.

questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-4 g Q9
questions.question: The chief risk officer of a mid-sized Australian bank is staffing its operational resilience program. The bank has identified nine important business services, and a first estimate suggests that mapping them end to end will involve more than 200 systems and 40 third-party suppliers. Which staffing plan is most consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: A multi-disciplinary team coordinated by ORM, with BCM, HR, third-party management, IT, operations and infrastructure, resourced for a complex mapping exercise.
A team coordinated by IT, with ORM, BCM and third-party management in a supporting role, since dependency mapping is mainly a systems inventory exercise.
A small team coordinated by ORM and drawn from ORM staff alone, since mapping becomes a light exercise once the important business services are known.
A multi-disciplinary team coordinated by internal audit, with ORM, BCM, HR, IT and operations, so that the program is independent of the first two lines.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank CRO staffing a resilience program with 200 systems and 40 suppliers.

**Concept and theory**

After IBS are identified, the firm must map the dependencies between services, identify critical paths to assess possible disruptions, and decide the resources needed to avoid them or recover quickly. GARP calls this a complex part of resilience assessment and reinforcement: complexity of dependencies grows exponentially in large institutions, requiring large teams, resources and data to get a proper view of the system and set realistic limits.

Because the dependencies cross people, suppliers, technology and premises, GARP says resilience requires a multi-disciplinary approach. Partners to the resilience team include the ORM department (usually as coordinator), BCM, Human Resources, Third-Party Management, IT, Operations and Infrastructure.

**Applying it to this question**

With 200 systems and 40 suppliers, the mapping is complex and cross-functional. The plan must (i) be multi-disciplinary, (ii) have ORM as the usual coordinator, and (iii) be resourced for a complex exercise. Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: ORM is usually the coordinator; BCM, HR, third-party management, IT, operations and infrastructure are partners.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5, text after Box 4.7 (mapping, complexity, multi-disciplinary approach). Schweser Reading 45 (larger banks need more data, IT resources and personnel from HR and IT). Schweser does not name ORM as coordinator; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: A matches GARP’s partner list and coordinator, and its recognition that mapping needs large teams, resources and data.

b.reason: (role misassignment). IT is a partner, not the usual coordinator; and treating mapping as a systems inventory ignores people, supplier and premises dependencies. B would be correct only if the stem asked which function owns the systems inventory within the mapping.

c.reason: (polarity flip on complexity). GARP says mapping is complex and grows exponentially with size, needing large teams; “light” and “ORM staff alone” reverse this. C would be correct only for a very small firm with few dependencies, which the stem rules out.

d.reason: (role misassignment). Internal audit is not in GARP’s partner list and does not coordinate the program; ORM does. D would be correct only for a stem about independent assurance of the program after it is built.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is mapping the corporate lending service, one of the bank’s important business services, end to end. The mapping so far is shown below.

| Stage of the lending service | Systems used | System recovery time (hours) |
|---|---|---|
| Credit approval | S1, S2 | 6 |
| Documentation | S2 | 6 |
| Disbursement | S2, S3 | 18 |
| Loan servicing | S4 | 10 |

Recovery time shown is for the slowest system used in each stage: S1 4 hours, S2 6 hours, S3 18 hours, S4 10 hours.

Which conclusion is best supported by the mapping?

options.text: S1 is the key dependency, because credit approval is the first stage of the service, so the bank should direct its recovery resources to S1 first.
S3 is the key dependency, because it has the longest recovery time, so the bank should direct its recovery resources to S3 first.
S2 is the key dependency node, because three of the four stages rely on it, so the mapping should feed the resources needed to avoid or quickly recover its disruption.
S2 is the key dependency node, because three of the four stages rely on it, so the bank should set an impact tolerance for S2 instead of for the lending service.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank analyst reading an end-to-end map of the corporate lending service.

**Concept and theory**

Step 3 maps each IBS end to end: the stages that deliver it and the resources (systems, people, suppliers) each stage needs. GARP describes the purpose as mapping the dependencies, identifying critical paths to assess possible disruptions, and identifying the resources to put in place to avoid them or recover them quickly. The Canadian bank case (Box 4.8) shows exactly this structure: a critical business service such as corporate lending is broken into stages (issue commitment, pre-funding, release funding, post-funding, administration), each with time limits and system dependencies. GARP’s Table 4.2 lists “key systems dependency: critical path mapping, dependency nodes” as a resilience KRI. A dependency node is a resource on which many stages depend, so its failure disrupts much of the service at once.

Impact tolerances, however, stay attached to the important business service, not to systems or processes.

**Applying it to this question**

Count stage dependencies per system:

$S$1 : 1 stage (credit approval)

$S$2 : 3 stages (credit approval, documentation, disbursement)

$S$3 : 1 stage (disbursement)

$S$4 : 1 stage (loan servicing)

S2 is the dependency node on the critical path. The recovery-time column is a distractor: it says how long a system takes to restore, not how much of the service depends on it. The mapping’s purpose is to direct resources to avoid or quickly recover the disruption of S2.

**Fragile fact.** Node = most shared dependency, not the slowest or the first; tolerances stay at the IBS level.

**Reference**

LO 45.g (verbatim as above). GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.5 (mapping and critical paths), Box 4.8 “Case Study: Critical Path and Critical Business Services in Canada”, Table 4.2 “KRIs for Resilience”. Schweser Reading 45, Step 3. Box 4.8 column headings are only partly legible in the source text; the question uses only its stage-and-system structure.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-4 g, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: (assumption error (sequence mistaken for dependency)). Being first in the sequence does not make S1 a node; it supports one stage only. A would be correct if S1 were shared by most stages.

b.reason: (irrelevant-input trap). It ranks systems by recovery time, the deliberately irrelevant column, rather than by how many stages depend on them. B would be correct if the question asked which system is slowest to restore.

c.reason: C identifies S2 as the node and states GARP’s purpose for mapping: the resources to put in place to avoid disruptions or recover quickly.

d.reason: (scope error). The node identification is right, but tolerances are set for important business services, not for a system. D would be correct only if the reading set tolerances at resource level, which it does not.
