questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Chinese commercial bank is reviewing three controls in the CNY lending operation and wants to classify each by its type of weak design.

I. A branch head must sign off about 300 loan files on the last afternoon of each quarter, without summaries or time to read them.

II. Each disbursement is checked by a maker, a checker and a third peer reviewer from the same team, and no one is named as accountable for the verification.

III. After a loss in which staff bypassed an onboarding check that they found too cumbersome, the bank added two further approval steps of the same design.

Which of the following classifications of controls I, II and III, in that order, is correct?

options.text: Optimistic control; collective control; more of the same
Collective control; optimistic control; more of the same
Optimistic control; more of the same; collective control
More of the same; collective control; optimistic control

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank lending controls: classify three weak designs.

**Concept and theory**

GARP names three types of weakly designed controls (citing Chapelle, 2018):

| Type | What goes wrong | GARP examples |
|---|---|---|
| Optimistic | Requires exceptional ability or exceptional motivation from the controller; cursory, “tick-box” | Sign-offs for large volumes of documents just before a deadline; any sign-off where the authorizer lacks information or time to understand what is validated |
| Collective | Dilutes accountability by spreading verification across several people | Four-eyes check, maker-checker |
| More of the same | Responds to a control failure by adding more controls of the same design that already failed | Adding more controllers after a collective control fails; reinforcing an onboarding process already bypassed because it is too cumbersome |

**Applying it to this question**

Control I: 300 files signed off on the last afternoon of the quarter with no time or summaries. That is GARP’s optimistic example almost exactly.

Control II: three peers check, no one is accountable. Verification is spread across several people: collective.

Control III: the response to a failed, bypassed onboarding check is more steps of the same design: more of the same.

**Fragile fact.** More of the same is defined by the response to a failure; collective by shared responsibility; optimistic by reliance on exceptional effort.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Design.” Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing” (examples of poorly designed controls). Schweser describes optimistic controls as “highly dependent on the individual”; GARP’s wording is “exceptional ability or exceptional motivation.” No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: Option A (optimistic; collective; more of the same) matches each control to its GARP definition.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B swaps I and II. Mass sign-off under deadline pressure is optimistic, not collective (only one person signs). B would be correct if Control I involved several officers each initialing the files and Control II were a single rushed sign-off.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C swaps II and III. Control II is a standing multi-person check, not a response to a failure; Control III is a response that adds the same design. C would be correct if Control II had been created by adding a third reviewer after a loss and Control III were a standing peer check.

d.reason: (sibling swap). D swaps I and III. Control III is the remedial addition of the same failed design, not Control I. D would be correct if Control I had been introduced after a loss as an extra copy of a failed check and Control III were a rushed bulk sign-off.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-5 c Q8
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a US broker-dealer is reviewing the four-eyes check on outgoing client wire transfers. Two clerks of equal rank in the payments team each verify every wire, and each has admitted relying on the other to catch errors. Which of the following changes would make this control most effective?

options.text: Add a third clerk from the same payments team, so that each wire is seen by more people before release.
Share responsibility for the check evenly across the whole team, so that no one person is held accountable.
Have the check carried out by a manager and a subordinate, with accountability clearly attributed to each.
Replace the check with a single sign-off of the full daily wire batch by one senior officer just before cut-off.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US broker-dealer wire transfers: how to make a four-eyes check effective.

**Concept and theory**

The four-eyes check (maker-checker) is GARP’s most common collective control. Its weakness is behavioral: “having more than one person check the same information can dilute accountability. Also, because too much trust may be placed in collective controls, individual attention and focus may be less rigorous, increasing the overall risk.”

GARP gives the remedy: “Four-eyes checks are more effective when carried out by a manager and a subordinate, or by people from different departments, and more generally when accountability is clearly attributed to those performing the tasks.” Schweser says the same: double checks are best performed by people at different hierarchy levels or in different departments.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem shows the textbook failure: two equal-rank clerks from the same team, each relying on the other. The fix must break the symmetry (different levels or departments) and attach accountability to named people.

**Fragile fact.** Four-eyes works when the two pairs of eyes differ (manager and subordinate, or different departments) and each owner is accountable.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Design” (collective controls). Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing” (collective controls, double checks). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: (more of the same). Adding another peer from the same team adds more of the failed design and dilutes accountability further. A would be correct only if the problem were lack of capacity rather than diluted accountability, which the stem rules out.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Spreading responsibility so that no one is accountable is exactly what makes collective controls weak; GARP asks for accountability to be clearly attributed. B would be correct if it read “attribute accountability clearly to each person performing the check.”

c.reason: Option C applies both elements of GARP’s remedy: a manager and a subordinate, with accountability clearly attributed.

d.reason: (sibling swap: optimistic control). A single bulk sign-off of the day’s wires just before cut-off is GARP’s optimistic control: it depends on exceptional effort by the signer, who lacks the time to review. D would be correct if the question asked which change would create an optimistic control.

questions.topic: Risk Mitigation
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-5 c Q9
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a French bank is reviewing a remediation plan. A four-eyes check missed a mispriced EUR swap, causing a loss of EUR 3.2 million. Management proposes adding a third and a fourth checker of the same seniority to the same check. Which of the following best describes the likely effect of the proposal?

options.text: Risk falls, because each extra checker independently lowers the probability that an error passes unnoticed.
Accountability is diluted further, so the change may raise rather than lower the vulnerability of the process.
The check becomes a key control, because four checkers can together mitigate the pricing risk on their own.
The check becomes an optimistic control, which is acceptable because the risk involved is a high inherent risk.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French bank remediation: adding more checkers after a four-eyes failure.

**Concept and theory**

“More of the same” is GARP’s name for responding to an incident caused by a control failure by “adding more controls of the same design, even though the previous ones failed.” GARP’s first example is this exact pattern: “responding to a failure of collective controls by adding more controllers has the effect of diluting accountability even more.” The general principle: “More controls do not necessarily mean less risk. Poorly designed controls can increase the vulnerability of a process. Conversely, proper process design reduces inherent risk simply through organization of tasks, without the need to add controls.”

**Applying it to this question**

The original failure is a collective (four-eyes) control. The proposal adds two more checkers of the same seniority to the same check, so it is more of the same, and GARP predicts further dilution of accountability. The EUR 3.2 million loss size is irrelevant to the classification.

**Fragile fact.** After a collective control fails, adding controllers makes accountability worse, not better.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Design” (more of the same). Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing” (“adding more controls here will not reduce risk”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: (absolute claim, independence assumption). A assumes each checker acts independently, so misses multiply away. GARP’s point is that checkers rely on each other, so attention falls as numbers rise. A would be correct if each checker were fully independent and accountable, for example in different departments.

b.reason: Option B states GARP’s predicted consequence: accountability is diluted further and the process may become more, not less, vulnerable.

c.reason: (sibling swap: key control). A key control is one that is sufficient on its own. Stacking weak checks of the same design does not create a control that can mitigate the risk alone. C would be correct if the check were redesigned so that one control could prevent mispricing by itself, such as an independent automated price validation.

d.reason: (sibling swap and scope error). Optimistic controls rely on exceptional effort by one controller; the proposal is a collective control made larger. Also, the source never calls a weak design acceptable for high inherent risk; higher inherent risk calls for stronger controls and testing. D would be correct only if the proposal were a rushed one-person sign-off and the risk were low.

questions.question: A banking supervisor at the Australian prudential regulator is reviewing a bank’s control testing plan, which pairs each control with a type of control testing. Which of the following pairings is most consistent with sound practice?

options.text: Self-certification for a key control over high-value AUD payments, since the control owner knows the control best.
Observation for an automated reconciliation, since observation provides moderate assurance from written evidence.
Examination for secondary controls, since it is the lightest form of testing and does not require any evidence.
Examination for an automated data validation check, since it relies on documentation and evidence of results.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian supervisor reviews how a bank pairs controls with testing types.

**Concept and theory**

GARP presents four main types of control testing in increasing level of scrutiny, and states: “The higher the inherent risk, the stronger the control testing required.”

| Rank | Type | How it works | Best suited to |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Self-certification or inquiry | Owner attests; no evidence provided | Secondary controls, or controls in low inherent risk environments |
| 2 | Examination | Supporting evidence and documentation of the process and written evidence of results; moderate assurance; usefulness depends on the documentation | Automated controls and sampling of manual controls |
| 3 | Observation | Real-time oversight of execution (or audio/video recording); more stringent; on a sample, as observation is limited in time | Key controls |
| 4 | Reperformance (reproduction or parallel testing) | Tester reproduces the control on a sample and compares results; the strongest form | Highest scrutiny; model validation, mystery shopping, bogus transactions |

**Applying it to this question**

Check each pairing against the table. Only D pairs an automated control with examination and gives examination’s true basis, documentation and written evidence of results.

**Fragile fact.** Order of scrutiny: self-certification, examination, observation, reperformance. Examination fits automated controls; observation fits key controls.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Testing” and “Control Effectiveness.” Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing.” Differences: Schweser calls the first type “self-assessment” and limits it for “lack of objectivity”; GARP calls it “self-certification or inquiry” and limits it for lack of evidence. Schweser says examination’s “limited scope” makes it most appropriate for automated controls; GARP says it gives moderate assurance and suits automated controls and sampling of manual controls. GARP used for content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: (scope error). Self-certification provides no evidence and is limited to secondary controls or low inherent risk. A key control over high-value payments needs stronger testing. A would be correct if the control were a secondary control in a low inherent risk environment.

b.reason: (sibling swap). “Moderate assurance” and “written evidence” are features of examination, not observation. Observation is real-time oversight, more stringent, and suited to key controls. B would be correct if it read “Examination for an automated reconciliation.”

c.reason: (sibling swap). The lightest form, requiring no evidence, is self-certification. Examination requires documentation and evidence. C would be correct if it read “Self-certification for secondary controls.”

d.reason: Option D matches GARP: examination “requires supporting evidence and documentation of the controls” and “is better suited for automated controls and sampling of manual controls.”

questions.question: The head of operational risk at a Japanese securities firm is describing four activities in this year’s control testing program for the JPY equity desk. Which of the following activities is an example of reperformance testing?

options.text: Testers insert fictitious trades into the trading system to check whether the middle office detects them.
Testers watch a video recording of staff executing the end-of-day trade confirmation control.
Testers review the written process documentation and the signed evidence of past control results.
Testers ask each desk head to confirm in writing that the confirmation control operated all quarter.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese securities firm: which testing activity is reperformance.

**Concept and theory**

Reperformance (also called reproduction or parallel testing) is GARP’s strongest form of control testing: “the tester reproduces the control process on a sample of transactions and compares the results with those previously obtained by the process.” GARP’s examples:

- “mystery shopping” to assess customer service or call center effectiveness;
- insertion of bogus data or fictitious transactions into trading systems or models to test error detection in control functions such as the middle office or back office;
- model validation: verifying model output with different data sets or with independently written code.

The other three types differ in what the tester does: asks (self-certification), reads evidence (examination), or watches (observation).

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each activity by what the tester does. Inserting fictitious trades makes the tester run the control process and compare outcomes: reperformance. Watching a recording is observation; reviewing documentation and signed evidence is examination; asking for written confirmation is self-certification.

**Fragile fact.** Reperformance means the tester does the control again; observation means the tester watches it, even on video.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Testing.” Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing” (reperformance: erroneous data introduced into the system; model validation). Schweser does not describe reperformance as the strongest form; GARP does. GARP used for content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: Option A is GARP’s own example of reperformance: “the insertion of bogus data or fictitious transactions into trading systems . . . to test the effectiveness of error detection in control functions, such as middle-office.”

b.reason: (sibling swap: observation). GARP explicitly includes audio and video recording within observation, which is oversight of execution, not reproduction. B would be correct if the question asked for an example of observation.

c.reason: (sibling swap: examination). Reviewing written documentation and written evidence of results is examination. Reperformance would require the tester to rerun the control; here the tester only reads. C would be correct if the question asked for an example of examination.

d.reason: (sibling swap: self-certification). A written attestation by the control owner is self-certification or inquiry, the weakest type, with no evidence provided. D would be correct if the question asked for the least stringent type of testing.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at an Indian private sector bank is writing guidance on what makes control testing effective. The draft contains the following statements:

I. The testing party should be independent from the owner of the control process, except in the case of self-certification.

II. The frequency of control assessment should be proportionate to the severity of the risk, with more frequent assessments in unstable risk environments.

III. Controls over higher risks are tested with stronger methods such as reperformance, so they can be tested less frequently than controls over lower risks.

IV. A large enough sample guarantees reliable test results, whatever the way in which the items in the sample were selected.

Which of the statements should the analyst keep?

options.text: I only
I, II and IV only
I and II only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Indian bank guidance: which statements on effective control testing to keep.

**Concept and theory**

GARP names three elements that influence the effectiveness of control testing:

1. **Independence of the testing party.** To avoid conflict of interest and bias, the tester should be independent from the owner of the control process, “except in the case of self-certification.”
2. **Frequency of testing.** “Proportionate to the severity of the risk, with more frequent assessments for higher risks or unstable risk environments.”
3. **Scope and sample.** The sample “should be as representative as possible of the full population”; reliability must be judged against the time and effort committed; “insufficient sampling or biased sample tests can easily give a false view of the control effectiveness.”

These factors are separate from the four testing types (self-certification, examination, observation, reperformance), which describe how a test is done.

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s independence factor with its exception. True.

II: GARP’s frequency factor, including unstable environments. True.

III: reverses the frequency rule; higher risk means more frequent assessment, and a stronger method does not offset frequency. False.

IV: size cannot cure bias; GARP wants the sample representative. False.

Keep I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Higher severity or an unstable environment means more frequent testing; a bigger biased sample is still biased.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Testing” (elements that influence effectiveness). Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing” (independence, frequency, sample selection). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: (scope error, too narrow). A rejects the true Statement II. A would be correct if II had said “frequency should be the same for all risks,” which would be false.

b.reason: (absolute claim). B accepts IV, which promises reliable results from any large sample. GARP warns that biased samples give a false view of effectiveness whatever their size. B would be correct if IV read “a sample should be large enough and as representative as possible of the full population.”

c.reason: Option C (I and II only) matches GARP’s list of elements that influence the effectiveness of control testing.

d.reason: (polarity flip and absolute claim). D drops the true I and accepts III (frequency reversed) and IV (absolute). D would be correct only if testing frequency fell with risk severity and sample size alone guaranteed reliability, both contrary to GARP.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Swiss private bank is reviewing how the daily CHF nostro reconciliation, a key control, was tested this year.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Tester | Head of the reconciliation unit, who owns the control |
| Sample | 25 items, all from the lowest-volume week of the year |
| Population | About 11,000 reconciliation items over the year |
| Frequency | Annual; the core banking system was migrated in Q3 |
| Unit headcount | 14 staff |
| Result | No exceptions; control reported as effective |

Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this testing?

options.text: It is acceptable, because the first line routinely tests key controls and the owner exception for testing applies here.
It may give a false view of effectiveness, as the tester lacks independence, the sample is biased and testing is too rare.
It is reliable once the sample is raised to 250 items from the same week, as sample size is its only weakness.
It is inadequate, and the remedy is for the operational risk function to take over the testing of this key control.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Swiss private bank: diagnose how a key reconciliation control was tested.

**Concept and theory**

Three elements decide whether a control test is credible (GARP Section 5.2):

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Independence | Tester independent from the owner of the control process, except in self-certification |
| Frequency | Proportionate to the severity of the risk; more frequent for higher risks or unstable risk environments |
| Scope and sample | Sample as representative as possible of the full population; insufficient or biased samples give a false view of effectiveness |

Testing also has a governance side: the first line routinely tests key controls, but that does not remove the independence requirement for the person who owns the control.

**Applying it to this question**

Check the table in the stem against each element:

- Tester: the head of the unit owns the control, and the test is a sample test, not self-certification. Independence fails.
- Sample: 25 items from the lowest-volume week, out of about 11,000 items. Not representative of the population. Scope and sample fail.
- Frequency: annual testing despite a core system migration in Q3, an unstable environment, on a key control. Frequency is too low.
- Headcount of 14 is irrelevant.

A zero-exception result produced under these conditions can easily give a false view of effectiveness.

**Fragile fact.** The independence exception belongs to self-certification only, not to any test done by the first line.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Testing” and “Control Testing and Risk Governance.” Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). The first line does routinely test key controls, but GARP’s exception to independence covers only self-certification. This was a sample test by the owner, so the exception does not apply. A would be correct if the exercise were explicitly a self-certification of a secondary control in a low-risk area.

b.reason: Option B names all three failures (independence, biased sample, insufficient frequency) and GARP’s consequence, a false view of control effectiveness.

c.reason: (scope error). Ten times as many items from the same quiet week remain biased, and the independence and frequency problems remain. C would be correct only if size were the sole defect and the sample were drawn across the whole year.

d.reason: (role misassignment). GARP: the ORM function does not usually test the controls itself; it receives assurance that controls are well designed and well operated. The fix is an independent tester (for example internal audit), a representative sample and higher frequency. D would be correct if it named internal audit or another independent tester.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising the board of a Brazilian bank on who should test internal controls. Which of the following statements best describes the allocation of responsibility for control testing?

options.text: Internal audit has historically tested controls; the first line also routinely tests key controls; the ORM function usually tests them too.
The ORM function has historically tested controls; the first line also routinely tests key controls; internal audit receives assurance on them.
Internal audit has historically tested controls; the first line is not allowed to test key controls; the ORM function receives assurance on them.
Internal audit has historically tested controls; the first line also routinely tests key controls; the ORM function receives assurance on them.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank board: who tests internal controls and who receives assurance.

**Concept and theory**

GARP, “Control Testing and Risk Governance”:

| Actor | Role in control testing |
|---|---|
| Internal audit (third line) | Historically responsible for control testing |
| First line of defense | In many organizations also routinely tests internal key controls, especially with the increase of operational risk |
| ORM function (second line) | Does not usually test the controls itself; should receive assurance that controls are well designed and well operated; requires evidence that controls are assessed and that the assessment is included in the operational risk assessment, qualitatively and quantitatively |

GARP adds that the Sarbanes-Oxley Act required US operating companies to develop and attest to internal controls over financial and accounting information (SOX controls), and that practices from SOX, the IIA and COSO can inspire operational risk managers.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has three clauses, one per actor. Check each clause against the table: only D has the correct historical owner, the correct first-line role and the correct ORM role.

**Fragile fact.** Second line (ORM) receives assurance and evidence; it does not usually test. Third line has historically tested; first line also tests key controls.

**Reference**

LO 46.c (verbatim as on the cover). GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2, “Control Testing and Risk Governance.” Schweser LO 46.c, “Control Testing”: “usually done by the internal audit department” (GARP: “historically”); ORM “not typically involved” but “must receive confirmation.” Consistent in substance; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-5 c, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: (role misassignment). A says the ORM function usually tests controls too. GARP: ORM “does not usually test the controls themselves” but receives assurance. A would be correct if the third clause read “the ORM function receives assurance on them.”

b.reason: (role misassignment). B swaps internal audit and ORM: internal audit, not ORM, has historically tested controls. B would be correct if “ORM function” and “internal audit” traded places.

c.reason: (polarity flip). GARP says the first line routinely tests key controls in many organizations; C forbids it. C would be correct if the second clause read “the first line also routinely tests key controls.”

d.reason: Option D matches GARP on all three actors.

questions.question: The head of regulatory affairs at an Indian private sector bank is presenting to newly hired risk analysts on the purpose of prudential regulation issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). One analyst asks how the BCBS pursues its stated objectives. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: All three objectives, namely solvency, customer protection and efficient competitive performance, are attained primarily through regulatory capital requirements.
Solvency and soundness, the primary objective, is addressed mainly through regulatory capital requirements; the other two through fit-and-proper criteria, monitoring and reporting.
Customer protection, the primary objective, is addressed mainly through regulatory capital requirements; solvency through fit-and-proper criteria, monitoring and reporting.
Solvency and soundness, the primary objective, is addressed mainly through mandatory market disclosures; the other two through regulatory capital requirements.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Indian bank: how the BCBS pursues its three objectives.

**Concept and theory**

Regulatory capital is, in GARP’s words, “the minimum level of equity and long-term, stable funding prescribed by the supervisors of banks and insurance companies, given their systemic importance in the economy.” To understand why such a minimum exists, start from what the regulator is trying to achieve. GARP states that BCBS prudential regulation has a threefold objective:

| # | Objective | Main instrument (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Solvency and soundness of all financial intermediaries (the primary objective, tied to the BCBS mandate of international financial stability) | Regulatory capital requirements |
| 2 | Protection of customers from undue risks (failure, fraud, opportunistic behavior) | Requirements on senior management’s history and competence (“fit and proper”), monitoring and reporting |
| 3 | Efficient and competitive performance of financial institutions | Same as objective 2 |

The logic is intuitive: capital is a loss-absorbing cushion, so it is the natural tool for keeping an intermediary solvent. Customer protection and efficient competition are about behavior and transparency, so they are pursued through who runs the bank and how its activities are monitored and reported. This is why the regulator’s capital number is a floor for solvency, not a full description of how the bank should be run.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks how the objectives are pursued, so you need two facts: which objective is primary, and which instrument serves which objective. GARP: solvency is primary and is addressed “primarily through regulatory capital requirements, while the other two objectives are attained through requirements on the bank’s senior management’s history and competence (the ‘fit and proper’ criteria), monitoring and reporting.” Only one option has both facts right.

**Fragile fact.** Solvency is the primary BCBS objective and capital is its tool; the other two objectives run through fit-and-proper criteria, monitoring and reporting, not through capital.

**Reference**

LO 48.b: “Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.” GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.1 and Section 7.3, “The Role of Regulatory Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b, “Regulatory Capital,” lists the three objectives and states that the first is the most important and is addressed through regulatory capital; the fit-and-proper, monitoring and reporting instruments are GARP only (Schweser omits them). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (scope error, overextension). A extends the capital instrument to all three objectives. GARP restricts capital to the solvency objective. A would be correct if the stem asked only “which objective is addressed primarily through regulatory capital requirements” and the option named solvency alone.

b.reason: Option B states the primary objective (solvency and soundness), its instrument (regulatory capital) and the instruments for the other two objectives (fit-and-proper criteria, monitoring and reporting), exactly as in GARP Section 7.3.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C swaps the roles of objectives 1 and 2: it makes customer protection primary and capital its instrument. GARP is explicit that solvency is primary. C would be correct only for a hypothetical conduct regulator whose mandate puts customer protection first, which is not the BCBS.

d.reason: (sibling swap). D attaches Pillar 3 market disclosure to solvency and capital to the other objectives. Disclosure is a separate pillar of the framework, not the main instrument for solvency. D would be correct if it read “addressed mainly through regulatory capital requirements.”

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Swiss universal bank is reviewing a training deck on the history of Basel capital rules before it is released to staff. The deck contains the following statements:

I. Basel I (1988) recommended minimum capital to cover unexpected credit losses equal to 8% of risk-weighted assets, known as the Cooke ratio.

II. The 1996 extension of regulatory capital to market risk, using a value-at-risk approach, raised the overall minimum requirement above 8% of risk-weighted assets.

III. Basel II (2002) added regulatory capital for operational risk and reformed credit capital to be based on counterparty credit ratings, leaving the overall 8% requirement unchanged.

IV. Basel III added a minimum regulatory ratio for liquidity risk and a buffer of 2.5% of risk-weighted assets in addition to the 8% minimum.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Swiss bank training deck: which statements about Basel history are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel capital rules grew in layers, each adding a risk type or a tool while (until Basel III) keeping the same headline ratio:

| Date | Step | What changed (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| 1988 | Basel I | Minimum capital for unexpected credit losses: 8% of risk-weighted assets (RWA), the “Cooke ratio,” named after the BCBS president. Credit risk only. |
| 1996 | Market risk extension | Regulatory capital extended to market risk using value-at-risk (VaR), driven by derivatives and off-balance-sheet growth. Overall 8% RWA minimum did not change. |
| 2002 | Basel II | Added operational risk capital; major reform of credit capital based on counterparty credit ratings; introduced the three pillars. 8% RWA still unchanged. |
| Post 2007-2009 | Basel III | Added a minimum regulatory ratio for liquidity risk and a buffer adding 2.5% of RWA on top of the 8% minimum, built up in strong periods to protect in recessions or crises. |

The pattern to remember: the scope widened (credit, then market, then operational, then liquidity) while the 8% headline stayed fixed until Basel III added an extra buffer on top.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: Basel I, 1988, 8% of RWA for unexpected credit losses, Cooke ratio. True.

Statement II: claims the 1996 market risk extension raised the minimum above 8%. GARP: “the overall minimum requirement of 8% RWA did not change.” False.

Statement III: Basel II added operational risk, reformed credit capital around ratings, 8% unchanged. True.

Statement IV: Basel III added a liquidity ratio and a 2.5% RWA buffer in addition to 8%. True. The accurate set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** The 8% of RWA minimum survived 1996 and Basel II unchanged; only Basel III added an incremental 2.5% of RWA on top of it.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Regulatory Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b, “Regulatory Capital.” Note: GARP calls the 2.5% buffer a “countercyclical buffer”; Schweser describes the same 2.5% without naming it. Schweser also places the 1996 market risk extension in a sentence about Basel II (“Even with regulatory capital extended to market risk in 1996, Basel II kept the RWA level at 8%”); GARP dates Basel II to 2002, and GARP is followed here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: (scope error, too narrow). A drops Statement IV, as if Basel III had not added the liquidity ratio and the 2.5% buffer. A would be correct if IV had claimed, for example, that Basel III replaced the 8% minimum with 2.5%.

b.reason: (polarity flip accepted). B accepts Statement II, which flips “did not change” into “raised.” B would be correct if the 1996 market risk amendment had increased the headline ratio, which it did not; the first incremental requirement on top of 8% came with Basel III.

c.reason: (polarity flip accepted, true statements rejected). C accepts the false Statement II and rejects the true Statements I and III. C would be correct only in a world where Basel I had no 8% ratio and Basel II had not added operational risk, contradicting the source on both counts.

d.reason: Option D contains exactly the three true statements and excludes the false Statement II, matching GARP’s chronology in “The Role of Regulatory Capital.”

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Dutch commercial bank is preparing training material that reconstructs how the original 1988 Basel I accord would have applied to a simplified balance sheet. The risk weights shown are those of Basel I. The bank’s trading desk also reports a 10-day 99% value-at-risk (VaR) of EUR 35 million.

| Exposure | Amount (EUR million) | Basel I risk weight (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Commercial loans to corporates | 400 | 100 |
| Consumer loans | 150 | 100 |
| Uninsured mortgage loans | 300 | 50 |
| Interbank loans | 200 | 20 |
| Sovereign bonds of OECD countries | 500 | 0 |

What is the minimum regulatory capital that Basel I, as recommended in 1988, would have required for this balance sheet?

options.text: EUR 59.20 million
EUR 77.70 million
EUR 94.20 million
EUR 124.00 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Dutch bank: Basel I (1988) minimum capital on a five-line balance sheet.

**Concept and theory**

Basel I required capital equal to 8% of risk-weighted assets. Risk weights scale each exposure according to how risky the regulator judged the asset class. GARP’s footnote gives the weights: 100% for commercial or consumer loans, 50% for mortgages and banking guarantees, 20% for interbank loans and 0% for sovereign credit (to OECD countries). Hence GARP’s example: capital equal to 8% of private sector lending, 4% of uninsured mortgage loans (8% × 50%) and 1.6% of interbank loans (8% × 20%), and nothing for OECD sovereign credit.

Minimum capital = 8% $\times\text{RWA},$ RWA = $\sum_{i} w_{i} \times E_{i}$

where $E_{i}$ is the exposure amount in class $i$ and $w_{i}$ its risk weight. In 1988 the requirement covered credit risk only; market risk was added in 1996 and the 2.5% buffer only with Basel III.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line (EUR million):

$\text{RWA}_{\text{commercial}}$ = 400 × 100% = 400

$\text{RWA}_{\text{consumer}}$ = 150 × 100% = 150

$\text{RWA}_{\text{mortgage}}$ = 300 × 50% = 150

$\text{RWA}_{\text{interbank}}$ = 200 × 20% = 40

$\text{RWA}_{\text{OECD sovereign}}$ = 500 × 0% = 0

RWA = 400 + 150 + 150 + 40 + 0 = 740

Minimum capital = 8% × 740 = 59.20

The trading desk VaR is irrelevant: the 1988 accord set no capital for market risk. The bank would have needed EUR 59.20 million of capital, about 3.8% of its EUR 1,550 million gross exposures, because the large OECD sovereign book attracts no capital.

**Fragile fact.** In 1988 Basel I covered credit risk only; OECD sovereigns carried a 0% weight, and market risk capital arrived in 1996.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Regulatory Capital,” including footnote 8 (Basel I risk weights). Schweser LO 48.b gives the 8% Cooke ratio but not the risk weights (the weights are GARP only and are supplied in the stem). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: Option A applies the Cooke ratio of 8% to RWA of EUR 740 million, using only what Basel I covered in 1988 (credit risk).

b.reason: (scope error, wrong regime). 10.5% × 740 = 77.70. This adds the Basel III 2.5% buffer to the 8% minimum. B would be correct if the stem asked for the requirement under Basel III, including the additional 2.5% of RWA (and ignoring any other changes).

c.reason: (scope error, wrong regime (1996 extension)). 59.20 + 35 = 94.20. This adds the trading VaR as if it were a market risk charge. Market risk capital was introduced only in 1996, and in any case the VaR is not itself the capital charge. C would be correct only if the stem stated that the trading VaR figure were the market risk capital charge and asked for the post-1996 total.

d.reason: (dropped term (risk weights)). 8% × (400 + 150 + 300 + 200 + 500) = 8% × 1,550 = 124.00. This applies 8% to unweighted exposures. D would be correct only if every exposure carried a 100% risk weight.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-7 b Q4
questions.question: A newly appointed independent director on the board of a US bank holding company asks the chief compliance officer whether the Basel capital frameworks have legal force. Which of the following answers by the chief compliance officer is most accurate?

options.text: Basel frameworks are legally binding on all banks in BCBS member countries from the date the Committee publishes them, without any national legislation.
Basel frameworks are not laws, but in the United States Basel II was mandatory for banks with assets above USD 10 billion or foreign assets above USD 250 billion.
Basel frameworks are not laws, but in the United States Basel II was mandatory for banks with assets above USD 250 billion or foreign assets above USD 10 billion.
Basel frameworks are not laws, and no jurisdiction has enacted them in legislation, so adopting them remains voluntary for every bank in every country.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US bank board member asks whether Basel frameworks have legal force.

**Concept and theory**

The BCBS was established by the central bank governors of the Group of Ten countries and issues guidance for the regulation and supervision of banks in the G-10 and beyond. Two facts follow from GARP:

- Basel frameworks “are not laws and are not legally binding.”
- Some jurisdictions have passed legislation to enact them: some elements of Basel II and III became law in the European community, applying to most financial institutions. In the United States, Basel II was only mandatory for banks with assets in excess of USD 250 billion, or internationally active banks with foreign assets in excess of USD 10 billion, and these banks were required to adopt the Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) for operational risk.

So regulatory capital requirements are “prescribed” by the Basel framework as recommendations; their legal force comes from national or regional enactment.

**Applying it to this question**

Every option except A begins “Basel frameworks are not laws,” so the decision rests on the second half. Only one option states the US thresholds the right way round: USD 250 billion of total assets, or USD 10 billion of foreign assets for internationally active banks.

**Fragile fact.** Total assets USD 250 billion; foreign assets USD 10 billion. The larger number goes with total assets.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Regulatory Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b states only that “the Basel frameworks are recommendations, not laws”; the EU and US details are GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (absolute claim). A claims Basel rules bind all banks on publication. GARP says the frameworks are not laws and not legally binding. A would be correct only if it described a jurisdiction where national legislation had adopted the framework, and then only for the banks that legislation covers.

b.reason: (wrong input twin (thresholds swapped)). B swaps the two thresholds: USD 10 billion for total assets and USD 250 billion for foreign assets. B would be correct if the thresholds were stated in that order, which GARP does not do.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP: not laws, but given force in some jurisdictions; in the US, Basel II was mandatory for banks above USD 250 billion of assets or with foreign assets above USD 10 billion.

d.reason: (absolute claim). D says no jurisdiction has enacted the frameworks. GARP gives the European community and the United States as examples where they were enacted. D would be correct if it stopped at “Basel frameworks are not laws in themselves.”

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is mapping three recent regulatory items to the pillars of the Basel framework for an internal compliance inventory:

I. The supervisor imposed a capital add-on after assessing the bank’s specific risk profile and the quality of its risk management.

II. The bank published its quarterly report on its financial situation and risk information, as required by the rules.

III. The bank confirmed that it met the minimum liquidity ratio set by the framework.

Which of the following mappings is most accurate?

options.text: I: Pillar 2; II: Pillar 3; III: Pillar 1
I: Pillar 2; II: Pillar 3; III: Pillar 2
I: Pillar 1; II: Pillar 3; III: Pillar 1
I: Pillar 2; II: Pillar 2; III: Pillar 1

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank: map an add-on, a disclosure and a liquidity ratio to the pillars.

**Concept and theory**

Basel II introduced a three-pillar approach to regulation, “going beyond the simple need for capital”:

| Pillar | Content (GARP) |
|---|---|
| 1: Regulatory Capital | Mandatory minimum capital for credit, market and operational risks, and a minimum liquidity ratio; for operational risk, also the “Sound Principles for the Management of Operational Risk” (last updated 2021). |
| 2: Supervisory Review Process | Adjustments to Pillar 1 requirements based on the specific risk profile of an institution, its activities and the quality of its risk management, as assessed by the regulator and by the firm itself. Since 2007-2009 this has produced capital add-ons, sometimes substantial. |
| 3: Market Discipline | Rules on mandatory information disclosures, yearly or quarterly, on the institution’s financial situation and risk information. |

Pillar 1 is the formula floor. Pillar 2 is where the supervisor tailors it to the individual firm. Pillar 3 lets the market see enough to discipline the bank.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I: an add-on based on the bank’s specific risk profile and quality of risk management is the textbook Pillar 2 adjustment. Pillar 2.

Item II: mandatory quarterly disclosure of financial situation and risk information. Pillar 3.

Item III: the minimum liquidity ratio is listed by GARP inside Pillar 1. Pillar 1.

**Fragile fact.** The minimum liquidity ratio sits in Pillar 1 (with minimum capital); Pillar 2 is the firm-specific adjustment, including add-ons.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Regulatory Capital” (three pillars). Schweser LO 48.b, “The Basel regulatory framework has three associated pillars.” No conflict; GARP adds the Sound Principles and the add-on detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: Option A (2, 3, 1) matches the pillar definitions in GARP Section 7.3.

b.reason: (sibling swap (liquidity to Pillar 2)). B places the minimum liquidity ratio in Pillar 2, as if liquidity were a firm-specific supervisory adjustment. GARP lists “minimum liquidity ratio” in Pillar 1. B would be correct if Item III described a supervisor requiring this particular bank to hold extra liquidity after a review of its specific risk profile.

c.reason: (sibling swap (add-on to Pillar 1)). C treats the add-on as Pillar 1 because it is capital. The add-on comes from the supervisory assessment of the specific institution, which is Pillar 2. C would be correct if Item I described the standard minimum capital that every bank must hold under the formula.

d.reason: (sibling swap (disclosure to Pillar 2)). D places mandatory public disclosure in the supervisory review pillar. Disclosure to the market is Pillar 3. D would be correct if Item II described confidential reporting to the supervisor as an input to its review of the bank.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is asked by the board risk committee to explain in one sentence how regulatory capital differs from economic capital. Which of the following sentences is most accurate?

options.text: Regulatory capital is the level a bank calibrates to its own risk profile and target rating, while economic capital is the minimum prescribed by supervisors.
Regulatory capital is a supervisory minimum covering unexpected losses, while economic capital is the own funds a bank judges necessary to cover its expected losses.
Regulatory capital is a supervisory minimum, while economic capital equals the Pillar 1 requirement alone, because Pillar 2 is set by the supervisor only.
Regulatory capital is a supervisory minimum that is not very risk sensitive, while economic capital is the own funds a bank judges necessary for unexpected losses.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore CRO: one-sentence difference between regulatory and economic capital.

**Concept and theory**

The two capital measures answer different questions:

| Dimension | Regulatory capital | Economic capital |
|---|---|---|
| Who sets it | Supervisors, following BCBS rules | The bank itself (“judges necessary”) |
| What it is | Minimum equity and long-term stable funding | Own funds (equity and subordinated debt) |
| What it covers | Credit, market, operational risk minimums (plus liquidity ratio) | Any unexpected loss in one or more risk types |
| Risk sensitivity | “Not very risk sensitive,” especially under standardized Pillar 1 approaches | Intended to fully reflect the firm’s risk profile |
| Main driver of level | Formula minimum | Maintenance of credit rating, hence cost of funds |
| Closest regulatory proxy | Pillar 1 | Pillars 1 and 2 combined |

GARP’s motivation for economic capital: “Despite the efforts of regulators, the regulatory capital requirement is not very risk sensitive and is unlikely to fully reflect the risk profile of the firm and therefore may not serve as a reliable metric.”

**Applying it to this question**

A one-sentence differentiation must get three things right: who sets each measure, what economic capital covers (unexpected losses), and the weakness of regulatory capital (low risk sensitivity). Check each option against the table.

**Fragile fact.** Economic capital covers unexpected losses and is set by the bank; regulatory capital is the supervisory floor and is not very risk sensitive.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.1 and Section 7.3, “The Role of Regulatory Capital” and “The Role of Economic Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b, “Economic Capital.” Schweser does not mention low risk sensitivity or the own-funds composition (GARP only). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: (role misassignment). A reverses the actors: it gives the bank’s own calibration to regulatory capital and the supervisory minimum to economic capital. A would be correct if the two labels were swapped.

b.reason: (sibling swap (expected for unexpected loss)). B says economic capital covers expected losses. GARP says it covers “any unexpected loss”; expected losses are deducted in the RAROC numerator, not funded by capital. B would be correct if “expected” were replaced by “unexpected.”

c.reason: (scope error). C equates economic capital with Pillar 1 alone and claims Pillar 2 is set by the supervisor only. GARP says Pillars 1 and 2 combined are the closest regulatory equivalent to economic capital, and Pillar 2 is assessed “by the regulator and by the firm itself.” C would be correct if it read “closest to the Pillar 1 plus Pillar 2 requirement.”

d.reason: Option D states the supervisory, not very risk-sensitive nature of regulatory capital and GARP’s definition of economic capital as the own funds a bank judges necessary to cover unexpected losses.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a large UK bank is validating the methodology document for the bank’s economic capital model. The document contains the statements below. Which of the following statements in the document is NOT correct?

options.text: Pillar 2 assessments compensate for insufficiencies in Pillar 1 approaches, so Pillars 1 and 2 combined are the closest regulatory equivalent to economic capital.
Because economic capital is an internal measure, it should exclude qualitative capital overlays and rely only on risks that can be measured with internal models.
The own funds counted as economic capital are made of equity and subordinated debt, held to cover unexpected losses arising in one or more risk types.
Economic capital is calculated like a value-at-risk on the bank’s revenue distribution, taking into account a diversification effect across all risk types.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK bank: which statement in the economic capital methodology is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s description of how economic capital is built has four parts:

1. **Why Pillar 2 matters.** Regulatory capital is not very risk sensitive, especially under standardized approaches. “Pillar 2 assessment requirements are meant to compensate for the insufficiencies of the Pillar 1 regulatory capital approaches and adjust to cover risks not fully captured by Pillar 1. As such, the combined assessments of Pillars 1 and 2 are the closest regulatory equivalent to economic capital.”
2. **What it is made of.** “The level of own funds (made of equity and subordinated debt) that a bank or an insurance company judges necessary to cover for any unexpected loss that may arise for one or more risk types.”
3. **How it is estimated.** “Tier-1 banks calculate economic capital needs through internal modeling approaches and, often, qualitative capital overlays for hard to measure and emerging risks.”
4. **What it resembles.** It “is calculated like a VaR on the revenue distribution of the organization, considering a diversification effect across all risk types.”

The overlays matter because the purpose of economic capital is to capture the full risk profile, including risks that models cannot yet measure.

**Applying it to this question**

A, C and D restate points 1, 2 and 4. Option B says economic capital should exclude qualitative overlays and rely only on modelled risks; GARP says large banks often add qualitative overlays precisely for hard-to-measure and emerging risks. B is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** Economic capital includes qualitative overlays for hard-to-measure and emerging risks; “internal” does not mean “model-only.”

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Economic Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b states that Pillars 1 and 2 combined most accurately reflect economic capital; the own-funds composition, overlays and VaR description are GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (true statement (not the answer)). A restates GARP’s Pillar 2 logic and its conclusion. It would be the answer only if it said Pillar 1 alone is the closest equivalent.

b.reason: Option B contradicts GARP’s statement that economic capital uses internal models “and, often, qualitative capital overlays for hard to measure and emerging risks.” Excluding them would leave the very risks that Pillar 1 misses uncovered.

c.reason: (true statement (not the answer)). C restates GARP’s definition (equity and subordinated debt; unexpected losses in one or more risk types). It would be the answer if it said “expected losses” or “equity only.”

d.reason: (true statement (not the answer)). D restates GARP’s “like a VaR on the revenue distribution... considering a diversification effect across all risk types.” It would be the answer if it said economic capital is computed separately for each risk type with no diversification.

questions.question:
The treasurer of an Australian bank currently calibrates economic capital to its A rating. The board has approved a strategy to reach an AA rating. The treasurer uses the one-year default probabilities below. The bank’s Pillar 1 requirement is AUD 4.2 billion.

| Rating | One-year default probability (bp) |
|---|---|
| AAA | 1 |
| AA | 3 |
| A | 7 |
| BBB | 20 |

Which of the following best describes the confidence level at which economic capital must now cover unexpected losses, and the effect on the amount of economic capital?

options.text: 99.97%, and the bank will need less economic capital than it holds today.
99.70%, and the bank will need more economic capital than it holds today.
99.97%, and the bank will need more economic capital than it holds today.
99.90%, and the bank will need more economic capital than it holds today.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank moves its target rating from A to AA: confidence level and capital.

**Concept and theory**

A bank sizes economic capital so that the probability of losses exceeding it over one year equals the default probability of the rating it wants to keep. If the target rating has a one-year default probability $P D$, the confidence level is

Confidence level = 1 $- P D_{\text{target rating}}.$

GARP’s examples: AAA firms default on average 0.01% (1 basis point) per year, so a AAA target implies 99.99%; AA firms default 3 bp, so a bank aiming for AA “will calculate its economic capital such that it covers unexpected losses for any risk at a 99.97% confidence interval.” Figure 7.4 shows that the further out in the loss tail the bank sets its threshold (AA at 99.97%, AAA at 99.99%, versus the regulatory threshold at 99.9%), the more capital it needs. Remember that 1 bp = 0.01%.

**Applying it to this question**

$P D_{\text{AA}}$ = 3 bp = 0.03%

Confidence $\text{level}_{\text{AA}}$ = 100% − 0.03% = 99.97%

Current $\text{level}_{\text{A}}$ = 100% − 0.07% = 99.93%

Moving from 99.93% to 99.97% pushes the threshold further into the loss tail, so the bank must hold more economic capital. The Pillar 1 figure of AUD 4.2 billion is irrelevant: it does not depend on the target rating.

**Fragile fact.** 1 bp = 0.01%; a higher target rating means a higher confidence level and more economic capital.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Economic Capital,” and Figure 7.4 “Economic capital and credit rating.” Schweser LO 48.b gives the AAA example (0.01%, 99.99%). The A and BBB default probabilities are data supplied in the stem. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip). Right confidence level, wrong direction. A higher rating needs a higher confidence level and therefore more capital. A would be correct if the bank were moving from AA down to A.

b.reason: (unit slip (bp read as %)). 100% − 0.3% = 99.70% treats 3 bp as 0.3% instead of 0.03%. B would be correct only if the AA default probability were 30 bp.

c.reason: Option C gives the AA confidence level (99.97%) and the correct direction (more capital), consistent with GARP’s AA example and Figure 7.4.

d.reason: (sibling swap (regulatory threshold)). 99.90% is the regulatory threshold shown in GARP Figure 7.4, not the AA target. D would be correct if the stem asked for the confidence level of the regulatory capital threshold.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Brazilian bank argues that, because capital is an expensive source of funding, the bank should cut its economic capital down to the regulatory minimum to reduce its funding costs. Which of the following responses by the chief risk officer is most accurate?

options.text: Cutting economic capital raises the confidence level at which unexpected losses are covered, so the bank’s credit rating and funding costs would both improve.
Economic capital is set by the supervisor under Pillar 1, so the board can change only the regulatory capital, which is the bank’s own internal estimate.
Cutting economic capital leaves the credit rating unchanged, because the rating depends on regulatory capital only, so the funding saving would be fully realized.
Cutting economic capital shrinks the buffer against losses and weakens creditworthiness, which tends to raise the cost of raising funds and offsets the saving.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank: should economic capital be cut to the regulatory minimum to save funding costs?

**Concept and theory**

Why do banks hold more capital than the regulator requires? GARP: “The level of economic capital that large banks require for themselves is largely linked to the maintenance of their credit rating, which then influences their cost of funds. The larger the capital, the bigger the buffer against losses, the better the creditworthiness of the institution, the lower the costs of raising funds.” At the same time, “capital is an expensive source of funding,” which is why banks track the risk-return trade-off of their activities through RAROC. So there are two opposing costs:

- holding more capital: capital itself is expensive;
- holding less capital: a thinner buffer, weaker creditworthiness and a higher cost of all other funding.

The bank sets economic capital where this trade-off matches the rating it wants. The regulatory minimum is only a floor.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member sees only the first cost. The decisive fact is the chain: capital → buffer → creditworthiness → cost of raising funds. Cutting capital moves every link in the wrong direction, so the funding saving is offset.

**Fragile fact.** More capital → better creditworthiness → lower cost of funds, even though capital itself is an expensive source of funding.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “The Role of Economic Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b: “a larger amount of capital provides more protection against unexpected losses and will support a higher credit rating. Higher ratings translate to lower borrowing costs.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip). Cutting capital lowers, not raises, the confidence level at which unexpected losses are covered, so the rating would weaken. A would be correct if the member had proposed increasing economic capital (although capital itself is expensive).

b.reason: (role misassignment). B reverses the actors: economic capital is the bank’s own estimate, while regulatory capital is the supervisory requirement under Pillar 1. B would be correct if the two labels were swapped.

c.reason: (scope error, absolute claim). C claims the rating depends only on regulatory capital. GARP links the level of economic capital to maintaining the credit rating. C would be correct only if the bank had no rating target, in which case the trade-off with funding costs would disappear.

d.reason: Option D states GARP’s causal chain in the correct direction: less capital, smaller buffer, weaker creditworthiness, higher cost of raising funds.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is calculating the risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC) of its SME lending business line for the coming year, using the data below.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Expected revenues (CNY million) | 180 |
| Operating costs (CNY million) | 60 |
| Expected credit losses (CNY million) | 40 |
| Tax rate (%) | 25 |
| Economic capital allocated (CNY million) | 250 |
| Pillar 1 regulatory capital (CNY million) | 175 |

What is the RAROC of the business line?
questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank SME line: compute RAROC from revenues, costs, expected loss, tax and capital.

**Concept and theory**

RAROC was developed by Bankers Trust in the late 1970s and adopted widely in the 1980s and 1990s under Basel I. It is a risk-adjusted version of return on equity (ROE). Compared with return on capital (ROC), RAROC makes two changes: the numerator is adjusted for the expected losses (EL) generated by the risk of the activity, and the denominator is economic capital, “the equity needed to cover the risks taken.” GARP:

RAROC = $\frac{\text{Expected after-tax risk-adjusted net income}}{\text{Economic capital}}$

Here risk-adjusted net income is revenues minus costs minus EL; after tax means multiplying by (1 $- t$), where $t$ is the tax rate. Regulatory capital is not the denominator; economic capital is the capital the bank actually sets aside, or mobilizes, for the activity.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line (CNY million):

Risk-adjusted pre-tax income = 180 − 60 − 40 = 80

After-tax risk-adjusted income = 80 × (1 − 0.25) = 60

RAROC = $\frac{60}{250}$ = 24.00%

The Pillar 1 regulatory capital of CNY 175 million is an irrelevant input. The SME line earns 24% after tax on the economic capital it uses. That figure can be compared with the minimum RAROC the bank sets for pricing and for managing its commercial teams.

**Fragile fact.** The denominator is economic capital, not regulatory capital, and the numerator is after tax and net of EL.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “RAROC: Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital” (GARP notes that RAROC is covered in more detail in Chapter 18). Schweser LO 48.b, “Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: Option A uses expected after-tax risk-adjusted net income in the numerator and economic capital in the denominator, as GARP defines RAROC.

b.reason: (dropped term (tax)). 80/250 = 32.00% uses pre-tax income. B would be correct if the stem defined RAROC on a pre-tax basis or the tax rate were zero.

c.reason: (sibling swap (regulatory capital denominator)). 60/175 = 34.29% divides by Pillar 1 regulatory capital instead of economic capital. C would be correct only if the stem asked for a return on regulatory capital.

d.reason: (dropped term (expected loss)). (180 − 60) × 0.75/250 = 90/250 = 36.00% omits the EL adjustment, which is what makes the measure “risk-adjusted.” D would be correct if expected credit losses were zero.

questions.question:
A risk consultant engaged by a Hong Kong bank is drafting a policy note on extending risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC) beyond the lending book. The draft contains the following statements:

I. RAROC is more straightforward for credit activities, because expected losses can be estimated using historical data.

II. For market risk activities, expected loss in the RAROC numerator is less straightforward and is often set at zero.

III. RAROC is widely used for operational risk, because revenues can be attributed explicitly to operational risk taking.

IV. RAROC can be estimated at the level of a transaction, a client, a portfolio or an entire business line.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Hong Kong bank: which statements about extending RAROC beyond lending are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

RAROC needs two inputs that are easy to estimate in lending and harder elsewhere: an expected loss figure for the numerator, and revenues that can be attributed to the risk taken. GARP:

| Risk type | RAROC applicability (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Credit | “More straightforward,” because EL can be estimated using historical data; RAROC is “mostly applicable to credit risk.” |
| Market | EL “is less straightforward and is often set at 0.” |
| Operational | “Generally not used,” due to the difficulty of attributing explicit revenues to operational risk and the uncertainty of economic capital. |

Granularity: RAROC “can be estimated at different levels of granularity”: a transaction, a client, a portfolio or an entire business line. Minimum RAROC requirements at these levels let managers price transactions, quantify funding costs, manage scarce capital and manage commercial agents by objectives.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: credit is more straightforward because EL comes from historical data. True.

Statement II: for market risk, EL is often set at 0. True.

Statement III: says RAROC is widely used for operational risk because revenues are easy to attribute. GARP says the opposite on both counts. False.

Statement IV: transaction, client, portfolio or business line. True.

Accurate set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** RAROC: credit straightforward (EL from history); market EL often 0; operational risk generally not used.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “RAROC: Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital.” Schweser LO 48.b, “Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital” (“ELs are often set to zero for market risks, and RAROC is often not used for operational risks”). No conflict; the reason for not using RAROC for operational risk is GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: (scope error, too narrow). A rejects Statement IV, as if RAROC were computed only at one level. GARP lists all four levels. A would be correct if IV had said RAROC can be computed only at the business-line level.

b.reason:
(polarity flip accepted). B accepts Statement III, which reverses GARP on operational risk (“generally not used,” because revenues are hard to attribute), and drops the true Statement

II. B would be correct only if III described credit risk instead of operational risk and II were false.

c.reason: Option C contains exactly the true statements I, II and IV.

d.reason: (polarity flip accepted, true statement rejected). D accepts III and rejects I. D would be correct only if credit EL could not be estimated from history and operational risk revenues were easy to attribute, the reverse of GARP.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a German banking group is explaining to the supervisory board why the group’s aggregated capital is lower than the sum of its stand-alone capital for credit, market and operational risk. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Regulators allow no diversification across credit, market and operational risk, so the lower aggregate reflects only diversification within each risk class.
Operational risk tends to move relatively independently, while credit and market risk correlations tend to rise in crises, so it brings important diversification benefits.
Operational risk correlations with credit and market risk tend to rise sharply in crises, so its diversification benefit is small and largely disappears under stress.
Operational risk is perfectly correlated with credit risk because both are driven by the same economic and market conditions, so its benefit comes from market risk only.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German banking group: why aggregated capital is below the sum of stand-alone capital.

**Concept and theory**

Once capital is estimated for each risk class, the bank assesses aggregate capital needs. GARP:

- “Because not all risks will materialize at the same time, regulators allow for some diversification measures across the classes of credit risk, market risk, and operational risk.”
- Aggregation across classes is **inter-risk diversification**; it supplements **intra-risk diversi-** **fication**, which is diversification within each risk class.
- Because each risk class follows different dynamics, total aggregated capital is lower than the sum of stand-alone amounts; the reduction is the diversification benefit.
- Operational risk “can bring important diversification benefits to the total capital, as it typically has a low correlation to other types of financial risks, due to its different risk drivers. Whereas credit and market risk correlations tend to increase in times of crisis, operational risks tend to move relatively independently.” Diversified operational risk capital can be 30% to 40% lower than the sum of the components.

Intuition: credit and market losses share the same drivers (economic and market conditions), so they tend to arrive together in a crisis; operational losses come from processes, people and systems, so they do not.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks why the aggregate is lower. The decisive facts are (1) regulators allow cross-class diversification, and (2) operational risk moves relatively independently while credit and market risk correlations rise in crises. Only one option states both directions correctly.

**Fragile fact.** In a crisis, credit and market correlations rise; operational risk tends to move relatively independently.

**Reference**

LO 48.b (verbatim above). GARP Chapter 7, Section 7.3, “Risk Aggregation for Capital Assessment,” and Figure 7.5. Schweser LO 48.b, “Capital Assessment Risk Aggregation.” The crisis-correlation contrast and the 30% to 40% figure are GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-7 b, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (absolute claim). A says regulators allow no cross-class diversification. GARP says regulators allow “some diversification measures across the classes.” A would be correct if it described only intra-risk diversification and the stem said that the bank aggregates by simple summation across classes.

b.reason: Option B restates GARP: operational risk moves relatively independently, while credit and market risk correlations rise in crises, so operational risk brings important diversification benefits.

c.reason: (polarity flip / sibling swap). C attributes to operational risk the crisis behavior of credit and market risk (correlations rising in crises). C would be correct if “operational risk” were replaced by “market risk” when describing correlation with credit risk.

d.reason: (absolute claim, wrong drivers). D claims perfect correlation with credit risk and gives operational risk the drivers of credit and market risk. GARP says operational risk has low correlation and different drivers. D would be correct only for a pair of risk classes that truly share drivers, and even then GARP never claims perfect correlation.
