questions.source: High quality paper ORR-8 c Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a bank in Singapore is briefing the audit committee on what to expect from supervisory reviews of the bank’s information security controls. She has drafted four statements:

I. On-site reviews usually consist of one or more meetings with the institution at its premises, whereas off-site reviews usually consist of a desk-based assessment of documentation or a meeting at the regulator’s office.

II. Risk specialists typically draw on documentary evidence such as survey responses, physical inspections, incident reports and in-person meetings to assess the adequacy of controls.

III. Reviews of information security controls are completed either as part of general technology assessments or as part of risk management assessments more broadly.

IV. Because supervisory expectations are aligned with industry standards such as COBIT and NIST, the approach, depth and breadth of supervisory assessments are now largely uniform across jurisdictions.

Which of the statements are consistent with the practices observed by the Basel Committee?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor in Singapore briefing the audit committee on supervisory reviews of information security controls.

**Concept and theory**

Supervisors gather evidence on cyber controls in two settings.

| Mode | Typical form | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| On-site review | One or more meetings at the institution’s premises | Direct observation, talking to specialists |
| Off-site review | Desk-based assessment of documents, or a meeting at the regulator’s office | Lower-cost monitoring and preparation |

Most jurisdictions use both to assess compliance with regulatory standards and alignment with good practice. Risk specialists rely on documentary evidence: survey responses, physical inspections, incident reports and in-person meetings. Reviews sit either inside general technology assessments or inside broader risk management assessments. They tend to cover governance and strategy, management and frameworks, controls, third-party arrangements, training, monitoring and detection, response and recovery, and information-sharing and communication.

A key point: many supervisory expectations are aligned with industry standards such as COBIT and NIST, but the approach, depth and breadth of assessments still vary between jurisdictions. A common reference framework does not produce a common supervisory method.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the source.

- I matches the GARP footnote on on-site and off-site reviews. True.
- II matches the list of evidence risk specialists draw on. True.
- III matches “either as part of general technology assessments or risk management assessments more broadly”. True.
- IV states that alignment with standards makes assessments uniform. The source says the opposite: they vary. False.

So I, II and III only: option D.

**Fragile fact.** Common standards (COBIT, NIST) shape expectations, but approach, depth and breadth of supervision still vary. Do not infer uniform methods from common frameworks.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Methods for Supervising Cyber-Resilience: Risk Specialists Assess Information Security Management and Controls”, including footnote 12 on on-site and off-site reviews. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser compresses the evidence list (“survey responses, inspections, and meetings with risk personnel”) and does not give the on-site and off-site definitions; GARP is used. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q2 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A omits statement III, which is a true description of the context of reviews. It would be correct if III had said that reviews take place only within capital adequacy assessments.

b.reason: **Polarity flip (accepting IV).** B accepts IV, which reverses “vary” into “largely uniform”. B would be correct only if the source had found harmonised supervisory methods, which it does not. The report in fact notes that each authority designs its own assessment tools even when using common frameworks.

c.reason: **Polarity flip (accepting IV).** C includes IV and omits II. It inherits the polarity error and also drops a true evidence statement. It would be right only if IV were true and II false.

d.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “Many supervisory expectations are aligned with industry standards (eg COBIT, NIST) but approach, depth and breadth of supervisory assessments vary between jurisdictions.” Together with the evidence list, the footnote definitions and the two review contexts, this makes I, II and III true and IV false.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a newly established banking supervisor that has a small specialist IT risk team and many institutions to oversee. The supervisor asks which capacity-building practices have been observed in other jurisdictions. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Some jurisdictions give front-line supervisors guidelines, questionnaires and tools to triage IT risk issues, and some can appoint an auditor or other third party to report to the regulator, including on cyber.

Some jurisdictions equip front-line supervisors with tools to triage IT risk issues, and some can require the institution’s board to appoint an auditor whose cyber report is addressed only to that board.
Front-line supervisors are generally kept out of IT risk assessment, because the size of specialist risk teams is broadly similar across jurisdictions and triage tools are not used in practice.
Some jurisdictions equip front-line supervisors with tools to triage IT risk issues, and appointing a third party to report on cyber risk has replaced on-site inspection wherever that power exists.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant advising a new supervisor with a small IT risk team on capacity-building practices.

**Concept and theory**

The number, type and nature of regulated institutions vary by jurisdiction, and so does the size of the regulator’s specialist risk teams. Two capacity-building practices address this mismatch.

| Practice | Examples in GARP |  | How it helps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equip front-line supervisors to triage IT risk | Australia, Brazil, pore | Singa- | Guidelines on identifying and evaluating IT risk, questionnaires, risk assessments and tools to quantify risk assessments |
| Power to appoint an auditor or other third party | Australia, UK |  | The third party provides a report to the regulator on an aspect of risk management, including cyber |

Triage lets generalist supervisors spot and escalate IT issues so specialists focus where risk is highest. The appointment power lets the authority obtain expert evidence without having all skills in-house.

**Applying it to this question**

The supervisor has a small specialist team. The question asks which practices exist. The two deciding facts are: front-line supervisors in some jurisdictions are given triage tools, and some authorities can appoint a third party that reports to the regulator. Only option A gets both, with the report going to the regulator.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: the appointed auditor or third party reports to the regulator. Triage examples: Australia, Brazil, Singapore; appointment power examples: Australia, UK.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Methods for Supervising Cyber-Resilience: Risk Specialists Assess Information Security Management and Controls”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q3 of 20.

a.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “Some jurisdictions (eg Australia, Brazil and Singapore) have developed approaches to equip front-line supervisors with knowledge and tools to assess (triage) IT risk issues”, and “a number of jurisdictions (eg Australia and the UK) have powers to appoint an auditor or other third party to provide a report to the regulator on a particular aspect of the regulated institutions’ risk management, including cyber.”

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The appointed party reports to the regulator, not only to the institution’s board. B moves the recipient of the report. It would be correct if the stem described an institution commissioning its own external review for its board.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source says specialist team sizes vary and that some jurisdictions do equip front-line supervisors. C reverses both. It would be correct only if specialist capacity were uniform and triage tools were absent.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The appointment power is an additional tool, not a replacement for on-site inspection. The source still describes on-site reviews as standard. D would be right only if the report had said that third-party reports had displaced inspections.

questions.question: The head of policy at a prudential regulator is preparing a paper for the regulator’s executive committee on how the authority should engage with industry on cyber-resilience. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Industry engagement is used only to influence industry behaviour; authorities avoid using it to seek industry views, since doing so could compromise the independence of supervisory judgement.
Industry engagement is confined to regulated banks; third-party service providers are excluded from such events because they sit outside the prudential perimeter.
Industry engagement is used to influence industry behaviour or to seek feedback that informs regulatory work, and messages sent through these channels can be faster and more responsive.
Industry engagement relies mainly on binding discussion papers, such as those issued by the ACPR and the PRA in 2018, which set enforceable cyber-resilience standards for the sector.

questions.solution:
Head of policy at a regulator preparing a paper on industry engagement on cyber-resilience.

**Concept and theory**

Supervision is not only inspection. Jurisdictions increasingly engage with industry, and GARP names two purposes:

1. to influence industry behaviour, and
2. to seek feedback and views that inform regulatory work.

Channels include discussion papers (the French ACPR on IT risk and the UK PRA on operational resilience, both in 2018), speaking at conferences, and publications such as white papers, information papers, annual reports and letters to industry. Some jurisdictions include third-party service providers: in the EU, the European Commission EU FinTech Lab and the EBA FinTech Knowledge Hub organised events with regulators, supervisors, industry and third-party providers. GARP notes that communicating key messages through these channels can be faster and more responsive than formal rule-making.

**Applying it to this question**

The paper is about how and why to engage. The deciding facts are the two purposes (influence and feedback) and the speed advantage. Option C contains both; the others narrow the purpose, exclude third parties or confuse engagement with rule-making.

**Fragile fact.** Two purposes: influence behaviour and seek feedback. ACPR paper: IT risk; PRA paper: operational resilience (do not swap them).

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Jurisdictions Increasingly Engage With Industry to Address Cyber-Resilience”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q4 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A keeps one purpose and drops the other. Seeking feedback is expressly a purpose. A would be correct if the question asked for one purpose of engagement, without the word “only”.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says some jurisdictions include third-party service providers, citing the EU FinTech Lab and EBA FinTech Knowledge Hub events. B reverses this. It would be correct only for a jurisdiction that restricts engagement to banks, which the report does not present as the observed practice.

c.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Jurisdictions Increasingly Engage With Industry to Address Cyber-Resilience”: “Industry engagement is used to either influence industry behaviour, or to seek feedback and views to inform regulatory work” and “Communicating key messages through these channels can be faster and more responsive.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Discussion papers are consultative engagement tools, not binding standards. D gives them the property of enforceable regulation. It would be correct if the stem referred to prescriptive regulations (49.a material), not discussion papers.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of an Australian bank has proposed a project, budgeted at AUD 4.5 million over 18 months, to map and classify the bank’s business services and the assets and services that support them. A board member asks why this mapping matters for cyber-resilience. Which of the following justifications is most accurate?

options.text: The mapping removes the need for a separate business impact analysis, since criticality is captured directly in the asset register and no further impact assessment is then required.
The mapping is chiefly needed to calculate the bank’s minimum capital requirement for cyber-risk, which supervisors derive from the number of critical assets recorded.
The mapping should cover only internally provided services, since services that depend on external third parties are assessed under separate outsourcing rules instead.
Understanding business services and supporting assets, with their criticality and sensitivity, allows testing and assurance of end-to-end business services to be designed.

questions.solution:
CRO of an Australian bank justifying a project to map and classify business services and supporting assets.

**Concept and theory**

To test whether a bank can keep delivering what matters, it must first know what it delivers and what each service depends on. Most jurisdictions (for example Australia, the EU, Hong Kong, Singapore and the US) recognise mapping and classifying business services and their supporting assets and services as good practice and as a basis for building resilience. A clear understanding of business services and supporting assets, including their criticality and sensitivity, can be used to design testing and assurance of end-to-end business services. The mapping is typically completed as part of:

- business impact analysis;
- recovery and resolution planning;
- reviewing the dependency of critical services on external third parties; and
- scoping for assessments.

Think of it as the wiring diagram: without it, a test of one system says little about whether the whole service survives.

**Applying it to this question**

The budget figure (AUD 4.5 million over 18 months) is irrelevant to the decision. The question asks why mapping matters. The deciding fact is that it underpins the design of testing and assurance of end-to-end business services. Option D states this.

**Fragile fact.** Mapping feeds end-to-end testing and assurance, and includes third-party dependencies. It is done within BIA, not instead of it.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Information Security Controls Testing and Independent Assurance: Mapping and Classifying Business Services Should Inform Testing and Assurance”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists business impact analysis, recovery planning and scoping, and omits the third-party dependency review and the end-to-end purpose; GARP is used. Condensation, not a conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q5 of 20.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Mapping is typically done as part of business impact analysis; it does not replace it. A treats a component as a substitute for its parent process. It would be correct only if the source had said that mapping supersedes BIA.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** The report expressly approaches resilience beyond the purview of operational risk management and minimum capital requirements. Mapping supports testing and assurance, not a capital calculation. B would be correct only in a capital-modelling context unrelated to this reading.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP lists “reviewing dependency of critical services on external third parties” as one of the uses of mapping. Excluding third-party dependencies drops this condition. C would be correct only if the bank had no external dependencies.

d.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Mapping and Classifying Business Services Should Inform Testing and Assurance”: “A clear understanding of business services and supporting assets (and their criticality and sensitivity) can be used to design testing and assurance of end-to-end business services.”

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a supervisory authority is presenting to newly hired analysts on how supervisors assess institutions’ detection capabilities and the assurance placed on controls. Which of the following statements in her presentation is least accurate?

options.text: A number of jurisdictions assess institutions’ monitoring and surveillance of emerging threats, including real-time detection and the ability to detect adversaries before they move between systems.
Independent assurance tells management and regulators whether controls have been designed, but regulators generally do not use the management information that these activities produce.
Some jurisdictions perform thematic reviews, such as a review of access controls and of user access rights, while others apply existing international standards to other types of institution.
Reviewing controls is only one aspect of building cyber-resilience, but many jurisdictions find a review of controls a ready way to engage with the institutions they regulate.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst presenting to new hires on detection capability reviews and independent assurance; find the least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond mapping services, supervisors look at whether institutions can see attacks and whether anyone independent has checked the controls.

- **Monitoring and surveillance.** A number of jurisdictions assess monitoring and surveillance of emerging threats: real-time detection capability, the ability to detect adversaries before they move between systems, and relevant continuity and control policies.
- **Review styles.** Some jurisdictions run thematic reviews (Sweden reviewed access controls and management of user access rights). Others apply existing international standards to other types of institution (South Africa applies the CPMI-IOSCO guidance on cyber-resilience for FMIs to banks).
- **Independent assurance.** It gives management and regulators an evaluation of whether appropriate controls have been implemented effectively. Jurisdictions commonly also leverage the management information outputs of these activities as another input to their own assessments.
- **Controls as an entry point.** Controls are only one aspect of resilience, but many jurisdictions find a review of controls a ready way to engage with institutions.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is “least accurate”. Statements A, C and D track the source. Statement B makes two departures in one clause structure: it narrows assurance to design (the source says implemented effectively) and it says regulators do not use the management information, when the source says they commonly do. The core error is the polarity on use of management information.

**Fragile fact.** Independent assurance tests whether controls are implemented effectively, and regulators do leverage its management information outputs.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Information Security Controls Testing and Independent Assurance” and opening of “Taxonomy of Cyber-Risk Controls”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says audits check “whether appropriate controls exist”, which is weaker than GARP’s “implemented effectively”; GARP is used. Condensation, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q6 of 20.

a.reason: **True statement (qualifier trap).** A matches the monitoring and surveillance sentence, including real-time detection and detecting adversaries before they move between systems. Choosing it misreads “least accurate”. A would be the false one only if it claimed this assessment was universal.

b.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “Independent assurance also provides management and regulators with an evaluation of whether appropriate controls have been implemented effectively. Jurisdictions commonly also leverage the management information outputs of these activities, providing the regulator with another source of information for their own assessments.” B contradicts this, so it is the least accurate statement.

c.reason: **True statement (qualifier trap).** C matches the thematic review example (access controls and user access rights) and the practice of applying international standards to other institution types. It would be false only if it said thematic reviews had replaced all other approaches.

d.reason: **True statement (qualifier trap).** D matches the opening of the taxonomy discussion: controls are only one aspect of resilience but a ready way to engage. It would be false if it said controls reviews were sufficient on their own.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a large EUR-reporting bank is preparing a note for the CRO on supervisory penetration testing in Europe. The note contains four statements:

I. Five EU jurisdictions have developed programmes of regulator-led penetration tests, and three authorities (the ECB, the Netherlands and the UK) have provided guidance to institutions on how to test.

II. These tests are typically voluntary, funded by the supervisory authority that requests them, and targeted at larger, more systemic institutions.

III. Threat-led red team penetration tests delivered by third-party threat intelligence providers and penetration testers are becoming more widespread.

IV. The majority of directed penetration tests focus on institutions’ response and recovery capabilities, while only a few also test protective and detective capabilities.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a EUR bank auditing four statements on supervisory penetration testing in Europe.

**Concept and theory**

A penetration test simulates an attack to see whether controls hold. In the supervisory context GARP records these features:

| Feature | Observed practice |
|---|---|
| Regulator-led programmes | Five EU jurisdictions have developed programmes of regulator-led penetration tests |
| Guidance on how to test | Three authorities: the ECB, the Netherlands and the UK |
| Voluntary or mandatory | Typically voluntary |
| Who pays | Funded by the regulated institution |
| Who is tested | Targeted at larger, more systemic institutions |
| Trend | Threat-led red team tests by third-party threat intelligence and penetration testers becoming more widespread |
| Capabilities tested | Majority: protective and detective; a few: also response and recovery |

Red teaming is “threat-led” because current threat intelligence is used to design a realistic attack, rather than running a generic vulnerability scan.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: five EU jurisdictions with regulator-led programmes; ECB, Netherlands, UK guidance. True.
- II: voluntary and targeted at larger institutions are right, but “funded by the supervisory authority” is wrong; the regulated institution funds them. False.
- III: threat-led red teaming by third parties becoming more widespread. True.
- IV: reverses the focus; most tests target protective and detective capabilities. False.

So I and III only: option C.

**Fragile fact.** Voluntary, institution-funded, larger systemic institutions; majority test protect and detect, only a few test respond and recover. Five EU regulator-led programmes; three issuers of guidance (ECB, Netherlands, UK).

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Information Security Controls Testing and Independent Assurance: Penetration Testing”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says “several regulators in the EU” rather than five, and omits the targeting of larger, more systemic institutions and the threat-led red teaming trend; GARP is used. Condensation, not a conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q7 of 20.

a.reason: **Role misassignment (accepting II).** A accepts II, which assigns funding to the supervisor instead of the institution, and omits the true statement III. A would be correct only if II had said “funded by the regulated institution” and III were false.

b.reason: **Role misassignment and polarity flip.** B accepts both false statements (II’s funding actor and IV’s reversed focus) and rejects both true ones. It would be correct only if the funding and the capability focus were the reverse of what GARP reports.

c.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Penetration Testing”: “Five EU jurisdictions have developed programmes of regulator-led penetration tests and three (the ECB, the Netherlands and the UK) have provided guidance for regulated institutions on how to test. Tests are typically voluntary, funded by the regulated institution and targeted at larger, more systemic institutions. In particular, threat-led red team penetration tests delivered by third-party threat intelligence and penetration testers are becoming more widespread. The majority of directed penetration tests focus on regulated institutions’ protective and detective cyber-resilience capabilities, while a few also test response and recovery capabilities.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip (accepting IV).** D adds IV, which swaps “majority” and “few” between the two capability groups. D would be correct if IV read “the majority focus on protective and detective capabilities, while a few also test response and recovery”.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian bank (total assets CAD 310 billion) is reviewing the bank’s information security control testing programme before a supervisory visit. The CIO asks what the supervisor’s role in control testing typically is. Which of the following statements best describes the observed practice?

options.text: Supervisors review and challenge the institution’s approach to testing controls and its remediation of issues found, drawing on inputs such as vulnerability assessments and control testing reports.

Supervisors carry out the institution’s control testing themselves and set its cyber-risk appetite, so that controls are implemented against a supervisor-defined appetite rather than the institution’s own.
Supervisors review the results of the institution’s control tests but not the remediation of issues identified, since remediation is treated as a matter solely for the institution’s management.
Supervisors accept the institution’s own control testing reports as conclusive evidence that its controls are effective, so further review or challenge of the testing approach is not applied.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Canadian bank asking what the supervisor’s role in information security control testing is.

**Concept and theory**

Who does what in control testing is the heart of this target.

- **The institution** implements cyber-security controls through risk-based decisions against its own risk appetite, and tests information security controls applied to hardware, software and data to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from cyber-incidents.
- **The supervisor** reviews and challenges the institution’s approach to testing controls and the remediation of issues identified. Evidence includes survey responses, threat and vulnerability assessments, risk assessments, audit reports and control testing reports (for example penetration tests and health checks).

The supervisor is a reviewer and challenger, not the tester and not the setter of the institution’s appetite. Review and challenge means the reports are inputs to be questioned, not certificates to be accepted.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s size (CAD 310 billion) does not change the roles. The CIO asks about the supervisor’s role. The deciding fact is “review and challenge” of both the testing approach and remediation. Option A states this with the correct evidence sources.

**Fragile fact.** Actor check: the institution tests against its own appetite; the supervisor reviews and challenges the testing approach and remediation.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Information Security Controls Testing and Independent Assurance: Penetration Testing”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says institutions test controls “to detect and prevent” incidents, while GARP says “to prevent, detect, respond and recover”; GARP’s fuller scope is used. Condensation, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q8 of 20.

a.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Penetration Testing”: “Supervisors review and challenge regulated institutions’ approach to testing controls and the remediation of issues identified. This can include reviewing survey responses, threat and vulnerability assessments, risk assessments, audit reports and control testing reports (eg penetration testing, health checks).”

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The institution performs testing and sets its own risk appetite; controls are implemented “through risk-based decisions against a regulated institution’s risk appetite”. B gives both actions to the supervisor. B would be correct only in a regime where supervisors run their own tests (as in regulator-led programmes) and set appetite, which GARP does not describe.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The supervisor’s review expressly covers “the remediation of issues identified”. C drops this part of the scope. It would be correct if the source limited review to test results.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Treating institution reports as conclusive contradicts the “review and challenge” role. D would be correct only if supervisors relied on reports without any challenge, which the source does not describe.

questions.question: The CRO of a banking group headquartered in Frankfurt, with significant operations in four other EU member states, is considering a test under the European Framework for Threat Intelligence-based Ethical Red Teaming (TIBER-EU). Which of the following statements about such a test is most accurate?

options.text: The test would be scheduled by the ECB alone, because the framework removes the tested entity from any decision about whether or when a test is to be performed.
The test would follow a standard script common to all participating entities, so that the results can be ranked against those of peer institutions across Europe.
The test would end with a pass or fail rating, which the relevant authorities would then use to set the group’s category for cyber supervision.
The test could be run for the group as a cross-border entity under several authorities’ oversight, giving insight into strengths and weaknesses to improve cyber-maturity.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Frankfurt-headquartered group with operations in four other EU states considering a TIBER-EU test.

**Concept and theory**

In May 2018 the ECB published the European Framework for Threat Intelligence-based Ethical Red Teaming (TIBER-EU). Its key features:

| Feature | TIBER-EU |
|---|---|
| Status | First Europe-wide framework for controlled and bespoke tests against cyber-attacks in the financial market |
| Cross-border use | Facilitates testing of cross-border entities under the oversight of several authorities |
| Decision to test | Up to the relevant authorities and the entities themselves to decide if and when tests are performed |
| Design | Tailor-made |
| Outcome | No pass or fail; insight into strengths and weaknesses so the entity can learn and evolve its cyber-maturity |

The design reflects a learning purpose: a bespoke threat-led test against a realistic adversary is more useful for improvement than a standard exam that produces a grade.

**Applying it to this question**

The group is cross-border with operations in several member states. The deciding facts are that TIBER-EU facilitates testing of cross-border entities under the oversight of several authorities, and that its output is insight into strengths and weaknesses. Option D states both.

**Fragile fact.** TIBER-EU: ECB, May 2018; bespoke; authorities and entities decide if and when; cross-border entities under several authorities; no pass or fail.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Information Security Controls Testing and Independent Assurance: Penetration Testing” (TIBER-EU paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not name TIBER-EU in the text (only in a footnote) and omits the no pass or fail feature; GARP is used. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q9 of 20.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The decision on if and when to test rests with “the relevant authorities and the entities themselves”, not with the ECB alone. A would be correct only if the framework gave the ECB sole scheduling power.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B gives TIBER-EU the property of a standardised benchmarking exercise. TIBER-EU tests are bespoke and tailor-made, and are not designed to rank entities. B would describe a standardised survey or questionnaire programme, not TIBER-EU.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** TIBER-EU tests do not result in a pass or fail. C would be correct only for a compliance-style test with a graded outcome.

d.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: TIBER-EU “facilitates testing for cross-border entities under the oversight of several authorities” and tests “will not result in a pass or fail; rather they will provide the tested entity with insight into its strengths and weaknesses, and enable it to learn and evolve to improve cyber-maturity.”

questions.question: A supervisory authority has mapped its cyber supervision activities against its taxonomy of cyber and information security controls. It finds that none of its staff has the skills needed to assess banks’ cryptographic key management controls, although it has a general approach to reviewing access controls. How is this finding best characterised under the observed practices?

options.text: As a control deficiency at the banks concerned, which each bank must remediate before the authority’s next on-site inspection of its key management.
As a sign that the authority’s taxonomy departs from the harmonised international taxonomy of cyber-risk controls that authorities are expected to apply.
As a gap in the coverage of the authority’s supervisory approach, because the authority cannot assess that type of control without the required skillset.
As no gap, since a gap is recorded only where an authority has no supervisory approach at all, not where it lacks the skills to assess a control.

questions.solution:
Supervisor finds no staff can assess banks’ cryptographic key management controls after mapping against its control taxonomy.

**Concept and theory**

A taxonomy of cyber-risk controls is a structured list of control types (for example access control, key management, logging). Supervisors use it as a checklist for themselves: does our supervisory approach actually cover every control type? GARP states:

- some jurisdictions use taxonomies of controls to understand whether there are gaps in the coverage of their supervisory approach;
- taxonomies are currently jurisdiction-specific and do not rely on harmonised concepts and definitions;
- if an authority is unable to assess a type of control, for example because it has no supervisory approach, or no assessment method, or lacks the required skillset, that is identified as a gap.

The gap is in the supervisor’s coverage, not in the bank’s control environment.

**Applying it to this question**

The authority has a general approach to access controls (an irrelevant detail for key management) but no staff with skills to assess key management controls. Lack of skillset is one of the three named causes of a gap. So the finding is a gap in the coverage of the authority’s supervisory approach: option C.

**Fragile fact.** A taxonomy gap is the supervisor’s gap, caused by no approach, no method or no skillset. Taxonomies are jurisdiction-specific, not harmonised.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Information Security Controls Testing and Independent Assurance: Taxonomy of Cyber-Risk Controls”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says taxonomies identify “gaps in controls and supervision”, which blurs whose gap it is; GARP specifies gaps in the coverage of the supervisory approach and the three causes. GARP is used. Condensation, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q10 of 20.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The deficiency sits with the supervisor’s ability to assess, not with the banks’ controls. A would be correct if an inspection had found weak key management at the banks themselves.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** There is no harmonised international taxonomy; current taxonomies are jurisdiction-specific and do not rely on harmonised concepts and definitions. B would be correct only if a harmonised taxonomy existed.

c.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Taxonomy of Cyber-Risk Controls”: “If an authority is unable to assess a particular type of control, for example because it has no supervisory approach, assessment method or the required skillset to assess the control, then that is identified as a gap.”

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D keeps one cause (no supervisory approach) and drops the others (no assessment method, no skillset). D would be correct only if the definition of a gap were limited to the absence of a supervisory approach.

questions.question: A risk consultant is compiling a comparison of supervisory emphases in cyber-incident response for a client operating in several countries. Which of the following pairings of jurisdiction and emphasis is correct?

options.text: United States: assessing whether a bank’s internal and external communication plans and protocols include all relevant stakeholders, so as to avoid contagion.
Japan (JFSA and Bank of Japan): a focus on potential threats and on information-sharing in order to minimise delays in the reporting of cyber-incidents.
Canada: supervisory guidance on incident management covering identification of indicators of compromise, classification of events, and escalation and reporting.
China: no requirements beyond general business continuity rules, because the design of cyber-incident response is left wholly to the discretion of institutions.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant matching jurisdictions to their supervisory emphases in cyber-incident response.

**Concept and theory**

Although most response and recovery rules are general rather than cyber-specific, some jurisdictions have distinct emphases. GARP records the following.

| Jurisdiction |  | Emphasis |
|---|---|---|
| China (and India) |  | Prescribed a cyber-incident response framework as a key component of cyber-governance |
| United States |  | Supervisory guidance on incident management: identification of indicators of compromise, analysis and classification of events, and escalation and reporting of incidents |
| Japan (JFSA, Bank Japan) | of | Focus on potential threats and information-sharing to minimise delays in reporting cyber-incidents |
| Canada |  | Assessment of internal and external communication plans and protocols to see if all relevant stakeholders are included, to avoid contagion |

Each emphasis addresses a different failure point: governance design (China), the mechanics of handling an incident (US), speed of reporting (Japan), and communication that could otherwise spread the damage (Canada).

**Applying it to this question**

Check each pairing. A attaches Canada’s communication emphasis to the US. C attaches the US incident management guidance to Canada. D denies China’s prescribed framework. B matches the JFSA and Bank of Japan emphasis exactly.

**Fragile fact.** US: incident handling mechanics (IoC, classify, escalate, report). Japan: threats and sharing to cut reporting delays. Canada: stakeholder communication to avoid contagion. China: prescribed cyber-incident response framework.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Response and Recovery Testing and Exercising: Evaluation of Service Continuity, Response and Recovery Plans and Continuous Learning”. GARP vs Schweser conflict: Schweser names “China and Japan” as requiring cyber-specific frameworks within cyber-governance, whereas GARP names “China and India” and gives Japan a different emphasis (threats and information-sharing). Resolved from GARP; the question avoids making India or Japan’s framework status decisive. This looks like a transcription error in the condensed source rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q11 of 20.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Assessing communication plans to include all relevant stakeholders and avoid contagion is Canada’s emphasis. A would be correct with “Canada” in place of “United States”.

b.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “Some authorities, such as the Japanese Financial Services Agency (JFSA) and Bank of Japan, also focus on potential threats and information-sharing to minimise delays in reporting cyber-incidents.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Guidance on indicators of compromise, classification, escalation and reporting is the US emphasis. C would be correct with “United States” in place of “Canada”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** China is one of the few jurisdictions that prescribed a cyber-incident response framework as a key component of cyber-governance. D reverses this. It would describe a jurisdiction with only general continuity rules, which is the majority pattern but not China.

questions.question: A board member of a Japanese regional bank (balance sheet JPY 6.2 trillion) asks the chief compliance officer whether regulators generally impose cyber-specific rules on response and recovery. Which of the following answers best reflects the range of practices observed by the Basel Committee?

options.text: Most regulators require a framework or policy for prevention, detection, response and recovery, including incident reporting, but most rules are not cyber-specific and few have cyber-specific continuity rules.

Most regulators require a framework or policy for prevention, detection, response and recovery, and most such rules are cyber-specific, with the majority of regulators issuing cyber-specific continuity rules.
Most regulators maintain a single response and recovery framework for the whole sector themselves, and regulated institutions are required only to report their incidents into that framework.
Most regulators require a framework or policy covering response and recovery only, because prevention and detection are addressed entirely by separate information security control rules.

questions.solution:
CCO of a Japanese regional bank answering whether regulators impose cyber-specific response and recovery rules.

**Concept and theory**

Response and recovery is where resilience is proven: an incident has happened, and the question is how fast and how safely the institution restores service. GARP observes:

- the majority of regulators require entities to establish a framework or policy for prevention, detection, response and recovery activities, including incident reporting;
- specific requirements vary across supervisory authorities, and most are not specific to cyber-risk;
- few regulators have issued cyber-specific business continuity or disaster recovery requirements for the sector;
- a few jurisdictions (China and India) have prescribed a cyber-incident response framework as a key component of cyber-governance.

The reason is the same as for governance: cyber is generally supervised through the lens of IT and general operational risk, so continuity rules are written for all disruptions and apply to cyber as one cause.

**Applying it to this question**

The balance sheet figure (JPY 6.2 trillion) is irrelevant. The board member asks whether rules are cyber-specific. The deciding facts are “most are not specific to cyber-risk” and “few” cyber-specific BC or DR requirements, with the general framework covering all four activities. Option A states this.

**Fragile fact.** Majority require a framework for prevent, detect, respond, recover (with incident reporting); most are not cyber-specific; few have cyber-specific BC or DR rules.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Response and Recovery Testing and Exercising: Evaluation of Service Continuity, Response and Recovery Plans and Continuous Learning”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says regulators require a framework “for risk detection and response and recovery” and omits prevention and the point that few regulators have cyber-specific BC or DR rules; GARP is used. Condensation, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q12 of 20.

a.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “The majority of regulators require entities to establish a framework or policy for prevention, detection, response and recovery activities, including incident reporting. Specific requirements vary across supervisory authorities, and most are not specific to cyber-risk. Indeed, few regulators have issued cyber-specific business continuity or disaster recovery regulatory requirements for the sector.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses “most are not specific” and “few” into “most are cyber-specific” and “the majority”. It would be correct only if cyber-specific continuity rules were the norm.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Regulators require entities to establish the framework; they do not run a single sector framework into which institutions merely report. C would describe a centralised national incident response scheme, not the observed requirement on institutions.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The required framework covers prevention and detection as well as response and recovery. D drops two of the four activities. It would be correct only if the framework were limited to post-incident activities.

questions.question:
A senior supervisor is preparing an on-site review programme for a GBP-reporting bank. The programme has two workstreams: evaluation of service continuity plans, and evaluation of incident response and recovery plans. She lists four review items:

I. How the plans are triggered.

II. The bank’s IT disaster recovery arrangements and data centre strategies.

III. Preservation of data and specific actions for critical technology.

IV. Alignment of the plans with the bank’s risk management framework and chosen business continuity management strategies.

Which of the items belong to the evaluation of incident response and recovery plans, rather than to the evaluation of service continuity plans?

options.text: I and IV only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Senior supervisor sorting review items between service continuity plan evaluation and incident response and recovery plan evaluation.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two evaluations that are easy to merge.

| Evaluation of service continuity plans | Evaluation of incident response and recovery plans |
|---|---|
| Alignment with the institution’s risk management framework | How plans are triggered |
| Business continuity management strategies chosen | The institution’s ability to implement the plans |
| IT disaster recovery arrangements | Preservation of data |
| Data centre strategies | Specific actions for “critical” technology |

Service continuity evaluation asks whether the strategic architecture for staying up is sound (strategy, DR set-up, data centres, fit with the risk framework). Incident response evaluation asks whether the operational playbook works when an incident hits (trigger, execution, data, critical technology).

**Applying it to this question**

- I, how plans are triggered: incident response and recovery evaluation.
- II, IT DR arrangements and data centre strategies: service continuity evaluation.
- III, preservation of data and actions for critical technology: incident response and recovery evaluation.
- IV, alignment with the risk management framework and BCM strategies: service continuity evaluation.

So I and III only: option C.

**Fragile fact.** DR arrangements and data centre strategies sit under service continuity evaluation, not incident response evaluation, even though both sound like “recovery”.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Response and Recovery Testing and Exercising: Evaluation of Service Continuity, Response and Recovery Plans and Continuous Learning”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not describe either evaluation; this content is from GARP only, and it is within the LO’s “incident response approaches”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q13 of 20.

a.reason: **Sibling swap (item IV).** A includes IV, which belongs to service continuity plan evaluation (“alignment with institutions’ risk management frameworks, the business continuity management strategies chosen”), and omits III. A would be correct if the question asked for one item from each evaluation.

b.reason: **Sibling swap (item II).** B includes II, which is a service continuity item (IT disaster recovery arrangements and data centre strategies), and omits I. B would be correct with I in place of II.

c.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “Evaluation of regulated institutions’ incident response and recovery plans focuses on how plans are triggered, institutions’ ability to implement plans, preservation of data and specific actions for ‘critical’ technology.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap (item II).** D correctly includes I and III but adds the service continuity item II. D would be correct if the question asked which items appear in either evaluation, excluding IV.

questions.question: A Hong Kong bank suffered a ransomware incident that disrupted its retail payment services for 30 hours and cost an estimated HKD 85 million. Its supervisor intends to carry out a supervisory review of the bank’s post-incident learning. Which of the following statements best describes how such reviews are conducted in the jurisdictions that perform them?

options.text: The review follows a standard international template that scores the bank’s response against peer benchmarks and produces a ranking across institutions.
The review is performed by the bank’s external auditor, and the supervisor receives only the auditor’s opinion on whether the lessons were adequately learnt.
The review is undertaken only where the incident’s financial loss exceeds a reporting threshold, so incidents below that threshold are excluded from review.
The review is conducted by discussing the bank’s response and its root cause analysis, with no further standard practice observed across jurisdictions.

questions.solution:
Supervisor reviewing post-incident learning after a ransomware incident at a Hong Kong bank.

**Concept and theory**

Resilience includes learning: after an incident, an institution should understand what happened and fix the cause so it does not recur. Several jurisdictions (for example Australia, Belgium, Hong Kong, Japan and the US) complete a supervisory review of post-incident learning. GARP specifies the method and its limits:

- it is conducted through discussion of the institution’s response and its root cause analysis;
- no further standard practice could be observed.

Root cause analysis looks past the symptom (encrypted servers) to the cause (for example an unpatched system or a compromised credential). The supervisor’s discussion tests whether the bank has found and addressed that cause.

**Applying it to this question**

The loss figure (HKD 85 million) and outage length (30 hours) are not decisive. The question asks how the review is conducted. The deciding fact is “discussion of regulated institutions’ response and the root cause analysis, but no further standard practice could be observed.” Option D states this.

**Fragile fact.** Post-incident learning review: by the supervisor, through discussion of the response and root cause analysis; no further standard practice.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Response and Recovery Testing and Exercising: Evaluation of Service Continuity, Response and Recovery Plans and Continuous Learning”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists the same jurisdictions but does not describe the method (discussion of response and root cause analysis) or the absence of a standard practice; GARP is used. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q14 of 20.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** No standard practice exists, let alone a standard international template with peer scoring. A promises a uniformity that the source denies. It would be correct only if a harmonised post-incident review methodology existed.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The review is a supervisory review carried out through discussion with the institution, not delegated to the external auditor. B would describe a jurisdiction using its power to appoint a third party to report, which is a different tool (see Q3).

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The source places no loss threshold on post-incident learning reviews. Reporting thresholds belong to incident reporting (LO 49.d). C imports a condition from a neighbouring topic. It would be correct only if a jurisdiction had set such a threshold for these reviews.

d.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: several jurisdictions “complete a supervisory review of post-incident learning. This is conducted through the discussion of regulated institutions’ response and the root cause analysis, but no further standard practice could be observed.”

questions.question: A member of a bank’s board risk committee asks what Exercise Resilient Shield, held in 2015, illustrates about cyber-resilience practice. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.text: A joint UK/US exercise with leading financial firms that rehearsed information-sharing, incident response handling and public communications, rather than testing individual firms.
A live-play cyber war game in which UK and US authorities simulated attacks on participating firms in order to test the strength of their protective and detective controls.
A crisis communication exercise for euro area financial market infrastructures, designed to rehearse how they would coordinate messages during a major operational disruption.
A joint UK/US exercise designed to test the actions of law enforcement and the security and intelligence agencies in responding to an attack on the entire finance sector.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member asking what Exercise Resilient Shield (2015) illustrates.

**Concept and theory**

GARP separates testing from exercising. Testing probes whether controls or capabilities work (for example a penetration test). Exercising, “distinct from testing”, is used by most supervisors and banks to train and practise how they would respond to an incident. Cross-border international exercises have made this more visible.

Box 8.4 (Case Study 4) describes Exercise Resilient Shield, a joint UK/US exercise in 2015 with leading global financial firms.

| What it did | What it did not do |
|---|---|
| Enhanced shared awareness of cyber threats between US and UK governments and the private sector | Amount to a “cyber war game” or include live play |
| Furthered understanding of each country’s information-sharing and incident response coordination, including public communications | Test the actions of law enforcement or the security and intelligence agencies |
| Exchanged best practices government to government and government to financial sector | Involve the entire range of the UK and US finance sectors |
| Rehearsed communication and coordination links | Test individual firms or financial systems |

Participants were UK and US supervisory authorities, government departments and cyber-agencies, together with leading global financial firms.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks what the exercise illustrates. The deciding facts are that it was joint UK/US, rehearsed information-sharing, incident response handling and public communications, and was not a test of individual firms or systems. Option A states this.

**Fragile fact.** Exercise is distinct from testing. Resilient Shield: UK/US, 2015, no live play, not a test of firms, rehearsed communication and coordination links.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Response and Recovery Testing and Exercising: Joint Public-Private Exercising” and Box 8.4, “Case Study 4: Exercise Resilient Shield”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser mentions only “joint U.S.-UK exercises” without the case detail; GARP is used. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q15 of 20.

a.reason: GARP, Box 8.4: Resilient Shield was “a joint exercise with leading global financial firms to enhance cooperation and ability to respond effectively to a cyber-incident in the finance sector. The exercise was not a test of individual financial firms or financial systems, but was designed to improve understanding across governments and industry of information-sharing, incident response handling and public communications.”

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B describes a threat-led red team test (protective and detective controls under simulated attack). Resilient Shield expressly did not amount to a cyber war game or include live play. B would describe a TIBER-EU or CBEST-style test, not this exercise.

c.reason: **Sibling swap (other case).** C describes TITUS, the crisis communication exercise for euro area financial market infrastructures held in November 2015. It is a true lesson of a different exercise. C would be correct if the question asked about TITUS.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Resilient Shield did not test law enforcement or the security and intelligence agencies, and did not seek to involve the entire finance sector. D reverses two of the listed exclusions. It would be correct only for an exercise designed around agency response.

questions.question: A treasury analyst seconded to a bank’s operational resilience team is summarising observed practices on cyber exercises for the treasurer. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Distinct from testing, most supervisors and banks use exercises to train and practise how they would respond to an incident, and cross-border exercises have made this more visible.
In the UK, the Sector Exercising Group manages the sector’s annual exercise regime, which excludes cyber-specific scenarios because cyber is covered by penetration testing.
The Japanese FSA has run tabletop exercises to improve cyber-security, in particular the communication and coordination of response mechanisms across participating institutions.
More than 100 regulated institutions took part in a 2017 Japanese exercise covering two cyber scenarios, after which a summary of the results was published for others to learn from.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst summarising observed cyber exercising practices; identify the statement that is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

Exercises rehearse the human and organisational side of a response: who calls whom, who decides, what is said publicly. GARP’s observations on joint public-private exercising:

- distinct from testing, most supervisors and banks use exercises to train and practise how they would respond to an incident; cross-border exercises (Resilient Shield, TITUS in 2015, a G7 exercise under planning in 2018) have made this more visible;
- in the UK, the Sector Exercising Group (SEG), a sub-group of the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), manages the sector’s annual exercise regime, which incorporates cyber-specific scenarios; CMORG is an industry forum co-chaired by the Bank of England and UK Finance;
- in Japan, the JFSA has conducted tabletop exercises to improve cyber-security, in particular communication and coordination of response mechanisms; over 100 regulated institutions (banks, credit unions, insurers, securities companies) took part in the 2017 exercise, which covered two cyber scenarios, and a summary of results was published so others could draw lessons.

Publishing a summary turns a single exercise into sector-wide learning.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is “NOT correct”. A, C and D match the source. B says the UK annual regime excludes cyber-specific scenarios; GARP says it incorporates them. B is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** UK SEG sits under CMORG (not the PRA) and its annual regime incorporates cyber scenarios. JFSA 2017: over 100 institutions, two scenarios, summary published.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Response and Recovery Testing and Exercising: Joint Public-Private Exercising”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says joint exercises “recently included the Group of Seven (G7)”, whereas GARP describes the G7 exercise as under planning in 2018; this is a wording or timing difference and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q16 of 20.

a.reason: **True statement (qualifier trap).** A restates “Distinct from testing, most supervisors and banks use exercises to train and practise how they would respond to an incident. Cross-border international exercises have made this more visible.” It would be the incorrect one only if it called exercises a form of testing.

b.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “In the UK, the Sector Exercising Group (SEG), which is a sub-group of the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), manages the sector’s annual exercise regime, which incorporates cyber-specific scenarios.” Statement B reverses this, so B is the answer.

c.reason: **True statement (qualifier trap).** C matches the JFSA tabletop exercises focused on communication and coordination of response mechanisms. It would be incorrect if it had said the JFSA exercises were live penetration tests.

d.reason: **True statement (qualifier trap).** D matches the 2017 exercise: over 100 institutions, two cyber scenarios, published summary. It would be incorrect if the summary had been kept confidential to participants.

questions.question: A portfolio manager who sits on the board of a Singapore bank (total assets SGD 95 billion) asks the CRO for a single quantitative cyber-resilience measure, comparable to value-at-risk, that supervisors use to benchmark banks. Which of the following replies is most accurate?

options.text: Supervisors have converged on standardised quantitative cyber metrics comparable to financial risk measures, derived mainly from the results of penetration tests.
Supervisory methodologies avoid reported incidents and surveys and rely solely on on-site inspections, which produce a single quantitative cyber-resilience score per bank.
Supervisors rely on banks’ own management information, which is now mature and consistent across entities, so it allows direct quantitative benchmarking of banks.
Methodologies based on incidents, surveys, penetration tests and inspections yield no metrics comparable to financial risk measures; indicators describe the bank’s approach.

questions.solution:
Board member of a Singapore bank asking for a VaR-like quantitative cyber-resilience measure used by supervisors.

**Concept and theory**

Financial risks have mature quantitative measures because there are long, standardised data series (prices, defaults, losses) and agreed models. Cyber is different. GARP states that cyber-security and resilience metrics are not yet mature:

- some jurisdictions have methodologies to assess or benchmark cyber-security and resilience, focused on reported incidents, surveys, penetration tests and on-site inspections;
- none of these methodologies produce quantitative metrics or risk indicators comparable to those for financial risks, for example standardised quantitative metrics where established data are available;
- indicators instead provide information on the institution’s approach to building and ensuring cyber-security and resilience more broadly;
- supervisory authorities also rely on entities’ own management information, which differs across entities and is not yet mature.

**Applying it to this question**

The asset figure (SGD 95 billion) is irrelevant. The board member wants a VaR equivalent. The deciding fact is that no supervisory methodology yields metrics comparable to financial risk measures; indicators describe approach. Option D states this.

**Fragile fact.** No cyber metric is comparable to financial risk measures; supervisors rely on entities’ own MI, which is not yet mature and differs across entities.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Cyber-Security and Resilience Metrics: Cyber-Security and Resilience Metrics are Not Yet Mature”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q17 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** There is no convergence on standardised quantitative cyber metrics. A reverses “none of these methodologies produce” comparable metrics. It would be correct only in a future state where such metrics exist.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Methodologies use reported incidents, surveys, penetration tests and on-site inspections; B drops three of four and invents a single score. It would be correct only if inspections were the sole input and produced a score.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Entities’ management information “differs across entities and is not yet mature”. C reverses both attributes. It would be correct only if management information were standardised and mature.

d.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Cyber-Security and Resilience Metrics are Not Yet Mature”: methodologies “have focused on reported incidents, surveys, penetration tests and on-site inspections. None of these methodologies produce quantitative metrics or risk indicators comparable to those available for financial risks ... Instead, indicators provide information on regulated institutions’ approach to building and ensuring cyber-security and resilience more broadly.”

questions.question: The CRO of a Brazilian bank notes that all of the backward-looking indicators of the technology function in the board’s management information have been stable for three years. Over the same period the bank has faced distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks whose traffic volume has grown sharply, with attackers changing technique in response to the bank’s defences. Which statement best explains why the CRO should not rely on the backward-looking indicators alone?

options.text: Backward-looking indicators are never informative about future performance, so they should be removed from the board’s management information and replaced entirely by forward-looking ones.
Backward-looking indicators are reliable for cyber-risk because adversaries’ tactics stay fixed once identified, so three years of stability is itself strong evidence of resilience.
Backward-looking indicators are a reasonable guide only when operations and the risk environment are stable and largely independent of outside influences, which adaptive adversaries undermine.
Backward-looking indicators show whether the bank is likely to be more or less resilient if a risk crystallises, but they are distorted by the much higher DDoS traffic volumes seen in recent years.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Brazilian bank with stable backward-looking indicators while adaptive DDoS attacks grow.

**Concept and theory**

Two kinds of indicator:

| Type | What it does | When it works |
|---|---|---|
| Backward-looking | Comments on past performance (often of the technology function) as an indicator of future performance | When operations and the risk environment are relatively stable over time and more or less independent from outside influences |
| Forward-looking | Direct and indirect metrics of resilience, indicating whether the institution is likely to be more or less resilient if a risk crystallises | Needed when the threat adapts |

Why cyber breaks the backward-looking logic: adversaries are dynamic. They adapt to institutions’ responses and protective measures, sometimes changing tactics even within a single incident. GARP’s example is DDoS: traffic volume and scale had increased significantly in the two years before the report, and adversaries adapt their techniques to the institution’s defences. A calm past is therefore weak evidence of a calm future. Backward-looking metrics remain important, but jurisdictions increasingly recognise the need for forward-looking indicators.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives the two facts that matter: indicators are stable (backward-looking), and attackers are adapting (the stability condition fails). The deciding fact is the condition under which backward-looking indicators are a reasonable guide. Option C states it and links it to adaptive adversaries.

**Fragile fact.** Backward-looking is reasonable only if the environment is stable and independent of outside influences. “More or less resilient if a risk crystallises” describes forward-looking indicators.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Cyber-Security and Resilience Metrics: Emerging Forward-Looking Indicators of Resilience”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser defines DDoS as a single system attacked from multiple malicious sources, which is not in GARP; GARP uses DDoS only as an example of adaptive adversaries and rising traffic volumes. The question relies on GARP’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q18 of 20.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP says backward-looking metrics “continue to be important”; they are insufficient, not useless. A would be correct only if backward-looking data had no predictive value in any environment.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Adversaries do not stay fixed; they adapt, sometimes within one incident. B reverses this and treats stability as proof. It would be correct only in a static threat environment.

c.reason: GARP, Section 8.4, “Emerging Forward-Looking Indicators of Resilience”: backward-looking indicators comment on past performance as an indicator of future performance, “which is reasonable when institutions’ operations and risk environment are relatively stable over time and more or less independent from outside influences. However, cyber-risk frustrates this because adversaries are dynamic, themselves adapting to institutions’ responses and protective measures.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Indicating “whether a regulated institution is likely to be more or less resilient in the event of a risk crystallising” is the defining property of forward-looking indicators. D attaches it to backward-looking ones. D would be correct with “forward-looking” in place of “backward-looking” (and without the distortion clause).

questions.question:
A risk committee member at a UK bank is reviewing the following extract from the board’s cyber management information pack.

| Indicator | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patch ageing: median days to apply critical patches | 18 | 22 | 27 | 31 |
| Staff completing phishing awareness training (%) | 92 | 95 | 96 | 97 |
| DDoS incidents recorded (number) | 3 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| Net interest margin (%) | 2.1 | 2.0 | 2.2 | 2.1 |

Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the observed practices on cyber-security and resilience metrics?

options.text: Patch ageing has risen by 13 days, a worsening on a metric that is widespread and comparable, but no single metric taken in isolation is a sufficient measure of cyber-resilience.
Training completion has risen every quarter, so the board can conclude that overall cyber-resilience has improved, since one consistently improving metric is a sufficient measure of resilience.
Patch ageing cannot be compared with other institutions because no cyber metric is widespread or comparable, so the 13-day rise can be benchmarked only against the bank’s own history.
The stable count of DDoS incidents shows that DDoS exposure is unchanged, since backward-looking incident counts remain reliable when adversaries adapt their techniques to defences.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at a UK bank interpreting a quarterly cyber management information extract.

**Concept and theory**

Annex C of the BCBS report collects cyber-centric metrics that a sample of institutions present to boards and board sub-committees. GARP summarises their properties:

- the data typically allow trend information, so the reviewer can assess whether the situation is getting better or worse;
- some metrics track compliance with internal policies, while others measure inherent risk;
- patch ageing in particular is a widespread and comparable metric;
- collectively, indicators can inform on the broad adequacy of an institution’s cyber and operational resilience for its business needs and risk appetite;
- no single item taken in isolation is a sufficient metric, and no standard set of indicators provides a meaningful benchmark so far.

Patch ageing measures how long known vulnerabilities stay open. Longer ageing means a longer window for attackers, so a rising value is a deterioration.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the trend, ignoring the irrelevant net interest margin row.

$\Delta\text{patch ageing} =$ 31 − 18 = 13 days

Relative change $= \frac{13}{18} \approx$ 72%

The rising value means the position is worsening on this measure. Patch ageing is the one metric GARP names as widespread and comparable. Training completion is improving, and DDoS counts are flat, but no single item is sufficient. Option A combines all three correct points.

**Fragile fact.** Rising patch ageing is worse, not better. Patch ageing is the one metric named as widespread and comparable, yet no single metric is sufficient.

**Reference**

LO 49.c: “Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.4, “Cyber-Security and Resilience Metrics: Emerging Forward-Looking Indicators of Resilience”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser notes that trend analysis shows whether risks are increasing or declining but does not mention patch ageing or the “no single metric” point; GARP is used. The specific metric values are illustrative and not from either source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 c, where it is Q19 of 20.

a.reason: GARP, Section 8.4: “the data provided typically allow for trend information so that the reviewer can assess if the situation is getting better or worse ... Patch ageing in particular is a widespread and comparable metric ... However, no single item taken in isolation is seen as a sufficient metric.”

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B treats one improving metric (training completion, 92% to 97%) as sufficient to conclude on overall resilience. GARP says no single item in isolation is sufficient. B would be correct only if a single metric could capture resilience.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Patch ageing is expressly “a widespread and comparable metric”. C reverses this. The 13-day arithmetic is right, but the conclusion is wrong. C would be correct for a bank-specific metric with no common definition.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** A flat count of DDoS incidents (3, 2, 4, 3) is backward-looking, and backward-looking data are a weaker guide precisely when adversaries adapt. D reverses the condition. It would be correct only in a stable threat environment.
