questions.question: The head of operational risk at an Australian wealth manager is presenting to newly hired analysts on the boundaries of information security risk. She asks them to identify the one accurate statement among four drafted for the induction pack. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Information security risk is a subset of cyber risk, covering only incidents in which digital data leaves the firm through its networks.
Data stolen through collusion between an employee and a supplier falls outside the typology, which covers only purely internal or purely external perpetrators.
A physical security assessment report forgotten on an office printer is an incident that falls within the scope of information security risk management.
Since insiders initiate the majority of data leaks, nearly all of them deliberately, controls should target malicious staff rather than accidental disclosure.

questions.solution:
Head of operational risk at an Australian wealth manager: which statement on the boundaries of information security risk is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Information security risk is the risk that information held by a firm is stolen, lost or unintentionally disclosed. It is deliberately broader than cyber risk. Cyber risk concerns attacks on digital systems and networks (hacking, virus infection, phishing). Information security covers those attacks and, in addition, everything else that can compromise information: an e-mail sent to the wrong person through the autofill function, a leak by a disgruntled employee, a lost laptop, and the loss or theft of paper documents and other non-digital data.

Why the wider scope? The motivation is practical. A firm’s clients and regulators do not care whether confidential information escaped through a network or through a briefcase left on a train: the damage (privacy breach, reputational harm, regulatory fines) is the same. GARP therefore places loss due to the compromise or theft of paper documentation explicitly inside information risk management, and gives two examples: an audit report left on a train and a physical security assessment report left on a printer.

Two further points define the perimeter:

- **Perpetrators.** They may be internal or external to the firm, and sometimes work in collusion or are hybrid, such as third parties and suppliers. The typology does not exclude mixed cases.
- **Insider share.** A 2017 McAfee study cited by GARP found that 43% of data leaks are initiated by insiders, and half of those unintentionally. Insiders are therefore a large minority, and accidental disclosure is as important as malice within that group.

| Fact | Value in GARP |
|---|---|
| Leaks initiated by insiders | 43% of all leaks |
| Of which unintentional | about half (roughly 21.5% of all leaks) |
| Of which deliberate | about half (roughly 21.5% of all leaks) |

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst is asked for the one statement that matches the perimeter. Test each statement against three questions: is cyber the whole or a part; are mixed perpetrators covered; is non-digital information covered. The deciding fact is GARP’s explicit inclusion of paper documents, using almost exactly the printer example in option C.

**Fragile fact.** Cyber risk sits inside information security risk, never the reverse; 43% of leaks start with insiders, and half of those are accidents.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Context and Scope” and “Typology of Information Security Risks”. Schweser makes the same point (information security risk “refers to more than just cyber risk” and includes nondigital data) but omits the McAfee statistic and the collusion or hybrid point, which come from GARP only. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q1 of 19.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The direction of inclusion is reversed. Cyber risk is a subset of information security risk, not the other way round; information security also covers lost, misdirected and paper-based information. The statement would be correct if it read “Cyber risk is a subset of information security risk”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP notes that perpetrators of data thefts can be internal or external and sometimes work in collusion, or are hybrid, such as third parties and suppliers. The option invents a restriction to “pure” perpetrators. It would be correct only for a typology that explicitly excluded hybrid cases, which this one does not.

c.reason: GARP states that information loss due to the compromise or theft of paper documentation and other non-digital data belongs within the scope of information risk management, and cites a physical security assessment report left on a printer as an incident that controls should address.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** The McAfee figures are distorted twice in one direction: insiders initiate 43% of leaks (a minority), and half of those are unintentional, not “nearly all deliberate”. Controls must therefore address accidental disclosure as much as malice. The statement would be correct for a data set in which insiders caused most leaks and almost always deliberately.

questions.question:
A compliance officer at a Singapore private bank is logging four recent data incidents into the four-quadrant typology of information security risks.

| Incident | Description |
|---|---|
| I | A consultant working on site copies a client database to a personal drive shortly before his contract ends. |
| II | An outage at the bank’s cloud service provider destroys the only copy of a client reporting data set. |
| III | A relationship manager relies on the e-mail autofill function and sends a client statement to the wrong external address. |
| IV | A caller posing as IT support persuades a staff member to reveal credentials and then extracts client files. |

Which of the following classifications (cause, then incident type) is most accurate?

options.text: I: internal, theft; II: external, loss; III: internal, loss; IV: external, theft
I: external, theft; II: external, loss; III: internal, loss; IV: external, theft
I: internal, theft; II: external, loss; III: external, loss; IV: external, theft
I: internal, theft; II: internal, loss; III: internal, loss; IV: external, theft

questions.solution:
Compliance officer at a Singapore private bank: classify four incidents in the four-quadrant typology.

**Concept and theory**

GARP (Table 9.1, from Chapelle) organises information security incidents in a two-by-two grid.

- **Cause (rows).** Internal causes include the firm’s staff and also contractors and consultants working on site. External causes include outsiders and third parties.
- **Nature (columns).** Theft or corruption covers deliberate acts, including voluntary corruption of data. Loss or involuntary disclosure covers accidents, including involuntary corruption and accidental disclosure. Schweser expresses the same column split as intentional versus unintentional.

|  | Theft or corruption | Loss or involuntary disclosure |
|---|---|---|
| External or third parties | Digital: hacking, virus, phishing. Physical: theft, social engineering | Disaster, systems disruptions, third-party failure |
| Internal | Theft and transfer by infiltrated employee or contractor; departing employees taking IP (mishandled exits) | Digital: database or back-up loss, lost devices, e-mail errors. Physical: lost printed documents, accidental mentions to outsiders, loss of archives |

The point of the grid is that causes and controls differ by quadrant: external theft calls for perimeter defences, internal loss calls for training and data governance, and so on.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each incident by asking first “who or what caused it?” and then “was it deliberate?”.

- I: an on-site consultant is internal by definition; copying a database deliberately is theft. Internal, theft.
- II: the cloud provider is a third party; an outage is not deliberate. This is third-party failure or systems disruption. External, loss.
- III: the relationship manager is staff; autofill misdirection is an error when sending documents. The recipient being external does not change the cause. Internal, loss.
- IV: the caller is an outsider who deliberately manipulates staff (social engineering). External, theft.

**Fragile fact.** Classify by cause, not by destination: on-site contractors are internal, and an e-mail sent outside by an employee is still an internal incident.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Typology of Information Security Risks”, Table 9.1. GARP labels the columns theft or corruption versus loss or involuntary disclosure; Schweser labels them intentional versus unintentional. The two are equivalent for classification; no substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q2 of 19.

a.reason: It matches all four rows of Table 9.1: on-site contractor theft (internal, theft), third-party failure (external, loss), e-mail recipient error (internal, loss) and social engineering (external, theft).

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Incident I is placed in the external row because a consultant is not an employee. GARP’s internal causes explicitly include contractors and consultants on site. B would be correct if the consultant had worked remotely as an outside third party with no on-site presence.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Incident III is classified by the location of the recipient rather than by the cause. The cause is the firm’s own employee making an error, which is internal loss (“errors when sending documents”). C would be correct if an outside party, say a vendor, had misdirected the file.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Incident II is treated as an internal database or back-up loss because the data belonged to the bank. The trigger was a third-party failure, which sits in the external loss quadrant. D would be correct if the data set had been lost through the bank’s own failed back-up process.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian life insurer is reviewing a draft policy paper that describes the firm’s taxonomy of information security risks. The paper contains the following statements:

I. The typology crosses the cause of an incident (internal, including on-site contractors and consultants, versus external, including third parties) with its nature (theft, including voluntary corruption, versus loss, including involuntary corruption and accidental disclosure).

II. Digital versus physical information is a third axis of the typology which, combined with the other two, produces eight distinct cells.

III. Departing employees who take proprietary information or intellectual property with them are an example of an internal theft incident.

IV. Disasters, systems disruptions and third-party failures are examples of external theft or corruption incidents.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and IV only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Canadian life insurer: which statements about the taxonomy of information security risks are correct.

**Concept and theory**

The four-quadrant typology has exactly two axes. The first is cause: internal (staff, plus contractors and consultants on site) versus external (outsiders, plus third parties). The second is the nature of the incident: theft or corruption (deliberate, including voluntary corruption) versus loss or involuntary disclosure (accidental, including involuntary corruption and accidental disclosure).

The digital versus physical distinction is used inside the cells, as a way of listing examples (external theft is split into digital and physical; internal loss is split into digital and physical). It is not a third axis, which is why the approach is called four-quadrant and not eight-cell. Schweser makes the same point: both intentional and unintentional incidents can be digital or physical.

Two examples that are often misplaced:

- Departing employees who take proprietary information or intellectual property (“mishandled exits”) are internal theft, item 5 of Table 9.1.
- Disasters, systems disruptions and third-party failures are external but involuntary, item 3: external loss, not theft.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates GARP’s definition of both axes accurately. Statement II adds a third axis, contradicting the four-quadrant structure. Statement III places mishandled exits in internal theft, which is correct. Statement IV puts disasters and third-party failures in the theft column, which is wrong: nobody acted deliberately. The correct statements are I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Two axes, four quadrants: digital versus physical is a sub-label inside cells, and disasters or third-party failures are external loss, not external theft.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Typology of Information Security Risks”, Table 9.1. Schweser describes the axes as internal versus external and intentional versus unintentional; GARP uses theft or corruption versus loss or involuntary disclosure. Equivalent framing; no GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q3 of 19.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It omits statement III, which is true. A reader who thinks theft requires an outside attacker, or that departing staff are no longer insiders, drops III. A would be correct if statement III had placed mishandled exits in the external row.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts statement IV, which flips disasters and third-party failures from the loss column to the theft column. These events are involuntary. B would be correct if statement IV had read “external loss or involuntary disclosure incidents”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts statement II, which promotes the within-cell digital versus physical split to a third axis, and rejects the true statement I. C would be correct only for a different typology built on three dimensions.

d.reason: GARP describes the taxonomy as internal causes (including contractors and consultants on site) versus external causes (including third parties), crossed with data theft (including voluntary corruption) versus data loss (including involuntary corruption and accidental disclosure), and lists departing employees taking proprietary information as an internal theft example. Statements I and III are therefore correct and II and IV are not.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Brazilian bank is preparing a training deck that pairs well-known information security incidents with a summary of what happened. A reviewer has flagged that only one of the draft pairings is accurate. Which of the following pairings is most accurate?

options.text: Paradise Papers: an employee of a UK insurance company copied the data of 500,000 customers and offered it for sale on the dark web.
Paradise Papers: 1.4 terabytes of data were stolen from the offshore law firm Appleby and sent to a German newspaper, which shared it with a journalists’ consortium.
bZx: a hacker exploited an administrator’s private key, possibly in an inside job, and the platform offered a reward to help retrieve the funds.
Equifax: a phishing attack on a developer gave attackers private keys, and the resulting breach exposed the data of 147 million customers.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant at a Brazilian bank: which pairing of a named incident with its description is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP illustrates the LO with two boxes of real incidents. Box 9.1 covers high-profile data hacks (external attacks); Box 9.2 covers data leaks (transfer of confidential information, often by insiders) and recent cryptocurrency thefts. Knowing what happened in each case, and in particular the attack vector and the actor, is exactly what “provide examples of cyber threats” requires.

| Case | What happened (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Paradise Papers | Nov 2017: 1.4 TB of private data stolen from Appleby, offshore law firm and tax adviser in Bermuda; sent to Süddeutsche Zeitung, which shared it with the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. Second largest data hack after the Panama Papers. |
| Equifax | 2017: external intrusion through an unpatched (known) vulnerability; data of 147 million US customers exposed; about \$5bn of market value lost in the week after the announcement (out of \$15.5bn). |
| UK insurer | July 2017: an employee fraudulently copied data of 500,000 customers and posted it for sale on the dark web; £175,000 fine; little coverage outside the specialised press. |
| IRS / ProPublica | Suspected leak of tax data of the wealthiest Americans by an IRS employee; origin never firmly established. |
| bZx | Nov 2021: US lending and trading platform; developer’s private keys stolen in a phishing attack; \$55 million lost. |
| BXH Exchange | Nov 2021: China-based exchange; hacker exploited an administrator’s private key, possibly an inside job; \$139.2 million lost; \$1 million reward offered. |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option attaches a true fact to a case. The test is whether the fact belongs to the named case. Only option B’s description belongs to the Paradise Papers; the other three borrow the facts of the UK insurer, BXH Exchange and bZx respectively.

**Fragile fact.** bZx is phishing for a developer’s keys (\$55m); BXH is an administrator’s key, possibly an inside job (\$139.2m); Equifax is an unpatched known vulnerability.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Cyberattacks: Cases and Threats” (Box 9.1) and “Information Leaks: Malicious Insiders” (Box 9.2). Schweser mentions only Equifax, Appleby and leaks in insurance, journalism and cryptocurrencies, without details; the case facts come from GARP. The detailed Equifax lessons belong to LO 50.b and are not tested here. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q4 of 19.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The description is the UK insurance company leak in Box 9.2 (500,000 customers, dark web sale, malicious employee). It is attached to the Paradise Papers, which was an external hack of a law firm. A would be correct with “UK insurer” as the case name.

b.reason: GARP’s Box 9.1 states that in November 2017, 1.4 terabytes of private information was stolen from Appleby in Bermuda and sent to the Süddeutsche Zeitung, which shared it with the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** The administrator’s private key, the suspected inside job and the reward all belong to BXH Exchange. bZx lost its funds when a developer’s private keys were stolen in a phishing attack. C would be correct with “BXH Exchange” as the case name.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Phishing for a developer’s private keys is the bZx vector. Equifax’s breach was an external intrusion exploiting an unpatched, known vulnerability, although the 147 million figure is right. D would be correct if it described an unpatched vulnerability as the cause.

questions.question: The CRO of a Japanese securities firm is briefing the board on the cyberthreat landscape and the place of insider leaks within it. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Cyberthreats facing financial firms are specific to the financial industry and do not arise in other sectors of the economy.
The 2017 leak by an employee of a UK insurer attracted wide coverage in the general press, although the regulatory fine was only £175,000.
Leaks by disgruntled or corrupt staff resemble internal fraud more than external cyberattacks, but remain within the scope of information security.
The COVID-19 pandemic reduced the cyberthreats facing financial firms, because remote working cut the volume of digital data handled by staff.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Japanese securities firm: which statement about the cyberthreat landscape and insider leaks is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Three ideas frame the threat landscape in GARP.

- **Industry exposure.** Cyberthreats are not specific to the financial industry, but the industry is particularly exposed because of the value of the transactions it facilitates. The threats are common; the exposure is higher.
- **Malicious insiders.** Information leaks by disgruntled or corrupt staff are more like internal fraud cases than external cyberattacks. They nevertheless stay within the scope of information security. (Fraud and financial crime management is then covered separately.)
- **COVID-19.** The pandemic changed work habits and locations, accelerated digitalisation, disrupted supply chains, generalised QR codes and intensified social media traffic. These changes affected the cyberthreat landscape of all sectors, including financial services, and heightened the need to protect digital information.

The UK insurer leak in Box 9.2 is GARP’s example of a malicious insider: the employee was dismissed, the regulator fined the firm £175,000 and increased scrutiny, but the case did not attract much coverage outside the specialised press.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is GARP’s classification of malicious insider leaks: closer to internal fraud in nature, still inside information security in scope. Option C states exactly this. The other options reverse a direction (industry-specific threats, wide coverage, reduced threats).

**Fragile fact.** Insider leaks look like internal fraud but stay inside information security; cyberthreats are common to all sectors, finance is simply more exposed.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Cyberattacks: Cases and Threats” and “Information Leaks: Malicious Insiders”, Box 9.2. Schweser covers COVID-19 and the industry’s vulnerability but not the internal fraud comparison or the UK insurer case, which come from GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q5 of 19.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP states that cyberthreats are not specific to the financial industry; the industry is particularly exposed because of the value of transactions. The option turns “particularly exposed” into “exclusively affected”. It would be correct only if it read “the financial industry is particularly exposed to cyberthreats that also affect other sectors”.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The fine of £175,000 is right, but the coverage is reversed: GARP notes the case did not attract much coverage outside the specialised press. The option would be correct if it said “attracted little coverage outside the specialised press”.

c.reason: GARP: “Information leaks that result from disgruntled or corrupt staff are more like internal fraud cases than external cyberattacks, but are still within the scope of information security.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** The pandemic accelerated digitalisation, generalised QR codes and intensified social media traffic, which raised, not reduced, the need to protect digital information. The option would be correct if it said the pandemic “reshaped and heightened” the threat landscape.

questions.question: The head of technology risk at the London branch of a Chinese commercial bank is explaining to the branch risk committee why the bank benchmarks itself against published cybersecurity frameworks. Which of the following best describes the role of such frameworks?

options.text: They give security managers a systematic way to mitigate cyberthreats and to benchmark against good market practice, and are often mandatory or strongly encouraged for regulatory compliance.
They are issued by national regulators, which is why all three dominant standards, including the NIST framework, are legally binding on every financial firm that adopts them.
They are designed as one-off certification exercises, so once a firm has been assessed against a standard, the standard itself is not refreshed or republished.
They are designed to measure cyber fraud losses for capital purposes, leaving the development of cybersecurity protection entirely to each firm’s own IT department.

questions.solution:
Head of technology risk at a Chinese bank’s London branch: what role do published cybersecurity frameworks play.

**Concept and theory**

Cyber risk changes fast and is technical, so few firms can build a complete defence model from scratch. The market has responded with standards and guidance documents that are published and refreshed regularly. GARP gives them three functions:

- help firms develop cybersecurity protection;
- provide quality benchmarks useful for mitigating and measuring cyber fraud and technology risks;
- give security managers a systematic way to mitigate cyberthreats and to benchmark themselves against good market practice.

Regulatory status is nuanced. GARP notes that cybersecurity frameworks are often mandatory, or at least strongly encouraged, for companies that want to comply with industry-related regulations. Yet the frameworks themselves are produced by bodies that are not financial regulators (NIST is an agency of the US Department of Commerce; CIS was built by a volunteer-expert coalition; ISO is an international standards body), and the NIST framework is explicitly voluntary.

Three standards dominate the market: the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (NIST CSF), the CIS Critical Security Controls, and the ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 standards.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee wants to know why the bank benchmarks itself. The answer has to combine the purpose (systematic mitigation and benchmarking) with the correct regulatory status (often mandatory or strongly encouraged for compliance, but not legally binding in themselves). Only option A combines both correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Frameworks are often mandatory or strongly encouraged for regulatory compliance, yet NIST CSF itself is voluntary: hold both facts at once.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Cyber Risk Management: Frameworks and Standards”. Schweser lists the three standards as “globally recognized and adopted” but does not state that frameworks are often mandatory or strongly encouraged; that point is from GARP. GARP names ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, while Schweser names only ISO 27001. No conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q6 of 19.

a.reason: GARP: “Cybersecurity management frameworks are designed to give security managers a systematic way to mitigate cyberthreats and benchmark themselves to good market practice. Cybersecurity frameworks are often mandatory, or at least strongly encouraged, for companies that want to comply with industry related regulations.”

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The standards are not issued by national financial regulators, and the NIST framework is expressly voluntary. The option gives the issuer role to regulators and turns “often mandatory or encouraged for compliance” into “legally binding on all adopters”. It would be correct for a rulebook that a supervisor had written into regulation.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP stresses that the standards are “published and refreshed regularly”, and the CIS list in particular has been updated for cloud computing, virtualisation, mobility, outsourcing, work-from-home and changing attacker tactics. The option would be correct only for a fixed, never-revised standard.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The frameworks are meant to help firms develop protection as well as provide benchmarks for mitigation and measurement. Narrowing them to loss measurement for capital purposes misstates their scope. It would describe a capital-modelling methodology, not a cybersecurity framework.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an Indian private-sector bank is validating a board paper that summarises the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity. Which of the following statements in the paper is most accurate?

options.text: It was designed from the outset for financial institutions and was only later extended to critical infrastructure such as power plants and dams.
It is a mandatory standard of the US Department of Commerce, and its adoption is a precondition for a firm seeking ISO 27001 certification.
Its organisation differs fundamentally from an operational risk framework, since cyber risk is handled by response rather than by identification and assessment.
It promotes root-cause analysis and lessons learned after incidents, and gives firms an outline of where to focus time and money on cybersecurity protection.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at an Indian bank: which statement about the NIST cybersecurity framework is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (NIST CSF) was developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology at the US Department of Commerce. Its key features in GARP:

| Feature | GARP description |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Help businesses of all sizes understand, manage and reduce cybersecurity risk and protect networks and data |
| Status | Voluntary; gives an outline of best practices to help decide where to focus time and money on protection |
| Origin | Originally intended for critical infrastructure such as power plants and dams; many financial organisations later adopted it |
| Approach | Analyse threats and vulnerabilities, assess their effects, reduce risk with customised measures; guidance on response and recovery promoting root-cause analysis and lessons learned |
| Structure | Similar organisation to an ORMF (identification, assessment, mitigation, monitoring); core of five functions: identify, protect, detect, respond, recover |

The analogy with an ORMF is worth understanding. Identify plays the role of risk identification (inventory of assets and policies); Protect is mitigation; Detect is monitoring; Respond and Recover extend the cycle into incident management and lessons learned. GARP adds that infrastructure security is just one of several NIST standards covering cybersecurity.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option states one feature. A reverses the origin, B misstates the status and invents a link with ISO, C reverses the ORMF analogy. D states two features GARP lists directly: root-cause analysis and lessons learned, and an outline of where to focus time and money.

**Fragile fact.** NIST CSF: voluntary, critical infrastructure first, finance later, and structurally similar to an ORMF.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “The NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity”. Schweser adds that NIST was founded by the US Congress; this is not in GARP and is not tested. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the tested points.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q7 of 19.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The direction of extension is reversed. NIST CSF was originally meant for critical infrastructure, and its use then extended to other industries, with many financial organisations adopting it. A would be correct if the two sectors were swapped.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The framework is voluntary, and ISO 27001 certification depends on ISO’s own requirements (an ISMS, controls, an ongoing process), not on NIST adoption. B would be correct only if NIST were a mandatory rulebook and ISO made it a prerequisite, neither of which holds.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says the opposite: though specific to IT, NIST has a similar organisation to an operational risk management framework of identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring. C would be correct if “differs fundamentally from” read “mirrors”.

d.reason: GARP: the framework “gives businesses an outline of best practices to help determine where to focus time and money for cybersecurity protection” and “provides guidance in response and recovery from cybersecurity incidents, promoting the practice of root-cause analysis and lessons learned”.

An internal auditor at a German savings bank is checking that each activity in the bank’s cybersecurity procedures has been mapped to the correct function of the NIST cybersecurity framework.

| Activity | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Monitoring workstations for unauthorised devices such as USB drives |
| II | Encrypting sensitive data at rest and in transit |
| III | Regularly testing a plan for notifying customers whose data may be at risk |
| IV | Listing all laptops, smartphones, tablets and point-of-sale devices in use |

Which of the following mappings is most accurate?

options.text: I: Detect; II: Protect; III: Recover; IV: Identify
I: Detect; II: Protect; III: Respond; IV: Identify
I: Protect; II: Protect; III: Respond; IV: Identify
I: Detect; II: Protect; III: Respond; IV: Protect

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a German savings bank: map four activities to the NIST functions.

**Concept and theory**

The core of NIST CSF is a list of five functions that follow the basic sequence of cyber defence. It helps to read them as a timeline around an attack: before (Identify, Protect), during (Detect, Respond) and after (Recover).

| Function | GARP guidance |
|---|---|
| Identify | List all equipment, software and data in use (laptops, smartphones, tablets, point-of-sale devices); create and share a cybersecurity policy covering roles and responsibilities and the steps to protect against and limit an attack |
| Protect | Control who logs on; use security software; encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit; back up regularly; update security software (automatically if possible); formal policies for disposing of files and old devices; train everyone |
| Detect | Monitor computers for unauthorised personnel access, devices (such as USB drives) and software; investigate unusual activity; check for unauthorised users or connections |
| Respond | Create and regularly test a plan for notifying those whose data may be at risk, keeping operations running, reporting to authorities, investigating and containing, updating the policy with lessons learned, preparing for inadvertent events |
| Recover | Repair and restore affected equipment and network; keep employees and customers informed of response and recovery activities |

In financial risk management, GARP summarises implementation as an asset inventory first (identifying risks and assets that need protection), then protection, detection, response and recovery.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: monitoring for unauthorised USB drives is listed verbatim under Detect.
- II: encrypting sensitive data at rest and in transit is a Protect protocol.
- III: creating and regularly testing a notification plan is Respond (the plan is prepared in advance, but it belongs to Respond).
- IV: listing laptops, smartphones, tablets and point-of-sale devices is the Identify inventory.

**Fragile fact.** A plan that is written in advance can still be Respond: the notification plan is a Respond item, while informing customers of recovery progress is Recover.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “The NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity”, guidance for each of the five functions. Schweser’s summary is consistent but less detailed (it omits “at rest and in transit” and the USB example, which come from GARP). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q8 of 19.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Activity III is moved to Recover because notifying people sounds like “keeping customers informed”. Recover covers informing employees and customers about response and recovery activities after an attack; the plan for notifying those whose data may be at risk is under Respond. A would be correct if III read “keeping customers informed of recovery activities after the attack”.

b.reason: Every activity is placed in the function under which GARP lists it: Detect, Protect, Respond, Identify.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Activity I is moved to Protect, confusing “control who logs on” (Protect) with monitoring for unauthorised devices (Detect). C would be correct if I read “restricting which staff can log on to workstations”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The asset inventory is placed in Protect because it lists assets “that require protection”. GARP places the list of equipment, software and data under Identify. D would be correct if IV described installing security software on those devices.

questions.question: The CRO of an Australian regional bank is reviewing a draft incident playbook written after a ransomware attack at a peer. Each item in the playbook is labelled with the NIST cybersecurity framework function to which it belongs. Which of the following items is least likely to belong to the Respond function?

options.text: Repairing and restoring the equipment and parts of the network affected by an attack
Preparing for inadvertent events, such as weather emergencies, that may put data at risk
Updating the cybersecurity policy and plan with the lessons learned from an attack
Keeping business operations up and running while an attack is being dealt with

questions.solution:
CRO of an Australian regional bank: which playbook item is least likely to belong to the NIST Respond function.

**Concept and theory**

Respond and Recover are the two post-detection functions of NIST CSF, and they are easy to confuse because both happen “after something has gone wrong”. The distinction GARP draws:

- **Respond** is about managing the incident and its aftermath at the level of the organisation: create and regularly test a plan for notifying those whose data may be at risk, keeping business operations up and running, reporting to law enforcement and other authorities, investigating and containing the attack, updating the cybersecurity policy and plan with lessons learned, and preparing for inadvertent events (such as weather emergencies) that may put data at risk.
- **Recover** is about restoring what was damaged: after an attack, repair and restore the equipment and parts of the network that were affected, and keep employees and customers informed of response and recovery activities.

Two Respond items look misplaced at first sight and are classic traps: “updating the policy with lessons learned” (sounds like Recover or Identify) and “preparing for inadvertent events” (sounds like Protect or Identify).

**Applying it to this question**

Options B, C and D are each a line of GARP’s Respond list. Option A, repairing and restoring affected equipment and network parts, is the first line of Recover. It is the item least likely to be classified under Respond.

**Fragile fact.** Lessons learned, weather preparedness and keeping operations running are Respond; repairing and restoring damaged equipment is Recover.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “The NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity”. Schweser lists the same Respond items (it writes “unpredictable events” where GARP writes “inadvertent events”). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q9 of 19.

a.reason: GARP: “Recover: After an attack, repair and restore the equipment and parts of your network that were affected.” This is a Recover activity, not a Respond activity.

b.reason: **Sibling swap; trap: a true Respond item.** Preparing for inadvertent events such as weather emergencies looks like Protect or Identify, but GARP lists it under the Respond plan. It would be the answer only if the question asked which item is least likely to belong to Protect.

c.reason: **Sibling swap; trap: a true Respond item.** Updating the cybersecurity policy with lessons learned looks like Recover, because it follows the incident, or like Identify, because the policy is created there. GARP places it under Respond. It would be the answer if the question asked about Recover.

d.reason: **Sibling swap; trap: a true Respond item.** Keeping business operations running sounds like recovery or business continuity, but GARP lists it in the Respond plan. It would be the answer only for a question on Recover.

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Singapore payments fintech is reviewing a summary of the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Critical Security Controls prepared by the firm’s IT team. Which of the following statements in the summary is most accurate?

options.text: The controls were built by the US Department of Commerce in the late 2000s and are licensed only to firms that are seeking formal certification.
Version 8 lists 18 critical controls, each of which is a single specific control rather than a control theme that is subdivided further.
The controls are prioritised to mitigate the most prevalent attacks, and are mapped to and referenced by multiple legal, regulatory and policy frameworks.
Because the controls form a stand-alone regime, they cannot be used alongside NIST or as a route towards ISO 27001 certification.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant at a Singapore fintech: which statement about the CIS Critical Security Controls is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The CIS Critical Security Controls are the most granular of the three dominant standards. GARP’s description:

| Feature | GARP description |
|---|---|
| Origin | Built in the late 2000s by a volunteer-expert coalition to protect companies from cybersecurity threats |
| Content | Key controls, regularly updated by experts from all fields; prioritised to mitigate the most prevalent attacks against systems and networks |
| Standing | Mapped to and referenced by multiple legal, regulatory and policy frameworks |
| Version | Version 8 (at the time of writing): 18 critical controls, freely accessible on the CIS website |
| Structure | Each critical control is a control theme or type, subdivided into about 10 specific controls |
| Refresh | Updated for cloud computing, virtualisation, mobility, outsourcing, work-from-home and changing attacker tactics |
| Use | Detailed; suits firms establishing or reviewing their measures; can coexist with other standards such as NIST, or help achieve ISO 27001 certification |

Examples from Table 9.2 include Control 1 (inventory and control of enterprise assets), Control 9 (e-mail and web browser protections), Control 11 (data recovery), Control 15 (service provider management) and Control 18 (penetration testing).

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the prioritisation of CIS controls against the most prevalent attacks and their mapping into legal, regulatory and policy frameworks, both stated together in GARP. The other statements misstate the origin, the structure and the compatibility.

**Fragile fact.** CIS v8: 18 themes, each about 10 controls, built by volunteers, free to access, and compatible with NIST and ISO 27001.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “CIS: Center for Internet Security” and Table 9.2. Schweser omits the origin, version number, count and structure, which come from GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q10 of 19.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The late-2000s date is right, but the builder was a volunteer-expert coalition, not the US Department of Commerce (which houses NIST), and the controls are freely accessible, not restricted to firms seeking certification. A would describe the origin of the NIST framework more closely.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The count of 18 is right, but each critical control is a theme subdivided into about 10 specific controls. B would be correct only if CIS had flattened its list to 18 single controls.

c.reason: GARP: “CIS controls are prioritized to mitigate the most prevalent cyberattacks against systems and networks. They are mapped to and referenced by multiple legal, regulatory, and policy frameworks.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP presents CIS as a good additional framework that can coexist with other standards such as NIST, or help achieve ISO 27001 certification. D would be correct if “cannot” read “can”.

questions.question:
The newly appointed chief information security officer of a Canadian credit union is choosing a framework. The credit union has no structured cybersecurity programme. She wants detailed, prioritised control-level guidance that her team can implement directly, covering items such as software asset inventory, e-mail and web browser protections and penetration testing, while keeping open the option of an ISO certification later.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Annual cybersecurity budget (CAD m) | 2.4 |
| Number of staff | 1150 |
| Branches | 38 |

Which of the following approaches is most appropriate?

options.text: Adopt ISO/IEC 27001 on its own, since its clauses supply the directly implementable technical controls she needs.
Adopt the CIS Critical Security Controls, which can coexist with other standards and support a later ISO 27001 certification.
Defer adopting any framework until a regulator mandates one, since the NIST and CIS frameworks are both voluntary.
Adopt the NIST framework, because it is the only one of the three that sets out specific controls such as penetration testing.

questions.solution:
New CISO of a Canadian credit union: which framework suits a firm that needs detailed, directly implementable controls and a path to ISO certification.

**Concept and theory**

The three dominant standards operate at different levels, and choosing between them is a matter of fit.

| Standard | Level of guidance | Best use (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| NIST CSF | Five functions with best-practice guidance; voluntary | Organising cyber risk management in a way similar to an ORMF |
| CIS Controls | 18 prioritised control themes, each with about 10 specific controls | Firms establishing or reviewing their measures; can coexist with NIST or support ISO 27001 certification |
| ISO/IEC 27001 | Evaluation grid, not implementable guidance per se | Firms seeking certification; requires an ISMS and controls |

The CIS list includes, among others, Control 2 (inventory and control of software assets), Control 9 (e-mail and web browser protections) and Control 18 (penetration testing).

**Applying it to this question**

Three conditions define the need: (1) no existing programme, (2) detailed control-level guidance that can be implemented directly, (3) a possible ISO certification later. The items listed in the stem are CIS control names. CIS works well for firms establishing their measures and can help achieve ISO 27001 certification. The budget, headcount and branch count are irrelevant: GARP’s choice criterion is the type of guidance needed, not the firm’s size.

**Fragile fact.** Detailed and implementable is CIS; evaluation grid for certification is ISO 27001; function-based, ORMF-like and voluntary is NIST.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “CIS: Center for Internet Security”, Table 9.2, and “ISO/IEC 27001: International Standard Organization”. Schweser agrees (CIS “can also be used to complement existing compliance standards, including NIST, or to help with ISO 27001 cybersecurity certification”). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q11 of 19.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The property “detailed and directly implementable” belongs to CIS. ISO standards “do not provide implementable guidance to firms per se, but rather act as evaluation grids” for certification. A would be correct if the CISO’s only goal were certification and she already had detailed controls in place.

b.reason: GARP: “The CIS guidance is detailed and works well for companies establishing or reviewing their cybersecurity measures. It is also a good option as an additional framework that can coexist with other, industry-specific compliance standards, such as NIST, or to achieve a certification in cybersecurity, such as ISO 27001.”

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Being voluntary does not make a framework unnecessary. Frameworks exist to give a systematic way to mitigate cyberthreats and benchmark to good practice, which the credit union lacks. C would be correct only if the question asked which frameworks a regulator could not enforce.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Penetration testing is CIS Control 18; NIST CSF sets out five functions with guidance, not a numbered list of specific controls. D would be correct if “NIST” read “CIS”.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a UK general insurer is reviewing a paper on the international standard ISO/IEC 27001 ahead of a certification decision. Which of the following statements about ISO/IEC 27001 is NOT correct?

options.text: It gives general guidance on organising information security risk management, including its governance, policies, support, communication and awareness.
In its final sections, it explains the role of audit and of management review in the context of information security.
It provides guidance on operational planning and control, on information security risk assessment and on risk treatment.
It provides directly implementable, step-by-step technical guidance to firms, rather than acting as an evaluation grid for certification.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at a UK insurer: which statement about ISO/IEC 27001 is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

ISO/IEC 27001 (the 2013 edition in GARP) is the internationally recognised standard for cybersecurity. Its content in GARP:

- general guidance to organise the risk management activities for information security, its governance, policies, support, and communication and awareness;
- guidance on operational planning and control, information security risk assessment and risk treatment;
- in its final sections, the role of audit and of management review in the context of information security.

Its nature is what distinguishes it from CIS. ISO standards do not provide implementable guidance to firms per se; they act as evaluation grids for those who want to achieve certification. In Schweser’s words, ISO 27001 provides a checklist of what firms need to achieve to gain certification. The practical work of choosing and implementing controls is left to the firm, which is why CIS can be used as a route to ISO certification.

**Applying it to this question**

Statements A, B and C each reproduce a line of GARP’s description of the standard’s content. Statement D reverses its nature: ISO 27001 is an evaluation grid, not step-by-step technical guidance. D is therefore the statement that is NOT correct.

**Fragile fact.** ISO 27001 tells a firm what it must achieve to be certified, not how to implement controls; the “how” comes from guidance such as CIS.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “ISO/IEC 27001: International Standard Organization”. GARP refers to ISO/IEC 27001:2013 and also names 27002; Schweser refers to ISO 27001 only and adds “guidance on . . . communications about the firm”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the tested point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q12 of 19.

a.reason: **True statement; trap: sounds too broad.** GARP states that the standard provides general guidance to organise information security risk management, its governance, policies, support, and communication and awareness. Some readers reject it because “awareness” sounds like a behavioural control rather than a standard’s content. It would be the answer only if it attributed this content to CIS.

b.reason: **True statement; trap: role confusion.** The final sections of ISO 27001 explain the role of audit and of management review. Readers who associate audit only with the external certification auditor may think this is outside the standard. It would be the answer if it said the standard excludes audit.

c.reason: **True statement; trap: sibling with NIST.** Operational planning and control, risk assessment and risk treatment are part of ISO 27001. The words “risk assessment” can make it look like a description of NIST’s Identify function. It would be the answer only if it named NIST’s five functions as ISO content.

d.reason: GARP: “ISO standards do not provide implementable guidance to firms per se, but rather act as evaluation grids for those who want to achieve certification in ISO standards.” Statement D says the opposite, so it is the incorrect statement the question asks for.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a French asset manager that intends to become certified as ISO 27001-compliant within 18 months. The managing partner asks what the framework requires the firm to have in place. Which of the following best describes a requirement for certification?

options.text: An information security management system that identifies threats and vulnerabilities, with effective controls and an ongoing, improving risk management process.
Full implementation of all 18 CIS critical security controls and their specific sub-controls, verified by the auditor before any ISO assessment can begin.
Evidence that each of the five NIST functions has been executed, with the Identify and Recover steps documented in a single external audit report.
A risk assessment performed once at the certification date, after which the framework requires no further updating or improvement of the controls.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant advising a French asset manager: what ISO 27001 requires for certification.

**Concept and theory**

Certification under ISO 27001 rests on a management system rather than on a fixed control list. GARP sets out the sequence:

1. The framework mandates that an adopting organisation have an **Information Security Man-** **agement System (ISMS)** that systematically manages the organisation’s information security risks by identifying threats and vulnerabilities.
2. The organisation is required to design and implement information security, including **effective** **and comprehensive controls** to mitigate the risks identified.
3. The organisation should adopt an **ongoing risk management process**, continuously striving to update and improve.
4. To be certified, it must demonstrate to the auditor that it uses the “POCA cycle” (presented in an earlier chapter of the GARP book).

The logic is that of a living system: certification attests that the firm identifies risks, controls them, and keeps improving, not that it passed a one-day snapshot.

**Applying it to this question**

The managing partner asks what must be in place. The deciding facts are the ISMS that identifies threats and vulnerabilities, the effective controls, and the ongoing, improving process. Option A contains all three. The other options import requirements from CIS or NIST, or deny the ongoing nature of the process.

**Fragile fact.** ISO 27001 certification needs an ISMS, effective controls and continuous improvement, demonstrated to an auditor; it does not require CIS or NIST adoption.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “ISO/IEC 27001: International Standard Organization”. Schweser agrees (an ISMS, effective and comprehensive controls, and a comprehensive risk management process with ongoing improvements) and does not mention the POCA cycle, which is from GARP. The POCA cycle itself is Chapter 5 material and is not tested. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q13 of 19.

a.reason: GARP: the framework “mandates that an organization adopting ISO 27001 have an Information Security Management System (ISMS) that systematically manages the organization’s information security risks, by identifying threats and vulnerabilities”, requires effective and comprehensive controls, and suggests “an ongoing risk management process, continuously striving to update and improve”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** The 18 critical controls belong to CIS. CIS can help a firm achieve ISO 27001 certification, but its full implementation is not an ISO requirement. B would be correct for a firm seeking to claim full CIS v8 adoption, not ISO certification.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** The five functions (identify, protect, detect, respond, recover) are NIST CSF, which is voluntary and separate from ISO certification. C would be correct if the question asked how to evidence NIST CSF adoption.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** ISO 27001 expects an ongoing risk management process, continuously striving to update and improve. A one-off assessment with no further updating is the opposite. D would be correct only if the standard were a point-in-time checklist with no maintenance requirement.

questions.question:
The operational resilience lead at a Japanese trust bank is classifying three recent events against the three dimensions of information protection (confidentiality, integrity, availability) and the discipline each dimension relates to (“security” for information security, “continuity” for business continuity).

| Event | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | A system failure takes the online banking platform offline for six hours |
| 2 | Payment instructions stored in a database are altered without authorisation |
| 3 | A client list is disclosed to an unauthorised outside party |

Which of the following classifications is most accurate?

options.text: 1: availability, security; 2: integrity, security; 3: confidentiality, security
1: availability, continuity; 2: confidentiality, security; 3: confidentiality, security
1: availability, continuity; 2: integrity, security; 3: confidentiality, security
1: availability, continuity; 2: integrity, continuity; 3: confidentiality, security

questions.solution:
Operational resilience lead at a Japanese trust bank: classify three events by CIA dimension and related discipline.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes the protection of information in three dimensions, the CIA triad:

| Dimension | What is protected | Relates to (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Information is seen only by those authorised | Information security |
| Integrity | Information is accurate and not altered without authorisation | Information security |
| Availability | Information and systems are accessible when needed | Business continuity and systems uptime, now in the scope of resilience |

The split matters for organisation. Confidentiality and integrity failures are information security events, handled by the security function and its controls. Availability failures are continuity events: they belong with business continuity and operational resilience, which is why GARP says availability is “now in the scope of resilience”. (The short definitions in the middle column are standard meanings of the terms; GARP names the dimensions and their mapping but does not define them further.)

**Applying it to this question**

- Event 1: the platform is offline; information is not accessible. Availability, which relates to business continuity and systems uptime.
- Event 2: data altered without authorisation. Integrity, which relates to information security.
- Event 3: information seen by an unauthorised party. Confidentiality, which relates to information security.

**Fragile fact.** C and I belong to information security; A (availability) belongs to business continuity and resilience.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Essentials of Cybersecurity Protection and Monitoring”. Schweser agrees on the mapping but omits “systems uptime” and “now in the scope of resilience”, which come from GARP. The working definitions of each dimension are general knowledge used only to read the events, and are flagged as such. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q14 of 19.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** All three dimensions are put under information security. GARP assigns availability to business continuity and systems uptime. A would be correct only under a framework that treated every CIA dimension as a security matter.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Event 2 is labelled confidentiality. Unauthorised alteration is a failure of integrity; nothing has been disclosed. B would be correct if event 2 had been the unauthorised viewing, not alteration, of payment instructions.

c.reason: GARP: “The protection of information has three dimensions often referred to as CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. The first two relate to information security, while the third relates to business continuity and systems uptime, now in the scope of resilience.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Integrity is mapped to business continuity. Only availability relates to continuity; integrity stays with information security. D would be correct if the mapping were “integrity and availability relate to continuity”, which is not GARP’s.

questions.question:
The head of information security at a Brazilian investment bank is sorting a list of controls into behavioural and technical controls for the annual control inventory.

I. Fake phishing tests sent to staff

II. Password cracking attempts run by the IT department

III. Penetration testing of systems

IV. Data transfer rules

V. A honeypot on the internal network

Which of the controls should be classified as behavioural controls?

options.text: I and IV only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV only
I, IV and V only

questions.solution:
Head of information security at a Brazilian investment bank: which controls are behavioural.

**Concept and theory**

GARP says effective mitigation comes from a combination of technical protection measures and appropriate human behaviours, and groups information controls in two categories.

- **Behavioural controls** address human behaviour and fallibility in handling and protecting information: awareness campaigns, rules of conduct and prudence for employees and contractors, online training, password management, supervision and sanctions. They apply to all types of information security risk, not just cyberattacks.
- **Technical controls** relate to all technical aspects of systems, for prevention, detection or mitigation.

Table 9.3 lists key controls in each category.

| Category | Group | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Behavioural | Awareness and prudence | Awareness campaign; training; fake phishing test; password cracking attempt (from IT department) |
| Behavioural | Conduct rules | Rules of confidentiality; code of conduct; sanctions rules |
| Behavioural | Data governance | Data transfer rules |
| Technical | Architecture, access, encryption | Network partitioning; firewalls; password rules; encryption levels and rules |
| Technical | Detection | DLPD; honeypot |
| Technical | Testing | Penetration testing |

The key insight: a control is behavioural if its object is human behaviour, even if it is run with technical tools. A fake phishing e-mail and a password cracking attempt test whether staff behave prudently (do they click, did they choose weak passwords); penetration testing and honeypots test or watch systems.

**Applying it to this question**

I (fake phishing tests): awareness and prudence, behavioural. II (password cracking attempts run by IT): awareness and prudence, behavioural, despite being run by the IT department. III (penetration testing): technical testing. IV (data transfer rules): data governance, behavioural. V (honeypot): technical detection. Behavioural set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Password cracking attempts run by IT are behavioural (they test staff); password rules and penetration testing are technical (they configure or test systems).

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Essentials of Cybersecurity Protection and Monitoring”, Table 9.3. Schweser lists awareness campaigns, rules of conduct, training, password management, supervision and sanctions as behavioural, but omits Table 9.3 (fake phishing tests, password cracking attempts, data transfer rules), which comes from GARP. The exact sub-grouping of the technical rows of Table 9.3 is not tested; the classification of the five tested items is unambiguous. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q15 of 19.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It drops II because the IT department runs it, treating the actor as decisive. GARP classifies password cracking attempts as behavioural even though they come from IT, because they target staff password habits. A would be correct if II were “password rules enforced by the system”, which GARP lists as technical.

b.reason: GARP’s Table 9.3 places fake phishing tests and password cracking attempts (from the IT department) under “Awareness and Prudence” and data transfer rules under “Data Governance”, all within behavioural controls.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It adds penetration testing, which tests system defences and sits under “Testing” in technical controls. C would be correct if III were a social engineering exercise aimed at staff rather than a test of systems.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps II for the honeypot, a technical detective control that creates a virtual trap to lure attackers. D would be correct only if the honeypot were classified as an awareness tool, which GARP does not do.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a US broker-dealer is reviewing the descriptions of technical controls in the firm’s information security policy. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.text: Preventive controls, such as firewalls, encryption, passwords and patching, are essentially directed at internal threats.
Detective controls, such as data loss prevention and detection, give early warning only of leaks initiated by external attackers.
Mitigating controls consist mainly of honeypots, which create a virtual trap designed to lure attackers away from real systems.
Mitigating controls, the third technical category after preventive and detective controls, focus on keeping redundancies and back-ups offline.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a US broker-dealer: which description of technical controls is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Technical controls relate to all technical aspects of systems. GARP divides them by what they do in time relative to an incident:

| Type | Purpose | Examples (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| Preventive | Stop incidents happening; essentially directed at external threats | System architecture, access, firewalls, encryption, passwords, patching |
| Detective | Early warning of data leaks, whether initiated internally or externally | DLPD (monitors access to and exchange of confidential data to identify unauthorised disclosure or improper usage); honeypot (a virtual trap to lure attackers) |
| Mitigating | Limit the consequences | Keeping redundancies and back-ups offline |

Why keep back-ups offline? An online back-up connected to the network can be reached by the same attacker who compromised the primary systems; an offline copy survives the attack and allows restoration.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each description against two attributes: the examples and the direction of threat. Option D gives the right example (redundancies and back-ups offline) for the right category (mitigating). The others misstate the threat direction (A, B) or misplace an example (C).

**Fragile fact.** Preventive is aimed at external threats; detective covers leaks from inside or outside; honeypots detect, offline back-ups mitigate.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Essentials of Cybersecurity Protection and Monitoring”. Schweser says detective controls give “early warnings of data incidents” and omits the honeypot and the “internally or externally” wording, which come from GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q16 of 19.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The examples are right but the direction is reversed: GARP says preventive controls “are essentially directed at external threats”. A would be correct if “internal” read “external”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP says detective controls provide early warnings of data leaks “whether initiated internally or externally”. Restricting them to external attackers drops half of the stated condition. B would be correct if it said “leaks initiated internally or externally”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** The honeypot is described correctly, but it is a detective control, listed with DLPD. Mitigating controls keep redundancies and back-ups offline. C would be correct if “mitigating” read “detective”.

d.reason: GARP: “Finally, mitigating controls focus on keeping redundancies and backups offline.” Mitigating controls are the third technical category after preventive and detective controls.

questions.question: The board of a Hong Kong-based private bank has stated that it has zero tolerance for information security breaches. The CRO is asked how the intensity of information security controls should be set across the bank’s data holdings. Which of the following recommendations is most consistent with good practice?

options.text: Apply the strongest available controls uniformly to all information, because cost, convenience and speed cease to matter once zero tolerance is declared.
Leave the number and intensity of controls to the IT department alone, because risk appetite has no bearing on information security controls.
Categorise information by sensitivity level, and balance the benefits of risk reduction against the cost of controls, convenience and speed.
Rely on the zero-tolerance statement itself, since all firms that claim it share the same commitment to governance, discipline and technical controls.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Hong Kong private bank with a zero-tolerance board statement: how to set the intensity of information security controls.

**Concept and theory**

Controls are never free. GARP makes three linked points about how many controls a firm should have and how strong they should be.

1. **Risk appetite and consistency.** The number and intensity of controls are a matter of risk appetite and consistency of choices. Every firm claims zero tolerance for information security breaches, but firms do not necessarily have the same commitment to the governance, discipline and technical controls needed to guarantee a high level of security. A zero-tolerance statement is therefore not evidence of security.
2. **Cost-benefit.** Information security measures cost time, money and effort, so the benefits of risk reduction must be balanced against the cost of controls, convenience and speed.
3. **Sensitivity levels.** Categorising information sensitivity levels helps a firm adjust the resources dedicated to protecting each type of information: the most sensitive data gets the strongest controls, less sensitive data proportionately less.

**Applying it to this question**

The board’s zero-tolerance statement tempts the CRO toward maximum controls everywhere. GARP’s position is that the statement does not change the economics: control intensity should still be calibrated by sensitivity and by cost-benefit. Option C is the only recommendation that applies both points.

**Fragile fact.** Zero tolerance is claimed by everyone and proves nothing; intensity follows risk appetite, sensitivity categorisation and cost-benefit.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “Essentials of Cybersecurity Protection and Monitoring”. Schweser states the cost-benefit point (each firm must weigh the cost of controls, convenience and speed against the benefits of risk reduction) but omits the zero-tolerance remark and the sensitivity categorisation, which come from GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q17 of 19.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It removes the cost-benefit condition because of the zero-tolerance statement. GARP requires the balance against cost, convenience and speed regardless of what firms claim. A would be correct only if controls were costless.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It hands the decision to IT alone and denies the link to risk appetite. GARP says the number and intensity of controls are a matter of risk appetite, which is set by the firm’s governance. B would be correct only if risk appetite played no role, the reverse of GARP.

c.reason: GARP: “Information security measures cost time, money, and effort, so the benefits of risk reduction need to be balanced against the cost of controls, convenience, and speed. In that regard, categorizing information sensitivity levels is important to aid in adjusting the resources dedicated to information protection.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says firms claiming zero tolerance “do not necessarily have the same level of commitment” to governance, discipline and technical controls. D asserts that they do. It would be correct if “share the same commitment” read “do not necessarily share the same commitment”.
