questions.question: A banking supervisor in Singapore is reviewing how a domestic bank organises the monitoring of information security and cyber risks across its lines of defence. Which of the following arrangements is most consistent with common practice?

options.text: Nearly all technical monitoring takes place in IT, the first line, while a separate information security department, often second line, designs, maintains and monitors the controls.
Nearly all technical monitoring takes place in the information security department, the third line, while IT, the second line, designs and maintains the behavioural controls.
Monitoring concentrates on counting realised losses, because in highly controlled activities deviations from normality in exposure, traffic or staff behaviour carry no signal.
The information security department sits within IT in every firm, because information security involves nothing more than securing the business against cyberattacks.

questions.solution:
Banking supervisor in Singapore: how monitoring of information security is organised across the lines of defence.

**Concept and theory**

In highly controlled activities such as information security and cyber protection, GARP says risk monitoring focuses on the effectiveness of controls and on unexpected deviations from normality, such as changes in exposure, traffic or staff behaviour. The intuition: losses in a well-controlled area are rare, so waiting for losses gives no warning; the signal lies in weakening controls and unusual patterns.

Who does what:

| Function | Line | Role (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| IT department | First | Nearly all technical monitoring of cyberattacks and access breaches |
| Information security department | Most often second | In many firms separate from IT; designs, maintains and monitors a comprehensive set of behavioural and technical controls, where deviations and failings constitute KRIs |

The separation of information security from IT reflects the fact that information security involves more than securing the business against cyberattacks: it also covers paper, behaviour, leaks and data governance.

**Applying it to this question**

The supervisor is testing who monitors and who designs. The deciding facts: nearly all technical monitoring sits in IT (first line), and a separate information security department, most often second line, designs, maintains and monitors behavioural and technical controls. Only option A states both.

**Fragile fact.** IT monitors (first line); information security, often separate from IT, designs and monitors controls (most often second line).

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “KRIs for Information Security”. Schweser says most firms monitor cyberattacks and breaches within IT and many have a separate information security department that designs, maintains and monitors controls, but does not mention the lines of defence or the focus on deviations from normality; those come from GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q18 of 19.

a.reason: GARP: “At a technical level and for cyberattacks and access breaches, nearly all monitoring takes place in the IT department, in the first line of defense. In many firms the information security department is separate from IT . . . It is most often part of the second line of defense. The information security department should design, maintain, and monitor a comprehensive set of behavioral and technical controls.”

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The roles and lines are swapped: technical monitoring is given to information security, labelled third line, and control design to IT, labelled second line. Information security is most often second line and IT does the technical monitoring as first line. B would be correct only if the lines were relabelled in exactly that way, which GARP does not do.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says monitoring focuses on control effectiveness and on unexpected deviations from normality (exposure, traffic, staff behaviour). C reverses this and claims such deviations carry no signal. It would be correct only for an area with frequent losses and weak controls.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** “In every firm” and “nothing more than” are both contradicted: in many firms information security is separate from IT, precisely because it involves more than cyberattacks. D would be correct if it read “in some firms” and dropped the claim about scope.

questions.question:
The information security department of an Australian bank tracks the key risk indicator “percentage change in the number of IT help-desk requests per IT manager”. One IT manager joined at the start of the current quarter. Data for the last two quarters are shown below.

| Item | Previous quarter | Current quarter |
|---|---|---|
| IT help-desk requests | 3360 | 3900 |
| IT managers | 12 | 13 |
| Approved cybersecurity positions | 40 | 40 |
| Vacant cybersecurity positions | 6 | 7 |
| Annual IT budget (AUD m) | 18 | 18 |

What is the value of the KRI for the current quarter?
questions.solution:
Information security department of an Australian bank: compute the KRI “percentage change in IT help-desk requests per IT manager”.

**Concept and theory**

A key risk indicator (KRI) is a metric whose movement signals rising risk before losses occur. For information security, GARP explains that the information security department designs and monitors a set of controls “where deviations and failings constitute KRIs”, and Table 9.4 gives examples:

| Examples of KRIs for information security risk (GARP Table 9.4, selection) |
|---|
| Overdue vulnerability patching; overdue penetration tests or overdue resolution of their recommendations |
| Overdue replacement of obsolescent software; results of phishing tests and of password cracking attempts |
| Number of computers with inadequate access and overdue revisions of access |
| % change in number of IT help-desk requests, change requests or issues per IT manager |
| % vacancies in IT or cybersecurity teams; overcapacity usage of systems |
| Number of “repeat offenders” (staff failing more than one phishing test) in sensitive data areas |

The help-desk KRI is a workload ratio: it normalises demand by the size of the team supervising it. A rising ratio means each manager carries more issues, which signals strain and a higher chance that problems are missed. Normalising matters: if requests grow but the team grows equally, there is no extra strain.

Formula, with $\text{R}_{\text{t}}$ the number of help-desk requests and $\text{M}_{\text{t}}$ the number of IT managers in quarter t:

$\text{KRI}_{\text{t}} = \frac{\text{R}_{\text{t}}\text{/M}_{\text{t}}}{\text{R}_{\text{t}-1}\text{/M}_{\text{t}-1}} -$ 1

**Applying it to this question**

Requests per manager, previous quarter $= \frac{3360}{12} =$ 280.0

Requests per manager, current quarter $= \frac{3900}{13} =$ 300.0

KRI $= \frac{300.0}{280.0} -$ 1 = 0.0714 = +7.14%

The approved and vacant cybersecurity positions and the IT budget are irrelevant to this KRI (the vacancy data would feed a different KRI, % vacancies, which is 6/40 = 15.0% then 7/40 = 17.5%). Interpretation: each IT manager is handling about 7.1% more help-desk requests than a quarter ago, even after the new hire. Workload per manager is rising, which the information security department should compare with the KRI’s threshold.

**Fragile fact.** The KRI is per IT manager: normalise first, then take the change against the previous quarter’s ratio.

**Reference**

LO 50.a: “Provide examples of cyber threats and information security risks, and describe frameworks and best practices for managing cyber risks.” GARP Chapter 9, “KRIs for Information Security”, Table 9.4. Schweser does not cover KRIs for information security; the content is from GARP only. The calculation is an application of the GARP KRI definition, not a formula given in the source. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 a, where it is Q19 of 19.

a.reason: **Wrong base; direction of the denominator.** The change is divided by the current rather than the previous value: (300 − 280)/300 = 6.67%. A percentage change is measured relative to the starting value. A would be correct if the question asked how far the previous ratio lies below the current one, as a share of the current ratio.

b.reason: The KRI is the percentage change in the ratio of requests to IT managers, 300/280 − 1 = +7.14%, matching GARP’s definition “% change in # of IT help-desk requests . . . per IT manager”.

c.reason: **Intermediate result misused; approximation.** The growth rates of requests and managers are subtracted: requests +16.07%, managers 13/12 − 1 = +8.33%, difference 16.07% − 8.33% = 7.74%. Subtraction only approximates the change in a ratio; the exact figure is 1.1607/1.0833 − 1 = 7.14%. C would be correct only as a first-order approximation, which the KRI definition does not ask for.

d.reason: **Dropped term.** The manager headcount is ignored: 3900/3360 − 1 = +16.07%. This is the change in raw requests, the numerator alone, and omits the “per IT manager” normalisation. D would be correct if the KRI were “% change in the number of IT help-desk requests”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.
questions.reading: ORR-9: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
questions.topic: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-9 b Q1
questions.question: A junior operational risk analyst at a Canadian life insurer is preparing a briefing note for new analysts on how the 2017 Equifax intrusion began. Which of the following statements best describes the initial attack?

options.text: The attackers exploited a flaw introduced by a patch that Equifax had installed on Apache Struts a few days earlier, so the intrusion originated in the remediation itself.
The attackers exploited a zero-day flaw in Apache Struts for which no vendor patch yet existed, so even immediate patching by Equifax could not have closed the entry point.
The attackers exploited a known Apache Struts vulnerability through the online dispute portal, for which a patch had been released before the attack but never implemented by Equifax.
The attackers entered through a phishing e-mail that captured an employee’s credentials, and used the Apache Struts flaw only later to move from the portal into other databases.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Canadian life insurer describing how the 2017 Equifax intrusion began.

**Concept and theory**

A vulnerability is a weakness in software that an attacker can exploit. When a software vendor learns of one, it publishes a patch (a code fix) and the vulnerability becomes known: from that moment, the risk sits with every user who has not yet installed the fix. A zero-day vulnerability is the opposite case, a flaw that attackers exploit before any patch exists. The distinction matters for lessons learned: a zero-day breach points to detection and response, while a breach through a known, patchable flaw points to failures in asset inventory, patch management and internal communication, which are exactly the failures the Equifax case is used to teach.

GARP sets out the Equifax facts as follows:

- Equifax is one of the largest credit reporting agencies in the United States; banks, insurers, prospective employers and landlords use its data daily.
- On 10 March 2017, hackers breached its networks by exploiting a vulnerability in Apache Struts via Equifax’s online dispute portal, then moved quickly from the infected portal into other parts of the network.
- The patch for this vulnerability had been released on 7 March, three days before the attack; an alert reached Equifax on 8 March and was distributed to 400 employees by the Global Threats and Vulnerability Management (GTVM) team.
- NIST had assigned the vulnerability the highest criticality score, 10, under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Nevertheless, the patch was never implemented, for multiple reasons.
- For three months the hackers remained undetected while extracting names, addresses, dates of birth, social security numbers and credit card accounts.

Box 9.1 summarises the cause in one line: an external intrusion on Equifax servers following an unpatched (known) vulnerability.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks how the attack began. Three facts decide it: the entry point (the online dispute portal running Apache Struts), the status of the flaw (known, with a patch available from 7 March) and Equifax’s action (the patch was never applied). Only one option contains all three without corruption.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of the patch: released by the vendor on 7 March, never applied by Equifax; the breach exploited the unpatched flaw, not the patch.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, and Box 9.1 (High profile, egregious data hacks). GARP vs Schweser conflict: the condensed notes state that the attack happened a few days after Equifax applied a patch and that attackers exploited a vulnerability in the patch. GARP states that the patch was released by the vendor on 7 March and was never implemented. Resolved from GARP; this looks like a compression error in the condensed source rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the patch status: Equifax did not install the patch, and the flaw was not created by a fix. The attackers exploited the vulnerability that the patch was designed to close. This option reproduces a compressed account found in some condensed notes (see the reference note below). It would be correct only in a stem describing a faulty patch that itself introduced a new vulnerability, which is not the Equifax case.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the properties of a zero-day attack to the Equifax breach. A patch existed three days before the attack and the vulnerability carried a published CVSS score of 10, so prompt patching would have closed the entry point. The option would be correct for a breach in which attackers exploited a flaw before any vendor fix had been published.

c.reason: It matches GARP exactly: a known Apache Struts vulnerability, exploited through the online dispute portal, with a patch released before the attack (7 March) that Equifax never implemented. This is also the Box 9.1 characterisation of the cause as an external intrusion following an unpatched known vulnerability.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It imports the attack vector of a different case in the chapter: phishing to capture credentials (as in the bZx private-key theft). At Equifax, the Apache Struts flaw was the initial entry point, not a later tool for lateral movement. The option would fit a stem about a credential-phishing breach followed by exploitation of an internal system.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is building a cyber incident timeline for the bank’s operational risk committee, using the Equifax case as the worked example. She has collected the following data.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Vendor releases the Apache Struts patch | 7 March 2017 |
| Alert distributed internally by the GTVM team | 8 March 2017 |
| Attackers breach Equifax’s networks | 10 March 2017 |
| Certificate updated and suspicious activity noticed | 29 July 2017 |
| Public announcement of the breach | 7 September 2017 |
| Unpatched vulnerabilities found by the 2015 internal audit | 8,500 |
| Customers affected in the first public announcement | 143 million |

Which of the following correctly states (i) the number of days the attackers operated before the breach was noticed and (ii) the number of days between that discovery and the public announcement?

options.text: (i) 141 days; (ii) 40 days
(i) 143 days; (ii) 40 days
(i) 141 days; (ii) 181 days
(i) 92 days; (ii) 42 days

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at an Australian bank counting the undetected period and the disclosure delay in the Equifax timeline.

**Concept and theory**

An incident timeline separates three intervals that correspond to three different control failures:

| Interval | Measured from and to | Control failure it reflects at Equifax |
|---|---|---|
| Exposure window | Patch release to breach | Patch not applied (inventory, enforcement, communication) |
| Dwell time | Breach to discovery | Detection failure (expired SSL certificate) |
| Disclosure delay | Discovery to announcement | Crisis communication failure |

GARP gives the dates: patch released 7 March 2017; alert sent to Equifax on 8 March; breach on 10 March; suspicious activity noticed on 29 July after the certificate was finally updated (“over three months after it had started”); public announcement on 7 September 2017, described as “six weeks after its discovery”. The lesson is that each interval is a separate KRI-style measure of a separate weakness, so the dates must be anchored to the right events.

**Applying it to this question**

Dwell time is counted from the breach (10 March), not from the alert or the patch. Disclosure delay is counted from discovery (29 July), not from the breach.

Dwell time = (31 − 10) + 30 + 31 + 30 + 29

= 21 (rest of March) + 30 (April) + 31 (May) + 30 (June) + 29 (July) = 141 days

Disclosure delay = (31 − 29) + 31 + 7 = 2 (rest of July) + 31 (August) + 7 (September) = 40 days The 8,500 backlog and the 143 million customer figure are irrelevant inputs. Interpretation: the attackers had more than four and a half months inside the network, and customers then waited almost six weeks (40 days is 5.7 weeks) for disclosure.

**Fragile fact.** Anchor dates: breach 10 March (not the 7 March patch or 8 March alert), discovery 29 July, announcement 7 September 2017.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax” (attack narrative; weaknesses 4 and 5). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes give only “March 2017”, “late July 2017” and 7 September 2017, without the 10 March breach date or the 29 July discovery date; the day counts here use GARP’s dates. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: 141 days from the 10 March breach to the 29 July discovery, and 40 days from discovery to the 7 September announcement, consistent with GARP’s “over three months” and “six weeks after its discovery”.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin.** The dwell time is counted from the 8 March alert date instead of the 10 March breach date: 141 + 2 = 143 days. It would be correct if the question asked for the days from the internal alert to discovery.

c.reason: **Intermediate result.** The second figure is the cumulative period from the breach to the announcement, 141 + 40 = 181 days, rather than the period from discovery to announcement. It would be correct if part (ii) asked for days from the breach to the public announcement.

d.reason: **Unit slip.** Both figures convert the narrative durations instead of counting dates: “three months” from 10 March read as 92 days (to 10 June) and “six weeks” read as 6 × 7 = 42 days. GARP’s words are approximations (“over three months”, “six weeks”); the dates give 141 and 40. It would be correct only if the stem defined the intervals as exactly three calendar months and six weeks.

questions.loText: Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.
questions.reading: ORR-9: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
questions.topic: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-9 b Q3
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is preparing a report on what Equifax knew about its own weaknesses before the 2017 breach. She drafts the following statements.

I. A 2015 internal audit identified a backlog of about 8,500 unpatched vulnerabilities resulting from severe weaknesses in the patch management process.

II. At the time of that audit, the Chief Security Officer was developing the implementation of Equifax’s first patch management policy.

III. In May 2016, Equifax’s W-2 Express website was hacked, leaking the personal information of about 430,000 individuals.

IV. By early 2017 most of the deficiencies found in 2015 had been remediated, so the March breach exploited a weakness that had arisen only recently.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Singapore bank listing what Equifax knew of its weaknesses before the breach.

**Concept and theory**

A recurring lesson of large operational risk events is that they are rarely surprises: the warning signs are usually already in the firm’s own records, and the failure lies in not acting on them. GARP stresses that the Equifax attack “would probably have not taken place in a healthy cybersecurity environment, but it should not have come as a surprise to Equifax”. The evidence it cites:

- At the time, Equifax’s cybersecurity frameworks, policies and tools were outdated and poorly maintained.
- In 2015, an internal audit detected a backlog of 8,500 unpatched vulnerabilities resulting from severe weaknesses in the patch management process.
- The CSO was at the time developing the implementation of Equifax’s first patch management policy.
- In May 2016, a year before the major leak, the W-2 Express website was hacked, leaking 430,000 names, addresses, social security numbers and other personal information.
- By 2017, most of Equifax’s security deficiencies remained unremediated.

The audit finding, the immature policy and an actual prior breach are three independent signals; the lesson is that identified issues must be remediated and tracked, not merely recorded.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the list above. I matches the 2015 audit finding. II matches the CSO developing the first patch management policy at the time. III matches the May 2016 W-2 Express hack. IV states that the deficiencies had largely been remediated by early 2017, which reverses GARP’s statement that most deficiencies remained unremediated.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: by 2017 most deficiencies remained unremediated; the breach exploited old, known weakness, not a new one.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax” (paragraph beginning “Such an attack would probably have not taken place. . . ”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes mention the 2015 audit backlog and a 2016 website hack affecting 430,000 customers, but not the W-2 Express name, the May date or the CSO’s first patch policy; these details are from GARP. No conflict on the facts tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It omits statement II, treating the immaturity of the patch policy as not part of the record. GARP explicitly notes that the CSO was then implementing Equifax’s first patch management policy, which is itself evidence of an underdeveloped control. It would be correct only if statement II had misdated the policy or attributed it to the wrong executive.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts statement IV, which flips “remained unremediated” into “had been remediated”. It would be correct in a stem about a firm that had closed its audit findings and was then breached through a genuinely new weakness, and only if II were also judged false.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts the reversed statement IV and also rejects two true statements (I and III). It would be correct only if the audit backlog and the 2016 hack had not occurred, which contradicts the source.

d.reason: Statements I, II and III are each direct restatements of GARP’s account of the pre-breach environment; statement IV is false, so “I, II and III only” is the only correct combination.

questions.question:
A senior risk consultant is reviewing the vulnerability management process at a Brazilian retail bank. Bank policy requires critical vulnerabilities to be patched within 48 hours of an alert. The consultant reconstructs the bank’s handling of its most recent critical alert, on a software library used across several platforms.

| Step | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Vendor alert received by the security team | Hour 0 |
| Alert circulated to all registered system owners | Hour 2 |
| Platforms confirmed as running the library | 3 of 5 |
| Patching of the confirmed platforms completed | Hour 30 |
| Two further platforms found running the library | Day 9 |
| Annual vulnerability tooling budget | BRL 4.2 million |

Which of the following best describes the Equifax weakness this pattern most closely replicates, together with its consequence at Equifax?

options.text: Failure to enforce the patch management policy, which meant that Equifax had set no deadline at all for patching vulnerabilities rated critical.
Lack of a comprehensive inventory of IT assets, which left the GTVM teams unable to locate and patch Apache Struts within 48 hours of the alert.
Inconsistent internal communication, which meant that the GTVM team itself never received the vendor alert concerning Apache Struts.
Use of an expired SSL certificate, which prevented the GTVM teams from scanning the network to find the servers running Apache Struts.

questions.solution:
Senior risk consultant at a Brazilian bank whose patching missed two platforms nobody knew ran a critical library.

**Concept and theory**

You cannot patch what you do not know you own. An IT asset inventory is the list of all hardware, software and data a firm uses, and it is the precondition for every downstream security control: a vulnerability alert can only be acted on if the firm can map the vulnerable software to the specific systems that run it.

GARP’s first key weakness at Equifax, compared with market standards in information security management, was “a lack of a comprehensive inventory of IT assets”. Its direct consequence: the Equifax GTVM teams were unable to locate and patch Apache Struts, as they should have done within 48 hours of a critical vulnerability being alerted. The alert had been received (8 March) and circulated (to 400 employees), and the patch existed (7 March); what failed was the mapping from alert to system.

The table distinguishes this from the neighbouring weaknesses:

| Weakness at Equifax | What it directly prevented |
|---|---|
| 1. No comprehensive IT asset inventory | Locating the systems running Apache Struts |
| 2. Patch policy not enforced | Timely patching as a matter of discipline |
| 3. Inconsistent internal communication | The alert reaching every relevant person |
| 4. Expired SSL certificate | Monitoring encrypted traffic (detection) |

**Applying it to this question**

At the Brazilian bank, the alert was received and circulated promptly, and the three known platforms were patched within the 48-hour window (hour 30). The failure was that two platforms running the library were not on anyone’s list and were found only on day 9. This is the inventory weakness, not a communication or enforcement failure. The BRL 4.2 million budget is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and consequence: the GTVM teams received the alert but could not locate Apache Struts, so the 48-hour patch window was missed because of the inventory gap.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, key weakness 1 (“A lack of a comprehensive inventory of IT assets”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes describe the weakness as an insufficient inventory exposing Equifax to vulnerabilities, including the inability to patch quickly, but omit the GTVM team and the 48-hour window, which come from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns the pattern to weakness 2 and adds a false condition: GARP’s account implies a 48-hour patching expectation for critical alerts, so a deadline existed. The bank in the stem also enforced its deadline on the platforms it knew about. The option would be closer to correct in a stem where known systems were left unpatched past the deadline with no escalation.

b.reason: It names the matching weakness (lack of a comprehensive inventory of IT assets) and the consequence GARP attaches to it: the GTVM teams could not locate and patch Apache Struts within 48 hours of the alert.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** At Equifax the GTVM team did receive the alert and was the actor that distributed it to 400 employees; the communication failure involved one employee left off the list and a manager who did not relay it. The option would be correct only if the security team had never been notified by the vendor.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The expired SSL certificate was designed to inspect encrypted network traffic; its failure blinded detection of the hacking activity, not the ability to find servers running a given library. It would be correct in a stem asking why the intrusion went unnoticed for months.

questions.question: The CRO of a Japanese regional bank is reviewing an internal report on IT security. The bank has a board-approved patch management policy, but compliance with patching deadlines is not monitored and overdue patches trigger no escalation. The report notes that 37% of critical patches are overdue and that the bank spent JPY 180 million on security software last year. In briefing the board on the corresponding lesson from the Equifax case, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The lesson is that patching is routine maintenance outside the key IT security controls, so overdue patches call for an IT service review rather than board attention.
The lesson is that a board-approved patch policy guarantees timely patching, so the bank needs only to recirculate its existing policy to the relevant staff.
The lesson is that missed patches were a secondary weakness at Equifax, because the intrusion itself was made possible mainly by the expired SSL certificate.
The lesson is that failing to enforce patch management leaves systems exposed, much like leaving a door unlocked in the physical world, so enforcement must be fixed.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Japanese regional bank with an approved but unenforced patch policy and 37% of critical patches overdue.

**Concept and theory**

A policy is a statement of intent; a control exists only when the policy is applied, monitored and enforced, with breaches escalated. GARP’s second key weakness at Equifax was the “failure of risk management policy enforcement, and specifically the failure to enforce the patch management policy”. GARP explains why this matters: “patch management is a key control in IT security; failing to patch a system is equivalent to leaving a door unlocked in the physical world.”

The analogy carries the lesson. A lock that exists but is not turned gives no protection, and an intruder who finds the door open needs no sophistication. At Equifax, the backlog of 8,500 unpatched vulnerabilities in 2015 and the never-applied Apache Struts patch in 2017 show that the issue was not the absence of knowledge but the absence of enforcement. The fact that patching is a key control, not housekeeping, is why its failure belongs in front of senior management and the board.

**Applying it to this question**

The Japanese bank has the written policy but no monitoring of deadlines and no escalation, and 37% of critical patches are overdue. This is the enforcement failure, not an inventory or communication failure. The JPY 180 million software spend is irrelevant: spending on tools does not substitute for enforcing the patching discipline.

**Fragile fact.** Patching is a key IT security control; the unlocked-door analogy refers to failing to patch, not to the expired certificate.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, key weakness 2 (“Failure of risk management policy enforcement”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes state only that Equifax failed to enforce its patch management policy (part of risk management); the key-control characterisation and the unlocked-door analogy are from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP calls patch management a key control in IT security; this option demotes it to routine maintenance outside the key controls. It would be correct only for a non-security housekeeping task, such as cosmetic software updates with no security content.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It treats an approved policy as a guarantee of compliance. Equifax shows the opposite: a policy that is not enforced does not prevent unpatched systems. The option would be closer to correct only if the bank already had monitoring and escalation and the sole gap was staff awareness of the policy.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the intrusion to the expired SSL certificate. The certificate affected detection (the breach went unnoticed for months); the intrusion was made possible by the unpatched known vulnerability. The option would be correct in a stem asking why discovery was delayed, not why entry was possible.

d.reason: It states GARP’s lesson in GARP’s own terms: failing to enforce patch management leaves systems exposed, like leaving a door unlocked, so enforcement itself must be remedied.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a UK building society asks the head of operational risk to explain the internal communication failure at Equifax in 2017. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: The GTVM team sent the alert to about 400 employees, but an employee who knew of Equifax’s use of Apache Struts was not on the list, and that employee’s manager received it but did not relay it.
The GTVM team sent the alert to about 400 employees, and the employee who knew of Equifax’s use of Apache Struts received it, but chose not to inform the manager responsible for patching.
The vendor alert was never circulated within Equifax, because the GTVM team was waiting for the Chief Security Officer to finish the first patch management policy.
Internal communication worked as designed and the alert reached every employee who knew of Apache Struts; the communication failure lay only in the six-week delay to the public.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at a UK building society asking how Equifax’s internal communication failed.

**Concept and theory**

A vulnerability alert is only as useful as its routing. Internal security communication has to reach the people who know which systems run the affected software, and a chain of relay (alert team, distribution list, manager, system owner) has a weak point at every link. GARP’s third key weakness at Equifax was “inconsistent communication among employees on the remediation of security vulnerabilities”. The specifics:

- The GTVM team distributed the 8 March alert to 400 employees.
- One employee who knew of Equifax’s use of Apache Struts was not included on the e-mail distribution list and did not receive news of the vulnerability.
- That employee’s manager did receive the alert but failed to relay the information.

The lesson is twofold: distribution lists must reflect who actually owns or knows each system (which links back to the asset inventory), and receipt of an alert creates a duty to pass it on.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are role-sensitive: who was left off the list (the knowledgeable employee), who received the alert (the manager) and who failed to act (the manager, by not relaying it). An explanation is accurate only if it assigns each of these to the right person.

**Fragile fact.** Actors: the employee who knew of Apache Struts was off the list; the manager received the alert and failed to relay it.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, key weakness 3 (“Inconsistent communication among employees on the remediation of security vulnerabilities”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes say only that communications about the vulnerabilities missed key employees; the distribution to 400 employees and the employee and manager detail are from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: It states the GARP facts with the right actors: the GTVM team sent the alert to about 400 employees; the employee who knew of Apache Struts was not on the list; that employee’s manager received the alert but did not relay it.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It reverses who received the alert and who failed to pass it on: GARP says the knowledgeable employee did not receive the alert, and the manager received it and did not relay it. It would be correct only in a case where the system expert was alerted and withheld the information from management.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It imports the CSO’s development of the first patch management policy, a fact from the 2015 pre-breach environment, as the reason for non-distribution in 2017. In fact the GTVM team did distribute the alert to 400 employees on 8 March. It would be correct only if the stem described an alert held back pending a policy decision.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It confuses weakness 3 (internal communication among employees) with weakness 5 (poor external communication). Both were failures at Equifax; the internal one concerned the vulnerability alert not reaching the right person. It would be correct only as a description of the external communication weakness, without the claim that internal communication worked.

questions.question: An IT internal auditor at a Chinese commercial bank finds that the certificate used by the bank’s network inspection appliance to decrypt and inspect encrypted traffic expired five months ago. The renewal request is still open, and the appliance cost CNY 2.4 million to install. Recalling the Equifax case, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: At Equifax, the expired certificate let the attackers in, because it disabled the protection on the online dispute portal through which they first entered the network.
At Equifax, the expired certificate was first flagged by the 2015 internal audit, and its eventual renewal on 7 September prompted the public announcement of the breach.
At Equifax, the expired certificate left encrypted traffic unmonitored, and the breach was noticed only after the certificate was finally updated on 29 July 2017.
At Equifax, the expired certificate did not delay detection, because the GTVM team identified the intrusion within the 48 hours that followed the attack itself.

questions.solution:
IT internal auditor at a Chinese bank finding an expired certificate on the traffic inspection appliance.

**Concept and theory**

Much network traffic is encrypted, which protects data in transit but also hides malicious activity. To monitor it, firms use inspection tools that decrypt traffic for analysis, and these depend on a valid digital certificate (an SSL certificate). If the certificate expires, the tool can no longer inspect encrypted traffic, and the firm loses visibility without any obvious alarm: a silent failure of a detective control.

GARP’s fourth key weakness at Equifax was “an expired SSL certificate designed to inspect encrypted network traffic”. For months, because of the expired certificate, Equifax could not monitor its encrypted traffic, including the hacking activity. It was only on 29 July 2017, after it finally updated the certificate, that Equifax noticed the suspicious activity and discovered the breach, over three months after it had started. The lesson: a lapsed detective control extends dwell time, and the expiry of security certificates is itself a risk that needs tracking.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor’s finding (an inspection certificate expired five months ago, renewal still open) is the Equifax weakness 4 pattern. The deciding fact is the role of the certificate: it affected detection, and its renewal is what revealed the breach. The CNY 2.4 million installation cost is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** The expired certificate was a detection failure, not an entry point; discovery followed its renewal on 29 July.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, key weakness 4 (“An expired SSL certificate designed to inspect encrypted network traffic”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes say the breach was discovered in late July 2017; GARP gives 29 July. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns the entry point to the certificate. The attackers entered through the unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability in the online dispute portal; the certificate concerned inspection of traffic once they were inside. It would be correct only for a case in which a lapsed certificate disabled an access control at the perimeter.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It mixes in two other events: the 2015 audit (which found the 8,500 unpatched vulnerabilities, not the certificate) and 7 September (the date of the public announcement, not the renewal). The certificate was updated on 29 July. It would be correct only if the dates of renewal and announcement had coincided.

c.reason: It matches GARP: the expired certificate left encrypted traffic, including the hacking activity, unmonitored, and the breach was noticed only after the certificate was updated on 29 July 2017.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the effect: the expired certificate did delay detection, by months. The 48-hour figure is the patching expectation for a critical alert, not a detection time. It would be correct only for a firm whose monitoring had caught the intrusion within two days.

questions.question: The Chief Compliance Officer of a payment institution in the euro area is drafting a crisis communication playbook and uses Equifax as a cautionary example. Which of the following statements about Equifax’s external communication is NOT correct?

options.text: Equifax was blamed for its lack of transparency to customers as much as for the breach itself.
Equifax’s first public figure of 147 million affected customers was later revised down to 143 million.
Equifax’s public announcement came on 7 September 2017, about six weeks after the breach was discovered.
The three Rs of crisis communication, which aim to limit reputational damage, were not applied by Equifax.

questions.solution:
Chief Compliance Officer of a euro-area payment institution drafting a crisis playbook from the Equifax disclosure.

**Concept and theory**

After a large operational risk event, the damage to reputation depends heavily on how the firm communicates. Delay and opacity convert an operational loss into a crisis of trust. GARP’s fifth key weakness at Equifax was “poor external communication as part of the crisis management”:

- As much as for the breach, Equifax has been blamed for its lack of transparency to its customers.
- Only on 7 September 2017, six weeks after discovery, did Equifax announce that its networks had suffered a data breach exposing the personal information of 143 million customers, a number later increased to 147 million.
- The three Rs of crisis communication, presented in Chapter 5 to limit reputational damage in large operational risk events, were not applied.

The upward revision is itself a lesson: an initial figure that later grows signals that the firm did not yet understand the scope, compounding the loss of confidence.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT correct. Options A, C and D are restatements of the GARP text. Option B reverses the direction of the revision: the first figure was 143 million and it was increased to 147 million.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of revision: 143 million announced, later increased to 147 million; announcement six weeks after discovery, not after the breach.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, key weakness 5 (“Poor external communication as part of the crisis management”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes give only 147 million and the 7 September date, without the initial 143 million figure, the six-week interval or the three Rs reference; these are from GARP. No conflict. The content of the three Rs belongs to GARP Chapter 5 and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: **True statement.** GARP states that, as much as for the breach, Equifax was blamed for its lack of transparency to customers. It would be the answer only if the stem asked for a correct statement.

b.reason: It is the false statement: GARP says the announcement cited 143 million customers, a number later increased to 147 million, not revised down from 147 million.

c.reason: **True statement.** The announcement came on 7 September 2017, six weeks after discovery (29 July to 7 September is 40 days). It would be the answer only if the date or interval were altered, for example to six weeks after the breach.

d.reason: **True statement.** GARP notes that the three Rs of crisis communication, intended to limit reputational damage after large operational risk events, were not applied. It would be the answer only if the option claimed they had been applied.

questions.question: At a meeting of the risk committee of an Australian superannuation fund, a director summarises the Equifax case as follows: “The breach came down to one missed patch. Had that single patch been applied, there would be nothing else to learn.” Which of the following responses best reflects the overarching lesson of the case?

options.text: Large operational risk events do not have a single cause; this one emerged from a weak environment of governance and procedure deficiencies, communication breakdowns and poorly prioritised alerts.
The summary is accurate, because the other weaknesses at Equifax affected only the aftermath of the breach and contributed nothing to how long it lasted or how much data was taken.
The breach was a technology failure rather than a failure of risk management, so its lessons belong to the IT department and have little bearing on the operational risk function.
The breach shows that once a firm has adopted a recognised cybersecurity framework, weaknesses of this kind cannot arise, so the missed patch reflects the absence of any framework.

questions.solution:
Risk committee director at an Australian superannuation fund reducing Equifax to one missed patch.

**Concept and theory**

A single-cause narrative is attractive because it suggests a single fix. Operational risk practice rejects it: large losses typically occur when several controls fail at once, each failure allowing the next to matter. GARP closes the Equifax case with the overarching lesson: “Such large operational risk events do not have a single cause; they emerge in weak operating environments, characterized by multiple deficiencies in governance and procedures, breakdowns in communication, and lack of prioritization in alerts and actions.” Equifax “had a deficient environment with respect to its cybersecurity controls at the time of the event”, and GARP describes the fallout as resulting from “its failings in risk management”.

At Equifax the chain was: no complete asset inventory (could not find Apache Struts), an unenforced patch policy (no discipline to close it), inconsistent internal communication (the alert missed the right person), an expired SSL certificate (months undetected) and poor external communication (amplified reputational harm). Each link is a separate lesson.

**Applying it to this question**

The director’s claim is that one patch explains everything and nothing else is to be learned. The response that reflects the case must reject the single-cause view and name the weak-operating-environment characteristics.

**Fragile fact.** Equifax did not lack frameworks; its frameworks, policies and tools were outdated and poorly maintained, and the event had multiple causes.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax” (closing paragraph beginning “Such large operational risk events do not have a single cause. . . ”). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes attribute the vulnerability to outdated cybersecurity frameworks and policies and list the five weaknesses, but do not state the no-single-cause conclusion; that lesson is from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: It restates GARP’s conclusion: large operational risk events do not have a single cause, and the breach emerged from a weak operating environment with deficiencies in governance and procedures, breakdowns in communication and lack of prioritisation of alerts and actions.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It confines the other weaknesses to the aftermath. The expired SSL certificate extended the undetected period to over three months while data was being extracted, and the inventory and communication gaps are why the patch was never applied in the first place. It would be correct only for a weakness, such as external communication, that operated purely after discovery.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It assigns ownership of the lessons to IT alone. GARP frames the fallout as the result of Equifax’s failings in risk management and draws governance, procedure and communication lessons that apply to the operational risk function. It would be correct only for a narrowly technical defect with no control-environment dimension.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It treats adopting a framework as a guarantee and misstates the case: Equifax did have cybersecurity frameworks and policies, but they were outdated and poorly maintained. It would be closer to correct only if the claim were limited to saying that frameworks must be kept current and enforced.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is assessing whether a Canadian bank shows the characteristics of the weak operating environment in which, according to the Equifax case, large operational risk events emerge. She records the following findings.

I. Several information security policies exist on paper but are not enforced, and two approved procedures contradict each other.

II. The bank’s cyber insurance premium rose by CAD 0.4 million this year after a market-wide repricing.

III. All vulnerability alerts, whatever their criticality score, enter one queue and are worked on in order of arrival.

IV. Security alert distribution lists are reconciled every month against the current owners of each system.

Which findings are characteristics of the weak operating environment described in the case?

options.text: I, II and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Risk consultant testing whether a Canadian bank shows the weak operating environment described in the Equifax case.

**Concept and theory**

GARP characterises the environments in which large operational risk events emerge by three features, each of which can be observed in a firm before any loss occurs:

| Characteristic (GARP) | How it appeared at Equifax |
|---|---|
| Deficiencies in governance and procedures | Outdated policies; patch policy not enforced |
| Breakdowns in communication | Alert missed a key employee; manager did not relay it |
| Lack of prioritisation in alerts and actions | A CVSS 10 alert never acted on; 8,500 backlog |

The lesson for a reviewer is diagnostic: look for these features directly, rather than waiting for loss events. Not every adverse finding is one of these characteristics; external price changes or consequences of events are outcomes, not features of the control environment.

**Applying it to this question**

Finding I (policies on paper but unenforced, contradictory procedures) is a deficiency in governance and procedures. Finding II (an insurance premium rise from market-wide repricing) is an external cost movement, not a feature of the bank’s operating environment. Finding III (all alerts in a single first-come queue regardless of criticality) is a lack of prioritisation in alerts and actions. Finding IV (monthly reconciliation of distribution lists to current owners) is the healthy opposite of Equifax’s communication breakdown.

**Fragile fact.** Three characteristics, and only three: governance and procedure deficiencies, communication breakdowns, and lack of prioritisation in alerts and actions.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax” (closing paragraph), with key weaknesses 2 and 3. GARP vs Schweser: the weak-operating-environment characterisation appears only in GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It includes finding II. A premium change driven by market-wide repricing is an external cost, not a deficiency in governance, communication or prioritisation. It would be correct only if the premium rise had resulted from an insurer’s assessment of control failures at the bank and the question asked about indicators of a weak environment.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It treats finding IV as a weakness and omits finding I. Reconciled distribution lists are the control that would have prevented Equifax’s communication breakdown. It would be correct only if finding IV said that distribution lists were never reconciled and finding I described enforced policies.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It includes finding IV, the healthy communication practice, as a weakness. It would be correct only if finding IV described stale distribution lists, as at Equifax.

d.reason: Only findings I and III match GARP’s characteristics of a weak operating environment.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a GBP-denominated credit fund is reviewing the fallout from the Equifax breach before discussing cyber risk with the issuers she covers. Which of the following statements about the consequences of the breach is least accurate?

options.text: The Chief Executive Officer, the Chief Security Officer and the Chief Information Officer all resigned.
In July 2019, Equifax agreed to pay up to USD 700 million in fines and compensation for the breach.
USD 300 million of the settlement was set aside for regulatory fines, with the rest paid to individuals.
Affected consumers could choose up to USD 125 or free credit monitoring at the three largest bureaus.

questions.solution:
Credit fund portfolio manager reviewing the consequences of the Equifax breach.

**Concept and theory**

The consequences of a large operational risk event go well beyond the direct loss: market value, regulatory action, litigation, management accountability and remediation cost. GARP lists the fallout from the Equifax breach and its failings in risk management:

- A drop in share price (Box 9.1: about USD 5bn of market capitalisation lost in the week after the announcement, out of USD 15.5bn).
- Investigations by several US federal authorities, fines and lawsuits.
- Resignations by senior management: the CEO, CSO and CIO.
- In July 2019, an agreement to pay up to USD 700 million in fines and compensation, USD 300 million of which was distributed to the individuals whose personal information had been exposed.
- Affected consumers could choose a payment of up to USD 125 or free credit monitoring at all three of the largest credit reporting firms (Equifax, Experian and TransUnion).
- A major revision of Equifax’s IT security system and management.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is least accurate. Options A, B and D match the list. Option C reverses the recipient of the USD 300 million: it went to the affected individuals, not to regulatory fines.

**Fragile fact.** USD 300 million of the up to USD 700 million went to individuals; the rest is the remaining fines and compensation.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax” (closing paragraph) and Box 9.1. GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes state that Equifax paid USD 700 million in fines and compensation, including USD 300 million paid directly to individuals; GARP says it agreed in July 2019 to pay up to USD 700 million and adds the USD 125 or credit monitoring option. Minor difference in wording; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: **True statement.** GARP names the CEO, CSO and CIO among the resignations. It would be the answer only if one of the three roles were replaced, for example by the CFO.

b.reason: **True statement.** In July 2019 Equifax agreed to pay up to USD 700 million in fines and compensation. It would be the answer only if the amount or date were altered.

c.reason: It is the inaccurate statement: GARP states that USD 300 million of the settlement was distributed to the individuals whose information was exposed.

d.reason: **True statement.** Consumers could choose up to USD 125 or free credit monitoring at the three largest credit reporting firms. It would be the answer only if the choice were misdescribed, for example as monitoring at Equifax alone.

questions.topic: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks

questions.question:
A risk analyst at an SGD-based asset manager is quantifying the market impact of the Equifax breach for a presentation on cyber risk. She uses the following figures.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Market capitalisation before the announcement (USD bn) | 15.5 |
| Market capitalisation lost in the week after the announcement (USD bn) | 5.0 |
| Maximum settlement agreed in July 2019 (USD m) | 700.0 |
| Portion of the settlement distributed to individuals (USD m) | 300.0 |
| Records leaked in the May 2016 W-2 Express hack (thousands) | 430.0 |

Which of the following correctly states (i) the percentage of market capitalisation lost in the week after the announcement and (ii) the market value lost in that week as a multiple of the maximum settlement?
questions.solution:
Risk analyst at an SGD-based asset manager comparing Equifax’s market value loss with its settlement.

**Concept and theory**

The cost of a cyber breach to shareholders is not limited to the fines and compensation eventually paid. The market reprices the firm immediately, reflecting expected direct costs and the reputational damage to future business. GARP’s Box 9.1 records that Equifax lost about USD 5bn of its market capitalisation in the week after the announcement, out of a total of USD 15.5bn, while the July 2019 settlement was up to USD 700 million. Comparing the two shows how much of the economic loss is reputational and market driven rather than regulatory. Define:

$\text{L}_{\text{\%}} = \frac{\Delta\text{MV}}{\text{MV}_{0}}$ , M $= \frac{\Delta\text{MV}}{\text{S}_{\text{max}}}$

where $\text{MV}_{0}$ is the market capitalisation before the announcement, ∆MV the market capitalisation lost in the following week, and $\text{S}_{\text{max}}$ the maximum settlement.

**Applying it to this question**

Convert to the same unit first: $\Delta\text{MV} =$ USD 5.0bn = USD 5,000m.

$\text{L}_{\text{\%}} = \frac{5.0}{15.5} =$ 0.3226 = 32.3%

M $= \frac{5{,}000}{700} =$ 7.14 ≈ 7.1 times

The USD 300 million to individuals and the 430,000 records of 2016 are irrelevant inputs. Interpretation: in a single week, Equifax lost roughly a third of its market value, about seven times the maximum amount it later agreed to pay in fines and compensation.

**Fragile fact.** Denominator is the pre-announcement USD 15.5bn; the settlement comparison uses the USD 700 million maximum, not the USD 300 million to individuals.

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, Box 9.1 (High profile, egregious data hacks: Equifax) and section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax” (closing paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes mention a drop in share price but give no market capitalisation figures; these are from GARP Box 9.1. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: **Wrong input twin.** The loss is divided by the post-loss market capitalisation, 15.5 − 5.0 = 10.5, instead of the pre-announcement value: 5.0/10.5 = 47.6%. It would be correct only if the question asked for the loss as a percentage of the market value remaining after the week.

b.reason: 32.3% of market capitalisation lost, equal to about 7.1 times the maximum settlement.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin.** The multiple uses the USD 300 million distributed to individuals instead of the USD 700 million maximum settlement: 5,000/300 = 16.7. It would be correct if part (ii) asked for the market value lost as a multiple of the compensation paid to individuals.

d.reason: **Intermediate result.** The first figure is the fraction of market capitalisation retained: 10.5/15.5 = 67.7%, the complement of the loss. It would be correct if part (i) asked for the share of value remaining after the week.
