questions.topic: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-9 b Q13
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a US bank is presenting the Equifax case to newly hired analysts. She asks them to match each weakness to the effect it most directly produced, using the following effect codes.

| Code | Effect |
|---|---|
| P | Equifax could not locate and patch the vulnerable system in time |
| D | The intrusion remained unnoticed for months |
| R | Customers were left uninformed for weeks after the breach was found |

Which of the following matches is correct?

options.text: Incomplete IT asset inventory: P; expired SSL certificate: D; poor external communication: R
Incomplete IT asset inventory: D; expired SSL certificate: P; poor external communication: R
Incomplete IT asset inventory: P; expired SSL certificate: R; poor external communication: D
Incomplete IT asset inventory: R; expired SSL certificate: D; poor external communication: P

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a US bank asking new hires to match Equifax weaknesses to their effects.

**Concept and theory**

Each of Equifax’s five weaknesses damaged a different stage of the incident, and the lesson from each is specific to that stage:

| Weakness (GARP) | Most direct effect at Equifax |
|---|---|
| 1. No comprehensive IT asset inventory | GTVM teams could not locate and patch Apache Struts within 48 hours |
| 2. Patch management policy not enforced | Known vulnerabilities left open (an unlocked door) |
| 3. Inconsistent internal communication | Alert missed an employee who knew of Apache Struts |
| 4. Expired SSL certificate | Encrypted traffic unmonitored; breach unnoticed until 29 July |
| 5. Poor external communication | Announcement only on 7 September, six weeks after discovery |

Weaknesses 1 to 3 explain why the known vulnerability stayed open; weakness 4 explains why the intrusion lasted so long; weakness 5 explains why the reputational damage was amplified after discovery.

**Applying it to this question**

Incomplete inventory maps to P (could not locate and patch). Expired SSL certificate maps to D (intrusion unnoticed for months). Poor external communication maps to R (customers uninformed for weeks after discovery).

**Fragile fact.** Order of stages: inventory gap (March, no patch), certificate (March to 29 July, no detection), external communication (29 July to 7 September, no disclosure).

**Reference**

LO 50.b: “Describe lessons learned from the Equifax case study.” GARP Chapter 9, section “Case Study of a Cyberattack: Equifax”, key weaknesses 1 to 5. GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes list the same five weaknesses in the same order. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-9 b, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: Inventory to P, certificate to D and external communication to R is the mapping GARP gives in its description of each weakness.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the effects of the inventory and the certificate. The inventory gap stopped the GTVM teams locating Apache Struts; the expired certificate blinded monitoring of encrypted traffic. It would be correct only if the inventory had been a monitoring tool and the certificate an asset register.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the effects of the certificate and external communication. The certificate delayed discovery; external communication delayed telling customers after discovery. It would be correct only if discovery had depended on the public announcement, which reverses the sequence (29 July discovery, then 7 September announcement).

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns the post-discovery disclosure failure to the inventory and the patching failure to external communication. Public communication occurred after discovery and could not have affected patching in March. It would be correct only if the weaknesses’ labels were rotated.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 a Q1
questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a mid-sized Brazilian commercial bank is preparing a board briefing after a peer bank paid a BRL 310 million penalty for anti-money laundering failings. The board has asked what the Basel Committee guidance says about the exposures created by inadequate ML/FT risk management. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The main exposures are reputational, operational, compliance and market risks; these risks are interrelated, and the costs can extend to the termination of wholesale funding and facilities.
The main exposures are reputational, operational, compliance and concentration risks; these risks are interrelated, and the costs can extend to the termination of wholesale funding and facilities.
The main exposures are reputational, operational, compliance and concentration risks; these risks are separable, so a regulatory fine does not by itself lead to further financial costs.
The main exposures are reputational, operational, compliance and concentration risks; these risks are interrelated, but the costs are confined to regulatory fines, sanctions and investigation costs.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant briefing a Brazilian bank’s board on the exposures created by inadequate ML/FT risk management.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel Committee treats ML/FT risk management as a prudential issue, not only a legal one. Its argument runs in three steps. First, sound ML/FT risk management protects the reputation of banks and national banking systems and preserves the integrity of the international financial system. Second, the inadequacy or absence of sound ML/FT risk management exposes a bank to four named risk types. Third, these risks are interrelated, so a failure in one area tends to spill into the others, and the financial cost goes well beyond the fine itself.

| Element | What the guidance says |
|---|---|
| Risk types named | Reputational, operational, compliance and concentration risk |
| Relationship | “All these risks are interrelated” |
| Direct costs | Fines and sanctions by regulators |
| Further financial costs | Termination of wholesale funding and facilities, claims against the bank, investigation costs, asset seizures and freezes, loan losses |
| Indirect cost | Diversion of limited and valuable management time and operational resources |

GARP names concentration risk without elaborating, so learn it as part of the list rather than deriving it. The Committee also notes that the costs seen in recent enforcement cases could probably have been avoided had banks kept effective risk-based AML/CFT policies.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share the same structure: a list of four risk types, a claim about how they relate, and a claim about costs. The discrimination lives in one word in each clause. The list must read “concentration”, not “market”; the relationship must be “interrelated”, not “separable”; and the costs must extend beyond fines, sanctions and investigations to items such as the termination of wholesale funding. Only option B passes all three tests. The BRL 310 million penalty is context and plays no role in the answer.

**Fragile fact.** The fourth named risk is concentration risk (not market, liquidity or credit risk), and the guidance stresses that the four are interrelated.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.1 Introduction (paragraphs 5 to 7). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser lists the same four risks and the same costs but omits the statements that the risks are interrelated and that management time is diverted.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q1 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Market risk is a familiar sibling in the Basel risk taxonomy, but it is not one of the four risks the guidance names; concentration risk is. The option would be correct only if the stem asked for a generic list of Basel risk categories rather than the risks specifically created by weak ML/FT management.

b.reason: GARP states that inadequate ML/FT risk management exposes banks “especially” to reputational, operational, compliance and concentration risks, that “all these risks are interrelated”, and that beyond fines and sanctions any one of them can cause significant financial costs, explicitly including the termination of wholesale funding and facilities.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The guidance says the risks are interrelated; “separable” reverses this, and the conclusion that a fine creates no further financial cost contradicts the listed follow-on costs. It would be correct only under a stem claiming the guidance treats each risk in isolation, which it does not.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The cost list is truncated. GARP lists fines and sanctions, then adds termination of wholesale funding and facilities, claims against the bank, asset seizures and freezes, loan losses and the diversion of management time. The option would be correct only if the stem asked for the costs imposed directly by regulators.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 a Q2
questions.question:
A senior compliance analyst at a Japanese trust bank is presenting the Basel Committee’s ML/FT guidance to newly hired analysts. She has drafted the following statements for her slides:

I. The guidelines are intended to be consistent with and to supplement the FATF standards, and should not be read as either strengthening or weakening them.

II. The Committee’s commitment to combating ML and FT is aligned with its mandate to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability.

III. The guidelines apply to internationally active banks only; small or specialised institutions fall outside their scope.

IV. Under the 2012 Core Principles, “adequate policies and processes” are met by effective customer due diligence (CDD) rules alone, as CDD is the complete set of AML/CFT measures.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
Senior compliance analyst at a Japanese trust bank auditing four statements on the Committee’s mandate and positioning.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel Committee’s ML/FT guidance sits on top of two pillars.

- **The FATF standards.** The Financial Action Task Force sets the international standards on combating ML, FT and proliferation financing. The Committee supports their adoption, and its guidelines are intended to be consistent with and to supplement the FATF goals; they should “in no way” be read as modifying the FATF standards, “either by strengthening or weakening them”. The Committee adds value by covering complementary areas, especially how ML/FT risk fits into a bank’s overall risk management.
- **The Core Principles.** The 2012 Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision include a dedicated principle (BCP 29) on the abuse of financial services. All banks should have “adequate policies and processes, including strict customer due diligence (CDD) rules”. GARP adds that “adequate policies and processes” requires other measures in addition to effective CDD rules, and that these measures should be proportional and risk-based, informed by the bank’s own risk assessment.

The motivation is the Committee’s mandate “to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability”. Sound ML/FT risk management serves that mandate by protecting bank safety and soundness and the integrity of the international financial system. On scope, the guidelines apply to all banks; some requirements may need adaptation for small or specialised institutions, but those adjustments are outside the guidance.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the FATF relationship correctly (supplement, neither strengthen nor weaken).

Statement II restates the mandate correctly. Statement III turns “applicable to all banks, with possible adaptation for small or specialised institutions” into “internationally active banks only”, which is false. Statement IV claims CDD alone satisfies “adequate policies and processes”, which GARP explicitly denies. So exactly I and II are correct.

**Fragile fact.** The guidelines neither strengthen nor weaken the FATF standards, they apply to all banks (with possible adaptation for small or specialised ones), and “adequate policies and processes” means CDD plus other proportional, risk-based measures.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.1 Introduction (paragraphs 3, 5 and 11) and Section 10.2 Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management (paragraph 14). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser states the mandate and the BCP quotation but is silent on the FATF relationship and the scope of application, which are tested here from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q2 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Accepts statement III, which narrows “all banks” to internationally active banks, and drops the true statement II. The option would be correct only if the guidance were limited to internationally active banks, as some other Basel standards are.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Accepts statement IV, which turns CDD from one necessary element into the complete set of measures, and rejects the true statement I. It would be correct only under a stem stating that BCP 29 is satisfied by CDD rules alone.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** Correctly accepts I and II but also accepts the absolute claim in IV. The trap is that BCP 29 quotes “strict CDD rules” prominently, so the reader assumes CDD is the whole requirement. It would be correct only if GARP had not added that other measures are required.

d.reason: GARP paragraph 3 supports statement I, paragraph 5 supports statement II, paragraph 11 refutes statement III (“applicable to all banks”), and paragraph 14 refutes statement IV (“requires the implementation of other measures in addition to effective CDD rules”).

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 a Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian digital bank with total assets of AUD 12 billion and a CET1 ratio of 13.1% is reviewing the bank’s ML/FT risk assessment. The assessment covers the existing retail and small-business customer base, the current deposit and payment products, the mobile app and agent delivery channels, and the jurisdictions in which the bank is licensed. It does not cover a cross-border remittance product scheduled for launch next quarter, nor the jurisdictions in which the bank’s business customers trade but the bank has no presence. Which recommendation is most consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Extend the assessment to the remittance product before launch and to the jurisdictions in which the bank’s customers, and not only the bank, do business.
Extend the assessment to the remittance product before launch, but leave out customers’ jurisdictions, since only jurisdictions in which the bank is licensed need assessing.
Leave both gaps to the national risk assessment, since the risks of new products and foreign jurisdictions are assessed by the authorities rather than by the bank.
Extend the assessment to customers’ jurisdictions, but leave out the remittance product until it has generated enough transaction data to be assessed.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at an Australian digital bank reviewing gaps in the coverage of the ML/FT risk assessment.

**Concept and theory**

A risk-based approach starts from an inventory of inherent risk: the risk that exists before any controls are applied. GARP says a bank should develop a thorough understanding of the inherent ML/FT risks present in:

| Dimension | Scope stated in the guidance |
|---|---|
| Customer base | All customers of the bank |
| Products and services | Including products under development or to be launched |
| Delivery channels | How products and services reach customers |
| Jurisdictions | Those within which the bank or its customers do business |

Two scope features are easy to miss. The product dimension is forward-looking: a product that has not yet launched is still in scope, because controls should be designed before the risk materialises, not after transaction data reveal a problem. The jurisdiction dimension is customer-driven as well as bank-driven: a bank can be exposed to a country where it has no branch simply because its customers trade there. The bank then designs acceptance, due diligence and monitoring policies to control the inherent risks it has identified. The bank, not the authorities, owns this assessment; national risk assessments are an input to it.

**Applying it to this question**

The assessment covers customers, current products, channels and the bank’s own licensed jurisdictions. Two gaps are identified: the remittance product scheduled for launch and the jurisdictions in which customers trade without a bank presence. Both fall inside the stated scope (“products under development or to be launched” and jurisdictions in which “it or its customers do business”), so both must be added. The total assets of AUD 12 billion and the CET1 ratio of 13.1% are irrelevant: capital strength does not reduce inherent ML/FT risk.

**Fragile fact.** Inherent risk coverage includes products not yet launched and jurisdictions where the bank’s customers, not only the bank, do business.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, Assessment, Understanding, Management and Mitigation of Risks, (a) Assessment and Understanding of Risks (paragraph 16). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q3 of 18.

a.reason: It closes both gaps and states the decisive scope words: the product before launch and the jurisdictions of customers, not only of the bank. This matches GARP paragraph 16 exactly.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops “or its customers” from the jurisdiction dimension. It would be correct only if the guidance limited jurisdiction risk to the places where the bank itself is licensed or operates.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Hands the assessment to the authorities. National risk assessments are an external input to the bank’s own understanding, but the bank must identify and assess its own inherent risks. It would be correct only under a stem asking which source a supervisor uses to understand risks across the national sector.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Imposes a condition (wait for transaction data) that the guidance removes by naming products “under development or to be launched”. It would be correct only if the guidance limited the assessment to products already in use.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 a Q4
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is reviewing a proposal from the head of financial crime to set the bank’s inherent ML/FT risk rating equal to the rating that the national risk assessment assigns to the banking sector. The supporting data are shown below.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| National risk assessment rating, banking sector | Medium-low |
| Cross-border payments, share of bank’s payment value | 38% |
| Cross-border payments, sector average share | 9% |
| Bank’s total deposits | SGD 64 billion |

Which of the following best describes how the proposal should be assessed under the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Acceptable, since the national risk assessment is the authoritative source of inherent risk, while the bank’s own data reflect only the residual risk left after its controls.
Acceptable, provided the bank’s supervisor confirms that the sector rating applies, since the supervisor is responsible for assessing each bank’s inherent risk.
Not acceptable, since the bank’s understanding should combine its own operational and transaction data with external sources such as the national risk assessment.
Not acceptable, since external sources should be excluded from the bank’s assessment so that it reflects only the information the bank has collected itself.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank CRO assessing a proposal to adopt the national sector rating as the bank’s inherent ML/FT risk rating.

**Concept and theory**

The understanding of inherent ML/FT risk has to be evidence-based, and GARP names two families of evidence that must be combined:

| Family | Examples given in the guidance |
|---|---|
| Internal | Specific operational and transaction data and other internal information collected by the bank |
| External | National risk assessments; country reports from international organisations |

The logic is that each family sees something the other cannot. A national risk assessment describes the typical threats facing a sector or country, but it cannot know the particular mix of a single bank’s customers, products and flows. A bank’s own data show its actual profile, but not the threats and typologies identified across the system. The bank combines both, then designs policies to control the inherent risks and manages residual risk in line with its risk profile. The resulting understanding should be demonstrable to, and acceptable to, the supervisor; the supervisor does not produce it.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal uses one external input (the national sector rating) as the whole answer. The table shows why that fails here: 38% of the bank’s payment value is cross-border against a sector average of 9%, so the bank’s own transaction data indicate a profile quite different from the sector’s, and its jurisdiction and channel exposures are likely higher. The deposit base of SGD 64 billion is irrelevant to the question of method. The proposal is not acceptable because it ignores the internal half of the evidence.

**Fragile fact.** Internal = operational and transaction data the bank collects; external = national risk assessments and country reports from international organisations. Both are required, and the bank (not the supervisor) builds the assessment.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (a) Assessment and Understanding of Risks (paragraph 16). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q4 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Swaps inherent risk for residual risk. Transaction data describe what the bank actually does, which is exactly what drives its inherent exposure; residual risk is what remains after the controls that are designed from that understanding. The option would be correct only if the stem asked which information shows the effectiveness of controls already in place.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Makes the supervisor responsible for assessing the bank’s inherent risk. In the guidance the bank conducts the assessment, and the supervisor must find the bank’s understanding demonstrable and acceptable. It would be correct only under a stem describing the supervisor’s review of the bank’s assessment.

c.reason: GARP paragraph 16 requires the understanding of inherent risk to be “based on specific operational and transaction data and other internal information collected by the bank as well as external sources of information such as national risk assessments and country reports from international organisations”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason: it excludes external sources, whereas the guidance includes them. It would be correct only if the guidance limited the assessment to the bank’s own data, which it does not.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 a Q5
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is preparing a report on the bank’s ML/FT risk assessment methodology and must choose which statements to include. The draft statements are:

I. The bank should consider all relevant inherent and residual risk factors at the country, sectoral, bank and business relationship level, among others, to determine its risk profile.

II. Policies for customer acceptance, due diligence and ongoing monitoring should be designed to control the residual risks, with inherent risks managed in line with the bank’s risk profile.

III. The risk profile should determine the appropriate level of mitigation, and the bank should have mechanisms to document and provide risk assessment information to competent authorities such as supervisors.

IV. The bank’s understanding of its inherent risks should be capable of being demonstrated to, and be acceptable to, its supervisor.

Which statements are consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Canadian senior risk analyst choosing which statements on risk assessment methodology to include in a report.

**Concept and theory**

Sound ML/FT risk management requires identifying and analysing the ML/FT risks present in the bank and designing and implementing policies and procedures commensurate with them. GARP sets out a clear sequence.

1. **Assess** all relevant inherent and residual risk factors at the country, sectoral, bank and business relationship level, among others (and, where appropriate, supranational assessments), to determine the bank’s risk profile and the appropriate level of mitigation.
2. **Design** policies for CDD, customer acceptance, customer identification and monitoring of the business relationship and operations to take account of the risk assessment and risk profile. Policies for acceptance, due diligence and ongoing monitoring are designed to control the identified inherent risks.
3. **Manage the remainder**: any resulting residual risk is managed in line with the bank’s risk profile established through its risk assessment.
4. **Evidence**: the bank should have mechanisms to document and provide risk assessment information to competent authorities such as supervisors, and its understanding should be capable of being demonstrated to, and acceptable to, its supervisor.

The ordering matters. Inherent risk is what controls are aimed at; residual risk is what is left after them and is measured against the risk profile.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I repeats the four levels and the inherent and residual factors: correct. Statement II reverses the roles of inherent and residual risk: controls target inherent risk, and residual risk is managed in line with the risk profile; so II is false. Statement III links the profile to the level of mitigation and requires documentation to competent authorities: correct. Statement IV restates the demonstrability requirement: correct. The correct set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Policies control inherent risk; residual risk is managed in line with the risk profile. Levels: country, sectoral, bank, business relationship.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (a) Assessment and Understanding of Risks (paragraphs 15 and 16). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser gives the four levels and the five policy areas but omits the inherent versus residual distinction and the documentation to competent authorities, which are taken from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q5 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Omits the true statement IV, treating the supervisory demonstration requirement as optional. It would be correct only if the guidance asked the bank merely to document its assessment without needing it to be acceptable to the supervisor.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Accepts statement II, which swaps inherent and residual risk, and drops the true statement III. It would be correct only if the guidance said controls are designed against residual risk, which would be circular, since residual risk is defined after controls.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Accepts the swapped statement II and rejects statement I. The trap is to think residual factors cannot be “considered” at assessment stage; GARP explicitly says to consider inherent and residual factors at each level. It would be correct only if statement I omitted residual factors and statement II were stated the right way round.

d.reason: GARP paragraph 15 supports statements I and III, and paragraph 16 supports statement IV and refutes statement II: policies “should be designed and implemented to adequately control those identified inherent risks. Any resulting residual risk should be managed in line with the bank’s risk profile”.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a German Landesbank is reviewing proposals to strengthen board governance of ML/FT risk following a supervisory finding. Which proposal best reflects the Basel Committee guidance on governance arrangements?

options.text: The chief AML/CFT officer should approve the ML/FT risk policies, with the board informed of the risk assessment only when the officer chooses to escalate a specific issue.
The board should approve and oversee the ML/FT risk policies, and should receive risk assessment information in a timely, complete, understandable and accurate manner.
The board should approve the ML/FT risk policies, while a detailed understanding of ML/FT risk is left to senior management, with the board briefed once a year.
The board should approve the ML/FT risk policies, and its responsibility for ML/FT risk is fully discharged once it has appointed a chief AML/CFT officer.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at a German Landesbank choosing the proposal that best reflects board governance of ML/FT risk.

**Concept and theory**

Effective ML/FT risk management requires proper governance arrangements as described in earlier Committee papers (The internal audit function in banks, 2012; Corporate governance principles for banks, 2015; Compliance and the compliance function in banks, 2005). Three board duties follow.

| Duty | Content |
|---|---|
| Approve and oversee | The board approves and oversees the policies for risk, risk management and compliance; this is “fully relevant” to ML/FT risk |
| Understand | The board should have a clear understanding of ML/FT risks |
| Be informed | Information on the ML/FT risk assessment is communicated to the board in a timely, complete, understandable and accurate manner, so that it can make informed decisions |
| Allocate | The board allocates explicit responsibility, considering the governance structure, so that policies and procedures are managed effectively |

The point of the four information qualities is decision usefulness: a board that receives late, partial or opaque information cannot oversee a risk it is accountable for. Appointing a chief AML/CFT officer is part of the arrangements but does not replace the board’s own approval, oversight and understanding.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are who approves the policies (the board) and how the board is informed (on the four stated qualities, not on an exception basis or once a year). Option B states both. The other options either move approval away from the board, dilute the board’s own understanding, or treat an appointment as discharging the board’s duty.

**Fragile fact.** The board approves and oversees; the information it receives must be timely, complete, understandable and accurate (four qualities).

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (b) Proper Governance Arrangements (paragraphs 17 and 18). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q6 of 18.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** Gives policy approval to the chief AML/CFT officer, and makes board information depend on the officer’s choice to escalate. It would be correct only under a stem asking who monitors fulfilment of AML/CFT duties and alerts the board, which is the officer’s second-line role.

b.reason: GARP paragraph 17: “the requirement for the board of directors to approve and oversee the policies for risk, risk management and compliance is fully relevant” and risk assessment information “should be communicated to the board in a timely, complete, understandable and accurate manner”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The board “should have a clear understanding of ML/FT risks”; leaving the understanding to senior management with an annual briefing reverses this and fails the timeliness requirement. It would be correct only if the guidance asked for a high-level annual summary rather than a clear understanding.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Treats one act (the appointment) as fully discharging continuing duties to approve, oversee and understand. It would be correct only if the stem asked what the board and senior management must do about staffing the AML/CFT function, and even then the appointment is one duty among several.

questions.question: The board of a UK retail bank is filling the vacant post of chief AML/CFT officer and is debating how the post should be set up. Which of the following is most consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: The head of internal audit should make the appointment, so that the choice is independent of the business lines whose ML/FT risks the officer will monitor.
The board and senior management should make the appointment, and the officer’s decisions on all AML/CFT matters, including approval of the bank’s policies, should be final and unreviewable.
The board and senior management should make the appointment, and the officer should have the stature and authority to ensure that the issues raised receive the necessary attention.
The board and senior management should make the appointment, and overall responsibility for the AML/CFT function should be shared equally with each business-line head.

questions.solution:
UK retail bank board deciding how to set up the post of chief AML/CFT officer.

**Concept and theory**

Governance needs a single accountable owner for the AML/CFT function. GARP paragraph 18 specifies four things about that owner.

- **Who appoints:** the board of directors and senior management.
- **Profile:** an appropriately qualified chief AML/CFT officer.
- **Remit:** overall responsibility for the AML/CFT function.
- **Standing:** the stature and necessary authority within the bank such that issues raised by this senior officer receive the necessary attention from the board, senior management and business lines.

Stature exists to solve a practical problem: compliance concerns that cut against revenue are easy to ignore if raised by a junior employee. The officer’s authority is therefore about being heard and escalating, not about replacing the board’s approval of policies (paragraph 17) or taking over business-line decisions (the officer should have no business-line responsibilities, paragraph 23).

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the appointing actor (board and senior management), the officer’s overall responsibility for the function, and the purpose of stature (ensuring attention). Option C states the actor and the purpose correctly. Each other option corrupts one element: the actor, the extent of authority, or who holds overall responsibility.

**Fragile fact.** Appointing actor = board of directors and senior management; the officer holds overall responsibility for the AML/CFT function, and stature exists so the officer’s issues receive attention.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (b) Proper Governance Arrangements (paragraph 18). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser omits the words “overall responsibility”, which are taken from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q7 of 18.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** Moves the appointment to the head of internal audit. Internal audit is the third line and independently evaluates the function; making it the appointing body would compromise that independence. It would be correct only under a stem asking who evaluates the effectiveness of the AML/CFT function.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Inflates “stature and necessary authority” into final, unreviewable power, including over policy approval, which belongs to the board. It would be correct only if the guidance made the officer the ultimate decision-maker, which it does not; conflicts are instead to be considered objectively “at the highest level”.

c.reason: GARP: “The board of directors and senior management should appoint an appropriately qualified chief AML/CFT officer to have overall responsibility for the AML/CFT function with the stature and the necessary authority within the bank such that issues raised by this senior officer receive the necessary attention from the board, senior management and business lines.”

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Spreads overall responsibility across business-line heads, whereas GARP gives overall responsibility for the function to the officer. It would be correct only under a stem about the first line’s responsibility for identifying, assessing and controlling the risks of its own business.

questions.question: A newly appointed internal auditor at a Chinese city commercial bank is reviewing a chart that maps the bank’s functions to the three lines of defence for ML/FT risk. Which of the following mappings is NOT consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: The national financial intelligence unit, which receives the bank’s reports, as part of the third line of defence.
The human resources function, which supports the bank’s AML/CFT regime, as part of the second line of defence.
The technology function, which maintains the transaction monitoring system, as part of the second line of defence.
Customer-facing branch staff, who identify, assess and control the risks of their business, as part of the first line of defence.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Chinese city commercial bank checking a map of functions to the three lines of defence.

**Concept and theory**

The three lines of defence model allocates ML/FT risk responsibilities inside the bank. GARP paragraph 19 states the composition.

| Line | Who | Core task |
|---|---|---|
| First | Business units (front office, customer-facing activity) | Identify, assess and control the risks of their business |
| Second | Chief AML/CFT officer, the compliance function, and also human resources or technology | Ongoing monitoring of the fulfilment of AML/CFT duties (chief AML/CFT officer) |
| Third | Internal audit function | Independent evaluation of risk management and controls |

All three lines are internal to the bank. External bodies, such as supervisors and financial intelligence units (FIUs), are outside the model: the chief AML/CFT officer is the contact point for them (paragraph 22) and the bank reports suspicious transactions to them, but they are not one of the bank’s lines. External auditors can also evaluate controls (paragraph 27), but the third line as defined is internal audit.

The inclusion of human resources and technology in the second line is the detail most candidates miss. GARP names these functions without describing their tasks, so the question tests only their placement.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the mapping that is NOT consistent. Mapping the national FIU to the third line places an external authority inside the bank’s internal model, which is wrong. The HR and technology mappings look surprising but are stated in GARP, and customer-facing staff are the classic first line.

**Fragile fact.** Second line = chief AML/CFT officer + compliance + HR + technology; FIUs and supervisors are external and are not a line of defence.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraphs 19 and 22). GARP vs Schweser conflict: Schweser names only the chief AML/CFT officer as the second line, while GARP adds the compliance function, human resources and technology. Resolved from GARP; this looks like condensation in Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q8 of 18.

a.reason: The third line is “ensured by the internal audit function”. An FIU is an external authority that receives the bank’s reports; the guidance names it as an external party for which the chief AML/CFT officer is the contact point.

b.reason: **True statement; sibling-swap trap.** The reader who assumes HR is a support function outside the model selects this. GARP states that the second line “includes the chief officer in charge of AML/CFT, the compliance function but also human resources or technology”. The option would be inconsistent only if the guidance confined the second line to the chief AML/CFT officer.

c.reason: **True statement; sibling-swap trap.** Same trap as B, applied to technology. Technology is named in the second line. It would be inconsistent only under a narrower definition of the second line than GARP uses.

d.reason: **True statement; role-misassignment trap.** Customer-facing staff are the first line, which identifies, assesses and controls the risks of its business. A reader who thinks risk “control” belongs only to the second line might select it. It would be inconsistent only if the stem mapped branch staff to the second or third line.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of an Australian bank is reviewing the AML/CFT manual for its front-office business units. Which of the following practices in the manual is least consistent with the Basel Committee guidance on the first line of defence?

options.text: Policies and procedures are set out in writing and communicated to all personnel, with a clear description of each employee’s obligations and instructions.
Business units are allotted sufficient resources to know and carry out the AML/CFT policies and procedures effectively.
Internal procedures are in place for front-office staff to detect and report suspicious transactions.
Business units leave the identification and assessment of their ML/FT risks to the chief AML/CFT officer and confine themselves to executing transactions.

questions.solution:
Australian bank CCO identifying the front-office manual practice least consistent with first-line duties.

**Concept and theory**

The first line of defence is the business units (for example front office and customer-facing activity). GARP gives them ownership of the risks their business creates, and supports that ownership with four requirements.

1. **Ownership:** they are “in charge of identifying, assessing and controlling the risks of their business”.
2. **Knowledge and resources:** they should know and carry out the policies and procedures and be allotted sufficient resources to do this effectively.
3. **Written policies:** policies and procedures are clearly specified in writing and communicated to all personnel, with a clear description of employees’ obligations and instructions and guidance on keeping the bank’s activity compliant.
4. **Detection and reporting:** internal procedures exist for detecting and reporting suspicious transactions.

The rationale is proximity: the people who open accounts and execute transactions see the customer and the flow first, so the cheapest and fastest control point is at the front line. The second line monitors that the first line is doing this; it does not replace it.

**Applying it to this question**

Options A, B and C each restate one first-line requirement. Option D moves identification and assessment of the business’s own risks to the chief AML/CFT officer and leaves the business units executing transactions only. That breaks the ownership principle, so D is the least consistent practice.

**Fragile fact.** The first line identifies, assesses and controls the risks of its own business; the second line monitors, it does not take over.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraphs 19 and 20). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q9 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement; absolute-claim trap.** Written, communicated policies with clear descriptions of obligations are required by paragraph 20. A reader who thinks a manual should be addressed only to front-office staff, not “all personnel”, may select it. It would be inconsistent only if the policies were communicated to a subset of staff.

b.reason: **True statement; scope trap.** Sufficient resources for the first line are required by paragraph 19. It would be inconsistent only under a stem in which business units lacked the resources to carry out the procedures.

c.reason: **True statement; role-misassignment trap.** Procedures for detecting and reporting suspicious transactions are part of the first-line framework in paragraph 20. A reader who knows the chief AML/CFT officer is responsible for reporting suspicious transactions (paragraph 25) may wrongly think front-office staff need no reporting procedures; in fact they detect and escalate internally. It would be inconsistent only if front-office staff filed reports with the FIU directly, bypassing the officer.

d.reason: GARP paragraph 19 places identification, assessment and control of the risks of their business with the business units. Delegating identification and assessment upward to the second line is a role misassignment.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing the AML/CFT training programme summarised below.

| Feature | Current design |
|---|---|
| Content | One 90-minute e-learning module, identical for all staff |
| New employees | Enrolled in the next annual training cycle after joining |
| Refresher training | None after the first completion |
| Annual training budget | GBP 420,000 |

Which recommendation is most consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Tailor content, scope and frequency to each group’s functions and risk exposure, train new employees as soon as possible after hiring, and provide refresher training.
Keep one identical module for all staff so that knowledge is uniform across the bank, but require new employees to complete it as soon as possible after hiring.
Tailor content to each group’s functions and add refreshers, but defer new employees’ training until probation ends, so that resources focus on permanent staff.
Tailor content to each group’s functions and add refreshers, but restrict training to customer-facing staff, since other staff have no AML/CFT obligations.

questions.solution:
UK bank internal auditor reviewing an AML/CFT training programme with identical content, delayed induction and no refreshers.

**Concept and theory**

Policies only work if staff are able to apply them, so GARP paragraph 21 pairs staff screening (adequate policies and processes for screening prospective and existing staff to ensure high ethical and professional standards) with ongoing training programmes. The training requirements are specific.

| Feature | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Programme | Ongoing employee training so staff can implement AML/CFT policies and procedures |
| Content and timing | Adapted to the needs of each sector of staff and to the bank’s risk profile |
| Drivers of need | Staff functions, job responsibilities and length of service with the bank |
| Materials | Tailored to each employee’s specific responsibility or function |
| New employees | Attend training as soon as possible after being hired |
| Refreshers | Provided so that obligations are remembered and knowledge is kept up to date |
| Scope and frequency | Tailored to the risk factors to which employees are exposed and to the level and nature of risk in the bank |

The underlying idea is that ML/FT exposure differs across roles: a trade-finance officer, a teller and a payments engineer face different red flags, so one module cannot give each of them “sufficient knowledge and information”.

**Applying it to this question**

The programme has three deficiencies, each mapped to one requirement: identical content (fails tailoring), enrolment in the next annual cycle (fails “as soon as possible after being hired”) and no refresher (fails the refresher requirement). The budget of GBP 420,000 is irrelevant. Only option A fixes all three without introducing a new error.

**Fragile fact.** Training is tailored (function, responsibilities, length of service, risk exposure), starts as soon as possible after hiring, and is refreshed.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraph 21). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser mentions only that the bank should train employees on identifying and reporting suspicious transactions; the tailoring, new-hire and refresher detail is taken from GARP. Neither source assigns staff screening and training explicitly to one line, so the question does not test that attribution.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q10 of 18.

a.reason: It applies the tailoring, new-hire and refresher requirements of GARP paragraph 21, with scope and frequency tied to risk exposure.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Substitutes “uniform” for “tailored”. Consistency of knowledge sounds like a virtue, but the guidance requires content tailored to function and risk. It would be correct only if the stem asked about consistency of the bank’s written policies, which are communicated to all personnel.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses the timing rule: new employees should be trained as soon as possible after hiring, not after probation. It would be correct only if the guidance allowed training to wait until employment is confirmed.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Limits training to customer-facing staff. The guidance covers “various sectors of staff”, with content varying by function; the second line also includes HR and technology staff. It would be correct only if AML/CFT obligations rested solely with the first line.

questions.question: A board member at a French mutual bank is considering proposals to combine the role of chief AML/CFT officer with another senior role to save costs. Which combination is consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Combine it with the role of head of internal audit.
Combine it with the role of data protection officer.
Combine it with the role of chief compliance officer.
Combine it with the role of head of the retail branch network.

questions.solution:
French mutual bank board member assessing which senior role may be combined with that of chief AML/CFT officer.

**Concept and theory**

The chief AML/CFT officer must give unbiased judgments and impartial advice to management. GARP therefore says the business interests of the bank should in no way be opposed to the officer’s effective discharge of the role and that, regardless of size or structure, potential conflicts of interest should be avoided.

| Role combined with the officer | Permitted? | Reason in the guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Business-line responsibilities | No | Would oppose business interests to AML/CFT duties |
| Data protection | No | Named as a responsibility the officer should not be entrusted with |
| Internal audit | No | Third line must independently evaluate the second line |
| Chief risk officer | Yes | “May also perform the function of the chief risk officer” |
| Chief compliance officer or equivalent | Yes | Named alongside the CRO |

The pattern: roles that are themselves control or oversight functions of the second line (risk, compliance) are compatible; roles that generate business, that are evaluated by the officer’s area, or that evaluate the officer are not. Data protection is the counter-intuitive exclusion; GARP states it without giving a separate reason, so it should be memorised as a named exclusion.

**Applying it to this question**

The four options map directly to rows in the table. Only the chief compliance officer combination is expressly permitted; the other three are expressly excluded.

**Fragile fact.** May combine with: CRO or CCO (or equivalent). Must not hold: business-line, data protection or internal audit responsibilities.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraphs 23 and 24). GARP vs Schweser conflict: Schweser says the officer “may also be the chief risk officer” and omits the chief compliance officer; GARP names the CRO, the CCO or equivalent. Resolved from GARP; this looks like condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q11 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Combines the second line with the third line. The officer “should not be entrusted with responsibilities in the context of . . . the function of internal audit”. It would be correct only if the stem asked which function independently evaluates the officer’s work.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Data protection sounds like a natural compliance sibling, but it is named as an excluded responsibility. It would be correct only if the guidance listed data protection among the permitted combinations, as it does for the CRO and CCO.

c.reason: GARP paragraph 24: “The chief AML/CFT officer may also perform the function of the chief risk officer or the chief compliance officer or equivalent.”

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Gives the officer business-line responsibilities, which the guidance excludes to keep business interests from opposing AML/CFT duties. It would be correct only under a stem asking who is the first line of defence.

questions.question:
The newly appointed chief AML/CFT officer of a US regional bank with USD 85 billion in assets is drafting her role description. She proposes that the role include:

I. Ongoing monitoring of the fulfilment of all AML/CFT duties by the bank, including sample testing of compliance and review of exception reports.

II. Alerting senior management or the board if she believes management is failing to address AML/CFT procedures in a responsible manner.

III. Acting as the contact point on all AML/CFT issues for internal and external authorities, including supervisors and financial intelligence units.

IV. Leaving the reporting of suspicious transactions to the business units that detect them, since her role is limited to oversight.

Which items are consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
US regional bank’s new chief AML/CFT officer auditing four proposed items for her role description.

**Concept and theory**

The chief AML/CFT officer is the core of the second line. GARP paragraphs 22 and 25 define what the role does.

- **Ongoing monitoring** of the fulfilment of all AML/CFT duties by the bank, which “implies sample testing of compliance and review of exception reports”.
- **Escalation:** alerting senior management or the board of directors if it is believed management is failing to address AML/CFT procedures in a responsible manner.
- **Contact point** regarding all AML/CFT issues for internal and external authorities, including supervisory authorities and FIUs.
- **Suspicious transaction reporting:** the officer “should also have the responsibility for reporting suspicious transactions”.
- **Capacity:** sufficient resources, a central and proactive role, and full knowledge of the regime, its statutory and regulatory requirements and the ML/FT risks arising from the business.

The logic of placing STR reporting with the officer is consistency and independence: front-line staff detect and escalate internally under the first-line procedures, but the decision to report externally is centralised in an officer who is free of business-line interests and is the bank’s single contact point with the FIU.

**Applying it to this question**

Items I, II and III restate paragraph 22. Item IV contradicts paragraph 25 by leaving reporting with the business units on the theory that the officer is “limited to oversight”. So the correct set is I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Business units detect and escalate; the chief AML/CFT officer reports suspicious transactions and is the contact point for supervisors and FIUs.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraphs 22 and 25). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser covers ongoing monitoring and the contact-point role but not sample testing, exception reports, the escalation duty or the officer’s STR responsibility; those are taken from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q12 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Omits item II. The escalation duty is easy to drop because it reads like a governance matter, but it is stated as part of the officer’s ongoing monitoring role. It would be correct only if the guidance gave the escalation duty solely to internal audit.

b.reason: Paragraph 22 supports I (sample testing and exception reports), II (alerting senior management or the board) and III (contact point for supervisors and FIUs). Paragraph 25 refutes IV.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Accepts item IV, which places external suspicious transaction reporting with the business units, and drops item II. It would be correct only under a stem asking who detects suspicious transactions and escalates them internally.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Accepts all four items, including the misassigned item IV. It would be correct only if item IV stated that the officer is responsible for reporting suspicious transactions.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the AML/CFT governance of a Canadian bank. The chief AML/CFT officer reports to the head of commercial banking, the chief risk officer is a separate person whose relationship to the officer is undocumented, and when the officer and a business line disagree, the business-line head decides. Which recommendation most accurately reflects the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Give the officer a direct reporting line to senior management or the board, define the officer’s relationship with the CRO, and have disputed concerns considered objectively at the highest level.
Keep the reporting line to the head of commercial banking, but require that head to consult the CRO and record reasons before deciding any disputed AML/CFT concern.
Give the officer a direct reporting line to the board, and have the head of internal audit resolve disputed AML/CFT concerns, since internal audit is independent of both parties.
Merge the officer’s role into the CRO’s role, since the guidance requires the chief AML/CFT officer and the chief risk officer to be one and the same person in every bank.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant at a Canadian bank fixing the chief AML/CFT officer’s reporting line and the handling of disputes with business lines.

**Concept and theory**

Independence of the chief AML/CFT officer is protected by three structural rules in GARP paragraphs 23 and 24.

1. **Reporting line:** the officer “should have a direct reporting line to senior management or the board”.
2. **Defined relationships:** where the officer’s role is separated from that of the CRO or chief compliance officer, “the relationship between the aforementioned chief officers and their respective roles must be clearly defined and understood”.
3. **Conflict resolution:** where conflicts arise between business lines and the officer’s responsibilities, “procedures should be in place to ensure AML/CFT concerns are objectively considered at the highest level”.

The reason is simple: if the officer reports to, or can be overruled by, the head of the business whose risks are being challenged, business interests can override AML/CFT duties, which paragraph 23 says should “in no way” happen. Combining the officer’s role with the CRO’s is permitted (paragraph 24 uses “may”), but it is not required.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank has three defects: a reporting line into commercial banking, an undocumented relationship with a separate CRO, and business-line heads deciding disputes. Option A fixes all three with the exact remedies in the guidance. The other options either keep the business reporting line, send disputes to the wrong body, or turn “may” into “must”.

**Fragile fact.** Direct reporting line to senior management or the board; combining with the CRO is optional (“may”), and if roles are separate their relationship must be clearly defined.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraphs 23 and 24). No GARP vs Schweser conflict in substance; Schweser writes “senior management and/or the board” and omits the separation-of-duties and conflict-escalation rules, which are taken from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q13 of 18.

a.reason: It installs the direct reporting line to senior management or the board, defines the relationship with the separately held CRO role, and routes disputes to objective consideration at the highest level, as GARP paragraphs 23 and 24 require.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Leaves the business-line head as both the officer’s line manager and the decision-maker on disputes, with only a consultation step added. It would be correct only if the guidance permitted the officer to report into a business line, which it does not.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Gets the reporting line right but gives dispute resolution to internal audit, the third line, whose job is to evaluate the framework independently, not to decide live disputes between the first and second lines. It would be correct only under a stem asking who evaluates whether conflict procedures are working.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Converts a permission (“may also perform the function of the chief risk officer”) into a universal requirement. It would be correct only if the guidance said “must”, and it would still leave the business-line dispute process unfixed.

questions.question: The head of internal audit at a Japanese bank is drafting the bank’s AML/CFT audit policy. Which of the following statements is NOT consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Audits should cover the adequacy of the AML/CFT policies in addressing identified risks and the effectiveness of staff in implementing them.
Audits should cover the effectiveness of compliance oversight and quality control, including the parameters of criteria for automatic alerts.
Audit scope, methodology and frequency should be based on the bank’s risk profile, with AML/CFT audits conducted periodically on a bank-wide basis.
Internal audit should report the results of its periodic evaluations to the chief AML/CFT officer, who is responsible for the function.

questions.solution:
Head of internal audit at a Japanese bank identifying the statement in a draft AML/CFT audit policy that is not consistent with the guidance.

**Concept and theory**

Internal audit is the third line of defence. It plays an important role in independently evaluating risk management and controls, and it “discharges its responsibility to the audit committee of the board of directors or a similar oversight body through periodic evaluations of the effectiveness of compliance with AML/CFT policies and procedures”. GARP paragraph 26 specifies what the bank’s audit policies should cover.

| Item | Audit coverage |
|---|---|
| (i) | Adequacy of the bank’s AML/CFT policies and procedures in addressing identified risks |
| (ii) | Effectiveness of bank staff in implementing the policies and procedures |
| (iii) | Effectiveness of compliance oversight and quality control, including parameters of criteria for automatic alerts |
| (iv) | Effectiveness of the bank’s training of relevant personnel |

In addition: senior management ensures audit functions are staffed by knowledgeable people with appropriate expertise; audit scope and methodology are appropriate for the bank’s risk profile and frequency is risk-based; auditors periodically conduct bank-wide AML/CFT audits; they proactively follow up their findings; and audit processes are consistent with internal audit’s broader mandate. Internal audit also evaluates the IT monitoring system (paragraph 31). The reporting line to the audit committee is what makes the evaluation independent of the second line it is evaluating.

**Applying it to this question**

Options A and B restate audit items (i), (ii) and (iii). Option C restates the risk-based scope, methodology and frequency and the periodic bank-wide audits. Option D sends audit results to the chief AML/CFT officer, the head of the function being audited, instead of to the audit committee. That is the inconsistent statement.

**Fragile fact.** Internal audit reports to the audit committee of the board (or similar oversight body), not to the chief AML/CFT officer; frequency is risk-based, not fixed.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraph 26) and (d) Adequate Transaction Monitoring System (paragraph 31). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser states only that the bank should establish policies for internal audits of its AML/CFT policies; the four audit items and the audit committee reporting line are taken from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q14 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement; scope trap.** Items (i) and (ii) are both in the list. A reader who thinks audit only tests policy design, not staff implementation, may pick it. It would be inconsistent only if internal audit were told not to assess how staff apply the policies.

b.reason: **True statement; role-misassignment trap.** Item (iii) explicitly includes alert parameters. A reader who thinks alert calibration belongs only to the chief AML/CFT officer may pick it. It would be inconsistent only if audit scope excluded quality control of automated alerts.

c.reason: **True statement; absolute-claim trap.** Risk-based scope, methodology and frequency, plus periodic bank-wide audits, are stated in GARP. A reader expecting a fixed audit cycle may pick it. It would be inconsistent only if the guidance prescribed a fixed frequency.

d.reason: Reporting to the officer whose function is under evaluation defeats the independence of the third line; GARP specifies reporting to the audit committee of the board or a similar oversight body.

questions.question: The audit committee chair of a Brazilian bank is approving the engagement of an external audit firm, for a fee of BRL 2.4 million, to evaluate the effectiveness of the bank’s AML/CFT policies and procedures. Which statement best describes the bank’s responsibilities under the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Once the external firm is engaged, internal audit no longer needs to evaluate AML/CFT controls, because the external firm replaces it as the third line of defence.
The bank should ensure that the audit scope addresses its risks, that the auditors have the requisite expertise and experience, and that it oversees the engagement appropriately.
The bank should ensure that the audit scope addresses its risks and that the auditors have the requisite expertise, while oversight of the engagement passes to the bank’s supervisor.
The bank should ensure that the audit scope addresses its risks, but external auditors may only test financial statement items, as AML/CFT compliance is outside their role.

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank audit committee chair engaging an external audit firm to evaluate AML/CFT effectiveness.

**Concept and theory**

External auditors sit alongside, not inside, the three lines. GARP paragraph 27 gives them two roles and puts three duties on the bank when it uses them.

| Aspect | Content |
|---|---|
| Role in financial audits | In many countries they evaluate banks’ internal controls and procedures in the course of their financial audits |
| Role on compliance | They confirm that controls and procedures are compliant with AML/CFT regulations and supervisory practice |
| Bank’s duty 1 | Ensure the scope of the audit is adequate to address the bank’s risks |
| Bank’s duty 2 | Ensure the auditors assigned have the requisite expertise and experience |
| Bank’s duty 3 | Exercise appropriate oversight of such engagements |

The rationale mirrors outsourcing generally: the bank can buy expertise, but it cannot outsource accountability. Internal audit remains the third line, and the bank remains responsible for the quality of the engagement.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank is engaging external auditors to evaluate the effectiveness of AML/CFT policies, which is exactly the case paragraph 27 addresses. The three duties (scope, expertise, oversight) all stay with the bank. The fee of BRL 2.4 million is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** When external auditors are used, scope, expertise and oversight remain the bank’s responsibility; external audit supplements, and does not replace, internal audit.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (c) The Three Lines of Defence (paragraph 27). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser says only that external audits “may also play a role”; the bank’s three duties are taken from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q15 of 18.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Treats the external firm as a full replacement for internal audit. The third line is “ensured by the internal audit function”; external auditors play an additional role. It would be correct only if the guidance defined the third line to include, and be substitutable by, external auditors.

b.reason: GARP: the bank “should ensure that the scope of the audit is adequate to address the bank’s risks and that the auditors assigned to the engagement have the requisite expertise and experience. A bank should also ensure that it exercises appropriate oversight of such engagements.”

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Moves oversight of the engagement to the supervisor. The bank must exercise oversight itself. It would be correct only under a stem about how a supervisor may use external auditors’ work in its own reviews.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses the role on compliance: external auditors do confirm that controls are compliant with AML/CFT regulations and supervisory practice. It would be correct only if the guidance limited external auditors to financial statement items.
