questions.question: A supervisor conducting an on-site review of a small Luxembourg private bank, with 600 clients and EUR 1.8 billion of assets under management, finds that the bank monitors transactions manually and has concluded that an IT monitoring system is not necessary in its situation. Which of the following best describes what the Basel Committee guidance expects of the bank?

options.text: It should implement an automated system in any case, since the guidance requires automated monitoring for all banks regardless of their size.
It should record the decision internally, and need do no more, since its monitoring only has to be adequate to its size, activities and complexity.
It should document the decision and be able to demonstrate to its supervisor or external auditors that it has an effective alternative in place.
It should document the decision and obtain prior approval from the national financial intelligence unit before relying on manual monitoring.

questions.solution:
Supervisor reviewing a small Luxembourg private bank that has decided not to use an IT monitoring system.

**Concept and theory**

A transaction monitoring system is the engine of ongoing risk monitoring. GARP paragraph 28 sets a proportionality rule with a burden of proof attached.

- **Adequacy:** the system should be adequate with respect to the bank’s size, activities and complexity and the risks present in the bank.
- **Automation as the norm:** for most banks, especially internationally active ones, effective monitoring is “likely to necessitate the automation of the monitoring process”.
- **Exception with a burden:** when a bank believes an IT system is not necessary in its specific situation, “it should document its decision and be able to demonstrate to its supervisor or external auditors that it has in place an effective alternative”.

Proportionality therefore cuts both ways: a small, simple bank may monitor without IT, but it must justify the choice on the record and prove the alternative works to an outside party.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank is small (600 clients) and has concluded IT is unnecessary. That is permitted, but only if the decision is documented and the bank can demonstrate an effective alternative to its supervisor or external auditors. The EUR 1.8 billion of assets under management is irrelevant to the procedural requirement.

**Fragile fact.** No IT system is allowed only if the bank documents the decision and can demonstrate an effective alternative to its supervisor or external auditors.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (d) Adequate Transaction Monitoring System (paragraph 28). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser says the bank must document its decision and demonstrate an effective alternative, without naming the supervisor or external auditors as the audience; the audience is taken from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q16 of 18.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Turns “likely to necessitate” for most banks into a requirement for all banks. It would be correct only if the guidance removed the exception for banks whose situation does not require IT.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Keeps the documentation but drops the demonstration condition, relying on proportionality alone. It would be correct only if the guidance required no external demonstration of the alternative’s effectiveness.

c.reason: It reproduces both conditions of paragraph 28: document the decision, and be able to demonstrate an effective alternative to the supervisor or external auditors.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Invents a prior approval by the FIU. The guidance names the supervisor or external auditors as the parties to whom the alternative is demonstrated, and requires no prior approval. It would be correct only under a stem asking to whom the bank reports suspicious transactions.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is validating a newly purchased transaction monitoring system. The vendor’s default parameters are used unchanged; alerts of unusual transactions are routed to the payments operations team, which closes them; and the chief AML/CFT officer receives only a monthly summary, because the system is owned and operated by the payments business line. Which recommendation most accurately reflects the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Adjust the parameters to reflect the bank’s own risk situation, give the officer access to the system as relevant to the role, and route alerts to the officer for further assessment.
Keep the vendor’s parameters unchanged, since developer parameters reflect wider experience, but route alerts to the chief AML/CFT officer for further assessment.
Adjust the parameters to reflect the bank’s own risk situation, but keep the officer’s access to summaries, since a system run by another business line is outside the officer’s remit.
Adjust the parameters and give the officer full access, but leave alert assessment with payments operations, since the first line owns the controls on its own transactions.

questions.solution:
Singapore junior risk analyst validating a vendor monitoring system with default parameters, alerts closed by operations and limited officer access.

**Concept and theory**

GARP paragraphs 29 and 30 describe how an IT monitoring system should be set up and who acts on its output.

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Parameters | Adequate parameters based on national and international experience of ML/FT methods and prevention; vendor standard parameters may be used, but “the parameters used must reflect and take into account the bank’s own risk situation” |
| Bank’s own criteria | The system should let the bank determine its own criteria for additional monitoring, filing an STR or other steps to minimise risk |
| Officer access | The chief AML/CFT officer should have access to and benefit from the system as far as relevant to the function, even if it is operated or used by other business lines |
| Alerts | Parameters should generate alerts of unusual transactions, which are then subject to further assessment by the chief AML/CFT officer |
| Risk criteria | Adequate with regard to the bank’s risk assessment |

The rationale: a vendor library is calibrated to an average bank, but ML/FT exposures are bank-specific, so the risk assessment must flow through into the parameters. The output then goes to the independent second line for assessment, so that the business that generated the activity does not clear its own alerts.

**Applying it to this question**

Three defects are described: unchanged vendor parameters, alerts assessed and closed by payments operations, and officer access limited to a monthly summary because another business line operates the system. Option A fixes each defect with the remedy stated in GARP.

**Fragile fact.** Vendor parameters are allowed but must reflect the bank’s own risk; alerts go to the chief AML/CFT officer for further assessment, and the officer has access even to systems run by other business lines.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (d) Adequate Transaction Monitoring System (paragraphs 29 and 30). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser states only that the IT system should let the bank determine its own criteria for monitoring and filing STRs; vendor parameters, officer access and alert assessment are taken from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q17 of 18.

a.reason: It aligns parameters with the bank’s own risk situation, gives the officer access as relevant to the function regardless of who operates the system, and routes alerts of unusual transactions to the officer for further assessment.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Treats vendor parameters as sufficient by virtue of wider calibration. Vendor parameters are permitted as a starting point only, and must reflect the bank’s own risk situation. It would be correct only if the guidance allowed standard parameters to be used without adjustment.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops the condition “even if operated or used by other business lines” from the access rule. It would be correct only if the officer’s access were limited to systems owned by the compliance function.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Leaves alert assessment with payments operations. The first line owns its controls, but GARP gives further assessment of alerts generated by the system to the chief AML/CFT officer. It would be correct only under a stem about who detects and escalates suspicious transactions at the front line.

questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.

questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 a Q18
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the IT transaction monitoring system of a Chinese joint-stock bank. Her findings are summarised below.

| Feature | Current design |
|---|---|
| Coverage | All corporate accounts; retail accounts with monthly turnover above CNY 70,000 |
| CDD feed | Customer profiles refreshed weekly from updated CDD records |
| Analytics | Alerts on individual transactions; no trend analysis of activity over time |
| Management information | Monthly report to senior management on changes in customers’ transactional profiles |
| Data organisation | Searchable by customer, product, group entity and time window; no unique group-wide customer file |

Which of the following best describes the deficiencies against the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: The system is deficient in its management information, since the guidance requires daily reporting to senior management on changes in customers’ transactional profiles.
The system is deficient in its data organisation, since the guidance requires each customer to have a unique customer file held across the group.
The system is adequate, since a turnover threshold on retail accounts is a proportionate, risk-based way of focusing monitoring on material activity.
The system is deficient in its coverage of retail accounts below the threshold and in its inability to perform trend analysis of transaction activity.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant at a Chinese joint-stock bank reviewing an IT monitoring system’s design against the guidance.

**Concept and theory**

When a bank uses an IT monitoring system, GARP paragraphs 28 and 29 set out what it must be able to do.

| Capability | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Coverage | “It should cover all accounts of the bank’s customers and transactions for the benefit of, or by order of, those customers” |
| Analytics | “It must enable the bank to undergo trend analysis of transaction activity and to identify unusual business relationships and transactions” |
| Management information | Accurate information for senior management on key aspects, including changes in the transactional profile of customers (no frequency is prescribed) |
| CDD input | The customer profile should incorporate updated, comprehensive and accurate CDD information |
| Centralised knowledge | Information organised by customer, product, across group entities, transactions in a timeframe, and so on |
| Customer file | “Without being requested to have a unique customer file”, banks should be able to risk-rate customers and manage alerts with all relevant information |

Two ideas sit underneath. First, a monitoring system is only as good as its perimeter: activity outside its coverage is invisible, which is why coverage is all accounts rather than accounts above a value threshold. Second, many ML patterns only appear over time, so single-transaction alerts without trend analysis will miss them. Risk-based thinking determines how intensively activity is monitored, not whether some accounts are monitored at all.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each feature against the table. Coverage excludes retail accounts with monthly turnover below CNY 70,000: deficient. Analytics lack trend analysis: deficient. The weekly CDD feed is consistent with incorporating updated CDD information. Monthly management information on profile changes meets the requirement, since no frequency is prescribed. Data organisation by customer, product, entity and time matches the centralised knowledge requirement, and no unique customer file is required. The two deficiencies are coverage and trend analysis.

**Fragile fact.** An IT system in use covers all accounts and must support trend analysis; a unique customer file is expressly not required.

**Reference**

LO 51.a: “Explain best practices recommended by the Basel Committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.”

GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2, (d) Adequate Transaction Monitoring System (paragraphs 28 and 29). GARP vs Schweser note: Schweser covers the management information on changes in transactional profiles; coverage of all accounts, trend analysis and the unique customer file point are taken from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 a, where it is Q18 of 18.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Invents a daily reporting requirement. The guidance requires accurate information on changes in transactional profiles without fixing a frequency. It would be correct only if the guidance specified daily reporting.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses “without being requested to have a unique customer file” into a requirement for one. It would be correct only if the guidance mandated a single group-wide customer file, which it expressly does not.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Applies risk-based reasoning to the perimeter of the system. Proportionality determines the intensity of monitoring, but an IT system in use must cover all accounts. It would be correct only if the guidance permitted value thresholds to exclude accounts from monitoring.

d.reason: GARP paragraph 28 requires coverage of all customer accounts and transactions and the capability for trend analysis of transaction activity; the system fails both.

questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q1
questions.question:
A junior compliance analyst at a Singapore private bank is preparing the acceptance file for a new applicant. The relationship manager has supplied the information below.

| Item | Applicant information |
|---|---|
| Occupation | Deputy director of a state-owned port operator abroad |
| Source of wealth | Inherited property portfolio and advisory fees |
| Country of origin / residence | Country X / Singapore |
| Product requested | Discretionary portfolio, SGD 6.5 million |
| Linked accounts | Two accounts held by family-owned companies |
| Preferred language | English |

Which of the following statements best describes how the bank should use this information under its CAP?

options.text: Because the applicant holds a public position, the bank must decline the relationship whatever the other factors show.
The bank should weigh the customer-oriented factors together, including linked accounts, to set the overall risk level and the measures to apply.
Country X can be disregarded because the applicant now resides in Singapore, so only the country of residence is relevant.
Linked accounts should be assessed only once the relationship is open, as part of ongoing monitoring rather than acceptance.

questions.solution:
Singapore private bank: how to use an applicant’s profile (public role, wealth, origin, product, linked accounts) under the CAP.

**Concept and theory**

A customer acceptance policy (CAP) is the bank’s front door. Its job is to sort prospective customers by the ML/FT risk they are likely to bring, so that the bank can decide whether to accept them and, if so, how much due diligence to apply. The guidance asks the bank to develop clear acceptance policies and procedures that identify the types of customer likely to pose a higher risk of ML and FT, pursuant to the bank’s own risk assessment.

The motivation is proportionality. A bank cannot apply maximum scrutiny to every customer without excluding ordinary people and wasting resources, and it cannot apply minimum scrutiny to everyone without becoming a conduit for criminal funds. Risk factors let the bank place each applicant somewhere on a scale. GARP lists the factors relevant to the situation:

| Factor | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Background | Who the customer is and their history |
| Occupation | Includes a public or high-profile position (exposure to corruption) |
| Source of income and wealth | Whether the funds have a plausible, legitimate origin |
| Country of origin and residence | Both, when different (jurisdictional exposure) |
| Products used | Some products move value faster or more opaquely |
| Nature and purpose of accounts | What the relationship is for |
| Linked accounts | Connected parties through which funds may be layered |
| Business activities | Cash-intensive or high-risk sectors |

The list closes with “other customer-oriented risk indicators”. The factors are used together “in determining what is the level of overall risk and the appropriate measures to be applied to manage those risks”. No single factor is an automatic verdict.

**Applying it to this question**

The table contains five genuine CAP factors: occupation (a public-sector role abroad), source of wealth, country of origin differing from residence, the product requested, and linked accounts held by family companies. The preferred language of correspondence is a deliberately irrelevant input: it is not a customer-oriented ML/FT risk indicator. The question asks how the bank should use the information. The guidance answers: combine the relevant factors into an overall risk level and then choose the measures. That is option B.

**Fragile fact.** The CAP factors are combined into an overall risk level; a public or high-profile occupation raises risk but does not by itself mean refusal, and origin and residence are both considered when they differ.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer Acceptance Policy, para 32. GARP and Schweser list the same factors; Schweser presents them as a bullet list without the phrase “other customer-oriented risk indicators”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Occupation, including a public or high-profile position, is a factor that raises the assessed risk; it does not compel refusal. The guidance expects higher-risk relationships to be handled through enhanced measures, such as senior management approval, not through automatic exclusion. A would be correct only if the stem said that the bank’s own CAP had defined this specific circumstance as one in which it will not accept a new relationship.

b.reason: GARP (Customer Acceptance Policy) states that the bank should consider the factors relevant to the situation, listing background, occupation, source of income and wealth, country of origin and residence, products used, nature and purpose of accounts, linked accounts and business activities, “in determining what is the level of overall risk and the appropriate measures to be applied”. Option B restates exactly this use.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP names “country of origin and residence (when different)”. The parenthesis means both countries are considered when they differ; it does not mean the country of origin drops out. The option overextends the condition. It would be correct only if origin and residence were the same country, in which case there is one country to assess.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Linked accounts are listed among the factors used at acceptance to set the overall risk level. Moving them to post-opening monitoring misplaces a stated acceptance factor. D would describe ongoing monitoring correctly only if the stem asked how the bank should track changes in linked-account activity after the relationship has begun.

questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian retail bank is reviewing a draft CAP. The draft contains the following statements:

I. All customers are subject to basic due diligence, with the intensity of due diligence rising as the customer’s risk rises.

II. Simplified measures may be applied to any customer whose opening deposit is below AUD 1,000, whether or not national law permits simplified measures.

III. Basic account-opening procedures may be appropriate for an individual who expects a small balance used for routine retail banking.

IV. Customers that the bank assesses as lower risk are exempt from due diligence altogether.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I only
I and II only
II and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Australian retail bank: internal auditor tests four CAP statements on basic, commensurate and simplified due diligence.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance builds due diligence as a floor plus a slope. The floor is basic due diligence for all customers: nobody is outside CDD. The slope is commensurate due diligence: as the risk associated with the customer varies, so does the depth of the measures. At the low end, simplified measures are possible, but GARP attaches two conditions:

| Condition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Proven lower risk | The low risk must be demonstrated, not assumed from one feature |
| Allowed by law | Simplified measures must be permitted by the applicable national law |

GARP gives an illustration: basic account-opening procedures may be appropriate for an individual who expects to maintain a small account balance and use it to conduct routine retail banking transactions. Note what the illustration says: basic procedures, not no procedures.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the floor plus slope: true. Statement II sets a single deposit threshold as the trigger for simplified measures and explicitly ignores national law: it fails both conditions.

Statement III paraphrases GARP’s own illustration: true. Statement IV removes the floor entirely for lower-risk customers: false. The consistent set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Simplified measures need both a proven lower risk and legal permission; and simplified or basic never means no due diligence.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer Acceptance Policy, para 33. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says simplified procedures “may be used” for lower-risk customers and omits the conditions “proven” and “if this is allowed by law”; GARP’s fuller wording is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” omits Statement III, which is GARP’s own example of where basic account-opening procedures may be appropriate. A would be correct only if Statement III had said that such an individual needs no procedures at all.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B accepts Statement II, which drops both conditions on simplified measures: the low risk must be proven, and simplification must be allowed by law. A deposit size below AUD 1,000 is one data point, not proof, and the phrase “whether or not national law permits” contradicts “if this is allowed by law”. B would be right only if II read “for proven lower-risk situations where national law allows”.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** C accepts Statements II and IV. Statement IV claims a complete exemption from due diligence for lower-risk customers, contradicting the requirement of basic due diligence for all. C would only work in a world where simplified meant none, which the guidance does not describe.

d.reason: GARP: “Such policies and procedures should require basic due diligence for all customers and commensurate due diligence as the level of risk associated with the customer varies. For proven lower risk situations, simplified measures may be permitted, if this is allowed by law.” The small-balance, routine-retail example supports III.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Brazilian commercial bank reviews a proposed CAP that would require every applicant to provide two years of salary slips and a utility bill in the applicant’s own name. A pilot shows that the rule would reject most informal-sector workers and recent migrants applying for BRL basic accounts. Which recommendation is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Revise the rule, because acceptance standards should not deny the general public access, especially disadvantaged people, while basic due diligence still applies to all.
Retain the rule, because a more restrictive acceptance standard is always consistent with sound ML/FT risk management for retail customers.
Revise the rule by exempting low-income applicants from identification and verification, because financial inclusion overrides CDD.
Retain the rule for all applicants, and apply EDD only to those applicants who are unable to provide the salary slips requested.

questions.solution:
Brazilian commercial bank: CCO reviews an acceptance rule (salary slips and utility bill) that would exclude informal-sector workers and migrants.

**Concept and theory**

AML/CFT controls can fail in two directions. Too weak, and the bank is used for criminal purposes. Too strong, and legitimate people are pushed out of the regulated system, often into cash or informal channels that are harder to monitor. The guidance therefore states that it is important that the CAP “is not so restrictive that it results in a denial of access by the general public to banking services, especially for people who are financially or socially disadvantaged”. GARP points to the FATF Financial Inclusion Guidance as a source of guidelines on designing procedures that are not overly restrictive.

The balance is struck inside the risk-based framework: everyone still receives basic due diligence, while the depth of measures follows the risk. Financial inclusion changes how demanding the acceptance standard is for low-risk retail customers; it does not switch off identification and verification.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposed rule applies a single, demanding documentary standard to every applicant regardless of risk, and the pilot shows it would exclude a large share of the disadvantaged population applying for basic accounts. That is exactly the outcome the guidance warns against. The right response is to revise the rule while keeping basic due diligence for all: option A.

**Fragile fact.** Financial inclusion limits how restrictive the CAP may be; it never removes basic due diligence or identification and verification.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer Acceptance Policy, para 33 (and the reference to the FATF Financial Inclusion Guidance). Schweser carries the same point (standards must not deny access to the general public, especially the financially or socially disadvantaged). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: It combines the two GARP statements: the CAP must not be so restrictive as to deny the general public access, especially the financially or socially disadvantaged, and the CAP must require basic due diligence for all customers.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** “Always consistent” promises that more restriction is never wrong. GARP explicitly identifies excessive restriction as a failure. B would be defensible only for a stem in which the restrictive rule targeted a demonstrated higher-risk segment, not the general retail population.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Inclusion is overextended into an exemption from identification and verification. The guidance requires banks to identify customers and verify their identity, and basic due diligence for all; inclusion affects the burden of the standard, not its existence. C would be right only if it said “apply basic, proportionate procedures to low-income applicants”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D attaches EDD to the inability to produce particular documents, borrowing the trigger that belongs to higher assessed risk. EDD follows higher risk (for example a large balance with regular cross-border wires, or a PEP), not a missing salary slip. D would be correct only if the stem had established that the applicants without slips presented higher ML/FT risk on the CAP factors.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK bank is classifying four prospective individual customers for the onboarding team.

| Applicant | Profile |
|---|---|
| W | Domestic salaried employee; expects a balance of about GBP 3,000 for routine payments |
| X | Expects a balance of about GBP 4 million with regular cross-border wire transfers |
| Y | Senior official of a foreign government |
| Z | Member of the domestic parliament |

Which statement about EDD is most accurate?

options.text: EDD is required for X and Z, and may be essential for Y.
EDD is required for X, Y and Z, since all three are higher risk.
EDD may be essential for X and Z, and is required for Y.
EDD is required only for Y; simplified measures suit X and Z.

questions.solution:
UK bank: classify four applicants (routine retail, large balance with cross-border wires, foreign official, domestic MP) for EDD.

**Concept and theory**

Where risks are higher, the guidance requires banks to take enhanced measures. GARP chooses its modal verbs carefully:

| Situation | GARP wording |
|---|---|
| Individual planning a large balance and regular cross-border wires | EDD may be essential |
| Individual who is a PEP | EDD may be essential |
| Foreign PEP | EDD is required |

The logic: large balances moved regularly across borders and the exposure of public officials to corruption both raise ML/FT risk, so EDD may well be essential; foreign PEPs combine public-office exposure with cross-jurisdiction opacity and limited local knowledge, so the guidance makes EDD mandatory for them (“In particular, such enhanced due diligence is required for foreign PEPs”).

**Applying it to this question**

W is a routine retail customer with a small balance: neither trigger applies and W is the irrelevant input. X matches the large-balance and regular cross-border-wire case: EDD may be essential. Y is a senior official of a foreign government: a foreign PEP, so EDD is required. Z is a domestic parliamentarian: a PEP but not foreign, so EDD may be essential. The matching option is C.

**Fragile fact.** “May be essential” for large balances with regular cross-border wires and for PEPs;

“required” only for foreign PEPs.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer Acceptance Policy, para 34. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says EDD “may be required” for large balances with regular cross-border wires and for a PEP, “especially foreign PEPs”, which softens GARP’s “is required for foreign PEPs”. GARP’s wording is used; this looks like condensation in Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q4 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A swaps the modal strengths between the domestic and the foreign PEP: it makes EDD required for X and Z and merely possibly essential for Y. That is the reverse of GARP. A would be correct only if Z were the foreign official and Y the domestic one, and even then X would remain “may be essential”.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B converts every higher-risk case into a mandatory requirement. Only foreign PEPs carry the word “required”. B would be correct only if the stem said that the bank’s own CAP mandates EDD for all three categories, which goes beyond what the guidance itself states.

c.reason: GARP: “Enhanced due diligence may be essential for an individual planning to maintain a large account balance and conduct regular cross-border wire transfers or an individual who is a politically exposed person (PEP). In particular, such enhanced due diligence is required for foreign PEPs.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D correctly isolates Y but flips X and Z to the low end, recommending simplified measures. Simplified measures are for proven lower-risk situations; large cross-border flows and PEP status point the other way. D would be correct only if X and Z had profiles like W.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a mid-sized bank asks how the bank’s CAP should handle applicants that the onboarding team has rated as higher risk. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Entry into each higher-risk relationship should be approved by internal audit, as the independent third line, before the account is opened.
Higher-risk applicants should be declined, because the CAP should not permit the bank to enter into relationships with higher-risk customers.
Once a higher-risk relationship is accepted with EDD, the CAP need not set out the circumstances in which that relationship would be terminated.
Such decisions should involve EDD, for example senior management approval to enter or continue the relationship, and the CAP should say when the bank would decline or terminate.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member asks how the CAP should handle applicants rated higher risk.

**Concept and theory**

A risk-based CAP does not simply say “no” to higher-risk applicants. It says “yes, but with more”: more scrutiny, more information, and decisions taken at a higher level. GARP states that decisions to enter into or pursue business relationships with higher-risk customers “should require the application of enhanced due diligence measures, such as approval to enter into or continue such relationships, being taken by senior management”. Escalation to senior management makes the risk acceptance a conscious, accountable business decision rather than a front-office default.

The CAP also has an outer boundary: it “should also define circumstances under which the bank would not accept a new business relationship or would terminate an existing one”. So the CAP defines both how higher-risk customers are accepted and when the bank walks away, at the start or later.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks about higher-risk applicants. The guidance gives two linked answers: apply EDD including senior management approval to enter or continue, and define the circumstances for non-acceptance and termination. Only option D contains both.

**Fragile fact.** Approval to enter into or continue a higher-risk relationship sits with senior management; the CAP covers both non-acceptance and termination.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer Acceptance Policy, para 34. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the bank must determine the risks it will accept and when it will not accept or will terminate a relationship, but does not mention senior management approval; that element is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The right action (a senior approval) is assigned to the wrong actor. GARP names senior management. Internal audit, as the third line, independently evaluates controls; approving individual relationships would compromise that independence. A would be right only if it asked who should periodically evaluate whether the approval process works.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B turns “higher risk” into “never accept”. The guidance expects the bank to decide the risks it will accept and to manage higher-risk customers with enhanced measures. B would be right only for the subset of cases the CAP itself defines as grounds for non-acceptance.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C drops the second half of the requirement: the CAP should define when the bank would terminate an existing relationship, not only when it would refuse a new one. C would be correct only if the guidance limited the CAP to account opening, which it does not.

d.reason: It reproduces GARP’s example of an EDD measure (senior management approval to enter into or continue the relationship) and the requirement that the CAP define when the bank would not accept a new relationship or would terminate an existing one.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a Japanese trust bank on onboarding Kaito Holdings KK, which wants a JPY operating account. The ownership and control information is summarised below.

- 70% of Kaito Holdings is held by the Mori Family Trust.
- Mr Mori, a natural person, ultimately controls the trust and so the company.
- Ms Sato, a director, will operate the account under a board resolution.
- The company’s auditor is a listed accounting firm.

Which statement best describes the persons to whom CDD should be applied?

options.text: Kaito Holdings only, because the customer is the legal entity that signs the account agreement with the bank.
Kaito Holdings, Ms Sato as the person acting on its behalf, and Mr Mori as the natural person who ultimately controls it.
Kaito Holdings, Ms Sato and the Mori Family Trust, with the trust treated as beneficial owner as it holds the controlling stake.
Kaito Holdings and Mr Mori only, because persons acting on the customer’s behalf are covered by the customer’s own CDD.

questions.solution:
Japanese trust bank: corporate applicant owned through a family trust controlled by a natural person, with a director operating the account.

**Concept and theory**

Criminals rarely put their own names on accounts. They use companies, trusts and agents. The guidance closes this gap in three steps.

| Element | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Customer | Per FATF Recommendation 10, any person who enters into a business relationship or carries out an occasional financial transaction with the bank; “person” covers natural and legal persons and legal arrangements |
| Persons acting on behalf | CDD applies to them as well as to the customer |
| Beneficial owner | The natural person(s) who ultimately owns or controls a customer and/or on whose behalf a transaction is conducted, including those exercising ultimate effective control over a legal person or arrangement |

GARP states that CDD “should be applied not only to customers but also to persons acting on their behalf and beneficial owners”. The beneficial-owner concept exists precisely to look through legal layers until a human being is reached.

**Applying it to this question**

Kaito Holdings is the customer (a legal person). Ms Sato operates the account on its behalf, so CDD extends to her. The Mori Family Trust is a legal arrangement in the ownership chain; it is not itself the beneficial owner, because the beneficial owner must be a natural person. Mr Mori, who ultimately controls the trust and therefore the company, is the beneficial owner. The listed auditor is irrelevant to whom CDD covers. The correct set is the company, Ms Sato and Mr Mori: option B.

**Fragile fact.** The beneficial owner is always a natural person; a trust or holding company in the chain is never the end point.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 35 and footnotes on “person” and “beneficial owner”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says that in some cases the bank must identify and verify “a person acting on behalf of a beneficial owner(s)”, which compresses GARP; GARP is clear that CDD covers the customer, persons acting on its behalf and beneficial owners. GARP wording is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A stops at the signing entity and drops the two extensions GARP adds: persons acting on behalf and beneficial owners. A would be correct only for the narrower question “which party is the customer under FATF Recommendation 10?”.

b.reason: It applies CDD to the customer, to the person acting on its behalf and to the beneficial owner, with the beneficial owner identified as the natural person who ultimately controls the customer, as in GARP’s definition (consistent with the FATF standards).

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** C attributes beneficial ownership to the trust, a legal arrangement, swapping in the property of a neighbouring concept (the controlling shareholder in the legal chain). The FATF definition requires a natural person. C would be correct only if the question asked which entity in the chain holds the controlling stake.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D drops persons acting on the customer’s behalf, claiming they are covered by the customer’s CDD. GARP applies CDD to them in their own right and requires the bank to verify that they are authorised and to verify their identity. D would be right only if no one other than the beneficial owner operated the account.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q7
questions.question: The head of branch operations at a German savings bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on customer identification and verification. Which of the following statements made in the presentation is least accurate?

options.text: A walk-in individual who carries out a single occasional EUR transaction is a customer for CDD purposes, even without an ongoing relationship.
Where an agent acts on behalf of a customer, the bank should verify both that the agent is so authorised and the identity of the agent.
Generally, identification and verification may be completed after the first transactions settle, because the relationship then already exists.
As part of a systematic procedure, the bank should also take reasonable measures to verify the identity of the beneficial owner.

questions.solution:
German savings bank: branch operations head presents to new analysts; identify the least accurate statement on identification and verification.

**Concept and theory**

GARP requires a bank to “establish a systematic procedure for identifying and verifying its customers and, where applicable, any person acting on their behalf and any beneficial owner(s)”. A systematic procedure means a defined, repeatable process rather than case-by-case discretion. Three features matter:

| Feature | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Timing | Generally, no banking relationship or transaction until identity has been satisfactorily established and verified (FATF Recommendation 10) |
| Beneficial owner | Reasonable measures to verify the beneficial owner’s identity |
| Agents | Verify that any person acting on behalf of the customer is so authorised, and verify that person’s identity |

The timing rule exists because once funds have moved, the damage may be done: verification after the fact cannot undo a laundering transaction. There is a narrow exception (Q12), but the general rule is verification first.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement A follows from the FATF Recommendation 10 definition: a person carrying out an occasional financial transaction is a customer. B restates the two-part check on agents. D restates the reasonable-measures requirement for beneficial owners. C reverses the timing rule into a general permission to verify after settlement. C is the least accurate.

In a “least accurate” question, each wrong option is a true statement. The error in choosing it is misjudging a true statement as false.

**Fragile fact.** The general rule is identify and verify before the relationship or any transaction; post-establishment verification is an exception, not the norm.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, paras 35 to 36. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser states that banks must establish a systematic procedure and defines the customer per FATF Recommendation 10, but does not state the “generally not before verification” timing rule explicitly; that rule is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: **True statement (misjudged by scope error).** A reader who limits “customer” to ongoing relationships drops half of the FATF definition. The customer is any person who enters into a business relationship or carries out an occasional financial transaction. A would become false only if it claimed that occasional customers fall outside CDD.

b.reason: **True statement (misjudged by scope error).** GARP requires both checks: that the person is authorised and that the person’s identity is verified. A reader who believes verifying the principal is enough would wrongly reject B. B would become false if it said only one of the two checks is required.

c.reason: GARP: “Generally, a bank should not establish a banking relationship, or carry out any transactions, until the identity of the customer has been satisfactorily established and verified in accordance with FATF Recommendation 10.” Statement C states the opposite as the general rule.

d.reason: **True statement (misjudged by absolute-claim reading).** The standard for beneficial owners is “reasonable measures to verify”, which is not a guarantee. A reader expecting full certainty might reject D, but D uses GARP’s own wording. D would become false if it said reasonable measures are optional or that verification of the beneficial owner is not required.

questions.loText: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q8
questions.question: A senior analyst in the operational risk validation team of a US bank is reviewing the bank’s identity verification standard and must recommend one improvement. Which recommendation is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Prefer documents that are hardest to obtain illicitly or counterfeit and, where non-documentary methods are used, confirm they suit the customer’s risk profile.
Accept a customer’s signed declaration of beneficial ownership as sufficient verification of the beneficial owner, as it is a written legal undertaking.
Prefer documents that are easiest for customers to obtain, because ease of access is the main criterion for choosing verification documents.
Limit verification to documents alone, because non-documentary sources such as financial statements and references are not acceptable evidence.

questions.solution:
US bank validation team: recommend one improvement to the identity verification standard.

**Concept and theory**

Verification answers the question “is this person really who they claim to be?”. GARP requires identity to be verified “by using reliable, independent source documents, data or information”. Two principles follow:

| Principle | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Document quality | The best documents are those most difficult to obtain illicitly or to counterfeit |
| Non-documentary sources | Allowed (for example references from other financial institutions, financial statements), but the methods and sources must be appropriate and in line with the bank’s policies and the customer’s risk profile |
| Declarations | A bank may require a written declaration of the beneficial owner’s identity, but should not rely solely on it |
| Extent | Set by the nature and level of risk presented by the customer |

The reasoning is adversarial: a criminal will choose whatever evidence is easiest to fake, so the bank should prefer evidence that is hardest to fake, and should never let the customer’s own word be the whole proof.

**Applying it to this question**

The validator must recommend a change consistent with the guidance. Option A captures both the document-quality principle and the condition on non-documentary methods. Every other option either over-trusts the customer, inverts the quality criterion, or excludes sources that GARP explicitly permits.

**Fragile fact.** Best documents are the ones hardest to obtain illicitly or counterfeit; a beneficial-owner declaration may be required but never relied on alone.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 37. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser carries the hardest-to-forge principle and the declaration rule but not the non-documentary methods; that element is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: GARP: “the best documents for the verification of identity are those most difficult to obtain illicitly or to counterfeit. When relying on other sources than documents, the bank must ensure that the methods . . . and sources of information are appropriate, and in accordance with the bank’s policies and procedures and risk profile of the customer.”

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B makes a written declaration sufficient on its own. GARP permits requiring such a declaration “although the bank should not rely solely on such declarations”. B would be correct only as “the bank may require a declaration as one element of beneficial owner verification”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses the direction of the quality criterion: from hardest to obtain illicitly to easiest to obtain. Ease of access for genuine customers is relevant to financial inclusion, but it is not the verification criterion. C would be correct only for a question about reducing onboarding friction, not about verification strength.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D removes non-documentary sources entirely. GARP explicitly contemplates them, citing references from other financial institutions and financial statements, subject to appropriateness. D would be correct only if the stem said that national law in the bank’s jurisdiction restricted verification to documents.

questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q9
questions.question:
A bank supervisor is reviewing an onboarding case. A non-resident applicant applied through the bank’s website to open a CAD deposit account, could not attend an interview, and is a national of a jurisdiction identified by the FATF as having strategic AML/CFT deficiencies, with a FATF call for enhanced due diligence. The supervisor considers four statements:

I. The bank may waive identification and verification because the applicant cannot be present for an interview.

II. The bank should consider why the applicant chose to open an account far from his seat, in particular in a foreign jurisdiction.

III. The bank should apply EDD because it is called for by the FATF in respect of the applicant’s jurisdiction.

IV. The bank must reject all applicants from such jurisdictions, because no level of due diligence can mitigate the risk.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II only
III and IV only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Supervisor reviews an online, non-face-to-face applicant from a jurisdiction with FATF-identified strategic deficiencies.

**Concept and theory**

Two risk features often arrive together in modern onboarding. First, the customer is not physically present (non-face-to-face). Second, the customer is connected to a jurisdiction with weak AML/CFT regimes. GARP addresses both in the same paragraph.

| Feature | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Non-face-to-face | In no case should the bank disregard identification and verification because the customer cannot attend an interview; it should also consider why the customer opened an account far from its seat or office, in particular in a foreign jurisdiction |
| Deficient jurisdictions | Take into account the risks of customers from jurisdictions known to have AML/CFT strategic deficiencies, and apply EDD when this is called for by the FATF, other international bodies or national authorities |

The logic: absence from an interview removes one control, so the bank compensates rather than relaxes; distance from home is itself a question the bank should ask; and jurisdictional weakness raises risk, which is met with EDD, not with automatic refusal.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: waiving verification because the applicant cannot attend is exactly what GARP prohibits (“in no case”): false. Statement II: considering why the account is opened far from the applicant’s seat is GARP’s own risk factor: true. Statement III: the FATF has called for EDD for this jurisdiction, which is GARP’s condition for applying EDD: true. Statement IV: blanket rejection with an absolute claim that no due diligence can mitigate the risk: false. Correct set: II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Non-face-to-face is a reason for more scrutiny, never for skipping verification; jurisdictional deficiencies lead to EDD when called for, not to automatic rejection.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 37. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says EDD “is called for” for customers from jurisdictions with AML/CFT deficiencies, stated without GARP’s condition (“when this is called for by the FATF, other international bodies or national authorities”); Schweser also omits the “far from its seat” factor. GARP wording is used; the stem satisfies both versions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A accepts Statement I, which reverses “in no case should a bank disregard” into “may waive”. A would be correct only if Statement I said the bank must not waive identification for non-face-to-face customers.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “II only” rejects Statement III, ignoring that the stated condition for EDD (a FATF call) is met in the stem. B would be correct if the stem said the jurisdiction had deficiencies but no body had called for EDD and the bank’s own assessment did not warrant it.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** C accepts Statement IV, which claims no level of due diligence can mitigate the risk and mandates rejection of all such applicants. GARP prescribes enhanced due diligence, not blanket exclusion. C would only be defensible if the bank’s CAP itself defined this as a non-acceptance circumstance, and even then Statement IV’s “no level of due diligence” remains an overstatement.

d.reason: GARP: “In no case should a bank disregard its customer identification and verification procedures just because the customer is unable to be present for an interview . . . the bank should also take into account risk factors such as why the customer has chosen to open an account far away from its seat/office, in particular in a foreign jurisdiction . . . and apply enhanced due diligence when this is called for by the FATF, other international bodies or national authorities.”

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q10
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is preparing a training note on customer risk profiles for new relationship managers who serve CNY corporate payroll clients. Which statement should the note include?

options.text: Profiles may cover individual customers or categories, reflect the purpose, expected activity, types of transactions and, where necessary, sources of funds, and help identify abnormal activity.
Profiles should be prepared only for customers already rated higher risk, because lower-risk customers and categories of customers do not need a profile of expected activity.
Profiles should be fixed at account opening and never updated, so that later account activity can always be compared against an unchanged baseline of expected behaviour.
Profiles must document the source of wealth for every customer in all cases, because the guidance makes source of funds a mandatory item for every profile.

questions.solution:
Chinese commercial bank: training note on what customer risk profiles contain and what they are for.

**Concept and theory**

Identification at the outset is not only about confirming a name. The bank also uses the information to understand the customer’s profile and behaviour. GARP lists information typically collected: the purpose of the relationship or occasional transaction, the level of assets or size of transactions, and the regularity or duration of the relationship. With it, the bank develops customer risk profiles “either for particular customers or categories of customers”.

What profiles do:

| Function | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Baseline | Define what is “normal” for the customer or category |
| Detection | Facilitate identification of activity that deviates from normal and may be unusual or even suspicious |
| Classification | Help determine whether the customer or category is higher risk and needs enhanced CDD |
| Content | Intended purpose and nature of the relationship, expected level of activity, type of transactions and, where necessary, sources of funds, income or wealth |
| Updating | Significant information on activity or behaviour should be used to update the bank’s risk assessment of the customer |

The information collected is itself risk-based: it depends on the risk of the customer’s business model and activities and on the products or services requested.

**Applying it to this question**

A training note should state what profiles contain and why they exist. Option A gives the coverage (individuals or categories), the content items with the “where necessary” qualifier on sources of funds, and the purpose (identifying abnormal activity). The other options each distort one feature.

**Fragile fact.** Sources of funds, income or wealth are in the profile “where necessary”, not always; profiles can be built for categories as well as individual customers.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 38. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists “frequency or length of the banking relationship” where GARP says “regularity or duration”; same meaning. Schweser files this material under the heading Customer Identification. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: GARP: profiles may be developed for particular customers or categories; they “facilitate the identification of any account activity that deviates from activity or behaviour that would be considered ‘normal’ ”; and they “should also reflect the bank’s understanding of the intended purpose and nature of the business relationship/occasional banking transaction, expected level of activity, type of transactions, and, where necessary, sources of customer funds, income or wealth”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B confines profiles to customers already rated higher risk. In GARP, profiles are part of what determines whether a customer or category is higher risk, so they cannot be limited to customers already classified. B would be closer to correct if it described the enhanced CDD measures, which do apply to higher-risk customers.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C freezes the profile. GARP requires that significant information collected on customer activity or behaviour be used to update the bank’s risk assessment of the customer. C would be correct only if it described the retained record of the original profile for audit purposes, not the working profile.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D makes sources of funds, income or wealth mandatory in every case. GARP qualifies this with “where necessary”. D would be correct only for higher-risk customers where the bank’s risk assessment requires source-of-wealth information.

questions.question: An external consultant is reviewing the onboarding file of a corporate customer at an Australian bank, opened with an expected turnover of AUD 40 million a year. Which statement about the records and information the bank should obtain is most accurate?

options.text: Copies of official identity documents only, since internal analysis such as the customer risk assessment need not be kept as part of the CDD file.
The same identification information for every applicant, since the nature and extent of verification information is fixed regardless of applicant type.
Identification papers plus CDD information such as account files, correspondence and analysis results, with verification extent set by risk, applicant type and account use.
Identification papers to a single Basel standard, since the guidance itself prescribes the specific requirements for identifying natural persons in every jurisdiction.

questions.solution:
Australian bank: consultant reviews a corporate onboarding file; what records and information should be obtained.

**Concept and theory**

Identification produces evidence, and the guidance wants that evidence kept. GARP says a bank should obtain customer identification papers “as well as any information and documentation obtained as a result of CDD conducted on the customer”. Examples:

| Category | Examples in GARP |
|---|---|
| Official documents | Copies or records of passports, identity cards, driving licences |
| Account files | For example financial transaction records |
| Business correspondence | Including the results of any analysis, such as the risk assessment and inquiries into the background and purpose of the relationship |

GARP then adds that the bank should obtain all information necessary to establish “to its full satisfaction” the identity of the customer, of persons acting on its behalf and of beneficial owners. The nature and extent of verification information depends on the risk assessment, including the type of applicant (personal, corporate and so on) and the expected size and use of the account. Specific requirements for natural persons are usually prescribed in national legislation. For complex relationships or significant account sizes, additional identification measures may be advisable.

**Applying it to this question**

The customer is a corporate with an expected turnover of AUD 40 million: a corporate applicant type with a significant expected account size. The bank should hold identification papers and the wider CDD record, including analysis results, and should calibrate verification to risk, applicant type and expected use. That is option C. The turnover figure is relevant only to the point that the extent of verification follows expected size and use.

**Fragile fact.** Extent of verification follows risk, applicant type and expected size and use; the detailed rules for natural persons come from national legislation, not from the Basel text.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, paras 39 to 40. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists the same document types (passports, identity cards, driving licences, account files, business correspondence) but omits the risk-dependent extent of verification and the national-legislation point; those are from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A drops the CDD information and analysis that GARP explicitly includes, such as the risk assessment and background inquiries. A would be correct only for a question asking which items are official identity documents.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B turns the risk-dependent extent of verification into a fixed standard. GARP says the nature and extent depend on risk assessment, applicant type and expected size and use. B would be correct only for the minimum basic due diligence that applies to all, not for the full extent of verification.

c.reason: It matches GARP: identification papers plus CDD information (account files, business correspondence including results of analysis), with “the nature and extent of the information required for verification” depending on “the type of applicant . . . and the expected size and use of the account”.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D assigns to the Basel guidance a role that GARP gives to national legislation: the specific requirements for ascertaining the identity of natural persons “are usually prescribed in national legislation”. D would be correct if it said national legislation prescribes them.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 b Q12
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a US commodity trading bank allows verification of some customers to be completed after the business relationship is established. The CRO’s policy memo contains the following statements:

I. Deferral is permissible only where it is essential not to interrupt the normal conduct of business.

II. During deferral, the bank applies risk management procedures that set conditions and restrictions on use of the relationship before verification.

III. If verification problems arise after opening and cannot be resolved, they are handled through ongoing monitoring, with no restriction on account access.

IV. Because deferral is a permitted exception, the bank need not consider filing an STR when verification is not completed.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and IV only
II and III only

questions.solution:
US bank CRO’s memo on deferring verification until after the relationship is established.

**Concept and theory**

The default rule is clear: when a bank is unable to complete CDD measures, it should not open the account, commence business relations or perform the transaction. GARP then recognises a narrow exception and surrounds it with safeguards.

| Element | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Verification after establishment may be permissible because it is essential not to interrupt the normal conduct of business |
| Safeguard | Adequate risk management procedures on the conditions and restrictions under which the customer may use the relationship before verification |
| Failure | Where verification problems arise that cannot be resolved, close or otherwise block access to the account |
| Reporting | In any event, consider filing an STR where there are problems completing CDD |

The exception exists because some business (for example fast-moving markets) cannot wait for every document; the safeguards exist because an unverified customer is exactly what a launderer wants to be.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the trigger: true. Statement II restates the safeguard: true. Statement III replaces “close or otherwise block access” with “no restriction”: false. Statement IV claims the exception removes STR consideration, contradicting “in any event”: false. Correct set: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** The STR obligation for incomplete CDD is “consider filing”, and it applies “in any event”; unresolved verification problems lead to closing or blocking the account.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 41. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says that if the bank proceeds before completing verification and cannot confirm identity it should consider filing an STR, but omits the conditions-and-restrictions safeguard and the close-or-block step; those are from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” drops Statement II, the safeguard that GARP attaches to the exception. A would be correct only if Statement II had said the customer may use the relationship without any conditions before verification.

b.reason: GARP: verification after establishment may be permissible “because it would be essential not to interrupt the normal conduct of business. In such circumstances, the bank should adopt adequate risk management procedures with respect to the conditions and restrictions under which a customer may utilise the banking relationship prior to verification.”

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C accepts Statement IV, which reverses “in any event, the bank should consider filing a STR” into “need not consider”. C would be correct only if Statement IV read “the bank should consider filing an STR even though deferral was permitted”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D accepts Statement III, which reverses “close or otherwise block access to the account” into “no restriction on account access”, and rejects the true Statement I. D would only become correct if III described closing or blocking access and I were false.

questions.question: The chief AML/CFT officer of a Dutch bank is told that CDD on a prospective customer, who wishes to deposit EUR 2.4 million, has produced reasonable grounds to suspect that the funds are the proceeds of a predicate offence. No account has yet been opened. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Do not voluntarily open the account, file an STR with the relevant authorities, and ensure the applicant is not informed, even indirectly, of the STR.
Open the account under restrictions and only consider filing an STR, because a suspicion raised by CDD is treated like incomplete verification.
Decline the account and tell the applicant that a report is being made to the authorities, so that the reason for the refusal is transparent.
Decline the account without filing any report, because an STR can be filed only after a business relationship with the customer exists.

questions.solution:
Dutch bank: CDD on a prospective EUR 2.4 million depositor raises reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds of crime.

**Concept and theory**

GARP separates two situations that look alike but carry different obligations.

| Situation | GARP response |
|---|---|
| CDD cannot be completed | Do not open; if opened, close or block when unresolved; consider filing an STR |
| CDD raises suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds of predicate offences or ML/FT | Do not voluntarily open the account; file an STR with the relevant authorities; ensure the customer is not informed, even indirectly, that an STR has been, is being or shall be filed |

The step up from “consider” to “file” reflects the step up from a gap in information to positive grounds for suspicion. The tipping-off prohibition protects the investigation: a warned suspect can move funds or destroy evidence.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem says CDD produced reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds of a predicate offence, and no account exists yet. This is the second row of the table: do not voluntarily open, file the STR, no tipping off. Option A.

**Fragile fact.** Incomplete CDD: consider an STR. Suspicion from CDD: do not open and file an STR, with no tipping off, even indirectly.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 41. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser attaches the no-tipping-off rule to the case of failed verification (“consider filing an STR”) and does not state the separate suspicion case with its “file an STR” obligation. GARP’s two-case structure is used; this looks like condensation in Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: GARP: “where CDD checks raise suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect that the assets or funds of the prospective customer may be the proceeds of predicate offences and crimes related to ML/FT, banks should not voluntarily agree to open accounts with such customers. In such situations, banks should file an STR with the relevant authorities accordingly and ensure that the customer is not informed, even indirectly, that an STR has been, is being or shall be filed.”

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B imports the response for incomplete CDD (“consider filing”) into the suspicion case, and even opens the account. B would describe the incomplete-verification case correctly only if the stem said that documents were missing with no grounds for suspicion, and even then the account should not be opened.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C turns “ensure that the customer is not informed” into informing the customer. This is tipping off. C would be correct only for an ordinary declined application with no suspicion and no report.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D imposes a condition that does not exist: that an STR requires an existing relationship. GARP’s rule applies to a prospective customer. D would be right only if the stem said CDD raised no suspicion and the bank simply declined on commercial grounds.
