questions.question: A branch manager at a Canadian bank reviews an application from an individual whose initial CAD 250,000 deposit will be transferred from an account in the applicant’s own name at another bank subject to the same CDD standard. The bank later obtains information giving it reason to believe that the other bank refused the applicant facilities because of concerns over illicit activities. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The transfer from an account under the same CDD standard allows the bank to rely on the other bank’s due diligence in place of its own.
Customers have the right to move their business, so the bank must accept the applicant and cannot use the prior refusal in its assessment.
The bank must file an STR and reject the applicant, because any account closed by another bank is an automatic ground for refusal.
The transfer gives some comfort, but the bank should do its own CDD and consider higher-risk status with EDD, an STR and/or not accepting.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: applicant’s deposit comes from own-name account at another bank under the same CDD standard; reason to believe that bank refused him over illicit-activity concerns.

**Concept and theory**

A transfer from another regulated bank feels reassuring, and GARP accepts that it “may provide some comfort” when the source account is in the customer’s name at a bank subject to the same CDD standard. But comfort is not a substitute. The receiving bank “should nevertheless conduct its own due diligence” and consider that the previous account manager may have asked for the account to be closed because of concerns about illicit activities.

GARP balances this with the customer’s rights: “customers have the right to move their business from one bank to another”. Where, however, the bank “has any reason to believe that an applicant has been refused banking facilities by another bank due to concerns over illicit activities”, it should consider:

I. classifying the applicant as higher risk and applying enhanced due diligence to the customer and the relationship;

II. filing an STR; and/or

III. not accepting the customer,

in accordance with its own risk assessments and procedures.

**Applying it to this question**

Both features of the stem are present: a transfer from an equivalent-standard bank (some comfort) and reason to believe there was a refusal for illicit-activity concerns (red flag). The guidance requires own CDD and consideration of the escalating responses. Option D.

**Fragile fact.** A transfer from an equivalent-standard bank gives “some comfort” only; the bank still does its own CDD, and a refusal elsewhere over illicit concerns leads to consider EDD, STR and/or non-acceptance.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 43. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the bank should consider classifying the customer as high risk with enhanced CDD or reject the customer, but omits the STR option and the point about transfers from a bank under the same CDD standard; those are from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A overextends “some comfort” into reliance in place of the bank’s own CDD. GARP says the bank should “nevertheless conduct its own due diligence”. A would be closer to a defensible statement in a different context, reliance on an introducer under equal or stricter standards, which belongs to LO 51.c and still leaves ultimate responsibility with the bank.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B turns the customer’s right to move business into a duty to accept and a ban on using the refusal. GARP acknowledges the right but immediately qualifies it. B would be correct only if the bank had no reason to believe the earlier refusal related to illicit activities.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** C makes STR and rejection automatic for any account closed by another bank. GARP says “consider” and offers options joined by “and/or”, and the trigger is a refusal due to concerns over illicit activities, not any closure. C would be closer to correct if it said the bank should consider these responses.

d.reason: It restates GARP: the transfer may give some comfort, the bank conducts its own due diligence, and given reason to believe of a refusal for illicit concerns it should consider higher-risk classification with EDD, filing an STR and/or not accepting the customer.

questions.question: A board member of a London private bank is reviewing the bank’s policy on numbered accounts after an applicant insisted on anonymity. Which statement in the policy is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: A numbered account may operate as an anonymous account, provided that one designated senior officer alone knows the holder’s identity.
Numbered accounts may be subject to lighter CDD than other accounts, because their confidentiality is itself an effective control.
Numbered accounts receive the same CDD as other accounts, even if done by selected staff, with the holder verified and known to enough staff.
The chief AML/CFT officer should not have access to the identities behind numbered accounts, so that customer confidentiality is preserved.

questions.solution:
London private bank: board member reviews the numbered-account policy after an applicant insists on anonymity.

**Concept and theory**

Anonymity is incompatible with CDD. GARP is unconditional: a bank should not open an account or conduct ongoing business with a customer who insists on anonymity or who gives an obviously fictitious name.

Numbered accounts are different. In a numbered account, the names of the customer and beneficial owner are known to the bank but are replaced by an account number or code name in later documentation. They offer confidentiality, not anonymity. GARP sets the conditions:

| Requirement | GARP content |
|---|---|
| Not anonymous | Numbered accounts should not function as anonymous accounts |
| Same CDD | Exactly the same CDD procedures as all other accounts, even if carried out by selected staff |
| Knowledge | Identity verified by the bank and known to a sufficient number of staff to allow effective due diligence, especially if other risk factors indicate higher risk |
| Access | Internal control, compliance, audit and other oversight functions, in particular the chief AML/CFT officer, and the supervisors, have full access as needed |

**Applying it to this question**

The applicant who insists on anonymity must be refused. The policy question is how numbered accounts are run. Only option C states the same-CDD rule with its two refinements (selected staff permitted; identity verified and known to enough staff).

**Fragile fact.** Numbered accounts are confidential, not anonymous: same CDD, identity known to a sufficient number of staff, and full access for the chief AML/CFT officer and supervisors.

**Reference**

LO 51.b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.2 (Essential Elements of Sound ML/FT Risk Management), subsection Customer and Beneficial Owner Identification, Verification and Risk Profiling, para 44 and the footnote defining numbered accounts. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser states that the bank must refuse a customer insisting on anonymity and must verify the identity of a numbered account holder, but omits the same-CDD, sufficient-number-of-staff and oversight-access details; those are from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 b, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A says a numbered account may operate as an anonymous account, the reverse of GARP’s “nor should confidential numbered accounts function as anonymous accounts”. Restricting knowledge to one officer also contradicts “a sufficient number of staff”. A would describe the rule correctly only if it said numbered accounts must not operate anonymously.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B treats confidentiality as if it were a mitigating control that justifies simplified measures, borrowing the treatment reserved for proven lower-risk situations. GARP requires exactly the same CDD. B would be correct only for a genuinely proven lower-risk retail account where law permits simplified measures, which a numbered account is not by virtue of its confidentiality.

c.reason: GARP: numbered accounts “should be subject to exactly the same CDD procedures as all other customers’ accounts, even if the procedures are carried out by selected staff . . . the identity of the latter must be verified by the bank and known to a sufficient number of staff to facilitate the conduct of effective due diligence”.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D denies access to the very actor GARP names as needing it. The oversight functions, “in particular the chief AML/CFT officer”, and the supervisors should have full access as needed. D would be correct only if it referred to general branch staff with no CDD role.

questions.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 c Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a banking group headquartered in Singapore is preparing an induction session for newly hired analysts. The group comprises two banks and their branches and subsidiaries in five jurisdictions, and each office currently writes its own AML/CFT manual. Which of the following statements best describes how the group’s AML/CFT policies should relate to those of its foreign offices?

options.text: Each branch and subsidiary should design its AML/CFT policies from host-country law alone, and the group policy should govern only the head office’s domestic operations.
The group should apply and supervise group-wide AML/CFT policies consistently, and local policies may reflect host requirements but must stay consistent with and supportive of group policy.
The group should apply identical AML/CFT procedures in every office, because any local adaptation to host-country requirements would break the consistency of the group-wide policy across offices.
Group-wide AML/CFT policies should bind the branches of the group’s banks, while subsidiaries follow only host-country rules, because they are separately incorporated legal entities.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Singapore-headquartered group explaining how group-wide AML/CFT policies relate to foreign offices.

**Concept and theory**

A bank that operates in several jurisdictions is exposed to ML/FT risk that does not respect legal borders: the same customer may hold accounts with the group’s offices in different countries, and a launderer can exploit whichever office has the weakest controls. The Basel Committee’s answer is that each group should develop group-wide AML/CFT policies and procedures that are consistently applied and supervised across the group. In the guidance, “group” means an organisation’s one or more banks and the branches and subsidiaries of those banks, so a subsidiary is inside the group policy even though it is a separate legal entity.

Consistency does not mean uniformity. Branch and subsidiary policies may reflect local business considerations and the requirements of the host jurisdiction, but they must still be consistent with and supportive of the group’s broader policies and procedures.

| Layer | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Group (head office) | Develops group-wide policies, applies and supervises them consistently across the group |
| Branch or subsidiary | May reflect local business needs and host requirements, but stays consistent with and supportive of group policy |

**Applying it to this question**

The group has two banks plus branches and subsidiaries, and each office currently writes its own manual. The question asks for the relationship between group and local policy. The deciding facts are (i) that a group-wide policy must exist and be applied consistently across the whole group, and (ii) that local adaptation is allowed as long as it remains consistent with and supportive of group policy. Only option B states both.

**Fragile fact.** Consistent does not mean identical: local policies may differ, but must be consistent with and supportive of group policy; and “group” includes subsidiaries, not only branches.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3 AML/CFT in a Group-Wide and Cross-Border Context (paragraph 63 and footnote 30). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q1 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It confines group policy to the head office’s domestic operations and lets each office build policy from host law alone. Option B restates this.

The guidance expressly permits local policies to reflect host requirements, and where host rules are stricter the group policy should allow the office to adopt them. The option would be right only if the stem asked what the baseline must be, without reference to local adaptation.

The definition of group in the guidance covers the banks and their branches and subsidiaries, and the information-sharing requirement expressly applies to both branches and subsidiaries. It would be right only if “group” were defined as a single legal entity and its branches.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a Canadian banking group is reviewing a subsidiary in Country

X. Country X requires beneficial-owner verification for a wider set of legal-entity customers than the group policy does, and requires CDD records to be refreshed more often. The subsidiary has asked which standard it should follow. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?

options.text: The subsidiary should follow the group policy, because group-wide consistency means that group standards prevail over local requirements in every jurisdiction.
The subsidiary should follow the Country X rules, and from then on group policy no longer governs any aspect of the subsidiary’s AML/CFT procedures.
The chief AML/CFT officer should inform the home supervisors that Country X does not permit the proper implementation of the FATF standards.
Group policy should allow the subsidiary to adopt and implement the Country X rules, while its procedures stay consistent with and supportive of group policy.

questions.solution:
Chief compliance officer of a Canadian group deciding which standard a subsidiary follows when the host country’s rules are stricter.

**Concept and theory**

Home and host requirements will often differ. The guidance resolves this with a one-directional rule designed so that a group never operates below the stricter standard in any location:

| Situation | Rule |
|---|---|
| Host requirements stricter than the group’s | Group policy should allow the branch or subsidiary to adopt and implement the host requirements |
| Minimum requirements of home and host differ (either way) | Offices in host jurisdictions apply the higher standard of the two |
| Host country does not permit proper implementation of FATF standards | Chief AML/CFT officer informs home supervisors; additional measures, possibly closure |

Adopting the host rule does not release the office from group policy: its policies must still be consistent with and supportive of the group’s broader policies. The motivation is that the group’s policy is a floor, not a ceiling, and that local law cannot be overridden by an internal policy.

**Applying it to this question**

Country X requires beneficial-owner verification for more legal-entity customers and more frequent CDD refreshes, so Country X is stricter than the group. Nothing in the stem says the FATF standards cannot be implemented in Country X. The first row of the table applies: the subsidiary adopts the Country X rules, and group policy continues to govern it in all other respects.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: when the host is stricter, the host rule is adopted locally; group policy is the floor, never a cap on stricter local law.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3 AML/CFT in a Group-Wide and Cross-Border Context (paragraph 63). Wording difference: GARP says group policy “should allow” the branch or subsidiary to adopt the stricter host requirements; Schweser compresses this to “the branch or subsidiary should adopt” them. The practical outcome is the same; GARP’s framing is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q2 of 18.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction of the rule, so that the group standard prevails over the stricter local rule. The guidance runs the other way: the stricter standard wins. The option would be correct only if the group’s standard were the stricter one (see Q14), in which case the higher, group standard applies.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It over-extends the rule: adopting stricter host requirements does not take the subsidiary outside group policy. The office must remain consistent with and supportive of the group’s broader policies. The option would be correct only if the subsidiary had been sold and left the group.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It imports the escalation rule that applies when the host country does not permit the proper implementation of FATF standards. A stricter host regime is the opposite situation. The option would be correct if Country X blocked beneficial-owner verification or information-sharing so that the FATF standards could not be implemented.

d.reason: GARP paragraph 63: “In cases where the host jurisdiction requirements are stricter than the group’s, group policy should allow the relevant branch or subsidiary to adopt and implement the host jurisdiction local requirements.” The same paragraph keeps local policy “consistent with and supportive of the group’s broader policies”. Option D states both halves.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Japanese banking group on its planned expansion into Country Y, whose law restricts the transmission of customer names and balances across national borders. The group will operate in Country Y through both a branch and a locally incorporated subsidiary. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Group-wide AML/CFT is harder to implement than many other risk processes for this reason, yet it is essential that both offices be authorised to share customer information with the head office, subject to adequate legal protection.

Group-wide AML/CFT is harder to implement for this reason, and the need to share customer information with the head office applies to the branch only, because the subsidiary is a separately incorporated host-country entity.

Group-wide AML/CFT is harder to implement for this reason, so the group should accept anonymised aggregate reports from Country Y, because head-office access to customer names is not needed for group-wide monitoring.

Group-wide AML/CFT is harder to implement for this reason, so the Country Y offices should transmit customer names and balances to the head office regardless of host law, because group policy overrides any local legal restrictions.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant advising a Japanese group expanding into a country that restricts cross-border transmission of customer names and balances.

**Concept and theory**

Most risk processes (market or credit risk aggregation, for example) can work with positions and exposures. AML/CFT needs identities: to see that the same person is moving funds through several offices, the head office must know who the customer is. The Basel Committee therefore recognises that implementing group-wide AML/CFT procedures is more challenging than many other risk management processes, because some jurisdictions still restrict banks’ ability to transmit customer names and balances across national borders.

Its response is not to give up on group monitoring, nor to ignore local law. It states that, for effective group-wide monitoring and ML/FT risk management, it is essential that banks be authorised to share information about their customers, subject to adequate legal protection, with their head offices or parent bank, and that this applies to both branches and subsidiaries. Group-wide policies must also take local data protection and privacy laws into account.

**Applying it to this question**

Country Y restricts the transmission of names and balances, and the group will use both a branch and a subsidiary. Three facts decide the answer: the restriction makes group-wide AML/CFT harder; head-office access to customer information is essential; and it is to be obtained through legal authorisation and protection, for both forms of presence.

**Fragile fact.** The sharing requirement covers both branches and subsidiaries, and it operates

“subject to adequate legal protection”, not in defiance of host law.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Global Process for Managing Customer Risks (paragraph 66), and Group-Wide Information-Sharing (paragraph 78). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser omits the explicit “both branches and subsidiaries” sentence.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q3 of 18.

a.reason: GARP paragraph 66 states that implementing group-wide AML/CFT procedures is more challenging because some jurisdictions restrict the transmission of customer names and balances, and that “it is essential that banks be authorised to share information about their customers, subject to adequate legal protection, with their head offices or parent bank. This applies in the case of both branches and subsidiaries.”

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops subsidiaries from the sharing requirement. The guidance says the requirement applies to both branches and subsidiaries. It would be correct only if the stem asked about an entity outside the group, such as an unaffiliated correspondent.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses “essential” into “not needed”. Anonymised aggregates cannot reveal that one customer is active across several offices, which is the purpose of group-wide monitoring. It would be correct only for a risk process that needs exposures rather than identities, such as aggregating interest-rate positions.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** It drops the condition “subject to adequate legal protection” and claims group policy overrides local law. The guidance seeks legal authorisation to share and requires group policies to take local data protection and privacy laws into account. It would be correct only if the host law permitted the transfer, in which case no override would be needed.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian bank is reviewing the private banking desk, which accepts customers referred by four introducer banks. Local legislation permits reliance on introducers, and in every case the desk obtains the customer information from the introducer. The auditor has compiled the following summary.

| Introducer | Same group? | Standards vs bank’s own | Supervised at group level? | Years known |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | No | Less strict | n/a | 12 |
| Q | No | Equally strict | n/a | 3 |
| R | Yes | Same standards | Yes | 8 |
| S | Yes | Less strict (local) | No | 15 |

On which introducers may the desk rely, consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: R only
Q, R and S only
Q and R only
P, Q and R only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at an Australian bank deciding on which of four introducers the private banking desk may rely.

**Concept and theory**

Business is often referred or introduced by another bank, which may already have performed CDD on the customer. Reliance saves duplicated work, but it lets the weakest link set the standard. The guidance therefore asks a bank to:

1. understand the extent to which AML/CFT legislation allows it to rely on other banks’ procedures;
2. not rely on introducers subject to standards less strict than those governing its own AML/CFT procedures, which requires monitoring and evaluating the standards in the referring bank’s jurisdiction;
3. consider a higher level of reliance on an introducer in the same financial group, provided it is subject to the same standards and their application is supervised at group level;
4. in every case obtain the customer information from the referring bank, because it may need to be reported to FIUs.

The decisive variable is therefore the strictness of the introducer’s standards relative to the bank’s own, not group membership by itself and not the length of the relationship.

**Applying it to this question**

Legislation permits reliance, and the desk obtains the customer information in every case. Test each introducer against the “no less strict” condition:

| Introducer | Test | Reliance? |
|---|---|---|
| P | Less strict standards | No |
| Q | Equally strict standards, unaffiliated | Yes |
| R | Same group, same standards, supervised at group level | Yes (higher reliance possible) |
| S | Same group, but less strict local standards | No |

The “Years known” column is irrelevant: the guidance attaches no weight to relationship length. The answer is Q and R only.

**Fragile fact.** The test is the introducer’s standards relative to the bank’s own: equal or stricter is acceptable; group membership raises the possible level of reliance only when standards are the same and supervised at group level.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraph 69). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser compresses the rule to “the bank’s own AML/CFT standards must be used . . . unless the introducer is in a jurisdiction with equal or stricter standards” and omits the same-group higher-reliance condition; the outcome here is identical under both sources, and GARP’s fuller rule is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q4 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It treats group membership as a precondition for any reliance and excludes Q. The guidance bars only introducers with less strict standards; group membership merely permits a higher level of reliance. “R only” would be correct if local legislation allowed reliance only on group entities.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It applies the same-group treatment to S, as if group membership alone justified reliance. The higher-reliance treatment requires the introducer to be subject to the same standards and supervised at group level; S’s local standards are less strict. It would be correct if S were subject to the group’s own standards with group-level supervision.

c.reason: GARP paragraph 69: “A bank should not rely on introducers that are subject to standards that are less strict than those governing the bank’s own AML/CFT procedures.” Q (equally strict) passes; R passes and qualifies for the higher-reliance treatment because it is in the same group, under the same standards and supervised at group level. P and S fail the strictness test.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts P, whose standards are less strict, perhaps swayed by the 12-year relationship. The guidance says the bank should not rely on such an introducer. It would be correct only if P’s jurisdiction applied standards at least as strict as the bank’s.

questions.question:
An AML analyst at a London-headquartered banking group is checking whether a corporate customer is a “significant relationship” under group policy, which requires a consolidated relationship review when the customer’s balances across the group exceed GBP 10.0 million. The analyst has extracted the following data.

| Group entity | Holding | GBP million |
|---|---|---|
| UK parent bank | Current and deposit accounts (on-balance-sheet) | 3.2 |
| UK parent bank | Letters of credit issued for the customer (off-balance-sheet) | 1.8 |
| Singapore subsidiary | Discretionary portfolio (assets under management) | 2.9 |
| Swiss branch | Deposits held on a fiduciary basis | 2.4 |
| Customer file | Declared annual net income of the customer | 0.9 |

Which of the following is the correct consolidated figure and conclusion?

options.text: GBP 5.0 million; below the threshold, so no consolidated review is required
GBP 8.5 million; below the threshold, so no consolidated review is required
GBP 11.2 million; above the threshold, so a consolidated review is required
GBP 10.3 million; above the threshold, so a consolidated review is required

questions.solution:
AML analyst at a London-headquartered group consolidating a corporate customer’s holdings across group entities against a GBP 10.0 million threshold.

**Concept and theory**

A customer that looks modest in one office may be significant across the group. The guidance therefore requires a bank to monitor significant customer relationships, balances and activity on a consolidated basis, “regardless of whether the accounts are held on-balance sheet, off-balance sheet, as assets under management or on a fiduciary basis, and regardless of where they are held”. Two dimensions of consolidation are required:

| Dimension | What must be included |
|---|---|
| Form | On-balance-sheet, off-balance-sheet, assets under management, fiduciary |
| Location | Every group entity, at home and abroad (branches and subsidiaries) |

Items that are not balances or activity held with the group (for example a customer’s declared income) are risk-profile information, not part of the consolidated relationship figure.

**Applying it to this question**

Let $\text{B}_{\text{cons}}$ be the consolidated group balance of the customer:

$\text{B}_{\text{cons}} = \text{B}_{\text{on}} + \text{B}_{\text{off}} + \text{B}_{\text{AUM}} + \text{B}_{\text{fid}}$

where $\text{B}_{\text{on}}$ is on-balance-sheet balances, $\text{B}_{\text{off}}$ off-balance-sheet positions, $\text{B}_{\text{AUM}}$ assets under management and $\text{B}_{\text{fid}}$ fiduciary holdings, all summed across every group entity. Step by step (GBP million):

$\text{B}_{\text{on}} =$ 3.2 (UK parent deposits)

$\text{B}_{\text{off}} =$ 1.8 (UK parent letters of credit)

$\text{B}_{\text{AUM}} =$ 2.9 (Singapore subsidiary portfolio)

$\text{B}_{\text{fid}} =$ 2.4 (Swiss branch fiduciary deposits)

$\text{B}_{\text{cons}} =$ 3.2 + 1.8 + 2.9 + 2.4 = 10.3

The declared annual income of 0.9 is excluded because it is not a balance held with the group. Since 10.3 > 10.0, the customer is a significant relationship and the consolidated relationship review is required. The number means that the group’s combined exposure to this customer’s activity crosses its internal significance line even though no single office holds more than GBP 5.0 million of it.

**Fragile fact.** Consolidate across both form (on- and off-balance-sheet, AUM, fiduciary) and location (every branch and subsidiary); declared income is not a group balance.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraph 73). The threshold is a hypothetical group policy given in the stem; the guidance sets no numerical threshold. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q5 of 18.

a.reason: **Dropped term (location).** GBP 5.0 million = 3.2 + 1.8 consolidates only the UK parent and drops the Singapore subsidiary and Swiss branch, ignoring “regardless of where they are held”. It would be correct only if group policy defined the threshold per legal entity in the home country.

b.reason: **Dropped term (form).** GBP 8.5 million = 3.2 + 2.9 + 2.4 omits the off-balance-sheet letters of credit, ignoring “regardless of whether the accounts are held on-balance sheet, off-balance sheet”. It would be correct only if the policy counted funded balances alone.

c.reason: **Wrong input (irrelevant data included).** GBP 11.2 million = 10.3 + 0.9 adds the customer’s declared income, which is profile information and not a balance held with the group. The conclusion happens to match, but the figure is wrong. It would be correct only if the 0.9 were a further balance held with a group entity.

d.reason: GBP 10.3 million is the sum of all four forms of holding across all three entities, as GARP paragraph 73 requires, and it exceeds the GBP 10.0 million threshold.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Brazilian bank is reviewing a report on the bank’s branch in Country Z. A new secrecy law in Country Z prevents the branch from verifying beneficial owners and blocks the transfer of any customer information to the head office, so the FATF standards cannot be properly implemented there. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: The branch manager should inform the Country Z supervisor and continue operating under Country Z law, since host requirements always govern branches located there.
The chief AML/CFT officer should inform the home supervisors, and additional measures should be considered, including, as appropriate, closing operations there.
The chief AML/CFT officer should inform the home supervisors, and the group must then close its operations in Country Z immediately after that notification.
The chief AML/CFT officer should apply the higher standard of the two jurisdictions, which resolves the issue without any escalation outside the bank.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at a Brazilian bank responding to a host-country secrecy law that prevents proper implementation of FATF standards.

**Concept and theory**

The “higher standard” rules (Q2, Q14) assume that both jurisdictions allow the FATF standards to be implemented and differ only in strictness. A different problem arises when the host country does not permit proper implementation of the FATF standards at all, for example because its law blocks beneficial-owner verification or information-sharing. Following the FATF standards (the interpretive note to Recommendation 18 on internal controls and foreign branches and subsidiaries), the guidance prescribes an escalation:

1. **Actor and addressee:** the chief AML/CFT officer should inform the home supervisors.
2. **Response:** additional measures should be considered, including, as appropriate, the financial group closing its operations in the host country.

The home supervisor is informed because it supervises the group on a consolidated basis; closure is a possible measure, not an automatic consequence.

**Applying it to this question**

Country Z’s law prevents verification of beneficial owners and blocks all transfer of customer information, and the stem states that the FATF standards cannot be properly implemented. This is the escalation case, not a difference in strictness. The right actor is the chief AML/CFT officer, the right addressee is the home supervisor, and closure is one measure to consider.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and addressee: the chief AML/CFT officer informs the home supervisors (not the host supervisor), and closure is “as appropriate”, not automatic.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Global Process for Managing Customer Risks (paragraph 65). Wording difference: Schweser says “in some instances, the bank may need to close operations”; GARP frames it as an additional measure to be considered, as appropriate. Same meaning; GARP’s framing is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q6 of 18.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives the escalation to the branch manager and sends it to the host supervisor, then continues business as usual. The guidance names the chief AML/CFT officer and the home supervisors. Continuing under host law would be appropriate only where host law permits proper FATF implementation and is merely different in detail.

b.reason: GARP paragraph 65: “if the host country does not permit the proper implementation of those standards, the chief AML/CFT officer should inform the home supervisors. Additional measures should be considered, including, as appropriate, the financial group closing its operations in the host country.”

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** It turns “should be considered, including, as appropriate” into a mandatory, immediate closure. The guidance treats closure as one of the additional measures to be considered. The option would be correct only if the home supervisor, having been informed, required closure.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It applies the “higher standard of the two” rule, which resolves differences in minimum requirements between home and host. When the host country does not permit implementation, applying a higher internal standard is impossible, so escalation is required. It would be correct if Country Z’s rules were merely weaker but still allowed the group standard to be applied.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Shanghai-headquartered banking group is drafting the section of a CNY-denominated board report that covers group-wide customer risk assessment. The analyst is considering the following statements.

I. Criteria for identifying higher-risk customers should be applied across the bank, its branches and its subsidiaries, and through outsourced activities.

II. Because customer categories are defined centrally, a given customer category should be treated as posing the same ML/FT risk in every jurisdiction where the group operates.

III. Customer risk assessments should be applied on a group-wide basis or, at a minimum, be consistent with the group-wide risk assessment.

IV. Internationally active groups should rely mainly on local business-line management, rather than on internal audit and a global compliance function, to monitor the application of global CDD.

Which of the statements should the analyst include as accurate?

options.text: I, II and III only
III only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Shanghai-headquartered group selecting accurate statements on group-wide customer risk assessment.

**Concept and theory**

At group level, the bank should have a thorough understanding of all the risks associated with its customers across the group, individually or by category, documented and updated regularly in proportion to the level and nature of group risk. The guidance builds this in four steps:

| Step | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Identify factors | Geographical location, patterns of transaction activity (declared or self-stated), usage of products and services |
| Set criteria | Criteria for identifying higher-risk customers, applied across the bank, its branches, its subsidiaries and through outsourced activities |
| Assess | Customer risk assessments applied group-wide, or at least consistent with the group-wide assessment; customers in the same category may pose different risks in different jurisdictions |
| Mitigate and check | Group controls (more information, tighter monitoring, more frequent updating, staff visits); compliance and internal audit (in particular the chief AML/CFT officer) or external auditors evaluate compliance; a strong internal audit and global compliance function are the primary mechanisms for monitoring global CDD |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches the criteria step, including outsourced activities. Statement II contradicts the explicit warning that the same category may carry different risk in different jurisdictions. Statement III matches the assessment step. Statement IV moves the primary monitoring of global CDD from internal audit and the global compliance function to local business management. Only I and III are accurate.

**Fragile fact.** Same customer category, different risk in different jurisdictions; and the primary monitors of global CDD are internal audit and the global compliance function, not business lines.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Risk Assessment and Management (paragraphs 67 to 68). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser summarises this section only as customer and group-wide risk assessments and audits applying to multinational banks.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q7 of 18.

a.reason: **Polarity flip (statement II accepted).** It accepts II. GARP paragraph 67 says group policy should recognise that customers in the same category “may pose different risks in different jurisdictions”. II would be true only if the group operated in a single jurisdiction.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error (statement I rejected).** It rejects I, typically because the reader believes outsourced activities fall outside the criteria. The guidance applies the criteria “through outsourced activities” as well. “III only” would be right if I had said the criteria apply only to in-house offices.

c.reason: GARP paragraph 67: criteria “should be applied across the bank, its branches and its subsidiaries and through outsourced activities” (I), and “Customer risk assessments should be applied on a group-wide basis or at least be consistent with the group-wide risk assessment” (III).

d.reason: **Role misassignment (statement IV accepted).** It accepts IV, which gives the primary monitoring role to local business-line management. GARP paragraph 68 states that internationally active groups should have a strong internal audit and a global compliance function, since these are the primary mechanisms for monitoring the overall application of global CDD. IV would be true only for first-line day-to-day controls, not for monitoring group-wide application.

questions.question: A home-country supervisor is reviewing the mandate of the group AML/CFT officer at a Frankfurt-headquartered banking group with branches and subsidiaries in twelve countries and total assets of EUR 310 billion. Which of the following descriptions of the group AML/CFT officer’s role is most accurate?

options.text: The officer creates and coordinates a single group AML/CFT strategy, assesses its implementation group-wide, and may give orders to branches and subsidiaries nationally and abroad.
The officer creates the group AML/CFT strategy, but monitoring of compliance at foreign subsidiaries rests solely with local officers, since the officer’s mandate ends at national borders.
The officer coordinates a single group AML/CFT strategy but may only recommend measures to foreign subsidiaries, since the authority to give orders rests with each host-country board.
The officer confirms group-wide compliance through annual written attestations from each office, since regular on-site visits to offices are the responsibility of internal audit.

questions.solution:
Home-country supervisor reviewing the mandate of the group AML/CFT officer of a Frankfurt-headquartered group.

**Concept and theory**

A bank operating nationally and abroad should appoint a chief AML/CFT officer for the whole group (the group AML/CFT officer). Without a single owner, each office would run its own strategy and no one would see, or be able to correct, weaknesses across the group. The guidance gives this officer:

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Responsibility | As part of global risk management, creating, coordinating and assessing group-wide the implementation of a single AML/CFT strategy |
| Authority | Mandatory policies and procedures, and authorisation to give orders to all branches, subsidiaries and subordinated entities nationally and abroad |
| Monitoring | Ongoing monitoring of fulfilment of all AML/CFT requirements group-wide, nationally and abroad, including through regular on-site visits |
| Powers | If needed, empowered to give orders or take the necessary measures for the whole group |

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the most accurate description. The deciding facts are a single strategy, a group-wide (cross-border) monitoring mandate and the authority to give orders. Option A has all three; each other option cuts one element.

**Fragile fact.** The group AML/CFT officer can give orders to all branches and subsidiaries nationally and abroad, and personally checks compliance through regular on-site visits.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraphs 75 to 76). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser states only that the group officer must ensure group-wide compliance across borders.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q8 of 18.

a.reason: GARP paragraph 75: the group AML/CFT officer has responsibility “for creating, coordinating and group-wide assessment of the implementation of a single AML/CFT strategy (including mandatory policies and procedures and the authorisation to give orders for all branches, subsidiaries and subordinated entities nationally and abroad)”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It ends the officer’s monitoring mandate at the national border. Paragraph 76 requires ongoing monitoring on a group-wide basis, “nationally and abroad”. It would be correct only for a bank that operates nationally and therefore has no group officer.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves the authority to give orders from the group officer to the host-country boards. The guidance gives the group officer authorisation to give orders to all branches and subsidiaries and, if needed, to take the necessary measures for the whole group. It would describe a purely advisory function, which is not what the guidance provides.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns regular on-site visits to internal audit and reduces the officer to collecting attestations. Paragraph 76 says the group officer should satisfy himself or herself, “including through on-site visits on a regular basis”, that there is group-wide compliance. Internal audit also evaluates compliance, but that does not remove the officer’s own duty.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the draft “global process for managing customer risks” of a New York-headquartered bank with USD 85 billion of deposits held across 14 countries. Which of the following draft statements is most consistent with the Basel Committee guidance on consolidated risk management?

options.text: “Group AML/CFT policies are designed to ensure strict compliance with all relevant laws and regulations in each jurisdiction, and that compliance is their sole objective.”
“Group AML/CFT policies set a consistent and comprehensive baseline across international operations, and local changes required by law must not impair the group’s access to information.”
“Group AML/CFT policies set a consistent baseline, and where local law requires changes, the group accepts reduced access to that office’s information as the cost of local compliance.”
“Group AML/CFT policies set a consistent baseline, which each branch and subsidiary administers independently, so information-sharing with the head office is left to local discretion.”

questions.solution:
Risk consultant reviewing a New York bank’s draft global process for managing customer risks.

**Concept and theory**

Consolidated risk management means “establishing and administering a process to coordinate and apply policies and procedures on a group-wide basis, thereby implementing a consistent and comprehensive baseline for managing the bank’s risks across its international operations”. Two design principles follow:

1. **Purpose beyond compliance.** Policies should be designed “not merely to comply strictly with all relevant laws and regulations, but more broadly to identify, monitor and mitigate group-wide risks”. Legal compliance office by office can still miss a pattern that spans offices.
2. **Protection of information access.** Every effort should be made to ensure that the group’s ability to obtain and review information under its global policies is not impaired by local modifications required by local law, supported by robust information-sharing between the head office and all branches and subsidiaries.

**Applying it to this question**

Each draft statement either keeps or breaks these two principles. Option B keeps both (consistent, comprehensive baseline; information access protected). The others either reduce the purpose to legal compliance, accept impaired access, or decentralise administration and make sharing optional.

**Fragile fact.** The group baseline must be consistent and comprehensive, and is meant to manage group-wide risk, not merely to tick local legal boxes.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Global Process for Managing Customer Risks (paragraph 64). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser does not reproduce the “not merely to comply” sentence.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q9 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the purpose to strict legal compliance. The guidance says policies should be designed “not merely” to comply but to identify, monitor and mitigate group-wide risks. It would be correct only as a description of a minimum legal obligation, not of consolidated risk management.

b.reason: GARP paragraph 64 defines the baseline as “consistent and comprehensive” and states that “Every effort should be made to ensure that the group’s ability to obtain and review information . . . is not impaired as a result of modifications to local policies or procedures necessitated by local legal requirements.”

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts impaired access as the cost of local compliance. The guidance says every effort should be made to ensure access is not impaired. It would describe the outcome only after every effort had failed, which then triggers escalation rather than acceptance.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives administration of the process to each office and makes sharing discretionary. Consolidated risk management is a process the group establishes and administers to coordinate policies group-wide, with robust information-sharing among the head office and all branches and subsidiaries. It would be correct only for a set of unrelated banks, not a group.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Swiss banking group that also runs securities and insurance businesses is presenting to the risk committee on ML/FT risk controls in mixed financial groups. Which of the following statements made in the presentation is NOT correct?

options.text: The group should be able to monitor and share information on customers’ identity and on their transaction and account activity across the entire group.
Differences in the nature of activities and customer relationships between sectors may require or justify variations in the AML/CFT requirements for each sector.
When cross-selling products from different business arms, the group should apply the AML/CFT requirements that are appropriate for the relevant sector.
Because customer risk is set at group level, the group should apply the banking arm’s AML/CFT requirements unchanged to its securities and insurance businesses.

questions.solution:
Chief risk officer of a Swiss mixed financial group identifying the incorrect statement about ML/FT controls across banking, securities and insurance.

**Concept and theory**

Many banking groups also run securities and insurance businesses. These mixed financial groups face issues not present in deposit-taking and lending, because a customer can move value through several sectors of the same group, each with its own patterns of activity. The guidance requires:

| Requirement | Content |
|---|---|
| Group-wide visibility | Ability to monitor and share information on customer identity and on transaction and account activity across the entire group; alertness to customers using services in different sectors |
| Sector variation | Differences in activities and relationship patterns may require or justify variations in AML/CFT requirements for each sector |
| Cross-selling | When cross-selling products from different business arms, apply the AML/CFT requirements appropriate for the relevant sector |

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT-correct question, so three options are true and one is false. A, B and C each restate one row of the table. D claims that the banking arm’s requirements should be applied unchanged to the other sectors, which contradicts the sector-variation and cross-selling rules.

**Fragile fact.** In mixed groups, information is shared across the whole group, but requirements may vary by sector; the banking arm’s rules are not copied unchanged.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Mixed Financial Groups (paragraphs 82 to 83). This section is in GARP only; Schweser does not cover mixed financial groups, so the content is taken from GARP within the LO’s scope of group-wide practices.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q10 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement.** Accurate: paragraph 82 requires mixed groups to be able to monitor and share information on customer identity and on transaction and account activity across the entire group. It would be the answer if the stem asked which statement is correct.

b.reason: **True statement.** Accurate: paragraph 83 states that sector differences may require or justify variations in the requirements imposed on each sector. A reader who thinks group-wide consistency forbids any variation (an absolute-claim trap) would wrongly pick it.

c.reason: **True statement.** Accurate: paragraph 83 requires the group to be alert to sector differences when cross-selling and to apply the requirements appropriate to the relevant sectors. It would be the answer if the stem asked which statement is correct.

d.reason: D is the incorrect statement. GARP paragraph 83: differences between sectors “may require or justify variations in the AML/CFT requirements imposed on each sector”, and “the appropriate AML/CFT requirements for the relevant sectors should be applied”. Uniform banking rules across all arms contradict this.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a large Paris-based bank is reviewing a project that moves transaction monitoring for all European offices to a central hub, after which the local offices would stop their own monitoring. Which of the following recommendations should the auditor make?

options.text: Document and integrate the local and centralised monitoring functions, so that suspicious patterns can be monitored across the group, not just locally or centrally.
Retire local monitoring once the hub is live, because a centralised database on its own gives a complete group-wide view of all patterns of potential suspicious activity.
Keep monitoring purely local and avoid centralising databases, because centralising processing systems conflicts with host-country AML/CFT requirements.
Limit centralisation to banks without foreign subsidiaries, because the guidance on centralised processing systems applies only to domestic branch networks.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Paris-based bank reviewing a move of all European transaction monitoring to a central hub.

**Concept and theory**

Many large banks with the capability to do so centralise certain processing systems and databases for more effective management or for efficiency. Schweser summarises the benefit as more effective and efficient risk management for larger banks. Centralisation creates a risk of its own: a central engine sees patterns visible only in aggregated data, while a local team sees context visible only on the ground. The guidance therefore requires that, when centralising, a bank should “adequately document and integrate the local and centralised transaction/account monitoring functions” so that it can monitor for patterns of potential suspicious activity “across the group and not just at either the local or centralised levels”. Separately, each office, regardless of location, should establish and maintain effective monitoring appropriate to the risks in its jurisdiction.

**Applying it to this question**

The project would make local offices stop their own monitoring, so only the centralised level would remain. That is exactly the gap the guidance warns about. The auditor’s recommendation should be to document and integrate the two levels, not to choose one of them.

**Fragile fact.** Centralisation is allowed but must be integrated with local monitoring: patterns are monitored across the group, “not just” locally or centrally.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraphs 72 and 74). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser states only that centralisation may allow more effective and efficient risk management for larger banks and omits the integration requirement.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q11 of 18.

a.reason: It restates GARP paragraph 74: document and integrate local and centralised monitoring so the bank can monitor for patterns “across the group and not just at either the local or centralised levels”.

b.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** It asserts that a central database on its own gives a complete view. The guidance requires integration with local monitoring precisely because neither level is complete alone, and paragraph 72 requires every office to maintain effective monitoring. It would be correct only if “complete” were replaced by “additional”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It treats centralisation as something to avoid. The guidance recognises centralisation as a legitimate route to more effective management or efficiency, provided the levels are integrated. It would be correct only if host law prohibited the transfer of the data, which the stem does not state.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It invents a limitation to domestic branch networks. Paragraph 74 refers to many large banks centralising systems and requires monitoring across the group, which includes foreign branches and subsidiaries. It would be correct only if the guidance restricted centralisation by geography, which it does not.

questions.question: A compliance manager at a Singapore-headquartered banking group finds that its offices in three jurisdictions collect CDD information in different formats and retain it under different local rules. Each approach was adopted to meet a local regulatory requirement. Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: The practice is inconsistent with the guidance, because customer acceptance, CDD and recordkeeping procedures must be identical in every office of the group.
The practice is acceptable, and the head office need not have access to the records, because local rules govern each office’s customer information.
The practice is acceptable, provided each approach is consistent with the group-wide standards and relevant information remains accessible to the head office.
The practice is acceptable only where the local rule is less strict than group policy, because stricter local rules must give way to the group standard.

questions.solution:
Compliance manager at a Singapore group assessing offices that collect and retain CDD information differently to meet local rules.

**Concept and theory**

Group-wide policy needs a common core and room for local law. The guidance draws the line as follows:

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Head-office access | Relevant information should be accessible by the head office to enforce group AML/CFT policies |
| Minimum standards | Each office should be able to comply with the minimum AML/CFT and accessibility policies applied by the head office |
| Consistency | Customer acceptance, CDD and record-keeping implemented consistently, with adjustments for specific business lines or geographical areas |
| Local variation | Different approaches to information collection and retention may be necessary to conform to local regulatory requirements or relative risk factors, but must be consistent with the group-wide standards |

**Applying it to this question**

The offices differ in format and retention because of local regulatory requirements. This is the “local variation” row: acceptable, provided it remains consistent with group-wide standards and head-office access to relevant information is preserved.

**Fragile fact.** Local collection and retention may differ, but must stay consistent with group-wide standards and keep relevant information accessible to the head office.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraphs 70 to 71). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser does not cover this paragraph explicitly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q12 of 18.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** It demands identical procedures in every office. The guidance requires consistent application “with adjustments as necessary” and explicitly accepts different approaches to collection and retention. It would be correct only if the stem asked about the group-wide standards themselves, which are common.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It removes head-office access. Paragraph 70 requires relevant information to be accessible to the head office for enforcing group policies. It would be correct only for information that is not relevant to enforcing group AML/CFT policies.

c.reason: GARP paragraph 71: “it is recognised that different approaches to information collection and retention may be necessary across jurisdictions to conform to local regulatory requirements . . . However, these approaches should be consistent with the group-wide standards”; and paragraph 70: “Relevant information should be accessible by the banking group’s head office for the purpose of enforcing group AML/CFT policies”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the stricter-standard rule, letting the group standard override stricter local rules. Where host requirements are stricter, group policy should allow the office to adopt them (paragraph 63). It would be correct only if “less strict” and “stricter” were swapped.

questions.question:
The head of financial crime at a GBP-reporting banking group is drafting group-wide information-sharing standards and is considering the following provisions.

I. Branches and subsidiaries should proactively provide the head office with information on higher-risk customers and activities relevant to the global AML/CFT standards.

II. Branches and subsidiaries should provide account information to the head office only when local law expressly requires such a transfer.

III. The standards should describe the process to be followed in all locations for identifying, monitoring and investigating unusual circumstances and for reporting suspicious activity.

IV. The standards should take into account local data protection and privacy laws and the requirements for storage, retrieval, sharing and disposal of the information.

Which of the provisions are consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
III and IV only

questions.solution:
Head of financial crime at a GBP-reporting group selecting provisions for group-wide information-sharing standards.

**Concept and theory**

Group-wide information-sharing is what makes the group policies operational. Banks should oversee the coordination of information-sharing, and the guidance sets out who sends what, and how:

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Proactive flow | Subsidiaries and branches should proactively provide the head office with information on higher-risk customers and activities relevant to the global AML/CFT standards |
| Responsive flow | They should respond to requests for account information from the head office or parent bank in a timely manner |
| Process | Group-wide standards should describe the process followed in all locations for identifying, monitoring and investigating potential unusual circumstances and reporting suspicious activity |
| Legal and data handling | Policies should take into account local data protection and privacy laws, the types of information that may be shared, and the requirements for storage, retrieval, sharing or distribution and disposal |

**Applying it to this question**

Provision I is the proactive flow. Provision II restricts the responsive flow to cases where local law requires a transfer, which inverts the obligation to respond to head-office requests in a timely manner. Provision III is the process requirement. Provision IV is the legal and data-handling requirement. The accurate set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of flow: branches and subsidiaries send higher-risk information to the head office proactively, and answer head-office requests in a timely manner.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Group-Wide Information-Sharing (paragraphs 77 to 78). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser condenses this to “the head office should be informed of information regarding high-risk customers” and “local data protection and privacy laws must be considered”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q13 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error (provision IV rejected).** It omits IV, as if data protection and handling rules were outside group-wide sharing policy. Paragraph 78 expressly includes them. “I and III only” would be correct only if IV had said that local privacy law should be disregarded.

b.reason: GARP paragraph 77 supports I and III, and paragraph 78 supports IV. Provision II conflicts with paragraph 77’s requirement to “respond to requests for account information from the head office or parent bank in a timely manner”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip (provision II accepted).** It accepts II. The guidance requires timely responses to head-office requests; it does not limit sharing to transfers that local law compels. II would be acceptable only if reworded to “subject to adequate legal protection”, which is a limit on how, not on whether, information is shared.

d.reason: **Polarity flip (provision I rejected).** It drops I, treating the flow to the head office as request-only. The guidance requires branches and subsidiaries to provide higher-risk information proactively. “III and IV only” would be correct only if I had said “only on request”.

questions.question: A treasury analyst on secondment to the compliance unit of a Brazilian banking group is reviewing its branch in Country K. Group policy requires enhanced due diligence for any customer who maintains a large balance and makes regular cross-border wire transfers. Country K’s minimum requirements set no such rule, and Country K’s FATF standards are otherwise properly implemented. Which approach should the Country K branch apply?

options.text: The group standard, because where home and host minimum requirements differ, offices in host jurisdictions should apply the higher standard of the two.
The Country K standard, because the requirements of a host jurisdiction always govern the branches and subsidiaries that a group operates in that jurisdiction.
The Country K standard, with the chief AML/CFT officer informing the home supervisors that Country K does not permit proper implementation of the FATF standards.
Whichever standard local management judges more cost-effective, provided the group AML/CFT officer approves the choice and documents it for the home supervisor.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst on secondment to compliance at a Brazilian group deciding which standard a host-country branch applies when the group’s rule is stricter.

**Concept and theory**

Q2 dealt with a host country that is stricter than the group. This question covers the mirror case. The guidance states the general rule in paragraph 64: “Where the minimum regulatory or legal requirements of the home and host countries differ, offices in host jurisdictions should apply the higher standard of the two.” Together the two rules mean the strictest applicable standard always governs locally:

| Home (group) standard | Host standard | Standard applied in host office |
|---|---|---|
| Lower | Higher | Host (Q2) |
| Higher | Lower | Home, the group standard (this question) |

The escalation rule (inform home supervisors, consider closure) is reserved for a host country that does not permit proper implementation of the FATF standards.

**Applying it to this question**

Group policy requires enhanced due diligence for customers with large balances and regular cross-border wires; Country K’s minimum requirements contain no such rule, so the group standard is higher. Country K otherwise implements the FATF standards properly, so the escalation rule does not apply. The branch applies the higher, group standard.

**Fragile fact.** The higher standard of the two always applies in the host office, whichever jurisdiction it comes from; “host governs” is true only when the host is stricter.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Global Process for Managing Customer Risks (paragraph 64) and the introduction to Section 10.3 (paragraph 63). Schweser places the “stricter of the two jurisdictions” rule in its list of supervisors’ duties, while GARP states it as a duty of the bank’s offices; there is no conflict in outcome, and GARP’s bank-level framing is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q14 of 18.

a.reason: GARP paragraph 64: where home and host minimum requirements differ, “offices in host jurisdictions should apply the higher standard of the two”. Here the higher standard is the group’s.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns the stricter-host rule into a “host always governs” rule. Host requirements are adopted only when they are stricter; when they are weaker, the group standard applies. B would be correct only in Q2’s situation, where the host rule is the stricter one.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It imports the FATF escalation rule. The stem states that Country K properly implements the FATF standards; it merely sets a lower minimum. C would be correct only if Country K’s law prevented the branch from applying the group’s EDD rule.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It replaces the “higher standard” condition with a cost-effectiveness test chosen by local management. Neither cost nor local discretion appears in the rule. It would be correct only if both standards were equally strict, so that the choice between them had no effect on the level of protection.

questions.question: A senior analyst in the group ML/FT risk management function of a Dubai-headquartered bank is preparing guidance after a branch reported suspicious activity on a corporate account. Which of the following statements in the draft guidance is least accurate?

options.text: The group function should evaluate the potential risks posed by activity reported by the branch and, where appropriate, assess the group-wide risk of that customer or category.
The group function should have procedures to ascertain whether other branches or subsidiaries hold accounts for the same customer, including any related or affiliated parties.
The head office should be able to require all branches and subsidiaries to search their files against specified lists of suspected individuals or organisations and report matches.
Branches and subsidiaries should refer all requests from local law enforcement agencies and FIUs to the home supervisor rather than respond to them under their own domestic laws.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst in a Dubai bank’s group ML/FT risk function identifying the least accurate statement in post-STR guidance.

**Concept and theory**

Once a branch reports suspicious activity, the question becomes whether the risk is local or group-wide. The guidance gives the group’s overall ML/FT risk management function the following tasks and tools:

| Task or tool | Content |
|---|---|
| Evaluate | Evaluate potential risks posed by activity reported by branches and subsidiaries and, where appropriate, assess the group-wide risks of a customer or category |
| Find linked accounts | Procedures to ascertain whether other branches or subsidiaries hold accounts for the same customer, including related or affiliated parties |
| Escalate | Policies for higher-risk or potentially suspicious global relationships, including escalation and restricting or closing accounts |
| Respond to authorities | The bank and its branches and subsidiaries should, in accordance with their respective domestic laws, be responsive to requests from law enforcement agencies, supervisory authorities or FIUs |
| Search | The head office should be able to require all branches and subsidiaries to search files against specified lists or requests and report matches |

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C each restate one row. D instructs offices to send all local law enforcement and FIU requests to the home supervisor rather than respond themselves, which contradicts the duty of each office to respond in accordance with its own domestic laws.

**Fragile fact.** Each office responds to law enforcement, supervisor and FIU requests under its own domestic law; the head office can order group-wide file searches.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Group-Wide Information-Sharing (paragraphs 79 to 80). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser does not reproduce these paragraphs.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q15 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement.** Accurate restatement of paragraph 79 on evaluating activity reported by branches and subsidiaries. It would be the answer if the stem asked for the most accurate statement.

b.reason: **True statement.** Accurate restatement of paragraph 79 on ascertaining whether other offices hold accounts for the same customer, including related or affiliated parties. A reader who forgets the “related or affiliated parties” extension may doubt it, but it is in the source.

c.reason: **True statement.** Accurate restatement of paragraph 80 on the head office’s power to require all branches and subsidiaries to search their files and report matches. A reader who thinks subsidiaries are outside head-office instructions (scope error) would wrongly select it.

d.reason: D is the least accurate statement, built by role misassignment. GARP paragraph 80: “a bank and its branches and subsidiaries should, in accordance with their respective domestic laws, be responsive to requests from law enforcement agencies, supervisory authorities or FIUs for information about customers”.
