questions.question:
A model validator at a Canadian bank is reviewing the machine-learning transaction monitoring model that went live in 2023. The model owner’s monitoring practices are summarised below.

| Item | Tracked | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Alerts generated | Yes | Daily |
| Alerts closed as false positives | Yes | Monthly |
| Suspicious cases later found that raised no alert | No | Not applicable |
| Model parameters | Set at go-live | Not reviewed since |
| Vendor licence cost (CAD 1.2 million a year) | Yes | Annually |

Which recommendation is most consistent with the lessons drawn from the USAA FSB case?

options.text: Review the parametrization and run a feedback loop on both false positives and false negatives, so that the bank and its model learn as financial crime evolves.
Keep the feedback loop on false positives only, because false negatives cannot be observed and therefore have no bearing on the bank’s legal requirements.
Keep the parameters frozen at their go-live values, because recalibration would break the comparability of alert volumes from one year to the next.
Track false positives and false negatives, but review them only once a year, because the nature of financial crime is stable enough for annual updates.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank’s model validator recommending changes to a monitoring model with no false negative tracking and frozen parameters.

**Concept and theory**

An automated detection model makes two kinds of error (the definitions here are standard terminology; the source names both errors without defining them):

| Error | What happens | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| False positive | An alert is raised on activity that proves legitimate | Wasted review effort; if excessive, an unmanageable backlog (as at USAA FSB) |
| False negative | Suspicious activity raises no alert | Criminal activity goes undetected and unreported |

GARP’s lesson from the case: “Technology and automation of detection and alerts is most useful in AML, but in creating any such detection system, proper parametrization of the model and a feedback loop on false positives and false negatives is crucial for the financial institution (and any models it uses) to learn and improve. Without proper tracking of false positives, false negatives, and the evolving nature of financial crime, financial institutions may fall behind in their legal requirements to limit criminal or terrorist access to the financial system.”

Three requirements follow: set the parameters properly, track both error types and feed them back, and keep up with how financial crime evolves.

**Applying it to this question**

The table shows three gaps against GARP’s requirements: false negatives are not tracked (“suspicious cases later found that raised no alert: not tracked”), the parameters have not been reviewed since go-live in 2023, and there is no link to the evolving nature of financial crime. The licence cost is irrelevant. The recommendation must close all three gaps, and only option A does.

**Fragile fact.** The feedback loop covers false positives and false negatives, and tracks the evolving nature of financial crime; parameters are not set once and forgotten.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser compresses this to ensuring alerts “do not create a large number of false positives or false negatives” and that the number is manageable “with adequate monitoring, assessment, and feedback”. No conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: It prescribes proper parametrization and a feedback loop on both false positives and false negatives so that the bank and its model learn and improve as financial crime evolves, which is GARP’s lesson in substance.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B drops false negatives from the loop. GARP requires tracking of both false positives and false negatives and warns that without it institutions may fall behind their legal requirements. B would be correct only if the bank’s sole concern were review workload.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses the lesson on parametrization: it treats frozen parameters as a virtue, whereas GARP requires proper parametrization and continuous learning. C would be correct only if financial crime patterns never changed and the go-live calibration were known to be right.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D accepts both error types but describes financial crime as stable. GARP stresses “the evolving nature of financial crime” and that AML and fraud risk management are “in constant evolution”. D would be correct only if crime patterns were static enough for annual review.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is reviewing the bank’s automated AML alerting in light of the USAA FSB case and drafts the following statements:

I. Automating detection and alerts is especially valuable in AML, provided that the detection model is properly parametrized.

II. A feedback loop on false positives and false negatives allows the institution, and the models it uses, to learn and improve.

III. Once a detection model has been properly parametrized at implementation, an ongoing feedback loop adds little further value.

IV. Without tracking the evolving nature of financial crime, an institution may fall behind its legal requirements to limit criminal or terrorist access to the financial system.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank internal auditor checking four statements on automated AML alerting.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s technology lesson from the USAA FSB case has four parts:

1. **Value of automation.** Technology and automation of detection and alerts is “most useful in AML”.
2. **Condition: parametrization.** In creating any such detection system, “proper parametrization of the model” is crucial.
3. **Condition: feedback.** “A feedback loop on false positives and false negatives is crucial for the financial institution (and any models it uses) to learn and improve.”
4. **Consequence of neglect.** “Without proper tracking of false positives, false negatives, and the evolving nature of financial crime, financial institutions may fall behind in their legal requirements to limit criminal or terrorist access to the financial system.”

The USAA FSB system illustrates what happens when the second and third conditions are missing: a system that was too sensitive produced an unmanageable number of alerts. Parametrization and feedback are complements, not substitutes: parametrization sets the starting point, and feedback keeps it right as behaviour and crime change.

**Applying it to this question**

- Statement I: automation is valuable in AML, provided the model is properly parametrized (GARP: parametrization is “crucial”). **Correct.**
- Statement II: the feedback loop on both error types lets the institution and its models learn and improve. **Correct.**
- Statement III: claims feedback adds little once parameters are set. This treats parametrization as a substitute for feedback, contradicting GARP. **Incorrect.**
- Statement IV: without tracking the evolving nature of financial crime, institutions may fall behind their legal requirements. **Correct.**

The correct set is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Parametrization and the false positive and false negative feedback loop are both required; one does not replace the other.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser compresses this paragraph (manageable alerts, few false positives and false negatives, adequate feedback); GARP’s fuller wording is used. No conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A rejects IV, perhaps because it reads the consequence of neglect as overstated. GARP states it directly: without proper tracking, institutions may fall behind their legal requirements to limit criminal or terrorist access to the financial system. A would be correct only if IV had promised certainty (“will” rather than “may”) or omitted the tracking condition.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B accepts III, which reverses the role of the feedback loop, and rejects the true statements I and IV. B would be correct only if detection models, once parametrized, did not need to learn.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C accepts III and rejects II, inverting the feedback lesson twice. C would be correct only if GARP had said that parametrization made feedback unnecessary.

d.reason: Statements I, II and IV each restate part of GARP’s lesson; III contradicts the requirement for a continuing feedback loop.

questions.question: A supervisor at an EU national competent authority is drafting a letter to bank chief executives that draws on the closing observations of the USAA FSB case discussion. Which of the following statements best describes those observations?

options.text: The pandemic reduced remote transactions, which made anomalies easier to identify, so banks can now hold their AML and fraud control frameworks largely stable.
The pandemic increased remote transactions, which made anomalies harder to identify, and as fraud patterns keep changing, banks must continuously adapt their control frameworks.
The pandemic increased remote transactions, which made anomalies harder to identify, and as fraud patterns keep changing, regulators rather than banks must adapt the control frameworks.
The pandemic increased remote transactions, which made anomalies harder to identify, but as fraud patterns have now settled, a one-off redesign of the control framework is sufficient.

EU supervisor drafting a letter on the closing observations of the USAA FSB case discussion.

GARP ends the case discussion by placing it in a changing environment:

- “The COVID-19 pandemic triggered changes in customer and business behavior, in particular a rise in remote transactions, that make it more difficult for financial institutions to identify anomalies.”
- “Greatly affected by the external environment, AML and fraud risk management are in constant evolution, responding to fraud patterns and tactics that change as new opportunities arise for fraudsters in new business and economic environments.”
- “Banks and other financial institutions are in the front line of fraud and AML risk management, facing the continuous challenge of adapting their control framework to these evolving threats.”

The logic links back to the USAA FSB failures. A monitoring system calibrated for one pattern of customer behaviour becomes miscalibrated when behaviour shifts, for example toward remote transactions. That is why GARP insists on parametrization and a feedback loop, and why the control framework is never finished.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has three slots: the direction of the change in remote transactions, the effect on identifying anomalies, and who must adapt the control framework and how often. GARP’s answers are: remote transactions rose; anomalies became harder to identify; banks, in the front line, face a continuous challenge of adaptation. Only option B fills all three slots correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Remote transactions rose, anomalies became harder to spot, and it is the banks (front line) that must keep adapting.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2), closing paragraphs. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser makes the remote-transactions point but omits the “constant evolution” and “front line” observations; GARP is used. The pandemic fraud statistics in the section “Context and Scope” belong to LO 52.a and are not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A reverses the direction: the pandemic increased remote transactions and made anomalies harder to identify. A would be correct only for an environment in which remote activity had declined.

b.reason: It states the rise in remote transactions, the greater difficulty of identifying anomalies, and the need for banks to adapt their control frameworks continuously as fraud patterns change.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** C gives the task of adapting control frameworks to regulators. GARP says banks and other financial institutions are in the front line and face the continuous challenge of adapting their control framework. C would be correct only if regulators designed and operated banks’ controls.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D asserts that fraud patterns have settled and that a one-off redesign is enough. GARP describes AML and fraud risk management as “in constant evolution” and the challenge of adaptation as “continuous”. D would be correct only if threats had stopped evolving.

questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 a Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a U.S. state member bank is classifying three recent events linked to the bank’s outsourced mortgage loan servicing provider, using the risk categories in the Federal Reserve’s guidance on managing outsourcing risk.

I. A failed batch process in the provider’s servicing system posted customer payments to the wrong accounts for two days.

II. Following press coverage of the provider’s slow and careless handling of customer queries, customers publicly blame the bank.

III. The provider’s escrow statements sent to the bank’s customers do not meet the requirements of applicable U.S. regulations.

Which mapping of events to risk categories best matches the definitions in the guidance?

options.text: I operational risk; II reputational risk; III legal risk
I operational risk; II reputational risk; III compliance risk
I compliance risk; II reputational risk; III operational risk
I legal risk; II reputational risk; III compliance risk

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst mapping three servicing-provider events to the guidance’s risk categories.

**Concept and theory**

The Federal Reserve’s guidance (SR 13-19) starts from a simple observation: when a bank hands an operational function to a service provider, the provider’s failures become the bank’s problems. The guidance therefore names six risks that a bank should consider before entering into and while managing an outsourcing arrangement. Each one is defined by its cause, not by its eventual cost, which is why classification questions are decided by asking “what went wrong, and through what channel does it hurt the bank?”

| Risk | Arises when (GARP 12.2 wording, condensed) |
|---|---|
| Compliance | the provider’s services, products or activities fail to comply with applicable U.S. laws and regulations |
| Concentration | services are provided by a limited number of providers or concentrated in limited geographic locations |
| Reputational | actions or poor performance of the provider cause the public to form a negative opinion of the bank |
| Country | a foreign-based provider exposes the bank to economic, social and political conditions and events in its country |
| Operational | the provider exposes the bank to losses from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems, or from external events and human error |
| Legal | the provider exposes the bank to legal expenses and possible lawsuits |

Two pairs are habitually confused. Compliance risk (a breach of applicable law or regulation) is not the same as legal risk (legal expenses and lawsuits); a breach may later lead to litigation, but the breach itself is compliance risk. Reputational risk is about public opinion, whatever the underlying cause.

**Applying it to this question**

Event I is a failed batch process inside the provider’s system: an inadequate or failed internal process or system, which is the definition of operational risk. Event II is poor performance by the provider that causes the public to think less of the bank: reputational risk. Event III is a provider output (escrow statements) that does not meet applicable U.S. regulations: the provider’s products or activities fail to comply with applicable laws and regulations, which is compliance risk. The mapping is therefore operational, reputational, compliance.

**Fragile fact.** Compliance risk is the breach of applicable U.S. law or regulation; legal risk is the resulting legal expense and lawsuits. Classify by the event described, not by its possible later consequence.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.2 “Risks from the Use of Service Providers”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser defines compliance risk against “relevant local laws and regulations”, whereas GARP specifies “applicable U.S. laws and regulations”; GARP is used. Schweser also narrows operational risk to internal control breaches and human error; GARP’s wider definition is used. Neither difference changes the answer.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q1 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It labels Event III legal risk. Legal risk in the guidance is exposure to legal expenses and possible lawsuits; a regulatory shortfall in a document is the compliance definition. Option A would be correct if Event III read “customers have filed suit against the bank over the escrow statements, and the bank is incurring legal fees”.

b.reason: It reproduces the three definitions exactly: failed processes or systems (operational), negative public opinion caused by poor performance (reputational), and failure to comply with applicable U.S. laws and regulations (compliance), as listed in GARP 12.2.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the labels of Events I and III, calling a failed batch process compliance risk and a regulatory breach operational risk. It would be correct only if Event I described a breach of a regulation and Event III a processing failure, which reverses the facts given.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It calls the failed batch process legal risk. Nothing in Event I involves lawsuits or legal expenses; it is a process and system failure. Option D would be correct if Event I described customers suing the bank over the misposted payments.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a bank holding company is reviewing the governance of the group’s outsourcing arrangements against the Federal Reserve’s guidance and must select one statement for the audit report as accurate. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Once a contract is signed, accountability for the safe-and-sound conduct of an outsourced activity passes to the board and senior management of the service provider.
Policies governing the use of service providers should be established and approved by senior management, with the board informed of them annually.
The board is responsible for ensuring that board-approved policies are appropriately executed, including building the reporting framework.
Service provider policies may be approved by an executive committee of the board, and senior management should report regularly to the board on adherence.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor choosing the accurate statement on board and senior management responsibilities for outsourcing.

**Concept and theory**

A recurring principle of outsourcing supervision is that a bank can delegate a task but not its accountability. GARP 12.3 states that the use of service providers does not relieve a bank’s board of directors and senior management of their responsibility to ensure that outsourced activities are conducted in a safe-and-sound manner and in compliance with applicable laws and regulations. The guidance then splits the work between two actors:

| Actor | Responsibility in GARP 12.3 |
|---|---|
| Board of directors, or an executive committee of the board | Establishes and approves the policies governing the use of service providers. These policies establish a program addressing risk assessments and due diligence, standards for contract provisions, ongoing monitoring, and business continuity and contingency planning. |
| Senior management | Ensures the board-approved policies are appropriately executed, which includes overseeing the development and implementation of an appropriate risk management and reporting framework; regularly reports to the board on adherence to the policies. |

The logic is the familiar governance split: the board sets direction and approves; management executes and reports back so that the board can hold it to account.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor must pick the one statement that matches this split. The deciding facts are (i) who approves the policies (the board or an executive committee of the board) and (ii) who reports on adherence (senior management, to the board). Only option D states both correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Board (or an executive committee of the board) approves policies; senior management executes them, oversees the framework and reports to the board. Outsourcing never moves accountability to the provider.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.3 “Board of Directors and Senior Management Responsibilities”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s notes for LO 53.a do not cover board and senior management responsibilities; this content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q2 of 17.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves accountability to the provider’s board and senior management. The guidance states that the use of service providers does not relieve the bank’s own board and senior management of responsibility. No alternate stem under the guidance makes this correct; it would describe a regime in which outsourcing transfers accountability, which the guidance rejects.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives policy approval to senior management. Approval sits with the board or an executive committee of the board; senior management executes. The option would be correct if it described who ensures the policies are executed rather than who approves them.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives the board the task of ensuring execution and building the reporting framework. That is senior management’s duty under GARP 12.3. The option would be correct if “the board” were replaced by “senior management”.

d.reason: GARP 12.3 says policies “should be established and approved by the board of directors, or an executive committee of the board” and that senior management “is also responsible for regularly reporting to the board of directors on adherence to policies”. Option D restates both points.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a regional bank is reviewing four plans, prepared by different teams, for the risk assessment that will precede a decision on whether to outsource the bank’s appraisal management function. Which plan is most consistent with the guidance on the risk assessment element of a service provider risk management program?

options.text: First confirm that outsourcing the function is consistent with the bank’s strategic direction and overall business strategy; then analyse the benefits and risks, the service provider risk and the cost implications.
First analyse the benefits and risks, the service provider risk and the cost implications; then confirm that the chosen provider is consistent with the bank’s strategic direction.
First select a preferred provider through due diligence on its financial condition and controls; then perform the risk assessment of outsourcing the function to that provider.
First confirm that outsourcing the function is consistent with the bank’s strategic direction; then adopt the preferred provider’s own risk assessment of the function in place of the bank’s analysis.

questions.solution:
CRO choosing the plan that sequences the outsourcing risk assessment correctly.

**Concept and theory**

Risk assessment is the first core element of a service provider risk management program, and the guidance calls the assessment of a business activity, and of the implications of performing it in-house or through a provider, “fundamental to the decision of whether or not to outsource”. It is a decision tool, so it must come before any provider is selected. GARP 12.4 A sets out a clear order:

1. Determine whether outsourcing the activity is consistent with the strategic direction and overall business strategy of the organisation.
2. “After that determination is made”, analyse the benefits and risks of outsourcing the proposed activity, the service provider risk, and the cost implications of establishing the arrangement.
3. Consider the availability of qualified and experienced providers to perform the service on an ongoing basis, and the bank’s own ability and expertise to oversee and manage the relationship.
4. Update the assessment at appropriate intervals and revise risk mitigation plans, if appropriate, based on the updated assessment.

Schweser compresses the same logic into “the crucial first step” of deciding whether the activity is best executed in-house or by a third party, followed by cost-benefit and risk analysis.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO needs the plan in which strategic consistency is confirmed first and the benefit, risk and cost analysis follows, all performed by the bank before choosing a provider. Plan A does exactly this. Plans B, C and D each break the order or the ownership of the analysis.

**Fragile fact.** Order matters: strategic fit first, then benefits, risks, provider risk and cost; and the assessment comes before due diligence on any provider.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4 “Service Provider Risk Management Programs”, subsection A “Risk Assessments”. GARP vs Schweser: consistent; Schweser phrases the first step as deciding whether the activity is best executed in-house or by a third party and then performing cost-benefit and risk analysis. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q3 of 17.

a.reason: It follows GARP 12.4 A word for word in sequence: strategic direction and overall business strategy first, then benefits and risks, service provider risk and cost implications.

b.reason: **Polarity flip (sequence reversed).** It runs the cost and risk analysis first and checks strategic fit last. The guidance states that the benefit and risk analysis is done “after that determination is made”, so the order is inverted. It would be correct only if the guidance placed strategy review at the end of the assessment.

c.reason: **Sibling swap (wrong element first).** It puts due diligence and provider selection ahead of the risk assessment. Due diligence is the second core element and is performed on a prospective provider once outsourcing has been judged appropriate. Option C would describe the correct sequence for due diligence and contracting, not for the risk assessment.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It lets the provider’s own risk assessment replace the bank’s. The assessment is the bank’s decision tool, and GARP 12.3 makes clear that outsourcing does not relieve the bank’s board and management of responsibility. It would be correct only if the stem asked what input the bank might consider alongside its own analysis.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is helping a U.S. savings and loan holding company decide where its service provider risk management program should concentrate oversight and controls. The company’s outsourced activities are summarised below.

| Activity | Annual fee (USD m) | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Core deposit processing | 4.2 | Critical to daily operations |
| Mortgage loan servicing | 1.8 | Holds sensitive customer information |
| Internal mail courier | 0.9 | No customer data; not critical |
| Prepaid card distribution | 0.3 | Newly launched bank product |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The internal mail courier should receive more intensive oversight than prepaid card distribution, because program intensity is calibrated mainly to contract value.
Core deposit processing warrants focus only if it also involves sensitive customer information, because criticality to operations is not sufficient on its own.
Prepaid card distribution warrants focus despite carrying the smallest fee, because the activity involves a new bank product offered through a service provider.
Mortgage loan servicing can rely on lighter oversight, because handling of sensitive customer information is governed by the contract rather than the program.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant identifying where the program should focus oversight among four outsourced activities.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance requires the program to be risk-focused: oversight and controls should be commensurate with the level of risk presented by the outsourcing arrangements. To make that concrete, GARP 12.4 lists four alternative grounds on which an outsourced activity deserves focus. The program should focus on outsourced activities that:

1. have a substantial impact on the bank’s financial condition;
2. are critical to the bank’s ongoing operations;
3. involve sensitive customer information or new bank products or services; or
4. pose material compliance risk.

The connective is “or”: any one ground is sufficient. Contract value is not on the list. A small contract can be high risk (a new product, sensitive data) and a large contract can, in principle, be low risk. The aim is to direct scarce oversight resources where a provider failure would hurt most.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each activity against the four grounds. Core deposit processing is critical to daily operations (ground 2). Mortgage loan servicing holds sensitive customer information (ground 3). Prepaid card distribution involves a newly launched bank product (ground 3). The internal mail courier meets none of the grounds. The fee column is a deliberately irrelevant input: ranking by fee would place the courier (USD 0.9 m) above prepaid card distribution (USD 0.3 m), which is the wrong conclusion.

**Fragile fact.** The four focus grounds are joined by “or”. Fee size is not one of them; a new product or sensitive customer data is enough on its own.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4 “Service Provider Risk Management Programs” (introductory paragraphs). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser refers to activities with a “material impact on the institution’s finances and operations” and adds emphasis on sensitive customer information and new products and services, but omits GARP’s ground of “material compliance risk”; GARP’s fuller list is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q4 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It calibrates oversight to contract value, a criterion the guidance does not use. It would be correct only if the guidance tied program intensity to fees, or if the courier service involved sensitive customer information or another focus ground.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error (“or” read as “and”).** It demands that criticality be combined with sensitive customer information. The guidance lists the grounds as alternatives, so criticality to ongoing operations is sufficient alone. It would be correct if the guidance required all grounds to be met jointly.

c.reason: New bank products or services offered through a provider are one of the named focus grounds in GARP 12.4, and the grounds do not depend on fee size. The smallest contract therefore still warrants focus.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It treats contractual coverage as a substitute for program oversight. Activities involving sensitive customer information are explicitly a program focus; contract terms are one element of the program, not a replacement for it. It would be correct only if mortgage servicing involved no sensitive data and met no other ground.

questions.question:
A risk committee member at a bank is checking a draft slide that lists the core elements of an effective service provider risk management program. The slide makes the following claims:

I. Incentive compensation review is listed as a core element in its own right.

II. Board approval of service provider policies is listed as one of the core elements.

III. Business continuity and contingency plans are listed as a core element.

IV. Concentration risk assessment is listed as a core element separate from risk assessments.

Which of the claims are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Risk committee member checking claims about the core elements of a service provider risk management program.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 12.4 says that, while activities vary with the scope and nature of a bank’s outsourcing, effective programs usually include six core elements:

| Element | Name in the guidance | Core question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| A | Risk assessments | Should we outsource this at all? |
| B | Due diligence and selection of service providers | Is this provider fit to do it? |
| C | Contract provisions and considerations | What are the binding terms? |
| D | Incentive compensation review | Do embedded incentives encourage imprudent risk? |
| E | Oversight and monitoring of service providers | Is the provider performing, and when do we escalate? |
| F | Business continuity and contingency plans | What if the provider cannot perform? |

Two things sit near this list but are not on it. Board approval of policies is a governance responsibility (GARP 12.3), not a program element. The named risks (compliance, concentration and so on) are things the program manages, assessed within element A, not separate elements.

**Applying it to this question**

Claim I: incentive compensation review is element D, listed separately from contract provisions (element C). Consistent. Claim II: board approval belongs to 12.3 responsibilities, not the element list. Not consistent. Claim III: business continuity and contingency plans is element F. Consistent. Claim IV: concentration is one of the six risks, not a seventh element. Not consistent. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Incentive compensation review is its own element (D), separate from contract provisions (C). Board approval of policies is a responsibility, not an element.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4 “Service Provider Risk Management Programs” (list of core elements A to F) and Section 12.3. GARP vs Schweser: both list the same six elements; Schweser later discusses incentive compensation under contract provisions (LO 53.c), but still lists incentive compensation review as a separate program element under LO 53.a. No conflict on the list.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q5 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts Claim II, treating a board responsibility from 12.3 as a program element. It would be correct if the question asked which items are required by the guidance as a whole, since board approval of policies is required, just not as a core program element.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts Claims II and IV and rejects both true claims, mixing governance duties and risk categories into the element list. It would fit only a list of “things the guidance mentions” rather than its core elements.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts Claim IV, promoting a risk category (concentration) to a stand-alone element, and rejects Claim I. It would be correct only if the guidance treated incentive compensation as part of contract provisions and listed concentration separately, which it does not.

d.reason: Claims I and III name elements D and F of the GARP 12.4 list exactly; claims II and IV do not appear in that list.

questions.question: A senior treasury analyst at a bank is preparing a briefing note for the board on how risk arises when the bank outsources activities, and must choose one statement to include. Which statement is most consistent with the Federal Reserve’s guidance?

options.text: Outsourcing transfers the risk inherent in an activity to the provider, so the bank need consider only the additional risks introduced by the provider’s involvement in it.
Some risks are inherent in the activity and others are introduced by the provider, and both should be considered before entering into and while managing the arrangement.
The listed outsourcing risks should be assessed when the bank enters into the arrangement, after which oversight relies on the contract’s performance metrics alone.
Entities affiliated with the bank within the same holding company fall outside the definition of service provider, so intragroup outsourcing creates no outsourcing risk.

questions.solution:
Senior treasury analyst choosing the briefing statement on how outsourcing risk arises.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 12.2 opens with the mechanism by which outsourcing creates risk. Using providers to perform operational functions presents various risks: “some risks are inherent to the outsourced activity itself, whereas others are introduced with the involvement of a service provider”. The distinction matters. Inherent risk (the risk that exists in the activity whoever performs it) does not disappear when someone else performs the activity; the bank still bears it. On top of that, the provider relationship adds new risks (a provider’s failed systems, its location, its reputation). If not managed effectively, these can lead to regulatory action, financial loss, litigation and loss of reputation. The guidance therefore tells banks to consider the risks “before entering into and while managing” outsourcing arrangements, so the analysis is continuous, not a one-off at signing.

GARP 12.1 also defines “service providers” broadly: all entities that have a contractual relationship with the bank to provide business functions or activities, whether bank or nonbank, affiliated or non-affiliated, regulated or non-regulated, domestic or foreign.

**Applying it to this question**

The briefing statement must capture both sources of risk and the time dimension. Option B is the only statement that says both inherent and provider-introduced risks exist and that both must be considered before entering into and while managing the arrangement.

**Fragile fact.** Inherent risk stays with the bank; the provider adds risk. Risks are considered before entering into and while managing the arrangement, and affiliates count as service providers.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Sections 12.1 “Purpose” and 12.2 “Risks from the Use of Service Providers”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists the six risks but does not state the inherent versus introduced distinction or the broad definition of service provider; these points are from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q6 of 17.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It claims inherent risk is transferred to the provider. The guidance says inherent risks remain alongside the introduced ones, and 12.3 confirms that outsourcing does not relieve the bank’s board and management of responsibility. It would be correct only under a regime where outsourcing transfers risk, which the guidance rejects.

b.reason: It paraphrases GARP 12.2 directly: inherent and introduced risks, considered before entering into and while managing outsourcing arrangements.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the “while managing” condition and narrows ongoing oversight to performance metrics. The guidance requires the risks to be considered throughout the arrangement, and oversight (element E) covers financial condition, internal controls and escalation as well as metrics. It would be correct if the stem asked only what is assessed at the point of entering into the arrangement.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It excludes affiliates. GARP 12.1 defines service providers to include affiliated as well as non-affiliated entities. It would be correct only under a definition limited to non-affiliated providers.

questions.question:
A relationship manager at the U.S. branch of a Canadian banking organisation reviews quarterly results for a provider that runs the branch’s cash management platform under a contract worth CAD 12.5 million a year.

| Quarter | Availability target (%) | Actual (%) | Other events |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 99.5 | 98.1 | None |
| Q2 | 99.5 | 97.6 | None |
| Q3 | 99.5 | 97.9 | Security incident at provider |

Which response is most consistent with the guidance on oversight and monitoring of service providers?

options.text: Escalate to more frequent and stringent monitoring, consider on-site control reviews and the right to audit, and apply pre-set termination criteria if issues are not addressed in time.
Terminate the contract at once, because any failure to meet performance expectations is itself a termination event that leaves no room for escalation, follow-up or remediation.
Keep monitoring at the current frequency, because monitoring intensity is fixed at onboarding by the provider’s initial risk rating and is reassessed only at contract renewal.
Ask the provider’s internal audit function to set the triggers for heightened monitoring, because the provider is best placed to judge when its own service performance has become unacceptable.

questions.solution:
Relationship manager responding to three quarters of missed availability targets and a security incident at a provider.

**Concept and theory**

Oversight and monitoring (element E) is how the bank keeps the arrangement under control after the contract is signed. GARP 12.4 E builds it in layers:

- **Performance metrics**: the bank establishes acceptable performance metrics that the business line or relationship management determines to be indicative of acceptable performance.
- **Risk-focused intensity**: higher-risk providers may require more frequent assessment and monitoring, a designated point of contact, and risk mitigation plans such as additional reporting by the provider or heightened monitoring by the bank; more frequent and stringent monitoring is needed for providers with performance, financial, compliance or control concerns; for lower-risk providers monitoring can be lessened.
- **Financial condition and internal controls**: ongoing review of financial statements and of the control environment; security incidents at the provider may necessitate elevated monitoring.
- **Escalation of oversight activities**: risk management processes should include triggers to escalate oversight when providers fail to meet performance, compliance, control or viability expectations. Escalation procedures include more frequent and stringent monitoring and follow-up on identified issues, on-site control reviews, and deciding when to exercise the right to audit. The bank should also develop criteria for engaging alternative arrangements and terminating the contract if identified issues are not adequately addressed in a timely manner.

The design is graduated: intensify oversight first, keep termination as a defined end point if remediation fails.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider has missed its availability target in every quarter (98.1, 97.6 and 97.9 against 99.5) and suffered a security incident in Q3. Both are escalation triggers: failure to meet performance expectations, and a security incident that may necessitate elevated monitoring. The contract value of CAD 12.5 million is irrelevant to the choice of response. The guidance’s response is escalation (more frequent and stringent monitoring, on-site control reviews, consideration of the right to audit) together with pre-set criteria for alternatives or termination if the issues are not addressed in a timely manner.

**Fragile fact.** The bank, not the provider, sets the escalation triggers. Escalate first (frequency, on-site reviews, right to audit); terminate under pre-set criteria only if issues are not addressed in a timely manner.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection E “Oversight and Monitoring of Service Providers” (including “Escalation of oversight activities”). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s LO 53.a notes list oversight and monitoring as an element but do not describe escalation; this content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q7 of 17.

a.reason: It lists the escalation tools named in GARP 12.4 E and keeps termination conditional on issues not being addressed in a timely manner, as the guidance requires.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It makes any shortfall an immediate termination event with no follow-up. The guidance escalates oversight first and uses termination criteria for issues “not adequately addressed in a timely manner”. It would be correct only if the stem stated that the bank had already escalated and the provider had failed to remediate within the agreed time.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It holds monitoring constant when the guidance says it should rise. Monitoring is risk-focused and must become more frequent and stringent when a provider shows performance or control concerns. It would be correct only for a provider meeting all expectations and rated low risk.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It hands the escalation triggers to the provider. The guidance places the triggers within the bank’s own risk management processes, and performance metrics are determined by the bank’s business line or relationship management. It would be correct only if it described the provider’s internal self-monitoring, not the bank’s oversight.

questions.question: A business continuity manager at a bank is preparing contingency plans for critical services delivered by an outsourced payments processor. Which of the following actions is least consistent with the guidance on business continuity and contingency considerations?

options.text: Assess the adequacy and effectiveness of the provider’s disaster recovery and business continuity plan and its alignment with the bank’s own plan.
Document the roles and responsibilities for maintaining and testing the provider’s business continuity and contingency plans.
Accept the provider’s annual self-certification of its plan in place of periodic testing, because testing the plan is solely the provider’s responsibility.
Maintain an exit strategy, including a pool of comparable service providers, in the event that the contracted provider is unable to perform.

questions.solution:
Business continuity manager identifying the action least consistent with contingency planning for an outsourced payments processor.

**Concept and theory**

Element F starts from the fact that many events can stop a provider from delivering: performance failure, operational disruption, financial difficulty, or failure of its business continuity and contingency plans during operational disruptions or natural disasters. Because the bank remains responsible for the outsourced activity, its own contingency plans should focus on critical services provided by service providers and consider alternative arrangements if a provider cannot perform. GARP 12.4 F lists what the bank should do when preparing contingency plans:

1. ensure that a disaster recovery and business continuity plan exists for the contracted services and products;
2. assess the adequacy and effectiveness of the provider’s plan and its alignment with the bank’s own plan;
3. document the roles and responsibilities for maintaining and testing the provider’s plans;
4. test the provider’s business continuity and contingency plans on a periodic basis to ensure adequacy and effectiveness; and
5. maintain an exit strategy, including a pool of comparable service providers, in case the contracted provider is unable to perform.

The common thread is verification: the bank does not take the provider’s plan on trust.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the action least consistent with the guidance. Options A, B and D reproduce items 2, 3 and 5 of the list. Option C replaces periodic testing (item 4) with acceptance of a self-certification and assigns testing solely to the provider, which contradicts both the testing requirement and the need to document shared roles for maintaining and testing.

**Fragile fact.** The bank tests the provider’s plans periodically and documents who maintains and tests them; it also keeps an exit strategy with a pool of comparable providers.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection F “Business Continuity and Contingency Considerations”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s LO 53.a notes only name this element; the detail is from GARP only. Schweser’s LO 53.c contract provision on the provider’s business resumption plans is a separate, contract-level topic. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q8 of 17.

a.reason: **Consistent with the guidance (not the exception).** Assessing the adequacy and effectiveness of the provider’s plan and its alignment with the bank’s own plan is item 2 of GARP 12.4 F. It would be the answer only if the stem asked which action is most consistent.

b.reason: **Consistent with the guidance (not the exception).** Documenting roles and responsibilities for maintaining and testing the provider’s plans is item 3. It would be the answer under a “most consistent” qualifier.

c.reason: The guidance tells the bank to test the provider’s plans on a periodic basis and to document the roles and responsibilities for maintaining and testing them. A self-certification relied on in place of testing, with testing treated as the provider’s sole responsibility, is inconsistent with GARP 12.4 F, so C is the action least consistent with the guidance. It is built from a role misassignment (testing given solely to the provider) combined with a scope error (self-certification substituted for periodic testing).

d.reason: **Consistent with the guidance (not the exception).** An exit strategy including a pool of comparable providers is item 5. A reader who thinks exit planning belongs only to contract termination provisions (LO 53.c) commits a sibling swap by choosing D; the guidance places it squarely in contingency planning.

questions.question:
A compliance officer at a bank is reviewing a proposed contract under which an outside sales firm will sell the bank’s credit cards to new customers. The proposed variable fees are shown below.

| Card product | Fee per account opened (USD) | Bank margin (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Standard card | 40 | 6.5 |
| Premium revolving card | 115 | 14.0 |

Which assessment is most consistent with the guidance on incentive compensation review?

options.text: The fee design is a matter for the sales firm alone, because the guidance requires the bank to review only the fixed fees embedded in a service provider contract.
The bank should review and approve the embedded incentives and the adequacy of related controls, since fees steering customers to higher-margin cards may cause reputational damage and litigation.
The structure is acceptable provided total variable fees stay below the fixed fee, because the guidance limits incentive concerns to the share of variable pay.
The main risk created is concentration risk, because the fee structure concentrates the sales firm’s selling effort on a single higher-margin card product line.

questions.solution:
Compliance officer assessing variable fees in a contract with an outside sales firm selling the bank’s credit cards.

**Concept and theory**

Incentive compensation review (element D) exists because some providers do not just process the bank’s business, they represent the bank by selling its products or services. How the provider is paid then shapes how the bank’s customers are treated. GARP 12.4 D requires the bank to ensure that an effective process is in place to review and approve any incentive compensation embedded in service provider contracts, including a review of whether existing governance and controls are adequate in light of the risks arising from those arrangements. The bank should consider whether the incentives might encourage the provider to take imprudent risks. Inappropriately structured incentives may result in reputational damage, increased litigation or other risks. The guidance’s own example of an inappropriate incentive is one where variable fees or commissions encourage the provider to direct customers to products with higher profit margins without due consideration of whether those products are suitable for the customer. GARP’s cost and compensation discussion reinforces this: incentives in the form of variable charges such as fees or commissions should not create incentives to take imprudent risks on the bank’s behalf.

**Applying it to this question**

The sales firm earns USD 115 per premium revolving account against USD 40 per standard account, almost three times as much, and the premium card carries the higher bank margin (14.0% against 6.5%). The margin column is context, not a calculation input; what matters is that the fee structure rewards steering customers to the higher-margin product. This is exactly the guidance’s example. The bank’s obligation is to have a process to review and approve these embedded incentives, assessing whether its governance and controls are adequate for the risk of unsuitable selling.

**Fragile fact.** The concern is variable fees or commissions that push customers to higher-margin products without regard to suitability; the bank must review and approve the embedded incentives.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection D “Incentive Compensation Review” (and the cost and compensation discussion in subsection C). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists incentive compensation review as a program element under LO 53.a but describes its content under contract provisions (LO 53.c), framing it as ensuring the provider places customers’ interests over its own; this is consistent with GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q9 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It limits review to fixed fees. The guidance targets precisely the variable fees and commissions that create incentives. It would be correct only if the provider were paid a fixed fee with no variable or commission element, in which case no incentive compensation would be embedded.

b.reason: It names the required action (review and approve embedded incentives, including the adequacy of controls) and the risk mechanism (steering to higher-margin products, causing reputational damage and litigation) from GARP 12.4 D.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It invents a threshold (variable fees below the fixed fee) as the test. The guidance asks whether incentives might encourage imprudent risk-taking or unsuitable selling, whatever their share of pay. It would be correct only under a rule that defined acceptability by the proportion of variable pay, which the guidance does not contain.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It labels the problem concentration risk. Concentration risk concerns reliance on a limited number of providers or limited geographic locations, not the product mix of sales. It would be correct if the stem said the bank relied on a single sales firm with no alternatives.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a bank is auditing definitions that a colleague has drafted for a training note on outsourcing risk:

I. Concentration risk arises when outsourced services or products are provided by a limited number of service providers or are concentrated in limited geographic locations.

II. Country risk arises when a foreign-based service provider fails to comply with the laws and regulations of the country in which it is located.

III. Operational risk arises when a service provider exposes the institution to losses due to inadequate or failed internal processes or systems, or from external events and human error.

IV. Reputational risk arises only when a service provider’s actions breach applicable law and the breach causes the public to form a negative opinion of the institution.

Which of the definitions are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV
I and III only

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst auditing four drafted definitions of outsourcing risks.

**Concept and theory**

Each outsourcing risk in GARP 12.2 is defined by a specific trigger. The traps in definition questions come from attaching the wrong trigger to a risk name or adding a condition the guidance does not contain.

| Risk | Correct trigger | Common corruption |
|---|---|---|
| Concentration | limited number of providers, or limited geographic locations | treating one city as country risk |
| Country | economic, social and political conditions and events in the provider’s country | treating it as a legal-compliance failure |
| Operational | inadequate or failed processes or systems, external events, human error | dropping external events |
| Reputational | actions or poor performance causing negative public opinion | requiring a breach of law |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches the concentration definition, including both alternatives (number and geography). Consistent. Statement II gives country risk a compliance trigger; the guidance’s country risk is about economic, social and political conditions and events in the provider’s country. Not consistent.

Statement III matches the operational definition, including external events. Consistent. Statement IV adds “only when ... breach applicable law”; the guidance says actions or poor performance causing negative public opinion, with no breach required. Not consistent. Correct set: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Reputational risk needs no breach of law: poor performance alone suffices. Country risk is about conditions and events in the provider’s country, not the provider’s legal compliance.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.2 “Risks from the Use of Service Providers”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s operational risk definition (“internal control breaches and human error”) omits GARP’s “external events”, and Schweser’s country risk mentions only “economic and political” risks; GARP’s wording is used. Under Schweser’s narrower wording, Statement III could look overextended; it is accurate against GARP. This appears to be condensation by Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q10 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts Statement II, which assigns the compliance trigger (failure to comply with laws) to country risk. It would be correct if Statement II read “exposes the institution to possible economic, social and political conditions and events from the country where the provider is located”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap and scope error.** It accepts the two corrupted statements and rejects the two accurate ones. It would be correct only if the guidance defined country risk by legal non-compliance and limited reputational risk to unlawful conduct.

c.reason:
**Scope or condition error.** It accepts Statement IV, which adds a breach-of-law condition to reputational risk. Poor performance alone can create reputational risk. It would be correct if

Statement IV read “arises when actions or poor performance of a service provider cause the public to form a negative opinion”.

d.reason: Statements I and III reproduce the GARP 12.2 definitions; II and IV each contain one corruption.

questions.question:
A regulator examining a U.S. bank’s outsourcing program reviews the following statements in the bank’s policy on additional risk considerations:

I. The confidentiality of suspicious activity reporting makes outsourcing of any SAR-related function more complex, so management should understand the risks and any BSA-specific guidance.

II. For a foreign-based service provider, compliance with the laws of the provider’s home country substitutes for compliance with applicable U.S. laws and regulations.

III. The bank should consider the authority or ability of home country supervisors to gain access to the bank’s customer information while examining a foreign-based provider.

IV. The bank should refer to existing guidance when engaging public accounting firms and other outside professionals to perform work traditionally carried out by internal auditors.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I, III and IV
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Regulator reviewing a bank’s policy statements on additional outsourcing risk considerations.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 12.4 G (“Additional Risk Considerations”) flags four situations in which outsourcing needs extra care:

| Topic | What the guidance says |
|---|---|
| SAR reporting functions | The confidentiality of suspicious activity reporting makes outsourcing any SAR-related function more complex. Banks must identify and monitor the risks of using providers for certain SAR functions in compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act, and management should understand the risks and any BSA-specific guidance. |
| Foreign-based providers | Banks should ensure foreign-based providers comply with applicable U.S. laws, regulations and regulatory guidance. They may also consider the provider’s home-country laws on the bank’s ability to perform on-site reviews, and the authority or ability of home country supervisors to access the bank’s customer information while examining the provider. |
| Internal audit | Banks should refer to existing guidance on engaging independent public accounting firms and other outside professionals to perform work traditionally done by internal auditors. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 prohibits a registered public accounting firm from performing certain non-audit services for a public company client whose financial statements it audits. |
| Risk management activities | Banks may outsource activities such as aspects of interest rate risk and model risk management, subject to developmental evidence and consistency with model risk management guidance. |

The foreign-provider point is additive: home-country law is also considered, but it never replaces compliance with U.S. requirements.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the SAR point. Consistent. Statement II says home-country compliance substitutes for U.S. compliance; the guidance requires compliance with applicable U.S. laws and treats foreign law as an additional consideration. Not consistent. Statement III restates the home-supervisor access point. Consistent. Statement IV restates the internal audit point. Consistent. Correct set: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Foreign-based providers must comply with applicable U.S. laws; the provider’s home-country law is an additional consideration (on-site review access, home supervisor access to customer data), never a substitute.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection G “Additional Risk Considerations”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not cover subsection G; this content is from GARP only, within the LO’s “elements of an effective program”. Schweser’s LO 53.c contract provision on foreign-based providers (choice of law) is a separate contract-level point. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q11 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error (true statement excluded).** It omits Statement IV, treating the internal audit consideration as outside the guidance. It would be correct only if Statement IV were false, for example if it claimed that SOX bars any outsourcing of internal audit work.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts Statement II and rejects I and III. Statement II turns “also consider” foreign law into “substitute for” U.S. law. It would be correct only if the guidance allowed home-country compliance to replace U.S. compliance.

c.reason: Statements I, III and IV match GARP 12.4 G; Statement II reverses the relationship between U.S. and foreign law.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts all four, including Statement II. It would be correct if Statement II read “a foreign-based provider must comply with applicable U.S. laws, and the bank may also consider the laws of the provider’s country”.

questions.question: The corporate secretary of a bank holding company is finalising the board’s governance charter for outsourcing. Which allocation of responsibilities is most consistent with the guidance on board of directors and senior management responsibilities?

options.text: Board or its executive committee: establish and approve service provider policies. Senior management: ensure the policies are executed, oversee the risk management and reporting framework, and report regularly to the board on adherence.

Board or its executive committee: establish and approve service provider policies and oversee development of the risk management and reporting framework. Senior management: ensure the policies are executed and report on adherence.

Senior management: establish and approve service provider policies. Board or its executive committee: ensure the policies are executed, oversee the risk management and reporting framework, and review adherence regularly.

Board or its executive committee: establish and approve service provider policies. Chief audit executive: ensure the policies are executed, oversee the risk management and reporting framework, and report regularly to the board on adherence.

questions.solution:
Corporate secretary allocating outsourcing responsibilities between the board and senior management.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 12.3 gives a precise division of labour, which the table summarises.

| Duty | Actor named in GARP 12.3 |
|---|---|
| Establish and approve policies governing the use of service providers | Board of directors, or an executive committee of the board |
| Ensure board-approved policies are appropriately executed | Senior management |
| Oversee development and implementation of the risk management and reporting framework | Senior management (as part of executing the policies) |
| Regularly report to the board on adherence to policies | Senior management |

The policies themselves should establish a program that addresses risk assessments and due diligence, standards for contract provisions and considerations, ongoing monitoring of service providers, and business continuity and contingency planning. The framework-building task sits with senior management because it is part of execution; the board’s role is to approve and to receive reports.

**Applying it to this question**

The charter must allocate four duties. Option A gives approval to the board (or its executive committee) and gives execution, framework oversight and reporting to senior management. Each other option moves one duty to the wrong actor.

**Fragile fact.** Overseeing the development of the risk management and reporting framework is a senior management duty, not a board duty; the board approves and receives reports.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.3 “Board of Directors and Senior Management Responsibilities”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s notes do not cover this section; content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q12 of 17.

a.reason: It reproduces GARP 12.3: board or executive committee approves; senior management ensures execution, which “includes overseeing the development and implementation of an appropriate risk management and reporting framework”, and regularly reports to the board on adherence.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives framework oversight to the board. GARP 12.3 places overseeing the development and implementation of the framework within senior management’s execution role. It would be correct only if the guidance assigned framework development to the board.

c.reason: **Role misassignment (actors swapped).** It gives approval to senior management and execution to the board, inverting the split. It would be correct if “senior management” and “board” were exchanged throughout.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives execution, framework oversight and reporting to the chief audit executive. The guidance names senior management for these tasks; internal audit is not the actor. It would be correct if “chief audit executive” were replaced by “senior management”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant reviewing a bank’s outsourcing risk assessment procedure records the following statements:

I. The risk assessment should be updated at appropriate intervals consistent with the bank’s service provider risk management program.

II. The bank should revise its risk mitigation plans, if appropriate, based on the results of the updated risk assessment.

III. The bank should revise its risk assessment, if appropriate, based on the results of its updated risk mitigation plans.

IV. The assessment should consider the availability of qualified and experienced providers on an ongoing basis and the bank’s own ability and expertise to oversee the relationship.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III
I, II and IV

questions.solution:
Risk consultant checking statements on updating the outsourcing risk assessment.

**Concept and theory**

A risk assessment is not a one-time gate. GARP 12.4 A ends with two linked instructions: the assessment “should be updated at appropriate intervals consistent with the financial institution’s service provider risk management program”, and the bank “should revise its risk mitigation plans, if appropriate, based on the results of the updated risk assessment”. The causal arrow runs one way:

updated risk assessment −→ revised risk mitigation plans

The assessment measures the risk; mitigation responds to it. Reversing the arrow would let the chosen controls dictate how much risk the bank believes it has, which defeats the purpose of assessment. The same subsection lists two forward-looking considerations: the availability of qualified and experienced providers to perform the service on an ongoing basis, and the bank’s own ability and expertise to provide appropriate oversight and management of the relationship. Schweser frames these as the two key questions: do qualified and experienced providers exist, and is the bank sufficiently qualified to oversee and manage the relationship?

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the updating requirement. Consistent. Statement II states the correct direction (mitigation plans revised from the updated assessment). Consistent. Statement III reverses the direction (assessment revised from updated mitigation plans). Not consistent. Statement IV restates the two considerations. Consistent. Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the updated risk assessment drives revision of risk mitigation plans, never the reverse.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection A “Risk Assessments”. GARP vs Schweser: consistent; Schweser states that “risk mitigation techniques should be updated on a sufficiently regular basis as a result of updated risk assessments”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q13 of 17.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts the reversed Statement III and rejects the correctly directed Statement II, as well as omitting IV. It would be correct only if the guidance said assessments are revised in light of updated mitigation plans.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts both II and III, treating the two directions as equivalent, and omits I and IV. The guidance states only one direction. It would be correct only if the stem asked which statements mention risk mitigation plans.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts Statement III alongside I and II and omits IV. Including the reversed direction makes the set wrong, and IV is an explicit consideration in the same subsection. It would be correct if Statement III were replaced by Statement IV.

d.reason: Statements I, II and IV match GARP 12.4 A; Statement III inverts the stated causality.
