questions.question:
A risk committee member compares the outsourcing profiles of two U.S. banking organisations.

| Organisation | Assets (USD bn) | Providers | Material activities | Spend (% of opex) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Community bank | 1.6 | 14 | 3 | 22 |
| Large bank holding company | 420.0 | 2600 | 85 | 9 |

The community bank’s three material activities are critical and are outsourced to highly reputable providers. Which statement best describes the appropriate design of the two programs?

options.text: The community bank’s program must match the large organisation’s in depth and formality, because each of its material outsourced activities is critical.
The community bank’s program may be simpler and use fewer elements, while the large organisation may need many more elements, given criticality, complexity and number.
The large organisation’s program may be simpler than the community bank’s, because outsourcing spend as a share of operating expense is lower at the large organisation.
The community bank may dispense with a formal program altogether, because all of its material activities are placed with highly reputable service providers.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member comparing program design for a community bank and a large bank holding company.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance is proportional. GARP 12.4 states that “the depth and formality of the service provider risk management program will depend on the criticality, complexity, and number of material business activities being outsourced”. It then gives two reference points:

| Profile | Program implication in GARP 12.4 |
|---|---|
| Community banking organisation with critical activities outsourced, but few, and to highly reputable providers | The program may be simpler and use fewer elements and considerations. |
| Institution using hundreds or thousands of providers for numerous activities with material risk | May need many more elements and considerations to manage the higher level of risk and reliance on providers. |

Two points are easy to miss. First, criticality alone does not force maximum formality: the community bank example explicitly includes critical activities and still permits a simpler program because they are few and placed with highly reputable providers. Second, simpler does not mean absent; the program still exists, with fewer elements and considerations. Schweser expresses the same idea: depth and complexity may be relatively low when there are few outsourced activities to established, reliable providers, and relatively high when many providers are involved.

**Applying it to this question**

The community bank has three material activities, all critical but placed with highly reputable providers, across 14 providers. The large organisation has 85 material activities across 2,600 providers. By criticality, complexity and number, the large organisation needs the deeper, more formal program; the community bank may run a simpler one. Total assets and outsourcing spend as a percentage of operating expense (22% against 9%) are deliberately irrelevant inputs: they are not among the factors the guidance uses.

**Fragile fact.** Depth and formality scale with criticality, complexity and number. Critical but few activities with highly reputable providers can justify a simpler program, never no program.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4 “Service Provider Risk Management Programs” (paragraph on depth and formality). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser speaks of “depth and complexity” and “established and reliable” providers where GARP says “depth and formality” and “highly reputable” providers; the substance is the same. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q14 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It treats criticality as sufficient to require maximum depth. The guidance’s own community bank example has critical activities yet allows a simpler program because they are few and with highly reputable providers. It would be correct if the community bank outsourced many critical activities to providers of unknown standing.

b.reason: It matches GARP 12.4: depth and formality depend on criticality, complexity and number, the community bank example permits a simpler program with fewer elements, and the large user of providers may need many more elements.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It uses outsourcing spend relative to operating expense, a measure the guidance does not use, and reaches the reverse conclusion. It would be correct only if program depth were defined by spend share; under the guidance’s factors, the large organisation’s 85 material activities and 2,600 providers point the other way.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It lets the community bank dispense with a program. The guidance says the program “may be simpler and use less elements”, not that it may be dropped; policies establishing the program are required of every institution under 12.3. It would be correct only if the bank outsourced no material activities at all.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a bank is preparing a report on how the bank monitors a significant service provider that delivers information technology services, and must choose one statement for the report. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The bank can request the FFIEC Technology Service Provider examination report for the provider directly from the provider’s external audit firm rather than from a regulator.
Acceptable performance metrics for the provider should be determined by the provider, because it is best placed to define achievable service levels.
The bank can review an available AICPA SOC 2 report and request the FFIEC Technology Service Provider examination report from its primary federal regulator.
Lower-risk providers should be monitored with the same frequency as higher-risk providers, so that the bank’s oversight process is applied consistently.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst choosing the accurate statement on monitoring a significant IT service provider.

**Concept and theory**

Within oversight and monitoring (element E), GARP 12.4 E assigns specific actors and sources to each task:

| Task | What the guidance says |
|---|---|
| Performance metrics | The bank establishes acceptable performance metrics that the business line or relationship management determines to be indicative of acceptable performance levels. |
| Oversight staff | Personnel with oversight and management responsibilities should have the appropriate level of expertise and stature. |
| Risk-focused intensity | Higher-risk providers may require more frequent assessment and monitoring and a designated point of contact; for lower-risk providers, monitoring can be lessened. |
| Internal controls | For significant relationships, assess the provider’s control environment, including available audits or reports such as the AICPA Service Organization Control 2 report. If the provider delivers IT services, the bank can request the FFIEC Technology Service Provider examination report from its primary federal regulator. |

The FFIEC TSP report is a supervisory examination report, so it comes from the bank’s own primary federal regulator, not from the provider or its auditors.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider is significant and delivers IT services, so both internal-controls sources apply: the SOC 2 report where available, and the FFIEC TSP examination report requested from the bank’s primary federal regulator. Option C states both correctly. The other options misplace an actor or invert the risk-focused principle.

**Fragile fact.** FFIEC TSP examination report: requested by the bank from its primary federal regulator. Performance metrics: set by the bank’s business line or relationship management.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection E “Oversight and Monitoring of Service Providers” (“Internal controls”). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser mentions the SOC 2 and FFIEC TSP reports under the right-to-audit contract provision (LO 53.c), describing their receipt “relating to the service provider at stipulated intervals” without naming the regulator as the source of the TSP report. GARP places them in ongoing oversight and names the primary federal regulator; GARP is used. This looks like Schweser condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q15 of 17.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It names the provider’s external auditor as the source of the FFIEC TSP report. The guidance names the bank’s primary federal regulator. It would be correct if it referred to the SOC 2 report, which is an auditor’s report on the service organisation’s controls.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It lets the provider set its own performance metrics. The guidance assigns this to the bank’s business line or relationship management. It would be correct only if it said the provider’s input may inform metrics that the bank then determines.

c.reason: GARP 12.4 E: assessments should include reviewing available audits or reports such as the AICPA SOC 2 report, and if the provider delivers IT services the bank can request the FFIEC TSP examination report from its primary federal regulator.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It applies equal monitoring frequency to all providers. Oversight is risk-focused: higher-risk providers get more frequent monitoring, and for lower-risk providers monitoring can be lessened. It would be correct only if both providers had the same risk profile.

questions.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 a Q16
questions.question: The head of asset-liability management at the U.S. operations of a Japanese banking organisation proposes outsourcing interest rate risk modelling, and validation of the resulting models, to a consultancy for a fee of JPY 180 million a year. Which approach is most consistent with the guidance on outsourcing risk management activities?

options.text: Outsource, but require evidence on product components, design and intended use, and ensure any validation service is consistent with existing model risk management guidance.
Do not outsource, because interest rate risk and model risk management are core risk activities that the guidance reserves for the bank’s own staff.
Outsource, and waive the request for developmental evidence on the models if the consultancy is a regulated entity with proprietary model designs.
Outsource, and treat responsibility for the models’ fit to the bank’s exposures as transferred to the consultancy under the terms of the contract.

questions.solution:
Head of ALM at U.S. operations of a Japanese bank deciding how to outsource interest rate risk modelling and validation.

**Concept and theory**

A tempting intuition is that risk management is too central to outsource. The guidance does not take that view. GARP 12.4 G states that banks may outsource various risk management activities, such as aspects of interest rate risk and model risk management, but sets two conditions:

1. **Developmental evidence.** The bank should require the provider to supply information demonstrating developmental evidence that explains the product’s components, design and intended use, so the bank can determine whether the products or services are appropriate for its exposures and risks.
2. **Consistency with model risk guidance.** The bank should have standards and processes to ensure that providers offering model risk management services, such as validation, do so consistently with existing model risk management guidance (SR 11-7).

Behind both conditions is the 12.3 principle: outsourcing does not relieve the bank’s board and senior management of responsibility, so the bank must be able to judge whether a vendor model fits its own exposures.

**Applying it to this question**

The head of ALM proposes outsourcing both interest rate risk modelling and model validation. The fee of JPY 180 million is irrelevant to the answer. The guidance permits the outsourcing, provided the bank obtains developmental evidence on components, design and intended use and ensures the validation service is consistent with existing model risk management guidance. Option A states exactly this.

**Fragile fact.** Risk management activities may be outsourced; the bank still demands developmental evidence (components, design, intended use) and keeps validation consistent with model risk management guidance.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, subsection G “Additional Risk Considerations” (“Risk management activities”). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not cover this subsection; content is from GARP only, within the LO’s “elements of an effective program”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q16 of 17.

a.reason: It combines the permission (“may outsource”) with both conditions set out in GARP 12.4 G.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It forbids what the guidance permits. GARP 12.4 G expressly names aspects of interest rate risk and model risk management as activities banks may outsource. It would be correct only under a rule reserving these activities to in-house staff, which the guidance does not contain.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It waives developmental evidence for regulated or proprietary providers. The guidance sets no such exemption; the evidence is needed for the bank to judge appropriateness for its exposures. It would be correct only if the bank already held equivalent developmental evidence from another source.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves responsibility for fit to the bank’s exposures onto the consultancy. The bank must itself determine appropriateness, and 12.3 states that outsourcing does not relieve the bank of responsibility. It would be correct if it said the consultancy is contractually responsible for delivering the agreed service, which is a different matter.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 a Q17
questions.question:
A CRO at a U.S. bank is reviewing a proposal to outsource specialised trade-finance document processing to a provider in Brazil.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Eligible providers worldwide | Two, both located in São Paulo |
| Host country conditions | Recent political unrest and new currency controls |
| Proposed contract value | BRL 48 million over four years |
| Provider service level achieved last year | 99.2% |

A committee member argues that the fact that both eligible providers are located in São Paulo is an example of country risk. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: The committee member is right, because geographic clustering of providers within a single foreign city is the defining feature of country risk.
The clustering of a limited number of providers in one location is concentration risk, while the conditions in Brazil give rise to country risk.
Both facts are concentration risk, because country risk arises only when a foreign provider fails to comply with the laws of its own country.
Both facts are operational risk, because the guidance’s definition of operational risk covers losses from external events affecting a provider.

questions.solution:
CRO assessing whether two providers clustered in São Paulo represent country risk.

**Concept and theory**

Concentration risk and country risk both involve geography, which is why they are confused. The guidance separates them by mechanism:

| Risk | Trigger in GARP 12.2 | Question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| Concentration | services provided by a limited number of providers or concentrated in limited geographic locations | How many alternatives do we have, and are they all in the same place? |
| Country | a foreign-based provider exposes the bank to economic, social and political conditions and events in its country | What could happen in that country that disrupts the provider? |
| Operational | inadequate or failed processes or systems, external events, human error at the provider | Did the provider’s processes, systems or people fail? |

Concentration is about the structure of supply (few providers, clustered locations), and it can arise entirely within one’s own country. Country risk is about the host-country environment and requires a foreign-based provider. Operational risk’s “external events” does not absorb either: the guidance names country and concentration as distinct risks precisely so that these channels are assessed separately.

**Applying it to this question**

Fact 1: only two eligible providers exist, and both are in São Paulo. That is a limited number of providers concentrated in a limited geographic location: concentration risk. Fact 2: recent political unrest and new currency controls in Brazil are political and economic conditions in the foreign provider’s country: country risk. The contract value (BRL 48 million) and the 99.2% service level are irrelevant to the classification. The committee member has attached the country label to a concentration fact.

**Fragile fact.** Few providers or clustered locations is concentration risk, even when the cluster is abroad; host-country economic, social or political conditions are country risk.

**Reference**

LO 53.a (verbatim): Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.2 “Risks from the Use of Service Providers”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes concentration risk as having “very few service providers to choose from or that the service providers are clustered in only a few geographic areas” and country risk as “economic and political risks” in a foreign country; GARP adds “social” conditions and events. Substance consistent; GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 a, where it is Q17 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It makes geographic clustering the defining feature of country risk. Clustering in limited geographic locations is part of the concentration definition; country risk is about host-country conditions and events. It would be correct if the stem said the concern was political or economic instability in the city where the providers are based.

b.reason: It matches both GARP 12.2 definitions: concentration risk for a limited number of providers in limited geographic locations, and country risk for economic, social and political conditions in the provider’s country.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It redefines country risk as the provider’s failure to comply with its own country’s laws, which borrows the compliance-risk trigger, and so files the Brazilian conditions under concentration. It would be correct only if the guidance defined country risk by legal noncompliance.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error (overextension).** It stretches “external events” in the operational risk definition to swallow both facts. The guidance lists concentration and country risk separately, and the clustering fact is a supply-structure feature, not an event. It would be correct only if the stem described a specific disruptive event, such as a power failure at the provider, without reference to supply structure or country conditions.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q1
questions.question:
The head of third-party risk at a Singapore bank is drafting an internal standard that sets how deep and how formal the due diligence on each prospective service provider must be. Her draft lists the following factors:

I. The scope, complexity and importance of the planned outsourcing arrangement.

II. The bank’s familiarity with the prospective service providers.

III. The reputation and industry standing of the service provider.

IV. The total number of material business activities the bank outsources across all of its service providers.

Which of the factors does the Federal Reserve guidance identify as determining the depth and formality of the due diligence performed on a prospective service provider?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Head of third-party risk at a Singapore bank listing the factors that set the depth and formality of due diligence.

**Concept and theory**

Due diligence is the second core element of a service provider risk management program. It is the evaluation an institution performs on a prospective provider before engaging it, to establish whether that provider can deliver the service safely, soundly and in compliance with the law. The guidance is deliberately proportional: it does not prescribe one fixed procedure for every provider. Instead it says the depth and formality of due diligence “will vary” with three named drivers.

| Driver named in GARP | Why it changes the effort required |
|---|---|
| Scope, complexity and importance of the planned arrangement | A critical, complex arrangement can hurt the institution more if the provider fails, so it warrants a deeper, more formal review. |
| Institution’s familiarity with prospective providers | Existing knowledge of a provider reduces the information gap that due diligence is meant to close. |
| Reputation and industry standing of the provider | A long-established, reputable provider carries less selection uncertainty than an unknown one. |

Be careful to keep this list separate from a similar list one level up. GARP also says that the depth and formality of the whole risk management program depends on the criticality, complexity and number of material business activities outsourced (a community bank with a few critical activities placed with highly reputable providers may run a simpler program; an institution with hundreds or thousands of providers needs many more elements). That is a statement about the program (LO 53.a), not about the due diligence on one prospective provider.

**Applying it to this question**

The standard is about due diligence on each prospective provider, so the test is whether each factor appears in GARP’s due diligence sentence. Statement I (scope, complexity and importance of the planned arrangement): named. Statement II (familiarity with prospective providers): named.

Statement III (reputation and industry standing of the provider): named. Statement IV (total number of material activities outsourced across all providers): this is the driver of the depth of the overall program, not of the due diligence on a given provider. So I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** The number of outsourced activities drives the depth of the program (LO 53.a); familiarity and reputation and industry standing drive the depth of due diligence on one provider.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, opening paragraph; contrast with Section 12.4 opening paragraphs on program depth. GARP vs Schweser: the Schweser summary of this LO does not list the three depth and formality drivers; the content here is from GARP. No conflict in substance, only an omission in the condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops a stated driver: it omits the provider’s reputation and industry standing (III). It would be correct only if the stem asked which factors relate to the institution and the arrangement, as opposed to the provider.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops the familiarity driver (II). It would be correct only if the question asked which factors are characteristics of the arrangement or the provider rather than of the institution’s own knowledge.

c.reason: GARP 12.4 B states that the depth and formality of the due diligence “will vary depending on the scope, complexity, and importance of the planned outsourcing arrangement, the financial institution’s familiarity with prospective service providers, and the reputation and industry standing of the service provider.” These are exactly statements I, II and III.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Adds statement IV, which belongs to the sibling concept: the depth and formality of the overall service provider risk management program depend on the criticality, complexity and number of material business activities outsourced. D would be correct if the stem asked what determines the depth and formality of the program as a whole (together with criticality and complexity).

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing the file for a recently outsourced loan servicing activity. The file records the following sequence of steps.

| Step | Date (2026) |
|---|---|
| Risk assessment approves outsourcing the activity | 3 February |
| Contract signed and provider engaged (annual fee EUR 4.5 million) | 10 March |
| References checked and financial statements reviewed, filed as “due diligence” | 2 to 20 May |
| Service Organization Control 2 report requested from the provider | 15 June |

Which of the following conclusions should the auditor reach?

options.text: The file is compliant, because due diligence and ongoing monitoring form a single element, so the order of the steps is immaterial.
The file is deficient, because due diligence should be performed before engaging the provider; reviews made after signing are monitoring.
The file is deficient, because due diligence on prospective providers should precede the risk assessment of whether to outsource at all.
The file is compliant, provided the Service Organization Control 2 report is received within the first year of the engagement.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a German bank reviewing a file in which “due diligence” was done after the contract was signed.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance arranges the service provider risk management program as a logical sequence. First comes the risk assessment: is outsourcing the activity consistent with strategy, what are its benefits, risks and costs, are qualified providers available, and can the institution oversee the relationship? Only once outsourcing is judged appropriate does the institution select a provider, and selection is where due diligence sits. GARP is explicit on timing: the institution “should conduct an evaluation of and perform the necessary due diligence for a prospective service provider prior to engaging the service provider.” Contract negotiation, incentive compensation review, and ongoing oversight and monitoring follow.

| Element | Question it answers | When |
|---|---|---|
| Risk assessment | Should we outsource this activity at all? | Before any provider is chosen |
| Due diligence | Is this prospective provider fit to perform it? | Before engaging the provider |
| Oversight and monitoring | Is the engaged provider still performing? | Throughout the relationship |

Why does timing matter? The purpose of due diligence is to inform the selection decision. A review carried out after the contract is signed cannot affect which provider was selected; it can only detect problems with a provider the institution is already committed to. Reviewing financial statements and requesting a Service Organization Control 2 report are legitimate activities after engagement, but GARP places them under oversight and monitoring (financial condition monitoring; internal controls assessment), not under due diligence.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the dates. The risk assessment (3 February) correctly comes first. The contract is signed on 10 March. The reference checks and financial statement review labelled “due diligence” occur from 2 to 20 May, after engagement. The deciding fact is the GARP requirement that due diligence be performed before engaging the provider. The EUR 4.5 million fee is irrelevant to the conclusion.

**Fragile fact.** Order: risk assessment, then due diligence before engagement, then contract, then monitoring. A financial statement review after signing is monitoring, not due diligence.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, opening paragraph; contrast with subsection A. Risk Assessments and subsection E. Oversight and Monitoring of Service Providers (Financial condition; Internal controls). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes due diligence “in selecting service providers” but does not state the “prior to engaging” wording; the timing point is from GARP. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Merges due diligence with its sibling element, oversight and monitoring. GARP lists them as separate core elements (B and E) with different timing and purpose. The option would be correct only for a monitoring activity, for example if the question asked whether a post-signing review of financial statements is an acceptable part of ongoing oversight.

b.reason: Due diligence is required “prior to engaging the service provider” (GARP 12.4 B). Reviews performed after signing may be useful, but they are monitoring of an engaged provider, so the file has no pre-engagement due diligence and is deficient.

c.reason: **Polarity flip (sequence reversed).** Reverses the order of the first two elements. The risk assessment of whether to outsource comes first, and due diligence on prospective providers follows. The option would be right if the sentence were reversed: the risk assessment should precede due diligence.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Invents a condition under which the timing failure is cured. Receiving a SOC 2 report is part of assessing an engaged provider’s control environment during monitoring; it cannot substitute for due diligence that was never performed before engagement. The option would be right only if the question asked about a monitoring requirement for a significant provider relationship.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q3
questions.question: A risk committee member at a Japanese regional bank asks the head of procurement who should take part in the due diligence on a prospective provider of core banking software, a JPY 900 million arrangement. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Every department of the bank should sign off on each due diligence review, whatever the scope and importance of the planned arrangement.
The bank’s technical experts should contribute to the review but be kept out of approval, so that approval stays independent of the review.
Once due diligence confirms the provider’s legal compliance, responsibility for the compliance of the outsourced service passes to the provider.
The bank’s technical experts and key stakeholders should be engaged in the review and approval process, as needed, throughout due diligence.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at a Japanese regional bank asking who should take part in due diligence on a core banking software provider.

**Concept and theory**

Due diligence is the institution’s own evaluation, and GARP names who inside the institution should be involved: “Throughout the due diligence process, financial institution technical experts and key stakeholders should be engaged in the review and approval process as needed.” Three features of that sentence carry weight.

- Who: the institution’s own technical experts (for example IT, information security, legal) and key stakeholders (for example the business line that will depend on the service).
- Which stages: both the review and the approval; experts are not merely consulted and then excluded.
- How much: “as needed”, which is consistent with the proportional design of due diligence.

Separately, the guidance never transfers accountability. The use of service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of their responsibility to ensure outsourced activities are safe, sound and compliant, and under operations and internal controls GARP states that institutions are responsible for ensuring that services provided by service providers comply with applicable laws and regulations.

**Applying it to this question**

The question is about participation in due diligence on a critical arrangement. The deciding fact is GARP’s sentence on engaging technical experts and key stakeholders in review and approval, as needed. The JPY 900 million size points to an important arrangement but does not change who should be engaged.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and stage: the institution’s technical experts and key stakeholders, in review and approval, as needed. Accountability never passes to the provider.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, opening paragraph; subsection B.3 Operations and Internal Controls (first sentence); Section 12.3 Board of Directors and Senior Management Responsibilities. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the institution should “involve any relevant technical specialists and/or important stakeholders” and that it “must ensure that the service provider follows all relevant laws and regulations”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; GARP adds that engagement covers the approval process.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Turns “as needed” into a requirement that every department signs off on every review, regardless of scope and importance. That contradicts both the “as needed” wording and the proportional depth of due diligence. It would be closer to correct only if the stem described a policy for engaging the relevant experts in proportion to the arrangement.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Narrows the stated scope from “review and approval” to review only. GARP engages experts in both stages. The option would be right only if the guidance confined experts to the review stage, which it does not.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Moves the compliance responsibility from the institution to the provider. GARP says the institution is responsible for ensuring that outsourced services comply with laws and regulations, and outsourcing does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility. It would be correct only if the actor were reversed: responsibility stays with the institution.

d.reason: It restates GARP 12.4 B: technical experts and key stakeholders of the institution are engaged in the review and approval process, as needed, throughout due diligence.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q4
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a US bank holding company has sorted items from a due diligence checklist into the three review areas set out in the Federal Reserve guidance. Her assignments are shown below.

| Checklist item | Review area assigned |
|---|---|
| Provider’s commitment of staff resources for the contract’s duration | Operations and internal controls |
| Verification of required licences and certifications | Business background, reputation and strategy |
| Maintenance and retention of records | Operations and internal controls |
| Adequacy of the provider’s insurance coverage | Financial performance and condition |

Which of the following assignments is NOT consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Commitment of staff resources for the contract’s duration, assigned to operations and internal controls.
Verification of required licences and certifications, assigned to business background, reputation and strategy.
Maintenance and retention of records, assigned to operations and internal controls.
Adequacy of the provider’s insurance coverage, assigned to financial performance and condition.

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst at a US bank holding company sorting checklist items into the three due diligence areas.

**Concept and theory**

GARP organises due diligence into three review areas. Each area answers a distinct question about the prospective provider.

| Area | Question it answers | Representative items in GARP |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Business background, reputation and strategy | Who is this provider and is its model durable? | Industry status, corporate history, qualifications; principals; employee background check program; experience; business model; references; licences and certifications; pending legal or regulatory issues |
| 2. Financial performance and condition | Can it afford to keep delivering for the contract term? | Financial statements and annual report; sustainability (time in business, market share growth); impact of the relationship on the provider; commitment of financial and staff resources; insurance; review of subcontractors’ finances; other current issues |
| 3. Operations and internal controls | Will it run the activity safely and lawfully? | Internal controls; facilities; training; security of systems; privacy; records; business resumption; systems development; service support; employee background checks; adherence to laws |

The commitment item sits in the financial area because GARP frames it as the provider’s commitment “(both in terms of financial and staff resources) to provide the contracted services to the financial institution for the duration of the contract.” The concern is capacity to sustain the service over the full term, which is a financial-viability question even when the resource in question is people.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each row against GARP. Commitment of staff resources for the contract’s duration is listed under financial performance and condition, so assigning it to operations and internal controls is the error. Licences and certifications are verified under business background. Maintenance and retention of records is an operations and internal controls item. Adequacy of insurance coverage is a financial performance and condition item. Exactly one row is misassigned.

**Fragile fact.** “Staff” does not mean “operations”: the provider’s commitment of financial and staff resources for the contract term is a financial performance and condition item.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, items 1 to 3. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser places the provider’s ability to provide the service for the length of the contract “in terms of capital and personnel” under financial performance and condition, consistent with GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 12.4 B.2 lists “the service provider’s commitment (both in terms of financial and staff resources) to provide the contracted services . . . for the duration of the contract” under financial performance and condition, not under operations and internal controls.

b.reason: **Sibling swap trap.** The assignment is correct: GARP 12.4 B.1 says institutions should “verify any required licenses and certifications” as part of business background, reputation and strategy. B would be the answer only if licence verification had been placed under, say, financial performance and condition.

c.reason: **Sibling swap trap.** The assignment is correct: “maintenance and retention of records” is in the GARP list for operations and internal controls. C would be the answer only if record retention had been put in a different area.

d.reason: **Sibling swap trap.** The assignment is correct: “the adequacy of the service provider’s insurance coverage” is listed under financial performance and condition. Readers who recall insurance as a contract provision (LO 53.c) may think it is misplaced, but it appears in both places. D would be the answer only if insurance had been assigned to operations and internal controls.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q5
questions.question: A risk consultant is presenting the Federal Reserve due diligence guidance to newly hired analysts at a bank holding company. An analyst asks where checks on the provider’s personnel appear in the three review areas. Which of the following answers best describes the guidance?

options.text: Background checks sit only under financial performance and condition, as part of the provider’s commitment of staff resources to the contract.
Under business background, the bank ensures the provider has an appropriate employee background check program; the operations review may also cover employee background checks.
Under business background, the bank itself carries out background checks on every provider employee who will be assigned to its account.
Background checks sit only under operations and internal controls; the business background area reviews only the background of the provider’s principals.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant explaining to new analysts where checks on the provider’s personnel appear in the three due diligence areas.

**Concept and theory**

Personnel risk at a provider is a real source of operational loss: an employee with a history of fraud who gains access to customer data or payment systems can cause damage no control framework fully offsets. The guidance therefore touches personnel checks twice, from two different angles.

| Area | GARP wording | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| Business background, reputation and strategy | “ensure that the service provider has an appropriate background check program for its employees”; also review “the background and reputation of the service provider and its principals” | Does the provider have a program? Who are its principals? |
| Operations and internal controls | “Employee background checks” among the items that may need review | Are checks actually being performed in operating the activity? |

The first is a check on the provider’s policies and its leadership; the second is a check on operating practice. Schweser expresses the same split: under business background the provider “should provide evidence of an adequate background check system for its new employees”, and under operations and internal controls the institution seeks “confirmation that employee background checks are being performed.”

Note the actor throughout: the institution ensures the provider has a program and confirms checks are performed; it does not run the background checks on the provider’s staff itself.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst’s question is “where” personnel checks appear. The deciding fact is that GARP places a background check program requirement under business background and lists employee background checks under operations and internal controls. Any answer that confines the topic to one area, moves it to the financial area, or makes the institution the party that performs the checks is wrong.

**Fragile fact.** Two placements: background check program under business background (with principals reviewed too); employee background checks under operations and internal controls. The provider performs the checks.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, items 1. Business Background, Reputation, and Strategy and 3. Operations and Internal Controls. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Moves background checks into the financial area by linking them to the provider’s commitment of staff resources. Commitment of staff resources concerns capacity to deliver for the contract term, not the vetting of staff. A would be correct only if the question asked where the provider’s staff capacity for the contract term is reviewed.

b.reason: It matches both GARP placements: under 12.4 B.1 the institution should “ensure that the service provider has an appropriate background check program for its employees”, and 12.4 B.3 includes “Employee background checks” among the operations and internal controls items that may need review.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Right action, wrong actor. The guidance requires the institution to ensure the provider has a program, and to confirm checks are performed; the provider screens its own employees. C would be correct only if the actor were the provider, checking its own staff.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops the business-background placement of the employee program and narrows business background to principals alone. GARP’s business background area covers both the principals and the employee background check program. D would be correct only if the guidance contained no employee-program requirement under business background.

questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk

questions.question: A treasurer at an Australian bank is preparing a report to the outsourcing committee on the business background, reputation and strategy of a prospective cash management provider. Which of the following statements should the treasurer include in the report?

options.text: Reference checks are used mainly to establish the provider’s capital strength and liquidity before the contract is signed.
The search for pending litigation, regulatory actions or complaints can be confined to the provider entity, leaving its principals aside.
The provider’s experience with the proposed service is evaluated mainly to benchmark the fee the bank will be charged for it.
The resiliency and adaptability of the provider’s business model are factors in assessing its future viability to perform the services.

questions.solution:
Treasurer at an Australian bank preparing a report on the business background, reputation and strategy of a cash management provider.

**Concept and theory**

The business background, reputation and strategy review answers the question “who is this provider, and will its business still be able to serve us in the future?” GARP builds the review from the following components.

| Component | What is reviewed and why |
|---|---|
| Industry status and history | Status in the industry, corporate history and qualifications. |
| People | Background and reputation of the provider and its principals; an appropriate employee background check program. |
| Experience | Experience in providing the proposed service, “in order to assess its qualifications and competencies to perform the service”. |
| Business model | Business strategy and mission, service philosophy, quality initiatives and organisational policies. |
| Future viability | “The resiliency and adaptability of the service provider’s business model as factors in assessing the future viability of the provider to perform services.” |
| References | Checked “to ascertain its performance record”. |
| Licences | Verify any required licences and certifications. |
| Legal and compliance issues | Pending litigation, regulatory actions or complaints associated with the provider and its principals. |

The future-viability point is distinctive. The institution is not only asking whether the provider is competent today, but whether its business model can absorb shocks (resiliency) and change with markets and technology (adaptability), so that it remains able to perform over the life of the relationship.

**Applying it to this question**

The treasurer needs a statement that correctly describes a business background component. Each option ties a component to a purpose or scope. The deciding fact is GARP’s sentence linking the resiliency and adaptability of the business model to the future viability of the provider.

**Fragile fact.** Resiliency and adaptability of the business model are viability factors under business background, not under financial condition; references establish the performance record.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, item 1. Business Background, Reputation, and Strategy. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser phrases the viability point as evaluating “the flexibility and feasibility of the service provider’s business model” to judge the likelihood of serving the institution “for the long term”. This is a wording difference in a condensed source, not a substantive conflict; GARP’s “resiliency and adaptability” wording is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Gives reference checks the purpose of a different area. References are checked “to ascertain its performance record”; capital strength and liquidity are assessed from the provider’s most recent financial statements and annual report under financial performance and condition. A would be correct if it said the financial statements are reviewed to establish capital strength and liquidity.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops a stated object: the verification of pending legal or regulatory compliance issues covers the prospective provider “and its principals”. B would be correct only if the guidance limited the search to the legal entity, which it does not.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Assigns the experience review a pricing purpose that belongs to contract terms (cost and compensation, LO 53.c). GARP says the experience review assesses the provider’s “qualifications and competencies to perform the service”. C would be correct if it said the experience review assesses qualifications and competencies.

d.reason: GARP 12.4 B.1: “Financial institutions should also consider the resiliency and adaptability of the service provider’s business model as factors in assessing the future viability of the provider to perform services.”

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is reviewing a colleague’s notes on the business background, reputation and strategy review of a prospective payroll provider. The notes contain these statements:

I. The review should cover the provider’s status in the industry, its corporate history and its qualifications.

II. The bank should verify whether there are pending legal or regulatory compliance issues associated with the provider and its principals.

III. Verification of required licences and certifications may be omitted where the provider’s references report a strong performance record.

IV. The provider’s service philosophy, quality initiatives and organisational policies are evaluated as part of its business model.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank auditing four statements about the business background review of a payroll provider.

**Concept and theory**

The business background, reputation and strategy review (see the component table in Solution

6) combines several independent checks. The important design feature is that the checks are cumulative: each addresses a different failure mode, so a strong result on one does not excuse another. References tell the institution how the provider has performed for others. Licence and certification verification tells it whether the provider is legally permitted and qualified to perform the service at all. A provider can have excellent references and still be unlicensed for the activity, or have a licence under threat because of a pending regulatory action. GARP therefore lists the checks side by side: “Financial institutions should check the service provider’s references to ascertain its performance record, and verify any required licenses and certifications.”

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against GARP 12.4 B.1.

| Statement | Test against GARP | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| I | “review a prospective service provider’s status in the industry and corporate history and qualifications” | True |
| II | “verify whether there are any pending legal or regulatory compliance issues . . . associated with the prospective service provider and its principals” | True |
| III | References and licence verification are both required; a good performance record does not waive the licence check | False |
| IV | The business model “including its business strategy and mission, service philosophy, quality initiatives, and organizational policies” is evaluated | True |

So I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** References and licence verification are both required; neither substitutes for the other. Legal and regulatory issues are checked for the provider and its principals.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, item 1. Business Background, Reputation, and Strategy. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser asks for a search for “any past or present legal and compliance problems”; GARP specifies “pending” issues such as litigation, regulatory actions or complaints. The statement tested uses GARP’s wording, which Schweser’s broader phrase also covers. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: Statements I, II and IV each restate a GARP 12.4 B.1 requirement. Statement III adds a waiver that GARP does not contain.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Omits statement IV, which is true: service philosophy, quality initiatives and organisational policies are explicitly part of the business model evaluation. B would be correct only if IV described something outside the guidance.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap (accepts III).** Accepts statement III, which treats favourable references as a complete substitute for licence verification, and drops statement I. GARP requires both reference checks and licence verification. C would be correct only if the guidance made licence verification conditional on weak references and statement I were false.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap (accepts III).** Treats all four statements as true, including the invented waiver in III. D would be correct only if statement III read “Verification of required licences and certifications is required in addition to reference checks.”

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a UK bank is reviewing the financial performance and condition of a prospective provider of mortgage document processing. She has gathered the following data.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Provider annual revenue (GBP million) | 48.0 |
| Proposed annual contract value (GBP million) | 9.6 |
| Provider years in business | 3.0 |
| Provider insurance cover (GBP million) | 5.0 |
| Bank total assets (GBP million) | 12 000.0 |

Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the guidance on the financial review of a prospective service provider?

options.text: The bank’s total assets of GBP 12.0 billion are a key input, since the review assesses the impact of the provider on the bank’s own financial condition.
The three-year operating history can be set aside, since the provider’s sustainability is judged only by its growth of market share for the service.
The contract would be 20% of the provider’s revenue, which matters because the review considers the impact of the bank’s relationship on the provider’s finances.
The GBP 5.0 million insurance cover can be set aside at this stage, since insurance is addressed only through the insurance provision of the contract.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses the direction of the impact item, from the institution’s relationship acting on the provider to the provider acting on the institution’s own financial condition. That turns an irrelevant input (bank total assets) into a “key” one. A would be correct only if the guidance asked for the impact of the provider on the institution’s financial condition, which it does not.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops one of the two stated sustainability factors. GARP lists “the length of time that the service provider has been in business and the service provider’s growth of market share for a given service.” A three-year history is a directly relevant input. B would be correct only if market share growth were the sole sustainability factor.

c.reason: The 20% share is correctly computed and correctly linked to GARP 12.4 B.2: the review includes “the potential impact of the financial institution’s business relationship on the service provider’s financial condition.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Confuses the due diligence item with its sibling contract provision. Insurance appears in both places: due diligence assesses “the adequacy of the service provider’s insurance coverage”, and the contract (LO 53.c) requires adequate insurance, proof of it, and notice of material changes. D would be correct only if insurance appeared in the contract provisions alone.

questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.

questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q9
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Chinese bank is planning the financial review of a prospective payments processor for a CNY 60 million arrangement. The processor is a subsidiary within a larger group and relies on two subcontractors for parts of the service. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Review the contracting entity alone, since its affiliates and subcontractors are addressed only through the contract’s subcontracting provision.
Review the processor and its affiliates, and rely on the subcontractors’ own review of the processor’s financial condition.
Review the processor’s affiliates only if its insurance coverage proves inadequate, and its subcontractors only after the contract is signed.
Review the processor and its closely-related affiliates, and assess the adequacy of the processor’s review of its subcontractors’ financial condition.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a Chinese bank planning the financial review of a group-owned payments processor that uses subcontractors.

**Concept and theory**

A provider’s financial strength rarely stops at its own legal entity. Two extensions matter.

- Affiliates. A subsidiary may depend on its group for funding, shared services or guarantees, and group distress can pass down to it. GARP therefore opens the financial review with: “Financial institutions should review the financial condition of the service provider and its closely-related affiliates.”
- Subcontractors. If parts of the service are subcontracted, a subcontractor’s failure can interrupt the service just as surely as the provider’s own failure. GARP’s response is layered: the institution reviews “the adequacy of the service provider’s review of the financial condition of any subcontractors.” In other words, the provider is expected to vet its subcontractors, and the institution evaluates whether that vetting is adequate.

The layered design reflects the structure of accountability elsewhere in the guidance: in the contract, the primary provider has overall accountability for all services that it and its subcontractors provide, and agreements should include the provider’s process for assessing the subcontractor’s financial condition.

**Applying it to this question**

The processor is (i) a subsidiary within a group and (ii) reliant on two subcontractors. Both features trigger an extension of the financial review. The deciding facts are GARP’s two phrases “and its closely-related affiliates” and “the adequacy of the service provider’s review of the financial condition of any subcontractors”. The CNY 60 million size does not change the approach.

**Fragile fact.** Actor chain: the provider reviews its subcontractors’ finances; the institution assesses the adequacy of that review, and reviews the provider together with its closely-related affiliates.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, item 2. Financial Performance and Condition; contrast with subsection C, Subcontracting provision. GARP vs Schweser: this is a conflict. Schweser says “financial information of any subcontractors should be obtained and analyzed”, implying the institution analyses subcontractors directly, and it omits affiliates. GARP says the institution reviews the adequacy of the provider’s own review of subcontractors, and includes closely-related affiliates. Resolved from GARP; it looks like compression in the condensed source rather than a version difference. No option in this question relies on the Schweser wording.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Narrows the review to the contracting entity and pushes affiliates and subcontractors entirely into the contract (the subcontracting provision of LO 53.c). GARP requires affiliates and the provider’s subcontractor review to be considered at due diligence. A would be correct only if the processor were a stand-alone entity with no subcontractors.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Reverses who reviews whom. GARP has the provider review its subcontractors’ financial condition, and the institution assess the adequacy of that review; subcontractors do not review the processor on the bank’s behalf. B would be correct if the actors were swapped: the processor reviews the subcontractors.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Attaches invented conditions and timing. Review of affiliates is not contingent on inadequate insurance, and the subcontractor point is part of due diligence before engagement, not an after-signing step. C would be correct only if the guidance made affiliate review conditional on an insurance shortfall.

d.reason: It reproduces both GARP 12.4 B.2 requirements: review the processor and its closely-related affiliates, and assess the adequacy of the processor’s own review of its subcontractors’ financial condition.

questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Swiss bank is validating the due diligence policy for outsourcing. The policy states: “For every outsourced activity, each item in the operations and internal controls checklist must be reviewed in full, whatever the activity.” Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Retain the policy as written, because the guidance requires every operations and internal controls item to be reviewed for every outsourced activity.
Revise the policy, because some or all items may need review depending on the activity, while the bank stays responsible for compliance and safe-and-sound practice.
Revise the policy, because the operations and internal controls review is needed only where the outsourced activity involves information technology services.
Revise the policy, because a provider’s written confirmation that it adheres to laws may replace the review, as compliance responsibility rests with the provider.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Swiss bank validating a policy that requires every operations and internal controls item for every activity.

**Concept and theory**

The operations and internal controls review answers: “will this provider run the activity safely and lawfully?” GARP frames it in three steps.

1. Responsibility. “Financial institutions are responsible for ensuring that services provided by service providers comply with applicable laws and regulations and are consistent with safe-and-sound banking practices.”
2. General test. “Financial institutions should evaluate the adequacy of standards, policies, and procedures.”
3. Tailored item list. “Depending on the characteristics of the outsourced activity, some or all of the following may need to be reviewed”: internal controls; facilities management (such as access requirements or sharing of facilities); training, including compliance training for staff; security of systems (for example, data and equipment); privacy protection of the institution’s confidential information; maintenance and retention of records; business resumption and contingency planning; systems development and maintenance; service support and delivery; employee background checks; and adherence to applicable laws, regulations and supervisory guidance.

The “some or all” wording matches the proportional design of due diligence generally: a facilities-relocation service and a core processing service raise different operational questions, and the review is matched to the activity. What does not vary is the institution’s responsibility.

**Applying it to this question**

The policy demands every item, in full, for every activity. The deciding fact is the conditional in GARP: some or all items, depending on the characteristics of the outsourced activity. An appropriate recommendation must (i) relax the blanket requirement and (ii) keep responsibility with the bank.

**Fragile fact.** The item list is conditional (“some or all . . . depending on the characteristics of the outsourced activity”); the institution’s responsibility for compliance and safe-and-sound practice is not.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, item 3. Operations and Internal Controls; Section 12.1 Purpose (range of outsourced activities). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser gives a shorter list without the “some or all, depending on the characteristics of the outsourced activity” condition and without the safe-and-sound wording; the content tested is from GARP. Not a conflict, an omission in the condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Converts “some or all . . . may need to be reviewed” into “every item for every activity”. The guidance tailors the list to the activity. A would be correct only if the guidance said “all of the following must be reviewed” for every outsourcing.

b.reason: It states the GARP condition (some or all items, depending on the activity) and keeps the responsibility with the institution for compliance and safe-and-sound banking practice, as GARP 12.4 B.3 requires.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Invents a condition that confines the review to IT services. The guidance applies to all outsourced business functions (accounting, internal audit, HR, loan servicing and others) and its item list includes non-IT matters such as facilities management and training. C would be correct only if the guidance applied solely to technology service providers.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Moves compliance responsibility to the provider and lets a self-certification replace the review. GARP states that the institution is responsible for ensuring outsourced services comply with laws and are consistent with safe-and-sound practices, and that it should evaluate the adequacy of standards, policies and procedures. D would be correct only if the actor bearing responsibility were the provider, which the guidance rules out.

questions.question: A senior analyst at a Brazilian bank is drafting the operations and internal controls section of a due diligence report on a prospective provider that would run a customer call centre handling the bank’s confidential information. Which of the following statements is most accurate for inclusion in the report?

options.text: Business resumption and contingency planning lies outside due diligence and is reviewed only once the contract has been signed.
Service support and delivery is assessed under financial performance and condition, since it depends on the provider’s staff resources.
Privacy protection of the bank’s confidential information and the maintenance and retention of records are among the items to review.
Systems development and maintenance need not be reviewed, since the provider rather than the bank owns and runs the call centre systems.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst at a Brazilian bank drafting the operations and internal controls section for an outsourced call centre.

**Concept and theory**

See Solution 10 for the structure of the operations and internal controls review. The point here is content: which items belong to the operations list, and which belong elsewhere. The table sorts the operations items by the risk they address.

| Risk addressed | Operations and internal controls items in GARP |
|---|---|
| Control environment | Internal controls; adherence to applicable laws, regulations and supervisory guidance |
| Physical and people | Facilities management (access requirements, sharing of facilities); training, including compliance training; employee background checks |
| Information | Security of systems (data and equipment); privacy protection of the institution’s confidential information; maintenance and retention of records |
| Continuity and delivery | Business resumption and contingency planning; systems development and maintenance; service support and delivery |

A call centre that handles the bank’s confidential information puts the information row at the centre of the review. Note also that business resumption and contingency planning appears in this list even though business continuity is also a separate program element (F) and a contract provision (LO 53.c): it is reviewed at due diligence and later.

**Applying it to this question**

The activity handles confidential information, so privacy protection of the institution’s confidential information and the maintenance and retention of records are natural, explicitly listed items. The deciding fact is the GARP item list in 12.4 B.3.

**Fragile fact.** Business resumption and contingency planning is reviewed at due diligence (operations and internal controls) and again in the contract and in contingency planning; do not drop it from due diligence.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, item 3. Operations and Internal Controls. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s list refers to “methods of securing confidential information” and “the process involved in maintaining records” and “disaster recovery processes”, consistent with GARP’s items. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error (timing).** Removes business resumption and contingency planning from due diligence and defers it until after signing. GARP lists it among the operations and internal controls items reviewed at due diligence; it is also addressed later in the contract and in contingency planning. A would be correct only if the guidance listed business resumption solely under program element F.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Moves service support and delivery into the financial area by linking it to staff resources. Service support and delivery is an operations and internal controls item; the provider’s commitment of staff resources for the contract term is the financial item. B would be correct if it described the commitment of staff resources rather than service support and delivery.

c.reason: Both “privacy protection of the financial institution’s confidential information” and “maintenance and retention of records” are named in GARP’s operations and internal controls list.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Uses the provider’s ownership of the systems to excuse the bank from reviewing them. The institution remains responsible for the outsourced service, and systems development and maintenance is an explicit review item precisely because the provider runs the systems. D would be correct only if responsibility followed ownership of the systems, which it does not.
