questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 b Q12
questions.question:
A board risk committee member at an Australian bank is reviewing a post-incident report on an outsourced mortgage document processing service.

- Before engagement, the bank reviewed the provider’s audited financial statements, confirmed its insurance cover, assessed its internal controls and IT security, and reviewed its tested business continuity plan.
- The bank did not verify the provider’s licence status and did not check for regulatory actions involving the provider’s two founding directors.
- Six months after go-live, the regulator suspended the provider’s licence following an enforcement action against the directors that had been pending at the time of selection. Services stopped and the bank incurred AUD 3.1 million of remediation costs.

Which of the following best describes the due diligence lesson from this case?

options.text: The business background review should have verified the required licences and checked for pending regulatory issues involving the provider and its principals.
The financial performance and condition review should have assessed the potential impact of the bank’s business relationship on the provider’s financial condition.
The operations and internal controls review should have covered business resumption and contingency planning, so that the stoppage could have been foreseen.
The gap lay in oversight and monitoring, because escalation triggers after go-live would have prevented the bank from selecting this provider.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at an Australian bank reviewing a case where a provider’s licence was suspended after go-live.

**Concept and theory**

The three due diligence areas are designed so that each catches a different kind of provider failure. Diagnosing a case therefore means asking: which area, done properly, would have revealed the fact that later caused the loss?

| Area | Failure it is designed to catch |
|---|---|
| Business background, reputation and strategy | Provider not qualified or not permitted to act (licences, certifications); reputation or integrity problems with the provider or its principals; pending litigation, regulatory actions or complaints; a fragile business model |
| Financial performance and condition | Provider unable to fund delivery for the contract term; excessive dependence on the institution’s business; inadequate insurance; weak subcontractor vetting |
| Operations and internal controls | Weak controls, security, privacy, records, continuity or service delivery in running the activity |

Due diligence is pre-engagement. Oversight and monitoring (program element E), including escalation triggers, operates after engagement; it can detect deterioration but cannot change a selection decision already made on incomplete information.

**Applying it to this question**

List what was and was not done. Done: financial statements, insurance (financial area); internal controls, IT security, business continuity (operations area). Not done: licence verification, and the check for regulatory actions involving the founding directors (business background area). Cause of loss: licence suspension arising from an enforcement action against the directors that was pending at selection. The only area whose omitted checks would have revealed this is business background, reputation and strategy. The AUD 3.1 million remediation cost is the irrelevant input.

**Fragile fact.** Pending regulatory issues and licences belong to business background, reputation and strategy, and the check covers the provider and its principals; a problem pending at selection is a due diligence failure, not a monitoring failure.

**Reference**

LO 53.b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, subsection B. Due Diligence and Selection of Service Providers, items 1 to 3; contrast with subsection E. Oversight and Monitoring of Service Providers (Escalation of oversight activities). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser asks for a search for “any past or present legal and compliance problems” and confirmation of licences and certifications; GARP specifies pending issues associated with the provider and its principals. Consistent in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 12.4 B.1 requires institutions to “verify any required licenses and certifications” and to “verify whether there are any pending legal or regulatory compliance issues (for example, litigation, regulatory actions, or complaints) that are associated with the prospective service provider and its principals.” Both omitted checks sit here, and both would have exposed the pending action.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: true lesson of a different case.** Assessing the impact of the bank’s relationship on the provider’s finances is a genuine GARP financial-review item, but the case reports a licence suspension, not financial distress or dependence. B would be the lesson if the provider had collapsed after losing the bank’s business or become over-reliant on it.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: true lesson of a different case.** Business resumption and contingency planning is a genuine operations item, but the file shows it was reviewed and tested, and no continuity plan can foresee a regulatory licence suspension rooted in the principals’ conduct. C would be the lesson if the stoppage had been caused by an operational disruption the plan failed to cover.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Attributes the gap to oversight and monitoring, the post-engagement element. Escalation triggers operate after go-live and cannot affect a selection already made; the issue was pending at the time of selection, which makes it a due diligence failure. D would be correct if the regulatory issue had first arisen after engagement and the bank had failed to escalate.

questions.question:
The head of vendor management at a U.S. state member bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the contracting stage of the bank’s service provider risk management programme. Her slides contain the following statements:

I. The terms of a service agreement should be set out in a written contract that the bank’s legal counsel has reviewed before the contract is executed.

II. The scope provision should define the rights and responsibilities of each party, including compliance with applicable laws, regulations and regulatory guidance.

III. For a routine activity, the contract terms should follow a standard template that does not depend on the characteristics of the activity or on the provider’s strategy for delivering it.

IV. The scope provision should address the distribution of any required statements or disclosures to the service provider’s own shareholders.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and IV only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Head of vendor management presenting four statements on the contracting stage and the scope provision.

**Concept and theory**

An outsourcing contract is the instrument that turns the institution’s expectations of a service provider into enforceable obligations. The guidance (Federal Reserve SR 13-19) treats “contract provisions and considerations” as one of six core elements of a service provider risk management programme, sitting after risk assessment and due diligence. Its starting points are procedural. First, the institution should understand the service contract and the legal issues of the proposed arrangement, and the terms of service should be defined in written contracts that the institution’s legal counsel has reviewed before execution. Second, the contract is not generic: the characteristics of the business activity being outsourced and the provider’s strategy for providing those services determine the terms of the contract.

The first substantive provision is **scope**: contracts should clearly define the rights and responsibilities of each party. GARP lists the matters the scope provision includes:

| Scope items (GARP) | What they settle |
|---|---|
| Support, maintenance and customer service | What the provider must keep running |
| Contract timeframes | Duration of the obligations |
| Compliance with applicable laws, regulations and regulatory guidance | Legal standard the service must meet |
| Training of financial institution employees | Who trains the institution’s staff |
| The ability to subcontract services | Whether work may be passed on |
| Distribution of required statements or disclosures to the institution’s customers | Who sends customer disclosures |
| Insurance coverage requirements | Coverage the provider must carry |
| Terms governing use of the institution’s property, equipment and staff | Use of the institution’s resources |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the procedural requirement word for word in substance: written contract, legal counsel review, before execution. True. Statement II is the definition of scope plus one of its listed items (compliance with laws, regulations and regulatory guidance). True. Statement III says the terms should not depend on the activity’s characteristics or the provider’s strategy; GARP says exactly the opposite, that these characteristics determine the terms. False. Statement IV keeps the right topic (distribution of required statements or disclosures) but names the wrong recipients: the guidance refers to disclosures to the financial institution’s customers, not the provider’s shareholders. False. Only I and II are correct.

**Fragile fact.** Required disclosures are distributed to the institution’s customers; the contract is reviewed by the institution’s legal counsel before execution; terms are tailored to the activity and the provider’s strategy.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Scope”, together with the opening paragraph of part C. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s scope list omits compliance with laws and the distribution of required customer disclosures, and does not repeat the legal counsel review; GARP is used for content. This looks like condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q1 of 22.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” rejects statement II, which is true: compliance with applicable laws, regulations and regulatory guidance is expressly listed within the scope provision. A reader who believes compliance sits only in due diligence (LO 53.b, operations and internal controls) would drop II. A would be right only if the stem had described scope as covering commercial terms alone.

b.reason: I and II match GARP’s opening paragraph of part C (written contracts reviewed by legal counsel prior to execution) and the scope bullet (rights and responsibilities of each party, including compliance with applicable laws, regulations and regulatory guidance). III and IV each contain a corruption, so “I and II only” is the only accurate combination.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Including IV accepts the swap of recipient. The scope item concerns statements or disclosures owed to the institution’s customers; the provider’s shareholders are not a party whose disclosures the institution’s contract regulates. C would be right if IV read “to the financial institution’s customers”.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Including III accepts a “one template fits all” claim that the guidance contradicts: the characteristics of the activity and the provider’s strategy determine the contract terms. It also omits the true statement I. D would need III to read “the characteristics of the activity and the provider’s strategy determine the terms”.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing the cost and compensation clause of a draft loan servicing agreement. The draft contains the following terms:

| Item | Draft treatment |
|---|---|
| Monthly base fee | USD 45,000, fixed |
| Per-loan boarding charge | USD 12 per loan boarded |
| Non-recurring items and special requests | “To be agreed informally when they arise” |
| Legal, audit and examination fees for the activity | Not addressed |
| Servicer’s long-term credit rating | BBB |

Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove the per-loan boarding charge, since compensation for an outsourced activity should be limited to a fixed fee that does not vary with volume.
Leave the examination fees unaddressed, since fees relating to supervisory examinations fall outside the contract and are settled with the regulator.
Require the servicer to bear all equipment, hardware and software costs, since the guidance assigns these expenses to the service provider by default.
Describe the fees for non-recurring items and special requests, and state which party pays the legal, audit and examination fees related to the activity.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor reviewing the cost and compensation clause of a draft loan servicing agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Fee disputes are a classic source of friction in outsourcing, and unclear fee terms can also hide incentives. The **cost and compensation** provision therefore requires the contract to be complete about money. GARP says contracts should describe:

- the compensation, the variable charges, and any fees to be paid for non-recurring items and special requests;
- which party is responsible for paying any legal, audit and examination fees related to the activity performed by the provider;
- where applicable, which party is responsible for the expense, purchasing and maintenance of any equipment, hardware, software or other item related to the activity;
- and the institution should ensure that any incentives in the contract (for example variable charges such as fees or commissions) do not create incentives to take imprudent risks on its behalf.

Notice the verb throughout: the contract must address or state who pays. The guidance does not itself allocate any cost to a particular party, and it does not forbid variable pricing; it forbids leaving cost items undefined and incentives unreviewed.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the table against the list. The fixed fee and the per-loan charge are compensation and a variable charge, which are permitted. Two rows breach the provision: non-recurring items and special requests are left “to be agreed informally”, and legal, audit and examination fees are not addressed at all. The credit rating is an irrelevant input: it belongs to due diligence on financial condition (LO 53.b), not to the cost clause. The appropriate recommendation must fix both gaps without inventing rules.

**Fragile fact.** The guidance requires the contract to state who pays legal, audit and examination fees and equipment costs; it does not decide who pays, and it permits variable charges subject to an imprudent-risk review.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Cost and compensation”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser mentions equipment purchases, legal fees and audit fees and “special charges”, but omits examination fees and the non-recurring items wording; GARP is used. Consistent in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q2 of 22.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The guidance expects contracts to describe “variable charges” alongside compensation, so variable pricing is allowed. What must be reviewed is whether variable charges create incentives to take imprudent risk, not whether they exist. A would be right only if the stem had shown that the per-loan charge rewarded imprudent risk-taking and asked how to remove that incentive.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The provision names examination fees explicitly: agreements should address which party pays legal, audit and examination fees related to the activity. Excluding them narrows the provision below what GARP requires. B would be right only if the guidance confined the clause to legal and audit fees, which it does not.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** GARP requires the agreement to address the party responsible for equipment, hardware and software expense “where applicable”; it does not assign that cost to the provider by default. The error is turning “state who pays” into “the provider pays”. C would be right if the stem asked which allocation the parties might choose, rather than what the guidance requires.

d.reason: Describing the fees for non-recurring items and special requests, and stating which party pays the legal, audit and examination fees related to the activity, are both explicit requirements of GARP’s cost and compensation bullet, and they repair exactly the two defective rows.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q3
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a savings and loan holding company is drafting a summary of the right to audit provision for a new payments processing agreement. Which of the following statements best describes the provision?

options.text: The agreement may give the institution or its representatives the right to audit the provider and/or to access its audit reports, and should define the types of reports and the frequency of the audits and reports.
The agreement must give the institution an on-site right to audit the provider, since access to the provider’s audit reports cannot substitute for an audit by the institution or its representatives.
The agreement should give the provider a reciprocal right to audit the institution’s processes connected with the service, so that oversight under the contract runs in both directions.
The agreement may give the institution a right to audit the provider, with the types of audit reports and their frequency to be settled after execution as issues come to light.

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst summarising the right to audit provision for a payments processing agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Outsourcing moves an activity out of the reach of the institution’s own internal audit. The **right to** **audit** provision restores visibility. GARP: agreements may provide for the right of the institution or its representatives to audit the service provider and/or to have access to audit reports; agreements should define the types of audit reports the institution will receive and the frequency of the audits and reports. Three features matter:

| Feature | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Strength | Permissive: “may provide”; this is the provision the guidance frames as optional |
| Who audits | The institution or its representatives (for example external auditors) |
| Form | An audit right, access to audit reports, or both (“and/or”) |
| What must be defined | Types of audit reports and frequency of audits and reports |

The right is one-directional: it protects the institution, which remains responsible for the outsourced activity. Later, under oversight (part E), the institution decides when to exercise the right as part of escalation, which is why the reports and frequency need to be fixed in the contract in advance.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks which statement “best describes” the provision, so each option must be checked on four attributes: may or must, who holds the right, audit versus reports, and what is defined at signing. Only one option gets all four right.

**Fragile fact.** Right to audit is the “may” provision, but once included, report types and frequency “should” be defined in the agreement; the right belongs to the institution or its representatives.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Right to audit”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser places the AICPA SOC 2 report and the FFIEC Technology Service Provider examination report inside this provision as examples of reports to be received. GARP mentions those reports under part E (Oversight and Monitoring, internal controls), and says the FFIEC TSP report is requested from the institution’s primary federal regulator. Both agree the right is optional (“could optionally”/“may”). This looks like Schweser condensation, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q3 of 22.

a.reason: It reproduces GARP’s wording: the agreement may provide for the institution or its representatives to audit the provider and/or access audit reports, and should define the types of reports and the frequency of the audits and reports.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It upgrades “may” to “must” and rejects audit reports as a substitute, whereas GARP says “audit the service provider and/or have access to audit reports”. Both moves overstate the provision. B would be right only if the guidance required an on-site audit in every arrangement.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** The right runs from the institution to the provider. Nothing in the guidance gives the provider a right to audit the institution. C would describe the provision only if the institution were the one providing services to the other party.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It keeps the permissive “may” but drops the condition that the agreement should define the types of reports and their frequency, deferring them to after execution. D would be right only if the guidance left report types and frequency to later negotiation.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q4
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a community bank is reviewing the draft service schedule for an outsourced online banking platform. The relevant extract is shown below.

| Service element | Draft wording |
|---|---|
| Platform availability | “High availability will be maintained” |
| Incident response | “Incidents will be addressed promptly” |
| Annual service fee | USD 1.2 million, invoiced quarterly |

Which of the following changes to the availability and incident response wording is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace both items with a right for the bank to audit the provider whenever service quality is in doubt, since audit rights make separate performance standards unnecessary.
Keep the wording, since acceptable performance levels are set by the business line after execution as part of ongoing monitoring rather than in the agreement.
Replace both items with measurable performance standards, for example a stated monthly availability percentage and a maximum time to respond to an incident.
Replace both items with standards that the provider may set and revise at its discretion, provided it informs the bank of each change in its annual report.

questions.solution:
CRO reviewing vague availability and incident wording in an online banking service schedule.

**Concept and theory**

A provider cannot be held to a promise that cannot be measured. The provision on **establishment** **and monitoring of performance standards** says agreements should define measurable performance standards for the services or products being provided. Measurable standards serve three later purposes: they let the institution monitor performance (part E says the institution should establish acceptable performance metrics that the business line or relationship management regards as indicative of acceptable performance); they define when the provider is failing; and they feed the default and termination provision, which lists “failure to meet performance standards” among termination rights. Without numbers, none of these mechanisms works.

**Applying it to this question**

“High availability” and “promptly” are qualitative. The deciding fact is the word measurable. The annual fee of USD 1.2 million is an irrelevant input: it belongs to cost and compensation and does not affect what the performance clause must contain. The fix is to replace the adjectives with quantities, such as an availability percentage per month and a maximum response time.

**Fragile fact.** The key word is measurable; the standards are defined in the agreement and then used by the institution’s business line for monitoring and, if breached, for termination.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Establishment and monitoring of performance standards”; see also part E, Oversight and Monitoring of Service Providers, on performance metrics. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: “specific and measurable performance standards (i.e., metrics)”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q4 of 22.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It substitutes the right to audit for performance standards. These are separate provisions with separate purposes: an audit tests controls and adherence, while performance standards define the service level. GARP requires measurable standards regardless of audit rights. A would be right if the stem asked how the bank could verify the provider’s controls.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It borrows the oversight idea that the business line determines acceptable performance metrics (part E) and uses it to excuse vague contract wording. The contract provision still requires the agreement itself to define measurable standards; monitoring then applies them. B would be right only if the guidance confined performance standards to post-signing monitoring.

c.reason: It converts both items into measurable performance standards, which is exactly what GARP requires agreements to define for the services being provided.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Standards that the provider sets and revises at will are not standards the institution can enforce. The guidance has the agreement define them, and has the institution’s business line judge acceptable performance. D would be right only if the provider were the party protected by the clause.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q5
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a U.S. state member bank is preparing a report on an incident at the provider that processes the bank’s outgoing wire transfers. A provider employee negligently sent customer payments to the wrong beneficiaries, and several customers have now filed claims against the bank. Which of the following provisions, as described, should the bank’s contract have contained to address the bank’s position?

options.text: A customer complaints provision, making the provider liable for any customer claim relating to a complaint that the provider has handled.
An indemnification provision, requiring the bank to indemnify the provider against claims caused by the provider’s negligence.
An indemnification provision, requiring the provider to indemnify the bank against all claims connected with the activity, whatever their cause.
An indemnification provision, requiring the provider to indemnify the bank against claims against the bank resulting from the provider’s negligence.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst reporting on negligent misrouting of wires at a provider and resulting customer claims.

**Concept and theory**

When a provider acts for an institution, the institution’s customers usually pursue the institution, not the provider, because the customer’s contract is with the bank. **Indemnification** reallocates that loss back to the party at fault. GARP: agreements should provide for service provider indemnification of financial institutions for any claims against financial institutions resulting from the service provider’s negligence. Four elements, each a possible trap:

| Element | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Who indemnifies | The service provider |
| Who is protected | The financial institution |
| What is covered | Claims against the institution |
| Trigger | Resulting from the service provider’s negligence |

Indemnification is distinct from limits on liability (which caps what the provider pays) and from insurance (which funds the provider’s ability to pay).

**Applying it to this question**

The facts supply every element: the provider’s employee acted negligently, customers filed claims against the bank, and the bank wants to recover. The correct option must name indemnification, run from provider to bank, and be triggered by the provider’s negligence.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and trigger: the provider indemnifies the institution for claims against the institution caused by the provider’s negligence.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Indemnification”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: hold harmless “in the event of any legal proceedings arising from the service provider’s negligence”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q5 of 22.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The customer complaints provision allocates responsibility for responding to complaints and, if the provider resolves them, requires summary reports on status and resolution. It does not allocate legal liability for claims. A would be right if the stem asked which provision governs who handles and reports customer complaints.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It reverses the direction: the institution indemnifying the provider for the provider’s own negligence would defeat the purpose of the clause. B would describe the provision only if the bank’s negligence had caused claims against the provider.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the negligence trigger and extends cover to all claims “whatever their cause”. The guidance ties indemnification to claims resulting from the provider’s negligence. C would be right only if the guidance required an unconditional indemnity.

d.reason: It states the provision exactly as GARP does: the provider indemnifies the bank against claims against the bank resulting from the provider’s negligence.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q6
questions.question: The treasurer of the U.S. operations of a Canadian banking organisation is reviewing the insurance clause in a draft agreement with a cash logistics provider. Which of the following draft clauses is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: The bank will purchase its own insurance against losses caused by the provider’s failures, and this replaces any requirement for the provider to hold coverage.
The provider will maintain adequate insurance, provide the bank with proof of insurance, and notify the bank when there is a material change in its coverage.
The provider will maintain adequate insurance; since adequacy was verified during due diligence, the provider need not report later changes in its coverage.
The provider will maintain insurance equal to the full contract value, which makes a separate indemnification provision in the agreement unnecessary.

questions.solution:
Treasurer reviewing the insurance clause of a cash logistics agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Insurance appears twice in the outsourcing guidance, at two different stages, and the distinction is a favourite trap. At due diligence (LO 53.b), the institution reviews “the adequacy of the service provider’s insurance coverage” as part of financial performance and condition: a one-off assessment before signing. In the contract, the **insurance** provision creates continuing obligations: service providers should have adequate insurance and provide financial institutions with proof of insurance, and should notify financial institutions when there is a material change in their insurance coverage. The notification duty exists precisely because coverage verified at selection can lapse or shrink during the term. Insurance also appears as a scope item (“insurance coverage requirements”).

**Applying it to this question**

A compliant clause needs three components, all on the provider: (1) adequate insurance, (2) proof of insurance, (3) notification of material changes. Check each option for all three and for any added claim.

**Fragile fact.** Adequacy of insurance is reviewed at due diligence; in the contract the provider must hold adequate cover, give proof, and notify the institution of any material change.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Insurance”; contrast Section 12.4 B.2, Financial Performance and Condition (LO 53.b). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: carry sufficient insurance, provide evidence, communicate significant changes).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q6 of 22.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves the insurance obligation from the provider to the institution. The guidance places the obligation to hold adequate insurance on the service provider. A would be right only if the guidance asked the institution to insure itself in place of provider coverage.

b.reason: It contains all three components in GARP’s words: adequate insurance, proof of insurance, and notification of a material change in coverage.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the material-change notification by relying on the due diligence review. That confuses the one-off selection check (LO 53.b) with the ongoing contract obligation. C would be right only if the guidance stopped at adequacy and proof.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It invents a fixed coverage amount and claims insurance makes indemnification unnecessary. The guidance requires “adequate” insurance, not a specified amount, and lists indemnification as a separate provision. D would need the guidance to treat insurance as a substitute for indemnification, which it does not.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.

questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q7
questions.question:
An examiner from a Federal Reserve Bank is reviewing a bank’s internal contracting policy for outsourced functions that involve confidential information. The policy contains the following statements:

I. Information made available to a service provider should be limited to what is needed to provide the contracted services.

II. Information security measures for an outsourced function may be less stringent than those for the same function performed in-house, since the provider is responsible for its own systems.

III. The provider’s security measures should meet the objectives of the FFIEC information security guidelines and comply with section 501(b) of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, and should be included or referenced in the agreement.

IV. The provider may reveal confidential supervisory information whenever it judges that disclosure is in the bank’s interest.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Examiner auditing four statements in a bank’s contracting policy on confidential information.

**Concept and theory**

Outsourcing hands data to a third party, so the **confidentiality and security of information** provision is the most extensive in the guidance. Its general principles (before the NPPI rules) are:

- Consistent with laws, regulations and supervisory guidance, providers should ensure the security and confidentiality of both the institution’s confidential information and its customer information.
- **Equivalence**: information security measures for outsourced functions should be viewed as if the activity were performed by the institution and afforded the same protections.
- The institution must ensure providers take measures designed to meet the objectives of the FFIEC information security guidelines and comply with section 501(b) of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. These measures should be mapped directly to the institution’s own security processes and be included or referenced in the agreements.
- **Need to know**: information made available to the provider should be limited to what is needed to provide the contracted services.
- **Confidential supervisory information** may be revealed by providers only to the extent authorised under applicable laws and regulations.

The logic is that outsourcing must not create a weaker control environment than the institution would run itself; responsibility for the outcome stays with the institution.

**Applying it to this question**

I is the need-to-know rule. True. II says outsourced security may be weaker because the provider owns its systems; GARP’s equivalence principle says the same protections apply. False. III restates the FFIEC and GLBA 501(b) requirement and the need to include or reference the measures in the agreement. True. IV makes the provider the judge of disclosing confidential supervisory information; GARP limits disclosure to what applicable laws and regulations authorise. False. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Outsourced security gets the same protections as in-house; data shared is limited to what the service needs; supervisory information is disclosed only as law authorises.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Confidentiality and security of information”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser covers need to know and FFIEC/GLBA 501(b) but omits the equivalence principle and the confidential supervisory information rule; GARP is used. Condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q7 of 22.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” rejects III, which is true: the measures should meet the FFIEC information security objectives, comply with GLBA 501(b), and be included or referenced in the agreement. A would be right only if III had said the measures need not be referenced in the agreement.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Accepting II reverses the equivalence principle: outsourced security should be at least as protective as in-house security (“afforded the same protections”), not less. B would be right only if the guidance allowed lighter controls for outsourced functions.

c.reason: I and III are direct statements of GARP’s confidentiality bullet; II and IV each contradict a specific sentence of it.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Accepting IV hands the disclosure decision to the provider’s judgement. Disclosure of confidential supervisory information is permitted only to the extent authorised by applicable laws and regulations. D would be right only if IV read “only to the extent authorised under applicable laws and regulations”.

questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q8
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing the agreement with a provider that processes the bank’s credit card applications, after the provider reported a breach involving customers’ nonpublic personal information (NPPI). Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The agreement should require the provider to notify the bank of any breach involving disclosure of NPPI, and should incorporate the state legal requirements that apply when such a breach occurs.
Once NPPI has been passed to the provider, responsibility for the data and for any disclosure of it rests with the provider rather than with the bank.
Since breach notification requirements vary by state, the agreement should omit them and rely instead on the provider’s general privacy policy.
NPPI covers only an individual customer’s personally identifiable financial information, so customer lists derived from that information fall outside the privacy terms.

questions.solution:
CCO reviewing a card-application processor’s agreement after an NPPI breach.

**Concept and theory**

Nonpublic personal information (NPPI) is the most sensitive data an institution shares, and the guidance gives it its own rules within the confidentiality provision:

| Rule | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Definition | Any nonpublic personally identifiable financial information, and any list, description or other grouping of consumers (and publicly available information about them) derived using personally identifiable financial information that is not publicly available |
| Compliance | Providers handling NPPI must comply with applicable privacy laws and regulations |
| Breach notice | Institutions should require notification from providers of any breach involving disclosure of NPPI |
| Responsibility | Institutions and their providers that maintain, store or process NPPI are responsible for that information and any disclosure of it |
| Contract content | Security of, retention of, and access to NPPI should be addressed in the contract |
| State law | Breach requirements vary by state and should be made part of the contracts with providers that store, process or transmit NPPI |
| Roles | Contracts should clearly authorise and disclose the roles and responsibilities of each party regarding NPPI |

Misuse or unauthorised disclosure by providers can expose the institution to liability or regulatory action, which is why the contract has to anticipate a breach rather than react to one.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are three: who is responsible (both parties, not the provider alone), how state law is handled (incorporated, not omitted), and how wide NPPI is (it includes derived lists). Only one option is consistent on all three and adds the breach notification duty.

**Fragile fact.** NPPI responsibility sits with both the institution and the provider; state breach requirements go into the contract; derived customer lists are NPPI.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Confidentiality and security of information” (NPPI paragraphs). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser covers access, security and retention, breach notice and clarifying roles, but omits the joint responsibility sentence, the state-law point and the NPPI definition; GARP is used. Condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q8 of 22.

a.reason: GARP says institutions should require notification of any NPPI breach and that the state-varying legal requirements for breaches should be made part of the contracts with providers that store, process or transmit NPPI.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** GARP states that institutions and their providers who maintain, store or process NPPI are responsible for that information and any disclosure of it. Transferring data does not transfer responsibility. B would be right only if the guidance placed responsibility on the provider alone.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Variation by state is the reason the guidance wants the requirements written into the contract, not a reason to omit them. C reverses the instruction. It would be right only if the guidance said to rely on the provider’s general policy.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the definition of NPPI. The guidance includes any list, description or other grouping of consumers derived using nonpublic personally identifiable financial information. D would be right only if NPPI were limited to individual records.

questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q9
questions.question: A portfolio manager at the asset management subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company is negotiating an agreement with a provider of performance analytics. The provider will receive client holdings data, generate risk scores from it, and has asked to use the data to improve products it sells to other clients. Which of the following best describes how the agreement should deal with these matters?

options.text: The ownership and license provision should establish that information the provider generates from the institution’s data belongs to the provider.
The confidentiality and security provision should settle who owns the information the provider generates, as part of limiting the provider’s access to data.
The ownership and license provision should define when the provider may use institution property, including data, and address ownership and control of information it generates.
The ownership and license provision should prohibit the provider from using the institution’s data, hardware, software or intellectual property in any circumstances.

questions.solution:
Portfolio manager negotiating use of holdings data and ownership of derived risk scores with an analytics provider.

**Concept and theory**

Two property questions arise in almost every outsourcing arrangement: may the provider use what the institution gives it, and who owns what the provider creates? The **ownership and license** provision answers both. GARP: agreements should define the ability and circumstances under which service providers may use financial institution property, inclusive of data, hardware, software and intellectual property; and agreements should address the ownership and control of any information generated by service providers. (The same provision also covers software escrow, tested in Q10.) The design is deliberately neither permissive nor prohibitive: the provider often needs to use institution data to perform the service, so the contract defines when and how, rather than banning use. Separately, ownership of derived output must be settled expressly, because by default a provider may claim it.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem raises both questions: use of client holdings data (including for the provider’s other clients) and ownership of generated risk scores. The correct option must name ownership and license and must cover both halves without a ban or a pre-emptive award of ownership.

**Fragile fact.** Ownership and license defines circumstances of use (not a ban) and addresses ownership of information the provider generates; data counts as institution property.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Ownership and license”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: when providers may use the institution’s property, i.e. data and equipment, and ownership and control of data produced by a provider; GARP’s list also includes software and intellectual property).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q9 of 22.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The guidance requires the agreement to address ownership and control of generated information; it does not presume the provider owns it. Asserting provider ownership reverses the institution-protective purpose. A would be right only if the guidance set a default rule in the provider’s favour.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Confidentiality and security deals with protecting information and limiting access to what is needed; ownership and control of generated information is assigned to the ownership and license provision. B would be right if the question asked which provision limits how much data the provider receives.

c.reason: It restates both parts of the GARP provision: define when the provider may use institution property, including data, and address the ownership and control of information the provider generates.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** A total ban conflicts with “define the ability and circumstances under which service providers may use” institution property. Many services cannot be performed without using institution data. D would be right only if the guidance forbade any provider use of institution property.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q10
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at the U.S. operations of a German bank is reviewing the purchase of proprietary treasury management software from a small vendor. The analyst has gathered the following information:

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| One-off licence fee | EUR 850,000 |
| Annual support fee | EUR 120,000 |
| Vendor’s years in business | 4 |
| Source code | Proprietary, held only by the vendor |

The analyst is concerned that the vendor might stop supporting the product or fail. Which of the following contractual arrangements is most appropriate?

options.text: An escrow agreement giving the institution unrestricted access to the source code at any time and for any purpose once the licence fee has been paid.
An escrow agreement allowing the vendor to access the institution’s data and programs if the institution itself becomes insolvent during the licence term.
An indemnification provision giving the institution access to the source code and programs if the vendor is found to have acted negligently.
An escrow agreement giving the institution access to the source code and programs only under specified conditions, such as discontinued product support or vendor insolvency.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst assessing protection against a small software vendor ceasing support or failing.

**Concept and theory**

When an institution buys software built on proprietary code, it depends on the vendor to maintain it. If the vendor stops supporting the product or becomes insolvent, the institution could be left with an unmaintainable system. The ownership and license provision addresses this: if institutions purchase software from service providers, **escrow agreements** may be needed so that institutions can access the source code and programs under certain conditions. GARP’s footnote explains: escrow agreements are established with vendors when buying or leasing products with underlying proprietary software; the organisation can access the source program code only under specific conditions, such as discontinued product support or financial insolvency of the vendor.

Escrow is therefore a conditional release mechanism: the code is deposited with a third party and released to the institution only when a defined trigger occurs. It is not a transfer of the code and not an unconditional access right.

**Applying it to this question**

The table shows a proprietary product, code held only by the vendor and a young vendor (four years in business). The fees (EUR 850,000 and EUR 120,000) are irrelevant to the choice of mechanism. The analyst’s two worries, discontinued support and vendor failure, are exactly the two conditions in the GARP footnote.

**Fragile fact.** Escrow protects the institution as purchaser; access is conditional (discontinued support, vendor insolvency), not at will.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Ownership and license”, including footnote 8 on escrow agreements. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q10 of 22.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Escrow gives conditional access, “only under specific conditions”. Unrestricted access at any time and for any purpose is a transfer of the code, which escrow is not. A would be right only if the institution had bought the source code itself.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It reverses who is protected and who fails: escrow protects the purchaser (the institution) against the vendor’s failure or discontinued support. B would describe escrow only if the vendor were the purchaser.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Indemnification compensates the institution for claims arising from the provider’s negligence; it gives no access to source code. C would be right if the question asked how the institution recovers losses from third-party claims caused by the vendor’s negligence.

d.reason: An escrow agreement giving access to the source code and programs only under specified conditions, such as discontinued product support or vendor insolvency, is the arrangement GARP describes.

questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q11
questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a community bank on the default clause of an agreement to outsource its loan review function. Which of the following draft clauses is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Any breach of any term is an immediate default, giving the bank the right to terminate at once without notice and without any opportunity for the provider to cure.
The agreement defines the events that constitute a contractual default, lists acceptable remedies, and provides opportunities for the provider to cure a default.
The provider defines the events that constitute a default and the related remedies, since it is best placed to judge what its own operations can deliver.
Events of default are not defined in the agreement but are determined case by case under the dispute resolution process when a disagreement arises.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant advising on the default clause of a loan review outsourcing agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Termination is costly and disruptive for both sides, so the guidance asks for a graduated path. The first half of the **default and termination** provision deals with default. GARP: agreements should define events of a contractual default, provide a list of acceptable remedies, and provide opportunities for curing default. This creates a sequence:

defined default event ⇒ acceptable remedies and cure period ⇒ termination right if not cured

Defining events in advance avoids arguments over whether a default has occurred; listing remedies lets the institution respond proportionately; cure opportunities preserve a service the institution depends on. The second half of the provision (termination rights, transition and return of data) is tested in Q12.

**Applying it to this question**

The test is whether the clause has the three components (defined events, acceptable remedies, cure opportunities) and whether the institution’s agreement, rather than the provider or a later process, defines them.

**Fragile fact.** Default comes with remedies and an opportunity to cure before termination; the events are defined in the agreement, in advance.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Default and termination”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the contract should clarify actions that constitute a default, reasonable remedies, and “methods to overcome default”; GARP’s “opportunities for curing default” is used. Consistent in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q11 of 22.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** “Any breach of any term” with immediate termination and no cure removes the remedies and cure opportunities the guidance asks for. A would be right only if the guidance treated every breach as terminable without cure.

b.reason: It contains all three GARP components: defined events of contractual default, a list of acceptable remedies, and opportunities for curing default.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Letting the provider define its own default events defeats the protective purpose; the agreement between the parties defines them, in the institution’s interest. C would be right only if the provider were the protected party.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Dispute resolution expedites problem resolution and addresses continuation during a dispute; it is not a substitute for defining default events in advance. D would be right if the question asked how disagreements over the contract should be handled while the arrangement continues.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q12
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing the termination section of a proposed core processing agreement. Which of the following statements is NOT consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Termination rights may be limited to failures to meet performance standards, since a change in control, merger or acquisition of the provider does not itself affect the service.
Termination rights should include an increase in fees and the provider’s failure to provide required notices to the institution.
Termination and notification requirements should give the institution sufficient time to transfer the services to another service provider.
The agreement should address the provider’s preservation and timely return of the institution’s data, records and other resources.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member reviewing the termination section of a core processing agreement (NOT question).

**Concept and theory**

The second half of the **default and termination** provision covers how the relationship ends. GARP says agreements should define termination rights, including:

| Group | Termination rights listed by GARP |
|---|---|
| Ownership changes | Change in control; merger or acquisition |
| Commercial terms | Increase in fees |
| Performance and obligations | Failure to meet performance standards; failure to fulfil contractual obligations; failure to provide required notices |
| Legal and viability | Failure to prevent violations of law; bankruptcy, closure or insolvency |

Contracts should also include termination and notification requirements that give the institution sufficient time to transfer services to another service provider, and should address the provider’s preservation and timely return of the institution’s data, records and other resources. The motivation is continuity: the institution must be able to exit without losing service or data.

Ownership events are included because a new owner may change strategy, staffing or financial strength, all of which were assessed at due diligence.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT question, so three options are true statements from GARP and one is corrupted. B, C and D each restate a GARP sentence. A restricts termination rights to performance failures and asserts that a change in control or merger does not affect the service, contradicting the list.

**Fragile fact.** Termination rights include ownership events (change in control, merger, acquisition) and fee increases, not just performance failures; notice periods exist so the institution can transfer services.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Default and termination”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser cites only change in control, poor performance and nonperformance as common termination reasons, and frames notice as the provider giving sufficient notice when it terminates; GARP’s fuller list and its “sufficient time to transfer services” wording are used. Condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q12 of 22.

a.reason: It is the statement NOT consistent with the guidance: GARP lists change in control and merger or acquisition among the termination rights agreements should define, alongside performance and other triggers. Limiting termination to performance failures narrows the provision.

b.reason: **True statement, not the exception.** Increase in fees and failure to provide required notices both appear in GARP’s list of termination rights. B would be the answer only if the stem asked which statement is consistent with the guidance and B were the sole true one.

c.reason: **True statement, not the exception.** GARP: termination and notification requirements should provide institutions with sufficient time to transfer services to another provider. A reader who thinks notice periods protect the provider would wrongly pick C; the beneficiary is the institution.

d.reason: **True statement, not the exception.** GARP: agreements should address a provider’s preservation and timely return of institution data, records and other resources. A reader who confuses this with ownership and license might doubt it, but GARP places it in default and termination.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q13
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a regional bank is dealing with a billing disagreement with its domestic mortgage subservicer. The subservicer has threatened to stop servicing the bank’s loans until the disagreement is settled. Which of the following best describes what the dispute resolution provision of the agreement should have contained?

options.text: Express choice-of-law and jurisdictional terms, so that any disagreement is adjudicated under the laws of a single, specific jurisdiction.
Suspension of all services until the dispute is resolved, so that neither party is prejudiced by continuing to perform during the disagreement.
Referral of every disagreement to litigation in the institution’s home courts, so that each dispute ends with an enforceable judgment.
A process to expedite problem resolution that also addresses the continuation of the arrangement between the parties during the dispute resolution period.

questions.solution:
CCO facing a billing dispute in which the domestic subservicer threatens to stop servicing.

**Concept and theory**

In an outsourcing relationship a disagreement can do more damage than the amount in dispute, because the provider controls a service the institution depends on. The **dispute resolution** provision addresses both the disagreement and the service. GARP: agreements should include a dispute resolution process in order to (1) expedite problem resolution and (2) address the continuation of the arrangement between the parties during the dispute resolution period. The second purpose is the distinctive one: the clause is designed so that a billing or performance dispute does not interrupt the outsourced activity.

It is distinct from the foreign-based service provider provision, which concerns which law and jurisdiction govern disputes with a provider located abroad.

**Applying it to this question**

The subservicer is domestic, so choice of law across borders is not the issue. The threat to stop servicing is exactly the risk the second limb of the provision addresses. The right description must combine speed of resolution with continuation of the arrangement.

**Fragile fact.** Dispute resolution has two jobs: expedite resolution and keep the arrangement running during the dispute; choice of law is a different provision.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Dispute resolution”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says “resolve disputes quickly and minimize disruption during a dispute”; GARP’s “continuation of the arrangement” is used. Consistent in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q13 of 22.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Express choice-of-law and jurisdictional terms under a single jurisdiction belong to the foreign-based service providers provision. A would be right if the provider were based abroad and the question asked how to avoid conflicting national laws.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Suspending services during the dispute is the outcome the provision is meant to prevent; GARP wants the arrangement’s continuation addressed. B would be right only if the guidance treated suspension as the protective default.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** Mandatory litigation of every disagreement works against “expedite problem resolution” and says nothing about continuation. The guidance asks for a process, not a forum rule. C would be right only if the guidance required every dispute to be litigated.

d.reason: It states both limbs of GARP’s dispute resolution provision: a process to expedite problem resolution and to address continuation of the arrangement during the dispute resolution period.

questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q14
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of the U.S. operations of an Australian banking group, which reports to its parent in AUD, is reviewing a fund administration provider’s proposal to cap its contractual liability. The figures below have been converted into AUD.

| Item | AUD million |
|---|---|
| Annual fees payable to the provider | 0.9 |
| Proposed liability cap (12 months of fees) | 0.9 |
| Estimated loss to the institution if the provider fails to perform | 45.0 |

The provider employs about 1,200 staff across three countries. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The provider’s board should judge whether the cap is reasonable relative to the fees the provider earns, since the cap limits the provider’s own exposure.
The institution’s legal counsel alone should approve the cap, since a limitation on liability is a legal drafting matter rather than a risk decision.
The institution’s board of directors and senior management should determine whether the cap is reasonable when compared to the risks to the institution if the provider fails to perform.
The institution should reject the cap outright, since the guidance does not permit service providers to limit their liability contractually.

questions.solution:
CRO of an Australian group’s U.S. operations evaluating a provider’s proposed liability cap.

**Concept and theory**

Providers commonly seek to cap their exposure, typically at a multiple of fees. A low cap shifts the residual loss from a provider failure back onto the institution. The **limits on liability** provision does not forbid caps; it assigns the decision and sets the test. GARP: service providers may want to contractually limit their liability. The board of directors and senior management of the financial institution should determine whether the proposed limitations are reasonable when compared to the risks to the institution if a service provider fails to perform.

This fits the wider principle in Section 12.3: using service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility for outsourced activities, so a decision that leaves residual risk with the institution belongs at that level.

**Applying it to this question**

The comparison the guidance asks for can be expressed as a coverage ratio:

Coverage ratio $= \frac{\text{Liability cap}}{\text{Estimated loss if the provider fails to perform}}$

$= \frac{0.9}{45.0} =$ 0.02 = 2%

Residual loss retained = 45.0 − 0.9 = 44.1 AUD million

The cap equals 12 months of fees (AUD 0.9 million) but would cover only about 2% of the estimated loss, leaving about AUD 44.1 million with the institution. Whether that is acceptable is exactly the judgement the board and senior management must make. The headcount is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** The institution’s board and senior management decide; the benchmark is the risk to the institution if the provider fails, not the fees.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Limits on liability”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says providers may limit liability “subject to approval by the financial institution’s board of directors and management team” but omits GARP’s reasonableness criterion; GARP is used. Consistent on the actors.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q14 of 22.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The provider’s board is not the decision-maker, and fees earned are not the benchmark. The guidance compares the cap with the institution’s risk. A would be right only if the guidance sought to protect the provider’s exposure.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Legal counsel reviews contracts before execution, but the guidance assigns the reasonableness judgement on liability limits to the board and senior management, because it is a risk acceptance decision. B would be right only if the question asked who reviews the contract drafting.

c.reason: It names the correct actors (the institution’s board of directors and senior management) and the correct criterion (reasonableness compared with the risks to the institution if the provider fails to perform).

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP explicitly contemplates providers seeking to limit liability and asks the institution to assess reasonableness. There is no prohibition. D would be right only if the guidance banned limitation clauses.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q15
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing an agreement under which a provider runs the call centre that receives and resolves complaints from the bank’s credit card customers. Which of the following draft clauses is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: The agreement specifies each party’s responsibilities for responding to complaints and, as the provider resolves them, requires it to give the bank summary reports tracking their status and resolution.
The agreement assigns all complaint handling to the bank, since the guidance does not allow a service provider to take responsibility for resolving customer complaints.
The agreement requires the provider, which resolves the complaints, to report to the bank only those complaints that have escalated into litigation or regulatory action.
The agreement requires the bank to send the provider summary reports tracking the status and resolution of complaints, since the provider is the party resolving them.

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst reviewing complaint-handling terms for an outsourced call centre.

**Concept and theory**

Customers experience the institution through whoever answers the phone. When a provider deals with customers, the institution still bears the reputational and regulatory consequences of how complaints are handled, so it needs both clarity of roles and visibility. The **customer** **complaints** provision supplies both. GARP: agreements should specify the responsibilities of financial institutions and service providers related to responding to customer complaints. If service providers are responsible for customer complaint resolution, agreements should provide for summary reports to the financial institutions that track the status and resolution of complaints.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider resolves complaints, so the conditional limb applies. The correct clause must (1) allocate responsibilities between both parties, (2) have reports flow from provider to bank, and (3) cover status and resolution of complaints in general, not a subset.

**Fragile fact.** If the provider resolves complaints, it reports to the institution, and the reports track both status and resolution.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Customer complaints”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: state which party deals with complaints; if the provider, it reports the complaints and their status).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q15 of 22.

a.reason: It allocates responsibilities between the parties and, because the provider resolves complaints, requires the provider to give the bank summary reports tracking status and resolution.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP expressly contemplates providers being responsible for complaint resolution (“If service providers are responsible for customer complaint resolution. . . ”). There is no prohibition. B would be right only if the guidance barred providers from resolving complaints.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the reports to complaints that escalate into litigation or regulatory action, whereas GARP’s summary reports track the status and resolution of complaints generally. C would be right only if reporting were confined to escalated cases.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It reverses the flow: reports go from the provider that resolves complaints to the institution. D would be right only if the institution resolved complaints and the provider needed to monitor it.
