questions.question:
An operational risk manager at a Canadian bank is reviewing two planned arrangements and wants each to reflect the lessons of the Capital One and Morgan Stanley cases.

| Arrangement | Description | Value (CAD m) |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud | Migration of card customer data to a public cloud provider | 12.0 |
| Disposal | Retirement of branch servers by a disposal vendor that uses a subcontractor | 1.5 |

Which of the following control designs best applies the lessons of the two cases?

options.text: Cloud: complete a risk assessment before migrating and check the bank’s own configuration and encryption. Disposal: vet and monitor the vendor and its subcontractor, and inventory the data on each device.

Cloud: rely on the provider’s built-in security once service levels have been agreed in the contract. Disposal: vet and monitor the vendor and its subcontractor, and inventory the data on each device.

Cloud: complete a risk assessment before migrating and check the bank’s own configuration and encryption. Disposal: vet and monitor the vendor only, leaving its subcontractor to the vendor, and inventory each device.
Cloud: keep an inventory of the customer data held on each device before migrating. Disposal: review the configuration of the web application firewall on the servers that are being retired.

questions.solution:
Operational risk manager at a Canadian bank designing controls for a cloud migration and a server disposal.

**Concept and theory**

The two cases teach different control lessons because they fail in different places of the vendor relationship. Applying them means matching each lesson to the arrangement that resembles its case.

|  | Capital One (cloud) | Morgan Stanley (decommissioning) |
|---|---|---|
| What failed | Risk assessment before migrating IT operations to the public cloud; the bank’s own configuration left data unencrypted | Assessment of decommissioning risk and of vendors including subcontractors; no data inventory; weak selection due diligence and monitoring |
| Control lesson | Assess risk before migration; configure and use the controls on offer; encrypt to make stolen data useless | Vet and monitor the vendor and its subcontractors; keep an inventory of the customer data on each device |

Common to both: accountability stays with the bank, so the bank cannot delegate these controls away.

**Applying it to this question**

The contract values (CAD 12.0 million and CAD 1.5 million) are irrelevant: the lessons apply whatever the size of the contract. For the cloud arrangement, the Capital One lessons point to a risk assessment before migration and to checking the bank’s own configuration and encryption. For the disposal arrangement, the Morgan Stanley lessons point to due diligence on and monitoring of both the vendor and its subcontractor, plus a data inventory for each device. Option A applies each lesson to the matching arrangement and leaves nothing out.

**Fragile fact.** Cloud lesson: assess before migrating and use the controls yourself. Disposal lesson: vendors and subcontractors, plus a data inventory per device.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, “Capital One Data Breach by Former Amazon Web Services (AWS) Employee” and “OCC Fines Morgan Stanley for Weak Third-Party Controls Over Decommissioning of Data Centers”. GARP vs Schweser: no conflict on the controls tested; the encryption attribution follows GARP (see Q2).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: The cloud half reflects the OCC’s finding that Capital One failed to establish effective risk assessment processes before migrating to the public cloud, and GARP’s point that the data was unencrypted because of Capital One’s own configuration. The disposal half reflects the OCC’s findings that Morgan Stanley failed to assess the risk of vendors including subcontractors, failed to maintain an inventory of customer data on its devices, and did not adequately select or monitor its vendors.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B’s disposal half is right, but its cloud half hands security to the provider once service levels are agreed. GARP is explicit that, despite providers’ strong security, risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance remain the business’s responsibility. B would be correct only if the source had said provider security makes the client’s own checks unnecessary.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C’s cloud half is right, but its disposal half limits due diligence and monitoring to the vendor and leaves the subcontractor to the vendor. The OCC faulted Morgan Stanley for failing to assess the risk of third-party vendors including subcontractors. C would be correct only if no subcontractor were involved.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D attaches each case’s control to the wrong arrangement: the device data inventory (Morgan Stanley) to the cloud migration, and the web application firewall review (Capital One) to the disposal. D would be correct only if the two cases had been the other way round.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is presenting the Capital One and Morgan Stanley cases to newly hired analysts and wants a single slide on what the two cases have in common. Which of the following best describes a feature common to both cases?

options.text: In both cases, the loss event was an intrusion by an outside hacker into systems that were hosted and operated by a vendor.
In both cases, the OCC imposed its fine on the vendor involved as well as on the bank that had used the vendor.
In both cases, the bank first learned of the control weakness through the findings of its own internal audit function.
In both cases, customer data held or handled by a vendor was exposed, and the regulator penalised the bank that used it.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank identifying the feature common to both case studies.

**Concept and theory**

GARP draws two general lessons from the cases: they highlight the close interconnection between data security and third-party risk management, and, although outsourcing may transfer some operational risk, accountability for that risk is not transferable. A feature common to both cases must therefore be one that holds in each:

| Feature | Capital One | Morgan Stanley |
|---|---|---|
| How data was exposed | Former AWS employee exploited a misconfigured firewall to reach files in an AWS database | Disposed hardware handled by vendors still contained customer data |
| Who was fined | The bank (USD 80 million, OCC) | The bank (USD 60 million, OCC) |
| Role of internal audit | 2015 audit failed to identify the weaknesses | Not reported |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each option against both columns. A (a hacker intrusion into vendor systems) roughly fits Capital One but not Morgan Stanley, where the exposure came from disposed hardware. B (the vendor fined too) fits neither: in both cases the OCC fined the bank. C (the weakness first found by internal audit) fits neither: Capital One’s 2015 audit failed to identify the weaknesses, and no audit finding is reported for Morgan Stanley. D (customer data held or handled by a vendor was exposed, and the bank was penalised) holds in both, and is the union of GARP’s two lessons.

**Fragile fact.** The common thread is data held or handled by a third party plus a fine on the bank; the mechanisms (intrusion vs disposed hardware) differ.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, both case sections and the closing paragraph of the Morgan Stanley section. GARP vs Schweser: GARP places the interconnection and accountability lessons in its Morgan Stanley commentary; the condensed notes state that both cases highlight the relationship between data security and TPRM. The facts of both cases support the shared reading. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A takes a feature of the Capital One case and extends it to Morgan Stanley. The Morgan Stanley exposure arose because hardware the bank had disposed of still held customer data. A would be correct only if the question had asked about the Capital One case alone.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B adds the vendor as a party fined. In both cases the OCC’s fine fell on the bank that used the vendor. B would be correct only if the OCC had also acted against AWS or the disposal vendors.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C turns Capital One’s audit failure into an audit success: the 2015 internal audit failed to identify numerous control weaknesses. C would be correct only if internal audit had detected the weakness in both cases.

d.reason: In both cases customer data in the hands of a third party (AWS’s database; vendors’ and subcontractors’ handling of retired hardware) was exposed, which is the interconnection between data security and TPRM that GARP highlights, and in both the OCC penalised the bank, consistent with accountability not being transferable.

I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Compliance trainer at an Australian asset manager auditing four statements on the purposes of investor protection.

**Concept and theory**

Investor protection, as the reading defines it, refers to legislation and regulation aimed at ensuring that investors are fully informed about their investments when they enter into financial transactions. The starting problem is an information gap: the firm that designs and sells a product knows far more about it than the investor who buys it. Left alone, that gap invites mis-selling, concealment of risk and abuse. Investor protection regimes close the gap by forcing disclosure and by setting conduct rules for the intermediaries that stand between investors and markets.

The reading lists a set of purposes that go beyond disclosure:

| Purpose | What it means |
|---|---|
| Full information | Investors understand what they buy when they enter a transaction |
| Protection from misrepresentation | Intermediaries and institutions may not misdescribe products or risks |
| Accountability | Responsibility can be established in cases of fraud or insider trading |
| Cross-jurisdictional cooperation | Regulators and law enforcement cooperate across borders in suspected fraud |
| KYC requirements | Strict know-your-customer filings ensure that money flowing into financial products is not of doubtful origin |

The last row is the bridge to anti-money laundering (AML). Because KYC filings exist to stop money of doubtful origin entering financial products, the reading states that investor protection and AML legislation are connected. The EU and the United States both have comprehensive investor protection laws, and firms operating there are expected to run robust risk assessments and controls to minimize violations, which have produced some of the largest settlements and penalties paid by banks and investment firms.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the definition section. Statement I restates the definition itself. Statement II combines two listed purposes: protection from misrepresentation by intermediaries and institutions, and accountability in case of fraud or insider trading. Statement III is the cross-jurisdictional cooperation purpose, with the right actors (regulators and law enforcement) and the right trigger (suspected fraudulent activity). Statement IV reverses the reading: strict KYC filings are named as a compliance requirement of investor protection mechanisms, and the reading says investor protection and AML legislation are connected, not separate. So I, II and III are correct and IV is false.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of the AML link: KYC filings sit inside investor protection compliance, and investor protection and AML legislation are connected; cooperation runs between regulators and law enforcement, across jurisdictions.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Context and Scope: Definition of Investor Protection. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser condenses the same purposes, including KYC due diligence).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q1 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope error.** Option A drops statement II, treating protection from misrepresentation and accountability for fraud or insider trading as outside investor protection. The reading lists both explicitly. Option A would be correct only if statement II had been corrupted, for example if it said accountability applied only to insider trading by retail investors.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option B accepts statement IV, whose single corruption is the reversal of “connected” into “kept separate”. It also discards I, the core definition. Option B would only fit a stem in which statement IV read “investor protection and AML legislation are connected through strict KYC filings” and statements I and III had been falsified.

c.reason: Statements I, II and III each restate a purpose listed under the definition of investor protection, and statement IV contradicts the reading’s explicit link between KYC filings, investor protection and AML. Only option C selects exactly I, II and III.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option D treats all four statements as true, which requires accepting the polarity-flipped statement IV. It would be correct only if statement IV said that strict KYC filings are among the compliance requirements of investor protection mechanisms.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is validating how two recent compliance events were classified in the operational loss database. Neither investigation found evidence of deliberate intent; both were attributed to faulty desk policies and staff error.

| Event | Description | Loss (SGD m) |
|---|---|---|
| X | Relationship managers sold a complex structured note to retail clients without assessing suitability or disclosing its key risks | 4.2 |
| Y | Equity traders repeatedly breached market conduct rules on how orders are placed and handled on the exchange | 7.5 |

Under the Basel operational risk event taxonomy, as the reading applies it to investor protection compliance, which classification is most accurate?

options.text: Both events fall in the fourth event type, Clients, Products and Business Practices; X under Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary and Y under Improper Business or Market Practices.
Both events fall in the fourth event type, Clients, Products and Business Practices; X under Improper Business or Market Practices and Y under Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary.
X falls in Clients, Products and Business Practices under Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary; Y falls in Execution, Delivery and Process Management as a processing failure.
Both events fall in Internal Fraud, because every compliance breach in market activities is an unauthorized activity and so a form of internal fraud.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Singapore bank classifying two non-intentional compliance events under the Basel taxonomy.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel operational risk taxonomy sorts loss events into seven Level 1 event types, each split into Level 2 categories. The reading places compliance with financial laws and regulations, and investor protection in particular, in the fourth event type, Clients, Products and Business Practices (CPBP; the chapter prints the abbreviation as “CBPB”). Within CPBP, investor protection compliance generally falls into one of two Level 2 subcategories:

| Subcategory | Typical content |
|---|---|
| 4.1 Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary | Duties owed to specific clients: suitability assessments, disclosure of risks, fiduciary and KYC obligations, retail disclosure violations |
| 4.2 Improper Business or Market Practices | Conduct towards the market as a whole: improper trade or market practices, market manipulation, antitrust, unlicensed activity |

The CPBP definition in the Basel taxonomy (reproduced in the GARP book’s taxonomy table) covers losses from an unintentional or negligent failure to meet a professional obligation to clients. So a compliance breach does not leave CPBP merely because it was caused by staff error or poor policy. Execution, Delivery and Process Management (EDPM) instead covers failed transaction processing and process management, such as data entry or settlement errors. Internal Fraud requires intentional, unauthorized acts: the reading says a compliance breach is a form of internal fraud only when intentional.

**Applying it to this question**

Event X is a failure of duties owed to specific clients: no suitability assessment and no disclosure of key risks. That is subcategory 4.1. Event Y is a breach of market conduct rules on how orders are placed and handled on the exchange, conduct directed at the market rather than at a specific client’s suitability, so it is subcategory 4.2. Both sit in event type 4, CPBP. The stem’s statement that neither event involved deliberate intent rules out Internal Fraud, and the fact that staff error contributed does not move Y to EDPM, because the loss arises from breaching a conduct rule, not from a failed processing step. The loss amounts (SGD 4.2 m and SGD 7.5 m) are irrelevant: classification depends on the nature of the event, not its size.

**Fragile fact.** Number and name: investor protection compliance is event type 4, CPBP; client-level duties are 4.1 (Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary), market-level conduct is 4.2 (Improper Business or Market Practices). Intent alone turns a breach into internal fraud.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Context and Scope: Definition of Investor Protection; Compliance Risk Management in Investment Activities. GARP prints the event type as “CBPB”; the standard abbreviation, used elsewhere in the GARP book, is CPBP. Schweser describes the two categories without the Basel numbering; no conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q2 of 17.

a.reason: The reading states that compliance with investor protections generally falls into CPBP subcategory 4.1, Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary, or 4.2, Improper Business or Market Practices. X is a suitability and disclosure failure (4.1) and Y a market practice breach (4.2).

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option B gets the event type right but exchanges the two subcategories, attributing the client-level suitability failure to market practices and vice versa. It would be correct only if X had been, say, manipulation of exchange prices and Y a failure to disclose product risks to retail clients.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C moves Y into a neighbouring event type, EDPM, because staff error was involved. EDPM covers failed transaction processing; breaching market conduct rules is a business practice failure captured by CPBP even when unintentional. Option C would be correct if Y had been, for example, a mis-keyed trade quantity or a missed settlement deadline.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option D asserts that every compliance breach is internal fraud. The reading limits this to intentional breaches (“when intentional, a compliance breach . . . is a form of internal fraud”), and the stem rules out intent. Option D would be defensible only if the investigations had found that staff deliberately breached the rules for their own or the desk’s benefit.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a German investment firm is drafting a one-page summary of the original Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID) for the firm’s compliance manual. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: MiFID prescribes authorization requirements for investment firms and conduct of business and organizational requirements for regulated markets.
MiFID was promulgated in 2004 and remained in force across the EU from November 2007 until 2014, when the revised framework was adopted.
MiFID defined regulatory reporting obligations but left trade transparency obligations to be introduced for the first time under MiFID II.
MiFID defined trade transparency obligations intended to prevent market abuse and set rules on the acceptance of financial instruments for public trading.

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst at a German investment firm summarizing the original MiFID.

**Concept and theory**

MiFID is the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (2004/39/EC), an EU directive promulgated in 2004 and applicable across the EU since November 2007. It is one of the central EU rule sets for financial market activities and aims at a high degree of protection for investors in financial instruments. The reading states that MiFID was in force from 2007 to 2018, when the revised framework (MiFID II and MiFIR) took over.

What MiFID does, and to whom, is the most testable part:

| MiFID element | Addressed to or purpose |
|---|---|
| Conduct of business and organizational requirements | Investment firms |
| Authorization requirements | Regulated markets |
| Regulatory reporting and trade transparency obligations | To prevent market abuse |
| Rules on acceptance of financial instruments for public trading | Admission of instruments to trading |

So trade transparency and regulatory reporting already existed in MiFID. The 2014 revision added further requirements on public disclosure of trading data and on disclosure of transaction data to regulators and supervisors; it did not introduce transparency from nothing.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst needs the statement that matches MiFID’s content, actors and dates. Check each claim: who receives conduct requirements (investment firms) and who receives authorization requirements (regulated markets); when MiFID stopped applying (2018, not 2014, which is when the revision was adopted); and whether trade transparency was original (it was). Option D restates two MiFID elements precisely: trade transparency obligations to prevent market abuse, and rules on acceptance of instruments for public trading.

**Fragile fact.** Dates and actors: promulgated 2004, applicable November 2007, in force until 2018; conduct and organizational rules go to investment firms, authorization rules to regulated markets.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, MIFID: Definition. Schweser says MiFID was “enacted in 2004 and implemented across the EU in 2007”, consistent with GARP; Schweser does not give the 2018 end date (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q3 of 17.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** Option A swaps the addressees. MiFID prescribes conduct of business and organizational requirements for investment firms and authorization requirements for regulated markets. Option A would be correct if it read “conduct of business and organizational requirements for investment firms and authorization requirements for regulated markets”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Option B confuses the adoption of the successor framework (June 2014) with the end of MiFID’s application. The reading says MiFID was in force from 2007 to 2018. Option B would be correct if the stem asked when the European Commission adopted the rules revising MiFID.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C credits MiFID II with introducing trade transparency, a feature the original MiFID already had. MiFID II added requirements on public disclosure of trading activity data and on transaction reporting to supervisors. Option C would be correct only if it said MiFID II set out additional public disclosure requirements on trading activity.

d.reason: GARP states that MiFID “defines regulatory reporting and trade transparency obligation to prevent market abuse and defines the rules on the acceptance of financial instruments for public trading”. Option D says exactly this.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at the Luxembourg subsidiary of a Brazilian bank is asked by head office why the 2014 EU reform package consisted of both a directive (MiFID II) and a regulation (MiFIR), and how the directive takes effect in member states. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: MiFIR, being a regulation, must be turned into national rules by each member state, whereas MiFID II, being a directive, applies directly in all member states.
MiFID II, being a directive, must be turned into national rules by each member state, and each member state may be more stringent, but not less, than the directive.
MiFID II, being a directive, must be turned into national rules by each member state, and each member state may be more or less stringent than the directive.
MiFID II, being a directive, applies directly and uniformly in all member states, and no member state may be more stringent than the directive.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a Luxembourg subsidiary explaining the directive and regulation in the 2014 EU package.

**Concept and theory**

The EU uses two different legal instruments, and MiFID’s history uses both. GARP explains the difference in a footnote to the MiFID section:

| Instrument | How it takes effect | Room for member states |
|---|---|---|
| Regulation | Applicable in all member states directly | None needed: the text itself applies |
| Directive | Must be turned into national rules in each member state | May be more stringent, but not less, than the directive |

The original MiFID was a directive. In June 2014 the European Commission adopted a package made up of a revised directive, MiFID II, and a regulation, MiFIR (Markets in Financial Instruments Regulation). The regulation gives directly applicable, uniform rules; the directive sets a floor that each member state transposes and may tighten. The asymmetry matters: a directive is a minimum, so national rules may go further but cannot fall below it.

**Applying it to this question**

Head office asks two things: why both instruments exist, and how the directive takes effect. MiFID II is the directive, so it must be turned into national rules; MiFIR is the regulation and applies directly. The deciding detail is the direction of national discretion: more stringent is allowed, less stringent is not.

**Fragile fact.** Directive equals transposition plus a floor (more stringent allowed, less not); regulation equals direct application. MiFID and MiFID II are directives, MiFIR is the regulation.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, MIFID: Definition, footnote 1, and Evolution in Recent Years: MIFID II. Schweser does not cover the directive versus regulation distinction; content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q4 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option A exchanges the properties of the two instruments: it says the regulation (MiFIR) needs national transposition and the directive (MiFID II) applies directly. The reading says the opposite. Option A would be correct if the labels were reversed, that is, if MiFID II were the regulation and MiFIR the directive.

b.reason: GARP’s footnote states that EU directives need to be turned into regulation in each member state, with each country having the freedom to be more stringent (but not less) than the directive. Option B states this for MiFID II.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Option C keeps the transposition step but drops the condition that national rules may not be less stringent. A directive is a floor. Option C would describe a regime in which the EU text was merely a recommended model, which is not how the reading describes directives.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option D reverses both features of a directive: it says the directive applies directly and uniformly, and that member states may not be more stringent. Under the reading, a directive must be transposed and member states may be more stringent. Option D would be correct only if the reading described a directive as directly applicable and as a ceiling on national rules; it describes it as needing transposition and as a floor.

questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing a short report for the board of a Spanish brokerage on why the European Commission revised the MiFID framework in June 2014. Which of the following statements is the most appropriate to include in the report?

options.text: After the 2008 crisis, the revision aimed to further strengthen investor protection and to address the development of new trading platforms and activities.
After the 2008 crisis, the revision aimed to stop commercial banks from proprietary trading and to limit their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.
After the 2008 crisis, the revision aimed to replace the directive with a single regulation, MiFIR, and so remove any further role for a revised directive.
After the 2008 crisis, the revision added public disclosure of trading activity data but removed the disclosure of transaction data to regulators and supervisors.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant reporting to a Spanish brokerage board on why the EU revised MiFID in 2014.

**Concept and theory**

After the 2008 financial crisis, the need for a more robust regulatory framework became clear. GARP gives two motivations for revising MiFID: to further strengthen investor protection, and to address the development of new trading platforms and activities. In June 2014 the European Commission adopted new rules revising the MiFID framework, made up of a revised directive (MiFID II) and a regulation (MiFIR).

What the revision added:

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Reinforced investor protection | Stronger conduct and incentive rules, set out in MiFIR |
| Public disclosure | Additional requirements on public disclosure of data on trading activity |
| Regulatory disclosure | Disclosure of transaction data to regulators and supervisors |
| Legal form | Revised directive (MiFID II) plus a new regulation (MiFIR) |

The revision therefore pushed transparency in two directions at once: outward to the public (trading activity data) and upward to supervisors (transaction data).

**Applying it to this question**

The board wants the reason for the revision. The statement to include must give the post-crisis motivation in the reading’s terms and must not import features of US law or misstate the package. Option A gives both motivations exactly. Each other option either attributes a US Dodd-Frank feature to the EU, misstates the package’s legal form, or reverses one of its disclosure requirements.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the 2014 revision added disclosure both to the public (trading activity data) and to regulators and supervisors (transaction data); nothing was removed. Motivation includes new trading platforms and activities, not bank proprietary trading.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Evolution in Recent Years: MIFID

II. Schweser says the revision aimed “to improve public disclosure requirements for trading data” and that MiFID II “came into force in 2014”; GARP says the rules were adopted in June 2014 and that MiFID remained in force until 2018. GARP used; this looks like a wording compression in Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q5 of 17.

a.reason: GARP: after the 2008 crisis a more robust framework was needed “to further strengthen investor protection and address the development of new trading platforms and activities”. Option A restates this.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option B attributes to the EU revision the purpose of the Volcker Rule, a US provision in the Dodd-Frank Act that intends to prevent commercial banks from speculative activities and proprietary trading and limits their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds. It would be correct if the question asked about the Volcker Rule.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Option C drops the revised directive from the package. The 2014 rules consisted of a revised directive, MiFID II, and a regulation, MiFIR. Option C would be correct only if the reform had been delivered solely by regulation.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option D keeps the added public disclosure of trading data but reverses the second requirement: MiFID II added disclosure of transaction data to regulators and supervisors rather than removing it. Option D would be correct if “removed” were replaced by “added”.

The chief compliance officer of a French investment firm is reviewing a draft gap analysis that maps proposed workstreams to the activities addressed by the Markets in Financial Instruments Regulation (MiFIR). The budget column was added by the finance team.

| No. | Proposed workstream | Budget (EUR 000) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Review of remuneration of traders and advisors, and of conflicts of interest | 240 |
| 2 | Controls ensuring communication to customers is fair and non-misleading | 180 |
| 3 | Enhanced protection programme for whistleblowers | 95 |
| 4 | Redesign of the sales process and product governance | 310 |
| 5 | Best execution of trades for clients | 275 |
| 6 | Committee to consult the US SEC on fee structures and trading strategies | 60 |
| 7 | Procedures for dealings with eligible counterparties | 120 |

Which workstreams correspond to activities that MiFIR addresses?

options.text: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 only
1, 2, 4 and 7 only
1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 only

Chief compliance officer at a French investment firm checking which workstreams map to MiFIR topics.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes MiFIR as a stronger version of the original regulation. It addresses the incentive structures and other aspects of the investment activities of financial firms. The reading lists six areas:

| No. | MiFIR area | Problem it targets |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Remuneration of traders and advisors, and conflicts of interest | Pay that rewards selling over client outcomes |
| 2 | Communication to customers to be fair and non-misleading | Marketing that obscures risk |
| 3 | Definition and independence of investment advice | Advice labelled independent that is not |
| 4 | Sales process and product governance | Products sold to the wrong clients |
| 5 | Best execution of trades for the clients | Orders not executed on the best terms |
| 6 | Dealings with eligible counterparties | Treatment of professional counterparties |

**Applying it to this question**

Map each workstream:

| No. | Workstream | Maps to |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Remuneration and conflicts of interest | MiFIR |
| 2 | Fair and non-misleading communication | MiFIR |
| 3 | Whistleblower protection | Dodd-Frank, Investor Protection Act |
| 4 | Sales process and product governance | MiFIR |
| 5 | Best execution | MiFIR |
| 6 | Committee consulting the SEC | Dodd-Frank, Investor Protection Act |
| 7 | Eligible counterparties | MiFIR |

The MiFIR set is therefore 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7. The budget column (EUR 000) is irrelevant: the question is about content, and no budget figure changes the mapping.

**Fragile fact.** Attribution: whistleblower protection and the SEC consultation committee are US (Investor Protection Act); best execution and eligible counterparties are EU (MiFIR).

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Evolution in Recent Years: MIFID II; The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. GARP attributes the six-item list to MiFIR (“a stronger version of the original regulation”); Schweser attributes it to “MiFID II and MiFIR” jointly. The list itself is identical; the question attributes it to MiFIR, which is consistent with both.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q6 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option A adds workstream 3, attributing whistleblower protection (a Dodd-Frank Investor Protection Act feature) to MiFIR. It would be correct if workstream 3 described, for example, a review of how investment advice is defined and kept independent.

Option B would be correct only if workstream 5 described something outside the list, such as US clearing of OTC derivatives.

c.reason: Workstreams 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 are each a named MiFIR area; workstreams 3 and 6 are Investor Protection Act features. Only option C selects exactly the five MiFIR items.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option D accepts all seven workstreams, treating every investor protection topic as a MiFIR topic, including two US Investor Protection Act features. It would be correct only if workstreams 3 and 6 were replaced by MiFIR areas.

questions.question: An internal auditor at an Italian investment firm is reviewing its wealth management unit. The audit finds that advisors receive bonuses linked to sales of the firm’s in-house funds, that client brochures highlight past returns while giving little prominence to risks, and that advice marketed as independent considers only in-house products. Which group of MiFIR topics is most directly engaged by these findings?

options.text: Best execution of trades for clients, dealings with eligible counterparties, and sales process and product governance.
Remuneration and conflicts of interest, fair and non-misleading communication, and definition and independence of investment advice.
Remuneration and conflicts of interest, fair and non-misleading communication, and increased protections for whistleblowers.
Authorization requirements for regulated markets, rules on acceptance of financial instruments for public trading, and best execution.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at an Italian investment firm linking wealth management findings to MiFIR topics.

**Concept and theory**

MiFIR targets the incentive structures inside investment firms as well as their outward conduct. Its six areas (remuneration and conflicts of interest; fair and non-misleading communication; definition and independence of investment advice; sales process and product governance; best execution; dealings with eligible counterparties) can be read as answers to specific failure modes:

| Failure mode | MiFIR area that addresses it |
|---|---|
| Pay that rewards product sales | Remuneration of traders, advisors, and conflicts of interest |
| Marketing that stresses returns and hides risk | Communication to customers to be fair and non-misleading |
| “Independent” advice limited to own products | Definition and independence of investment advice |
| Products reaching unsuitable clients | Sales process and product governance |
| Client orders filled on poor terms | Best execution of trades for the clients |
| Treatment of professional counterparties | Dealings with eligible counterparties |

Original MiFID, by contrast, contains the authorization requirements for regulated markets and the rules on acceptance of instruments for public trading. Whistleblower protection is a US feature of the Investor Protection Act.

**Applying it to this question**

Match each finding to the area it engages most directly. Bonuses linked to in-house fund sales are a remuneration incentive that creates a conflict of interest. Brochures that highlight returns but downplay risks breach the requirement that communication be fair and non-misleading. Advice marketed as independent that considers only in-house products goes to the definition and independence of investment advice. That is the trio in option B. Nothing in the findings concerns execution of orders or counterparties, so those areas are not “most directly” engaged.

**Fragile fact.** Attribution: advisor remuneration, fair communication and independent advice are MiFIR areas; authorization of regulated markets is original MiFID; whistleblowers are US Dodd-Frank.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Evolution in Recent Years: MIFID II; MIFID: Definition. GARP attributes the list to MiFIR; Schweser to “MiFID II and MiFIR”. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q7 of 17.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option A names three genuine MiFIR areas, but the wrong ones for these facts. Product governance is arguably related, yet best execution and eligible counterparties are not engaged by any finding. Option A would be correct if the audit had found client orders routed for the firm’s benefit and poor handling of professional counterparties.

b.reason: Each finding maps to one MiFIR area named in GARP’s list: remuneration and conflicts of interest, fair and non-misleading communication, and definition and independence of investment advice.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C replaces investment advice independence with increased protection for whistleblowers, a Dodd-Frank Investor Protection Act feature that is not on the MiFIR list. It would be correct only for a stem asking which mix of EU and US provisions applies, and the third finding would still be unaddressed.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank with US operations is summarizing the Investor Protection Act for the bank’s regulatory change committee. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The act established a committee to which all new financial products, fee structures and trading strategies must be submitted for approval before launch.
The act established a committee to consult with the CFTC about regulatory priorities surrounding new financial products, fee structures and trading strategies.
The act was introduced ahead of the 2007 financial crisis as a pre-emptive measure, and its provisions were later absorbed into the Dodd-Frank Act.
The act established a committee to consult with the SEC about regulatory priorities surrounding new financial products, fee structures and trading strategies.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank summarizing the Investor Protection Act.

**Concept and theory**

In the United States, the Investor Protection Act is a component of the broader Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. It was introduced as a regulatory response to the financial crisis of 2007, in an attempt to prevent any future recurrence. The reading attributes two features to the act itself:

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Consultative committee | Established to consult with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) about regulatory priorities surrounding new financial products, fee structures and trading strategies |
| Whistleblowers | Granted increased protections under the act |

Three details are fragile. The counterparty of the consultation is the SEC (the CFTC appears in the reading only in connection with OTC derivatives). The committee consults on regulatory priorities; it is not an approval gate. And the act came after the crisis, as a response to it, as part of Dodd-Frank.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options describe either the committee or the act’s origin. Option D gets every element right: committee, consultation, SEC, and the three subjects (new financial products, fee structures, trading strategies). Options A and B differ from D in one element each, and option C misstates timing and structure.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the Investor Protection Act committee consults the SEC (not the CFTC), and it consults on priorities; it does not approve products.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. Schweser condenses the same content (“a committee to consult with the SEC about new financial products, fees, and trading strategies”). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q8 of 17.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option A turns a consultative committee into a mandatory preapproval gate for all new products, fees and strategies. The reading describes consultation about regulatory priorities, not product approval. Option A would be correct only if the act had created a licensing regime for new products.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Option B has the right committee and the right subjects but the wrong agency: the committee consults the SEC, not the CFTC. The CFTC appears in the reading only alongside the SEC as a regulator to which OTC derivatives trading is delegated. Option B would be correct if “CFTC” were replaced by “SEC”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option C reverses the sequence. The act was introduced as a regulatory response to the 2007 crisis, as a component of Dodd-Frank, not as a pre-emptive measure absorbed later. Option C would be correct only if the act had pre-dated the crisis.

d.reason: GARP: “The act established a committee to consult with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) about regulatory priorities surrounding new financial products, fee structures, and trading strategies.” Option D is this sentence.

questions.question:
A regulatory affairs analyst at a Japanese bank’s New York branch is checking a slide that links US provisions to the legislation that contains them. The slide makes the following pairings:

I. Increased protections for whistleblowers: the Investor Protection Act component of the Dodd-Frank Act.

II. Limits on commercial banks’ investments in hedge funds and private equity funds: the Investor Protection Act component of the Dodd-Frank Act.

III. Creation of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: the Dodd-Frank Act.

IV. A requirement that firms buying and selling derivatives use clearinghouses: the Dodd-Frank Act.

Which pairings are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Regulatory affairs analyst at a Japanese bank’s New York branch checking provision-to-legislation pairings.

**Concept and theory**

The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act is a large statute with several distinct parts. The Investor Protection Act is one component of it; the Volcker Rule is another element the act contains; and the act also creates institutions and mandates of its own. Keeping the part-versus-whole structure straight is the core of this target:

| Provision | Where the reading places it |
|---|---|
| Committee consulting the SEC on new products, fees, strategies | Investor Protection Act |
| Increased protections for whistleblowers | Investor Protection Act |
| OTC derivatives regulation delegated to SEC and CFTC | Dodd-Frank Act |
| Mandatory use of clearinghouses for derivatives | Dodd-Frank Act |
| Financial stability, federal oversight, oversight council | Dodd-Frank Act |
| Prevent commercial banks’ speculative and proprietary trading; limit hedge fund and PE investments | Volcker Rule, contained in the Dodd-Frank Act |
| Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) | Created under the Dodd-Frank Act |

The reading attributes the hedge fund and private equity limits to the Volcker Rule. It does not place them in the Investor Protection Act.

**Applying it to this question**

Pairing I is correct: whistleblowers were granted increased protections under the Investor Protection Act. Pairing II is wrong: limits on commercial banks’ investments in hedge funds and private equity funds come from the Volcker Rule. Pairing III is correct: the CFPB was created under Dodd-Frank. Pairing IV is correct: the Dodd-Frank Act mandates that firms buying and selling derivatives use clearinghouses. So I, III and IV are correct.

**Fragile fact.** Part versus whole: whistleblowers belong to the Investor Protection Act; hedge fund and private equity limits belong to the Volcker Rule; both sit inside the Dodd-Frank Act.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. Schweser presents the clearinghouse requirement as part of how “the act enhances investor protection”, while GARP attributes it to “the Dodd-Frank Act”. Pairing IV uses the GARP attribution (the whole act), which is correct under both sources.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q9 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Option A drops pairing IV, as if the clearinghouse requirement were outside Dodd-Frank. The reading says the Dodd-Frank Act mandates clearinghouse use. Option A would be correct if pairing IV attributed the clearing mandate to, say, MiFIR.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option B accepts all four pairings, which requires crediting the Investor Protection Act with the Volcker Rule’s hedge fund and private equity limits. It would be correct only if pairing II named the Volcker Rule instead.

c.reason: Pairings I, III and IV match GARP’s attributions; pairing II misattributes a Volcker Rule feature. Option C selects exactly I, III and IV.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option D rejects the correct whistleblower pairing and accepts the incorrect hedge fund pairing, in effect exchanging the Investor Protection Act’s feature with the Volcker Rule’s. It would be correct only if pairing I attributed whistleblower protection to the Volcker Rule (making I false) and pairing II attributed the fund limits to the Volcker Rule (making II true).

questions.question: A risk consultant is validating a memo prepared for a US derivatives dealer that summarizes how the Dodd-Frank Act treats over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives. Which of the following statements in the memo is most accurate?

options.text: Regulation of OTC derivatives trading is delegated to both the SEC and the CFTC, and firms buying and selling derivatives must use clearinghouses.
Regulation of OTC derivatives trading is delegated solely to the SEC, and firms buying and selling derivatives must use clearinghouses to do so.
Regulation of OTC derivatives trading is delegated to both the SEC and the CFTC, and clearinghouse use is left to each firm’s discretion.
Regulation of OTC derivatives trading is delegated to the CFPB, since derivatives sold to clients fall within the consumer finance markets.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant validating a memo on how Dodd-Frank treats OTC derivatives.

**Concept and theory**

OTC derivatives were at the centre of the 2007 to 2009 crisis because they were traded bilaterally, with limited transparency and with counterparty exposures that were hard to see and hard to unwind. The Dodd-Frank Act regulates multiple aspects of investor protection, including those relating to the trading of OTC derivatives. GARP states two things:

| Element | What the reading says |
|---|---|
| Who regulates trading | Regulation of OTC derivatives trading is delegated to the SEC and the CFTC (Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission) |
| How trades are made | Firms buying and selling derivatives need to use clearinghouses to do so |

A clearinghouse stands between the two parties, so each faces the clearinghouse rather than each other; that is why mandatory clearing reduces bilateral counterparty risk. The CFPB, a separate Dodd-Frank creation, oversees consumer finance markets (mortgages, student loans, credit cards), not derivatives.

**Applying it to this question**

The memo must name both regulators and state the clearing requirement as mandatory. Option A does both. Option B drops one regulator, option C weakens the mandate, and option D names the wrong agency entirely.

**Fragile fact.** Actors: OTC derivatives trading regulation is delegated to the SEC and the CFTC; clearinghouse use is mandatory, not optional.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. GARP vs Schweser conflict: Schweser says the act “gave the SEC greater oversight responsibilities for OTC derivatives” and does not mention the CFTC; GARP says regulation is delegated to the SEC and the CFTC. Resolved from GARP; this looks like a compression in Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q10 of 17.

a.reason: GARP: “the trading of over the counter (OTC) derivatives, of which the regulation of trading is delegated to the SEC and the CFTC” and “the Dodd-Frank Act also mandates that firms buying and selling derivatives need to use clearinghouses to do so”.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Option B gives the SEC sole responsibility, dropping the CFTC. This is the trap created by condensed summaries that say Dodd-Frank gave the SEC greater oversight of OTC derivatives. GARP names both agencies. Option B would be correct only if the reading had delegated OTC derivatives regulation to the SEC alone.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option C turns a mandate into a choice. The act mandates that firms buying and selling derivatives use clearinghouses. Option C would be correct if the act had merely encouraged central clearing.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Option D assigns OTC derivatives to the CFPB, whose remit is consumer finance markets such as mortgages, student loans and credit cards. It would be correct only if the question asked which body oversees consumer credit cards.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a US-listed insurer asks for a summary of the elements of the Dodd-Frank Act that sit beyond the Investor Protection Act and the Volcker Rule. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Elements of the act are aimed at ensuring greater financial stability of the markets, with federal oversight.
The act provided for the creation of a financial stability oversight council and a reorganization of financial regulation.
The act created the CFPB as an independent financial regulator overseeing mortgages, student loans and credit cards.
The act created the CFPB within the SEC to supervise the best execution of retail customer orders by brokerage firms.

Insurer risk committee member asking about Dodd-Frank elements beyond the Investor Protection Act and Volcker Rule.

Beyond its investor protection provisions, GARP describes Dodd-Frank elements aimed at the stability of the financial system as a whole and at consumers:

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Financial stability | Greater financial stability of the markets, with federal oversight |
| Institutions | Creation of a financial stability oversight council |
| Structure | Reorganization of financial regulation |
| Consumer protection | The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), created as an independent financial regulator to oversee consumer finance markets, including mortgages, student loans and credit cards |

The CFPB’s two defining attributes are that it is independent and that its remit is consumer finance. Best execution of customer orders by brokerage firms belongs to a different world: in the reading it is the subject of FINRA rules, and FINRA is overseen by the SEC.

Because the qualifier is NOT correct, three options must be true. A states the stability and federal oversight aim; B states the oversight council and the reorganization; C states the CFPB’s independence and remit. D places the CFPB inside the SEC and gives it the wrong remit (best execution of brokerage orders). D is the false statement.

**Fragile fact.** The CFPB is an independent regulator of consumer finance markets (mortgages, student loans, credit cards); it is not part of the SEC and does not supervise best execution.

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. Schweser covers the CFPB but not the financial stability oversight council or the reorganization of financial regulation; those elements are from GARP only. No conflict.

Choosing it would mean treating the act as purely an investor protection statute. A “NOT correct” option would need it to say, for example, that the act left oversight to the states.

b.reason: **Qualifier misread.** Option B is true: the reading lists the creation of a financial stability oversight council and the reorganization of financial regulation. It would be the answer only if it claimed the council was created by MiFID II or that regulation was left unchanged.

c.reason: **Qualifier misread.** Option C is true and close to verbatim. Choosing it would come from doubting the CFPB’s independence. It would be the answer only if it described the CFPB as a self-regulatory body or as a derivatives regulator.

questions.question: The treasurer of a US commercial bank is presenting to newly hired treasury analysts on the Volcker Rule. Which of the following best describes the rule?

options.text: It prohibits all financial firms, including asset managers and insurers, from making any investment in hedge funds or private equity funds.
It intends to prevent commercial banks from speculative activities and proprietary trading for profit, and limits their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.
It intends to prevent commercial banks from trading OTC derivatives except through clearinghouses, and limits their exposures to hedge funds.
It intends to prevent hedge funds and private equity funds from proprietary trading for profit, and limits commercial banks’ lending to such funds.

questions.solution:
Treasurer of a US commercial bank describing the Volcker Rule to new analysts.

**Concept and theory**

The Dodd-Frank Act contains the Volcker Rule. Its logic is to separate the deposit-funded, systemically important business of commercial banking from risk-taking for the bank’s own profit. GARP states it in two parts:

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| Trading | Intends to prevent commercial banks from engaging in speculative activities and proprietary trading for profit |
| Fund investments | In particular, limits banks’ investments in hedge funds and private equity funds |

Three words carry the meaning. “Commercial banks” fixes the actor: the rule restricts banks, not funds or asset managers. “Proprietary” means trading for the bank’s own account and profit. “Limits” fixes the strength of the fund restriction: investments are limited, not banned outright in the reading’s wording. Clearing of OTC derivatives and the CFPB are separate Dodd-Frank provisions.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option describes an actor, an activity, and a restriction. Only option B names commercial banks as the restricted actor, speculative and proprietary trading as the activity, and a limit on hedge fund and private equity investments as the second restriction.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the Volcker Rule restricts commercial banks (their speculative and proprietary trading and their hedge fund and private equity investments), not the funds themselves.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. Schweser says the rule “prohibits” commercial banks from speculative and proprietary trading; GARP says it “intends to prevent” them. Same substance; GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q12 of 17.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option A extends the rule to all financial firms and turns a limit into a total ban on any investment. The reading restricts commercial banks and limits their fund investments. Option A would be correct only if the rule applied economy-wide and prohibited every such investment.

b.reason: GARP: “The Volcker Rule intends to prevent commercial banks from engaging in speculative activities and proprietary trading for profit. In particular, it limits banks’ investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C attributes to the Volcker Rule the clearinghouse requirement for derivatives, a separate Dodd-Frank provision. It would describe the Dodd-Frank clearing mandate if its hedge fund clause were removed and its actor widened to all firms buying and selling derivatives.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Option D keeps the activity (proprietary trading for profit) but moves the restriction onto hedge funds and private equity funds, and recasts the fund limit as a lending limit. The rule restricts commercial banks. Option D would be correct only if the rule targeted fund managers’ own trading.

questions.question:
A US regulator is reviewing four institutions as part of a thematic study. The table summarizes the activity observed at each.

| Ref. | Institution | Activity observed |
|---|---|---|
| P | Commercial bank, USD 85 bn assets | Runs a desk trading the bank’s own capital for short-term profit and holds a large stake in a private equity fund |
| Q | Asset manager (not a bank), USD 40 bn under management | Allocates client portfolios to hedge funds and private equity funds |
| R | Credit card issuer, USD 12 bn receivables | Changes the fees and terms it applies to consumer credit card accounts |
| S | Derivatives dealer, USD 30 bn notional | Trades derivatives bilaterally with clients without using a clearinghouse |

Which institution’s activity is the Volcker Rule most directly designed to restrict?

options.text: Institution P
Institution Q
Institution R
Institution S

questions.solution:
US regulator identifying which of four institutions’ activities the Volcker Rule targets.

**Concept and theory**

Applying the Volcker Rule to facts requires checking two conditions together: the actor must be a commercial bank, and the activity must be speculative or proprietary trading for profit, or investment in hedge funds or private equity funds. GARP: the rule “intends to prevent commercial banks from engaging in speculative activities and proprietary trading for profit. In particular, it limits banks’ investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.” Neighbouring Dodd-Frank provisions cover the other activities that appear in this kind of question:

| Activity | Dodd-Frank provision in the reading |
|---|---|
| Bank’s own-account trading; bank stakes in HF or PE funds | Volcker Rule |
| Consumer credit cards, mortgages, student loans | CFPB oversight of consumer finance markets |
| Derivatives bought and sold without a clearinghouse | Mandate to use clearinghouses |
| Non-bank investing client money in funds | No Volcker restriction: actor is not a commercial bank |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each row against both conditions. P: actor is a commercial bank; activity is own-capital trading for short-term profit plus a large private equity stake. Both conditions met. Q: activity (hedge fund and PE allocations) resembles the rule’s fund clause, but the actor is a non-bank asset manager investing client money. Actor condition fails. R: consumer credit card terms are a consumer finance matter for the CFPB. Activity condition fails. S: trading derivatives without a clearinghouse engages the clearing mandate. Activity condition fails. The size figures (USD 85 bn, 40 bn, 12 bn, 30 bn) are irrelevant to which provision applies.

**Fragile fact.** Both conditions must hold: commercial bank and proprietary or speculative trading or hedge fund or private equity investment. A non-bank doing the same thing is outside the rule.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, The Investor Protection Act: Dodd-Frank. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q13 of 17.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Option B matches the activity but drops the actor condition: the Volcker Rule limits commercial banks’ investments in hedge funds and private equity funds, and Q is an asset manager that is not a bank. Option B would be correct if Q were a commercial bank investing its own capital in such funds.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C attributes a consumer finance matter to the Volcker Rule. Consumer credit card markets are overseen by the CFPB, another Dodd-Frank creation. Option C would be correct if the question asked which institution falls within the CFPB’s remit.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option D attributes the clearing mandate to the Volcker Rule. The requirement that firms buying and selling derivatives use clearinghouses is a separate Dodd-Frank provision. Option D would be correct if the question asked which activity the clearinghouse mandate targets.

questions.question: The head of operational risk at a Hong Kong securities firm is reviewing two compliance breaches. In breach 1, a trader deliberately exceeded a client’s mandate limits to boost the desk’s results and concealed the positions. In breach 2, an operations clerk applied an outdated internal policy and sent clients incorrect product disclosures. Which of the following best describes how these breaches should be understood?

options.text: Both are forms of internal fraud, since any compliance breach is an unauthorized activity whatever the intention of the perpetrator.
Breach 1 is an unintentional breach and breach 2 is a form of internal fraud, since breach 2 directly misinformed the firm’s clients.
Breach 1 is a form of internal fraud and breach 2 an unintentional breach; the key difference between them is the intention of the perpetrator.
Breach 1 is a form of internal fraud and breach 2 an unintentional breach; the key difference between them is the size of the client harm.

questions.solution:
Head of operational risk at a Hong Kong securities firm characterizing a deliberate and an accidental compliance breach.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s section on compliance risk management in investment activities starts by splitting compliance breaches by intent:

| Type | What the reading says | Consequence for controls |
|---|---|---|
| Intentional | A form of internal fraud, as it is an unauthorized activity | Most of the internal fraud control framework applies |
| Unintentional | Often due to human error or faulty policies | Many internal fraud controls also apply, except deterrent controls |

The reading names the deciding variable explicitly: “the key difference between an error and a fraud is the intention of the perpetrator.” Neither the size of the loss nor the degree of harm to clients decides the category. A small deliberate breach is still fraud; a large accidental one is still an error.

**Applying it to this question**

Breach 1: the trader deliberately exceeded mandate limits and concealed the positions. Deliberate and unauthorized, so it is a form of internal fraud. Breach 2: the clerk applied an outdated policy. There is no intent; the cause is a faulty policy and human error, so it is an unintentional breach. The distinguishing feature is intention.

**Fragile fact.** The single deciding variable between error and fraud is the intention of the perpetrator; not loss size, not client harm, not whether a policy existed.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Compliance Risk Management in Investment Activities. Schweser says breaches “can be unintentional as a result of human error or ineffective policies, or intentional due to fraud”; consistent with GARP, though Schweser omits the statement that intention is the key difference. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q14 of 17.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option B reverses the classification of the two breaches and grounds it in client impact. The deliberate, concealed breach is the fraud; the outdated-policy breach is the error. Option B would be correct only if the trader had acted by mistake and the clerk had sent false disclosures on purpose.

c.reason: GARP: “When intentional, a compliance breach in financial market activities is a form of internal fraud, as it is an unauthorized activity . . . When unintentional, compliance breaches are often due to human error or faulty policies . . . the key difference between an error and a fraud is the intention of the perpetrator.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option D classifies both breaches correctly but substitutes the size of client harm for intention as the distinguishing feature. Severity is a property of the loss, not of the event type. Option D would be correct only if the reading had defined fraud by loss size, which it does not.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of an Australian broker is reviewing a proposal to reuse the firm’s internal fraud control framework to prevent unintentional compliance breaches (errors) in its trading activities. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: None of the internal fraud controls carry over to errors, because errors involve no intention and so need an entirely separate framework.
All of the internal fraud controls carry over to errors, including deterrent controls, because errors and fraud share the same drivers.
Many internal fraud controls carry over to errors, except detective controls, because the key difference between error and fraud is intention.
Many internal fraud controls carry over to errors, except deterrent controls, because the key difference between error and fraud is intention.

questions.solution:
Chief compliance officer at an Australian broker reusing internal fraud controls to prevent errors.

**Concept and theory**

Because an intentional compliance breach is a form of internal fraud, GARP says most of the control framework for internal fraud applies to the prevention of compliance breaches. It then extends the point to unintentional breaches: “Many of the controls designed to prevent internal fraud also apply to the prevention of errors (with the exception of deterrent controls), as the key difference between an error and a fraud is the intention of the perpetrator.”

Why deterrent controls are the exception follows from first principles. Controls work through different mechanisms:

| Control type | Mechanism | Useful against errors? |
|---|---|---|
| Preventive | Stops the event happening (limits, segregation, four-eyes) | Yes |
| Detective | Finds the event after it happens (reconciliation, monitoring) | Yes |
| Deterrent | Discourages a person from choosing to act (sanctions, visible consequences) | No: an error is not chosen |

Deterrence acts on intention. A person who makes a mistake did not decide to breach, so the threat of consequences does not prevent the mistake. Preventive and detective controls act on the event, so they work whether or not anyone intended it. (The three-way control typology in the table is a teaching frame; the reading itself names only the deterrent exception.)

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal reuses the internal fraud framework to prevent errors. The reading supports reuse of “many” controls, not all and not none, and singles out deterrent controls as the exception, giving intention as the reason. Option D states this. Option C has the right structure and reason but names the wrong control type.

**Fragile fact.** The exception is deterrent controls (they act on intention); detective and preventive controls carry over to errors.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Compliance Risk Management in Investment Activities. Schweser does not mention the deterrent-control exception; content is from GARP. The preventive, detective, deterrent typology in part a is a teaching aid, not a statement of the reading. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q15 of 17.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Option A says none of the controls carry over. The reading says many do. Option A would be correct only if errors and fraud shared no control mechanisms at all.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option B says all controls carry over, including deterrent controls, dropping the stated exception. It would be correct only if errors were deliberate choices that sanctions could discourage, which contradicts the definition of an error.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C keeps the structure and the reason but swaps deterrent controls for detective controls. Detective controls (finding breaches after the fact) work regardless of intent and are useful against errors. Option C would be correct if “detective” were replaced by “deterrent”.

d.reason: It restates GARP’s sentence: many internal fraud controls apply to errors, except deterrent controls, because the key difference between an error and a fraud is the intention of the perpetrator.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Chinese asset management firm is compiling a register of compliance risk drivers for its trading business. The observations below were collected during interviews.

| No. | Observation |
|---|---|
| 1 | A staff survey shows low employee engagement on the trading floor |
| 2 | Retail clients are far less informed about the firm’s structured products than its sales staff |
| 3 | Several traders manage both client orders and the firm’s own trading book |
| 4 | Budget cuts have left the middle office with insufficient resources |
| 5 | A spike in market volatility has sharply increased transaction volumes |
| 6 | The firm moved its head office from Shenzhen to Shanghai in the last year |

Which observations correspond to the drivers that the reading identifies as specific to compliance risk in market activities, as opposed to the general drivers shared with internal fraud?

options.text: 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 5 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst at a Chinese asset manager separating specific from general compliance risk drivers.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains compliance breaches in two layers. The first layer is shared with internal fraud in general; the second is specific to market activities:

| Layer | Drivers |
|---|---|
| General (shared with internal fraud) | Poor employee engagement within the firm; employee dissatisfaction or stress; allocation of insufficient resources to business units or activities; weak ethics culture |
| Specific to market activities | (1) Information asymmetry between buyers and sellers: retail investors are usually far less informed about products than the banks and asset managers selling them. (2) Conflicts of interest of traders who trade both for their clients’ books and for the firm’s own trading book. (3) Economic conditions, such as spikes in market volatility, that increase the number of transactions, leading to more errors and making abnormal transactions or insider trading easier to hide |

The direction in each specific driver matters. The seller knows more than the buyer. The trader’s conflict arises from serving clients and the firm at once. Volatility spikes raise transaction counts, and more transactions produce more errors and more cover for abuse.

**Applying it to this question**

Sort the observations:

| No. | Observation | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Low employee engagement | General |
| 2 | Retail clients far less informed than sales staff | Specific: information asymmetry |
| 3 | Traders run client orders and the firm’s own book | Specific: conflicts of interest |
| 4 | Middle office under-resourced | General: insufficient resources |
| 5 | Volatility spike raises transaction volumes | Specific: economic conditions |
| 6 | Head office relocation | Neither (irrelevant) |

The specific drivers are 2, 3 and 5.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: sellers know more than retail buyers; volatility spikes increase transactions, which raises errors and hides abuse. Engagement, stress, resources and ethics culture are the general layer.

**Reference**

LO 55.a: “Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFID, MiFID II, and Dodd-Frank.” GARP Chapter 14, Compliance Risk Management in Investment Activities. Schweser lists the same drivers in one paragraph, labelling the specific ones “broader drivers”; GARP calls them “more specific drivers of compliance risks in market activities”. The question follows GARP’s label. Content is otherwise identical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-14 a, where it is Q16 of 17.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Option A omits observation 5, treating economic conditions as outside the specific drivers. GARP lists spikes in market volatility, which increase transactions, as the third specific driver. Option A would be correct if observation 5 had described, say, a fall in interest rates with no effect on trading activity.

b.reason: Observations 2, 3 and 5 are, respectively, the information asymmetry, trader conflict of interest and economic conditions drivers that GARP lists as specific to compliance risk in market activities.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Option C adds observation 4. Insufficient resources allocated to business units is a general driver shared with internal fraud, not a market-specific one. Option C would be correct if the question asked for all drivers of compliance risk among the observations other than 1.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Option D accepts every relevant observation, merging the general and specific layers. It would be correct if the question asked which observations are drivers of compliance breaches of any kind (general or specific).
