questions.question:
A model risk consultant is reviewing the development test plan for a JPY interest rate risk model at a Japanese regional bank. The model is intended for three deposit products, and its outputs feed the bank’s funds transfer pricing model. The plan contains the following features:

I. Testing is limited to market conditions observed in the development sample, because scenarios outside ordinary expectations are left to later validation.

II. Extreme values for the inputs are evaluated to identify any boundaries of the model’s effectiveness.

III. The impact of the model’s results on the funds transfer pricing model, which uses them as inputs, is evaluated.

IV. Testing covers only the first of the three deposit products, because the model was originally designed for that product.

Which of the features are consistent with best practice for model testing?

options.text: I and II only
II only
II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Model risk consultant auditing four features of a JPY interest rate risk model’s development test plan.

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls testing an integral part of model development: the components of a model and its overall functioning are evaluated to determine whether it performs as intended. The guidance lists what testing should cover:

| Testing element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Accuracy, robustness, stability | Confirm the model is correct and does not behave erratically |
| Potential limitations; impact of assumptions | Expose where the model’s simplifications bite |
| Behaviour over a range of input values | Show how outputs respond across inputs |
| Situations of poor performance | Identify where the model becomes unreliable |
| Variety of market conditions | Apply to actual circumstances, including scenarios outside the range of ordinary expectations |
| Variety of products or applications | Cover every product or application the model is intended for |
| Extreme input values | Identify the boundaries of model effectiveness |
| Downstream models | Evaluate the impact on other models that use the results as inputs |

The common thread is that testing must reflect how the model will actually be used. A model tested only in calm conditions, on one product, in isolation, gives no information about the circumstances in which it is most likely to fail.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each feature against the list:

I. Limits testing to observed conditions and defers unusual scenarios. GARP requires scenarios outside the range of ordinary expectations during development testing. Inconsistent.

II. Extreme input values to find boundaries of effectiveness. Stated directly in GARP. Consistent.

III. Evaluates the effect on the funds transfer pricing model that uses the outputs. Stated directly in GARP. Consistent.

IV. Tests one product although three are intended. GARP requires testing to encompass the variety of products or applications for which the model is intended. Inconsistent.

Only II and III are consistent, which is option C.

**Fragile fact.** Scope: development testing must already include unusual scenarios outside ordinary expectations and every intended product; it is not deferred to validation.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser phrases the condition as testing in normal and extreme (stressed) states, including unusual but still plausible conditions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q4 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A accepts I, which drops the condition that testing must include scenarios outside ordinary expectations and wrongly defers it to validation. A would be correct only if the guidance limited development testing to the historical sample, which it does not. It also omits III.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B omits III, treating downstream models as outside the scope of testing. GARP expressly includes them. B would be correct only for a stand-alone model whose outputs feed no other model, which the stem rules out.

c.reason: GARP states that extreme values for inputs should be evaluated to identify any boundaries of model effectiveness (II), and that the impact of model results on other models that rely on those results as inputs should also be evaluated (III).

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D accepts IV, which narrows testing to the product the model was originally built for. GARP requires testing across all intended products or applications. D would be correct only if the model were intended for that one product alone.

questions.question: A senior quantitative analyst at a German bank is developing a EUR probability of default model. She proposes to accept the model’s calibration on the basis of one statistical test at the 95% confidence level, which did not reject the null hypothesis that the model is correctly calibrated. Which of the following statements about her proposal is most accurate?

options.text: Relying on one test is insufficient, because tests cannot unambiguously reject false hypotheses or accept true ones on sample information, and a variety of tests should be applied.
Relying on one test is sufficient, provided its confidence level is set high enough to eliminate the possibility of both Type I and Type II errors from the conclusion.
Relying on one test is insufficient, because failing to reject the null of correct calibration when it is false is a Type I error, which only a second test can detect.
Relying on one test is sufficient, because the appropriate statistical test depends only on the purpose of the model and not on its distributional assumptions.

questions.solution:
Senior quantitative analyst at a German bank proposing to accept a EUR PD model’s calibration on one test.

**Concept and theory**

Statistical tests are run on samples, and a sample is only a partial view of the population. A test therefore never proves a hypothesis true or false; it only tells us whether the sample evidence is strong enough to reject it at a chosen confidence level. Two kinds of error are always possible:

| Error | Definition | In a calibration test (null: model is correctly calibrated) |
|---|---|---|
| Type I | Rejecting the null when it is true | Rejecting a model that is in fact well calibrated |
| Type II | Failing to reject the null when it is false | Accepting a model that is in fact miscalibrated |

GARP makes three related points. First, the nature of testing depends on the type of model and its context; for example, the appropriate statistical tests depend on specific distributional assumptions and on the purpose of the model. Second, in many cases statistical tests cannot unambiguously reject false hypotheses or accept true ones based on sample information. Third, different tests have different strengths and weaknesses under different conditions, so any single test is rarely sufficient and banks should apply a variety of tests to develop a sound model. Raising the confidence level does not escape the problem: as a standard statistical result (not stated in the reading), for a given sample it lowers the chance of a Type I error but raises the chance of a Type II error.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst has one test that did not reject correct calibration. That outcome is consistent with a well-calibrated model, but it is also consistent with a miscalibrated model that the test lacked the power to detect (a Type II error). The 95% confidence level does not resolve this. The guidance’s answer is a variety of tests, which is A.

**Fragile fact.** Type I = reject a true null; Type II = fail to reject a false null. A test that “passes” a model is exposed to Type II error.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. The Type I and Type II labels come from Schweser, which frames the use of multiple tests as a way to avoid these errors; GARP states the same idea without the labels. No conflict on substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q5 of 16.

a.reason: GARP states that statistical tests cannot unambiguously reject false hypotheses or accept true ones based on sample information, that different tests have different strengths and weaknesses, and that any single test is rarely sufficient, so banks should apply a variety of tests.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B claims a high enough confidence level can eliminate both error types. GARP’s point is that tests based on sample information cannot unambiguously reject false hypotheses or accept true ones, so no choice of confidence level removes both risks (and, as standard statistics adds, for a given sample reducing one error type increases the other). B would be correct only with complete population data, in which case no inference would be needed.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reaches the right conclusion but mislabels the error. Failing to reject a null that is false is a Type II error, not Type I. C would be correct if it described rejecting a correctly calibrated model, which is the Type I case.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D drops one of the two conditions GARP gives: the appropriate test depends on distributional assumptions and on purpose. D also concludes that one test suffices, which contradicts the guidance. It would be closer to correct only if the stem asked which single factor is irrelevant to test choice, and none is.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q6
questions.question: The CRO of a Chinese bank is reviewing the development of a CNY loss model for small business loans. For borrowers in one industry sector, the developers have raised the model’s statistical loss estimate by 15% to reflect their view of a recent change in sector conditions. The rationale for the adjustment is recorded only in an informal email between two developers. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The adjustment is not permitted, because statistical output from a model must not be modified with judgmental or qualitative adjustments during development.
The adjustment may be appropriate, but it should be made in an appropriate and systematic manner and be well documented as part of the development process.
The adjustment needs no further documentation, because judgmental adjustments fall outside the development process and so outside model risk management.
The adjustment may be appropriate, but only the validation function, and never the developers, may make judgmental adjustments to a model’s statistical output.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Chinese bank reviewing a 15% judgmental uplift to a CNY small business loss model, recorded only in an email.

**Concept and theory**

Statistical output is rarely the whole story. A model estimated on past data may miss a recent change that experienced staff can see, so developers sometimes take the statistical output and modify it with judgmental or qualitative adjustments as part of development. GARP accepts that “such practices may be appropriate”, and adds that banks should ensure the development of the more judgmental and qualitative aspects of their models is also sound.

The safeguard is process, not prohibition. Any such adjustment made during development should be:

- conducted in an appropriate and systematic manner (a defined basis and method rather than ad hoc discretion), and
- well documented, so that others can understand why it was made and test whether it remains justified.

Schweser expresses the same requirement as alterations having a reasonable or logical basis and being clearly documented. Without documentation, the adjustment becomes an untraceable part of the model that no validator or user can assess.

**Applying it to this question**

The uplift itself is not the problem; a sector change is a legitimate reason for judgment. The problem is that the rationale sits only in an informal email between two developers, which is neither systematic nor well documented. The size of the uplift (15%) does not decide the answer: the guidance sets no numerical limit, only process requirements. B states the correct treatment.

**Fragile fact.** Judgmental adjustments are allowed in development; what is required is that they be systematic and well documented. There is no numerical cap.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. No GARP vs Schweser conflict (Schweser: reasonable or logical basis, clearly documented).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q6 of 16.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A forbids judgmental adjustments outright. GARP explicitly says they may be appropriate. A would be correct only under a policy banning overlays, which the guidance does not impose.

b.reason: GARP states that banks may modify statistical output with judgmental or qualitative adjustments as part of development, that such practices may be appropriate, and that banks should ensure the adjustments are conducted in an appropriate and systematic manner and are well documented.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C places judgmental adjustments outside development and outside model risk management. GARP treats them as part of the development process and requires the judgmental aspects of models to be sound. C would be correct only for analysis that is not part of a model at all.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D accepts the adjustment but reassigns it to the validation function. GARP describes such adjustments as part of model development, made by the bank in building the model; validation later reviews them. D would be correct only if the question asked who evaluates judgmental adjustments, not who makes them.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK bank is preparing a report on the role of model users in the bank’s model development and use. Which of the following statements should the auditor include as most accurate?

options.text: Model users should be kept out of the development process, because their business insight would compromise the objectivity of the developers’ modeling choices.
Questioning of a model’s assumptions by business managers who disagree with its outcomes is unhealthy and should be discouraged during model development.
Because users have a strong interest in well-functioning models, their challenge can serve as the bank’s main source of criticism independent of the line of business.
Model use provides an additional opportunity to test whether a model is functioning effectively and to assess its performance over time as conditions change.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a UK bank choosing the most accurate statement on the role of model users.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Model Use subsection treats use as a continuation of development rather than a separate world. Its main points are:

- Model use provides an additional opportunity to test whether a model is functioning effectively and to assess its performance over time as conditions and applications change.
- Users are a knowledgeable internal constituency with a strong interest in models that work well and reflect economic and business realities, so they are a source of productive feedback.
- Users can provide valuable business insight during the development process.
- Business managers affected by model outcomes may question methods or assumptions; this can be healthy if it is constructive and makes developers explain and justify their choices.
- But user challenge has limits (it may be weak, not comprehensive and asymmetric), so its motivation should be evaluated and banks should also seek criticism from sources independent of the line of business using the model.

The motivation is practical: users see the model in action every day, so they notice problems early; but they also have a stake in its outputs, so their view cannot be the only check.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor needs a statement that matches the guidance. D restates the first bullet directly. A and B treat user input as harmful, and C treats it as sufficient and even as independent, which the guidance rejects.

**Fragile fact.** Users are a valuable but not independent source of challenge: helpful during development and use, but independent criticism must still be sought.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4 Model Development, Implementation, and Use, subsection Model Use. Schweser’s LO 56.c section does not cover the Model Use material; content is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q7 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says users can provide valuable business insight during development. A reverses this into a reason for exclusion. It would be correct only if user input were a conflict that the guidance wanted removed, which it is not.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says such questioning can be healthy if it is constructive and causes developers to explain and justify assumptions. B calls it unhealthy. B would be closer to correct only for challenge that is not constructive, and even then the guidance asks banks to evaluate its motivation, not to discourage it.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** C treats the users as the independent source of criticism. GARP says banks should solicit constructive criticism from sources independent of the line of business using the model, precisely because users’ challenge is limited. C would be correct only if the challenging party were outside the business line.

d.reason: GARP states that model use provides additional opportunity to test whether a model is functioning effectively and to assess its performance over time as conditions and model applications change.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Swiss bank complains that the reports produced from the bank’s CHF mortgage loss model are hard to interpret. The modelers report one base-case loss figure, written in technical terms. Which of the following recommendations is most consistent with best practice for reports used in business decision making?

options.text: Reports need be comprehensible only to the modelers, because decision makers and modelers can be assumed to interpret their contents in the same way.
Reports should show only the base-case figure, because estimates under alternative input scenarios would reveal limitations that weaken confidence in the model.
Reports should be clear and comprehensible, and a range of estimates for different input and assumption values can indicate the model’s robustness, stability and limitations.
Reports lie outside model risk management, because translating estimates into business information cannot itself contribute to decisions based on misleading outputs.

questions.solution:
Swiss bank risk committee member finding the CHF mortgage loss model’s single technical base-case figure hard to interpret.

**Concept and theory**

A model reaches decision makers through reports, so GARP says reports used for business decision making play a critical role in model risk management. Two requirements follow:

1. **Clarity.** Reports should be clear and comprehensible, taking into account that decision makers and modelers often come from quite different backgrounds and may interpret the contents in different ways.
2. **Ranges.** Reports that provide a range of estimates for different input-value scenarios and assumption values can give decision makers important indications of the model’s accuracy, robustness and stability, as well as information on its limitations.

The idea is that a single figure in technical language hides both the meaning of the number and how fragile it is. Showing how the estimate moves when inputs and assumptions change lets a non-specialist see whether the model is stable and where its limits lie.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem identifies two failings: technical language and a single base-case figure. C addresses both, by requiring clarity and a range of estimates across scenarios. The other options defend one of the failings or deny that reports matter.

**Fragile fact.** Showing limitations is the point of a range of estimates in a report; it is a feature of good reporting, not a weakness to hide.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4 Model Development, Implementation, and Use, subsection Model Use. Schweser’s LO 56.c section does not cover reporting practice; content is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q8 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says decision makers and modelers often come from different backgrounds and may interpret contents differently. A assumes the opposite. It would be correct only in an organisation where the decision makers were themselves the modelers.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP presents the disclosure of limitations through ranges as a benefit to decision makers. B treats revealing limitations as a reason to suppress the ranges. It would be correct only if the goal of reporting were to maximise confidence in the model, which is the opposite of the guidance’s intent.

c.reason: GARP states that reports should be clear and comprehensible, and that reports providing a range of estimates for different input-value scenarios and assumption values can indicate the model’s accuracy, robustness and stability as well as its limitations.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D removes reports from model risk management. GARP says reports play a critical role in it. D would be correct only for output that is not used in business decisions.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q9
questions.question: An operational risk manager at a US bank is reviewing the implementation plan for a new USD credit loss model. In production the model will draw data from three source systems and feed its results into two reporting systems. The project budget funds the coding of the model’s calculations only; no money is allocated to data feeds, controls or reporting systems. Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: The plan is adequate, because information systems are a technology matter that lies outside the scope of model risk management.
The plan is adequate if the mathematics is correct, because data flows and aggregation affect how results are presented but not their accuracy.
The plan is inadequate, and the remedy is to build all data management into the model’s code so that no supporting systems are needed.
The plan is inadequate, because sound model risk management depends on investment in supporting systems, controls and testing for effective systems integration.

questions.solution:
Operational risk manager at a US bank reviewing a USD credit loss model implementation budget that funds only the model’s code.

**Concept and theory**

Implementation is where a correct model on paper becomes a working tool. GARP notes that models are typically embedded in larger information systems that manage the flow of data from various sources into the model and handle the aggregation and reporting of model outcomes. Three practices follow:

- Model calculations should be properly coordinated with the capabilities and requirements of information systems.
- Sound model risk management depends on substantial investment in supporting systems to ensure data and reporting integrity.
- That investment should come with controls and testing to ensure proper implementation of models, effective systems integration and appropriate use.

The reasoning is that model risk can arise anywhere from design through implementation. A mathematically correct model that receives incomplete data from a feed, or whose results are mis-aggregated on the way to a report, produces wrong decisions just as surely as a flawed formula. Schweser summarises the same point as a robust internal control system, involving both individuals and computers, supporting effective development and implementation.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem shows a model that depends on three source systems and two reporting systems, with no budget for feeds, controls or reporting. That leaves data and reporting integrity, systems integration and implementation testing unfunded. The plan is therefore inadequate for the reason given in D.

**Fragile fact.** Implementation risk sits in the systems around the model (data in, aggregation and reporting out), not only in the model’s own code.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. No GARP vs Schweser conflict (Schweser: a robust internal control system involving individuals and computers).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q9 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A excludes information systems from model risk management. GARP places supporting systems at the centre of sound model risk management. A would be correct only for a model that runs entirely on its own with no data feeds or reporting, which is not this model.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B claims correct mathematics is enough because data flows affect only presentation. GARP says the information systems manage the flow of data into the model as well as aggregation and reporting, so they affect accuracy. B would be correct only if the inputs were guaranteed complete and accurate by some other means.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** C reaches the right verdict but proposes eliminating supporting systems entirely. GARP expects calculations to be coordinated with information systems and backed by investment in them, not replaced. C would be correct only if a model could operate with no external data sources or reporting outputs.

d.reason: GARP states that sound model risk management depends on substantial investment in supporting systems to ensure data and reporting integrity, together with controls and testing to ensure proper implementation of models, effective systems integration and appropriate use.

questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at an Australian bank is reviewing a proposal to address model risk in a AUD commercial property loss model. The model fits a parametric loss distribution, and the proposal is to report the 99.9th percentile of the fitted distribution instead of the 99th, describing the change as conservative.

| Percentile of fitted distribution | Loss (AUD m) |
|---|---|
| 99th | 410 |
| 99.9th | 655 |

Which of the following statements about the proposal is most accurate?

options.text: The change is not necessarily conservative, because if the distribution was misestimated or misspecified in the first place, the more extreme point may still understate the risk.
The change is necessarily conservative, because a higher percentile of any fitted distribution must lie above the true loss at the lower percentile, whatever the specification.
The change is conservative and, once accepted, will remain conservative over time, because assumptions that are conservative at the outset stay conservative as conditions change.
The change is not conservative, because conservatism may be introduced only through the model’s inputs and never through choices or adjustments made to the model’s outputs.

questions.solution:
Australian bank credit risk analyst assessing a proposal to report the 99.9th rather than the 99th percentile of a fitted AUD loss distribution as “conservative”.

**Concept and theory**

Because all models are imperfect, GARP says it can be prudent to account for model uncertainty in the interest of conservatism. But it warns that banks should be careful in applying conservatism broadly or in claiming that adjustments are conservative, because the impact of conservatism in complex models may not be obvious or intuitive. Its specific warnings are:

- Aspects that appear conservative in one model may not be truly conservative compared with alternative methods.
- Simply picking an extreme point on a given modeled distribution may not be conservative if the distribution was misestimated or misspecified in the first place.
- Initially conservative assumptions may not remain conservative over time.

The key insight is that a percentile is only as good as the distribution it is read from. If the fitted tail is too thin, every percentile of it is too low; moving further into a wrong tail does not guarantee coverage of the true risk.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal moves from AUD 410 million to AUD 655 million by reading a higher percentile from the same fitted distribution. The table is a distractor: the size of the increase tells us nothing about whether the true 99.9th or even 99th percentile loss is higher still. The deciding fact is that the distribution itself may be misestimated or misspecified, which is A.

**Fragile fact.** A higher percentile of a misspecified distribution is not automatically conservative; conservatism must be demonstrated, not assumed.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4 Model Development, Implementation, and Use, subsection Model Use. Schweser’s LO 56.c section does not cover the conservatism caveats; content is from GARP only. (The general principle of informed conservatism appears in GARP 15.3 and belongs to LO 56.b.)

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q10 of 16.

a.reason: GARP states that simply picking an extreme point on a given modeled distribution may not be conservative if the distribution was misestimated or misspecified in the first place.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B asserts the change is necessarily conservative whatever the specification. That is exactly the claim GARP warns against; if the specification is wrong, the higher percentile of the fitted distribution can still lie below the true loss. B would be correct only if the distribution were known to be correctly specified and estimated.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C says initially conservative assumptions stay conservative. GARP says they may not remain conservative over time. C would be correct only if market conditions and the portfolio never changed.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D restricts conservatism to inputs. GARP lists several channels: adjusting inputs or calculations to produce more severe output, judgmental conservative adjustments to model output, placing less emphasis on the output, or supplementing it with other models. D would be correct only if the guidance limited conservatism to inputs, which it does not.

questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q11
questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the development of a GBP probability of default model for a new small business lending product at a UK challenger bank. Because the bank has no history for the product, the developers built the model on an external dataset bought from a data vendor, pooled from lenders whose borrowers differ from the bank’s target market. The developers reweighted the observations to resemble the expected portfolio. Which of the following best describes best practice in this situation?

options.text: Because the data come from an established vendor, the bank may rely on the vendor’s own quality checks and need not assess the data’s relevance itself.
Because the data were reweighted to resemble the portfolio, the adjustment removes the limitation, which therefore need not be communicated to users.
The lack of representativeness and the reweighting should be tracked and analysed so users are aware of limitations, which matters especially for external data and new products.
External data may be used only as a benchmark in later validation, because data used to develop a model must come from the bank’s own portfolio.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant reviewing a UK challenger bank’s GBP PD model built on reweighted external vendor data for a new product.

**Concept and theory**

The data requirements in development are graded by risk. Every model needs a rigorous assessment of data quality and relevance, but GARP singles out cases where the data may not match the bank:

- If data and information are not representative of the bank’s portfolio or other characteristics, or
- if assumptions are made to adjust the data and information,

then these factors should be properly tracked and analysed so that users are aware of potential limitations. GARP adds that this is particularly important for external data and information (from a vendor or outside party), especially as they relate to new products, instruments or activities.

The motivation is that an adjustment such as reweighting is itself an assumption: it assumes the reweighted pool behaves like the bank’s future portfolio. That assumption may be wrong, so the limitation does not disappear when the data are adjusted; it changes form and must be made visible to the people relying on the model.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem combines all three high-risk features: external vendor data, a new product, and data that are not representative and have been adjusted. GARP’s requirement is to track and analyse these factors so users know the limitations, which is C. The vendor’s reputation and the reweighting do not remove the requirement.

**Fragile fact.** An adjustment to unrepresentative data is itself something to track and disclose; it does not cure the limitation.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. No GARP vs Schweser conflict (Schweser: proxies, unrepresentative data and adjustments, for example from external sources, must be clearly documented and made clear to users so they can judge the usefulness of the data).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q11 of 16.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** A hands the relevance assessment to the vendor. GARP requires the bank’s developers to assess data quality and relevance and demonstrate suitability. A vendor can check that its data are accurate, but only the bank can judge relevance to its own portfolio. A would be correct only if the question asked who is responsible for the vendor’s internal data checks.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B treats the adjustment as removing the need for disclosure. GARP lists adjustments to data as one of the very factors that must be tracked and analysed for users. B would be correct only if no adjustment or representativeness issue existed.

c.reason: GARP states that if data are not representative of the bank’s portfolio, or if assumptions are made to adjust the data, these factors should be properly tracked and analysed so that users are aware of potential limitations, and that this is particularly important for external data, especially for new products.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D bans external data in development. GARP expressly contemplates external data in development and asks for tracking and analysis, not exclusion. D would be correct only under a rule that development data must be internal, which the guidance does not contain.

questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q12
questions.question:
The head of model risk at a French bank is reviewing the log of challenges raised by the retail lending business against the EUR credit limit model over two years.

| Direction of model output | Occasions | Challenges raised |
|---|---|---|
| Output reduced approved limits | 22 | 14 |
| Output increased approved limits | 19 | 0 |

The business head argues that the absence of challenges when the model increased limits shows that the model’s risk is low. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The log shows effective challenge, because users have the strongest incentive of any party to find model weaknesses, so their silence confirms that model risk is low.
The log suggests that user challenge is asymmetric, so the motivation behind it should be evaluated and criticism sought from sources independent of the business line.
The log suggests that user challenge is asymmetric, so the bank should stop accepting challenges from users and rely only on the developers’ own review of the model.
The log suggests that user challenge is comprehensive but infrequent, so the bank should increase it by linking users’ compensation more closely to model outputs.

questions.solution:
Head of model risk at a French bank reading a challenge log in which the business challenged the EUR limit model only when it cut limits.

**Concept and theory**

GARP values user feedback but sets out why user challenge cannot be relied on alone. User challenge:

- **may be weak** if the model does not materially affect the users’ results, if resulting changes are perceived to harm the business line, or if change is regarded as expensive or difficult;
- **tends not to be comprehensive**, because users focus on aspects with the most direct impact on their measured business performance or compensation and may ignore other elements and applications;
- **tends to be asymmetric**, because users are less likely to challenge an outcome that results in an advantage for them.

GARP adds that users may incorrectly believe model risk is low simply because outcomes from model-based decisions appear favourable. Its prescription: evaluate carefully the nature and motivation behind users’ input, and solicit constructive suggestions and criticism from sources independent of the line of business using the model.

**Applying it to this question**

The log shows 14 challenges in 22 occasions when the output cut limits, and none in 19 occasions when it raised them. That is the asymmetric pattern GARP describes. The business head’s argument (no challenge when outcomes are favourable means low model risk) is the incorrect belief GARP warns about. The appropriate response is B.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: users challenge unfavourable outcomes and stay silent on favourable ones; silence is not evidence of low model risk.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4 Model Development, Implementation, and Use, subsection Model Use. Schweser’s LO 56.c section does not cover user challenge; content is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q12 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A reads the silence as confirmation of low model risk. GARP says users may incorrectly believe model risk is low because outcomes appear favourable. A would be correct only if challenge were equally likely in both directions.

b.reason: GARP states that user challenges tend to be asymmetric because users are less likely to challenge an outcome that results in an advantage for them, and that the nature and motivation of users’ input should be evaluated and criticism solicited from sources independent of the line of business.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** C correctly diagnoses asymmetry but moves the challenge role to the developers. GARP asks for criticism from sources independent of the business line, and developers are not independent of their own model. It also does not tell banks to stop accepting user challenge, which remains a source of insight. C would be correct only if the developers were the independent party, which they are not.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D attributes “comprehensive” to user challenge, when GARP says it tends not to be comprehensive, and proposes strengthening the link to compensation, which is the very focus that narrows user challenge. D would be closer to correct only if the problem were simply too few challenges with no directional bias.

questions.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q13
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is reviewing the development testing file for a CAD market risk model. Which of the following features of the file is NOT consistent with best practice for testing during model development?

options.text: The file sets out the purpose, design and execution of each test plan used during development.
The file contains summary results with commentary and evaluation, and analysis of informative samples.
The file records only the tests the model passed, because failed tests are fixed before the model is released.
The file assesses the impact of assumptions and identifies situations in which the model performs poorly.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Canadian bank finding the feature of a CAD market risk model’s development testing file that is NOT consistent with best practice.

**Concept and theory**

Testing is only as useful as the record it leaves. GARP specifies what testing activities should include and that they should be documented:

| Element of testing activity | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Purpose, design and execution of test plans | Shows what was tested, how and why |
| Summary results with commentary and evaluation | Interprets the results, not just lists them |
| Detailed analysis of informative samples | Shows the evidence behind conclusions |
| Impact of assumptions; situations where the model performs poorly or becomes unreliable | Records the model’s limitations for users and validators |
| Appropriate documentation | Makes testing reviewable by others |

The purpose of testing includes assessing potential limitations and identifying situations where the model performs poorly. A test file that keeps only successes therefore defeats one of the main purposes of testing: the failures are exactly the evidence about where the model’s boundaries lie.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT consistent. A, B and D each restate a GARP requirement. C keeps only passed tests, which removes the record of limitations and poor-performance situations that testing is meant to produce. Even if a failure is fixed, the test that revealed it is informative about the model’s behaviour and must be documented. C is the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Testing exists partly to find weaknesses; failed tests and poor-performance situations must be documented, not edited out.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. No GARP vs Schweser conflict (Schweser: potential weaknesses and circumstances where the model does not work must be noted; proper documentation, analysis and summarisation of the testing process).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q13 of 16.

a.reason: **True statement, qualifier trap.** A is a direct GARP requirement (purpose, design and execution of test plans). Choosing it reads the stem as “consistent” rather than “NOT consistent”. A would be the answer to a stem asking which feature is consistent with best practice.

b.reason: **True statement, qualifier trap.** B combines two GARP requirements (summary results with commentary and evaluation; detailed analysis of informative samples). It is consistent with best practice, so it cannot answer a NOT question. It would be correct under a stem asking what testing documentation should contain.

c.reason: GARP states that testing should assess potential limitations and identify situations where the model performs poorly or becomes unreliable, and that testing activities, including summary results with commentary and evaluation, should be appropriately documented. Recording only passed tests is inconsistent with both.

d.reason: **True statement, qualifier trap.** D restates GARP’s requirement to assess the impact of assumptions and identify situations of poor performance. It is the very practice that C violates. D would be the answer to a stem asking which feature shows that the file records the model’s limitations.

questions.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q14
questions.question: A model validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing the development documentation for an SGD foreign exchange options pricing model. The documentation describes the chosen volatility model and states that the numerical scheme used to solve it is “standard”. It does not mention any other theory or approach that was considered. Which of the following recommendations best reflects best practice for model development?

options.text: Make no change, because comparing a model with alternative approaches is required only for models whose theory is not supported by published research.
Add a comparison with alternatives only if the model later performs poorly in use, because such comparison serves as a remedy once a model has been shown to be weak.
Replace the description of the numerical scheme with a summary of outputs, because numerical approximations are implementation details with no bearing on merits and limitations.
Document a comparison with alternative theories and approaches, and explain the numerical techniques and approximations in detail with attention to their merits and limitations.

questions.solution:
Model validator at a Singapore bank reviewing SGD FX options model documentation that calls its numerical scheme “standard” and considers no alternatives.

**Concept and theory**

GARP asks development documentation to make a model understandable and defensible. Two requirements are tested here:

1. The model methodologies and processing components that implement the theory, including the mathematical specification and the numerical techniques and approximations, should be explained in detail with particular attention to merits and limitations.
2. Comparison with alternative theories and approaches is a fundamental component of a sound modeling process.

Numerical techniques matter because a correct theory can be implemented badly: a discretisation, a convergence tolerance or an approximation can distort outputs even when the underlying theory is sound. Comparison with alternatives matters because a model’s choices only make sense relative to what else could have been chosen; it exposes where the chosen approach is strong and where it is weak.

**Applying it to this question**

The documentation fails both requirements: it labels the numerical scheme “standard” without explaining it or its merits and limitations, and it mentions no alternative theory or approach. D remedies both. The other options either excuse the gaps or make comparison conditional.

**Fragile fact.** GARP calls comparison with alternatives fundamental; it is a standing requirement of development, not an optional reasonableness check.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4, subsection Model Development and Implementation. GARP vs Schweser difference in emphasis: Schweser says a comparison with alternative models “may serve” as a reasonability check, while GARP calls comparison with alternative theories and approaches a fundamental component of sound modeling. Resolved from GARP; this looks like Schweser compressing the wording rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A makes comparison conditional on a lack of published support. GARP requires the design to be generally supported by published research and treats comparison with alternatives as fundamental; one does not replace the other. A would be correct only if the guidance treated comparison as an exception, which it does not.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B makes comparison a remedy triggered by poor performance in use. GARP places it within the development process as a fundamental component, before the model is used. B would describe a later redevelopment step, not development best practice.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C treats numerical approximations as irrelevant to merits and limitations. GARP names numerical techniques and approximations as items to be explained in detail precisely because of their merits and limitations. C would be correct only for a model with an exact closed-form solution and no approximation.

d.reason: GARP states that methodologies and processing components, including numerical techniques and approximations, should be explained in detail with attention to merits and limitations, and that comparison with alternative theories and approaches is a fundamental component of a sound modeling process.

questions.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.

questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q15
questions.question:
The CRO of a Canadian bank plans to address model risk in the bank’s CAD loss models by applying broad conservative overlays and by holding a CAD 50 million capital cushion. A risk committee member drafts four statements on the use of conservatism:

I. A claim that model outputs are conservative should be justified and substantiated with a definition and measurement of that conservatism that is communicated to model users.

II. Sensitivity analysis or other types of stress testing can be used to demonstrate that a model is indeed conservative.

III. Holding an additional cushion of capital against potential losses from model risk is not an acceptable way for a bank to be conservative.

IV. Excessive conservatism has no cost, because overstating risk cannot lead model users to place less weight on the model’s outputs.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
CRO of a Canadian bank planning broad conservative overlays and a CAD 50 million capital cushion; four statements on conservatism.

**Concept and theory**

GARP accepts conservatism as a response to model uncertainty but surrounds it with conditions, because conservatism that is assumed rather than demonstrated can be false comfort. The key points:

| Point | GARP position |
|---|---|
| Claims of conservatism | Should be justified and substantiated with a definition and measurement communicated to users |
| Demonstrating conservatism | Sensitivity analysis or other stress testing can be used |
| Capital cushion | An acceptable way to be conservative: hold additional capital against model risk losses |
| Conservatism as substitute for improvement | An impediment if it dissuades the bank from improving the model |
| Excessive conservatism | Can lead model users to discount the model outputs |

The reasoning is that conservatism has costs as well as benefits. If users learn that outputs are padded, they stop taking them at face value, and the model loses its usefulness for decisions.

**Applying it to this question**

Assess each statement:

I. Matches GARP’s requirement to justify and substantiate claims of conservatism. Correct.

II. Matches GARP’s statement that sensitivity analysis or stress testing can demonstrate conservatism. Correct.

III. GARP lists a capital cushion as one way a bank may choose to be conservative. Incorrect.

IV. GARP says excessive conservatism can lead users to discount outputs, so it has a cost. Incorrect.

Only I and II are correct, which is B. The CAD 50 million figure is irrelevant; no amount is judged in the guidance.

**Fragile fact.** A capital cushion is an accepted form of conservatism, but conservatism must be defined, measured and communicated, and too much of it makes users discount the model.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4 Model Development, Implementation, and Use, subsection Model Use. Schweser’s LO 56.c section does not cover these conservatism practices; content is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q15 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A drops II, treating sensitivity and stress testing as irrelevant to demonstrating conservatism. GARP names them as a way to do so. A would be correct only if II were false.

b.reason: GARP states that banks should justify and substantiate claims that outputs are conservative with a definition and measurement communicated to users (I), and that sensitivity analysis or other stress testing can be used to demonstrate that a model is indeed conservative (II).

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C accepts III, which reverses GARP’s statement that holding an additional capital cushion is a way a bank may choose to be conservative. C would be correct if III said a capital cushion is acceptable.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D accepts IV, which reverses GARP’s warning that excessive conservatism can lead users to discount outputs, and it drops the true statement I. D would be correct only if excessive conservatism were costless and I were false.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 c Q16
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank is presenting the output of a new BRL deposit outflow model, whose point estimate of the 30-day outflow is BRL 1.2 billion. Some factors that drive outflows are unobservable and are not fully incorporated in the model. Which of the following statements about how she should treat model uncertainty is most accurate?

options.text: Presenting a range of outputs rather than a point estimate can signal model uncertainty and avoid spurious precision, and inputs or calculations may be adjusted to produce more severe output.
Presenting the point estimate alone is preferable, because model uncertainty should be reflected only where it can be quantified through a confidence interval around the estimate.
Presenting a range is unnecessary, because a model whose development testing is complete no longer carries meaningful uncertainty or inaccuracy in its point estimate.
Presenting a range is preferable, but accounting for uncertainty must never involve placing less emphasis on the model’s output or supplementing it with other models.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank deciding how to present uncertainty around a BRL 1.2 billion deposit outflow estimate.

**Concept and theory**

Because models are by definition imperfect representations of reality, GARP says all models have some degree of uncertainty and inaccuracy, and that understanding this and demonstrating that the bank accounts for it are important outcomes of effective development, implementation and use.

- **Measuring it.** Uncertainty can sometimes be quantified, for example by assessing the potential impact of factors that are unobservable or not fully incorporated in the model, or by the confidence interval around a statistical point estimate. At other times only a qualitative assessment is possible.
- **Signalling it.** Using a range of outputs rather than a simple point estimate is a useful way to signal model uncertainty and avoid spurious precision.
- **Accounting for it.** In either case it can be prudent to adjust model inputs or calculations to produce more severe or adverse output in the interest of conservatism; to make judgmental conservative adjustments to output; to place less emphasis on the model’s output; or to use the model only when supplemented by other models or approaches.

“Spurious precision” is the false confidence created by a single number reported to many digits when the model cannot support that accuracy.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem flags unobservable factors that the model does not fully incorporate, which is GARP’s own example of a source of model uncertainty. A single BRL 1.2 billion figure would imply spurious precision. A states both the range-of-outputs practice and one of the accepted ways of accounting for uncertainty. The size of the estimate is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Uncertainty that can only be assessed qualitatively still has to be accounted for; a range of outputs avoids spurious precision.

**Reference**

LO 56.c: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.4 Model Development, Implementation, and Use, subsection Model Use. Schweser’s LO 56.c section does not cover model uncertainty; content is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 c, where it is Q16 of 16.

a.reason: GARP states that using a range of outputs rather than a simple point estimate can signal model uncertainty and avoid spurious precision, and that it can be prudent to account for uncertainty by adjusting model inputs or calculations to produce more severe or adverse output.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B limits recognition of uncertainty to cases where a confidence interval is available. GARP says that when only a qualitative assessment is possible, it can still be prudent to account for uncertainty. B would be correct only if uncertainty that cannot be quantified could be ignored, which the guidance rejects.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** C says a tested model carries no meaningful uncertainty. GARP says all models have some degree of uncertainty and inaccuracy because they are imperfect representations of reality. C would be correct only for a model that perfectly represents reality, which does not exist.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D forbids two of the methods GARP lists for accounting for uncertainty: placing less emphasis on the model’s output and supplementing it with other models. D would be correct if it said these methods may be used.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q1
questions.question:
A senior model validator at a Singapore bank is preparing a training note that maps validation activities to the three core elements of a comprehensive validation framework described in the supervisory guidance.

| Activity | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Reviewing the empirical evidence behind the variables selected and comparing the method with alternative theories |
| II | Confirming that the model’s computer code can be altered only by approved parties and that all changes are logged |
| III | Comparing realised default rates in a period not used in development with confidence intervals around the forecasts |
| IV | Comparing the model’s outputs with estimates from a vendor model and data from a retail credit bureau |

Which of the following correctly assigns each activity to the core element under which the guidance places it?

options.text: I: conceptual soundness; II: ongoing monitoring; III: outcomes analysis; IV: outcomes analysis
I: conceptual soundness; II: ongoing monitoring; III: outcomes analysis; IV: ongoing monitoring
I: conceptual soundness; II: conceptual soundness; III: outcomes analysis; IV: ongoing monitoring
I: ongoing monitoring; II: ongoing monitoring; III: outcomes analysis; IV: ongoing monitoring

questions.solution:
Senior validator at a Singapore bank mapping four validation activities to the three core elements.

**Concept and theory**

Model validation is the set of processes and activities intended to verify that models are performing as expected, in line with their design objectives and business uses. The supervisory guidance organises a comprehensive validation framework around three core elements, each with named sub-activities:

| Core element | Activities described under it | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluation of conceptual soundness | Developmental evidence; sensitivity analysis and stress testing; review of qualitative judgment | Is the design and construction of the model sound? |
| Ongoing monitoring | Process verification; benchmarking; override analysis | Is the model implemented, used and performing as intended now? |
| Outcomes analysis | Back-testing; parallel outcomes analysis; early-warning metrics | Do the model’s outputs agree with what actually happened? |

The logic of the split is temporal and evidential. Conceptual soundness looks at the model’s design (documentation, empirical evidence for methods and variables, comparison with alternative theories). Ongoing monitoring starts when the model enters production and checks that inputs, code, systems and reports still work and that the model still compares sensibly with alternatives. Outcomes analysis compares outputs with realised outcomes.

**Applying it to this question**

Activity I (evidence for variables, comparison with alternative theories) is the core of conceptual soundness. Activity II (code change control) is process verification, which the guidance places under ongoing monitoring. Activity III (realised outcomes against confidence intervals, in a period not used in development) is the definition of back-testing, part of outcomes analysis. Activity IV (comparison with a vendor model and credit bureau data) is benchmarking; the guidance gives exactly these examples for credit risk models and lists benchmarking under ongoing monitoring.

**Fragile fact.** Benchmarking sits under ongoing monitoring (with process verification), not under outcomes analysis; back-testing is the sub-activity of outcomes analysis.

**Reference**

LO 56.d: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process. GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5 Model Validation, “Key Elements of Comprehensive Validation”, “Ongoing Monitoring” and “Outcomes Analysis”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q1 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves benchmarking (IV) into outcomes analysis. Both compare model output with something else, but benchmarking compares with an alternative prediction (another model or data set), whereas outcomes analysis compares with realised outcomes. A would be right only if IV read “comparing outputs with realised default rates”.

b.reason: The guidance lists the elements as “Evaluation of conceptual soundness, including developmental evidence; Ongoing monitoring, including process verification and benchmarking; Outcomes analysis, including back-testing”. Option B is the only mapping that follows this list for all four activities.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It treats code change control (II) as part of conceptual soundness. Conceptual soundness assesses design and construction; checking that implemented code is correct and controlled is process verification within ongoing monitoring. C would be right if II read “reviewing the mathematical specification chosen by the developers”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It places the review of developmental evidence (I) in ongoing monitoring. Developmental evidence is reviewed before use and again at material changes, but the guidance names it under conceptual soundness. D would be right if I described checking that live data feeds remain complete.

questions.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q2
questions.question: The chief risk officer of an Irish bank is presenting to newly hired analysts in the model validation unit on the role of independence in validation. Which of the following statements should she include as the most accurate?

options.text: Independence is the ultimate objective of the validation framework, so validation is judged effective once validators sit in a separate unit.
Independence is established by a separate reporting line for validators, which is sufficient evidence that validation is objective and free of bias.
Validation is generally best performed by the model’s users, because their stake in whether the model is found valid gives them a strong incentive.
Some validation work may be done by developers or users, provided that an independent party critically reviews it and conducts additional activities.

questions.solution:
CRO of an Irish bank explaining independence in validation to new analysts.

**Concept and theory**

Validation is a form of effective challenge, so it needs people who are willing to find fault. The guidance therefore requires that validation involve a degree of independence from model development and use: generally it should be done by people who are not responsible for development or use and who have no stake in whether the model is found valid.

Three refinements matter for the exam:

- Independence is not an end in itself. Its purpose is to align incentives with the goals of validation.
- Independence may be supported by separate reporting lines, but it should be judged by actions and outcomes, since there may be other ways to ensure objectivity and prevent bias.
- As a practical matter some validation work may be most effectively done by developers and users. This is acceptable only if that work is subject to critical review by an independent party, who should conduct additional activities to ensure proper validation.

The overall quality of validation is judged by the manner in which models are subject to critical review: the extent and clarity of documentation, the issues identified by objective parties, and the actions management takes to address them.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO must choose the single statement that matches the guidance. The deciding facts are (i) independence is a means, not the goal, (ii) a reporting line is supporting evidence, not proof, and (iii) developer or user work is permitted when independently reviewed. Only D states (iii) correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: developers and users may perform some validation work, but never without critical review by an independent party; independence is judged by actions and outcomes, not by the organisation chart alone.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5 Model Validation (introductory text on independence). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says developers should generally not validate, with exceptions for “overly technical or specialized” areas subject to rigorous objective review; GARP frames the exception more broadly (work “most effectively done by model developers and users”) and adds that independence is judged by actions and outcomes. GARP used for content; this looks like Schweser compression rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q2 of 18.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It makes independence “the ultimate objective”. The guidance says the opposite: independence is not an end in itself but helps ensure that incentives are aligned with the goals of validation. A would be right if it said that the goal of validation is to verify that models perform as intended and independence serves that goal.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It treats a separate reporting line as sufficient evidence. The guidance says independence may be supported by separate reporting lines but should be judged by actions and outcomes. B would be right if “sufficient evidence” were replaced by “one supporting factor”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns the disqualifying feature into a qualification: validators should not have a stake in whether a model is found valid. A stake creates bias, not useful incentive. C would be right if it described users contributing validation work that an independent party then critically reviews.

d.reason: The guidance states that some validation work may be most effectively done by model developers and users, but it is essential that such work be subject to critical review by an independent party, who should conduct additional activities to ensure proper validation. D reproduces both conditions.

questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is assessing whether the model validation unit that reviews the bank’s CAD mortgage models has sufficient influence within the organisation. She has gathered four pieces of evidence. Which of the following most directly demonstrates that the unit has the influence the supervisory guidance requires of validation staff?

options.text: A record of past cases in which models, or the use of models, were changed as a result of the unit’s validation findings.
A record of the validators’ advanced technical qualifications and their long familiarity with the mortgage business line.
A record showing that the validators’ performance reviews are tied to the quality and critical rigour of their validations.
A record confirming that none of the validators is responsible for developing or using the models and none has a stake in them.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Canadian bank choosing evidence of the validation unit’s influence.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance says model validation, like other effective challenge, should be performed by staff with appropriate incentives, competence and influence. For validation specifically, it describes each condition:

| Condition | What the guidance requires of validation staff |
|---|---|
| Independence and incentives | No responsibility for development or use and no stake in the outcome; compensation and performance evaluation tied to the quality of validations and the degree of critical, unbiased review; a culture that encourages questioning. |
| Competence | Requisite knowledge, skills and expertise, often a high level of technical expertise, plus significant familiarity with the business line and the model’s intended use. |
| Influence | Explicit authority to challenge developers and users and to elevate findings; the unit they report to has sufficient influence or stature to ensure issues are addressed in a timely and substantive manner. |

Influence can be reflected in reporting lines, title, rank or designated responsibilities, but the guidance adds that it may be demonstrated by a pattern of actual instances in which models, or the use of models, have been appropriately changed as a result of validation. Authority on paper is not the same as authority that changes outcomes.

**Applying it to this question**

All four records are relevant to effective validation, but the auditor’s question is narrower: which demonstrates influence. Each wrong option evidences a different condition. A track record of changes caused by validation findings is the evidence the guidance itself names for influence.

**Fragile fact.** Influence is shown by outcomes: a pattern of models or model use actually changed because of validation, not merely by title or reporting line.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5 Model Validation (paragraphs on staff incentives, competence and influence). Schweser does not cover validator competence or influence for this LO; content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q3 of 18.

a.reason: The guidance states that influence may be demonstrated by a pattern of actual instances in which models, or the use of models, have been appropriately changed as a result of validation.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Technical qualifications and familiarity with the business line describe competence. B would be right if the question asked which evidence best shows that validators have the knowledge, skills and expertise required.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Performance reviews tied to the quality and rigour of validations describe incentives. B and C are both true features of good validation, but neither shows that findings get acted on. C would be right if the question asked how the bank supports appropriate incentives.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** No responsibility for development or use and no stake in the outcome describes independence. A fully independent unit can still be ignored. D would be right if the question asked about independence.

questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q4
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Mexican bank is preparing a recommendation on a newly developed prepayment model for an MXN product the bank has never offered. Because the product is new, there are too few observations to complete the planned validation activities before the model is first used, although no deficiencies have been found in the work done so far. According to the supervisory guidance, which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Reject the model, because a model that cannot be fully validated before first use must not be placed into production under any constraints.
Use the model without restriction, because the guidance exempts models for new products from validation until sufficient data have accumulated.
Document the limitation, communicate it in reports to users and senior management, and mitigate the resulting uncertainty with compensating controls.
Ask the model developers to sign off the validation themselves, because no independent data exist, and have internal audit review it at its next annual audit.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a Mexican bank with a new-product model that cannot be fully validated before first use.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance ties the range and rigour of validation before first use to the potential risk presented by use of the model, and it gives a decision ladder:

| Situation found before use | Required response |
|---|---|
| Significant deficiencies identified | Use not allowed, or permitted only under very tight constraints until the issues are resolved |
| Deficiencies too severe to be addressed within the model’s framework | Model rejected |
| Necessary validation not feasible before use (data paucity or other limitations) | Document the fact, communicate it in reports to users, senior management and other relevant parties, and mitigate the uncertainty with other compensating controls |

The guidance adds that the last case is particularly applicable to new models and to the use of existing models in new applications. Validation then continues after the model goes into use to track known limitations and identify new ones.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem states two facts: (i) data are too sparse to complete validation before use, and (ii) no deficiencies have been found. Fact (ii) rules out the “significant deficiencies” and “reject” rungs. Fact (i) is the infeasibility case, whose response is to document, communicate and compensate.

**Fragile fact.** Data paucity is not a deficiency: the response is document, communicate and use compensating controls, not reject. Rejection is for deficiencies too severe to fix within the model’s framework.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5 Model Validation (paragraph on validation prior to first use). Schweser does not address pre-use infeasibility; content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q4 of 18.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It forbids production “under any constraints”. Rejection is reserved for deficiencies too severe to fix within the model’s framework, and even significant deficiencies allow use under very tight constraints. A would be right if validation had found deficiencies too severe to address within the model’s framework.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** No exemption exists. Infeasibility triggers documentation, communication and compensating controls, not unrestricted use. B would be right only if it added that the limitation is reported and compensating controls are applied.

c.reason: The guidance states that if it is not feasible to conduct necessary validation activities prior to model use because of data paucity or other limitations, that fact should be documented and communicated in reports to users, senior management and other relevant parties, and the uncertainty should be mitigated by other compensating controls.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It hands sign-off to the developers. Developer work is acceptable only under critical review by an independent party, and internal audit’s role is to assess the framework, not to substitute for validation. D would be right if the developers’ work were critically reviewed by the independent validation function before use.
