questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q5
questions.question:
A risk committee member at a Hong Kong bank is reviewing the draft validation policy. The draft contains the following statements:

I. All model components, including input, processing and reporting, are subject to validation, whether the model is built in-house or purchased from a vendor.

II. Each model is reviewed at least annually, and more frequently if warranted, to determine whether it is working as intended and whether existing validation activities are sufficient.

III. Validation activity may be scaled back during periods of benign economic and financial conditions, because estimates of risk and potential loss are then at their most reliable.

IV. If deficiencies identified in validation are too severe to be addressed within the model’s framework, the model is rejected.

Which of the statements are consistent with the supervisory guidance?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at a Hong Kong bank auditing four validation policy statements on scope and timing.

**Concept and theory**

Scope and timing of validation in the guidance:

- **Scope.** All model components (input, processing and reporting) should be validated, equally for in-house models and for models purchased from or developed by vendors or consultants. Rigour is commensurate with the bank’s overall model use, the complexity and materiality of its models, and the size and complexity of its operations.
- **Continuity.** Validation continues after a model goes into use, to track known limitations and find new ones. The guidance stresses that validation is an important check during benign economic and financial conditions, when estimates of risk and potential loss can become overly optimistic and data may not reflect stressed conditions.
- **Periodic review.** At least annually, and more often if warranted, each model is reviewed to see whether it works as intended and whether existing validation activities are sufficient. Material changes are validated, and it is good practice for all models to undergo full validation at some fixed interval.
- **Consequences.** Significant deficiencies mean no use or use under tight constraints; deficiencies too severe to address within the model’s framework mean rejection.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the scope rule. Statement II restates the annual review rule. Statement III reverses the benign-period warning: benign conditions are when estimates become overly optimistic, so validation matters more, not less. Statement IV restates the rejection rule. The consistent set is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: benign conditions make risk estimates overly optimistic, so validation is an important check then. Review frequency is “at least annually”, not “annually”.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5 Model Validation (paragraphs on scope, rigour, ongoing validation, periodic review). Schweser does not cover these scope and timing rules; content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q5 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It omits IV, treating rejection as outside policy. The guidance explicitly says the model should be rejected when deficiencies are too severe to be addressed within its framework. A would be right if IV said deficiencies should always be fixed by adjustments within the model.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts III, which reverses the direction of the benign-period warning, and drops I and IV. B would be right only if III said validation is especially important in benign periods and I and IV were false.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It includes III. Benign periods make estimates look better than they are; the guidance does not permit validation to be scaled back then. C would be right if III were reworded to “maintained, because estimates of risk can become overly optimistic” and II were false.

d.reason: I, II and IV each match the guidance. III is inconsistent because the guidance describes validation as an important check on model use during benign conditions, when risk estimates can become overly optimistic.

questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q6
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an Australian bank is validating a probability of default model that the bank has extended from its AUD residential mortgage book to a new small business lending product. The model was rebuilt using external data purchased from a data vendor. Which of the following activities is least likely to form part of the evaluation of conceptual soundness?

options.text: Assessing whether the purchased external data are reasonably representative of the bank’s small business lending portfolio.
Comparing realised default rates in the year after deployment with the confidence intervals placed around the model’s forecasts.
Reviewing the developmental evidence again, because extending the model to a new product is a material change in the model.
Evaluating the logic, judgment and types of qualitative information used by the developers when constructing the model.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at an Australian bank validating a PD model extended to a new product with external data.

**Concept and theory**

The evaluation of conceptual soundness assesses the quality of the model’s design and construction. It entails:

- review of documentation and empirical evidence supporting the methods used and variables selected, including comparison with alternative theories and approaches;
- assessment of key assumptions and the choice of variables, with analysis of their impact on outputs and focus on limitations;
- evaluation of the relevance of the data used to build the model, to ensure it is reasonably representative of the bank’s portfolio or market conditions, which the guidance calls especially important when the bank uses external data or the model is used for new products or activities;
- sensitivity analysis and stress testing where appropriate;
- evaluation of qualitative information and judgment used in development (the logic, judgment and types of information), to ensure it is appropriate, systematic, well supported and documented.

Developmental evidence should be reviewed before a model goes into use and again as part of ongoing validation, in particular whenever there is a material change in the model.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst faces both flags the guidance names: external data and a new product. Options A, C and D are all design-stage reviews. Option B compares realised outcomes with forecast intervals after deployment, which is back-testing, part of outcomes analysis.

**Fragile fact.** External data and new products are the two triggers the guidance names for extra scrutiny of data representativeness within conceptual soundness.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5 Model Validation, “Evaluation of Conceptual Soundness”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q6 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Data representativeness is explicitly part of conceptual soundness, especially for external data and new products. Choosing A confuses it with process verification, which checks the ongoing accuracy of live data feeds. A would be the exception if it read “verifying that daily data feeds remain complete”.

b.reason: Comparing realised outcomes with confidence intervals around forecasts is back-testing, which the guidance describes as one form of outcomes analysis, the third core element. It is therefore the activity least likely to form part of the evaluation of conceptual soundness.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Developmental evidence is reviewed before use and also whenever there is a material change. Choosing C assumes the review happens only once. C would be the exception if the stem said the model was unchanged since its last validation.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The guidance requires qualitative information and judgment used in development to be evaluated as part of conceptual soundness. Choosing D treats judgment as outside validation. D would be the exception if it described evaluating overrides by model users, which belongs to ongoing monitoring.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q7
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is validating a net interest income (NII) model for the bank’s JPY balance sheet, which totals JPY 84 trillion. As part of the evaluation of conceptual soundness, she runs the following sensitivity tests and records the change in the one-year NII forecast.

| Test | Input change | Change in NII forecast (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Policy rate +5 bp only | −0.4 |
| 2 | Deposit beta +0.01 only | −0.3 |
| 3 | Policy rate +5 bp and deposit beta +0.01 together | −6.1 |
| 4 | Prepayment speed +1% only | 0.5 |

Each single-input result lies within the range the developers documented as expected. Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: Test 3 shows that the model is unstable, because a small change in a single input produced an unexpectedly large change in the output.
Test 3 confirms that the model is robust, because every single-input test produced an output change within the expected range.
Test 3 is evidence of an unexpected interaction between the two inputs, and management should consider remedies such as limits on use.
Test 3 can be disregarded, because sensitivity analysis is a development tool and is not part of the validation of a model already built.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Japanese bank interpreting single-input and joint sensitivity tests on an NII model.

**Concept and theory**

Within the evaluation of conceptual soundness, the guidance asks banks, where appropriate, to use sensitivity analysis in development and validation. It distinguishes three uses, each revealing a different weakness:

| Test | What is varied | What a bad result signals |
|---|---|---|
| Single-input sensitivity | Small changes in one input or parameter | Unexpectedly large output change: an unstable model |
| Joint sensitivity | Several inputs simultaneously | Evidence of unexpected interactions, particularly complex, non-intuitive ones |
| Stress testing | Wide range of inputs, including extreme values | Boundaries of model performance; conditions where it becomes unstable or inaccurate |

Management should have a clear plan for using the results. If testing indicates the model may be inaccurate or unstable in some circumstances, management should consider modifying model properties, putting less reliance on its outputs, placing limits on model use, or developing a new approach.

**Applying it to this question**

Compare the joint result with what the single-input results imply. The balance sheet size (JPY 84 trillion) and Test 4 are irrelevant to the conclusion.

Sum of single-input effects = (−0.4%) + (−0.3%) = −0.7%

Joint effect observed = −6.1%

Ratio $= \frac{6.1}{0.7} \approx$ 8.7

Each input on its own behaves within the documented range, so the single-input tests do not show instability. Moved together, the same small shocks produce an effect almost nine times the sum of their separate effects. That is the signature the guidance attributes to varying several inputs simultaneously: evidence of an unexpected interaction. The guidance then calls for a management response (modify, rely less, limit use or develop a new approach).

**Fragile fact.** Single-input: large response means instability. Multiple inputs: disproportionate joint response means unexpected interaction. Do not swap the two diagnoses.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Evaluation of Conceptual Soundness” (sensitivity analysis and stress testing paragraphs). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser describes the same single-variable, multiple-variable and stress testing sequence.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q7 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It applies the single-input diagnosis (instability) to a joint test. Test 3 changed two inputs, and each single change was within range. A would be right if Test 1 or Test 2 alone had produced the −6.1% change.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reads the anomaly as confirmation. Passing single-input tests does not establish robustness when joint testing reveals an interaction. B would be right if Test 3 had produced roughly −0.7%, close to the sum of the single effects.

c.reason: The guidance states that varying several inputs simultaneously as part of sensitivity analysis can provide evidence of unexpected interactions, and that if testing indicates the model may be inaccurate or unstable in some circumstances, management should consider remedies including placing limits on model use.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The guidance explicitly says banks should employ sensitivity analysis in model development and validation, and repeat it in ongoing monitoring. D would be right only if the bank had substituted an equivalent validation test for it, which the guidance does not provide for.

questions.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q8
questions.question:
The head of credit risk at a Brazilian bank is reviewing ongoing monitoring results for a retail credit scorecard. Credit officers may override the scorecard’s decision. The table compares the realised loss rate on overridden loans with the loss rate the scorecard predicted for the same loans. The average loan size is BRL 18,500.

| Quarter | Decisions | Overrides | Realised loss (%) | Predicted loss (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 12 000 | 480 | 1.8 | 2.9 |
| Q2 | 11 500 | 690 | 1.7 | 3.0 |
| Q3 | 12 400 | 930 | 1.9 | 3.1 |
| Q4 | 12 100 | 1210 | 1.6 | 2.8 |

Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: A rising override rate together with overrides that consistently improve performance is a sign that the scorecard needs revision or redevelopment.
Overrides that consistently improve performance show that the scorecard is performing as intended, so documenting the overrides is sufficient.
The overrides reflect errors by credit officers rather than limitations of the scorecard, so the bank should withdraw officers’ authority to override.
Override analysis belongs to outcomes analysis, so no conclusion should be drawn until the scorecard has completed a full back-test cycle.

questions.solution:
Head of credit risk at a Brazilian bank reading a rising override rate on a retail scorecard.

**Concept and theory**

Ongoing monitoring should include the analysis of overrides with appropriate documentation. In the use of virtually any model, users will sometimes ignore, alter or reverse model output on expert judgment. The guidance treats this as information about the model, not just about the users:

- Overrides indicate that in some respect the model is not performing as intended or has limitations.
- Banks should evaluate the reasons for overrides and track and analyse override performance.
- If the rate of overrides is high, or if the override process consistently improves model performance, it is often a sign that the underlying model needs revision or redevelopment.

The second trigger is the counter-intuitive one: overrides that work well are not reassuring, because they show that the model is leaving out information the users have.

**Applying it to this question**

Compute the override rate each quarter (the loan size is irrelevant):

Override rate $= \frac{\text{Overrides}}{\text{Decisions}}$

Q1 = 480/12,000 = 4.0%

Q2 = 690/11,500 = 6.0%

Q3 = 930/12,400 = 7.5%

Q4 = 1,210/12,100 = 10.0%

The rate rises every quarter, to one decision in ten. In every quarter the realised loss on overridden loans (1.6% to 1.9%) is well below the scorecard’s predicted loss on the same loans (2.8% to 3.1%), so the overrides consistently improve on the model. Both triggers in the guidance are present, pointing to revision or redevelopment.

**Fragile fact.** Two separate triggers, joined by “or”: a high override rate, or overrides that consistently improve performance. Good overrides are a warning about the model, not a comfort.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Ongoing Monitoring” (analysis of overrides). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the existence of overrides suggests problems and frequent overrides need deeper understanding; it omits the “consistently improves model performance” trigger. GARP used for content; Schweser compression, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q8 of 18.

a.reason: The guidance states that if the rate of overrides is high, or if the override process consistently improves model performance, it is often a sign that the underlying model needs revision or redevelopment. The data show both conditions.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reads successful overrides as proof the model works. The guidance says the reverse: overrides indicate the model is not performing as intended, and consistently beneficial overrides suggest revision. B would be right only if overrides were rare and their performance no better than the model’s.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It blames the users rather than the model. The guidance treats overrides as a sign of model limitations, and here the officers’ judgment beats the scorecard every quarter. C would be right if overridden loans had consistently performed worse than predicted, suggesting poor judgment by officers.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Override analysis is named under ongoing monitoring, not outcomes analysis, and monitoring begins when the model is first used. D would be right if the question concerned back-testing the scorecard’s loss forecasts against realised losses.

questions.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-15 d Q9
questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the ongoing monitoring programme of a German bank’s EUR market risk models. Which of the following statements about ongoing monitoring is most accurate?

options.text: Monitoring begins once the model has completed its first successful back-test, since earlier performance data are not yet meaningful.
Monitoring evaluates whether changes in products, exposures, clients or markets require the model to be adjusted, redeveloped or replaced.
Monitoring is performed at one standard frequency across all models, so that results are consistent and comparable across the model inventory.
Monitoring replaces the tests used in model development with benchmarking alone, since the development tests have already been passed.

questions.solution:
Consultant reviewing the purpose, start point and frequency of ongoing monitoring at a German bank.

**Concept and theory**

Ongoing monitoring is the second core element. It confirms that the model is appropriately implemented and is being used and performing as intended. Its key features in the guidance:

| Feature | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Evaluate whether changes in products, exposures, activities, clients or market conditions necessitate adjustment, redevelopment or replacement of the model, and verify that any extension beyond its original scope is valid; reassess limitations found in development |
| Start | When the model is first implemented in production systems for actual business use |
| Frequency | Periodic, with a frequency appropriate to the nature of the model, the availability of new data or modelling approaches, and the magnitude of the risk involved |
| Content | Process verification and benchmarking; many development tests repeated regularly; sensitivity analysis and robustness checks repeated; monitoring of input ranges; override analysis |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes a claim about purpose, start, frequency or content. Only B matches the guidance; the others misstate the start, the frequency rule or the content.

**Fragile fact.** Monitoring starts at production implementation, not after the first back-test; its frequency is model-specific, not uniform.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Ongoing Monitoring”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says monitoring should be done “on a frequent basis” considering the model’s purpose and risk exposures; GARP adds the availability of new data or modelling approaches. GARP used; minor compression, no substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q9 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It moves the start point to after the first back-test. Monitoring begins when the model is first implemented in production systems. A would be right if it described when the first full back-test results become available.

b.reason: The guidance states that ongoing monitoring is essential to evaluate whether changes in products, exposures, activities, clients or market conditions necessitate adjustment, redevelopment or replacement of the model.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** It imposes one standard frequency on all models. The guidance requires a frequency appropriate to the nature of the model, the availability of new data or approaches and the magnitude of risk. C would be right if it said the review of each model occurs at least annually, which is a floor, not a uniform frequency.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It says monitoring uses benchmarking alone. The guidance says many development tests should be included in ongoing monitoring and conducted regularly, with sensitivity analysis repeated periodically. D would be right if it said benchmarking is one of the activities in monitoring alongside process verification.

questions.question: A senior internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing the process verification work performed on the bank’s GBP asset and liability management model. Which of the following statements about process verification is NOT correct?

options.text: It verifies that internal and external data inputs continue to be accurate, complete, and consistent with the model’s purpose and design.
It confirms that the model’s code is subject to change control, so that it can be altered only by approved parties and every change is logged.
It reviews reports derived from model outputs to verify that they are accurate, complete and informative and indicate model limitations.
It excludes user-developed spreadsheets, because these are not production systems and therefore carry less model risk than core models.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a UK bank auditing statements about process verification.

**Concept and theory**

Process verification is the part of ongoing monitoring that checks that all model components are functioning as designed. The guidance lists:

- **Inputs.** Internal and external data inputs continue to be accurate, complete, consistent with model purpose and design, and of the highest quality available.
- **Code.** Computer code is subject to rigorous quality and change control, so that it is correct, cannot be altered except by approved parties, and all changes are logged and auditable.
- **System integration.** A challenge deserving special attention, because the processing component often draws from various data sources, processes large amounts of data and feeds multiple repositories and reporting systems.
- **User-developed applications.** Spreadsheets or ad hoc database applications used to generate quantitative estimates are particularly prone to model risk.
- **Change over time.** Systems may need updating as the content or composition of information changes.
- **Reports.** Reports derived from model outputs are reviewed to verify they are accurate, complete, informative and contain appropriate indicators of performance and limitations.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the statement that is NOT correct. A, B and C restate the inputs, code and reports items. D reverses the guidance on user-developed applications.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: user-developed spreadsheets are particularly prone to model risk, not less risky; system integration is singled out as a challenge.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Ongoing Monitoring” (process verification). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says inputs should remain “error free and complete”; GARP adds consistency with model purpose and design and highest quality available. GARP used; no substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q10 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement, so not the answer.** This restates the inputs requirement. A would be the exception if it said only internal inputs need verifying, since external inputs are named too.

b.reason: **True statement, so not the answer.** This restates the change-control requirement. B would be the exception if it allowed any developer to alter production code without logging.

c.reason: **True statement, so not the answer.** This restates the requirement to review reports derived from model outputs as part of validation. C would be the exception if it confined report review to the board pack only.

d.reason: The guidance states that user-developed applications, such as spreadsheets or ad hoc database applications used to generate quantitative estimates, are particularly prone to model risk. Excluding them because they carry less risk inverts that statement, so D is the incorrect statement.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese bank is benchmarking the bank’s CNY corporate credit model against an industry consortium model. The consortium model is well regarded and its data are accurate and complete.

**X.** For the manufacturing portfolio, the bank’s model and the consortium model produce closely matching estimates.

**Y.** For the property portfolio, the bank’s estimates are 35% below the consortium’s. The consortium model uses a different estimation method and data set.

Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: X is evidence in favour of the model, to be read with caution; Y should trigger an investigation of the sources and degree of the difference.
X confirms that the model is correctly specified for that portfolio; Y should trigger an investigation of the sources and degree of the difference.
X is evidence in favour of the model, to be read with caution; Y demonstrates that the model is in error and must be redeveloped for that portfolio.
X confirms that the model is correctly specified for that portfolio; Y can be set aside because the benchmark uses a different method and data set.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst at a Chinese bank interpreting a close benchmark match and a 35% discrepancy.

**Concept and theory**

Benchmarking is the comparison of a model’s inputs and outputs with estimates from alternative internal or external data or models. It can be used in development and in ongoing monitoring. For credit risk models, examples include vendor or industry consortium models and retail credit bureau data. Benchmark models should be rigorous and benchmark data accurate and complete.

The guidance is symmetric and cautious in interpreting results:

| Result | Interpretation in the guidance |
|---|---|
| Close match | Evidence in favour of the model, but to be interpreted with caution so that the bank does not get a false degree of comfort |
| Discrepancy | Should trigger investigation into the sources and degree of the differences and whether they are within an expected or appropriate range given the nature of the comparison; may suggest revisions. Differences do not necessarily mean the model is in error, since the benchmark is itself an alternative prediction and may use different data or methods |

**Applying it to this question**

Portfolio X: a close match is supportive evidence, not confirmation. Portfolio Y: a 35% gap against a rigorous benchmark using a different method is exactly the case where the guidance requires investigation, without presuming error and without dismissing the gap. Only A treats both portfolios correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Symmetry: a match is not confirmation and a mismatch is not proof of error; a mismatch always triggers investigation.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Ongoing Monitoring” (benchmarking). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q11 of 18.

a.reason: The guidance says a good match is evidence in favour of the model but should be interpreted with caution, and that discrepancies should trigger investigation into the sources and degree of the differences, since they do not necessarily indicate model error.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Its treatment of Y is right, but it upgrades X from evidence to confirmation, the false comfort the guidance warns against. B would be right if “confirms” were replaced by “is evidence in favour of”.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** Its treatment of X is right, but it treats the Y discrepancy as proof of error. The benchmark is an alternative prediction and the difference may stem from different data or methods. C would be right if investigation had shown the difference came from an error in the bank’s model.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It overstates X and dismisses Y. A different method is a reason to investigate whether the gap is within an appropriate range, not a reason to set it aside. D would be right only if the benchmark itself were shown to be unreliable, which the stem rules out.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Canadian bank is reviewing an adjustment to the bank’s CAD deposit run-off model. Both the original and the adjusted model were run in parallel for eight quarters, and their forecasts were compared with realised outflows.

| Metric | Original model | Adjusted model |
|---|---|---|
| In-sample $\text{R}^{2}$ on development data | 0.71 | 0.86 |
| Mean absolute forecast error vs realised outflows (%) | 3.1 | 3.4 |
| Quarters with errors outside the acceptable range | 2 | 3 |

Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: The adjusted model should replace the original model, because its higher in-sample fit demonstrates that the adjustment improved the model.
The adjusted model should replace the original model, because it incorporates newer data, so its weaker realised accuracy should be disregarded.
The adjusted model does not outperform the original on realised outcomes, so further changes or a wholesale redesign are likely needed first.
The comparison is not valid, because parallel outcomes analysis should compare the adjusted model with a benchmark rather than with the original.

questions.solution:
Validator at a Canadian bank comparing an adjusted deposit run-off model with the original in parallel.

**Concept and theory**

Outcomes analysis is the third core element: a comparison of model outputs with corresponding actual outcomes. Models are regularly adjusted for new data or techniques, or because performance has deteriorated. Parallel outcomes analysis tests such adjustments: both the original and the adjusted model’s forecasts are tested against realised outcomes. The guidance’s rule is direct:

- If the adjusted model does not outperform the original, developers, users and reviewers should realise that additional changes, or even a wholesale redesign, are likely necessary before the adjusted model replaces the original one.

A related point from the back-testing paragraph: analysis of in-sample fit and holdout performance are important parts of development but are not substitutes for testing against realised outcomes.

**Applying it to this question**

Use only the rows that compare forecasts with realised outcomes; the in-sample $\text{R}^{2}$ is the deliberately irrelevant input.

$\Delta\text{MAE} =$ 3.4% − 3.1% = +0.3 percentage points (adjusted worse)

∆ quarters outside range = 3 − 2 = +1 (adjusted worse)

On both realised-outcome measures the adjusted model is worse, so it does not outperform the original. The higher in-sample fit (0.86 against 0.71) says the adjusted model fits its own development data better, which is not evidence of better forecasting.

**Fragile fact.** In parallel outcomes analysis the comparator is the original model, judged on realised outcomes; better in-sample fit does not count.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Outcomes Analysis” (parallel outcomes analysis; in-sample fit and holdout samples). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says further amendments are needed if the amended model is “not noticeably better”; GARP says “does not outperform” and adds that a wholesale redesign may be needed. GARP used; no substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q12 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It uses in-sample fit, a development statistic, in place of performance against realised outcomes. A would be right if the adjusted model also had the lower forecast error and fewer breaches.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Newer data is a reason models are adjusted, not a reason to ignore the result of the test of that adjustment. B would be right if the adjusted model’s realised accuracy were at least as good as the original’s.

c.reason: The guidance says that if the adjusted model does not outperform the original model, additional changes or even a wholesale redesign are likely necessary before the adjusted model replaces the original one.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It confuses parallel outcomes analysis with benchmarking. Parallel outcomes analysis is defined as testing the original and adjusted models against realised outcomes. D would describe benchmarking, which compares a model with alternative models or data.

questions.question: A senior model validator at a French bank is designing a back-test of a 12-month probability of default model for its EUR corporate portfolio. The model was estimated on data from 2015 to 2021. Four designs have been proposed. Which design is most consistent with the supervisory guidance on back-testing?

options.text: Compare realised 12-month default rates for 2019 to 2021 with the model’s forecasts, using confidence intervals around the forecasts.
Compare realised 12-month default rates for 2022 to 2025 with the model’s forecasts, using confidence intervals around the forecasts.
Compare realised monthly default rates for 2022 to 2025 with the model’s 12-month forecasts, using confidence intervals around the forecasts.
Compare default rates in a holdout sample set aside from the 2015 to 2021 data with the model’s forecasts, using confidence intervals.

questions.solution:
Senior validator at a French bank choosing a back-test design for a 12-month PD model built on 2015 to 2021 data.

**Concept and theory**

Back-testing is one form of outcomes analysis. The guidance defines it by three design features:

| Design feature | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Sample period | A sample time period not used in model development |
| Observation frequency | Matches the forecast horizon or performance window of the model |
| Comparison standard | Expected ranges or statistical confidence intervals around the model forecasts; outcomes outside them are analysed and significant causes investigated |

The guidance adds that analysis of in-sample fit and of model performance in holdout samples (data set aside and not used to estimate the original model) are important parts of development but are not substitutes for back-testing. The reason is that a holdout sample is drawn from the same period and conditions as the development data, so it cannot show how the model performs on genuinely new outcomes.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each design against the three features. The model forecasts a 12-month default rate and was estimated on 2015 to 2021.

| Design | Out-of-development period? | Frequency matches horizon? | Intervals? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | No (2019 to 2021 is in-sample) | Yes | Yes | Fails |
| B | Yes (2022 to 2025) | Yes | Yes | Passes |
| C | Yes | No (monthly) | Yes | Fails |
| D | No (holdout from 2015 to 2021) | Yes | Yes | Not a substitute |

**Fragile fact.** Back-testing: out-of-development sample, frequency matching the forecast horizon, intervals around forecasts. Holdout samples and in-sample fit are development tools, not substitutes.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Outcomes Analysis” (back-testing). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser describes the period as “consistent with the model’s forecast horizon”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q13 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the out-of-sample condition: 2019 to 2021 lies inside the estimation period, so this is in-sample fit. A would be right if the model had been estimated on data ending in 2018.

b.reason: It compares actual outcomes with forecasts during a period not used in development, at an observation frequency matching the 12-month horizon, using confidence intervals, which is the guidance’s definition of back-testing.

c.reason: **Unit slip: horizon mismatch.** It observes monthly default rates against 12-month forecasts, so the observation frequency does not match the forecast horizon. C would be right if the model forecast one-month default rates.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Holdout-sample testing is a development technique that the guidance says is not a substitute for back-testing. D would describe a sound development step, not a back-test.

questions.question:
A market risk analyst at a US bank is back-testing the bank’s one-day VaR model for its USD trading book over 250 trading days. The results are below.

| VaR confidence level | Exceptions observed | Timing of exceptions |
|---|---|---|
| 99% | 3 | All within eight consecutive trading days in March |
| 95% | 24 | Spread across the year, with a concentration in March |

Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: The 99% exception count is close to its expected level, but the clustering and the 95% results suggest the model may not be capturing risk adequately.
The 99% exception count is close to its expected level, so the model passes, because exception frequency at a single percentile is the definitive test.
The 95% results should be disregarded, because back-testing compares outcomes with one chosen VaR percentile, and the 99% count is acceptable.
The 99% exception count is far below its expected level of 25, so the model is overly conservative and should be recalibrated to release capital.

questions.solution:
Market risk analyst at a US bank reading clustered 99% VaR exceptions and excess 95% exceptions.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance cites VaR as a well-known example of back-testing: actual profit and loss is compared with the model’s forecast loss distribution. Significant deviation between expected and actual performance, and unexplained P&L volatility, may indicate that hedging and pricing relationships are not adequately measured. The key instruction for this question is that, along with measuring the frequency of losses in excess of a single VaR percentile, banks should use other tests, such as:

- assessing any clustering of exceptions; and
- checking the distribution of losses against other estimated percentiles.

For a VaR at confidence level c over T days, the expected number of exceptions if the model is correct is

E$[\text{N}] = ($1 $- \text{c}) \times$ T,

where N is the number of days on which the loss exceeds VaR. This simple frequency arithmetic is implied by the guidance’s reference to measuring exception frequency; the guidance does not prescribe a particular statistical test.

**Applying it to this question**

Apply the expected-exception formula at each confidence level:

E$[\text{N}_{99}] = ($1 − 0.99) × 250 = 2.5 observed 3

E$[\text{N}_{95}] = ($1 − 0.95) × 250 = 12.5 observed 24

Ratio at 95% = 24/12.5 ≈ 1.9

At 99% the count alone looks acceptable. But all three exceptions fall within eight consecutive days, which is clustering, and at the 95% percentile the model produces almost twice the expected number of exceptions. Both are exactly the additional checks the guidance requires, and both point to a model that may not capture the distribution of losses adequately, so the discrepancies should be analysed.

**Fragile fact.** Expected exceptions use the tail probability (1 $- \text{c})$: 2.5 at 99% over 250 days, 12.5 at 95%. A good count at one percentile does not clear a model with clustered exceptions.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Outcomes Analysis” (VaR backtesting example). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser mentions supplementing one VaR percentile with another but omits clustering of exceptions; GARP includes both. GARP used for content. The expected-exception arithmetic is elementary and implied, not stated, in the source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q14 of 18.

a.reason: The guidance states that, along with measuring the frequency of losses in excess of a single VaR percentile estimator, banks should assess clustering of exceptions and check the distribution of losses against other estimated percentiles. Here the frequency test is passed but the other two checks raise concerns.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It treats frequency at a single percentile as definitive. The guidance explicitly says other tests are needed alongside it. B would be right only if the exceptions were scattered and the 95% count were close to 12.5, and even then “definitive” would overstate it.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It restricts back-testing to one chosen percentile, discarding the other-percentile check the guidance requires. C would be right if the guidance asked only for an exception count at the reporting percentile.

d.reason: **Wrong percentile.** It computes the expected count using 10% instead of 1%: 0.10 × 250 = 25. With the correct tail probability, 0.01 × 250 = 2.5, three exceptions are not “far below” expectation. D would be right only for a 90% VaR, and even then the clustering would still need analysis.

questions.question: The CRO of a Singapore bank is reviewing the validation plan for a new model that forecasts SGD mortgage losses over a five-year horizon. The board wants evidence on the model’s performance within its first year of use. According to the supervisory guidance, which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace back-testing with early-warning metrics, because the five-year horizon means the necessary data for a back-test will never accumulate in time.
Defer all outcomes analysis until five years of data are available, and rely only on the evaluation of conceptual soundness in the meantime.
Back-test each individual forecast as soon as it matures, and redevelop the model whenever any single forecast falls outside its interval.
Back-test over the longer period, and complement it with early-warning metrics from shortly after introduction and trend analysis over time.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Singapore bank planning validation of a five-year mortgage loss model with a one-year board deadline.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance recognises that back-testing, though essential, poses challenges:

- It is not a straightforward, mechanical process that always produces unambiguous results. Its purpose is to test the model, not individual forecast values, and it may involve many forecasts over different conditions and time periods.
- Statistical testing is essential but poses challenges in the choice of tests and the interpretation of results; banks should support and document both.
- Models with long forecast horizons should be back-tested, but because accumulating data takes time, testing should be supplemented by evaluation over shorter periods: “early warning” metrics designed to measure performance beginning very shortly after model introduction, and trend analysis of performance over time.
- These tools are not substitutes for back-testing, which should still be performed over the longer period, but very important complements.

**Applying it to this question**

The board’s one-year deadline is the trap: it tempts the reader to replace or skip the long-horizon back-test. The guidance keeps the back-test and adds short-period tools so that evidence arrives early. Only D keeps both.

**Fragile fact.** Early-warning metrics and trend analysis complement, never substitute for, the long-horizon back-test.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Outcomes Analysis” (challenges of back-testing; long forecast horizons). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q15 of 18.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It uses early-warning metrics as a replacement. The guidance says they are not substitutes for back-testing, which should still be performed over the longer period. A would be right if “replace” were changed to “complement”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It postpones all outcomes analysis. The guidance wants outcomes analysis on an ongoing basis, with early-warning metrics from shortly after introduction. B would be right only for the full five-year back-test, not for all outcomes analysis.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It tests individual forecasts and redevelops on a single breach. The guidance says the purpose of back-testing is to test the model, not individual forecast values, and that discrepancies significant in magnitude or frequency should be investigated. C would be right if outcomes fell consistently outside the acceptable range.

d.reason: The guidance says models with long horizons should be back-tested, supplemented by early-warning metrics measuring performance beginning very shortly after introduction and by trend analysis over time, and that these are complements, not substitutes.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a Swiss bank on the validation of its EUR pricing model for an illiquid structured product. Because prices for the product are rarely observable, the bank has a limited ability to back-test the model or perform sensitivity analysis. The consultant drafts the following statements:

I. Even more attention should be paid to the model’s limitations when considering whether its use is appropriate.

II. Senior management should be fully informed of those limitations when the model is used for decision making.

III. This scrutiny should be applied to the individual model only, since aggregate model risk is a matter for governance rather than validation.

IV. Any recalibration made after validation reveals errors should be governed by the principle of conservatism and undergo independent review.

Which of the statements are consistent with the supervisory guidance?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Consultant advising a Swiss bank whose illiquid EUR pricing model cannot be fully back-tested.

**Concept and theory**

Validation tools are sometimes unavailable. The guidance notes that banks may have a limited ability to use key tools such as back-testing or sensitivity analysis, for reasons such as lack of data or of price observability. In those cases:

- even more attention should be paid to the model’s limitations when considering the appropriateness of model usage;
- senior management should be fully informed of those limitations when using the models for decision making;
- such scrutiny should be applied to individual models and to models in the aggregate.

Separately, when outcomes analysis and other validation elements reveal significant errors, or outcomes consistently outside predetermined thresholds, model adjustment, recalibration or redevelopment is warranted. Adjustments and recalibration should be governed by the principle of conservatism and should undergo independent review, and material changes and all redevelopment should be validated before implementation.

**Applying it to this question**

I and II restate the first two bullets. III cuts off the aggregate dimension, which the guidance expressly includes. IV restates the conservatism and independent-review rule for recalibration. The consistent set is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** When tools are limited, scrutiny rises (not falls), senior management is fully informed, and the scrutiny covers individual models and the aggregate.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Outcomes Analysis” (closing paragraphs on adjustment, recalibration and limited validation tools). Schweser states that significant changes require validation before implementation but does not cover limited tools or conservatism in recalibration; content is from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q16 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It omits IV, treating recalibration as unconstrained. The guidance requires conservatism and independent review for adjustments and recalibration. A would be right if IV said recalibration can be made by the desk without review.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts III, which narrows scrutiny to the individual model. The guidance applies it to individual models and in the aggregate. B would be right if III included the aggregate and IV were false.

c.reason: Statements I, II and IV are each stated in the guidance; III contradicts the instruction that such scrutiny should be applied to individual models and models in the aggregate.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts III and drops I, the central instruction to pay even more attention to limitations. D would be right only if I were false, which contradicts the guidance.

questions.question: A risk manager at a mid-sized Australian bank is validating a vendor credit scoring model used for AUD personal loans. The vendor declines to give the bank access to the model’s computer code, describing it as proprietary. Which of the following actions is most appropriate?

options.text: Rely more on sensitivity analysis and benchmarking, obtain the vendor’s developmental evidence and test results, and monitor the bank’s own outcomes.
Accept the vendor’s own validation report as the bank’s validation of the model, because the modelling expertise and the code both sit outside the bank.
Implement the model only with the vendor’s default settings, because any customisation by the bank would invalidate the testing that the vendor has performed.
Limit validation to the processing component, because the vendor’s input data and the reporting of outputs fall outside the scope of the bank’s validation.

questions.solution:
Risk manager at an Australian bank validating a vendor scoring model without access to code.

**Concept and theory**

Vendor and other third-party products (data, parameter values and complete models) pose unique challenges for validation because the modelling expertise is external to the user and some components are proprietary. They should nevertheless follow the same principles as in-house models, with a modified process:

| Party | Expectations in the guidance |
|---|---|
| Vendor | Provide developmental evidence on components, design and intended use; provide testing results showing the product works as expected; disclose limitations and assumptions and where use may be problematic; conduct ongoing performance monitoring and outcomes analysis with disclosure to clients |
| Bank | Have selection processes; validate its own use of the product; rely more on sensitivity analysis and benchmarking where code is not accessible; document and justify customisation; investigate relevance of vendor data and assumptions; conduct ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis using its own outcomes; keep knowledge in-house and have contingency plans |

**Applying it to this question**

The vendor withholds code, which removes direct code verification. The guidance’s answer is to lean more on tools that do not need code (sensitivity analysis and benchmarking), to obtain the vendor’s evidence and test results, and to monitor using the bank’s own outcomes. A combines these three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the bank validates its own use of a vendor model; with no access to code it leans more on sensitivity analysis and benchmarking.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Validation of Vendor and Other Third-Party Products”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point; Schweser says validation “will likely have to focus more on sensitivity analysis and benchmarks”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q17 of 18.

a.reason: The guidance says external models may not allow full access to code, so the bank may have to rely more on sensitivity analysis and benchmarking; banks should require developmental evidence and testing results from vendors; and the bank should conduct ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis using its own outcomes.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It lets the vendor’s validation stand in for the bank’s. The guidance says banks are expected to validate their own use of vendor products. B would be right if it said the vendor’s testing results are an input to, not a replacement for, the bank’s validation.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It forbids customisation. The guidance notes vendor models may need to be customised for a bank’s circumstances; customisation choices should be documented and justified as part of validation. C would be right if it said customisation must be documented and justified.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It shrinks validation to the processing component. All components (input, processing, reporting) are subject to validation for vendor models too, and vendor input data must be checked for relevance. D would be right if it said validation must cover all components.

questions.question: A model risk officer at a UK bank is drafting the section of the validation policy that covers vendor and other third-party models. Which of the following draft statements is NOT consistent with the supervisory guidance?

options.text: The bank should maintain contingency plans for cases in which a vendor model is no longer available or can no longer be supported by the vendor.
The bank need not obtain information on the data used to build a vendor model, as the vendor’s test results address representativeness.
The bank’s choices in customising a vendor model to its own circumstances should be documented and justified as part of the validation.
The bank should expect vendors to conduct ongoing performance monitoring and outcomes analysis, with disclosure of the results to their clients.

questions.solution:
Model risk officer at a UK bank drafting vendor model policy and spotting the inconsistent statement.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond the testing approach (Solution 17), the guidance places continuing obligations on the bank for vendor models:

- **Data.** If vendors provide input data or assumptions, or use them to build models, their relevance to the bank’s situation should be investigated. Banks should obtain information about the data used to develop the model and assess the extent to which it is representative of the bank’s situation.
- **Customisation.** Customisation choices should be documented and justified as part of validation.
- **Vendor monitoring.** Banks should expect vendors to conduct ongoing performance monitoring and outcomes analysis, with disclosure to clients, and to make modifications and updates over time.
- **Knowledge and continuity.** Banks should have as much knowledge in-house as possible, in case the contract ends or the vendor goes out of business, and contingency plans for when the vendor model is no longer available or cannot be supported.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the statement that is NOT consistent. A, C and D restate continuity, customisation and vendor-monitoring expectations. B releases the bank from obtaining information on development data, which the guidance requires.

**Fragile fact.** Even for proprietary models, the bank must obtain information on the vendor’s development data and assess its representativeness for the bank.

**Reference**

LO 56.d (wording as above). GARP Chapter 15, Section 15.5, “Validation of Vendor and Other Third-Party Products”. Schweser covers vendor evidence and testing but not data representativeness, customisation documentation or contingency planning; content is from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-15 d, where it is Q18 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement, so not the answer.** Contingency plans for an unavailable or unsupported vendor model are required. A would be the answer if it said contingency planning is the vendor’s responsibility alone.

b.reason: The guidance says banks should obtain information regarding the data used to develop the model and assess the extent to which that data is representative of the bank’s situation. Relying on the vendor’s test results instead contradicts this, so B is the inconsistent statement.

c.reason: **True statement, so not the answer.** Customisation choices must be documented and justified as part of validation. C would be the answer if it said customisation should be avoided altogether.

d.reason: **True statement, so not the answer.** Banks should expect vendors to conduct ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis with disclosure to clients. D would be the answer if it said this expectation removes the bank’s own monitoring using its own outcomes.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-16 a Q1
questions.question:
The head of model governance at a Singapore bank with SGD 40 billion of assets is drafting the bank’s model inventory policy and wants the policy’s definition to follow the US Federal Reserve’s supervisory guidance SR 11-7 exactly. She lists the following statements:

I. A model may be a quantitative method, a system, or an approach.

II. A model applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories, techniques, and assumptions to input data.

III. A tool falls within the definition only if its input data are themselves wholly quantitative.

IV. A model processes its input data into quantitative estimates.

Which of the statements are consistent with the SR 11-7 definition?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Head of model governance at a Singapore bank testing four statements against the SR 11-7 definition of a model.

**Concept and theory**

Everything in model risk management starts with a decision about what counts as a model. GARP stresses that the definition “is essential in establishing the right governance for model risk management”: a tool that is classed as a model enters the inventory, is tiered, documented, validated and monitored; a tool that is not classed as a model escapes that governance. A definition that is too narrow therefore leaves risk unmanaged, and one that is too wide wastes validation effort.

The US Federal Reserve’s guidance SR 11-7 supplies the definition most widely used in the United States and adapted in many other jurisdictions. It is deliberately broad, and it has two parts:

1. “The term model refers to a quantitative method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories, techniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates.”
2. “The definition of model also covers quantitative approaches whose inputs are partially or wholly qualitative or based on expert judgment, provided that the output is quantitative in nature.”

It helps to read the definition as four components:

| Component | What SR 11-7 requires | What it does not require |
|---|---|---|
| Form | A method, a system, or an approach | Any particular level of complexity |
| Engine | Theories, techniques and assumptions (statistical, economic, financial or mathematical) | A statistical technique specifically |
| Input | Input data | Quantitative inputs: they may be partly or wholly qualitative or expert judgment |
| Output | Quantitative estimates | Certainty: the output is an estimate |

The asymmetry is the key: the input side is open, the output side is the gate.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I reproduces the form component (“method, system, or approach”): consistent. Statement II reproduces the engine and the input component: consistent. Statement III adds a requirement that the inputs be wholly quantitative; the second sentence of SR 11-7 says the opposite, covering inputs that are “partially or wholly qualitative or based on expert judgment”. Statement III is therefore inconsistent. Statement IV reproduces the output component (“into quantitative estimates”): consistent. The consistent set is I, II and IV. The SGD 40 billion asset figure plays no role in the definition.

**Fragile fact.** Under SR 11-7, qualitative or expert-judgment content is allowed on the input side, never on the output side: the output must be quantitative.

**Reference**

LO 57.a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. GARP Chapter 16, Definition and History, subsection 1. Model Definition. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point: Schweser quotes the same first sentence of SR 11-7 and notes that inputs can be qualitative as well as quantitative; it does not quote the “provided that the output is quantitative” proviso, which is taken from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops Statement IV, as if the definition said nothing about the output. The output requirement is in fact the condition on which the whole definition turns: qualitative inputs are acceptable only “provided that the output is quantitative”. Option A would be right only if the question asked which statements describe what a model does to its inputs, leaving aside what it produces.

b.reason: Statements I, II and IV restate the SR 11-7 wording as quoted in GARP Chapter 16, and Statement III contradicts the explicit extension of the definition to qualitative and expert-judgment inputs.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts Statement III, imposing a quantitative-input condition that SR 11-7 expressly removes, and in doing so it also omits the form component in Statement I. It would describe a narrow definition confined to quantitative data in which the form of the tool was left unstated, which is not the SR 11-7 text.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts all four statements, so it accepts the false input restriction in Statement III. This option would be correct under the early, narrow view of models as forecasting tools built on quantitative data, which SR 11-7 was written to go beyond.

questions.question: A risk consultant is briefing the board risk committee of a German insurer on why the firm’s model inventory changed after it adopted the definition of a model that now reflects the industry consensus. A committee member asks how the definition of a model has evolved since the early days of model risk management. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.text: It has narrowed from all estimation tools to complex statistical forecasting tools, and the emphasis has moved to the sophistication of the technique used.
It has broadened from complex statistical forecasting tools to a wider set of estimation techniques, and the emphasis has moved to the technique used rather than the forecast.
It has broadened from complex statistical forecasting tools to a wider set of estimation techniques, and the emphasis has moved to whether the output is used for regulatory capital.
It has broadened from complex statistical forecasting tools to a wider set of estimation techniques, and the emphasis has moved to the uncertain nature of the forecast.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant explaining to a German insurer’s board risk committee how the definition of a model has evolved.

**Concept and theory**

The definition of a model has a history, and the history explains why model inventories have grown. GARP describes three stages:

| Stage | What counted as a model | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Early days | Forecasting tools relying on complex statistical techniques, i.e. quantitative models | These were new techniques whose risks were not well understood, so a narrow focus made sense |
| Maturing MRM | A broader set of estimation techniques, including non-quantitative, so-called qualitative, models | As model risk management matured, the definition expanded significantly; SR 11-7 is purposefully broad |
| Current consensus | Any estimation method that uses data and relies on a set of assumptions to generate an uncertain estimate or forecast | The emphasis is more and more on the uncertain nature of the forecast rather than on the method or technique |

The last row is the conceptual shift: what makes something a model is no longer how sophisticated its machinery is, but the fact that it produces an estimate that could be wrong. That is also why model risk exists at all: if the output were certain, there would be nothing to manage.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks two things: the direction of change and where the emphasis now lies. Direction: from a narrow statistical scope to a wider set of estimation techniques (broadened). Emphasis: on the uncertainty of the forecast, not the technique. Only Option D gets both right.

**Fragile fact.** The definition moved from narrow to broad, and the emphasis moved from the technique to the uncertainty of the forecast; reversing either direction is the trap.

**Reference**

LO 57.a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. GARP Chapter 16, Definition and History, subsection 1. Model Definition. Schweser does not describe the evolution of the definition or the current industry consensus; this content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction of change (narrowed instead of broadened) and places the emphasis on technique. The narrow, technique-focused view is where the definition started, not where it ended. Option A would describe the change only if the question ran the history backwards, from today’s definition to the early days.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The direction is right but the emphasis is reversed: GARP says the emphasis is on the uncertain forecast rather than the technique, and Option B says the technique rather than the forecast. It would be an accurate description of the early-days definition, where the complexity of the statistical technique was what marked out a model.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Whether a model is used for regulatory purposes is one of the characteristics MRM functions consider when assigning a model to a risk tier (LO 57.b). It affects how intensively a model is validated, not whether it is a model. Option C would be correct if the question asked which characteristics help determine a model’s tier.

d.reason: GARP states that the definition “expanded significantly to encompass a broader set of estimation techniques” and that, under the current consensus, “the emphasis is more and more on the uncertain nature of the forecast rather than on the method or technique used to estimate it”.

questions.question:
A model validation analyst at a Brazilian development bank must decide whether two credit tools fall within the SR 11-7 definition of a model. The tools are summarised below.

| Tool | Inputs | Output | Loans covered (BRL m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | Credit officers’ ratings of each borrower’s management quality and governance (strong, adequate or weak), combined by fixed weights | Probability of default (%) for each borrower | 2400 |
| Y | Twelve financial ratios taken from audited accounts, read by a panel of senior officers | Written outlook (positive, stable or negative) with commentary | 1100 |

Which of the following classifications is most accurate under the wording of SR 11-7?

options.text: Only Tool X falls within the definition, because its output is quantitative even though its inputs are qualitative.
Only Tool Y falls within the definition, because its inputs are quantitative even though its output is qualitative.
Both tools fall within the definition, because each applies expert judgment to input data to reach a view.
Neither tool falls within the definition, because each relies on expert judgment at some stage of the process.

questions.solution:
Validation analyst at a Brazilian development bank classifying a qualitative-input scorecard and a qualitative-output outlook tool under SR 11-7.

**Concept and theory**

The second sentence of the SR 11-7 definition settles a question that troubled early model governance: are expert-judgment tools models? SR 11-7 answers by looking at the two ends of the tool separately.

| Inputs | Output | Inside SR 11-7? |
|---|---|---|
| Quantitative | Quantitative | Yes |
| Partly or wholly qualitative, or expert judgment | Quantitative | Yes (expressly covered) |
| Quantitative | Qualitative | No (output condition fails) |
| Qualitative | Qualitative | No (output condition fails) |

The reason for this design is that the definition was “purposefully broad to capture the wider set of estimation techniques” that institutions use, while still describing a process that turns data into quantitative estimates. Judgment can enter on the way in; what comes out must be a number.

**Applying it to this question**

Tool X: the inputs are qualitative grades (strong, adequate, weak) set by credit officers, but fixed weights turn them into a probability of default, a quantitative estimate. This is exactly the case covered by the proviso, so Tool X is within the definition. Tool Y: the inputs are quantitative ratios, but the output is a written outlook with commentary, which is not a quantitative estimate. The output condition fails, so Tool Y is outside the SR 11-7 wording. The column showing loans covered is irrelevant: materiality of output matters for tiering a model (LO 57.b), not for deciding whether a tool is a model.

**Fragile fact.** In SR 11-7 the proviso attaches to the output (“provided that the output is quantitative”), not to the inputs.

**Reference**

LO 57.a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. GARP Chapter 16, Definition and History, subsection 1. Model Definition. Note: GARP also says the definition has expanded to include “so-called qualitative” models, and the broader industry consensus focuses on an uncertain estimate; the stem therefore asks for the SR 11-7 wording specifically, whose output condition is explicit. Schweser says only that inputs can be qualitative as well as quantitative and does not state the output proviso; GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: SR 11-7 “also covers quantitative approaches whose inputs are partially or wholly qualitative or based on expert judgment, provided that the output is quantitative in nature”. Tool X satisfies the proviso and Tool Y does not.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It applies the quantitative requirement to the inputs instead of the output, which is the mirror image of SR 11-7. It would be correct only under a definition that required quantitative inputs and allowed qualitative outputs, the reverse of the guidance.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the output condition, treating any use of judgment on data as sufficient. Option C would be correct if Tool Y’s outlook were converted into a numerical score, for example a probability of downgrade, since both tools would then produce quantitative output.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It treats expert judgment as disqualifying, when SR 11-7 expressly brings expert-judgment inputs inside the definition. It would be correct only under the early narrow view in which models were statistical forecasting tools, a view SR 11-7 was written to go beyond.
