questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank finds that, after the MRM function doubled the size of its highly regarded validation team, the bank’s credit modelling team stopped running its own pre-release testing. The head of modelling explains: “MRM is better resourced than we are, so it will catch anything we miss.” Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: Acceptable: once MRM, as the independent second line, has validated a model, ownership of the model’s risk passes from the modelling team to MRM.
Not acceptable: MRM is an independent backstop for errors the first line misses, but the first line owns the risk and must not abdicate its responsibilities.
Not acceptable: the modelling team should instead have passed its pre-release testing to internal audit, the third line, which independently validates models.
Acceptable: provided the validation team is large and competent enough, it will catch all of the errors that the modelling team might make before release.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at an Australian bank finds the modelling team dropped its own testing after MRM expanded.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes its discussion of MRM with the three lines of defence and a warning: “The existence of large and competent validation teams can result in modeling teams becoming more complacent with regard to their risk management practices.”

The roles are:

- First line: model developers and model owners. They “generate the risk to which the institution is exposed. As such, they own the risk and should take the appropriate measures to mitigate it to the greatest extent possible.”
- Second line: MRM, which “exists as an independent backstop to ‘catch’ errors that the first line might have missed”, and does an independent assessment of the risk and of the first line’s risk management practices.

The key sentence: the second line’s “existence however should not result in an abdication by the first line of its own responsibilities.” A backstop catches what the first line misses; it is not a substitute for the first line’s own controls.

**Applying it to this question**

The modelling team cut its own testing because MRM became bigger and better. That is the complacency GARP warns about, and the head of modelling’s remark is an abdication of first-line responsibility. The practice is not acceptable, and the reason is first-line ownership of risk, not a need to hand the work to another line.

**Fragile fact.** Actor check: the first line (developers and owners) generates and owns the risk; the second line (MRM) is the backstop. A stronger MRM team is a complacency risk, not a reason for the first line to do less.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management” (three lines of defence paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser names “model users and developers” as the first line; GARP names “model developers and model owners”. GARP is used here; the difference looks like condensation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q12 of 16.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves ownership of the risk to MRM after validation. GARP is explicit that developers and owners own the risk; the second line assesses it independently. It would be correct only if the first and second lines’ roles were reversed.

b.reason: It identifies MRM as an independent backstop, states that the first line owns the risk, and rejects abdication, all as in GARP.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason, swapping in internal audit (third line) as the validator. Model validation is a second-line MRM activity, and the fix is for the first line to resume its own testing. It would be correct only if the third line were the validation function, which it is not in the source.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It assumes a large, competent validation team will catch all errors. GARP warns that such teams can breed complacency, and a backstop catches errors the first line “might have missed”, not every possible error. It would be correct only if a second line could guarantee zero errors, which no source supports.

questions.question: A regulator examining a Brazilian bank asks its CRO to map the parties involved in model risk to the three lines of defence. Which of the following mappings is most accurate?

options.text: Model developers and model owners are the first line and generate and own the risk; MRM is the second line and independently assesses the risk and the first line’s risk management practices.
Model developers and model owners are the first line and generate and own the risk; MRM is the second line and independently assesses the risk, but not the first line’s risk management practices.
MRM is the first line and generates and owns the risk; model developers and model owners are the second line and independently assess the risk and MRM’s risk management practices.
Model developers and model owners are the first line and generate the risk; MRM is the second line and owns the risk, mitigating it to the greatest extent possible.

questions.solution:
Regulator asks a Brazilian bank’s CRO to map developers, owners and MRM to the three lines of defence.

**Concept and theory**

In the three lines of defence model applied to model risk, GARP assigns the roles as follows:

| Line | Who | Role |
|---|---|---|
| First | Model developers and model owners | Generate the risk, own it, and mitigate it to the greatest extent possible |
| Second | MRM | Independent backstop; independent assessment of the risk and of the first line’s risk management practices |

GARP’s wording: developers and owners “are, in the context of model risk, the first line and thus the actors that generate the risk to which the institution is exposed. As such, they own the risk and should take the appropriate measures to mitigate it to the greatest extent possible, with the second line doing an independent assessment of the risk and of the risk management practices of the first line.”

The logic: whoever creates a risk is best placed, and most accountable, to control it. The second line assesses both the risk itself and how well the first line manages it.

**Applying it to this question**

Four facts must all be right: developers and owners are the first line; they generate and own the risk; MRM is the second line; MRM assesses both the risk and the first line’s practices. Option A states all four.

**Fragile fact.** Owners are first line, not second line. The second line assesses two things: the risk and the first line’s risk management practices.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management” (three lines of defence paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser names “model users and developers” as the first line, whereas GARP names “model developers and model owners”. GARP is used here; the difference looks like condensation in Schweser rather than a change of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q13 of 16.

a.reason: It matches GARP’s allocation of generation and ownership to the first line and of a two-part independent assessment (risk and first-line practices) to the second line.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the second half of MRM’s assessment remit. GARP says the second line assesses the risk and the risk management practices of the first line. It would be correct if “but not” read “and”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It inverts the two lines, making MRM the risk generator and owner and developers the independent assessors. It would be correct only if the labels “first” and “second” were swapped back.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives ownership and mitigation of the risk to MRM. GARP gives ownership and mitigation to the first line, with MRM assessing independently. It would be correct if “MRM is the second line and owns the risk” read “developers and owners own the risk”.

questions.question: At a mature UK insurer, the modelling teams have formed their own quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) team. A newly appointed chief compliance officer asks how this team fits into model risk management. Which of the following best describes its role?

options.text: It is part of the second line, acting as MRM’s own quality team, and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.
It is the first line’s risk team and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly the risk of conceptual errors.
It is the first line’s risk team and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.
It is the first line’s risk team and, by mitigating execution risk, removes the need for independent validation by the second line.

questions.solution:
Chief compliance officer at a mature UK insurer asks how the first-line QA/QC team fits into model risk management.

**Concept and theory**

The first line does not discharge its ownership of model risk only through individual developers’ diligence. GARP notes: “At more mature institutions, the modeling teams will form a quality control/quality assurance team. These QA/QC teams are the first line’s risk team and play a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.”

Why execution risk in particular? Execution risk arises when a model does not do what it is intended and designed to do, through coding errors, implementation errors, use of the wrong data and so on. These are checkable errors that a team close to the code and data is well placed to catch before release. Conceptual errors (wrong assumptions or techniques) are harder to identify and are not simply right or wrong; there MRM’s role of ensuring transparency is central.

| Team | Line | Main contribution |
|---|---|---|
| QA/QC team | First | Mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk |
| MRM | Second | Independent review and challenge; backstop |

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the line (first, because it is formed by the modelling teams) and the risk it mainly targets (execution risk). The QA/QC team supplements, but does not replace, second-line validation.

**Fragile fact.** QA/QC: first line (formed by the modelling teams), particularly execution risk. Not second line, not conceptual errors, not a substitute for MRM.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management” (three lines of defence paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not mention QA/QC teams; this content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The risk focus is right, but the team is placed in the second line as MRM’s quality team. GARP says it is formed by the modelling teams and is the first line’s risk team. It would be correct if “part of the second line, acting as MRM’s own quality team” read “the first line’s risk team”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps execution risk for its sibling, conceptual errors. GARP singles out execution risk; conceptual errors call for MRM’s transparency and challenge role. It would be correct if “conceptual errors” read “execution risk”.

c.reason: It restates GARP: QA/QC teams are the first line’s risk team and play a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It says the QA/QC team removes the need for second-line validation. GARP keeps the second line as an independent backstop to catch what the first line misses. It would be correct only if first-line controls could guarantee error-free models.

questions.question: A validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing an SGD mortgage prepayment model. She and the developer hold different views on a key prepayment assumption, and both views are reasonable and equally valid. The developer has noted the assumption’s limitations in the model documentation. Which course of action best reflects the role of MRM in this situation?

options.text: Decide which view of the assumption is correct and require the developer to adopt it, since conceptual questions of this kind are ultimately a matter of right or wrong.
Ensure transparency, making sure the assumption and its limitations are communicated to users so that they understand when the model can be safely used and when to stop.
Accept the assumption without further action, since limitations that are discussed in the model documentation can be relied on to be understood by all users.
Remove the conceptual risk entirely by requiring the developer to recalibrate the model until it is shown to be valid in every possible market environment.

questions.solution:
Validator at a Singapore bank and a developer hold equally reasonable but different views on a prepayment assumption.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two sources of model risk. Execution errors are errors in doing what the model is designed to do; they are matters of right or wrong. Conceptual errors arise from wrong assumptions or techniques and are “much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong. Different reasonable modelers can have different and equally valid opinions on an assumption.”

MRM cannot “correct” such a disagreement by decree. GARP states: “In those situations, the role of model risk management is to ensure transparency.” Understanding the limitations of a model and communicating them clearly to users, who might not be quantitatively savvy, is crucial. Modelers may discuss limitations in the documentation, “but this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them.” MRM should therefore ensure the assumptions are communicated “in a manner that is useful to their understanding of when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued.” A model can be right in one context and wrong if the context changes.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem builds the exact condition GARP describes: two reasonable, equally valid views on an assumption. That points to a conceptual question with no single right answer, so MRM’s role is transparency. The fact that the limitation is in the documentation is a trap: documentation alone does not ensure users understand it.

**Fragile fact.** Conceptual errors: MRM’s role is transparency and clear communication to users. Documentation by the modeler is not the same as users understanding the limitation.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “2. Model Risks”. Boundary call: the execution versus conceptual taxonomy belongs to LO 57.a; this question tests only MRM’s role when a conceptual question arises, which falls under the role of the MRM function. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says assumptions and limitations should be documented and effectively communicated to users (under LO 57.a). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q15 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It treats the conceptual question as a matter of right or wrong. GARP says conceptual errors may not be a matter of right or wrong, which is why MRM’s role is transparency. It would be correct for an execution error, such as a coding mistake, where one answer is right.

b.reason: It states the GARP role (ensure transparency) and the GARP purpose of communication (so users understand when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued).

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It treats mention in the documentation as enough. GARP says documented limitations do not mean users are aware of them or understand them; MRM must ensure clear communication. It would be correct only if every user were known to have read and understood the documentation.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It promises to remove conceptual risk and to make the model valid in every environment. GARP says a model can be right in one context and wrong if the context changes; the risk is managed through transparency, not eliminated. It would be correct only if a model could be valid in all environments, which the source rules out.

questions.question: The head of MRM at a US asset manager is training validators on the priorities of the function when reviewing a complex USD pricing model used by portfolio managers with little quantitative background. Which of the following statements is least accurate?

options.text: MRM should replicate the model to confirm that no coding errors exist and that the outputs generated are the intended ones.
MRM’s more critical responsibility, beyond replication, is challenging the assumptions upon which the model relies.
MRM should help users understand in non-technical terms what the model’s limitations are, so as to minimise its misuse.
MRM’s most important skill is technical modelling depth, since it is the modelers’ responsibility alone to ensure that the model works.

questions.solution:
Head of MRM at a US asset manager training validators on MRM priorities for a complex pricing model with non-quantitative users.

**Concept and theory**

GARP sets out what a risk management function contributes when a complex model is used by people who cannot see inside it. Its role is “primarily one of improving transparency by shedding light in the so-called black box.” The priorities are ranked:

| Priority | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Always required | Replicate the model to ensure no coding errors exist and that the prices generated are the intended ones |
| More critical | Challenge the assumptions on which the model relies and ensure users understand its limitations |
| Most important skill | Effective communication |
| Purpose | Help users understand in non-technical terms what the limitations are, to minimise misuse |

GARP explains why communication is the key skill: most model users at financial institutions do not have a quantitative background, and “it is easy for them to deflect responsibility by simply relying on the argument that they cannot understand the model and that it is the modelers’ responsibility to ensure that it works.” A good MRM function prevents that deflection by making the limitations understandable.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least accurate statement. A, B and C each restate a GARP point (replication, the more critical challenge of assumptions, non-technical explanation of limitations). D names the wrong skill and endorses the very deflection of responsibility GARP warns against.

**Fragile fact.** Replication is always needed, but challenging assumptions is the more critical responsibility, and effective communication is the most important skill.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing” (paragraph on the role of the risk management function). Boundary call: the case’s facts and lessons belong to LO 57.c; this question tests only the general MRM priorities and skill stated there, which describe the role of the MRM function. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser places the transparency and effective communication point under its LO 57.c case summary and does not rank replication against challenge; GARP is used. No conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q16 of 16.

a.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP says MRM always needs to replicate the model to ensure that no coding errors exist and that the outputs are the intended ones. Because it is true, it cannot be the least accurate statement. It would become the answer only if it claimed replication were MRM’s most critical responsibility.

b.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP says that MRM’s more critical responsibility, beyond replication, is challenging the assumptions on which the model relies. It would be the answer only under a polarity flip that ranked replication above challenge.

c.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP says a good MRM function helps users understand in non-technical terms what the limitations are, to minimise misuse. It would be the answer only if it said MRM should explain the model in technical terms or leave users to rely on the modelers.

d.reason: D is the inaccurate statement, so it is the answer. It is a sibling swap: GARP names effective communication, not technical modelling depth, as the most important skill, and it describes “it is the modelers’ responsibility” as an excuse users use to deflect responsibility, not as a principle.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on the Gaussian copula approach to CDO pricing that David X. Li published in the early 2000s. The slide must state how the approach obtained the correlations among the assets in a pool. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: It estimated the correlations from historical mortgage default data, since long default histories were available and could be observed directly for each pool.
It inferred the correlations from CDS prices, on the premise that efficient market prices should reflect them, so pools could be priced without observing the correlations.
It inferred the correlations from traded CDO tranche prices, on the premise that a deep and long-established tranche market already reflected the pool correlations.
It inferred the correlations from CDS prices, a premise that was robust because CDS markets had several decades of data spanning a number of housing cycles.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Japanese bank writing a slide on how Li’s Gaussian copula approach obtained pool correlations.

**Concept and theory**

A collateralised debt obligation (CDO) is backed by a pool of assets, such as the mortgages in the GARP case. Pricing it requires the correlation between the default probabilities of the assets in the pool, that is, how likely they are to default together. The practical problem in the early 2000s was that these correlations could not be observed or calculated directly for a given pool.

David X. Li’s paper offered a way round this. The concept at the centre of his approach was the Gaussian copula, used to model the correlations between default probabilities of the assets in the pool. The key modelling choice was where that correlation came from:

| Element | Li’s choice (GARP, Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing) |
|---|---|
| Correlation source | Prices of credit default swaps (CDSs), rather than observed historical correlations |
| Justification | If markets are efficient, market prices should already reflect the correlation |
| Benefit | Pools could be priced without being able to observe and calculate their correlations |
| Weakness | CDSs had existed for only about a decade, a short and relatively benign sample |

The CDO market took off on the back of this approach. The lesson of the case starts here: the model’s output was only as good as an assumption (that CDS prices over a benign decade told you the true correlation) whose validity depended on the environment.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must state how the correlations were obtained. Two facts decide it: the source (CDS prices, not history and not tranche prices) and the stated premise (efficient markets). A third fact, the length of the CDS sample, rules out the option that gets the source right but overstates the data.

**Fragile fact.** Source direction: Li used CDS prices instead of historical correlations, and the CDS sample was short (about a decade) and benign.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing. Schweser additionally calls the inferred correlation the “Gaussian constant” and notes that historical mortgage default correlations tended to be low; GARP does not use the term. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the CDS-implied source for its sibling, historical correlations. GARP says explicitly that Li’s formula used CDS prices “rather than observed historical correlations”, and the whole point was that correlations could not be observed directly for each pool. This option would be correct for a stem describing a traditional historical-estimation approach to default correlation, not Li’s.

b.reason: GARP states that the approach was about “how to price pools of assets without being able to observe and calculate their correlations”, and that it used “CDS prices to infer the correlation of assets (assuming market prices should reflect the correlation if they are efficient)”. Option B states exactly this.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin.** It names the wrong market instrument: CDO tranche prices instead of CDS prices. The CDO is the product being priced, so it cannot be the source of its own correlation input, and the CDO market only “took off” after the approach was published, so it was not deep or long established. It would be right only for a stem about a later practice of backing out correlations from quoted tranche prices, which is not this case.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The source and premise are right, but it overextends the data condition. GARP says CDSs had been in existence “for only about a decade”, a “very short and relatively benign sample” in which house prices rose consistently and defaults were at all-time lows. This option would be correct only if the CDS history had covered several housing downturns, which is precisely what it lacked.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is reviewing a draft board paper on why CDO pricing based on the Gaussian copula broke down in 2008. Which of the following statements in the draft is most accurate?

options.text: The Gaussian copula assumption was invalid even in normal markets, so the CDO values it generated were inaccurate throughout the years before the crisis.
Correlations implied by CDS prices were high during the benign period and fell sharply once house prices reversed, which destabilised CDO prices.
The CDS data covered a long sample that included stress periods, so the breakdown must have come from coding errors in the banks’ pricing tools.
Correlations implied by CDS prices over a short, benign sample were very low and sensitive to house prices, and they shot up once house prices reversed.

questions.solution:
Singapore CRO reviewing a board paper on why Gaussian copula CDO pricing broke down in 2008.

**Concept and theory**

The copula case is GARP’s illustration of a conceptual error: a model that is “right” in one context and “completely wrong” if the context changes. Nothing in the code needs to be broken for this to happen. The chain of cause and effect in the case runs as follows:

1. The correlation input came from CDS prices, and CDSs had only about a decade of history.
2. That decade was benign: house prices rose consistently and defaults were at all-time lows.
3. CDS-implied correlations were therefore very low and extremely sensitive to the trajectory of house prices.
4. In normal markets the Gaussian copula assumption was “perfectly valid and generated accurate values”.
5. The moment house prices reversed, implied correlations “shot up”, with dramatic consequences for CDO prices; the assumption was no longer valid, yet many kept using tools built on it.

The lesson is that validity is conditional on the environment, and that a model calibrated on a short, calm sample hides how fragile its key input is.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes a claim about (i) whether the assumption worked in normal markets, (ii) the level and direction of implied correlations, and (iii) the nature of the error. Only one option gets all three right: low correlations in the benign sample, high sensitivity to house prices, and a spike on reversal.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: CDS-implied correlations were low in the benign period and shot up when house prices fell. The assumption was valid in normal markets; it failed when the context changed.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; also Model Risks (paragraph on conceptual errors, which cites the CDO case). Schweser describes the model as incorporating changing correlations “with a lag”; GARP frames it as banks failing to update the model. This is a difference of framing, not of substance, and does not affect the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It extends the failure to all conditions. GARP says the Gaussian copula assumption was “perfectly valid and generated accurate values in normal market conditions”; it became invalid only when correlations spiked. This option would be correct for a model whose assumption was wrong from the outset, which is not what the case describes.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses both directions: implied correlations were low in the benign period and rose sharply when house prices reversed. It would be correct only for an imaginary market in which a housing downturn made defaults less likely to cluster.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the conceptual error for its sibling, an execution (coding) error, and it reverses the data condition: the sample was short and benign, not long and stressed. It would describe a different case, in which the model’s concept was sound and the implementation was faulty.

d.reason: GARP: “Correlations implied by CDS prices in this environment were very low and extremely sensitive to the trajectory of house prices. The moment house prices reversed course, correlations implied by CDS prices shot up with dramatic consequences to CDO prices.” The “short, benign sample” is GARP’s own description of the decade of CDS data.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a German asset manager is reviewing a lessons-learned note on the Gaussian copula case. The note records that the pricing approach was adopted by bond investors, banks, rating agencies and regulators, and became so entrenched that warnings about its limitations were largely ignored. Which of the following best describes where the case places the blame for the losses?

options.text: With those who used the formula blindly: the quants, who should have known better and warned users, and the users, who relied on black-box prices they did not understand.
With the formula itself, because its mathematics was flawed and would have produced wrong CDO prices under any market conditions, however carefully it was used.
With the users alone, because the quants had documented the model’s limitations, and documenting the limitations ensures that users are aware of and understand them.
With the rating agencies and regulators, because their adoption of the approach entitled the quants and users at banks to rely on its prices without further challenge.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a German asset manager reviewing where the copula case places the blame for losses.

**Concept and theory**

A tempting reading of the CDO collapse is “the formula was wrong”. GARP rejects this. It quotes the Wired account that Li’s method “was adopted by everybody from bond investors and Wall Street banks to ratings agencies and regulators”, and that it became “so deeply entrenched, and was making people so much money, that warnings about its limitations were largely ignored”. GARP then states: “While it might be easy to simply blame the formula, the reality is that the blame falls with those who used it blindly.” It names two groups:

| Actor | Failing identified by GARP |
|---|---|
| Quants at the financial institutions | Should have known better and warned users |
| Users of the model | Should not have relied blindly on prices “spat out of a black box” they did not understand |

GARP adds that “the problem was not with the formula itself” but with the failure to update it. The broader point from the Model Risks section is that modellers may be aware of limitations, and may even document them, but “this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them”.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives the entrenchment facts and asks where the blame lies. The deciding fact is GARP’s attribution to both quants and users, for blind use, and its explicit refusal to blame the formula.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the blame falls on both the quants (who should have warned) and the users (who relied blindly), not on the formula and not on the regulators or rating agencies.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; Model Risks (users’ awareness of documented limitations). Schweser condenses this to the model having encouraged quants and managers to ignore real-world randomness; it does not set out the attribution of blame. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: It reproduces GARP’s attribution: the blame “falls with those who used it blindly: both the quants at the various financial institutions who should have known better and warned users, as well as users who should not have blindly relied on prices spat out of a black box that they did not understand”.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It blames the formula under “any market conditions”. GARP says the problem “was not with the formula itself”, and that the Gaussian copula assumption generated accurate values in normal market conditions. This option would be correct for a model that is mathematically unsound in every regime.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It clears the quants and puts all the blame on users, on the premise that documentation guarantees understanding. GARP says the quants should have warned users, and states separately that documenting limitations does not mean users will be aware of them or understand them. It would be right only if documentation alone discharged the modellers’ duty, which GARP denies.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves the blame to rating agencies and regulators. GARP lists them only among the adopters that show how entrenched the approach became; it does not say their adoption entitled others to rely on it. The blame sits with the quants and users who relied on it blindly. This option would fit a stem about an endorsement that carried a formal guarantee, which is not in the case.

questions.question: A model validation lead at a US bank is asked by the risk committee what the model risk management function’s most critical responsibility would have been in a context like the Gaussian copula and CDO pricing case. Which of the following answers is most accurate?

options.text: Replicating the model to confirm that no coding errors exist and that the prices generated are the intended ones, since this is the core defence against such failures.
Taking ownership of CDO pricing decisions away from model users, since users without a quantitative background cannot be expected to use such models appropriately.
Challenging the assumptions on which the model relies and ensuring that users understand its limitations, so that the model is not misused when conditions change.
Certifying the correlation assumption as valid for all market conditions before approval, so that conceptual errors are eliminated before the model is put to use.

questions.solution:
US validation lead asked for MRM’s most critical responsibility in a context like the copula case.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes the role of a risk management function in the copula context as “primarily one of improving transparency by shedding light in the so-called black box”. It then distinguishes two layers of work:

| Layer | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Always required | Replicate the model to ensure that no coding errors exist and that the prices generated are the intended ones |
| More critical | Challenge the assumptions upon which the model relies and ensure that users understand its limitations |
| Key skill | Effective communication, because most users do not have a quantitative background |

The reason the second layer matters more here is that the copula failure was conceptual: the code could replicate perfectly and the model would still misprice once correlations spiked. Replication catches execution errors; only challenge and communication address an assumption whose validity depends on context.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee asks for the most critical responsibility. Replication is a genuine MRM task, so the question turns on GARP’s ranking: replication “always” needs doing, but the “more critical responsibility” is challenging assumptions and ensuring user understanding.

**Fragile fact.** Ranking: replication is always needed, but challenging assumptions and ensuring users understand limitations is the more critical responsibility in this case.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing (paragraph on the role of a risk management function). Schweser says MRM “would aim to increase the transparency regarding the assumptions and limitations”; it does not rank replication against challenge. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q4 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It promotes the always-required task, replication, to the most critical one. Replication confirms that the code does what was intended; it would not have caught the copula problem, which lay in the assumption. This option would be the best answer for a case of coding or implementation error, where replication is the decisive check.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives MRM ownership of the pricing decisions. MRM sheds light in the black box and helps users understand the limitations; it does not take over the users’ decisions. GARP’s remedy for users lacking a quantitative background is communication in non-technical terms, not removal of their role.

c.reason: GARP: “its more critical responsibility is that of challenging the assumptions upon which the model relies and ensuring that users understand its limitations”. Option C states this and links it to preventing misuse when conditions change.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It promises that conceptual errors can be eliminated by certifying an assumption as valid in all conditions. GARP’s whole point is that a model can be right in one context and wrong in another, and that MRM’s role for conceptual errors is to ensure transparency. It would be correct only if an assumption could be shown valid in every possible environment.

questions.question: The head of model risk management at a Brazilian bank meets business heads who use a BRL credit portfolio pricing model. They say: “We cannot understand this model, and making sure that it works is the modellers’ job.” Which of the following responses is most consistent with the lesson of the Gaussian copula case?

options.text: Accept the position, because model performance is the modellers’ responsibility, and users without a quantitative background need not understand the model’s limitations.
Require every user to complete quantitative training to the modellers’ level before using the model, because only technically expert users can understand its limitations.
Circulate the modellers’ full technical documentation, because once the modellers have documented the model’s limitations, users will be aware of them and understand them.
Explain the model’s limitations in non-technical terms, so that users understand when it can be safely used and when its use should stop, which minimises misuse of the model.

questions.solution:
Head of MRM at a Brazilian bank responding to business heads who say the model is the modellers’ job.

**Concept and theory**

The copula case ends with a lesson about people rather than mathematics. GARP says that “the most important skill required for the MRM function to be successful with this challenge is effective communication”. The reasoning is:

1. Most users of models at financial institutions do not have a quantitative background.
2. It is easy for them to “deflect responsibility by simply relying on the argument that they cannot understand the model and that it is the modelers’ responsibility to ensure that it works”.
3. A good MRM function “will help users understand in non-technical terms what the limitations are to minimize the mis-use of the models”.

The Model Risks section adds the purpose of the communication: users should understand “when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued”. Documentation alone is not enough, because modellers may document limitations without users being aware of them or understanding them.

**Applying it to this question**

The business heads use, almost word for word, the deflection argument that GARP describes. The question asks for the response consistent with the case. The deciding facts are the form of the remedy (non-technical explanation), its purpose (safe use and when to stop) and its aim (minimising misuse).

**Fragile fact.** Actor and form: MRM explains limitations to users in non-technical terms; the most important MRM skill named in this case is effective communication, not technical replication.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; Model Risks (communication of assumptions and limitations). Schweser: “Given that the model users lacked the necessary quantitative background, effective communication would have been critical to minimize the misuse of the model.” No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It accepts the deflection and leaves the whole responsibility with the modellers. GARP identifies this as the very attitude that let users rely blindly on a black box in the copula case. It would be correct only if users had no need to know when a model ceases to be safe to use, which GARP rejects.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It overextends the remedy: users need to understand the limitations, not to become quantitative experts. GARP’s prescription is explanation in non-technical terms, precisely because most users lack a quantitative background. It would be right for a stem about the competence of validators, not of business users.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the condition that documentation must be made understandable. GARP says modellers may discuss limitations in their documentation, “but this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them”. Circulating technical documentation would be adequate only for a technically trained audience.

d.reason: It matches GARP’s prescription: help users understand “in non-technical terms what the limitations are to minimize the mis-use of the models”, so that they know when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK bank is preparing a briefing on the Barclays bid for Lehman Brothers assets in September 2008. She has collected the following facts.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| File sent by Barclays | Excel file of 1,000 rows and 24,000 cells, sent at 7.50 p.m. on 18 September |
| Submission deadline | Midnight on 18 September, to the bankruptcy court’s website |
| Contracts not wanted | 179 trading contracts listed in the file |
| Discovery of the problem | 1 October |

Which of the following best describes how the error arose and was dealt with?

options.text: Barclays had deleted the 179 rows, but a junior law associate at Cleary Gottlieb restored them while reformatting the file, and a legal motion was later filed to exclude them.
The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted; a junior law associate at Cleary Gottlieb, reformatting the file to PDF, was unaware of them, and they became visible in the PDF.
The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted; a court clerk converting the file to PDF for the court’s website made them visible, and the court later excluded them itself.
The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted and became visible in the PDF, but the error was caught before the deal was approved, so no legal motion was needed.

questions.solution:
UK senior risk analyst briefing on how the Barclays and Lehman spreadsheet error arose and was dealt with.

**Concept and theory**

The second case is GARP’s example of a simple implementation error. The facts matter because each fact carries part of the lesson:

| Step | Fact (GARP, Barclays’ Acquisition of Lehman Brothers) |
|---|---|
| Context | Lehman filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008; three days later Barclays Capital offered to buy part of its assets, including trading positions |
| Submission | Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton, Barclays’ law firm, had to file the offer on the bankruptcy court’s website by midnight on 18 September |
| The file | Barclays sent an Excel file at 7.50 p.m. on 18 September: 1,000 rows, 24,000 cells, including 179 contracts it did not want to buy |
| The flaw | The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted |
| The trigger | A junior law associate at Cleary Gottlieb, on a tight schedule, reformatted the file to PDF; unaware of the hidden rows, he produced a PDF in which they were visible again |
| Discovery | 1 October, after the deal had been approved |
| Remedy | Cleary Gottlieb filed a legal motion to exclude those contracts |

The error was trivial in itself (forgetting to delete rows), arose under time pressure, passed through a hand-off between organisations and was caught only after approval. That combination is what GARP means when it says seemingly trivial execution errors, paired with bad luck and a confluence of events, can produce a “perfect storm”.

**Applying it to this question**

The table in the stem is mostly context: the row and cell counts and the 7.50 p.m. send time do not discriminate between the options. What decides the answer are four facts: hidden, not deleted; who converted the file (a junior associate at Cleary Gottlieb); the file format (PDF); and when the error was spotted (1 October, after approval).

**Fragile fact.** Actor and timing: the rows were hidden, not deleted; a junior associate at Cleary Gottlieb (Barclays’ law firm) converted the file; the error was spotted after approval, on 1 October.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Barclays’ Acquisition of Lehman Brothers and the Excel Spreadsheet Error. GARP vs Schweser difference: Schweser says the mistake was realised “several days later” and that Barclays had to file the legal motion; GARP gives 1 October and says Cleary Gottlieb filed it. GARP is used here; the difference looks like condensation in Schweser rather than a version change, and no option turns on who filed the motion.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the state of the rows: they were hidden, not deleted, and the associate did not restore anything; the conversion simply displayed what was still in the file. The option would be correct only if deleted data could reappear on conversion, which is the opposite of the case’s lesson that the rows should have been deleted.

b.reason: GARP: the 179 contracts “were, however, hidden rather than deleted”; a junior law associate at Cleary Gottlieb “was tasked with reformatting the Excel file to a PDF document” and “was not aware of those hidden rows, which were visible again in the PDF file”.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It puts the conversion in the hands of a court clerk and has the court exclude the contracts on its own initiative. In GARP the conversion was done by a junior associate at Barclays’ law firm, and the law firm filed the motion to exclude. This option would fit a case in which the court itself processed the submission.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It moves the discovery before approval. GARP says the mistake “was only spotted on October 1, after the deal had been approved”, which is why a legal motion was needed. The option would be correct only if the error had been caught in the window before approval.

questions.question: A model inventory reviewer at a Canadian bank is deciding whether a spreadsheet like the one in the Barclays and Lehman Brothers case belongs in the model inventory. The spreadsheet lists the trading contracts to be acquired and their values. Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the case study?

options.text: It is a model, because it processes quantitative information on trading contracts into an output that the bank relies on when it submits a binding purchase offer.
It is a model, because the contract values it contains may carry estimation errors, which makes the spreadsheet itself the source of model risk for those values.
It is not a model, because there is no uncertainty around its contents; any estimation error in the values belongs to the models used to value the contracts.
It is not a model, and therefore it falls outside the scope of review, challenge and controls, which apply only to tools that meet the definition of a model.

questions.solution:
Canadian model inventory reviewer deciding whether a Barclays-type spreadsheet is a model.

**Concept and theory**

The current industry consensus quoted in GARP is that a model is “any estimation method that uses data and relies on a set of assumptions to generate an uncertain estimate/forecast”, with the emphasis increasingly “on the uncertain nature of the forecast”. The Barclays case applies that test to a spreadsheet and concludes that it is not a model:

1. There is no uncertainty around the information it contains.
2. The list of assets is known, and their values are known or at least agreed upon.
3. If there are estimation errors in the asset values, “they would be model risks related to the models used to value them not the spreadsheet, which is really just inventorying them”.

The second half of the lesson is just as important: being outside the definition of a model does not put a tool outside control. GARP calls the case “an excellent example of why even seemingly simplistic tools or models still need the right review, challenge and controls”.

**Applying it to this question**

The reviewer must classify the spreadsheet. The deciding facts are the absence of uncertainty in its contents and the attribution of any valuation error to the upstream valuation models. A further fact, that non-model tools still need controls, rules out the option that reaches the right classification but the wrong consequence.

**Fragile fact.** Not a model does not mean no control: the spreadsheet is outside the model definition (no uncertainty), yet still needs review, challenge and controls.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Barclays’ Acquisition of Lehman Brothers and the Excel Spreadsheet Error; Definition and History (consensus definition, used only as applied in the case). Schweser: “The spreadsheet is not a model, but the failure to delete the unneeded rows posed a large potential loss.” No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the defining condition of a model, an uncertain estimate produced by applying assumptions to data. Processing quantitative information into an output that matters is not enough; a spreadsheet that only inventories known contracts produces no estimate. The option would be right for a spreadsheet that applied assumptions to generate forecast values.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the model risk of the upstream valuation models to the spreadsheet. GARP says such estimation errors “would be model risks related to the models used to value them”, with the spreadsheet “just inventorying them”. It would be correct only if the spreadsheet itself estimated the values, in which case it would be a valuation model.

c.reason: GARP: the spreadsheet “does not fit the definition of a model, there is no uncertainty around the information contained in the spreadsheet”; any estimation errors in asset values “would be model risks related to the models used to value them not the spreadsheet”.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The classification is right but the consequence is wrong: it treats “not a model” as “needs no control”. GARP draws the opposite lesson, that even seemingly simplistic tools need the right review, challenge and controls, and notes in the Model Risks section that execution-type errors are also found in tools that are not considered models.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is drafting an operational risk report and must choose one statement summarising the lesson of the Barclays spreadsheet error. Which of the following statements should she include?

options.text: The error was a simple implementation error in a tool, and although no loss materialised, it could have, so even seemingly simplistic tools need review, challenge and controls.
The error was a simple implementation error in a tool, and because no loss materialised, it shows that such errors are self-correcting and need no controls beyond legal process.
The error was a conceptual error in a tool, showing that invalid assumptions in simple spreadsheets are harder to identify than invalid assumptions in complex pricing models.
The error was an implementation error in a tool, showing that simple tools cannot create material losses, so review effort should be reserved for complex quantitative models.

questions.solution:
Australian treasury analyst choosing the statement that summarises the lesson of the Barclays spreadsheet error.

**Concept and theory**

GARP classifies the Barclays error as “a perfect example of a simple implementation error”. Three features of the lesson work together:

| Feature | GARP’s statement |
|---|---|
| Type of error | A simple implementation error, in a tool that is not a model |
| Severity | Seemingly innocuous (forgetting to delete hidden rows), yet it “nearly cost Barclays millions of dollars” |
| Outcome | “In this instance, the loss did not materialize, but under different circumstances, it could have” |
| Lesson | Even seemingly simplistic tools or models still need the right review, challenge and controls |

The near-miss character of the case is the point: an absence of loss here was luck, not evidence that the control environment worked.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option pairs an error type with a conclusion. The deciding facts are the type (implementation, not conceptual), the outcome (no loss, but one could have arisen) and the direction of the lesson (more control over simple tools, not less).

**Fragile fact.** Outcome: in the Barclays case the loss did not materialise, but it could have; the lesson is more control over simple tools, not less.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Barclays’ Acquisition of Lehman Brothers and the Excel Spreadsheet Error. Schweser: “This is an example of an implementation error.” No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: It combines GARP’s classification (“simple implementation error”), its outcome statement (the loss did not materialise but could have) and its conclusion (“even seemingly simplistic tools or models still need the right review, challenge and controls”).

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns the near-miss into evidence that no controls are needed. GARP draws the opposite conclusion: because the loss could have materialised under different circumstances, simple tools need review, challenge and controls. The legal motion was a costly after-the-event remedy, not a control. The option would be right only if errors of this kind reliably corrected themselves, which the case contradicts.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps implementation error for its sibling, conceptual error. There was no assumption in dispute: the contracts were known and the error was failing to delete rows. GARP reserves the “harder to identify” description for conceptual errors such as the copula assumption. The option would fit a stem about a spreadsheet resting on a debatable estimate.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It claims that simple tools “cannot” create material losses. GARP says the error nearly cost Barclays millions and that trivial-seeming errors have resulted in catastrophic losses. The option would be correct only for a tool whose failure could have no financial consequence.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Japanese insurer is reviewing four recent incidents and must identify the one that is the closest financial-world parallel to the NASA Mars orbiter case. The insurer’s total investment portfolio is JPY 2.4 trillion.

| Incident | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | A pricing model calibrated during a benign period stays in use after market-implied correlations spike, and nobody updates its correlation inputs. |
| 2 | Rows marking positions that should be excluded are hidden rather than deleted, and they reappear when the file is converted for submission. |
| 3 | Two experienced modellers hold different, equally valid views on which default correlation is appropriate for a new pool of loans. |
| 4 | One team supplies cash flows in JPY to a valuation model that another team built on the basis that all inputs are in USD, and the mismatch is never checked. |

Which incident is the closest parallel?

options.text: Incident 1
Incident 2
Incident 3
Incident 4

questions.solution:
Japanese insurer’s risk consultant identifying the closest financial parallel to the Mars orbiter case.

**Concept and theory**

NASA lost a USD 125 million Mars orbiter because a Lockheed Martin engineering team used English units of measurement while the agency’s team used the metric system for a key spacecraft operation. GARP calls this “an error in the ‘assumptions’ of the model, the choice of the unit (metric vs imperial)”, and then gives the financial translation:

| Mars orbiter | Financial parallel named by GARP |
|---|---|
| Choice of unit (metric vs imperial) | Use of the wrong currency |
|  | Use of the wrong discount factor “Other simple assumptions that are often taken for granted” |

The signature of a Mars-type error is: two parties, each internally consistent, working to different basic conventions that nobody thinks to reconcile, because the convention seems too obvious to check.

**Applying it to this question**

The insurer’s portfolio size is irrelevant. Each incident is matched to the signature of one case:

| Incident | Signature | Matching case |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Assumption valid in calm markets, not updated after correlations spike | Gaussian copula |
| 2 | Rows hidden rather than deleted, revealed on conversion | Barclays spreadsheet |
| 3 | Reasonable experts disagree on an assumption | Generic conceptual error (no case) |
| 4 | JPY inputs fed into a model built on the basis of USD inputs, never checked | Mars orbiter (wrong currency) |

**Fragile fact.** Parallel: the Mars orbiter error maps to the wrong currency or discount factor in finance, a simple convention taken for granted, not to a debatable modelling assumption.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: NASA Mars Orbiter; Model Risks (conceptual errors as matters of reasonable disagreement). Schweser does not give the financial parallel; it describes the error as a mistake in the measurement of model inputs. The parallel tested is from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Incident 1 is the Gaussian copula pattern: an assumption that was valid in a benign environment and was not updated when implied correlations rose. It would be the right answer if the question asked for the closest parallel to the CDO pricing case.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Incident 2 is the Barclays pattern: data hidden rather than deleted and revealed on conversion, a simple implementation error in a tool. It would be correct for a question asking for the parallel to the Barclays case.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Incident 3 is a conceptual disagreement where “different reasonable modelers can have different and equally valid opinions on an assumption”. Inconsistent units are not a matter of valid opinion. This incident would be the answer to a question about the kind of model risk for which MRM’s role is to ensure transparency.

d.reason: Incident 4 is a mismatch of a basic convention between two teams, the currency, which is exactly GARP’s parallel: “In the financial world, a parallel could be the use of the wrong currency, discount factor, or other simple assumptions that are often taken for granted.”

questions.question: A regulator at a Chinese banking supervisor is writing guidance that draws on the NASA Mars orbiter case, in which a Lockheed Martin engineering team and the agency’s team used different systems of units for a key spacecraft operation, and the USD 125 million orbiter was lost. Which of the following characterisations of the case is most accurate?

options.text: An error in a simple assumption taken for granted, the choice of unit; the error sounds too obvious to have been missed, yet it destroyed the orbiter.
An error that was hard to identify, because the choice of unit was a matter on which reasonable engineers could hold different, equally valid views.
An error in an assumption that was valid in normal conditions but failed once the operating environment changed, as with correlations under market stress.
An error in a simple assumption taken for granted, the choice of unit; the agency’s team used English units while Lockheed Martin used the metric system.

questions.solution:
Chinese regulator characterising the Mars orbiter error for supervisory guidance.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s description of the Mars orbiter case has four parts:

1. Facts: NASA lost a USD 125 million orbiter because a Lockheed Martin engineering team used English units while the agency’s team used the more conventional metric system for a key spacecraft operation.
2. Obviousness: “This error sounds too obvious to not have been caught earlier in the process”, yet it happened and destroyed the satellite.
3. Classification: “This is an error in the ‘assumptions’ of the model, the choice of the unit (metric vs imperial).” GARP puts the word assumptions in quotation marks: this is a simple convention taken for granted, not a debatable modelling judgment. In its Model Risks section, GARP groups the case with Barclays as a prime example of trivial-seeming execution errors that produced catastrophic losses.
4. Contrast with conceptual errors: conceptual errors are hard to identify because “they may not be a matter of right or wrong”; reasonable modellers may hold equally valid views. Inconsistent units are simply wrong.

**Applying it to this question**

Options A and D share the same correct classification, so the actors decide between them. Options B and C import the features of other kinds of error. The deciding facts are who used which units, and that the error was obvious rather than debatable or environment-dependent.

**Fragile fact.** Actors: Lockheed Martin used English units; NASA used metric. GARP calls the unit choice an “assumption” in quotation marks, a simple convention, not a debatable modelling judgment.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: NASA Mars Orbiter; Model Risks (Barclays and NASA cited as prime examples of execution errors). GARP vs Schweser difference: Schweser calls this “a mistake in the measurement of model inputs” and its key concepts call it “input measurement error”, while GARP calls it an error in the “assumptions” of the model. GARP is used here, and no option turns on the label “input” versus “assumption”; both sources agree that it was a simple, avoidable error.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: It follows GARP’s classification (an error in the “assumptions” of the model, the choice of unit, a simple assumption often taken for granted) and its observation that the error “sounds too obvious” to have been missed, yet led to the destruction of the satellite.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It gives the unit error the defining property of a conceptual error, one on which reasonable experts can hold different, equally valid views. There is no valid view in which two teams can use different unit systems for the same operation. The option would describe a genuine conceptual disagreement, such as the choice of default correlation for a new loan pool.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the copula case’s feature, an assumption valid in normal conditions that fails when the environment changes, to the orbiter. The unit mismatch was wrong from the start; no change in conditions made it wrong. This would be the right characterisation of the Gaussian copula case.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The classification is correct but the actors are swapped. GARP says Lockheed Martin’s engineering team used English units, while the agency (NASA) used the metric system. The option would be right only if the roles were reversed.

questions.question: A board member of a UK bank questions the cost of the model risk management function. Its annual budget is GBP 18 million, and it reported 312 model errors last year, almost all of which would have caused small losses, if any. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the lessons of the model risk case studies?

options.text: The function should review only the models whose errors have caused catastrophic losses in the past, because the other errors it catches are benign.
The function can identify in advance which mistakes will be catastrophic, so its reviews can be restricted to those mistakes and its budget reduced.
Most caught mistakes would cause benign losses, but a small subset could be catastrophic, and since these cannot be identified in advance, all models need review.
The board’s concern is unfounded, because most of the mistakes caught by the function would have caused catastrophic losses had they not been caught.

questions.solution:
UK board member questioning the cost of MRM when almost all caught errors would have caused small losses.

**Concept and theory**

The Mars orbiter section closes with GARP’s general argument for comprehensive model risk management. It anticipates exactly the objection a board might raise:

1. The cost of an MRM function that “reviews all models and double checks all the work often upsets executives because of the perceived benign nature of some of the mistakes that are caught”.
2. It is “undeniable that in most instances these benign mistakes would have resulted in benign losses, if any”.
3. It is “equally undeniable that a small subset of these mistakes could result in catastrophic losses, such as the loss of the Mars orbiter”.
4. “Unfortunately, it is impossible to determine which mistakes will lead to catastrophic losses and which ones will not!”

The logic is that of a tail risk. GARP’s Model Risks section explains that model risk is often underestimated because of its tail nature: most errors are benign, which leaves institutions with misplaced confidence, and the rarity of severe events makes the cost of MRM “seem disproportionate relative to the risk”. Since the catastrophic few cannot be singled out in advance, the only defence is to review everything. Schweser puts the same point as MRM being “sometimes viewed as a bureaucratic obstacle” whose importance “cannot be overstated”.

**Applying it to this question**

The budget (GBP 18 million) and the number of errors (312) are irrelevant inputs; the argument does not depend on them. The board member’s premise (almost all caught errors are benign) is true. The question is what follows from it. The deciding fact is that catastrophic mistakes cannot be identified in advance.

**Fragile fact.** Frequency: most caught mistakes are benign; a small subset could be catastrophic, and which ones cannot be determined in advance.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: NASA Mars Orbiter (closing paragraph); Definition and History (tail nature of model risk). Schweser: “Oftentimes, small mistakes result in losses; some of those losses, however, can be quite large.” No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows review to models with a history of catastrophic loss. The orbiter’s error had no such history; it was a simple convention nobody thought to check. Because catastrophic mistakes cannot be predicted, past catastrophes are not a usable filter. The option would hold only if catastrophic errors recurred in the same models.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It asserts that MRM can tell in advance which mistakes will be catastrophic. GARP says the opposite: “it is impossible to determine which mistakes will lead to catastrophic losses and which ones will not”. If that foresight existed, targeted review would indeed be efficient, which is why the option is tempting.

c.reason: It accepts the true premise, adds GARP’s “small subset” that could be catastrophic, and draws GARP’s conclusion from the impossibility of telling them apart in advance: all models need review.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the frequency: GARP says most caught mistakes would have caused benign losses, if any, and only a small subset could be catastrophic. Defending MRM on a false premise would be wrong even though the conclusion (keep MRM) is right. The option would be correct only in an institution where most errors were severe.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at a French bank is reviewing four statements in a paper on what the Barclays and NASA Mars orbiter cases teach about model risk.

I. Trivial-seeming execution errors, paired with bad luck and a confluence of events, have resulted in catastrophic losses.

II. Because most errors are benign or caught early, a record of few model-related losses shows that an institution manages model risk well.

III. Errors of the kind seen in the Barclays case are also found in tools that are not considered models.

IV. Both cases show that conceptual errors are easier to identify than execution errors, because conceptual errors are a matter of right or wrong.

Which of the statements are consistent with the case study reading?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
French risk committee member auditing four statements on what the Barclays and Mars orbiter cases teach.

**Concept and theory**

GARP uses the Barclays and Mars orbiter cases to make a point about execution errors in its Model Risks section:

- “Execution errors often seem like trivial errors that cannot result in a material loss. Yet over and over such trivial seeming errors, paired with bad luck and a confluence of events that set the right conditions for a ‘perfect storm,’ have resulted in catastrophic losses. The Barclays’ acquisition of Lehman Brothers and the NASA Mars orbiter case studies below are prime examples.”
- Such errors can be coding errors, implementation errors, use of the wrong data and so forth, and “such errors are also found in tools that are not considered models”; the Barclays spreadsheet is itself such a tool.
- Conceptual errors, by contrast, “are much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong”.

GARP adds that model risk is underestimated because most errors are benign and are either caught early or do not lead to material losses, which “often leaves institutions with misplaced confidence in their ability to manage the risk”.

**Applying it to this question**

| Statement | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| I | True | GARP’s own statement, with Barclays and NASA as prime examples |
| II | False | Polarity flip: a record of few losses creates misplaced confidence; it is not evidence of good management |
| III | True | Execution-type errors are also found in tools that are not models; the Barclays spreadsheet is one |
| IV | False | Polarity flip: conceptual errors are harder to identify, because they may not be a matter of right or wrong |

**Fragile fact.** Direction: execution errors seem trivial but can be catastrophic; conceptual errors are the harder ones to identify. Few past losses breed misplaced confidence.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Model Risks (execution errors and the two case studies); Definition and History (tail nature and misplaced confidence); Case Studies: Barclays’ Acquisition of Lehman Brothers. Boundary note: the passages are in the section serving LO 57.a, but they state what these two cases teach, so they are tested here only as case lessons. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” omits statement III. A reader who thinks the case lesson is confined to models will reject III, but GARP says expressly that such errors are also found in tools that are not considered models, and the Barclays spreadsheet “does not fit the definition of a model”. This option would be right only if III were limited to models.

b.reason: Only statements I and III are consistent with the reading: I is GARP’s description of what the two cases exemplify, and III is GARP’s statement that such errors also occur in tools not considered models, of which the Barclays spreadsheet is the case example.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts statement II, which reverses GARP’s point. A record of few losses is what produces “misplaced confidence”; the tail risks materialise under extreme conditions. II would be correct only if a short loss record were a reliable measure of tail exposure.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts statements II and IV, both of which reverse GARP, and drops the true statement I. IV inverts GARP’s comparison: conceptual errors are harder to identify than execution errors. This combination would be correct only if both directions were reversed in the source.
