questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is training new hires on the three model risk case studies. She asks them to choose the row that correctly matches each case with the nature of the error.

| Row | Gaussian copula and CDO pricing | Barclays spreadsheet | NASA Mars orbiter |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Assumption valid in normal markets became invalid as conditions changed | Simple implementation error in a tool that is not a model | Simple assumption taken for granted (choice of unit) |
| B | Coding error in the copula pricing routine | Simple implementation error in a tool that is not a model | Simple assumption taken for granted (choice of unit) |
| C | Assumption valid in normal markets became invalid as conditions changed | Invalid assumption in the spreadsheet’s estimated asset values | Simple assumption taken for granted (choice of unit) |
| D | Assumption valid in normal markets became invalid as conditions changed | Simple implementation error in a tool that is not a model | Debatable modelling judgment on which reasonable engineers could differ |

Which row is correct?

options.text: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.solution:
Singapore senior analyst training new hires to match each case study with the nature of its error.

**Concept and theory**

The three cases illustrate three different ways in which a model, or a tool, can fail. Schweser’s key concepts summarise them as the risk of using models given “(1) the invalidity of assumptions, (2) implementation error, or (3) input measurement error”. GARP’s text supports the following matrix:

| Case | Nature of the error | Key GARP wording |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian copula | Conceptual: an assumption valid in normal markets that became invalid when correlations spiked | “perfectly valid . . . in normal market conditions”; “no longer valid” |
| Barclays | Simple implementation error, in a tool that does not fit the definition of a model | “a perfect example of a simple implementation error” |
| Mars orbiter | Error in a simple assumption taken for granted, the choice of unit; execution-type | “an error in the ‘assumptions’ of the model, the choice of the unit” |

**Applying it to this question**

Each wrong row corrupts exactly one cell of Row A. The reader has to check every cell, not only the first column.

**Fragile fact.** Classification: copula = assumption that ceased to be valid (conceptual); Barclays = implementation error in a non-model tool; Mars = simple unit “assumption” (execution-type).

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies (all three sections); Model Risks. GARP vs Schweser difference: Schweser’s key concepts call the Mars orbiter case “input measurement error”, while GARP calls it an error in the “assumptions” of the model (the choice of unit). The matrix uses GARP’s wording, and no row turns on the input versus assumption label.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: Row A matches each case to GARP’s classification: the copula assumption valid in normal markets but invalid when conditions changed; the Barclays simple implementation error in a non-model tool; and the Mars orbiter error in the choice of unit, a simple assumption taken for granted.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Row B makes the copula case a coding error. GARP says MRM must always replicate a model to exclude coding errors, but the copula problem was “not with the formula itself”; it was the failure to update an assumption that was no longer valid. Row B would be correct for a case in which a correctly conceived model was coded wrongly.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Row C turns the Barclays case into an invalid assumption in estimated asset values. GARP says there is no uncertainty in the spreadsheet, the asset values are known or agreed, and any estimation error would belong to the valuation models. Row C would fit a case in which the spreadsheet was itself a valuation model.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Row D gives the Mars orbiter case the property of a conceptual error, a debatable judgment on which reasonable experts could differ. GARP says the error “sounds too obvious to not have been caught” and groups it with Barclays as an execution error. Row D would fit a genuine disagreement between experts about an assumption.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is checking a training handout that pairs each model risk case study with a lesson for model risk management. Which of the following pairings is NOT correct?

options.text: Gaussian copula: challenge the model’s assumptions and explain its limitations to users in non-technical terms, so that the model is not used blindly.
Barclays spreadsheet: even seemingly simplistic tools need the right review, challenge and controls, because simple errors can nearly cost millions.
Mars orbiter: check simple assumptions that are often taken for granted, such as the currency or the discount factor used in a financial model.
Barclays spreadsheet: replicate the spreadsheet’s valuation of the 179 contracts, because the error arose from estimation error in the spreadsheet’s values.

questions.solution:
Brazilian internal auditor finding the incorrect case-to-lesson pairing in a training handout.

**Concept and theory**

Each case carries its own lesson for model risk management:

| Case | MRM lesson (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Gaussian copula | Improve transparency; challenge assumptions; ensure users understand limitations, explained in non-technical terms, to minimise misuse |
| Barclays | Even seemingly simplistic tools or models need the right review, challenge and controls; the error nearly cost Barclays millions |
| Mars orbiter | Check simple assumptions taken for granted (in finance: currency, discount factor); review all models because catastrophic mistakes cannot be identified in advance |

In the Barclays case the risk lay in the handling of the file (rows hidden rather than deleted and then exposed by conversion), not in the values. GARP says the asset values were known or agreed, and that any estimation error in them would be model risk of the valuation models, not of the spreadsheet.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT correct, so three pairings are true and one misstates a lesson. The deciding fact is the location of the Barclays error: in implementation, not in estimation.

Here each of the remaining options is a correct pairing, so choosing it is the error.

**Fragile fact.** Location of the Barclays error: in implementation (hidden rows), not in the values; valuation estimation error belongs to the valuation models.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies (all three sections). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: **Qualifier misread.** This pairing is correct: in the copula case MRM’s critical responsibility is challenging assumptions and ensuring users understand limitations, communicated in non-technical terms to minimise misuse. A reader who picks A has probably been distracted by “blindly”, which is GARP’s own word for how the formula was used. This option would be the answer only if it paired the copula case with replicating the code to remove coding errors, which GARP ranks below challenging assumptions.

b.reason: **Qualifier misread.** This pairing is correct: GARP calls the Barclays case “an excellent example of why even seemingly simplistic tools or models still need the right review, challenge and controls”, and says the error “nearly cost Barclays millions of dollars”. Choosing B usually reflects the belief that a non-model tool needs no review, which the case refutes. This option would be the answer only if it said that a tool outside the model definition needs no review.

c.reason: **Qualifier misread.** This pairing is correct: GARP’s financial parallel for the unit error is “the use of the wrong currency, discount factor, or other simple assumptions that are often taken for granted”. A reader who rejects C may be thinking only of physical units and not of their financial equivalents. This option would be the answer only if it described the unit choice as a debatable modelling judgment.

d.reason: This pairing is the incorrect one, which makes D the answer. It attributes the Barclays error to estimation error in the spreadsheet’s values, which GARP rules out: there was “no uncertainty around the information contained in the spreadsheet”, and estimation errors in values “would be model risks related to the models used to value them not the spreadsheet”. Replicating a valuation would not have caught a hidden row.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing a US bank’s internal post-mortem on its CDO pricing losses in 2008. The bank had priced its CDOs with a Gaussian copula model that drew its correlations from CDS prices. As house prices fell, CDS prices rose sharply. Which of the following best explains what went wrong, according to the case study?

options.text: Banks updated the copula model promptly with the higher CDS-implied correlations, and the losses arose because the formula cannot produce valid prices at high correlations.
Banks switched from CDS-implied correlations to historical correlations once CDS prices rose, and the low historical correlations then understated the risk in their CDOs.
Banks failed to update the copula model with the new, higher correlation estimates implied by CDS prices, and they continued to price CDOs using the old assumptions.
Banks’ pricing tools contained coding errors that went unnoticed in benign markets, and the losses arose because these errors were magnified once CDS prices rose.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant reviewing a US bank’s post-mortem on its 2008 Gaussian copula CDO pricing losses.

**Concept and theory**

Having said that the blame falls on those who used the formula blindly, GARP pins down the mechanism of failure: “In actuality, the problem was not with the formula itself, but with the fact that banks failed to update the copula model with the new correlation estimates implied by the higher CDS prices, and instead continued to price CDOs using the old assumptions.”

The sequence is:

1. The model’s correlation input was meant to come from CDS prices.
2. As house prices fell in 2008, CDS prices rose, implying much higher correlations.
3. Banks did not feed these higher correlations back into the model; they kept the low correlations from the benign period.
4. CDO prices therefore rested on stale assumptions, until “the correlations implied by the CDSs, and consequently the CDO prices, swung dramatically, resulting in a collapse of the market”.

GARP’s conceptual-error paragraph says the same: many continued to use CDO pricing tools that relied on the assumption “without realizing the magnitude of the pricing errors that were resulting”. The lesson is that an assumption must be monitored and updated as the environment changes, and that users must know when a model should no longer be used.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks what went wrong. The deciding fact is the direction of the banks’ action: they did not update the model with the new CDS-implied correlations. Options that have banks updating promptly, switching to another data source, or suffering from code defects all contradict the source.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of action: banks failed to update the model with the higher CDS-implied correlations and kept the old assumptions; the formula itself was not the problem.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; Model Risks (conceptual errors paragraph). Schweser says the model “incorporated changing correlations with a lag”. That is compatible with GARP’s statement that banks failed to update the model and kept the old assumptions; GARP’s wording is used. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the banks’ action (they did not update promptly) and then blames the formula, which GARP says was not the problem. It would be correct only for a model that was kept current but could not handle high correlations, which is not what GARP describes.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin.** It replaces the CDS-implied input with its twin, historical correlations. The case says nothing about a switch to historical data; GARP says banks kept the old CDS-implied assumptions. This option would describe a different failure, in which a bank replaced a market-implied input with a backward-looking one.

c.reason: It restates GARP’s diagnosis: banks “failed to update the copula model with the new correlation estimates implied by the higher CDS prices, and instead continued to price CDOs using the old assumptions”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the conceptual failure for an execution failure (coding errors). GARP says the problem was not with the formula, and its conceptual-error paragraph cites this case as one where a valid assumption ceased to hold. It would be the right explanation for a case in which a correctly conceived model was implemented wrongly.

questions.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian regional bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on why broad-based supervisory stress testing became the regulators’ main tool for assessing bank capital adequacy during the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis. Which of the following statements should she include as most accurate?

options.text: Firms such as Lehman and Wachovia were adequately or even well capitalized under the regulatory capital rules disclosed in their filings before they failed or nearly failed, so published capital ratios lost credibility.
Stress testing was adopted because it answers a different question from regulatory and internal economic capital models, which do not seek the capital needed to support a bank’s risk taking.
Stress testing was favored because bank balance sheets are highly transparent, so supervisors could verify each bank’s results quickly from its public filings and existing reports.
Supervisory stress tests were designed to guarantee that no participating bank would fail, a goal that regulatory and economic capital models had never been calibrated to achieve.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst explaining to new hires why supervisory stress testing became the crisis capital tool.

**Concept and theory**

Schuermann opens with a simple taxonomy: there are three kinds of capital (and liquidity): (1) what the bank has, (2) what the bank needs to support its business activities, and (3) what the regulators think it needs. Regulatory capital rules, bank-internal “economic capital” models and stress tests all try to answer the same question: how much capital and liquidity is needed to support the institution’s risk taking. Capital adequacy concerns the right side of the balance sheet (net worth); liquidity concerns the left side (the share of liquid assets).

Why, then, did stress testing become the new tool? Because in the crisis the standard answers stopped being believed:

- Bear Stearns, Washington Mutual, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Lehman and Wachovia were adequately or even well capitalized according to the regulatory capital rules disclosed in their public filings, across several regimes and regulators (SEC and Basel 2, OCC/Fed and Basel 1, OTS, OFHEO). Yet “the capital you need vs. the capital you have” came out wrong in each case.
- Bank balance sheets are notoriously opaque and susceptible to asset substitution (easy swapping of low-risk for high-risk assets).
- Neither economic nor regulatory capital models can guarantee that failure is prevented: every firm accepts some probability of failure, sized by its risk appetite.

The cascading defaults and deep skepticism about stated capital adequacy forced regulators to find a credible new tool. Stress tests tailored to the situation, with openly disclosed results and approaches, could provide clarity and allow trust to be regained.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the reason the tool changed. The deciding fact is that the existing public measure (regulatory capital ratios) had lost credibility because institutions that failed had looked adequately or well capitalized under it. Option A states exactly that.

**Fragile fact.** All three approaches (regulatory, economic capital, stress testing) aim at the same quantity; what changed in the crisis was credibility, not the question.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, Abstract and section 17.1 “Introduction”; Conclusion. Schweser Reading 58, Module 58.1 “Stress Testing”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 17.1: “Prior to their failure or near-failure, financial institutions such as Bear Stearns, Washington Mutual, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Lehman and Wachovia were adequately or even well capitalized, at least according to the regulatory capital rules disclosed in their public filings.” The abstract adds that answers from standard approaches such as regulatory capital ratios “were no longer credible”. Schweser makes the same point: traditional measures such as regulatory capital ratios were insufficient.

b.reason: (sibling swap). The option claims stress testing answers a different question from regulatory and economic capital models. GARP says the opposite: all three “seek to do the same thing”, namely to assess the capital and liquidity needed to support the business. The option attributes to stress testing a distinct purpose that it does not have. It would be correct if the stem asked how stress testing differs from a model that estimates something other than required capital, such as a backtest of realized losses.

c.reason: (polarity flip). GARP says bank balance sheets are “notoriously opaque” and susceptible to asset substitution; that opacity is precisely why a tailored stress test with disclosure was needed. The option reverses “opaque” into “highly transparent”. It would be correct only if the stem described a hypothetical system where public filings already revealed true risk, in which case stress tests would add little.

d.reason: (absolute claim). GARP stresses that neither economic nor regulatory capital models can guarantee failure prevention, and that this is not their purpose, since every firm accepts some probability of failure sized by its risk appetite. Supervisory stress tests target adequate capitalization after a chosen stress, not certainty. The word “guarantee” makes the option false. It would be correct if reworded as “designed to show whether banks would remain adequately capitalized after a severe but plausible scenario”.

questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank is reviewing the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) as a case study for the bank’s AUD capital planning manual. She notes that a successful macro-prudential stress testing program in a crisis has two components. All US bank holding companies with assets above \$100 billion at year-end 2008 took part. Which of the following best describes how the SCAP delivered both components?

options.text: Banks’ internal economic capital models sized the capital hole, and the hole was filled by requiring the Federal Reserve to buy preferred shares in every participating bank.
A supervisory loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario sized the hole, and the Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program filled it by injecting equity into all participating banks.
A supervisory loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario sized the hole, and the Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program stood ready as a credible backstop that no bank needed to draw on.
A supervisory loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario sized the hole, and the backstop was credible because the participating banks, not the Treasury, were the strongest debt issuers.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian auditor reviewing how the 2009 SCAP sized and filled the capital hole.

**Concept and theory**

GARP states that a successful macro-prudential stress testing program, particularly in a crisis, has at least two components:

1. a credible assessment of the capital strength of the tested institutions, to size the capital “hole” that needs to be filled; and
2. a credible way of filling that hole.

The 2009 US SCAP is the worked example. The US entered 2009 with enormous uncertainty about its banks. Investors would not commit capital, partly because of the threat of later government dilution. By producing a credible estimate of losses under a sufficiently stressful macroeconomic scenario, supervisors drew “a line in the sand”: fill this hole and you will not be diluted later because the scenario was not tough enough. For institutions that could not convince investors, the Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program (CAP) stood ready to supply the capital. The CAP promise was credible because the US Treasury was itself a sufficiently credible debt issuer: a sovereign recapitalizes its banks by issuing debt and “downstreaming” it as equity. Participation covered all banks with assets above \$100 billion (about two-thirds of US banking assets). The banks that had to raise capital did so (\$77 billion of Tier 1 common equity against \$75 billion required), and none needed to draw on CAP funds.

**Applying it to this question**

Component 1 in the SCAP was the supervisors’ loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario. Component 2 was the CAP backstop, credible because of the Treasury’s own credit standing. The outcome: no bank drew on it. Only option C gets the actor (Treasury), the mechanism (backstop) and the outcome (not drawn) right.

**Fragile fact.** Actor check: the Treasury (CAP) was the backstop and the credible issuer; the backstop was never drawn.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.1 “Introduction” and footnote 5 (downstreaming). Schweser Reading 58, “Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP)”. Note: GARP says ten of the 19 SCAP banks had to raise \$75 billion; Schweser says the 19 SCAP banks were required to raise \$75 billion. GARP is used; the count is not a deciding fact here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (role misassignment). The hole was sized by a supervisory assessment, not by banks’ internal economic capital models (which, in the reading, had themselves proved unreliable), and the backstop was the Treasury’s CAP, not Federal Reserve purchases of preferred shares. Right actions, wrong actors. It would be closer to correct for a purely bank-internal capital planning exercise with no public backstop.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). The first half is right, but the option overextends the CAP’s role: it says the CAP actually injected equity into all participating banks. In fact the banks raised capital privately and none drew on CAP funds; the CAP mattered as a credible promise, not as a realized injection. It would be correct if the stem described a counterfactual in which private investors refused to fill the hole.

c.reason: GARP 17.1: “if some institutions could not convince investors to fill the hole, a US government program, namely the Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program (CAP), stood ready to supply the required capital. Importantly, the US Treasury was a sufficiently credible debt issuer that the CAP promise was itself credible.” And: “None needed to draw on CAP funds.”

d.reason: (role misassignment). The credibility of the backstop came from the Treasury being a sufficiently credible debt issuer; the option hands that property to the participating banks. If the banks had been the strongest issuers there would have been no hole to fill in the first place. It would be correct only for a different program in which banks self-insured each other.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK building society is preparing GBP training material that contrasts bank stress testing before and after the 2009 SCAP. She drafts the following statements:

I. Before the SCAP, stress tests were mostly single shocks applied at the product or business unit level.

II. After the SCAP, stress tests are applied at the product or business unit level rather than firm-wide.

III. After the SCAP, stress test results are tied to an explicit post-stress common equity threshold.

IV. Before the SCAP, stress tests covered losses, revenues and costs, but were not usually tied to capital adequacy.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK building society analyst auditing four statements on pre-SCAP vs post-SCAP stress testing.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes the SCAP as the first macro-prudential stress test of the crisis, but stresses that the changes at the micro-prudential (bank-specific) level were at least as significant. Table 17.2 summarizes them:

| Pre-SCAP | Post-SCAP |
|---|---|
| Mostly single shock | Broad macro scenario and market stress |
| Product or business unit level | Comprehensive, firm-wide |
| Static | Dynamic and path dependent |
| Not usually tied to capital adequacy | Explicit post-stress common equity threshold |
| Losses only | Losses, revenues and costs |

In words: stress testing went from a handful of single-factor shocks to a broad macro scenario with market-wide stresses; from business unit testing focused on losses to firm-wide testing of losses, revenues and costs; and all of it was tied to a post-stress capital ratio to ensure a going concern.

**Applying it to this question**

- Statement I: pre-SCAP, mostly single shock, product or business unit level. True.
- Statement II: assigns the product or business unit level to post-SCAP. False (post-SCAP is firm-wide).
- Statement III: post-SCAP has an explicit post-stress common equity threshold. True.
- Statement IV: pre-SCAP is “losses only”; the option gives it losses, revenues and costs. False.

Correct set: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** “Losses only” is the pre-SCAP column; “losses, revenues and costs” plus an explicit post-stress common equity threshold is post-SCAP.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.1, Table 17.2 “Features of Stress Testing, Pre- and Post-SCAP”. Schweser Reading 58, Figure 58.1 “Comparison of Stress Testing Pre-SCAP and Post-SCAP” (figure content not legible in the extracted Schweser text; GARP Table 17.2 used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason:
(polarity flip (via Statement II)). Includes II, which reverses the direction of the firm-wide shift: post-SCAP testing is comprehensive and firm-wide. Option A would be correct if

Statement II said “before the SCAP” instead of “after the SCAP”.

b.reason: Option B selects exactly the two statements that match Table 17.2 (I and III).

c.reason: (sibling swap (via Statement IV)). Drops the true Statement I and accepts IV, which gives the pre-SCAP column the post-SCAP output set (losses, revenues and costs). Only the second half of IV (not usually tied to capital adequacy) is true. Option C would be correct if IV said “covered losses only” and if I were false.

d.reason: (sibling swap (via Statement IV)). Contains I and III correctly but adds IV. A half-true statement is still false; the trap is accepting IV because its second clause is right. Option D would be correct if Statement IV read “covered losses only and were not usually tied to capital adequacy”.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is reviewing the design of the bank’s SGD enterprise stress test against the shift in practice that followed the 2009 SCAP. The design is summarized below.

| Feature | Element | Current design |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Scenario | Severe recession: GDP growth, unemployment, house prices and equity prices move together |
| 2 | Coverage | One common scenario applied to every business line across the whole firm |
| 3 | Hurdle | Results compared with a post-stress common equity ratio the board has set |
| 4 | Outputs | Projected credit and trading losses only; revenues and costs are not projected |
| 5 | Horizon | Nine quarters, starting from the third-quarter balance sheet |

Which feature is most consistent with pre-SCAP rather than post-SCAP practice?

options.text: Feature 1, because broad scenarios combining several macro variables were the norm before the SCAP.
Feature 2, because applying one scenario across every business line was the norm before the SCAP.
Feature 3, because comparing results with a post-stress capital ratio was the norm before the SCAP.
Feature 4, because projecting losses without revenues and costs was the norm before the SCAP.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore CRO checking which of five design features of the bank’s stress test is still pre-SCAP.

**Concept and theory**

The pre- to post-SCAP shift (GARP Table 17.2) has five paired features: single shock to broad macro scenario; product or business unit level to firm-wide; static to dynamic and path dependent; not tied to capital adequacy to an explicit post-stress common equity threshold; and losses only to losses, revenues and costs. A post-SCAP program needs both sides of the income statement, because whether capital survives a stress depends on losses and on the revenues (for example pre-provision net revenue) that can absorb them.

**Applying it to this question**

Map each feature to the table:

- Feature 1, multi-variable recession scenario: post-SCAP (broad macro scenario).
- Feature 2, common scenario across the whole firm: post-SCAP (comprehensive, firm-wide).
- Feature 3, explicit post-stress common equity ratio: post-SCAP.
- Feature 4, losses only, no revenues or costs: pre-SCAP.
- Feature 5, nine-quarter horizon from a third-quarter balance sheet: irrelevant input. It mirrors the CCAR’s nine-quarter horizon and is not a pre-SCAP marker.

**Fragile fact.** The capital hurdle is a post-SCAP feature; a program that projects only losses is still pre-SCAP even if its scenario is broad.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.1, Table 17.2; footnote 26 (nine-quarter CCAR horizon) for the irrelevant input. Schweser Reading 58, Figure 58.1.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (polarity flip). Broad scenarios combining several macro variables are the post-SCAP feature; pre-SCAP tests were “mostly single shock”. The option reverses the timeline. It would be correct if Feature 1 were a single shock, for example only a parallel rise in interest rates.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Firm-wide application of a common scenario is post-SCAP; pre-SCAP testing was at the product or business unit level. It would be correct if Feature 2 described separate, unconnected desk-level tests.

c.reason: (polarity flip). Pre-SCAP tests were “not usually tied to capital adequacy”; the explicit post-stress common equity threshold is the post-SCAP innovation. It would be correct if Feature 3 said results were reported without reference to any capital ratio.

d.reason: Only Feature 4 sits in the pre-SCAP column (“losses only”). Option D identifies it and gives the right reason.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Brazilian bank is preparing a BRL-denominated report for the bank’s board comparing how the 2009 SCAP and the 2011 European Banking Authority (EBA) stress test specified their stress scenarios. Which of the following statements should the consultant include as the most accurate comparison?

options.text: The SCAP specified eight macro factors for each participating country, while the 2011 EBA test used a tri-variate scenario of GDP growth, unemployment and house prices.
Both the SCAP and the 2011 EBA test took their market risk scenario from the historical risk factor changes observed between June 30 and December 31, 2008.
The SCAP had a three-variable macro state space and a historical market shock, while the 2011 EBA test set over 70 trading book factors and sovereign haircuts by maturity.
The 2011 EBA test left geographic differences across countries to individual banks, while US supervisors in the SCAP specified separate macro factors for each US state.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank consultant comparing the scenario specification of the 2009 SCAP and the 2011 EBA test.

**Concept and theory**

Scenario specification is where the exercises differ most visibly.

|  | 2009 SCAP (US) | 2011 EBA (Europe) |
|---|---|---|
| Macro state space | Three variables: GDP growth, unemployment, house price index (HPI) | Eight macro factors for each of 21 countries (GDP growth, inflation, unemployment, residential and commercial real estate prices, short and long government rates, stock prices) |
| Market risk | Historical: instantaneous shock equal to risk factor changes from June 30 to December 31, 2008 | Over 70 risk factors specified for the trading book |
| Sovereign | Not specified | Sovereign haircuts across seven maturity buckets |
| Geography | Left to individual firms | Confronted directly via country-level factors |
| Who generated | Supervisors | Macro scenario generated by ECB economists with reference to the EU Commission baseline |

The SCAP’s historical market shock achieved a “loose coherence” between real and financial stresses (that period featured a flight to quality and the Lehman failure), at the price that a historical scenario does not test for anything new.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the size of each state space and the market risk specification: SCAP was tri-variate with a historical market shock; EBA 2011 specified over 70 trading book risk factors plus sovereign haircuts by maturity bucket. Option C states both.

**Fragile fact.** SCAP = three macro variables plus a historical market shock; EBA 2011 = 8 factors × 21 countries, 70+ trading factors, sovereign haircuts in 7 buckets.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.3 “Stress Testing Design” and section 17.4 “Executing the Stress Scenario: Losses and Revenues” (opening and “Modeling Losses”). Schweser Reading 58 states the SCAP tri-variate scenario under LO 58.b; the EBA specification is GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: (sibling swap). The two specifications are swapped: the eight-factors-per-country design belongs to the 2011 EBA test and the tri-variate scenario to the SCAP. It would be correct with the names reversed.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). The historical June 30 to December 31, 2008 shock is a SCAP feature; the option extends it to the EBA test, which specified over 70 trading book risk factors and sovereign haircuts. It would be correct if it said “Only the SCAP took its market risk scenario from . . . ”.

c.reason: GARP 17.3: “The 2009 SCAP had a rather simple scenario specification. The state space had only three dimensions, GDP growth, unemployment, and the house price index (HPI), and the market risk scenario was based in historical experience.” GARP 17.3/17.4: “For the 2011 EBA test, the supervisors specified over 70 risk factors for the trading book, eight macro-factors for each of 21 countries . . . plus sovereign haircuts across seven maturity buckets.”

d.reason: (role misassignment). GARP says the EBA was forced to confront geographic heterogeneity directly (it spans 21 sovereign nations), while US supervisors left the task of accounting for geographic heterogeneity to individual firms. The option gives each supervisor the other’s approach. It would be correct with “EBA” and “US supervisors” exchanged.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee at a Japanese bank is reviewing a JPY briefing paper that compares the design of the major macro-prudential stress tests run between 2009 and 2011. Which of the following comparisons in the paper is most accurate?

options.text: The SCAP held risk-weighted assets constant, the 2010 CEBS and 2011 EBA tests held total assets constant, and the 2011 Irish test allowed balance sheet shrinkage.
The SCAP allowed balance sheet shrinkage, the 2011 Irish test held risk-weighted assets constant, and the 2010 CEBS and 2011 EBA tests held total assets constant.
The SCAP and the 2011 EBA test both used a 4% Tier 1 common hurdle, while the 2010 CEBS test used a 6% Tier 1 common hurdle for all participating banks.
The SCAP, the 2010 CEBS test and the 2011 Irish test all covered market, credit, liquidity and operational risk, as did the 2011 EBA test of 90 banks.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese risk committee member checking a comparison of balance sheet assumptions, hurdles and risk types across 2009 to 2011 stress tests.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Table 17.3 compares the macro-prudential stress tests on target capital ratio, number of banks, participation criteria, balance sheet assumptions, capital raised and risk types:

| Exercise | Target ratio | Banks | Balance sheet | Risk types |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SCAP, Mar 2009 | 4% T1C; 6% T1 | 19 | Constant RWA | M, C |
| CEBS, Jul 2010 | 6% T1 | 91 | Constant total assets | M, C |
| CCAR, Mar 2011 | 5% T1C | 19 | None | M, C |
| Ireland, Mar 2011 | 6% T1C (10.5% base) | 4 | Shrinkage allowed | M, C, L, O |
| EBA, Jul 2011 | 5% T1C | 90 | Constant total assets | M, C, L, O |
| CCAR, Mar 2012 | 5% T1C; 4% T1; 8% total; lev. | 19 (+11) | None | M, C, O |

M = market, C = credit, L = liquidity (funding), O = operational; T1C = Tier 1 common. For the EBA 2011 test, liquidity was not assessed directly, though funding stresses were taken into account. Only SCAP banks with at least \$100 billion of trading assets ran the market risk stress. GARP also notes that the static balance sheet appears in raw form in the 2011 EBA test and in risk-weighted form in the 2009 SCAP.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each claim against the balance sheet column: SCAP constant RWA (yes), CEBS and EBA constant total assets (yes), Ireland allowed shrinkage (yes). Option A matches every cell it cites.

**Fragile fact.** Constant RWA = SCAP; constant total assets = CEBS 2010 and EBA 2011; shrinkage = Ireland 2011.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.1, Table 17.3 “Summary of Macroprudential Stress Tests to Date” and its footnotes; section 17.4 “Modeling the Balance Sheet”. Schweser Figure 58.2 is not legible in the extracted text; content is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: Table 17.3 and the 17.4 text (“a static (be it in raw form, as in the 2011 EBA, or in risk weighted form, as in the 2009 SCAP)”) support every element of A.

b.reason: (sibling swap). The SCAP and Irish balance sheet assumptions are exchanged: SCAP held RWA constant and Ireland allowed shrinkage. It would be correct with “SCAP” and “2011 Irish test” swapped.

c.reason: (wrong input twin). Two hurdle errors. The 2011 EBA hurdle was 5% Tier 1 common, not 4% (4% T1C is the SCAP hurdle), and the 2010 CEBS hurdle was 6% Tier 1, not 6% Tier 1 common (6% T1C is the Irish stress hurdle). It would be correct if it read “the SCAP used 4% T1C, the 2011 EBA test 5% T1C and the 2010 CEBS test 6% Tier 1”.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). Overextends the risk coverage: SCAP and CEBS covered market and credit risk only. Liquidity and operational risk appear in the Irish and 2011 EBA rows. It would be correct if restricted to “the 2011 Irish test and the 2011 EBA test”.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a eurozone bank is replicating the post-stress capital hurdles of historical stress tests. For the bank’s adverse scenario, the projected end-of-horizon position (EUR billion) is shown below.

| Item | EUR billion |
|---|---|
| Tier 1 common capital | 9.0 |
| Tier 1 capital | 11.5 |
| Risk-weighted assets | 240.0 |
| Total assets | 610.0 |

Assuming risk-weighted assets are unchanged by any capital raised, how much additional Tier 1 common capital would the bank need to meet the post-stress hurdle used in the 2011 EBA stress test?

options.text: EUR 0.6 billion
EUR 21.5 billion
EUR 12.0 billion
EUR 3.0 billion

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Eurozone bank analyst computing the Tier 1 common shortfall against the 2011 EBA hurdle.

**Concept and theory**

A post-stress hurdle is the capital ratio a bank must still meet after the stress. GARP stresses that the target is not strict solvency but “adequate capitalization post-stress”. Capital adequacy is defined as a capital ratio, roughly capital over assets, where the numerator is the relevant form of capital (supervisors insisted on common equity) and the denominator is typically risk-weighted assets (RWA). The hurdles differ by exercise (Table 17.3): SCAP 4% Tier 1 common, CEBS 2010 6% Tier 1, Ireland 6% Tier 1 common under stress, EBA 2011 5% Tier 1 common, CCAR 5% Tier 1 common. The capital “hole” is the amount by which post-stress capital falls short of the hurdle:

Shortfall = max$($0$, h \times\text{RWA} - K)$

where $h$ is the hurdle ratio, RWA the post-stress risk-weighted assets and $K$ the post-stress capital of the type the hurdle names. (The shortfall formula is plain ratio arithmetic; the hurdle values and the RWA denominator are from GARP.)

**Applying it to this question**

$h$ = 5% (2011 EBA hurdle, Tier 1 common)

$K$ = Tier 1 common capital = 9.0

$h \times$ RWA = 0.05 × 240.0 = 12.0 (required Tier 1 common)

Shortfall = 12.0 − 9.0 = 3.0 EUR billion

Meaning: the bank’s post-stress Tier 1 common ratio is 9.0/240.0 = 3.75%, short of 5%, so it would need EUR 3.0 billion of new Tier 1 common equity. Tier 1 capital (11.5) and total assets (610.0) are distractor inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Hurdle 5% T1C for EBA 2011 (4% T1C for SCAP); the denominator is RWA even though the EBA held total assets constant.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, Table 17.3; section 17.3 (post-stress hurdle concept); section 17.4 “Modeling the Balance Sheet” (capital over RWA) and “Modeling Losses” (EBA RWA under Basel II). Hurdle values are GARP-only; Schweser does not list them.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (wrong input twin). EUR 0.6 billion is 0.04 × 240.0 − 9.0 = 9.6 − 9.0, using the SCAP’s 4% Tier 1 common hurdle. It would be correct if the stem asked for the shortfall against the hurdle used in the 2009 SCAP.

b.reason: (wrong input twin). EUR 21.5 billion is 0.05 × 610.0 − 9.0 = 30.5 − 9.0, using total assets as the denominator. The trap is confusing the EBA’s balance sheet assumption (constant total assets) with the ratio’s denominator, which is RWA. It would be correct for an unweighted capital-to-total-assets (leverage-style) ratio of 5%.

questions.question: A regulator at a national supervisory agency is presenting to newly hired bank examiners on how the US Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), in operation since 2011, changed scenario specification relative to the 2009 SCAP. Which of the following statements best describes the change and its purpose?

options.text: CCAR replaced the common supervisory scenario with bank-designed scenarios, because supervisors no longer needed to compare banks’ results under one scenario.
CCAR asked banks to submit results under their own baseline and stress scenarios in addition to the common scenario, revealing bank-specific and possibly common risks.
CCAR asked banks to submit results under their own stress scenarios, which helped microprudential supervision but by design gave supervisors no macro-prudential insight.
CCAR required supervisors to design a separate stress scenario for each bank, tailored to that bank’s business mix and geographic footprint, in place of one common scenario.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Regulator explaining to new examiners how CCAR changed scenario specification relative to SCAP.

**Concept and theory**

Until CCAR, every supervisory stress test imposed the same scenario on all banks. Any scenario is more severe for some banks than others depending on business mix and geographic footprint. GARP compares this one-size-fits-all approach with regulatory vs. economic capital: regulatory capital is the same for all banks by design, while economic capital reflects each bank’s own business mix. The problem becomes acute in normal times, when there is more debate about what a relevant adverse scenario looks like.

CCAR, in operation since 2011, recognized the problem and asked banks to submit results under their own scenarios (baseline and stress) in addition to results under the common supervisory scenario. This dual approach:

- reveals each bank’s particular sensitivities and vulnerabilities, so supervisors learn what banks themselves think are the high-risk scenarios (micro-prudential value);
- allows supervisors to learn about common risks across banks that may have been undiscovered or under-emphasized (macro-prudential value);
- keeps the common scenario, so results can still be compared across banks without sacrificing risk discovery.

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts decide the answer: banks (not supervisors) design the extra scenarios; they are additional to, not a replacement for, the common scenario; and the benefit is both micro- and macro-prudential. Only option B has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and conjunction: banks design their own scenarios, and these are in addition to the common supervisory scenario.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.3 “Stress Testing Design”. Schweser Reading 58, LO 58.b discussion and “Stress Test Comparisons” (2011 and 2012 CCAR required banks to submit results of their own baseline and stress scenarios). Schweser says this applied “prior to 2011”/“prior to the CCAR 2011”; consistent with GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). Drops the condition “in addition to”: the common scenario was kept so that supervisors could compare results across banks directly. It would be correct if CCAR had abandoned the supervisory scenario, which it did not.

b.reason: GARP 17.3: CCAR “asks banks to submit results using their own scenarios (baseline and stress) in addition to results under the common supervisory stress scenario. This was an important step forward from the 2009 SCAP . . . useful not just for micro-prudential supervision . . . but also for macro-prudential supervision.”

c.reason: (scope or condition error). Understates the scope of the benefit. GARP explicitly says bank-own scenarios also serve macro-prudential supervision by revealing common risks across banks. It would be correct if the stem asked only about the micro-prudential benefit and dropped “by design gave supervisors no macro-prudential insight”.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The tailored scenarios are designed by the banks, not by supervisors, and they supplement rather than replace the common scenario. It would be correct for a hypothetical regime in which supervisors wrote a bespoke scenario for each bank.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Chinese bank with CNY reporting and subsidiaries in both the US and the euro area is comparing how the capital ratio denominator was computed in the US tests (SCAP and CCAR) and in the 2011 EBA test. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The US tests used Basel I risk weights, which are not ratings sensitive, while the EBA test used Basel II risk weights, so banks needed stress migration matrices for the whole ratings distribution.
The US tests used Basel II risk weights, so banks needed stress migration matrices for the whole ratings distribution, while the EBA test used Basel I risk weights, which are not ratings sensitive.
The EBA test used Basel II risk weights, but banks needed only the default column of a stress migration matrix, because risk-weighted assets depend on projected defaults alone.
Because both regimes express capital over risk-weighted assets, a bank required to raise capital under the US risk weights would always be required to raise it under the EBA weights.

Stem summary: Chinese bank CRO comparing risk weight regimes in the US and EBA stress tests.

**Concept and theory**

The capital ratio’s denominator is typically RWA, where the risk weights come from the prevailing regulatory regime:

|  | US tests (SCAP, CCAR) | European tests (EBA) |
|---|---|---|
| Risk weight regime | Basel I | Basel II |
| Ratings sensitive? | No: weights do not depend on obligor ratings | Yes: weights depend on ratings |
| Consequence in stress | RWA not driven by downgrades | Banks must use stress migration matrices to project the entire future ratings distribution, not only defaults, to get RWA right |

GARP notes this “clearly complicates any comparison of US and European stress test results”: a bank may be forced to raise capital under one regime but not the other, and there is no way to know which regime is more favorable without detailed knowledge of the portfolio.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts: which regime each side used, and that ratings-sensitive Basel II weights required the full migration matrix. Option A is the only one with both.

**Fragile fact.** US = Basel I (not ratings sensitive); EBA = Basel II (ratings sensitive, full migration matrix).

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.4, “Modeling Losses” and “Modeling the Balance Sheet”. Schweser Reading 58 mentions only that RWA follows Basel II risk weight definitions (under LO 58.c) and does not draw the US Basel I contrast; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 17.4: “Since the EBA stress test was based on risk weighted assets (RWA) computed using Basel II risk weights, which are ratings sensitive, banks were forced to make use of stress migration matrices to compute not only increased defaults (the last column of the matrix), but also the entire future ratings distribution . . . The US stress tests were conducted under Basel I risk weights, which are not obligor ratings sensitive.”

(sibling swap). The two regimes are reversed: the US used Basel I and the EBA Basel

II. It would be correct with “US” and “EBA” exchanged.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). Narrows the requirement to the default column. Under ratings-sensitive weights, RWA depends on the whole ratings distribution, so banks needed the entire migration matrix. It would be correct for a pure expected-loss calculation, where only defaults (the last column) matter.

d.reason: (absolute claim). GARP says a bank “may be forced to raise capital under one regime but not the other”, and that it is not possible to know which is more favorable without portfolio detail. “Always” makes the option false. It would be correct only if both exercises used the same risk weight regime and hurdle.

questions.question:
A junior analyst at an Australian asset manager is preparing an AUD research note on what supervisors disclosed in the US and European stress tests. He drafts the following statements:

I. The SCAP disclosed projected losses for each participating bank across eight asset classes, plus resources other than capital, such as pre-provision net revenue and reserve releases.

II. The 2011 CCAR published bank-level loss rates by asset class, while the 2012 CCAR published only the macro scenario.

III. In the 2012 CCAR, the losses and pre-provision net revenue reported by the Federal Reserve were supervisory estimates, not the banks’ own estimates.

IV. The 2010 CEBS test released firm-level loss rates by detailed asset class, such as first-lien mortgages and credit cards.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian asset manager analyst auditing four statements on SCAP, CCAR and CEBS disclosures.

**Concept and theory**

Disclosure varied sharply across the exercises (GARP Table 17.1 and section 17.5):

| Exercise | What was disclosed |
|---|---|
| SCAP 2009 | Projected stress losses for each of the 19 banks for eight asset classes, plus resources other than capital (mostly PPNR and reserve releases). Until then, regulatory reports (e.g., Y-9C) showed only realized losses. “Opened Pandora’s box”. |
| CEBS 2010 | Less than SCAP: firm-level loss rates only for overall retail and overall corporate. |
| CCAR 2011 | Only the macro scenario; no bank-level results. Market read dividend increases as a “pass”. |
| CCAR 2012 | Nearly SCAP’s level: bank-level loss rates and dollar losses by regulatory asset class (FR Y-9C categories), PPNR, AFS/HTM gains and losses, trading and counterparty losses for the six firms with the largest trading portfolios. Numbers were supervisory estimates, not banks’ own. |
| Ireland 2011 | Very detailed, including bank vs third-party loss estimates. |
| EBA 2011 | Very detailed, bank-level data downloadable in spreadsheet form. |

**Applying it to this question**

I true (SCAP: eight asset classes plus PPNR and reserve releases). II false (years reversed). III true (supervisory estimates in 2012 CCAR, as in SCAP). IV false (CEBS gave only retail and corporate loss rates; the detailed asset classes were SCAP’s). Correct set: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** CCAR 2011 = macro only; CCAR 2012 = SCAP-like bank-level detail; both SCAP and 2012 CCAR figures are supervisory estimates.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.1 (CEBS disclosure) and Table 17.1 “Summary of Disclosures Across Stress Test Exercises”; section 17.5 “Stress Testing Disclosure”. Schweser Reading 58, “Stress Test Comparisons” and Key Concepts LO 58.a. Schweser lists six regulatory asset classes for the 2012 CCAR, consistent with GARP’s FR Y-9C categories; SCAP used eight.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q10 of 12.

b.reason: (sibling swap (via Statement IV) and polarity flip (via II)). Rejects both true statements and accepts the two false ones. IV gives the 2010 CEBS test the SCAP’s asset-class detail. Option B would be correct only if both II and IV were corrected into true statements and I and III were false.

c.reason: (sibling swap (via Statement IV)). Accepts IV, attributing SCAP’s detailed asset-class loss rates (first-lien mortgages, credit cards, commercial real estate) to the CEBS test, which disclosed only overall retail and corporate loss rates. Option C would be correct if IV named the SCAP instead of the CEBS test.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Canadian pension fund wants to apply her own sovereign haircuts to the exposures of individual European banks in order to test each bank’s solvency herself, rather than rely on the official pass or fail results. Which of the following statements best describes the stress test disclosure that made this possible?

options.text: The 2011 EBA test disclosed each bank’s funding liquidity stress results, so analysts could combine her haircuts with each bank’s projected liquidity position.
The 2011 Irish test disclosed only an aggregate system-wide capital need, without firm-specific results, so analysts could apply haircuts to the system.
The 2011 EBA test made all bank-level results downloadable in spreadsheet form, so analysts could impose their own loss rate assumptions on each bank.
The 2011 CCAR disclosed each bank’s own loss estimates next to third-party estimates, so analysts could apply their own haircuts to each bank’s exposures.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian pension fund manager wanting to apply her own sovereign haircuts to each European bank.

**Concept and theory**

European supervisors faced a credibility problem the US did not. The 2010 CEBS test of 91 banks gave limited disclosure and required only seven banks to raise EUR 3.5 billion; months later Ireland needed EU and IMF assistance, and subsequent tests of Irish banks run largely by outside advisors (BlackRock) found a EUR 24 billion capital need, although all had passed the CEBS test. To close the credibility gap, the March 2011 Irish exercise disclosed far more than any previous test, including bank vs third-party loss estimates (revealing the bias any bank has when estimating its own losses). The 2011 EBA test of 90 banks then approached that bar: exposures by asset class and geography, and all bank-level results downloadable in spreadsheet form so that analysts could impose their own loss rate assumptions. The “official” results were thus no longer final: analysts could and did apply their own sovereign haircuts to all exposures and test the solvency of each of the 90 institutions themselves. Funding liquidity was also stressed in the EBA test, but those results were not disclosed.

**Applying it to this question**

The investor needs bank-level exposure data in a usable form. That is exactly the EBA 2011 downloadable spreadsheet disclosure (option C).

**Fragile fact.** Downloadable bank-level spreadsheets = EBA 2011; bank vs third-party estimates = Ireland 2011; liquidity was stressed but not disclosed by the EBA.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.1 and section 17.5 “Stress Testing Disclosure”. Schweser Reading 58, “Stress Test Comparisons”. Conflict: Schweser calls the Irish exercise the “2011 EBA Irish” test; GARP describes it as a Central Bank of Ireland exercise conducted largely by outside advisors (BlackRock), separate from the July 2011 EBA test. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (polarity flip). GARP says funding liquidity was stressed in the EBA test “without disclosing the results”, because liquidity positions change rapidly and a delayed snapshot would not be informative. The option turns “not disclosed” into “disclosed”. It would be correct if the stem asked which risk the EBA stressed but did not disclose.

b.reason: (sibling swap). Aggregate, non-firm-specific disclosure is the Goldstein and Sapra proposal for normal times, the opposite of the Irish approach, which disclosed bank-level detail including bank vs third-party loss estimates. It would be correct as a description of the aggregated regime GARP suggests once trust is restored.

c.reason: GARP 17.1: “Importantly, all bank level results were available to download in spreadsheet form, to enable market analysts to easily impose their own loss rate assumptions. . . . analysts could (and did) easily apply their own sovereign haircuts on all exposures, and thus test the solvency of any of the 90 institutions themselves.”

d.reason: (sibling swap). Bank vs third-party loss estimates were the Irish 2011 disclosure feature. The 2011 CCAR published only the macro scenario with no bank-level results. It would be correct with “2011 CCAR” replaced by “2011 Irish test”.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a banking supervisor in a country where confidence in the banking system has recently been restored after a crisis. The supervisor asks how to set the disclosure regime for routine supervisory stress tests in normal times, in light of the SCAP, CCAR and European experience. Which recommendation is most consistent with that experience?

options.text: Keep full bank-by-bank disclosure in normal times, because more stress test disclosure always strengthens market discipline and never distorts bank behavior.
Tilt disclosure toward aggregated results such as loss rates by asset class, keeping system-wide information while preserving incentives to produce private information.
Disclose no results in normal times, because the market’s calm reaction to the 2011 CCAR shows that stress test disclosure has no value once trust is restored.
Reserve detailed bank-level disclosure for normal times, since in a crisis aggregated results suffice because markets can then readily distinguish good banks from bad.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant advising a supervisor on disclosure for routine stress tests once confidence is restored.

**Concept and theory**

The evolution of stress testing is also an evolution of disclosure. In a crisis, regulatory capital ratios are heavily discounted by the market, so supervisors must disclose enough for the market to “check the math”. The SCAP’s value came partly from its “pop quiz” nature: sprung at short notice, hard to manipulate by pre-positioning, and tailored to the situation, it revealed genuinely new information and trust was regained. Between March 2009 and March 2011 the 19 SCAP banks raised about \$300 billion and supervisors regained credibility; the market absorbed the near-nondisclosure of the 2011 CCAR “without a hiccup” (a state of “symmetric ignorance”).

In normal times the cost-benefit changes (Goldstein and Sapra): detailed disclosure can lead banks to window dress (poor portfolio choices to pass the test), traders to over-weight public information and stop producing private information, damaging the information content of prices and making them less useful to supervisors. GARP’s conclusion: some disclosure is still preferable to none; once trust is re-established, the balance tips from bank-specific toward aggregated information, such as loss rates by major asset class and total capital decline in the system. Aggregation is “less wrong” because idiosyncratic estimation errors average out, and it gives the market an anchor without diluting the incentive to analyze individual firms.

**Applying it to this question**

The supervisor is in normal times with trust restored. The recommendation consistent with GARP is aggregated disclosure that keeps system-wide information and preserves private information production: option B.

**Fragile fact.** Crisis: detailed, bank-specific disclosure; normal times: tilt to aggregated disclosure. The 2011 CCAR’s macro-only release caused no market disruption.

**Reference**

LO 58.a: “Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.” GARP Chapter 17, section 17.5 “Stress Testing Disclosure” and Conclusion. Schweser Reading 58, “Stress Test Comparisons” (costs of disclosure in normal times; Schweser places this text under LO 58.c, but its Key Concepts tie the disclosure comparison to LO 58.a). Boundary call: included as the disclosure strand of the LO’s “evolution”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (absolute claim). GARP says “it is not clear that more is always better” and lists costs of detailed disclosure in normal times (window dressing, crowding out of private information). “Always” and “never” make the option false. It would be correct for crisis times, where detailed bank-specific disclosure has significant benefits.

b.reason: GARP Conclusion: “Once that trust has been re-established, the cost-benefit of stress testing disclosures may tip away from bank-specific towards more aggregated information. This still provides the market with unique information . . . without taking away market participants’ incentives to produce private information.”

c.reason: (absolute claim). The quiet reaction to the 2011 CCAR shows the market could live with little disclosure, not that disclosure is worthless; GARP states “some disclosure is still preferable to no disclosure”. It would be correct only if the stem asked what the 2011 CCAR itself did (published the macro scenario only).

d.reason: (polarity flip). The timing is reversed: detailed bank-specific disclosure is most valuable in a crisis, when the market cannot distinguish good banks from bad; aggregated disclosure suits normal times. It would be correct with “normal times” and “crisis” exchanged and “can” changed to “cannot”.

questions.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
questions.topic: Stress Testing Banks
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-17 b Q1
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank holding company is presenting to newly hired analysts on how supervisory stress scenarios are designed. Her draft slide contains the following statements:

I. A stress scenario is inherently multi-factor: it describes adverse states of the world through several financial or real risk factors that take extreme yet possible values.

II. Specifying a severe value for one risk factor, such as only a sharp widening of credit spreads, is sufficient, provided that the shock is extreme enough.

III. The real difficulty in scenario design is specifying a coherent joint outcome of all relevant risk factors, because when one factor moves significantly the others move too.

IV. Coherence is mainly a concern for real economy factors; scenarios built only from financial market risk factors are coherent by construction.

Which of the statements should she keep on the slide as accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian BHC slide on what a coherent stress scenario requires.

**Concept and theory**

A stress test asks a simple question: how resilient is a bank to deteriorating conditions? Stresses come in two forms. A sensitivity shocks one thing (spreads double, prices drop, volatilities rise). A scenario describes a whole adverse state of the world (a severe recession, stagflation, the post-Lehman period). Supervisory macro-prudential stress tests use scenarios, and that is where the design problem of coherence arises.

GARP (Schuermann) puts it this way: scenarios are inherently multi-factor. The designer wants a rich description of adverse states of the world in the form of several risk factors, financial or real, “taking on extreme yet coherent (or possible) values.” Two requirements pull against each other:

| Requirement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Extreme | The scenario must be severe enough to be a genuine stress. |
| Coherent | The joint values of all risk factors must be possible together. |

Why is a single-factor shock not enough? Because risk factors do not move in isolation: “when one risk factor moves significantly, the others move too.” Specifying only high unemployment, only wider credit spreads or only a fall in equity prices leaves the other factors frozen at values they would not hold in that world. Hence GARP’s key sentence: “the real difficulty is in specifying a coherent joint outcome of all of the relevant risk factors.” GARP also stresses that while coherence is generic to all scenario design, it is especially acute for market risk, that is, for portfolios of traded securities and derivatives.

**Applying it to this question**

Audit each statement against the source.

- Statement I restates GARP’s description: multi-factor, financial or real factors, extreme yet coherent (possible) values. True.
- Statement II claims a single extreme shock suffices if severe enough. GARP says the opposite: it is not sufficient to specify only one factor, because the others move too. False.
- Statement III restates GARP’s “real difficulty” sentence. True.
- Statement IV says financial-only scenarios are coherent by construction. GARP says the coherence problem is especially acute for market risk scenarios. False.

The accurate set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Severity and coherence are different properties: making a shock larger never makes the scenario more coherent.

**Reference**

LO 58.b: “Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.” GARP Chapter 17, Section 17.3 Stress Testing Design. Schweser LO 58.b, “Challenges in Designing Stress Tests.” Schweser illustrates multi-factor linkages with its own examples (volatility freezing credit markets; unemployment and falling equity prices); GARP’s examples are unemployment, credit spreads and equity prices. No conflict on substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 b, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (absolute claim). A keeps Statement II, which claims that one sufficiently extreme shock is enough. That confuses severity with coherence: making one factor more extreme does nothing to make the other factors’ values consistent with it. A would be correct only if Statement II were rewritten as “specifying a severe value for only one risk factor is not sufficient, because the others move too.”

b.reason: Option B (I and III only) contains both true statements and neither false one. It matches GARP Section 17.3: scenarios are inherently multi-factor with extreme yet coherent values, and the real difficulty is specifying a coherent joint outcome of all relevant risk factors.

c.reason: (absolute claim and scope error). C rejects both true statements and accepts the two false ones. Statement IV narrows the coherence problem to real factors, whereas GARP says it is especially acute for traded market risk factors. C would be correct only if the slide described a sensitivity test (one factor, by design) rather than a scenario, which is not the case here.

d.reason: (scope error). D correctly keeps I and III but also accepts IV, which reverses where the problem bites hardest. Financial factors in a trading book are mapped to tens of thousands of risk factors, which makes coherence harder, not automatic. D would be correct if Statement IV read “the problem of coherence is generic to scenario design and especially acute for market risk.”

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-17 b Q2
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing a draft severely adverse scenario prepared by the treasury team of an Australian bank. The core assumptions over the stress horizon are shown below.

| Risk factor | Assumption over the horizon |
|---|---|
| Consumer price inflation | Rises from 2.5% to 8.0% a year |
| Central bank policy (cash) rate | Held unchanged at 3.6% |
| Unemployment rate | Rises from 4.1% to 7.5% |
| AUD against a trade-weighted basket | Depreciates by 15% |
| Number of branches in the bank’s network | Unchanged at 412 |

Which of the following revisions most directly addresses a coherence weakness in the draft?

options.text: Raise the inflation path to 12% a year, so that the scenario becomes more severe and therefore more credible.
Add an equal depreciation of the USD, EUR and JPY against the same basket, so that the currency shock is broad-based.
Hold all other risk factors at current levels while inflation rises, so that the effect of inflation can be isolated.
Add a monetary policy response consistent with the inflation shock, such as an increase in the policy interest rate.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank draft scenario: high inflation with an unchanged policy rate.

**Concept and theory**

Coherence means the joint outcome of all relevant risk factors must be possible. GARP gives concrete illustrations of what a coherent scenario must respect:

| Situation in the scenario | What coherence requires |
|---|---|
| Some exchange rates depreciate | Others must appreciate: not all exchange rates can depreciate at once. |
| High inflation | Account for likely monetary policy responses, such as an increase in the policy interest rate. |
| Flight to quality from risky assets | A (usually small) set of safe-haven assets to which capital flows. |

The idea behind each row is that markets and policymakers react. A scenario that shocks one variable but freezes the agents who would respond to it describes a world that cannot happen. Such a scenario may look severe, but its results are hard to interpret because the joint state is implausible.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the table row by row and ask: does any assumption contradict another?

- Inflation rises from 2.5% to 8.0%, a large high-inflation shock.
- The policy rate is held unchanged at 3.6% throughout. This is the incoherence: GARP states that a high inflation scenario needs to account for likely monetary policy responses, such as an increase in the policy rate.
- Unemployment rising and the AUD depreciating against a basket are plausible companions of a severe scenario.
- The branch count of 412 is an irrelevant input: it is not a risk factor at all.

The fix that targets the coherence gap is to add the policy response.

**Fragile fact.** The actor that must respond to high inflation is the monetary authority: the policy rate goes up, not unchanged.

**Reference**

LO 58.b: “Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.” GARP Chapter 17, Section 17.3 Stress Testing Design (coherence examples). The inflation and monetary policy example is in GARP only; Schweser LO 58.b gives the currency and flight-to-quality examples but omits it. Content from GARP; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-17 b, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error: severity confused with coherence). Raising inflation to 12% makes the scenario more extreme but leaves the frozen policy rate in place, so the joint outcome is even less plausible. Coherence requires extreme yet possible values. A would be correct if the question asked how to make an already coherent scenario more severe.

b.reason: (polarity flip). GARP states that not all exchange rates can depreciate at once; some have to appreciate. Adding an equal depreciation of the USD, EUR and JPY against the same basket that the AUD is already falling against would introduce a new incoherence. B would be correct if it read “add an appreciation of some other currencies, consistent with the AUD’s depreciation.”

c.reason: (scope error: single-factor shock). Holding every other factor fixed is the one-factor-ata-time approach that GARP says is not sufficient, because when one risk factor moves significantly the others move too. C describes a sensitivity analysis. It would be correct if the task were to measure the bank’s sensitivity to inflation alone, not to design a coherent scenario.

d.reason: Option D adds a monetary policy response consistent with the inflation shock. That is exactly GARP’s illustration: “a high inflation scenario needs to account for likely monetary policy responses, such as an increase in the policy interest rate.”
