questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a U.S. BHC that has just become subject to the Capital Plan Rule is preparing an internal briefing on how the Federal Reserve assesses capital plans. Which statement about the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) is most accurate, as described in the reading?

options.text: CCAR is the Dodd-Frank Act supervisory stress test itself, so passing the supervisory scenarios gives a complete assessment of the risks a BHC faces.
In 2013, CCAR assessed every BHC subject to the Capital Plan Rule, and from 2014 the smaller BHCs moved to a separate Capital Plan Review.
CCAR is a self-assessment in which each BHC’s internal audit function evaluates its own capital plan and certifies the result to the Federal Reserve.
CCAR is the Federal Reserve’s supervisory program for assessing capital plans, and in 2013 it covered the 18 BHCs that took part in the 2009 SCAP.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Junior analyst choosing the most accurate statement about CCAR.

**Concept and theory**

Three things are easily blurred: the Capital Plan Rule, CCAR and the Dodd-Frank Act stress tests.

| Item | What it is (GARP 20.1) |
|---|---|
| Capital Plan Rule | The rule requiring covered BHCs to develop and maintain a capital plan supported by a robust process for assessing capital adequacy. Its preamble sets out the seven CAP principles. |
| CCAR | “The Federal Reserve’s supervisory program for assessing the capital plans”; annual. In 2013 it covered the 18 BHCs that participated in the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP). The other BHCs subject to the rule were assessed through a separate Capital Plan Review; from 2014 all were to be evaluated “in a single, unified process through CCAR”. |
| Dodd-Frank Act supervisory stress tests | “Play an important role in CCAR” but “are not meant to be and should not be viewed as providing for an all-encompassing assessment of the possible risks a BHC may face”. |

The supervisory assessment within CCAR evaluates the BHC’s risk identification, measurement and management practices, its stressed loss and revenue estimation, and the governance and controls around them.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement for: what CCAR is (a supervisory program run by the Federal Reserve), who carries it out (the Federal Reserve, not the BHC), and the 2013 to 2014 history (18 SCAP BHCs in CCAR in 2013, the rest in the Capital Plan Review, unification in CCAR from 2014). Only option D is right on all three.

**Fragile fact.** CCAR is the Fed’s supervisory program; Dodd-Frank stress tests feed it but are not all-encompassing; 18 SCAP BHCs in 2013, unified CCAR from 2014.

**Reference**

LO 61.a: “Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.” GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 20 “Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies: Supervisory Expectations and Range of Current Practice”, Section 20.1 “Introduction” (including footnote 3). Schweser LO 61.a describes CCAR as “the Federal Reserve’s supervisory program for evaluating capital plans” but does not give the 2013 coverage, the Capital Plan Review or the 2014 unification; those facts are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 a, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: (sibling swap). A merges CCAR with the Dodd-Frank Act stress tests and then adds an absolute claim. The supervisory stress tests play an important role in CCAR but are explicitly not “an all-encompassing assessment”. A would be correct if it said the stress tests are one important input to CCAR.

b.reason: (polarity flip). The timeline is reversed. In 2013 the Capital Plan Review was the separate process for BHCs outside the 18; from 2014 everyone was to be assessed in CCAR. B would be correct if it said that in 2013 the BHCs outside the 18 were assessed through the separate Capital Plan Review, and that from 2014 all of them moved into CCAR.

c.reason: (role misassignment). CCAR is a supervisory program run by the Federal Reserve; it is not a self-assessment by the BHC’s internal audit. Internal audit reviews the capital adequacy process under the internal controls principle. C would be correct as a description of internal audit’s role within the BHC’s own controls, not of CCAR.

d.reason: GARP Section 20.1: “CCAR is the Federal Reserve’s supervisory program for assessing the capital plans. In 2013, CCAR covered 18 BHCs that participated in the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP).” Option D restates this.

questions.question:
An internal audit manager at a U.S. BHC is mapping the bank’s control inventory to the CAP principle on robust internal controls. She has listed four items:

I. Change control over the components of the capital adequacy process

II. Approval of capital decisions

III. Model validation and independent review

IV. Review of the capital adequacy process components by internal audit

Which of the items does the principle name as components of robust internal controls?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Internal audit manager deciding which of four items belong to the robust internal controls principle.

**Concept and theory**

Principle 6 exists because the capital plan is only as reliable as the machinery that produces it: data systems, models, aggregation and decision processes. GARP’s Figure 20.1 lists five named components of robust internal controls “governing capital adequacy process components”:

1. policies and procedures;
2. change control;
3. model validation and independent review;
4. comprehensive documentation;
5. review by internal audit.

Section 20.3 restates them as (1) regular and comprehensive review by internal audit, (2) robust and independent model review and validation, (3) comprehensive documentation including policies and procedures, and (4) change controls. By contrast, approval of capital decisions is a governance function (P7), carried out by the board and senior management.

**Applying it to this question**

| Item | Content | Principle |
|---|---|---|
| I | Change control | P6, named |
| II | Approval of capital decisions | P7, governance |
| III | Model validation and independent review | P6, named |
| IV | Review by internal audit | P6, named |

So the items named in P6 are I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Change control and internal audit are controls (P6); approval of capital decisions is governance (P7).

**Reference**

LO 61.a: “Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.” GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 20 “Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies: Supervisory Expectations and Range of Current Practice”, Figure 20.1 (Principle 6) and Section 20.3 “Internal Controls”. Schweser LO 61.a lists principle 6 as “independent review, model validation, documentation, and internal audit” and omits policies and procedures and change control; item I therefore rests on GARP. GARP is used for content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 a, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). Omitting IV drops internal audit from the controls principle, perhaps because audit is thought of as an independent oversight function. GARP names “review by internal audit” inside P6. A would be correct if item IV read “approval of capital actions by the audit committee” or another non-control item.

b.reason: GARP Figure 20.1, Principle 6: “robust internal controls governing capital adequacy process components, including policies and procedures; change control; model validation and independent review; comprehensive documentation; and review by internal audit.” Items I, III and IV are named; option B is correct.

c.reason: (sibling swap). Including II attributes P7’s “approval of capital decisions” to P6, and the option also leaves out change control, which P6 names. C would be correct if item II read “comprehensive documentation, including policies and procedures” (a named P6 component) and item I read “evaluation of capital goals” (a P7 element).

d.reason: (scope or condition error). Selecting all four overextends P6 to cover governance. D would be correct if the question asked which items are elements of the CAP as a whole, since approval of capital decisions is a CAP element (P7).

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the draft charter that a U.S. BHC has written for the oversight of its capital adequacy process. To test the draft, he wants a one-sentence description of the CAP principle on effective governance. Which description best matches that principle?

options.text: Board and senior management oversee the CAP, periodically reviewing the risk infrastructure and estimation methods, evaluating capital goals and approving capital decisions.
The Federal Reserve oversees the CAP through CCAR, periodically reviewing the risk infrastructure and estimation methods, evaluating capital goals and approving capital decisions.
Board and senior management approve the capital plan once at inception, after which reviews of the risk infrastructure and estimation methods are left to the business lines.
Board and senior management oversee the CAP and must eliminate all limitations and uncertainties in the estimates before approving any capital decision.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Risk consultant choosing the one-sentence description of the effective governance principle.

**Concept and theory**

Principle 7 answers “who is accountable for the CAP, and what must they actually do?” GARP’s wording: “The BHC has effective board and senior management oversight of the CAP, including

- periodic review of the BHC’s risk infrastructure and loss- and resource-estimation methodologies;
- evaluation of capital goals;
- assessment of the appropriateness of stressful scenarios considered;
- regular review of any limitations and uncertainties in all aspects of the CAP; and
- approval of capital decisions.”

Three features matter: the actor is the BHC’s own board and senior management; the review is periodic and regular, not one-off; and limitations and uncertainties are to be reviewed, not eliminated, because capital planning results are estimates. The Capital Plan Rule also requires the board to approve the capital plan.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each option on three attributes: actor (board and senior management), frequency (periodic), and the treatment of limitations (review). Option A has the right actor, periodic review, evaluation of goals and approval of capital decisions. It does not list every element, but nothing in it is wrong, and it is the only option with no error.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the BHC’s own board and senior management. Verb for limitations and uncertainties: review, not eliminate.

**Reference**

LO 61.a: “Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.” GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 20 “Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies: Supervisory Expectations and Range of Current Practice”, Figure 20.1 (Principle 7); board approval requirement in Section 20.4 “Governance”, Board Reporting. Schweser LO 61.a calls the principle “effective oversight” by “a board and senior management”; GARP calls it “effective governance”. Same content, different label.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 a, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: GARP Figure 20.1, Principle 7 assigns oversight of the CAP to the board and senior management and names periodic review of the risk infrastructure and estimation methodologies, evaluation of capital goals and approval of capital decisions. Option A states exactly these.

b.reason: (role misassignment). The tasks are right but the actor is the Federal Reserve. CCAR is the Fed’s supervisory assessment of the plan; oversight of the CAP itself is the BHC’s own board and senior management. B would be correct if it described what CCAR evaluates rather than who governs the CAP.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). The principle requires periodic review by board and senior management; a one-time approval followed by delegation to business lines drops that condition. C would be correct only for the single act of approving the plan, which is one element of P7, not the whole principle.

d.reason: (absolute claim). The principle requires “regular review of any limitations and uncertainties”, not their elimination. Capital planning results are estimates and cannot be made certain. D would be correct if “eliminate all” were replaced by “regularly review any”.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a U.S. BHC with USD 74 billion of total consolidated assets is preparing a compliance checklist for the bank’s first capital plan submission. Which of the following statements describe requirements of the Capital Plan Rule as set out in the reading?

I. The BHC’s board of directors must approve the capital plan.

II. The BHC must use a BHC-developed stress scenario that is appropriate for its business model and portfolios.

III. The BHC must use advanced measurement approach (AMA) models to estimate operational-risk losses under stress.

IV. The BHC must estimate revenue and expenses over a nine-quarter planning horizon.

options.text: I and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Senior analyst building a checklist of what the Capital Plan Rule itself requires (statements I to IV).

**Concept and theory**

Most of GARP Chapter 20 describes supervisory expectations and stronger or weaker practices (LO 61.b). A few sentences, however, state what the Capital Plan Rule itself requires. These describe the rule and are part of LO 61.a:

| Statement in GARP | Section |
|---|---|
| “The board of directors is required to approve a BHC’s capital plan under the Capital Plan Rule.” | 20.4 Governance |
| “Under the Capital Plan Rule, a BHC is required to use a BHC-developed stressed scenario that is appropriate for its business model and portfolios.” | 20.6 BHC Scenario Design |
| “The Capital Plan Rule requires BHCs to estimate revenue and expenses over the nine-quarter planning horizon.” | 20.7 PPNR Projection |
| “The Capital Plan Rule does not require BHCs to use advanced measurement approach (AMA) models for stressed operational-risk loss estimation.” | 20.7 Operational Risk |

The logic: the board owns the plan; the BHC’s own scenario must reflect its own vulnerabilities (the supervisory scenarios are not enough); a fixed nine-quarter horizon gives comparable projections; and because operational-risk modeling best practice “is still evolving”, no particular method such as AMA is mandated.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: required (board approval). True.
- II: required (BHC-developed scenario). True.
- III: the rule explicitly does not require AMA models. False.
- IV: required (nine-quarter horizon). True.

The USD 74 billion figure only confirms the BHC is above the \$50 billion threshold; it does not change any answer.

**Fragile fact.** Required: board approval, BHC-developed scenario, nine-quarter horizon. Not required: AMA for stressed operational-risk losses.

**Reference**

LO 61.a: “Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.” GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 20 “Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies: Supervisory Expectations and Range of Current Practice”, Section 20.4 “Governance” (Board Reporting), Section 20.6 “BHC Scenario Design”, Section 20.7 “Estimation Methodologies” (Operational Risk; PPNR Projection Methodologies). Schweser confirms the nine-quarter horizon (Reading 61, LO 61.b text) and management furnishing information “for its approval” to the board; the AMA statement is GARP-only. Boundary call: these four rule requirements are treated as describing the Capital Plan Rule (LO 61.a); the related practices remain LO 61.b.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 a, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). Omitting II assumes the supervisory scenarios are sufficient. GARP says the rule requires a BHC-developed scenario appropriate for its business model and portfolios. A would be correct if the checklist covered only BHCs exempted from running their own scenario, which the reading does not describe.

b.reason: (polarity flip). Including III reverses GARP’s statement that the rule “does not require” AMA models. B would be correct if III read “The BHC may, but need not, use AMA models” and the question asked which statements are consistent with the rule.

c.reason: Statements I, II and IV each restate a requirement GARP attributes to the Capital Plan Rule; III contradicts GARP Section 20.7. Option C (I, II and IV only) is correct.

d.reason: (role misassignment). Omitting I treats approval of the plan as a senior management matter, removing the board. The rule requires the board of directors to approve the plan. D would be correct if statement I said “the chief risk officer must approve the capital plan”, which the rule does not require.

questions.question: A board risk committee member at one of the largest and most complex U.S. BHCs is reviewing a consultant’s summary of the Federal Reserve’s supervisory stance on internal capital planning. Which statement in the summary is least accurate?

options.text: Practices the Federal Reserve identifies as leading or industry-best should not be treated as a safe harbor, since leading practice will keep evolving.
The Federal Reserve has heightened its expectations for the largest and most complex BHCs, expecting them to use widely recognized leading practices.
Many lagging practices rely on generic assumptions or “standard” modeling techniques without asking whether they suit the particular BHC.
An internal capital planning process designed to mirror the Federal Reserve’s own stress testing is a strong practice because it ensures consistency.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Risk committee member auditing a consultant’s summary of the Federal Reserve’s supervisory stance; find the least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s introduction frames how the Federal Reserve wants the seven principles to be read:

- **No safe harbor.** Practices described as leading or industry-best “should not be considered a safe harbor”. Leading practice will keep evolving as data, conditions, products and techniques change.
- **Tailoring.** Expectations are tailored to size, scope, activities and systemic importance. The Fed has “significantly heightened supervisory expectations for the largest and most complex BHCs” and expects them to have practices “widely considered to be leading practices”; it also recognizes the challenges for BHCs new to CCAR.
- **BHC-specific, not mirrored.** The supervisory stress tests are not all-encompassing, so internal planning should reflect BHC-specific factors that may “differ considerably” from the Fed’s. “Designing an internal capital planning process that simply seeks to mirror the Federal Reserve’s stress testing is a weak practice.”
- **Generic assumptions lag.** “Many lagging practices . . . rely on generic assumptions or ‘standard’ modeling techniques, without sufficient consideration of whether those assumptions or techniques are the most appropriate ones for the BHC.”

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is least accurate, so three statements are true and one is false. A, B and C each match a sentence in Section 20.1. D calls mirroring the Fed’s stress testing a strong practice; GARP calls it a weak practice.

**Fragile fact.** Mirroring the Fed’s stress tests is a weak practice; tailoring to BHC-specific factors is what the Fed wants.

**Reference**

LO 61.a: “Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.” GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 20 “Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies: Supervisory Expectations and Range of Current Practice”, Section 20.1 “Introduction”. These points are GARP-only; Schweser’s LO 61.a text does not cover the safe-harbor caveat, tailoring or mirroring (Schweser’s LO 61.b text says stress testing “should go above and beyond the general guidelines established by the supervisory authority”, which is consistent).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 a, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: (accurate statement; qualifier misread). A restates “should not be considered a safe harbor” and the reason (leading practices “will continue to evolve”). It would be the answer only if it said leading practices are a safe harbor.

b.reason: (accurate statement; qualifier misread). B restates the heightened expectations for the largest and most complex BHCs. It would be the answer only if it said expectations are uniform across all BHCs regardless of size.

c.reason: (accurate statement; qualifier misread). C restates GARP’s description of lagging practices. It would be the answer only if it said generic or “standard” techniques are a leading practice.

d.reason: GARP Section 20.1: “designing an internal capital planning process that simply seeks to mirror the Federal Reserve’s stress testing is a weak practice.” Statement D reverses this, so D is the least accurate statement and the correct answer.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a U.S. BHC with a large London branch receives four findings from a pre-submission review of the BHC’s capital adequacy process. The exposure figures are those quoted in the review report.

| Finding | Description | Exposure (GBP million) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Each business line estimates stressed losses for its own portfolio, but the estimates are never aggregated across the BHC. | 1,250 |
| 2 | Changes to the stressed loss models were put into production without approval or any record of what was changed. | 340 |
| 3 | The risk inventory omits a material exposure created by a product launched during the year. | 860 |
| 4 | Neither the board nor senior management has reviewed the limitations and uncertainties of the CAP for two years. | n/a |

Which mapping of each finding to the CAP principle it most directly breaches is correct?

options.text: 1: loss estimation; 2: internal controls; 3: foundational risk management; 4: governance
1: resource estimation; 2: internal controls; 3: foundational risk management; 4: governance
1: loss estimation; 2: governance; 3: foundational risk management; 4: governance
1: loss estimation; 2: internal controls; 3: capital adequacy impact assessment; 4: governance

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chief compliance officer mapping four review findings (aggregation, change control, risk inventory, review of limitations) to CAP principles.

**Concept and theory**

The seven principles are best used as a diagnostic map: each typical failure has one principle that “owns” it. The relevant extracts from GARP Figure 20.1:

| Principle | Deciding words |
|---|---|
| P1 Sound foundational risk management | infrastructure that supports “the identification, measurement, assessment, and control of all material risks” |
| P2 Effective loss-estimation methodologies | translating risk measures into potential losses “and for aggregating those estimated losses across the BHC” |
| P3 Solid resource-estimation methodologies | definition and estimation of available capital resources, including projected revenues |
| P4 Sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment | combining losses and resources against stated goals |
| P6 Robust internal controls | “policies and procedures; change control; model validation and independent review; comprehensive documentation; and review by internal audit” |
| P7 Effective governance | board and senior management oversight, including “regular review of any limitations and uncertainties in all aspects of the CAP” |

**Applying it to this question**

- Finding 1: losses estimated but not aggregated across the BHC. Aggregation is part of P2. Loss estimation.
- Finding 2: unapproved, unrecorded model changes. Change control is a named P6 component. Internal controls.
- Finding 3: a material risk from a new product is missing from the inventory. Identifying all material risks is P1. Foundational risk management.
- Finding 4: no board or senior management review of limitations and uncertainties. Named in P7. Governance.

The exposure column (GBP 1,250 million and so on) is irrelevant: the principle breached depends on the nature of the failure, not its size.

**Fragile fact.** Aggregation belongs to loss estimation (P2), change control to internal controls (P6), and review of limitations to governance (P7).

**Reference**

LO 61.a: “Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.” GARP FRM Part II, Operational Risk and Resilience, Chapter 20 “Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies: Supervisory Expectations and Range of Current Practice”, Figure 20.1 “Seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process”. Schweser LO 61.a names P1 “risk management foundation” (“identification, evaluation, measurement, and control” of all key risk exposures) and omits change control from principle 6; GARP is used for content. Detailed risk-identification practices (risk inventories, new products) belong to LO 61.b and are used here only as the setting.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 a, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: The mapping 1: P2, 2: P6, 3: P1, 4: P7 follows the wording of GARP Figure 20.1 for each principle. Option A is correct.

b.reason: (sibling swap). Finding 1 is assigned to resource estimation (P3). The missing step is aggregation of losses, which P2 names. B would be correct if finding 1 said the BHC had no clear definition of its available capital resources or did not project revenues under stress.

c.reason: (role misassignment). Finding 2 is assigned to governance. Change control is a component of internal controls (P6); governance is board and senior management oversight. C would be correct if finding 2 said the board had not reviewed or approved the model change policy.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Finding 3 is assigned to impact assessment (P4). An omitted risk is a failure of identification, which is P1’s “identification . . . of all material risks”; P4 combines losses and resources that have already been estimated. D would be correct if finding 3 said the BHC never compared its post-stress capital with its stated goals.

questions.question:
The newly appointed head of enterprise risk at a US bank holding company (BHC) with USD 180 billion of total consolidated assets is preparing a briefing for newly hired analysts on the risk-identification process that supports the firm’s internal capital planning. She drafts four statements:

I. The process should evaluate the full set of exposures arising from on- and off-balance sheet positions, including exposures that could arise from noncontractual support to off-balance sheet entities.

II. Assumptions about risk reduction from guarantees, netting and collateral agreements can be taken as given once their legal enforceability was confirmed when the exposures were originated.

III. Risk measures should capture changes in the risk profile on a timely basis, for example from new products, higher volumes or changes in portfolio quality, and can serve as early warning indicators in capital contingency plans.

IV. The capital planning team should maintain its own stand-alone risk inventory, kept separate from the enterprise-wide risk inventory so that it is not influenced by business-line input.

Which of the statements describe stronger risk-identification practice?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Head of enterprise risk audits four statements on risk identification for capital planning.

**Concept and theory**

Capital planning starts with knowing what can hurt capital. The Federal Reserve’s account of the financial crisis is blunt: many firms simply failed to identify the exposures arising from their firm-wide activities, partly because fractured information systems made aggregation hard, and more importantly because they did not consider how the size and risk of those exposures would evolve as conditions changed. Risk identification is therefore the foundation on which every later step (scenarios, loss estimates, capital goals) rests.

GARP sets out what a strong risk-identification process looks like:

- **Full scope.** It evaluates the full set of potential exposures from on- and off-balance sheet positions, including those that could arise from noncontractual support to off-balance sheet entities, and risks that depend on changing economic and market conditions in stress. It is systematic and repeatable.
- **Skepticism about mitigation.** The BHC should closely assess any assumed risk reduction from risk transfer or mitigation, including the enforceability and effectiveness of guarantees, netting and collateral agreements, and the access to and valuation of collateral when exposures and asset values are changing rapidly in a stressed market.
- **Dynamic measurement.** Risk measures should capture changes in the risk profile on a timely basis, whether from strategy, new products, increased volumes, concentration or portfolio quality, or the economic environment. They can act as early warning indicators or contingency triggers.
- **Enterprise-wide inventory.** Stronger BHCs keep a comprehensive risk inventory refreshed as conditions warrant, with input from senior representatives of business lines, risk, finance and treasury.

| Stronger practice | Lagging practice |
|---|---|
| Inventory linked to enterprise-wide risk governance, input from many units | Capital planning staff in silos with stand-alone inventories |

Statement II freezes the mitigation assessment at origination; GARP asks for close assessment of enforceability and effectiveness and of collateral access and valuation as conditions change in stress: false. A would be correct only if the stem asked which statements describe practices that a lagging BHC relied on, alongside I.

(polarity flip in II and IV). B selects the two statements that describe weak practice.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a US BHC with USD 95 billion of assets is explaining to the board risk committee how the firm treats reputational, strategic and compliance risk, none of which is directly attributable to the integrated firm-wide scenarios in its scenario-based stress test. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with stronger practice?

options.text: Holding a cushion above the internal capital target, stating which risks it covers and supporting with analysis how its size relates to them.
Holding a cushion above the internal capital target set at a fixed 1% of tier 1 capital, chosen by the expert judgment of senior risk managers.
Leaving these risks out of the capital plan, because the scenario-based stress test is expected to capture every material risk that the BHC faces.
Reflecting these risks in projected net income for the first four quarters only, because their effect beyond one year cannot be estimated reliably.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: CRO explains how reputational, strategic and compliance risks are reflected in capital planning.

**Concept and theory**

A scenario-based stress test runs a small number of discrete scenarios. GARP is explicit that such a test “cannot and is not expected to capture all potential risks” and should be one of several inputs to capital planning. Large BHCs face risks that are either hard to quantify or not attributable to any of the integrated firm-wide scenarios. GARP calls these **“other risks”** and names reputational, strategic and compliance risk as examples.

The supervisory expectation has three parts:

1. Identify and assess all risks, and capture the potential effect of all of them in capital planning, so capital is a sufficient buffer against every risk the BHC faces.
2. To the extent possible, incorporate their effect into projections of net income over the **nine-quarter** planning horizon, with assumptions and methods clearly articulated.
3. Where the effect is not built into the capital targets, stronger practice states clearly which risks a **cushion above the capital target** addresses and how the cushion relates to those risks. A simple rule (such as a percent of capital) or expert judgment without analysis or support is a **lagging** practice.

The range of observed practice: many BHCs held an incremental cushion above their targets; others assessed the effect through reduced revenue, added expenses or a management overlay on losses; lagging BHCs did not try at all.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO must choose a treatment for risks the stress test cannot capture. The deciding facts are: (i) the risks must stay in the capital plan, (ii) a cushion is acceptable only if its coverage is articulated and its size supported by analysis, and (iii) any income effects run over the full nine-quarter horizon. Only option A meets all three.

**Fragile fact.** Number and condition: other risks are reflected over nine quarters, and a cushion is only strong practice when its size is supported by analysis, not by a rule of thumb.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: risk identification. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.2, Box 20.1 “Incorporating Risks That Are More Difficult to Quantify”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Risk Identification” (Schweser compresses this to “a variety of methods . . . including internal capital targets”; the cushion-support condition is from GARP).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q2 of 17.

a.reason: A is correct because GARP Box 20.1 says stronger practices “included a clear articulation of which risks were being addressed by putting in place a cushion above the capital target, and how this cushion is related to identified risks”, and that BHCs “should clearly support the method they used”.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). B keeps the cushion but drops the condition that its size be supported by analysis. GARP names “a simple rule (such as a percent of capital) or expert judgments . . . without providing analysis or support” as lagging. B would be correct if the fixed percentage were backed by documented analysis linking it to the identified risks.

c.reason: (absolute-claim trap). C assumes the stress test captures every material risk. GARP says the opposite: a limited number of discrete scenarios cannot and is not expected to capture all risks, and BHCs that did not even attempt to account for other risks were lagging. C would be correct only in a world where the stem said the scenarios had been shown to cover these risks fully, which GARP rules out in principle.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). D truncates the horizon. GARP asks BHCs to incorporate the effect of other risks into projections of net income “over the nine-quarter planning horizon”. D would be correct if the stem’s planning horizon were four quarters.

questions.question: The head of model validation at a US BHC is presenting the scope of the capital planning validation program to the audit committee. Which of the following practices in the program is LEAST consistent with supervisory expectations for independent model review and validation?

options.text: Including in the model inventory the feeder models whose estimates are used as inputs by the models that produce final loss, revenue and expense projections.
Assessing whether models built for ongoing business activities remain valid for use under stressed conditions before they are used in the capital plan.
Supplementing the limited outcomes analysis of stress models with sensitivity analysis and with benchmark or challenger models.
Leaving management overlays outside the validation scope, because overlays are judgmental adjustments that the business lines review themselves.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Head of model validation presents the validation program scope; identify the practice LEAST consistent with expectations.

**Concept and theory**

Internal controls over capital planning have four pillars in GARP: (1) regular review by internal audit, (2) robust and independent model review and validation, (3) comprehensive documentation including policies and procedures, and (4) change controls. This question concerns pillar (2).

Why validate? Capital plan numbers are produced by chains of models. If one link is wrong, the capital ratio is wrong. Validation, consistent with SR 11-7, should be done by staff with technical competence, stature and independence from model developers and business areas, so the evaluation is unbiased. Its elements are:

- evaluation of **conceptual soundness**;
- **ongoing monitoring**, including process verification and benchmarking;
- **outcomes analysis**.

Further expectations:

- An inventory of all models, including input or **feeder** models whose estimates feed the models that produce final loss, revenue or expense projections.
- Consideration of whether a model is valid **under stressed conditions**, since models designed for ongoing business may be inappropriate for stress.
- Because realized stress outcomes are scarce, backtesting is hard; BHCs should compensate with **sensitivity analysis** or **benchmark or challenger models**.
- Validation should cover all models and assumptions, **including any management overlay**.
- Models not validated, or with known weaknesses, should have restricted use or be checked against challenger models.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the practice LEAST consistent with expectations, so three options are true restatements and one breaks a rule. A, B and C restate the feeder-model, stressed-use and compensate-for-backtesting expectations. D carves management overlays out of validation and leaves their review to the business lines, which breaks both the scope rule (overlays must be covered) and the independence rule (validation must be independent of business areas).

**Fragile fact.** Scope and actor: management overlays are inside validation scope, and validation must be independent of the business lines, not performed by them.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: internal controls, including model review and validation. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.3 Internal Controls, “Independent Model Review and Validation”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Internal Controls”. Note: the Schweser LO wording says “model review and valuation”; GARP’s LO and text say “model review and validation”, and the content is validation throughout. This paper follows GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q3 of 17.

a.reason: (true statement; qualifier misread if chosen). GARP: BHCs should maintain an inventory of all models “including all input or ‘feeder’ models”. Choosing A treats a required practice as a breach. A would be the answer if it said feeder models could be excluded because only final models drive capital.

b.reason: (true statement; qualifier misread if chosen). GARP: “Consideration should be given to the validity of the use of a model under stressed conditions”. B would be the answer if it said models validated for ongoing business need no further review before use in stress.

c.reason: (true statement; qualifier misread if chosen). GARP: BHCs should compensate for backtesting challenges “by conducting sensitivity analysis or by using benchmark or ‘challenger’ models”. C would be the answer if it said outcomes analysis could be skipped entirely because stress outcomes are rarely observed.

d.reason: D is correct (as the inconsistent practice) because GARP states that “BHCs should ensure that validation covers all models and assumptions used for capital planning purposes, including any adjustments management has made to the model estimates (management overlay)”.

questions.question: The internal audit director of a US BHC is drafting next year’s audit plan for the firm’s internal capital planning process and reviews four statements about the internal control framework. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Internal audit should concentrate on the individual components of the process, such as specific models, because the board itself reviews the process end to end.
Policies and procedures for the process should be reviewed at least annually, and exceptions should be rare and approved by the appropriate level of management.
Reports to the board should show aggregate enterprise-wide results net of manual adjustments made in aggregation, without describing those adjustments separately.
Documentation should cover loss- and resource-estimation methods but can omit the efficacy of control and governance functions, to keep it concise for decision-makers.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Internal audit director reviews statements on the internal control framework for capital planning.

**Concept and theory**

The internal control framework should cover the entire capital planning process: the risk measurement and management systems that produce input data, the models that generate loss and revenue estimates, the aggregation and reporting framework, and the process for making capital adequacy decisions. GARP breaks the expectations into several blocks:

- **Internal audit.** Reviews the full end-to-end process periodically, not just individual components; reviews how deficiencies are identified, tracked and remediated; has competence, influence and independence; reports regularly to senior management and the board.
- **Policies and procedures.** Cover the entire process, give a consistent and repeatable process and transparency to third parties; reviewed and updated **at least annually**; evidence of adherence; a formal exceptions process with exceptions that are **rare and approved** by the appropriate level of management.
- **Integrity of results.** Robust MIS able to run ad hoc analysis; reconciliation and data integrity for key reports; presentation of aggregate results that **describes any manual** **adjustments** made in aggregation and how they compensate for weaknesses; accurate, timely reports.
- **Documentation.** Clear and comprehensive for all aspects, including risk infrastructure, estimation methods, capital decision process and the **efficacy of control and governance** **functions**, with enough detail to allow review and challenge.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option tests one block. A narrows audit to components; B restates the policies block; C removes the description of manual adjustments; D narrows documentation. Only B matches GARP without alteration.

**Fragile fact.** Numbers and actors: policies at least annually; exceptions rare and approved by the appropriate level of management; audit covers the full process.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: internal controls. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.3, “Scope of Internal Controls”, “Internal Audit”, “Policies and Procedures”, “Ensuring Integrity of Results”, “Documentation”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Internal Controls”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q4 of 17.

a.reason: (scope error with role misassignment). GARP: audit “should perform a review of the full process, not just of the individual components”. A also hands the end-to-end review to the board, which oversees but is not the audit function. A would be correct if it said audit reviews components and the full end-to-end process.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP 20.3 states that policies “should be reviewed and updated at least annually and more frequently when warranted” and that exceptions “should be rare and approved by the appropriate level of management”.

c.reason: (polarity flip). GARP requires that the presentation of aggregate results “describe any manual adjustments made in the aggregation process and how those adjustments compensate for identified weaknesses”. C reverses this into suppressing the description. C would be correct if it said the reports must show and explain each manual adjustment.

d.reason: (scope error). GARP lists documentation of “efficacy of control and governance functions” among the required aspects, and asks for sufficient detail to allow review and challenge. D would be correct if it described what lagging documentation looked like rather than what is expected.

questions.question: A risk consultant is helping a US BHC write a responsibilities matrix for its capital planning process. Which of the following assignments of responsibility is consistent with supervisory expectations?

options.text: Senior management: ensuring that stress scenarios are sufficiently severe, and developing remediation plans for weaknesses that affect the reliability of results.
Board of directors: developing remediation plans with specific timelines for identified weaknesses, and then informing senior management once remediation is complete.
Internal audit: approving the capital plan and the capital policy under the Capital Plan Rule, after reviewing the end-to-end capital planning process.
Senior management: holding ultimate oversight responsibility for capital planning, and informing the board of capital adequacy matters at least once a year.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant builds a responsibilities matrix; choose the correct assignment of a governance task.

**Concept and theory**

Governance of the capital adequacy process splits responsibilities between the board and senior management, with internal audit as an independent control. GARP’s allocation:

| Actor | Responsibilities in GARP |
|---|---|
| Board of directors | Ultimate oversight responsibility and accountability; informed decisions on capital adequacy and capital actions; receives information at least quarterly or on material developments; approves the capital plan (Capital Plan Rule) and the capital policy (board or designated committee) |
| Senior management | Implements board-authorized activities, accountable to the board; ensures effective controls, including that stress scenarios are sufficiently severe and cover material risks; makes informed recommendations on capital goals and distributions; identifies weaknesses, evaluates materiality, develops remediation plans; reports limitations and plans to the board |
| Internal audit | Reviews the full process; reviews how deficiencies are identified, tracked and remediated; reports to senior management and the board |

**Applying it to this question**

The question is purely about who does what. Option A assigns two senior management duties correctly. Options B, C and D each move a duty to the wrong actor or change a frequency.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: senior management makes sure scenarios are severe enough and writes remediation plans; the board holds ultimate responsibility and approves; information flows to the board at least quarterly.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: corporate governance. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.4 Governance, “Board of Directors”, “Senior Management”, “Board Reporting”; Section 20.5 (capital policy approval). Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Governance”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q5 of 17.

a.reason: A is correct because GARP 20.4 says senior management “should ensure that effective controls are in place around the capital planning process, including ensuring that the BHC’s stress scenarios are sufficiently severe” and “should develop remediation plans for any weaknesses affecting the reliability of internal capital planning results”.

b.reason: (role misassignment). Remediation plans are developed by senior management, and both the limitations and the plans are reported to the board. B reverses the direction of reporting as well. B would be correct if it read “Senior management: developing remediation plans . . . and reporting them to the board”.

c.reason: (role misassignment). The board approves the capital plan under the Capital Plan Rule, and the capital policy must be approved by the board or a designated board committee. Internal audit reviews; it does not approve. C would be correct with “Board of directors” in place of “Internal audit”.

d.reason: (role misassignment with a frequency error). Ultimate oversight responsibility and accountability sit with the board, which should receive capital information at least quarterly, not annually. D would be correct if it read “Board of directors: holding ultimate oversight responsibility . . . and receiving capital adequacy information at least quarterly”.

questions.question:
The chair of the board risk committee of a US BHC asks the corporate secretary to check the committee’s information and record-keeping practices against supervisory expectations. The secretary lists four practices:

I. The board receives capital adequacy information at least quarterly, or sooner when material developments affect capital adequacy or the way it is assessed.

II. Capital information given to the board includes capital measures under current conditions and on a post-stress, pro forma basis, framed against the BHC’s capital goals and targets.

III. Where management makes judgmental adjustments to modeled loss estimates, the board receives only the adjusted results, because the unadjusted figures could mislead it.

IV. Board minutes record the final capital decisions; the information used and any challenge by the board need not be recorded, because minutes should be kept brief.

Which of the practices are consistent with stronger practice?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I and II only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Corporate secretary checks board information and minute-keeping practices.

**Concept and theory**

The board can only exercise oversight if it receives the right information and if its decisions are documented. GARP’s expectations:

- **Frequency.** Capital adequacy information at least quarterly, or when material developments affect capital adequacy or how it is assessed.
- **Content.** Capital measures under current conditions and on a post-stress, pro forma basis, framed against capital goals and targets; details of scenarios; key limitations, assumptions and uncertainties; summary mitigation strategies. Stronger practice adds independent model review and validation results, internal audit findings and sensitivity of capital to key assumptions.
- **Judgmental adjustments.** “In reporting to the board of directors, management should always provide both the initial results and the results after any judgmental adjustments.” Transparency about overlays lets the board challenge them.
- **Documenting decisions.** Decisions and the information used should be documented. Stronger practice: minutes describing how decisions were made, what information was used and evidence that the board challenged results. Weaker practice: minutes that were very brief and opaque.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches the frequency rule and II matches the content rule. III removes the unadjusted results that GARP says must always accompany the adjusted ones. IV describes the brief, opaque minutes that GARP labels weaker. Accurate set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the board gets both pre-adjustment and post-adjustment results; “brief” minutes are a weakness, not a virtue.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: corporate governance. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.4, “Board of Directors”, “Board Reporting”, “Documenting Decisions”; Section 20.7, “Qualitative Projections, Expert Judgment, and Adjustments” (initial and adjusted results). Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Governance”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q6 of 17.

a.reason: (omission of a true statement). A rejects II, which is a direct restatement of GARP. A would be correct if II had said the board receives only current-condition capital measures, without post-stress pro forma figures.

b.reason: (polarity flip in III). B accepts III, which reverses GARP’s “always provide both the initial results and the results after any judgmental adjustments”. B would be correct if III read “the board receives both the unadjusted and the adjusted results”.

c.reason: C is correct because GARP 20.4 states the board “should receive this information at least quarterly, or when there are material developments” (I) and that it “should include capital measures under current conditions as well as on a post-stress, pro forma basis and should be framed against the capital goals and targets” (II).

d.reason: (polarity flip in IV). D accepts IV, which presents the weaker practice (“very brief and opaque” minutes with little reference to the information used) as acceptable. D would be correct if IV said minutes describe how decisions were made, the information used and the board’s challenge.

questions.question: The treasurer of a US BHC is drafting a new capital policy for approval. A board member asks which of the proposed features reflects stronger practice in setting capital goals and targets. Which feature is most consistent with supervisory expectations?

options.text: Setting the internal capital goal at the ratio required to be considered well capitalized, as that ratio already reflects supervisory expectations.
Setting capital targets above the capital goals, allowing for the economic outlook, possible stress events and the uncertainty in the planning process.
Setting capital goals for the level of capital only, and leaving the composition of capital to the treasury function as market conditions allow.
Reevaluating the capital policy every three years, or earlier if the supervisor requests it, with each revision approved by the chief financial officer.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Treasurer drafts a capital policy; which goal-and-target feature is strongest?

**Concept and theory**

GARP defines a capital policy as the principles and guidelines a BHC uses for capital planning, issuance, usage and distributions. It is a distinct, comprehensive written document approved by the board or a designated board committee, reevaluated at a minimum frequency of **at least annually** and on other triggers.

Two levels of capital objective must be distinguished:

| Concept | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Capital goals | Aligned with risk appetite, risk profile and expectations of internal and external stakeholders (shareholders, rating agencies, counterparties, creditors, supervisors); specific goals for level and composition, current and under stress; sufficient to continue operating during and after stress |
| Capital targets | Set above the goals so that capital will not fall below the goals during stress; consider the economic outlook, financial condition, potential impact of stress events and uncertainty inherent in capital planning |

Weak practice: goals based solely on regulatory minimums and well-capitalized ratios, without regard to the BHC’s own risk profile, business model and sensitivity to changing conditions.

**Applying it to this question**

The board member asks which feature reflects stronger practice. A anchors the goal to a regulatory ratio, which GARP calls weak. C drops composition. D gets both the frequency and the approver wrong. B states the target-above-goal rule with its forward-looking inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: targets sit above goals (targets are the buffer that protects the goals), not the other way round.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: capital policy, including setting of goals and targets. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.5 Capital Policy, “Capital Goals and Targets”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Capital Policy”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q7 of 17.

a.reason: (sibling swap). A substitutes the regulatory benchmark for the BHC’s own goal. GARP lists “establishing capital goals based solely on regulatory minimums and the ratios required to be considered well-capitalized” as weak. A would be correct if the stem asked which practice supervisors observed at BHCs with weaker capital policies.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP 20.5 states that “BHCs should also establish capital targets above their capital goals to ensure that capital levels will not fall below the goals during periods of stress” and that targets should reflect the economic outlook, stress events and “the uncertainty inherent in the capital planning process”.

c.reason: (scope error). GARP requires “specific goals for the level and composition of capital”. C drops composition. C would be correct only if the policy item under review concerned the level of capital alone and the stem said composition goals were set elsewhere in the policy.

d.reason: (scope error with role misassignment). The minimum reevaluation frequency is at least annually, and the policy must be approved by the board or a designated board committee, not the CFO. D would be correct if it read “at least annually . . . approved by the board”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the capital contingency plan of a US BHC with USD 140 billion of total assets. Extracts from the plan are shown below.

| Plan element | Current design |
|---|---|
| Capital triggers | Common equity tier 1 ratio at 0.5 percentage points above the regulatory minimum, measured on reported quarter-end results |
| Scenarios covered | Baseline only |
| Other trigger metrics | None |
| Contingency actions | Common equity issuance; sale of the credit card business; listed in the order in which they were approved |
| Feasibility support | Both actions were executed successfully in 2009 |

Which recommendation by the consultant is most consistent with supervisory expectations?

options.text: Keep the current trigger level and its measurement basis, but extend the triggers to the stress scenario so that both scenarios are covered.
Rank the contingency actions by the amount of capital each would raise in normal markets, and test their feasibility once a trigger is breached.
Retain both actions without further analysis, because their successful execution in 2009 shows that they are feasible during a stress period.
Measure triggers on projected and reported results in baseline and stress, against capital targets, and add triggers such as CDS spreads.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant reviews a contingency plan with actual-only, baseline-only, minimum-based triggers.

**Concept and theory**

A capital contingency plan says what the BHC will do if capital deteriorates, and when. GARP’s expectations:

- **Circumstances and actions.** The policy explains when it will reduce or suspend dividends or repurchases or not execute a planned capital action, and lists contingency actions to remedy current or prospective deficiencies.
- **Triggers.** Defined for both baseline and stress scenarios and measured against the BHC’s capital targets; they give early warning, with target ranges for normal operation and thresholds that trigger escalation to the board, suspension of capital actions or activation of the plan. Triggers should also be set on other metrics: liquidity, earnings, debt and CDS spreads, ratings downgrades, stock performance, supervisory actions, market stress.
- **Actions.** Flexible and realistic for stress; mindful of market capacity constraints; ranked by ease of execution and impact, with stakeholder reactions assessed.

Weak practice, per GARP: few options or no feasibility analysis; overly optimistic assumptions or excessive reliance on past history; triggers based on actual but not projected results, or on minimum regulatory ratios only with no regard to other stakeholders or other metrics.

**Applying it to this question**

The table shows four weaknesses: triggers measured on reported results only, keyed to the regulatory minimum, baseline only, and no other metrics; plus actions ordered arbitrarily and supported only by 2009 history. The recommendation that repairs the triggers on all counts is D. A fixes only coverage, B misranks actions and defers feasibility, C relies on history.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and basis: triggers should be measured on projected results (not only actual), in baseline and stress, against capital targets (not regulatory minimums).

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: capital policy, including contingency planning. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.5, “Capital Contingency Plan”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Capital Policy” (triggers “based on the projected results, regulatory requirements, and the expectations of various stakeholders”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q8 of 17.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). A fixes only scenario coverage and keeps two weak features: measurement on reported results only and a level tied to the regulatory minimum. A would be correct if the plan’s only defect were that triggers covered the baseline alone.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). GARP ranks actions by ease of execution and impact and expects them to be realistic during stress, recognizing that some capital-raising actions may not be feasible then. Ranking by normal-market size and deferring the feasibility test drops both conditions. B would be correct if it said rank by ease of execution and impact under stress.

c.reason: (assumption miss). GARP lists “excessive reliance on past history (in terms of both possible contingency situations and options to address those situations)” as weak. Past success does not show feasibility in a future stress, where market access may differ. C would be correct if the stem asked for a feature typical of weak plans.

d.reason: D is correct because GARP 20.5 states triggers “should be established for both baseline and stress scenarios and measured against the BHC’s capital targets in those scenarios”, lists triggers “based on actual results but not on projected results” as weak, and expects triggers on other metrics such as “debt and credit default swap spreads, ratings downgrades”.

Because the BHC is seen as stronger than its competitors, the scenario may assume modest market share gains, provided the gains are explained in the scenario narrative.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Board member reviews the BHC-designed stress scenario for a regionally concentrated CRE lender.

**Concept and theory**

The Capital Plan Rule requires a BHC-developed stress scenario appropriate for its business model and portfolios. The point is that supervisory scenarios are generic; the BHC’s own scenario should hit the BHC where it is weakest. GARP’s expectations:

- **Tailoring.** Reflect the BHC’s unique vulnerabilities: business model, asset and liability mix, geographic footprint, portfolio characteristics and revenue drivers. A generic macroeconomic weakening similar in size to the supervisory severely adverse scenario does not meet expectations. Stronger examples: a significant counterparty default; a natural disaster or operational event; more acute stress on a region, industry or asset class.
- **Severity, but no safe harbor.** The scenario should place substantial strain on revenue and loss absorption. A scenario with post-stress ratios lower than under the supervisory severely adverse scenario “is not, in and of itself, a safe harbor”.
- **No self-serving assumptions.** Assuming the BHC will look strong relative to peers and gain market share is contrary to supervisory expectations.
- **Method.** Stronger internal designers combine internal models with expert judgment rather than relying solely on either; users of vendor scenarios tailor them; selection engages a broad range of stakeholders; a suite of scenarios is developed even though one is submitted.
- **Variables and narrative.** Variables sufficient for all material risks (regional or industry variables where concentrated); a clear narrative tying variable paths to vulnerabilities.

**Applying it to this question**

The BHC has a regional CRE concentration, so the scenario must stress that concentration. A states the no-safe-harbor rule and the tailoring rule. B, C and D each contradict a GARP statement.

**Fragile fact.** Severity is necessary but not sufficient: “worse than the supervisory severely adverse” is not a safe harbor.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: stress testing and stress scenario design. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.6 BHC Scenario Design, “Scenario Design and Severity”, “Variable Coverage”, “Clear Narratives”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Stress Testing and Stress Scenario Design”. Conflict note: Schweser describes expert judgment as “an outside expert’s opinion”; GARP says only “expert judgment” combined with internal models, with no requirement that the expert be external. This paper follows GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q9 of 17.

a.reason: A is correct because GARP 20.6 states that a scenario “that produces post-stress capital ratios lower than those under the supervisory severely adverse scenario is not, in and of itself, a safe harbor” and that BHC stress scenarios should be “tailored specifically to stress a BHC’s key vulnerabilities and idiosyncratic risks”.

b.reason: (polarity flip). GARP cites BHCs that “assumed that they would be viewed as strong compared to their competitors . . . and would therefore experience increased market share” as weaker practice, contrary to supervisory intent. Explaining it in the narrative does not cure it. B would be correct if it said the scenario should not assume market share gains.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). GARP says a scenario that “simply features a generic weakening of macroeconomic conditions similar in magnitude to the supervisory severely adverse scenario does not meet these expectations”. Applying it to every line does not add tailoring. C would be correct if the stem asked what supervisors found insufficient.

d.reason: (absolute-claim trap). GARP finds stronger designers “used internal models in combination with expert judgment rather than relying solely on either”. D would be correct if it said models and expert judgment should be combined.

questions.question: A senior model risk consultant is reviewing how a US BHC estimates losses, revenues and expenses for its enterprise-wide scenario analysis. Which of the following practices is NOT consistent with supervisory expectations?

options.text: Segmenting portfolios by common risk characteristics, such as credit score or loan-to-value ranges, while ensuring each segment has sufficient data observations.
Quantifying the impact of extensive judgmental adjustments relative to the unadjusted estimates, and treating heavy use of adjustments as a reason to review the models.
Projecting annual losses for a material loan portfolio and spreading them evenly over the four quarters of each year, because quarterly paths are hard to model.
Using external data where internal history is limited by acquisitions, and adjusting model outputs for risk differences between the internal and external data.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant reviews estimation practices; identify the one NOT consistent with expectations.

**Concept and theory**

Projections of losses, revenues and expenses are the building blocks of the pro forma capital analysis. GARP’s general expectations:

- **Quantitative basis.** Models or other quantitative methods are generally expected. Internal data first; external data where internal data are insufficient (systems limits, acquisitions, new products), with adjustments for differences in risk characteristics.
- **Granularity and segmentation.** Leading practice segments by common risk characteristics (credit score or LTV ranges) that show meaningful performance differences, with enough observations per segment for reliable estimates.
- **Testing.** Sensitivity analysis and challenger models supplement out-of-sample testing, because historical relationships may not hold in a hypothetical stress.
- **Timing.** Generating annual projections and spreading them evenly over four quarters “does not reflect a careful estimate of the expected quarterly path” and is acceptable only if the item is highly uncertain and the practice is likely conservative.
- **Qualitative methods.** Expert judgment and overlays are allowed where well supported, transparent and repeatable. Extensive adjustments should be quantified against unadjusted estimates, documented, and should trigger discussion of whether new or improved models are needed.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT question: three options restate expectations and one breaks a condition. C applies even spreading to a material portfolio and justifies it by modeling difficulty, not by high uncertainty and demonstrable conservatism. A, B and D restate GARP.

**Fragile fact.** Condition: even quarterly spreading is acceptable only when the item is highly uncertain and the result is likely conservative; both must be shown.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: estimating losses, revenues and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.7, “General Expectations”, “Establishing a Quantitative Basis for Enterprise-Wide Scenario Analysis”, “Qualitative Projections, Expert Judgment, and Adjustments”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Estimating Losses, Revenues, and Expenses”. The even-spreading condition is from GARP only (Schweser does not cover it).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q10 of 17.

a.reason: (true statement; qualifier misread if chosen). GARP: the leading practice is to segment on common risk characteristics, “e.g., credit score ranges or loan-to-value ratio ranges”, ensuring “each risk segment has sufficient data observations”. A would be the answer if it said segments should be as fine as possible regardless of data depth.

b.reason: (true statement; qualifier misread if chosen). GARP: the impact of extensive adjustments “should be quantified relative to unadjusted estimates” and extensive use “should trigger review and discussion as to whether new or improved modeling approaches are needed”. B would be the answer if it said adjustments need not be quantified.

c.reason: C is correct (as the inconsistent practice) because GARP 20.7 says even distribution over four quarters “is only acceptable when a BHC can clearly demonstrate that the projected item is highly uncertain and the practice likely results in a conservative estimate”. Difficulty of modeling is not one of those conditions.

d.reason: (true statement; qualifier misread if chosen). GARP: external data may be more appropriate when internal data are limited by “systems limitations, acquisitions, or new products”, with adjustments “to modeled outputs to account for identified differences”. D would be the answer if it omitted the adjustment step.

questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at a US BHC is projecting stressed credit losses over the nine-quarter planning horizon for a segment of revolving commercial credit lines, using an expected loss approach consistent with leading practice. The following information is available (amounts in USD million).

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Total committed lines | 2,000.0 |
| Drawn balance | 1,200.0 |
| Loan equivalent factor (additional drawdown, % of unused commitments) | 40.0 |
| Cumulative PD over the horizon, conditional on the stress scenario (%) | 6.0 |
| Long-run average PD of the segment (%) | 2.5 |
| LGD reflecting the fall in collateral values under the stress scenario (%) | 45.0 |
| Historical average LGD of the segment (%) | 35.0 |
| Average annual net charge-off rate, last five years (%) | 1.1 |

The projected stressed credit loss for the segment is closest to:

options.text: USD 17.10 million
USD 32.40 million
USD 54.00 million
USD 41.04 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Analyst projects stressed credit loss on revolving lines with loan equivalents and stressed parameters.

**Concept and theory**

Under the **expected loss (economic loss) approach**, GARP says losses are estimated as a function of three components: probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD) and exposure at default (EAD). Schweser (Reading 62) gives the product form:

EL = PD $\times\text{LGD} \times$ EAD

where PD is the probability of default over the horizon (decimal), LGD is the fraction of exposure lost if default occurs (decimal), and EAD is the exposure at the time of default (currency).

GARP’s leading-practice requirements for each component under stress:

| Input | Leading or stronger practice | Not appropriate or weaker |
|---|---|---|
| PD | Conditioned on the macroeconomic scenario | Long-run average PD over a mix of expansions and downturns |
| LGD | Tied to risk drivers, including the likely decline in collateral values under stress | Historical or weighted-average LGD not consistent with scenario severity |
| EAD | Loan equivalents (additional drawdowns as % of unused commitments, added to the drawn balance) or credit conversion factors | Ignoring undrawn commitments or assuming lines can be managed down in stress |

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Unused commitments = 2,000.0 − 1,200.0 = 800.0

Additional drawdown = 0.40 × 800.0 = 320.0

EAD = 1,200.0 + 320.0 = 1,520.0

PD × LGD = 0.060 × 0.45 = 0.027

Stressed loss = 0.027 × 1,520.0 = 41.04

The long-run PD (2.5%), historical LGD (35%) and the net charge-off rate (1.1%) are not used: the first two are inputs GARP says are inappropriate for stress, and the third belongs to a different (accounting-based) loss approach. The result means the segment is expected to lose about USD 41 million over the nine-quarter stress horizon, about 2.1% of total commitments.

**Fragile fact.** Base convention: the loan equivalent factor applies to unused commitments and is added to the drawn balance; the stressed loss uses the scenario-conditioned PD, never the long-run average.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: estimating losses (quantitative methodologies). GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.7, “Loss-Estimation Methodologies”, “Common Credit Loan Loss-Estimation Approaches”, “Expected Loss Approaches”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Loss Estimation Methods”. The multiplicative EL formula is from Schweser Reading 62 (“Recall from Book 2 that the expected loss (EL) from default is computed as . . . ”); GARP Chapter 20 names the three components but does not print the product. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q11 of 17.

a.reason: (wrong input twin: long-run average PD). 0.025 × 0.45 × 1,520.0 = 17.10. GARP: estimates “based on long-run average behavior over a mix of conditions . . . are not appropriate for projecting losses under stress and should not be used”. A would be correct for a long-run average loss estimate with no stress scenario.

b.reason: (dropped term: undrawn exposure ignored). 0.06 × 0.45 × 1,200.0 = 32.40. This is the weaker practice of not projecting stressed exposures on undrawn commitments. B would be correct if the lines were fully drawn or the stem gave a loan equivalent factor of zero.

c.reason: (wrong input twin: LEQ applied to total commitment). 1,200.0+0.40×2,000.0 = 2,000.0, then 0.06 × 0.45 × 2,000.0 = 54.00. This applies the loan equivalent factor to drawn plus undrawn amounts, confusing it with the base of a credit conversion factor. C would be correct if the 40% were defined as additional drawdown as a percentage of total commitments.

d.reason: D is correct because it uses the scenario-conditioned PD, the LGD that reflects collateral decline under stress, and an EAD that adds loan-equivalent drawdowns on unused commitments to the drawn balance, exactly as GARP 20.7 describes for stronger practice.
