questions.question:
A model validator at a US BHC is reviewing the credit loss-estimation methods used in the firm’s capital plan and drafts four statements for her report:

I. Roll-rate models are transparent and easy to use, but they often have weak predictive power beyond the near future, especially if they are not conditioned on scenario variables.

II. Scalar adjustments that scale up baseline loss estimates are acceptable as the primary method for material portfolios, provided the scalars are calibrated to historical performance.

III. Vintage loss models are well suited to stress testing because they assume that different cohorts experience similar losses over time, which produces results representative of a stress period.

IV. A net charge-off model that lacks sufficient segmentation, or that ignores changing portfolio composition, should not be the primary loss-estimation approach for a material portfolio.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and IV only
II and III only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Validator audits statements on roll-rate, scalar, vintage and NCO credit loss models.

**Concept and theory**

GARP surveys the credit loss models BHCs used in CCAR. Each has a characteristic weakness under stress:

| Model | What it does | Supervisory view |
|---|---|---|
| Roll-rate | Rate at which current or delinquent loans roll into delinquency or default next period (retail) | Transparent, easy to use; weak predictive power outside the near future, especially if not conditioned on scenario variables; limited use over nine quarters |
| Vintage (age-cohort-time) | Seasoning curve by segment plus regression of losses on macro variables at each seasoning level | Natural cohort segmentation, good for lifecycle products; hard to build and validate; assumes cohorts have similar losses, so results represent average years, not stress |
| Net charge-off (NCO) | Regresses portfolio charge-off rates on macro variables, often with lagged NCO | Lower explanatory power; assumes history predicts the future; without segmentation or changing composition, avoid as primary model for a material portfolio |
| Scalar | Scales baseline loss up for stress | Easy, but opaque and insensitive to composition and scenario; at most for immaterial portfolios |

**Applying it to this question**

I restates the roll-rate assessment: true. II promotes scalars to material portfolios: false. III takes the vintage-model assumption that cohorts behave alike and claims it produces stress-representative results, when GARP says it produces results representative of average years: false. IV restates the NCO restriction: true. Accurate set: I and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the vintage assumption that cohorts behave alike pushes results toward average years, which is a weakness for stress testing, not a strength.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: estimating losses (quantitative methodologies). GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.7, “Roll-Rate Models”, “Vintage Loss Models”, “Charge-Off Models”, “Scalar Adjustments”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.2, “Loss Estimation Methods” (Schweser covers roll-rate and charge-off models only; vintage and scalar content is from GARP).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q12 of 17.

a.reason: (scope error in II). A accepts II. GARP: scalar approaches have “lack of transparency and lack of sensitivity to changes in portfolio composition and scenario variables” and should be “at most, limited to immaterial portfolios”. Calibration to history does not lift that limit. A would be correct if II referred to immaterial portfolios.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP states that roll-rate models “often have a weak predictive power outside the near future, particularly if they are not properly conditioned on scenario variables” (I), and that BHCs “should avoid using such a NCO model as the primary loss-estimation approach for a material portfolio” (IV).

c.reason: (scope error in II and polarity flip in III). C picks the two false statements. III reverses GARP: the similar-cohort assumption generates “results that are representative of average years, rather than during the period of stress”. C would be correct if the question asked which statements are inaccurate.

d.reason: (polarity flip in III). D keeps the true IV but accepts III and rejects the true I. D would be correct only if III said vintage models’ similar-cohort assumption makes outputs representative of average years, and I were false.

questions.question: An operational risk modeler at a US BHC is designing the stressed operational loss projections for the capital plan. Statistical tests show a significant relationship between macroeconomic variables and loss frequency for some event types, but no meaningful relationship with loss severity. Which of the following design choices is most consistent with supervisory expectations?

options.text: Use a regression model for loss frequency, apply a severity assumption based on the most recent crisis period, and support the estimation period with statistical evidence.
Use a modified loss distribution approach at the 99.9th percentile for the stressed estimates, because the Federal Reserve requires the AMA percentile for capital planning.
Remove legal reserves and losses from discontinued business lines from the internal loss data, because these losses would distort the loss distribution of ongoing operations.
Use historical averages of internal losses as the sole approach for the stressed estimates, because this anchors the projections firmly to the BHC’s own loss experience.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Operational risk modeler designs stressed loss projections when only frequency correlates with macro variables.

**Concept and theory**

Operational losses arise from inadequate or failed internal processes, people or systems, or from external events. The Capital Plan Rule does not require AMA models for stressed operational losses, but BHCs with AMA data should leverage them. GARP’s survey of methods:

- **Data.** Start from internal loss data, add forward-looking elements, idiosyncratic risks and tail events; supplement with scaled external data. Use complete internal data; lagging BHCs excluded large items such as legal reserves, losses from acquired firms and losses from discontinued business lines.
- **Regression models.** Estimate loss frequency and loss severity. Most BHCs found no meaningful correlation between macro variables and severity, so those using regression for frequency typically applied a severity assumption (static or four-quarter moving average) based on the most recent crisis period. Most BHCs chose estimation periods judgmentally; Schweser states they should provide statistical support instead.
- **Modified LDA.** The AMA uses the 99.9th percentile; for CCAR BHCs used a lower confidence level (typically 70th to 98th percentile for stress; mean or median for baseline) or adjusted frequency for correlation. The Federal Reserve does not require a particular percentile, but expects a credible, transparent selection, a rationale and sensitivity analysis.
- **Scenario analysis.** Expert-driven overlays for idiosyncratic or unexperienced events; quantitative effect on final estimates must be shown.
- **Historical averages.** Acceptable in combination (for event types with no correlation); used alone, backward-looking and excludes unexperienced risks.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives frequency correlation but no severity correlation. That is exactly the case GARP describes: regression for frequency, severity from the recent crisis period. A adds the requirement to support the estimation period with statistical evidence. B, C and D each break a stated expectation.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: for CCAR, modified LDA uses a lower percentile than the AMA’s 99.9th (typically 70th to 98th), and no particular percentile is mandated.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: estimating losses (operational risk). GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.7, “Operational Risk”, “Regression Models”, “Modified Loss-Distribution Approach (LDA)”, “Historical Averages”, “Legal Exposures”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.3, “Operational Risk”. Conflict note: Schweser gives the LDA confidence level example as “90% or 95%”; GARP reports a range of 70th to 98th percentile for stressed estimates. These are consistent (Schweser’s examples sit inside GARP’s range); GARP’s range is used here. The statistical-support requirement for the estimation period is stated explicitly in Schweser; GARP reports that most BHCs chose periods judgmentally and, for historical averages, that BHCs should support chosen time periods.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q13 of 17.

a.reason: A is correct because GARP reports that BHCs using regression for frequency “typically applied the loss-severity assumption . . . based on the most recent crisis period”, and Schweser states that BHCs using regression models “should provide statistical support for the period chosen for estimation purposes instead of arbitrary and judgmental selection”.

b.reason: (absolute-claim trap). GARP: “The Federal Reserve does not require BHCs to use a particular percentile to produce stressed estimates”; CCAR LDA users typically used a lower confidence level than the AMA’s 99.9th. B would be correct if it said the BHC must justify its chosen percentile and test its sensitivity.

c.reason: (polarity flip). GARP lists “excluding large items such as legal reserves” and “excluding loss data from discontinued business lines, even though the loss events were reasonably generic” as lagging practices; it expects all legal reserves and settled legal losses in the total. C would be correct if the stem asked what lagging BHCs did.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). Historical averages are acceptable in combination with other methods, but “when used alone, this approach is backward-looking and excludes potential risks the BHCs have not experienced”. D would be correct if historical averages were used only for event types without identified correlation, alongside regression for the others.

questions.question: The head of market risk at a US BHC with sizeable EUR and GBP interest rate trading books is presenting the trading and counterparty stress loss methodology to newly hired analysts. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The Federal Reserve prefers probabilistic approaches for capital planning, because a full distribution of P/L is easier to communicate to senior management and the board.
The approximation methods used for daily VaR are appropriate for stress testing, because they perform adequately for the risk-factor moves seen in normal conditions.
Instantaneous market shock scenarios already embed counterparty defaults, so an explicit default scenario for the largest counterparties would double count losses.
Assuming that stressful moves occurring over weeks or months happen instantaneously is suitably conservative, given uncertainty about exiting positions under stress.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Head of market risk explains trading and counterparty stress methodology.

**Concept and theory**

BHCs with sizeable trading operations can lose money under stress from market moves (rates, spreads, equities, commodities) and from counterparty credit deterioration or default. GARP groups methods into two families:

| Approach | Strength | Weakness and expectation |
|---|---|---|
| Probabilistic (distribution of P/L) | Insight into a range of scenarios a deterministic test may miss | Complex, less transparent, hard to communicate and to tie to actions; must show it can produce scenarios more severe than history |
| Deterministic (point estimate under a scenario) | Easier to communicate to management and board; used by most BHCs in CCAR | Limited scenario set may miss large-loss scenarios; must show a range of scenarios stressing key exposures |

Implementation expectations: **full revaluation** for stress (approximations used for daily VaR may misstate large, nonlinear moves); **instantaneous shocks** are appropriate and suitably conservative given uncertainty about exiting positions; shocks must give plausible results; **counterparty** **defaults** are typically not embedded in instantaneous market shocks, so leading BHCs added an explicit default scenario for their largest counterparties; risk-mitigation assumptions must be conservative.

**Applying it to this question**

D states the instantaneous-shock rationale exactly. A inverts the communication strengths of the two approaches, B carries VaR approximations into stress, and C claims defaults are already embedded.

**Fragile fact.** Convention: instantaneous shocks are the conservative choice; full revaluation, not VaR approximations, is the default for stress.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: estimating losses (market risk and counterparty credit risk). GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.7, “Market Risk and Counterparty Credit Risk”, “Translating Scenarios to Risk Factor Shocks”, “Revaluation Methodologies and P/L Estimates”, “Counterparty and Issuer Defaults”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.3, “Market Risk and Counterparty Credit Risk”. Full revaluation and instantaneous shocks are from GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q14 of 17.

a.reason: (sibling swap). A gives the probabilistic approach the deterministic approach’s strength. GARP: the probabilistic approach “is complex and often lacks transparency” and is hard to communicate; the deterministic approach “generally produces scenarios that are easier to communicate”. The Federal Reserve expresses no general preference. A would be correct with “deterministic” in place of “probabilistic” and without the claimed Federal Reserve preference.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). GARP: approximations “may perform adequately for the risk-factor moves that are considered in normal conditions”, but BHCs “should generally use full-revaluation methods for stress testing”; approximations only on a limited basis if tests show mismeasurement is not significant. B would be correct only under that tested exception.

c.reason: (polarity flip). GARP: defaults “are typically not embedded directly within the instantaneous market shock scenario”; leading practice adds an explicit default scenario for the largest counterparties. C would be correct only if the shock scenario modeled counterparty defaults directly.

d.reason: D is correct because GARP says most BHCs “used instantaneous market shocks . . . which assumed highly stressful outcomes that have typically occurred over a period of time (days, weeks, or months) will occur instantaneously. Given the uncertainty surrounding a firm’s ability to exit or manage positions during a period of severe market stress, this is an appropriate practice and suitably conservative”.

questions.question: A supervisor is reviewing the pre-provision net revenue (PPNR) projections in a US BHC’s capital plan. The BHC has large credit card, trading and retail deposit businesses. Which of the following projection practices is most consistent with stronger practice?

options.text: Projecting net interest income on balance sheet assumptions built by treasury independently of the balance sheet used in loss estimation, so each projection reflects its specialist owner.
Projecting trading revenue by assuming a perfect correlation between trading revenue and a broad equity index, because the index is already one of the scenario variables.
Projecting credit card interchange revenue by first modeling consumer spending under the scenario and then applying fee rates, instead of regressing revenue on scenario factors.
Projecting a fall in non-interest expense from the first stressed quarter through cuts in marketing and compensation, because management will respond as soon as the downturn begins.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Supervisor reviews PPNR projection practices at a card, trading and deposit BHC.

**Concept and theory**

Pre-provision net revenue (PPNR) is net revenue before adjusting for loss provisions (Schweser); GARP projects it through three components: net interest income, non-interest income and noninterest expense. The Capital Plan Rule requires revenue and expense estimates over the nine-quarter horizon, across the same scenarios used for losses. GARP’s central theme is **coherence**: projections of PPNR, losses, balance sheet and RWA must tell one consistent story in each scenario.

- **Net interest income.** Balance sheet assumptions must be the same as those used in loss estimation; capture prepayments, repricing, embedded options, loan performance, premium and discount amortization; check constant-spread pricing assumptions.
- **Non-interest income.** Estimate at a granular level and model the drivers (volume) before applying fees: GARP says modeling interchange revenue directly is likely less effective than modeling customer spending and then fee and rate movement. Do not assume perfect correlation between trading or private equity revenue and broad indices; estimate the sensitivity.
- **Non-interest expense.** Include costs that rise in a downturn (other real estate owned, collections); do not assume immediate dramatic cuts; such assumptions imply perfect foresight.

**Applying it to this question**

The supervisor needs the one stronger practice. C models the driver (consumer spending) and then applies fee rates, exactly GARP’s preferred structure. A breaks the shared-balance-sheet rule, B assumes perfect correlation, D assumes immediate cuts.

**Fragile fact.** Order of modeling: project the driver (spending, AUM, volume) under the scenario first, then apply the fee or rate; do not regress the revenue line itself.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: estimating revenues and expenses. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.7, “PPNR Projection Methodologies”, “Net Interest Income”, “Non-Interest Income”, “Non-Interest Expense”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.3, “PPNR Projection Methodologies”. Note: Schweser places PPNR under Module 61.3 (“Assessing the Impact of Capital Adequacy”); GARP places it under 20.7 (estimation methodologies). Both lie inside LO 61.b; this question is classed under estimating revenues and expenses, following GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q15 of 17.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). GARP: “Balance sheet assumptions used to project net interest income should be consistent with balance sheet assumptions considered as part of loss estimation”. Independent construction breaks that condition. A would be correct if treasury’s balance sheet were the single shared set used for both projections.

b.reason: (absolute-claim trap). GARP: the BHC “should establish the level of sensitivity of its positions relative to the indices and not automatically assume a perfect correlation between the two”. B would be correct if it said the BHC estimates the sensitivity of trading revenue to index moves.

c.reason: C is correct because GARP states that “modeling interchange revenues or asset management fees is likely to be less effective than modeling customer spending or assets under management, respectively, given the scenario being used, and then considering fee and/or rate movement”.

d.reason: (assumption miss). GARP calls immediate dramatic cuts in marketing, rewards, compensation or discretionary costs unrealistic and notes such assumptions “imply perfect knowledge of the conditions as they unfold”. D would be correct only if the cuts were supported by analysis of their timing and feasibility, not assumed from the first stressed quarter.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US BHC is validating the balance sheet and risk-weighted asset (RWA) projections that feed the post-stress capital ratios in the capital plan. Which of the following projection practices is most consistent with stronger practice?

options.text: Projecting a target balance for each major balance sheet segment directly from the strategic plan, and then aligning the PPNR projections with those target balances.
Projecting asset balances from separately assessed drivers such as paydowns, prepayments, nonperformance and new business, each checked against the scenario.
Assuming RWA reductions over the horizon from planned enhancements to the internal RWA models, because the enhancements have been approved by the model committee.
Assuming flight-to-quality deposit inflows that lower funding costs under stress, because the BHC’s deposit franchise attracted deposits in the last financial crisis.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Senior analyst validates balance sheet and RWA projections feeding post-stress ratios.

**Concept and theory**

Post-stress capital ratios depend on the numerator (capital after losses and PPNR) and on the denominator (RWA). Balance sheet projections drive losses, PPNR and RWA together, so GARP calls them a key input. Expectations:

- **Drivers, not targets.** Balances evolve through originations, purchases, sales, maturities, prepayments and defaults. Stronger BHCs separately considered drivers (contractual paydowns, modeled prepayments, nonperformance, new business) and checked each against scenario conditions, “rather than simply projecting targeted balances directly”.
- **No favorable assumptions.** GARP lists aggressive assumptions: (1) large asset-mix shifts that lower risk weights, (2) flight-to-quality deposit inflows that cut funding costs, (3) shrinkage without the losses of selling in stressed markets, (4) operating margin improvement. These need evidence that they can be reasonably assured.
- **RWA.** Consistent with projected exposures and scenario severity; trading RWA may rise with volatility; no assumed RWA reductions from data or model enhancements during the horizon; assumptions documented and independently validated.

**Applying it to this question**

B describes driver-based projection with a scenario check. A projects target balances and bends PPNR to fit. C assumes model-enhancement RWA relief. D is the flight-to-quality example GARP names as aggressive.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: under stress, assume no RWA relief from model changes and no favorable deposit inflows; RWA per dollar may rise.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including RWA and balance sheet projections. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.8 Assessing Capital Adequacy Impact, “Balance Sheet and RWAs”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.3, “Generating Projections”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q16 of 17.

a.reason: (sibling swap: common practice presented as stronger practice). Projecting target balances directly is what stronger BHCs avoided, and adjusting PPNR to fit reverses the causal chain. A would be correct if the question asked for a weaker practice that BHCs with stronger practices avoided; GARP notes that most BHCs made direct projections of balances by segment, which is why the option looks familiar.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP 20.8 says BHCs with stronger practices “separately considered the drivers of change to asset and funding balances, such as contractual paydowns, modeled prepayments, nonperformance, and new business activity”, with each element “separately assessed for consistency with scenario conditions”.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). GARP: “Where RWA projections are based on internal risk models, BHCs should not assume any RWA reductions from potential data or model enhancements . . . over the projection period.” Internal approval does not change this. C would be correct if the enhancements were already implemented before the projection start date.

d.reason: (assumption miss). GARP names “‘flight-to-quality’ assumptions and funding mix changes that increase deposits and reduce the dollar cost of funding” as aggressive or favorable. Past experience alone does not give reasonable assurance in the assumed stress. D would be correct only with sufficient evidence that the inflows can be reasonably assured in the scenario.

questions.question:
The head of the central group that aggregates enterprise-wide scenario results at a US BHC is reviewing the consolidated projections below before they are reported to senior management (amounts in USD billion unless stated).

| Item | Baseline | BHC stress scenario |
|---|---|---|
| Cumulative PPNR over nine quarters | 14.2 | 15.6 |
| Cumulative provisions over nine quarters | 5.8 | 19.4 |
| Loan balances at end of horizon | 212.0 | 191.0 |
| RWA at end of horizon | 238.0 | 243.0 |
| Minimum CET1 ratio over the horizon (%) | 11.6 | 7.9 |
| Effective tax rate assumption (%) | 21.0 | 21.0 |

Which observation should the group most likely escalate for further investigation?

options.text: The minimum CET1 ratio over the horizon is lower in the stress scenario than in the baseline.
Cumulative provisions in the stress scenario are more than three times those in the baseline.
RWA at end of horizon are higher in the stress scenario even though loan balances are lower.
Cumulative PPNR is higher in the stress scenario than the baseline while loan balances fall.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Central aggregation group reviews consolidated baseline and stress projections.

**Concept and theory**

Aggregation turns component estimates into post-stress capital ratios. GARP expects a well-established process, ideally run by a **centralized group** that combines loss, revenue, balance sheet and RWA projections, provides governance and controls, ensures coherence of components and aggregate results, and applies and documents adjustments. The group should:

- check that paths of losses and revenues are consistent with paths of balances, RWA and the overall scenario. GARP’s example: “an increase in PPNR amid declining balances would appear generally inconsistent and should warrant further investigation”;
- critically evaluate assumptions if post-stress outcomes are more favorable than baseline;
- use business planning and reporting systems rather than standalone spreadsheets, and reconcile results to management and regulatory reports.

Expected features of a severe BHC scenario: substantial strain on revenue and loss absorption, and a significant reduction in capital ratios relative to baseline.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the table row by row. CET1 lower under stress (7.9% versus 11.6%): expected. Provisions more than three times baseline (19.4/5.8 ≈ 3.3): expected for a severe scenario. RWA higher under stress despite lower loans: consistent with risk parameters (for example RWA per dollar of trading positions) rising with volatility and with RWA tracking scenario severity. PPNR higher under stress (15.6 versus 14.2) while loans fall (191 versus 212): this is GARP’s own example of an inconsistency and a post-stress outcome more favorable than baseline. The tax rate row is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: under stress, PPNR should not rise while balances fall; any post-stress result better than baseline is a red flag to investigate.

**Reference**

LO 61.b (ORR 20.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas”, followed by the seven areas listed on the cover. Area: assessing the impact of capital adequacy. GARP Chapter 20, Section 20.8, “Aggregation of Projections”; Section 20.6, “Scenario Design and Severity”. Schweser Reading 61, Module 61.3, “Generating Projections” (“If an enterprise-wide scenario analysis produces post-stress results that are more favorable than the baseline conditions”). Conflict note: Schweser says BHCs should use automated processes “without manual intervention or managerial adjustments”; GARP’s leading practice is automated processes with mechanisms “requiring approval and logging of judgmental adjustments and overrides”, so adjustments are allowed if controlled and documented. This paper follows GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-20 b, where it is Q17 of 17.

a.reason: (polarity flip: expected outcome treated as anomaly). GARP expects the BHC stress scenario to produce “a significant reduction in capital ratios relative to baseline projections”. A would warrant escalation if the stress ratio were higher than baseline.

b.reason: (polarity flip: expected outcome treated as anomaly). Much higher provisions are what a scenario placing “substantial strains on its ability to . . . absorb losses” should produce. B would warrant escalation if stress provisions were close to or below baseline.

c.reason: (sibling swap: RWA path confused with the aggressive asset-mix case). GARP expects RWA consistent with scenario severity and notes RWA per dollar of some trading positions may increase in volatile periods. The aggressive case GARP flags is the opposite: asset-mix changes that decrease risk weights. C would warrant escalation if RWA fell sharply under stress through an unsupported shift in asset mix.

d.reason: D is correct because GARP 20.8 states that “an increase in PPNR amid declining balances would appear generally inconsistent and should warrant further investigation”, and that more favorable post-stress outcomes than baseline require critical evaluation of assumptions.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank is preparing a training module on how bank regulation developed before the Basel Committee existed. She drafts four statements:

I. Early clearinghouse members shared financial statements with one another and had rights of inspection, so solvency monitoring existed but was carried out privately.

II. Government-controlled central banks replaced clearinghouses as lenders of last resort chiefly because clearinghouse members refused to share their financial statements.

III. Customers complained of unfairness and of the difficulty of monitoring an institution’s safety and soundness, even when a failure was not associated with fraud.

IV. A run or panic could bring down only an institution that was already insolvent, because a solvent institution could always meet its withdrawals.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese trust bank training module: four statements on regulation before the Basel Committee.

**Concept and theory**

Regulation of banks did not begin with governments. GARP opens Chapter 21 by tracing how it grew incrementally, usually in response to stress that exposed the limits of what came before.

Stage 1: reputation. Before any official approval was needed, a bank succeeded only if clients trusted it. Banks therefore enlisted prominent local figures, carried large amounts of capital at creation and built imposing buildings, all to signal that deposits would be returned.

Stage 2: why trust was not enough. Failures were frequent, and sometimes happened not because of insolvency but because of a loss of confidence. When clients rushed to withdraw, even a solvent institution could fail if it could not liquidate assets or raise new funds quickly enough. A run is a liquidity event that can kill a solvent bank.

Stage 3: private mutual support. The first “regulations” were private. The Bank of England began as a private-sector entity that supported other banks; clearinghouses were partly mutual-support clubs whose members shared financial statements and had rights of inspection. Solvency monitoring and enforcement therefore existed, but privately.

Stage 4: limits of private arrangements (GARP lists four triggers):

| Trigger | What it showed |
|---|---|
| Size of panics | No entity without the power to print money could support the system in a big enough panic, so government-controlled central banks replaced clearinghouses and private banks as lenders of last resort. |
| Cost to the economy | Crises imposed large economy-wide costs (often followed by depressions), so governments sought to keep institutions solvent and liquid enough to survive plausible distress. |
| Customer complaints | Fraud was not uncommon, but even without fraud customers complained of unfairness and of the difficulty of monitoring safety and soundness. |
| Globalization | Interlinked international banks, competitive concerns and settlement failures (Herstatt) required official international coordination. |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the four-stage story. Statement I describes Stage 3 exactly: shared statements, rights of inspection, done privately. Accurate. Statement II gives a reason for the move to central banks that GARP never gives. The reason was the size of panics relative to private resources and the unique power of a central bank to print money. Inaccurate. Statement III is the third trigger, including the qualifier “even when a failure was not associated with fraud”. Accurate. Statement IV says only insolvent banks could be brought down by a run. GARP says the opposite: a solvent institution could fail if it could not liquidate assets or raise funds quickly enough. Inaccurate. Accurate set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Runs can kill solvent banks (a liquidity problem); central banks became lenders of last resort because they can print money, not because clearinghouses withheld information.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, introduction (before section 21.1), on early private arrangements and their limitations. Schweser Reading 62, LO 62.a, gives the same list in condensed form; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (sibling swap). It includes Statement II, which attaches a plausible but wrong cause (an information-sharing failure) to the move to central-bank lending of last resort. The real cause belongs to the panic-size trigger: only an entity that can print money can stop a big enough panic. A would be right if the stem asked for statements I and II where II read “. . . because no entity without the power to print money had enough resources in a large panic”.

b.reason: Option B (I and III only) matches the source: GARP describes clearinghouse members sharing financial statements with rights of inspection, “however, this was done privately”, and lists customer complaints of unfairness and monitoring difficulty “even when a failure was not associated with fraud”.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It includes Statement IV and drops Statement I. Statement IV reverses the source’s direction on runs: GARP’s point is that a run can bring down a solvent institution. C would be right only if IV said “even a solvent institution could fail if it could not liquidate assets or raise funds quickly enough” and I were false.

d.reason: (polarity flip). It accepts I and III correctly but also accepts the reversed Statement IV. D would be right if Statement IV were restated with the correct polarity (runs can topple solvent institutions).

questions.question: A risk consultant at a London foreign exchange dealer is preparing a GBP settlement-risk training session built around the failure of Herstatt Bank in the summer of 1974. Which of the following best describes what the failure exposed and the institutional response that followed?

options.text: Capital rules set as ratios to total assets ignored off-balance-sheet exposures, and the official sector responded by creating the BCBS in 1974.
Different currency delivery times across time zones caused large FX trades to fail to clear, and banks responded through private clearinghouse arrangements.
Different currency delivery times across time zones caused large FX trades to fail to clear, and the official sector responded by creating IOSCO and the IAIS in 1974.
Different currency delivery times across time zones caused large FX trades to fail to clear, and the official sector responded by creating the BCBS in 1974.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: London FX dealer: what the 1974 Herstatt failure exposed and the official response.

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls globalization the fourth trigger of regulation, and especially of international coordination of regulation. As international trade blossomed in the 1960s and 1970s and multinationals multiplied, FX and capital flows grew very large. Multinationals valued providers that operated in many countries, which raised three issues:

1. Interlinkage: large international banks became connected, so one failure could cause problems in many countries, not just its home country.
2. Competitive (dis)advantage: banks and regulators worried about differences in capital requirements across nations.
3. Clearing and settlement: when Herstatt Bank failed in the summer of 1974, differences in required delivery times for currencies across countries and time zones caused large amounts of FX transactions to fail to clear, raising concern about a potential collapse of the global financial system. Schweser names this settlement risk.

GARP’s conclusion: “only official-sector cooperation and coordination could address these risks”. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) was therefore created in 1974, following the Herstatt failure. Its perceived success may have encouraged the creation of sister bodies for other sectors, but at different dates:

| Body | Sector | Created |
|---|---|---|
| BCBS | Banking supervision | 1974 |
| IOSCO | Securities regulators | 1983 |
| IAIS | Insurance supervisors | 1994 |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks two things: what the failure exposed (cause) and what response followed (actor and institution). The cause is a settlement and time-zone problem in FX clearing; the actor is the official sector; the institution is the BCBS; the year is 1974. Only one option gets all four right.

**Fragile fact.** Herstatt (1974) → BCBS (1974); IOSCO 1983 and IAIS 1994 came later. The response was official-sector, not private.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, introduction (globalization as the fourth trigger; Herstatt; creation of the BCBS, IAIS and IOSCO). Schweser LO 62.a agrees (“settlement risk”) but does not give the IOSCO and IAIS dates; those come from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: (sibling swap). It attaches the wrong cause to the right institution. Capital requirements set as ratios to total assets, and their blindness to off-balance-sheet exposures, are the pre-1988 problems that motivated the risk-based ratio of Basel I, not the Herstatt failure. A would be right if the stem asked “which pre-1988 weakness did Basel I’s risk-weighted assets address?” with a response of “the 1988 accord”.

b.reason: (role misassignment). The cause is right, but the actor is wrong. Private mutual support is exactly what GARP says had reached its limits: “only official-sector cooperation and coordination could address these risks”. B would describe the earlier private response to bank runs (the Bank of England as a private-sector entity, mutual-support clearinghouses), not the response to Herstatt.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The cause and actor are right, but the institution is a sibling body. IOSCO was created in 1983 and the IAIS in 1994, possibly inspired by the BCBS’s perceived success. C would be right only if the stem asked which bodies later followed the BCBS model, and dropped the 1974 date.

d.reason: Option D states the time-zone delivery problem, failed FX clearing, an official-sector response and the creation of the BCBS in 1974, exactly as GARP describes it.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the two events that motivated the creation of Basel I. Which of the following statements on her slides is **least** accurate?

options.text: The negotiations were purely about safety and soundness, with no element of manoeuvring by member nations for perceived competitive advantage.
Cross-border finance kept growing after Herstatt, giving the G10 nations a common interest in banks holding enough equity to absorb large losses.
International banks competed vigorously in each other’s home countries while minimum levels of required capital varied significantly across nations.
Members of the BCBS developed a global minimum standard in order to level the playing field and to avoid a race to the bottom in capital requirements.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank presentation: which slide on the two events motivating Basel I is least accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The BCBS existed from 1974, but its first capital accord came later. GARP names two events that motivated Basel I:

1. **Solvency motive.** Cross-border finance kept growing after Herstatt, so the G10 nations had a common interest in ensuring that banks had enough equity capital to absorb large losses. A failing bank abroad is now everyone’s problem.
2. **Competitive motive.** International banks competed vigorously in each other’s home countries, but minimum required capital varied significantly across nations. Banks headquartered in low-minimum countries were perceived to have a competitive advantage (they could lever more and price more aggressively). The BCBS therefore set a global minimum standard to “level the playing field” and avoid a “race to the bottom”, in which each country would cut its minimums to help its own banks.

GARP adds a candid remark: while the accord was partly about safety and soundness, “negotiations also had an element of manoeuvring for perceived competitive advantage”. In other words, the negotiators were not neutral engineers: each nation also sought terms that suited its own banks.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a **least** accurate question, so three options are faithful to the source and one is not. B restates motive 1; C restates the premise of motive 2; D restates the BCBS’s response to motive 2. Option A claims the negotiations were purely about safety and soundness with no competitive manoeuvring, which directly contradicts GARP’s remark.

**Fragile fact.** Basel I had two motives (solvency and level playing field), and the negotiations themselves were not purely technical: there was competitive manoeuvring.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1 “The Basel Accord: Basel I” (two events motivating Basel I). Schweser LO 62.a covers the competitive point under globalization but does not mention the manoeuvring remark; deciding fact from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: Option A is the inaccurate statement and therefore the answer. It applies an absolute claim (“purely”, “no element”) where GARP explicitly says the negotiations had an element of manoeuvring for perceived competitive advantage.

b.reason: (accurate statement, not the answer to a LEAST qualifier). This is motive 1 nearly word for word. It would be the answer only if the stem asked which statement is most accurate about the solvency motive.

c.reason: (accurate statement, not the answer to a LEAST qualifier). This is the factual premise of motive 2. It would become the answer only if it reversed a fact, for example “minimum levels of required capital were broadly similar across nations”.

d.reason: (accurate statement, not the answer to a LEAST qualifier). This is the response to motive 2, including both of GARP’s phrases. It would be the answer if it said the standard was set to maximise each nation’s flexibility, which is the opposite of a common minimum.

questions.question: A board risk committee member at a Chinese bank with branches in several G10 markets asks the treasurer to explain the competitive concern that Basel I was designed to address. The treasurer notes that, before 1988, international banks competing in the same markets were held to widely differing home-country capital minimums. Which of the following best describes the concern and the response?

options.text: Banks headquartered in low-minimum countries were seen as advantaged; Basel I harmonised risk weights but left each nation free to choose its own minimum ratio.
Banks headquartered in high-minimum countries were seen as advantaged; Basel I set a global minimum ratio so that banks from low-minimum countries could catch up.
Banks headquartered in low-minimum countries were seen as advantaged; Basel I set a global minimum ratio to level the playing field and avoid a race to the bottom.
Banks headquartered in low-minimum countries were seen as advantaged; Basel I set minimums in absolute currency amounts so that every bank held the same capital.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank risk committee: direction of the competitive concern and Basel I’s response.

**Concept and theory**

Why would lower capital minimums be an advantage? Capital is expensive relative to deposits and debt. A bank allowed to hold less capital per unit of assets can either grow more for the same equity or accept thinner margins while still meeting its return target. When two banks compete for the same client in the same market, the bank from the low-minimum country can underprice the other. That is the perceived advantage GARP describes.

If nothing were done, each national regulator would face pressure to lower its own minimum to protect its banks: a race to the bottom that would erode solvency everywhere. The BCBS response was a common global minimum (a risk-based ratio with a minimum value of 8% total capital to RWA, 4% Tier 1), expressed as a ratio so it could apply to banks of every size.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has two halves: the direction of the advantage, and the response. Direction: low-minimum countries’ banks were seen as advantaged (A, C, D agree; B reverses it). Response: a global minimum ratio to level the playing field and avoid a race to the bottom. A leaves national minimums free, D uses absolute amounts. Only C has both halves right.

**Fragile fact.** Low minimums = perceived advantage; the fix was a common minimum ratio, not harmonised weights alone and not absolute amounts.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1 (two events motivating Basel I; “The Risk-Based Capital Ratio”). Schweser LO 62.a: banks in countries with lax standards were perceived to have a competitive advantage. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). The direction is right, but the response drops the key condition that the minimum itself was common. Harmonising risk weights while letting each nation choose its own minimum ratio would leave the very gap that caused the concern. A would describe an imaginary accord that standardised only the denominator.

b.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the direction of the advantage. Higher required capital is a cost, not an advantage, in head-to-head competition. B would be right only if the stem were about which banks were perceived as safer by depositors, which is a different question.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP: minimums “varied significantly across nations, creating a perception that banks headquartered in countries with low minimums had a competitive advantage. In response, members of the BCBS decided to develop a global minimum standard to level the playing field and avoid a race to the bottom.”

d.reason: (sibling swap). The direction is right, but the response borrows a design that GARP says the BCBS rejected. Because banks differ greatly in size, “specifying minimum amounts of capital (in dollars, pounds, etc.) would be infeasible”; that is why a ratio was used. D would be right only if every bank were the same size.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising an Australian bank’s board is explaining why the BCBS chose a risk-based capital ratio rather than a leverage ratio. She compares two hypothetical banks with identical book assets. Under Basel I, total capital must be at least 8% of risk-weighted assets, using the Basel I risk weights shown; the illustrative leverage rule requires capital of 5% of book assets.

| Asset category | Weight (%) | Kestrel (AUD m) | Osprey (AUD m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 0 | 100.0 | 0.0 |
| Bonds of OECD central governments | 0 | 300.0 | 0.0 |
| Claims on OECD banks | 20 | 200.0 | 0.0 |
| Uninsured residential mortgages | 50 | 200.0 | 0.0 |
| Commercial and consumer loans | 100 | 0.0 | 800.0 |
| Total book assets |  | 800.0 | 800.0 |
| Return on equity, last year (%) |  | 11.4 | 13.9 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The leverage rule requires AUD 40m at each bank; Basel I requires AUD 140m at Kestrel and AUD 800m at Osprey, so the leverage rule penalises low-risk Kestrel.
The leverage rule requires AUD 40m at each bank; Basel I requires AUD 5.6m at Kestrel and AUD 32m at Osprey, so the leverage rule penalises low-risk Kestrel.
The leverage rule requires AUD 40m at each bank; Basel I requires AUD 11.2m at Kestrel and AUD 64m at Osprey, so the leverage rule penalises high-risk Osprey.
The leverage rule requires AUD 40m at each bank; Basel I requires AUD 11.2m at Kestrel and AUD 64m at Osprey, so the leverage rule penalises low-risk Kestrel.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian board report: two banks with equal book assets under a leverage rule versus Basel I.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains the choice of the Basel I ratio in three steps.

1. Why a ratio? Banks differ greatly in size, so minimum amounts of capital are infeasible.
2. Why not a leverage ratio? Capital to book assets would be a universal standard, but banks also differ greatly in the composition and riskiness of their balance sheets. A leverage minimum would **disadvantage banks with low-risk portfolios and advantage those with high-** **risk portfolios**, because both hold the same capital per unit of assets regardless of risk.
3. So a risk-based ratio: capital to risk-weighted assets, including off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures. Crude by modern standards, it was a major innovation at the time.

The ratio is built from

RWA = $\sum_{i\text{=1}}^{N} w_{i}A_{i},$ Required total capital = 8% $\times\text{RWA},$

where $w_{i}$ is the Basel I risk weight of asset category $i$ and $A_{i}$ is its on-balance-sheet amount. The illustrative leverage rule is Required capital = 5% × book assets. The return on equity row is irrelevant to both rules.

**Applying it to this question**

Leverage rule (same for both banks):

$\text{Capital}_{\text{lev}}$ = 0.05 × 800 = AUD 40m at Kestrel and at Osprey

Kestrel under Basel I:

$\text{RWA}_{K}$ = 0 × 100 + 0 × 300 + 0.20 × 200 + 0.50 × 200 = 0 + 0 + 40 + 100 = AUD 140m

$\text{Capital}_{K}$ = 0.08 × 140 = AUD 11.2m

Osprey under Basel I:

$\text{RWA}_{O}$ = 1.00 × 800 = AUD 800m

$\text{Capital}_{O}$ = 0.08 × 800 = AUD 64m

Interpretation: under the leverage rule Kestrel must hold AUD 40m although its risk warrants only AUD 11.2m (it is over-charged by AUD 28.8m), while Osprey holds AUD 40m although its risk warrants AUD 64m (it is under-charged by AUD 24m). The leverage rule therefore penalises the low-risk bank and favours the high-risk one, which is exactly GARP’s reason for rejecting it.

**Fragile fact.** A leverage-ratio minimum disadvantages low-risk banks and advantages high-risk banks; use the 8% total capital minimum, not 4% Tier 1, for total capital.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1, “The Risk-Based Capital Ratio” and “Risk-Weighted Assets” (Table 21.1 weights). Boundary call: the RWA arithmetic belongs to LO 62.b; it is used here only to illustrate the LO 62.a motivation, and the risk weights are given in the stem.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (intermediate result). It reports RWA (AUD 140m and AUD 800m) as if it were required capital, stopping before the 8% step. A would be right if the question asked for each bank’s risk-weighted assets rather than its capital requirement.

b.reason: (wrong input twin). It applies the 4% Tier 1 minimum instead of the 8% total capital minimum: 0.04 × 140 = 5.6 and 0.04 × 800 = 32. B would be right if the stem asked for the minimum Tier 1 capital.

c.reason: (polarity flip). The figures are right but the conclusion reverses the direction: the leverage rule under-charges high-risk Osprey (40 versus 64), it does not penalise it. C would be right only if the leverage rule were replaced by a risk-based rule and the comparison were reversed.

d.reason: Option D has the correct leverage figure (AUD 40m each), the correct Basel I capital (AUD 11.2m and AUD 64m) and the correct direction: the leverage rule penalises low-risk Kestrel, as GARP states.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US bank is reviewing a historical memo for the audit committee on bank capital regulation before 1988 and on how Basel I responded. The memo makes four claims:

I. Requirements were commonly stated as minimum ratios of capital to total assets or as maximum ratios of total assets to capital.

II. Growth in OTC interest rate swaps, currency swaps and options did not change total assets, so it did not change the capital a bank was required to hold.

III. The original Basel I denominator covered on-balance-sheet assets only, with off-balance-sheet exposures left for a later amendment to address.

IV. Enforcement was uniform across countries, so the inconsistency in capital regulation lay only in the levels of the required ratios.

Which of the claims are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US bank audit memo: four claims on pre-1988 capital regulation and Basel I’s response.

**Concept and theory**

Before 1988, capital regulation had three weaknesses that together fuelled the belief that total assets did not reflect a bank’s total risk:

| Weakness before 1988 | Basel I response |
|---|---|
| Ratios to total assets (minimum capital to assets, or maximum assets to capital) ignored the riskiness of each bank | Capital measured against risk-weighted assets |
| Growing off-balance-sheet OTC derivatives (interest rate swaps, currency swaps, options) did not affect total assets, so did not affect required capital | RWA included off-balance-sheet exposures (via credit conversion factors) and derivative exposures (via credit equivalent amounts) from 1988 |
| Inconsistent rules and enforcement across countries; some authorities were more diligent than others | A common international minimum |

GARP is explicit that the Basel I RWA “included not only assets on the balance sheet . . . but also off-balance-sheet exposures (e.g., loan commitments) and derivative exposures”. What came later (1995) was better treatment of derivatives through netting, not their first inclusion.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: Schweser states pre-1988 requirements were minimum ratios of capital to total assets or maximum ratios of total assets to capital. Accurate. Statement II: Schweser states off-balance-sheet OTC deals did not affect total assets and so did not affect required capital. Accurate. Statement III: contradicts GARP; off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures were in the original RWA. Inaccurate. Statement IV: contradicts Schweser; some authorities were more diligent in enforcement than others, so enforcement was not uniform. Inaccurate. Accurate set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Off-balance-sheet exposures were in Basel I’s RWA from 1988 ; the 1995 change concerned netting, not inclusion.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” Schweser Reading 62, LO 62.a (pre-1988 regulation; content for I, II and IV from Schweser, a condensed source). GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1, “The Risk-Based Capital Ratio” (inclusion of off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures; deciding fact for III). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It drops Statement II, which is accurate. Omitting the off-balance-sheet point removes one of the main reasons total assets were judged a poor measure of risk. A would be right only if Statement II wrongly claimed that derivative growth raised total assets and so raised required capital.

b.reason: Option B (I and II only) matches Schweser’s description of pre-1988 regulation; III and IV are both contradicted by the sources.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). It adds Statement III, which narrows Basel I’s denominator to on-balance-sheet assets. GARP says off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures were included from the start; only the netting treatment came in 1995. C would be right if III read “the 1995 Amendment allowed reductions in credit equivalent amounts where enforceable bilateral netting agreements were in place”.

d.reason: (polarity flip). It accepts Statement IV, which reverses the source on enforcement (uneven, not uniform), and drops Statement I. D would be right only if IV said enforcement was inconsistent and I were false.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Hong Kong bank is preparing a timeline slide for the risk committee showing which key risk exposure each stage of the Basel framework brought into minimum capital requirements. Which of the following timelines is most accurate?

options.text: Basel I (1988): credit risk; 1996 Amendment: market risk on both trading book and banking book assets; Basel II: operational risk.
Basel I (1988): credit risk; 1996 Amendment: operational risk; Basel II: market risk on trading book assets.
Basel I (1988): credit risk; 1996 Amendment: market risk on trading book assets; Basel II: operational risk.
Basel I (1988): credit risk; 1996 Amendment: market risk on trading book assets; Basel II: operational risk, replacing the market risk charge.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Hong Kong bank timeline slide: key risk exposure added at each Basel stage.

**Concept and theory**

The LO asks for the “key risk exposures addressed”. The Basel framework added them one at a time:

| Stage | Risk added | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Basel I (1988) | Credit risk | On-balance-sheet, off-balance-sheet and derivative counterparty exposures, through RWA |
| 1996 Amendment | Market risk | Changes in market value of trading book assets, the primary risk of the trading book, which credit-based RWA did not capture |
| Basel II (2004) | Operational risk | Required “in addition to credit risk and market risk”; market risk charges unchanged from 1996 |

The total capital rule under Basel II became Total capital = 0.08 × (credit RWA + market RWA + operational RWA), where market and operational charges are converted to RWA by multiplying by 12.5 (the inverse of 8%).

**Applying it to this question**

All four options start with credit risk for Basel I. The discrimination lies in what the 1996 Amendment added (market risk, and for which book) and what Basel II added (operational risk, and whether anything was removed). Only C has market risk on trading book assets in 1996 and operational risk added in Basel II, with nothing replaced.

**Fragile fact.** Order of addition: credit (1988) → market, trading book only (1996) → operational (Basel II), each added to the previous ones.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, sections 21.1 (“Capital for Market Risks Associated with Trading Activities”) and 21.2 (four innovations of Basel II), and Summary. Schweser LO 62.a key concepts and LO 62.d (Pillar 1). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It overextends the 1996 charge to banking book assets. The amendment targeted market risk on trading book assets, the risk the trading book primarily carries; banking book loans stayed under credit RWA. A would be right if “both trading book and banking book” were replaced by “trading book”.

b.reason: (sibling swap). It swaps the two later additions: operational risk is attributed to 1996 and market risk to Basel II. B would be right if the two labels were exchanged, so that 1996 added market risk and Basel II added operational risk.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP: market risk for trading book assets “was not captured by the requirements described previously” and the 1996 Amendment added it; Basel II required capital for operational risk “in addition to credit risk and market risk”. Schweser’s key concepts for LO 62.a state the same sequence.

d.reason: (absolute claim). It says operational risk replaced the market risk charge. Basel II added operational risk on top; Schweser states that market risk capital charges remained unchanged from the 1996 Amendment. D would be right if “replacing” read “in addition to”.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a Singapore bank is drafting a board briefing on the legal status of the original Basel Accord. Her draft includes the following dates.

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Accord first published by the BCBS | December 1987 |
| Accord formally agreed | July 1988 |
| Accord fully implemented | End of 1992 |

Which of the following statements about the accord is most accurate?

options.text: Agreed by roughly the G10 members, it had no legal standing of its own and became a de facto global minimum as nations adopted it through domestic law.
Agreed by roughly the G10 members, it carried legal standing of its own and bound the banks of member nations directly from the date of agreement.
Agreed by roughly the G10 members, it had no legal standing of its own and stayed confined to G10 banks, as non-members had no means to adopt it.
Agreed by roughly the G10 members, it had no legal standing of its own and was enforced by the BCBS through direct inspection of member banks.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore CCO board briefing: legal status and adoption of the original Basel Accord.

**Concept and theory**

Basel I was first published in December 1987, formally agreed in July 1988 and fully implemented by the end of 1992. Three facts define its legal and geographic reach:

1. **Who agreed it:** the members of the BCBS, roughly the G10 nations.
2. **Legal standing:** none “in and of itself”. The BCBS is a committee of supervisors, not a legislature. Nations chose to incorporate its standards through domestic law and regulation, and it is the national authority that supervises and enforces.
3. **Reach:** although agreed by the G10, by the early 2000s it had become a de facto global minimum capital standard.

This matters for interpretation: a “Basel requirement” binds a bank only through its home country’s own rules. That is also why later revisions (Pillar 2 in Basel II) had to address national differences in how the accord was applied.

**Applying it to this question**

The dates in the table are context and do not discriminate between the options. All four options agree on “roughly the G10”. The discriminating facts are (i) whether the accord had legal standing, (ii) who enforced it, and (iii) how far it spread.

**Fragile fact.** The BCBS writes the standard; nations give it legal force and enforce it. Agreed by the G10, global in practice by the early 2000s.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1 “The Basel Accord: Basel I” (opening paragraphs). Schweser LO 62.a: Basel I has no legal authority; countries adopt it through domestic laws and regulations. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: Option A states all three correctly: no legal standing of its own, adoption through domestic law, and de facto global minimum status, exactly as GARP and Schweser describe.

b.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the legal-standing fact: GARP says “Basel I has no legal standing in and of itself”. B would be right only for a legally binding instrument such as a national statute implementing the accord.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). It confines the accord to G10 banks. GARP says that by the early 2000s it had become a de facto global minimum standard, and the same domestic-law route was open to any nation. C would be right if the stem asked about the accord’s scope at the date of agreement (members only) without the “no means to adopt” clause.

d.reason: (role misassignment). The legal-standing fact is right, but enforcement is attributed to the BCBS. Enforcement sits with national authorities, which incorporate the standard into domestic law and regulation. D would be right if “the BCBS” read “national supervisors”.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a German bank is explaining the original 1988 treatment of derivatives to new analysts. In her example, Bank A enters a EUR 50 million interest rate swap with Bank B to buy protection against rising rates, and later enters a swap of identical notional with Bank B to sell that protection. Rates have not moved in between. Which of the following best describes the capital treatment under the original Basel I and its rationale?

options.text: Only the net exposure attracted capital, because the two swaps were documented under a single bilateral master netting agreement.
Each swap attracted its own add-on, because the BCBS held that netting could never reduce a bank’s loss on a counterparty default.
Each swap attracted its own add-on, a treatment the BCBS designed to encourage banks to hedge with a single counterparty.
Each swap attracted its own add-on, because master netting agreements had not yet been sufficiently tested in bankruptcy courts.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German bank example: two offsetting swaps with the same counterparty under the original Basel I.

**Concept and theory**

Netting means that, if a counterparty defaults, all transactions with it are treated as one, so positive and negative market values offset. OTC derivative counterparties sign an ISDA master agreement that makes this possible. If Bank A has two swaps with Bank B worth +$V$ and $-V$ , its true credit exposure to B is zero.

Original Basel I (1988). It allowed almost no capital credit for netting: an add-on for potential future exposure was applied to each swap. In GARP’s words this disincentivised hedging, because hedging with the same counterparty increased, rather than reduced, required capital.

Why? As of 1988, master agreements “had not been sufficiently tested in bankruptcy courts”. Regulators could not be sure a court would honour netting when a counterparty failed.

Revision (1995 Amendment). By 1995, BCBS members were more confident the agreements would work, and the amendment allowed reductions in credit equivalent amounts where enforceable bilateral netting agreements were in place. Even then, add-ons were not removed: they were scaled by 0.4 + 0.6 × NRR, where NRR (net replacement ratio) is net current exposure divided by gross positive current exposure (mechanics belong to LO 62.c).

**Applying it to this question**

The stem is GARP’s own illustration: offsetting swaps with the same counterparty, rates unchanged, net value zero. The question is about the original treatment and its rationale. Treatment: an add-on on each swap. Rationale: legal uncertainty about master agreements in bankruptcy. That is option D.

**Fragile fact.** Original Basel I disincentivised hedging; the reason was legal (untested in bankruptcy courts), and the fix came in 1995.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1, “Netting” (under “The 1995 and 1996 Amendments”). Schweser LO 62.c describes the same disincentive but does not give the bankruptcy-court rationale; deciding fact from GARP. Boundary call: netting mechanics (NRR, CEA formula) belong to LO 62.c; this question tests only the reason for the revision, which LO 62.a names.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (sibling swap). It describes something close to the later 1995 Amendment treatment (credit for enforceable bilateral netting) and attributes it to the original 1988 accord. A would be right if the stem asked about the treatment after 1995, and even then it overstates, because add-ons were reduced rather than removed.

b.reason: (absolute claim). The treatment is right but the rationale is an absolute statement the BCBS never held. Netting obviously can reduce the loss on default (Schweser’s example: gross loss of 25 becomes a net loss of 18); the BCBS’s doubt was about legal enforceability at that time, which is why it later accepted netting. B would be right if “could never” read “might not, if courts did not uphold the agreement”.

c.reason: (polarity flip). The treatment is right, but its effect is reversed. Charging an add-on on each leg disincentivised hedging; it did not encourage it. C would be right if it read “a treatment that discouraged banks from hedging with a single counterparty”.

d.reason: Option D gives both the treatment (an add-on per swap) and GARP’s stated rationale (master agreements not yet sufficiently tested in bankruptcy courts).

questions.question: A portfolio manager on a Canadian bank’s trading desk asks the market risk team why the original 1988 accord carried no capital charge for market risk, while the 1996 Amendment introduced one. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: The 1987 crash had already shown VaR models to be unreliable, so the 1988 designers deliberately left market risk out of the accord until better models existed.
Market risk on trading assets was already captured through the 100% risk weight, so the 1996 Amendment merely refined a charge that banks were already holding.
When Basel I was designed, VaR was not in wide use and the 1987 crash had not occurred; by 1995 this had changed, and trading book market risk was uncaptured.
The Nordic banking crises showed that systemic problems could arise even in well-capitalised systems, so the 1996 Amendment extended capital to market risk.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian trading desk: why 1988 had no market risk charge and why 1996 added one.

**Concept and theory**

Basel I’s RWA measured credit risk: the chance that a borrower or counterparty fails to pay. A trading book carries a different primary risk: market risk, the change in market value of trading assets as prices move. A bond held for trading can lose value without any default at all. Credit-based RWA “did not capture” this.

Why was it missing in 1988? GARP gives the state of the art at the time: when Basel I was being developed, the 1987 stock market crash had not yet occurred, VaR was not in widespread use, and quantitative market risk management was in its infancy. By 1995, “all of this had changed”. The 1995 and 1996 Amendments (the “Market Risk Amendment”) therefore introduced market risk capital for the trading book, with a standardised approach and an internal models approach based on 10-day 99% VaR (mechanics in LO 62.c).

| Condition | When Basel I was developed | By 1995 |
|---|---|---|
| 1987 stock market crash | Not yet occurred | Occurred |
| Value at risk | Not in widespread use | Widespread |
| Quantitative market risk management | In its infancy | Established |

**Applying it to this question**

The question has two parts: why absent in 1988 and why added in 1996. The first is about the state of risk measurement; the second is that market risk is the trading book’s primary risk and was uncaptured. Option C gives both. The others either reverse the timing, deny the gap, or borrow a Basel II reason.

**Fragile fact.** In 1988 the crash had not yet happened and VaR was not yet widespread; the Nordic crises belong to Basel II, not to 1996.

**Reference**

LO 62.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.” GARP Chapter 21, section 21.1, “The 1995 and 1996 Amendments” and “Capital for Market Risks Associated with Trading Activities”. Schweser LO 62.c (opening paragraph) and LO 62.a key concepts give the same reasons in condensed form. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-21 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the sequence: the crash had not yet occurred when Basel I was being designed, and VaR was not yet in widespread use, so it could not have been “shown unreliable”. A would be right only for a hypothetical accord designed after 1987 that rejected VaR on evidence.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It overextends the credit RWA framework to cover market risk. The 100% weight measures counterparty credit risk; GARP says market risk on the trading book was not captured. B would be right if the stem asked about the credit risk of a corporate bond held in the trading book.

c.reason: Option C reflects GARP: as Basel I was developed “the 1987 stock market crash had not yet occurred, value-at-risk (VaR) was not in widespread use . . . By 1995, all of this had changed”, and market risk, the primary risk for the trading book, “was not captured by the requirements described previously”.

d.reason: (sibling swap). The Nordic banking crises are a reason GARP gives for Basel II, showing systemic problems could occur even in well-capitalised systems. They are not the reason for the 1996 market risk charge. D would be right if “the 1996 Amendment extended capital to market risk” read “supervisors pushed for a more risk-sensitive revised accord”.
