questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-22 b Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Canadian universal bank is preparing a briefing for newly hired analysts on why, in 2005, the Basel Committee began work on an incremental charge for positions held in the trading book. Which of the following statements best describes the problem that this work was designed to correct?

options.text: Trading-book positions often attracted more capital than equivalent banking-book positions, so banks moved illiquid credit exposures into the banking book.
Trading-book VaR drawn from calm recent history fell during low volatility, so capital lagged when volatility rose again in stressed markets.
Trading-book positions often attracted less capital than equivalent banking-book positions, so banks placed illiquid instruments posing default risk in the trading book.
Trading-book securitization tranches were capitalized as if correlations were constant, so senior tranches looked safe until correlations changed.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank briefing: what problem the 2005 incremental charge work was designed to correct.

**Concept and theory**

Banks hold assets in two regulatory “books”. The banking book holds instruments the bank intends to keep, such as loans and some debt securities. The trading book holds positions held for trading, such as bonds, marketable equities, commodities, currencies and most derivatives. The two books were capitalized by different rules. Banking-book credit exposures attracted credit risk capital calibrated, under the IRB approach, to a one-year horizon at the 99.9th percentile. Trading-book positions attracted market risk capital under the 1996 Amendment: a 10-day, 99% VaR scaled by a multiplier, plus a specific risk charge.

GARP explains that although the specific risk charge was intended to capture default risk (and other idiosyncratic risk), banks had learned by the early 2000s that most banking-book type exposures needed less capital in the trading book than in the banking book. The predictable response was regulatory arbitrage: many illiquid instruments posing default risk were placed in the trading book. The incremental default risk charge (IDRC), proposed in 2005, was designed “to remove this incentive”. It later became the incremental risk charge (IRC).

|  | Banking book | Trading book (pre-2005) |
|---|---|---|
| Horizon | One year | 10 days |
| Confidence | 99.9% | 99% (times multiplier) |
| Capital for the same exposure | Higher | Lower |
| Bank incentive |  | Book illiquid, default-risky assets here |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the problem behind the 2005 work on an incremental trading-book charge. The deciding fact is the direction of the capital gap (trading book lower) and the resulting behaviour (illiquid, default-risky instruments moved into the trading book). Only option C states both correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: before the IDRC, the trading book was the cheaper book, so the arbitrage moved default-risky illiquid assets into the trading book.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2 Basel 2.5, “Incremental Risk Charge”. Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b. No conflict on the direction; Schweser adds the horizon and confidence contrast, which GARP gives in Chapter 21 (1996 Amendment) and through the IRB calibration.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the direction of the capital gap (“more” instead of “less”) and therefore the direction of the migration (into the banking book). It would be correct only in a world where the trading-book charge was the stricter one, which is the opposite of what GARP and Schweser describe.

b.reason: (sibling swap). This is the motivation for the stressed VaR, the first Basel 2.5 change (LO 63.a): historical simulation drawn from a calm period produced low VaR and was slow to follow when volatility returned. It would be correct if the stem asked why Basel 2.5 required a stressed-VaR measure.

c.reason: GARP: “even with the specific risk charge, most banking-book exposures had smaller capital requirements in the trading book than in the banking book. Thus, many illiquid instruments posing default risk were placed in the trading book.” Schweser makes the same point: trading-book capital “was generally lower”, so some banks would “shift illiquid instruments that could potentially default to the trading book”. Option C restates this.

d.reason: (sibling swap). This is the motivation for the comprehensive risk charge for the correlation book (LO 63.c): the Basel II assumption of a constant correlation parameter failed for tranched securitizations. It would be correct if the stem asked why securitizations and re-securitizations received a separate charge.

questions.question:
The head of market risk at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing a consultant’s memo on how credit exposures were capitalized before the Basel Committee’s 2005 proposal for an incremental default charge. The memo contains the following statements:

I. Banking-book credit capital was calibrated to a one-year horizon at a 99.9% confidence level.

II. Trading-book capital applied a multiplier of at least 3 to a 10-day VaR at a 99% confidence level.

III. The specific risk charge was intended to capture default risk, among other idiosyncratic risks, yet most banking-book type exposures still needed less capital when booked in the trading book.

IV. Because the specific risk charge fully absorbed default risk, the book in which an illiquid loan was placed had no effect on its capital.

Which of the statements in the memo are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, II, III and IV
II and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese trust bank: audit of four statements on pre-2005 capitalization of credit exposures.

**Concept and theory**

To see why a gap existed, compare how each book was capitalized before 2005.

- **Banking book.** Under the IRB approach, credit capital was calibrated to the 99.9th percentile of the loss distribution at a one-year horizon. Schweser: “A one-year, 99.9% confidence level VaR was required for calculating capital for the banking book.”
- **Trading book.** Under the 1996 Amendment, market risk capital was $\text{max(VaR}_{t-1}, m\times\text{VaR}_{\text{avg}}$), where VaR is a 10-day, 99% measure and the multiplier $m$ is never less than 3 (GARP Chapter 21). Schweser: “a multiplier was applied to a 10-day, 99% VaR for capital to back the trading book.” A separate specific risk charge applied to fixed income, equity instruments and derivatives.
- **The gap.** A 10-day, 99% loss quantile, even multiplied by 3, plus the specific risk charge, typically produced less capital than a one-year, 99.9% credit loss quantile for an illiquid default-risky position. GARP: the specific risk charge “was intended to capture default risk (as well as other sources of idiosyncratic risk)”, but “even with the specific risk charge, most banking-book exposures had smaller capital requirements in the trading book than in the banking book.”

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement.

- I: one year, 99.9%, banking book. True (Schweser LO 63.b; GARP’s IRB calibration).
- II: multiplier of at least 3 on a 10-day, 99% VaR, trading book. True (Schweser LO 63.b; GARP Chapter 21).
- III: the specific risk charge was meant to capture default risk, yet the trading book still needed less capital. True (GARP 22.2).
- IV: claims the specific risk charge “fully absorbed” default risk so the choice of book did not matter. False: the whole point of the IDRC was that the choice of book did matter.

The accurate set is I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Horizon and confidence by book: banking book one year at 99.9%; trading book 10 days at 99% times a multiplier of at least 3. Do not swap them.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge”; GARP Chapter 21, 1996 Amendment, “Capital for Market Risks Associated with Trading Activities” (multiplier at least 3; specific risk). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b. Schweser states the horizon and confidence contrast directly; GARP states the capital gap directly. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). Rejecting II implies the trading book was already on the banking-book basis (one year, 99.9%). That basis is what the 2005 IDRC proposal introduced for default-sensitive trading positions, so this attributes the later fix to the earlier regime. “I and III only” would be right if II had said the trading book used a one-year, 99.9% VaR, which would then be false.

b.reason: (absolute claim). Including IV accepts the claim that the specific risk charge “fully” absorbed default risk. GARP says it was intended to capture default risk, not that it did so; the persistent capital gap shows it did not. “I, II, III and IV” would be right only if IV said the specific risk charge was intended to capture default risk.

c.reason: (condition error). Rejecting I misreads the banking-book calibration, for example by assuming the banking book also used a 10-day horizon. If the horizons and confidence levels had been the same in both books, the gap that motivated the IDRC would not have arisen. “II and III only” would be right if I had stated a 10-day horizon for the banking book.

d.reason: Option D (I, II and III only) is the only option that includes all three true statements and excludes IV, which contradicts GARP’s statement that many illiquid default-risky instruments were placed in the trading book because it required less capital.

questions.question: A policy analyst at the Australian prudential regulator is drafting a history note on the incremental default risk charge (IDRC) that the Basel Committee proposed in 2005. She wants to describe the treatment a bank would have faced if it held default-sensitive positions in its trading book but did not have an internal model of default risk. Which of the following is the most accurate description of that treatment under the proposal?

options.text: A standardized or current exposure approach bearing some similarity to the Basel I capital charges for specific risk.
An internal default model at the 99.9th percentile over one year, because the proposal offered banks no other route.
The existing 10-day, 99% VaR scaled by a multiplier of at least 3, which the proposal left unchanged for such banks.
A rating-based table expressing capital as a fraction of exposure, of the kind later specified for the correlation book.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian regulator’s history note: IDRC treatment for a bank without an internal default model.

**Concept and theory**

In 2005, the Basel Committee proposed adding an incremental default risk charge (IDRC) to remove the incentive to book illiquid default-risky positions in the trading book. GARP says “two variants were proposed”:

1. An internal model of default risk calibrated to the same 99.9th percentile at a one-year horizon as the Committee’s IRB approach; or
2. In the absence of such a model, either a “standardized” or a “current exposure” approach that had some similarity to Basel I capital charges for specific risk.

The idea of offering two routes is the usual Basel design: sophisticated banks use an internal model calibrated to a regulatory standard, and others use a simpler, prescribed method. Either way, as a practical matter, trading-book capital became the greater of market risk capital and banking-book capital (see Q4).

**Applying it to this question**

The stem fixes the condition: the bank has default-sensitive trading positions but no internal model of default risk. That condition selects the second variant, the standardized or current exposure approach resembling Basel I specific risk charges.

**Fragile fact.** Two variants in 2005: an IRB-style internal model (99.9th percentile, one year) or, absent a model, a standardized or current exposure approach like Basel I specific risk charges.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge” (two IDRC variants; footnote to BCBS, July 2005). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b mentions only the 99.9%, one-year VaR and omits the fallback variant; the deciding fact here is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: GARP lists the fallback “in the absence of such a model” as “either a ‘standardized’ or a ‘current exposure’ approach that had some similarity to Basel I capital charges for specific risk”. Option A states exactly this.

b.reason: (absolute claim). It turns the internal model into the only route (“no other route”). The 99.9th percentile, one-year model was one of two variants. Option B would be correct if the stem asked for the treatment of a bank that did have an internal default model.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The 10-day, 99% VaR with a multiplier of at least 3 is the 1996 Amendment market risk charge, the very treatment that left trading-book capital too low. It would be correct if the stem asked how general market risk in the trading book was capitalized before 2005.

d.reason: (sibling swap). A rating-based table with capital expressed as a fraction of exposure is the standardized approach for the comprehensive risk charge on the correlation book (GARP Table 22.1, LO 63.c). It would be correct if the stem asked about rated securitizations under the CR standardized approach.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank is estimating capital for a desk that holds illiquid corporate loans in its trading book. She applies the practical outcome of the Basel Committee’s 2005 incremental default risk charge proposal for trading-book capital. Her inputs are shown below.

| Item | BRL million |
|---|---|
| General market risk capital (10-day 99% VaR, multiplier 3) | 26.0 |
| Specific risk capital (internal model, multiplier 4) | 22.0 |
| Banking-book capital for the same positions (IRB, 99.9%, one year) | 75.0 |
| Desk’s average daily trading revenue | 3.1 |

Market risk capital for the desk is the sum of general market risk capital and specific risk capital. Under the practical outcome of the proposal, the capital for the desk is closest to:

options.text: BRL 48.0 million
BRL 75.0 million
BRL 97.0 million
BRL 123.0 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian desk of illiquid loans: trading-book capital under the IDRC’s practical outcome.

**Concept and theory**

The IDRC was designed so that a default-sensitive position could not obtain lower capital simply by being booked in the trading book. GARP: “As a practical matter, capital in the trading book would be the greater of market risk capital and banking book capital.” Schweser says the change “had the effect of requiring roughly the same capital for trading book instruments as banking book instruments (trading book capital was the greater of market risk capital and banking book capital).” Define:

- MRC = market risk capital for the positions = general market risk capital + specific risk capital;
- BBC = banking-book capital the same positions would attract (IRB, 99.9%, one year).

Then

Trading-book capital = max(MRC, BBC).

The “greater of” rule is what ends the arbitrage: if the trading book is cheaper, the banking-book figure binds; if it is dearer, the market risk figure binds.

**Applying it to this question**

MRC = 26.0 + 22.0 = 48.0 (BRL million)

BBC = 75.0 (BRL million)

Trading-book capital = max(48.0, 75.0) = 75.0 (BRL million)

The average daily trading revenue (3.1) is irrelevant to capital. The result means the banking-book figure binds: booking these illiquid loans in the trading book no longer saves capital.

**Fragile fact.** “Greater of”, not “sum of”: trading-book capital = max(market risk capital, banking-book capital).

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge” (“as a practical matter, capital in the trading book would be the greater of market risk capital and banking book capital”). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b (same rule). GARP Chapter 21 for the composition of market risk capital (general market risk and specific risk; multipliers 3 and 4). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (intermediate result). BRL 48.0 million = 26.0 + 22.0 is market risk capital, the first input to the max function and the pre-IDRC answer. It would be correct if the stem asked for capital under the 1996 Amendment alone, or if banking-book capital were below 48.0.

b.reason: BRL 75.0 million is the greater of market risk capital (48.0) and banking-book capital (75.0), which is the rule stated in both GARP and Schweser.

c.reason: (added term, double count). BRL 97.0 million = 75.0 + 22.0 adds the specific risk charge on top of banking-book capital, as if the specific risk charge sat outside the comparison. The specific risk capital is already inside market risk capital. It would be correct only if a rule required banking-book capital plus a separate specific risk add-on, which neither source describes.

d.reason: (sibling swap). BRL 123.0 million = 48.0 + 75.0 sums the two capital figures, borrowing the additive structure of the Basel 2.5 formula in which VaR and stressed VaR terms are added (LO 63.a). The IDRC rule takes the greater of the two, not the sum. It would be correct if the stem asked for a charge defined as the sum of the two figures.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is explaining to the board why the Basel Committee revised its 2005 incremental default risk charge late in the 2007 to 2009 crisis, producing the incremental risk charge (IRC). Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Most credit-related losses were driven by issuer defaults, so the revised charge kept default as its only loss event and kept the 99.9th percentile.
Most credit-related losses came from ratings, spreads or liquidity, so the revised charge moved to a 10-day horizon at the 99th percentile.
Most credit-related losses came from ratings, spreads or liquidity, so losses from rating downgrades were added while the 99.9th percentile was kept.
Most credit-related losses came from ratings, spreads or liquidity, so the comprehensive risk charge replaced the IRC for every credit position.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore CRO to the board: why the 2005 default charge was revised into the IRC.

**Concept and theory**

The 2005 IDRC captured only default losses on default-sensitive trading positions. GARP: “Late in the crisis, however, the Committee had realized that most losses in portfolio value associated with credit risk had been due to changes in ratings, credit spreads, or liquidity, not defaults. As a result, the scope of the proposal was increased to include changes in ratings. The same 99.9th percentile was used, but in addition to defaults, banks were required to estimate losses associated with rating downgrades.”

| Feature | IDRC (2005) | IRC (post-crisis) |
|---|---|---|
| Loss events | Default only | Default and rating migration |
| Instruments | Default-sensitive | Credit-sensitive |
| Percentile, horizon | 99.9th, one year | 99.9th, one year (unchanged) |
| Replacement |  | Constant level of risk, liquidity horizons |

**Applying it to this question**

Three of the four options agree on the cause (ratings, spreads, liquidity). The discrimination lies in what the Committee did: it (1) added downgrade losses and (2) kept the 99.9th percentile. Only option C states both.

**Fragile fact.** The crisis revision changed the scope (default plus downgrades), not the calibration (99.9th percentile, one year stayed).

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge”. Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b. Minor wording difference: Schweser says losses came from “downgrades, widening credit spreads, and losses of liquidity” and that the IRC covers “credit-sensitive instruments”; GARP says the scope was increased to “changes in ratings”. GARP is used for the deciding fact.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the crisis finding (defaults drove losses) and therefore keeps default as the only loss event. That describes the 2005 IDRC, not the revision. It would be correct if the stem asked for the rationale of the original 2005 proposal’s default-only scope.

b.reason: (condition error). The cause is right, but the calibration is changed to 10 days and the 99th percentile, the old trading-book VaR standard. The revision kept the 99.9th percentile at one year. It would be correct only if the stem asked about the standard 1996 Amendment market risk VaR.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP’s text in substance: scope “increased to include changes in ratings” and “the same 99.9th percentile was used”. Schweser agrees: banks “must consider ratings change sensitivities in addition to default sensitivity”.

d.reason: (scope error). The comprehensive risk charge replaced the IRC and the specific risk charge only for the correlation book (securitizations, re-securitizations and related instruments), not for every credit position. It would be correct if the stem were restricted to correlation-book positions.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK investment bank is documenting the origins of the incremental risk charge (IRC) for a model inventory file. The IRC is described in the regulatory literature as combining two strands of work: one released in 2005 and one released in the wake of the 2007 to 2009 crisis. Which of the following best describes the trigger for each strand?

options.text: 2005 strand: regulatory arbitrage between the banking and trading books. Crisis strand: credit losses driven mostly by ratings, spreads and liquidity rather than defaults.
2005 strand: credit losses driven mostly by ratings, spreads and liquidity rather than defaults. Crisis strand: regulatory arbitrage between the banking and trading books.
2005 strand: regulatory arbitrage between the banking and trading books. Crisis strand: historical simulation VaR that was drawn mostly from calm, low-volatility periods.
2005 strand: securitization tranches whose capital assumed constant default correlations. Crisis strand: credit losses driven mostly by ratings, spreads and liquidity.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK auditor’s model inventory: matching the two strands of work behind the IRC to their triggers.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens its IRC section with: “The incremental risk charge (IRC) combines two strands of work, one released in 2005 as a reaction to regulatory arbitrage opportunities between the banking and trading book, and the other released in the wake of the crisis.” The two strands answer two different problems:

| Strand | Trigger | Response |
|---|---|---|
| 2005 | Regulatory arbitrage: trading book needed less capital than banking book | IDRC: default risk at the 99.9th percentile, one year; capital = greater of market risk and banking-book capital |
| Post-crisis | Most credit losses came from ratings, spreads and liquidity, not defaults | Scope widened to rating changes; constant level of risk and liquidity horizons |

The other two Basel 2.5 changes had different triggers: stressed VaR answered the slow response of historical-simulation VaR after calm periods, and the comprehensive risk charge answered the failure of the constant-correlation assumption for tranched securitizations.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the trigger of each strand. The 2005 strand is the arbitrage problem; the crisis strand is the discovery that credit losses were mostly non-default losses. Option A pairs them correctly in the right order.

**Fragile fact.** Order: arbitrage first (2005), non-default credit losses second (crisis). The IRC fuses both.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge” (two strands). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b gives the same sequence (IDRC in 2005, revised into the IRC after the crisis) without the “two strands” framing. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: Option A reproduces GARP’s two strands and the crisis finding (“changes in ratings, credit spreads, or liquidity, not defaults”).

b.reason: (role misassignment, timing swap). Both triggers are right but attached to the wrong strand. The arbitrage problem was recognized “by the early 2000s” and drove the 2005 proposal; the ratings and spreads finding came “late in the crisis”. B would be correct if the stem listed the strands as “crisis strand” first and “2005 strand” second.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The crisis strand is replaced with the motivation for stressed VaR (historical simulation drawn from calm periods). That was a separate Basel 2.5 change (LO 63.a). C would be correct if the stem asked about the strands behind the Basel 2.5 market risk capital changes as a whole, pairing the IDRC with stressed VaR.

d.reason: (sibling swap). The 2005 strand is replaced with the motivation for the comprehensive risk charge (constant correlations in tranched securitizations, LO 63.c). D would be correct if the stem asked about the trigger for the CR charge.

questions.question:
A model validation manager at a German Landesbank is reviewing the methodology document for the bank’s incremental risk charge (IRC) on its EUR credit trading book. The document makes the following statements about liquidity horizons:

I. A liquidity horizon is estimated for each position, and horizons differ across positions according to their liquidity.

II. A single liquidity horizon of one year applies to every position, matching the one-year capital horizon.

III. No position may be assigned a liquidity horizon shorter than three months.

IV. A position with a three-month liquidity horizon is assumed, if it has been downgraded or has defaulted, to be replaced at the end of each three-month period through the year.

Which of the statements are consistent with the IRC rules?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German Landesbank validation: four statements on IRC liquidity horizons.

**Concept and theory**

The IRC is a one-year, 99.9th percentile measure, but banks are not assumed to sit on a deteriorating position for the whole year. Each position has a liquidity horizon: the time the bank would need to sell or replace it. GARP: “The period over which replacement could occur differs across positions according to their liquidity but is never less than three months.” Schweser: banks “are required to estimate a liquidity horizon for each instrument in the portfolio” and “The Basel Committee set the minimum liquidity horizon at three months.”

At the end of each liquidity horizon, a position that has been downgraded or has defaulted is assumed sold (recording a loss) and replaced by a position with the original rating. Schweser’s example: for a six-month horizon, “This rebalancing is assumed at the end of each six-month period (or three months, nine months, etc., depending on the estimated liquidity horizon).”

**Applying it to this question**

- I: horizons are set per position and differ by liquidity. True (GARP; Schweser).
- II: a single one-year horizon for every position. False: horizons differ by position; a uniform one-year horizon would remove intra-year rebalancing altogether.
- III: three-month floor. True (GARP “never less than three months”; Schweser minimum three months).
- IV: three-month horizon implies replacement, if downgraded or defaulted, at the end of each three-month period. True (Schweser’s rebalancing example).

**Fragile fact.** Three months is a floor, not a fixed value; horizons vary by position, and rebalancing happens at the end of every horizon within the year.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge” (footnote 2: BCBS guidelines for computing capital for incremental risk in the trading book). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b. The “end of each period” rebalancing example is in Schweser; GARP states the same mechanism more compactly. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (condition error). “I and III only” rejects IV, treating rebalancing as something that happens once, rather than at the end of each liquidity horizon through the year. A would be correct if IV had said replacement occurs only once, at the end of the year.

b.reason: (scope error). “II and IV only” accepts a uniform one-year horizon and rejects both the per-position estimate and the floor. It ignores that horizons “differ across positions according to their liquidity”. B would be correct only if I and III had been corrupted (for example, a one-month floor) and II had described differing horizons.

c.reason: (absolute claim). “I, II, III and IV” accepts all four, including II, which contradicts I (horizons cannot both differ by position and be a single value for all). It would be correct only if II had read “each position is assigned its own liquidity horizon”.

d.reason: Option D (I, III and IV only) contains exactly the three true statements.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the liquidity horizons that a trading desk at a UK bank has proposed for its incremental risk charge (IRC) calculation. The proposals are shown below.

| Position | Rating | Notional (GBP million) | Proposed liquidity horizon |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bond P | AA | 40 | 6 months |
| Bond Q | BBB | 25 | 2 months |
| Bond R | A | 60 | 3 months |
| Bond S | BB | 15 | 12 months |

Which of the following conclusions in the consultant’s report is most accurate?

options.text: No proposal breaches a rule, because banks may set any liquidity horizon that is shorter than the one-year capital horizon.
Bond Q breaches the three-month floor; Bond P is assumed replaced, if downgraded or defaulted, at the end of each six-month period.
Bond R breaches a floor, because positions rated A or lower must be given a liquidity horizon of at least six months.
Bond Q breaches the three-month floor; Bond P is assumed replaced only if it defaults, and only at the end of the year.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK desk’s proposed liquidity horizons: which conclusion in the consultant’s report holds.

**Concept and theory**

Two rules from the source govern liquidity horizons in the IRC (see Q7 for the full build):

1. **Floor.** The liquidity horizon is “never less than three months” (GARP); “the Basel Committee set the minimum liquidity horizon at three months” (Schweser).
2. **Rebalancing frequency.** At the end of each liquidity horizon, a position that has defaulted or been downgraded is assumed replaced by one with the original rating, a loss being recorded on the sale. A six-month horizon means rebalancing “at the end of each six-month period” (Schweser).

Schweser illustrates the mechanism with an AA-rated bond and a six-month horizon. That is an example, not a rule linking ratings to horizons; the source links horizons to each position’s liquidity.

**Applying it to this question**

- Bond P: 6 months. Above the floor. Replacement, if downgraded or defaulted, at months 6 and 12.
- Bond Q: 2 months. Below the three-month floor: must be raised to at least 3 months.
- Bond R: 3 months. Exactly at the floor: compliant.
- Bond S: 12 months. Above the floor: compliant on the floor test.

Notional amounts are irrelevant to the floor test and to the rebalancing rule.

**Fragile fact.** Three months is the minimum; any proposal below it breaches the rule, whatever the position’s rating.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge”. Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b (six-month AA example; minimum three months). Note: the Schweser module quiz answer uses an AA+ bond with a three-month horizon for the same illustration, confirming that the rating in the example is not a rule. No GARP vs Schweser conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). It replaces the three-month floor with a one-year ceiling and so passes Bond Q. The source sets a minimum, not just a maximum. A would be correct if Bond Q’s proposal had been three months or more.

b.reason: Option B identifies the one breach (Bond Q) and correctly describes Bond P’s treatment: replacement, if downgraded or defaulted, at the end of each six-month period.

c.reason: (condition error). It overextends Schweser’s illustrative six-month AA example into a rating-based rule. No source rule ties a minimum of six months to ratings; Bond R’s three months sits exactly on the floor. C would be correct only if the rules set a six-month minimum for positions rated A or lower, which they do not.

d.reason: (scope error). It treats Bond P as replaced only on default and only at year end, which is the default-only, hold-to-horizon view of the original IDRC. Under the IRC, downgrades also trigger replacement, at the end of every liquidity horizon. D would be correct if the rules ignored rating migration and used no liquidity horizon shorter than one year.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese bank compares two internal runs of a one-year, 99.9% credit loss model on the same CNY bond portfolio held in the trading book. Run 1 holds every position for the full year with no replacement. Run 2 applies the constant level of risk assumption used in the incremental risk charge, with three-month liquidity horizons. Which of the following best describes how Run 2 is expected to differ from Run 1?

options.text: Run 2 records small losses on sales of downgraded positions, lessens the likelihood of default, and generally produces a lower 99.9% VaR.
Run 2 records no losses on downgraded positions, since each is swapped for a new one, and generally produces a lower 99.9% VaR.
Run 2 records small losses on sales of downgraded positions, raises the likelihood of default, and generally produces a higher 99.9% VaR.
Run 2 replaces each downgraded position with one at its new, lower rating, so portfolio credit quality drifts down as in Run 1.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank: buy-and-hold run versus constant level of risk run of a one-year, 99.9% model.

**Concept and theory**

Without replacement (Run 1), a bond that is downgraded stays in the portfolio, is more likely to default later in the year, and the portfolio’s credit quality drifts down. The tail of the one-year loss distribution is then dominated by defaults.

The IRC instead uses the constant level of risk assumption. GARP: “Portfolio credit quality is held approximately constant by an assumption that any position that is downgraded or that defaults is replaced by a position with the same pre-downgrade rating. A loss is recorded from sale of the downgraded or defaulted position.” Schweser names the assumption and states its effect: “Small losses occur as bonds are downgraded and the portfolio is rebalanced, but the likelihood of default is lessened. Generally, this assumption reduces the one-year 99.9% VaR.”

|  | Run 1: hold to one year | Run 2: constant level of risk |
|---|---|---|
| Downgraded positions | Kept | Sold at horizon end, loss recorded |
| Replacement rating | None | Same pre-downgrade rating |
| Portfolio credit quality | Drifts down | Held approximately constant |
| Default likelihood | Higher | Lessened |
| One-year 99.9% VaR | Higher | Generally lower |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for three things: what happens to losses on downgrades, to default likelihood, and to VaR in Run 2. Run 2 records small sale losses, lessens default likelihood, and generally lowers the 99.9% VaR.

**Fragile fact.** Replacement is at the pre-downgrade (original) rating; the effect is small sale losses, lower default likelihood and generally a lower 99.9% VaR.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge”. Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b (“constant level of risk assumption”). The name of the assumption and the statement that it generally reduces the one-year 99.9% VaR are content from Schweser, a condensed source; GARP states the replacement rule and the recorded loss but not the VaR effect.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: Option A matches all three elements of Schweser’s description and is consistent with GARP’s statement that a loss is recorded on the sale and credit quality is held approximately constant.

b.reason: (dropped term). It drops the sale loss: replacement does not erase the loss on the downgraded position. GARP: “A loss is recorded from sale of the downgraded or defaulted position.” B would be correct only if positions were replaced at their purchase value with no mark-to-market loss, which the IRC does not assume.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the direction of both the default likelihood and the VaR effect. Replacing deteriorating positions with ones of the original rating reduces default risk. C would describe Run 1 relative to Run 2, not Run 2 relative to Run 1.

d.reason: (sibling swap). It replaces the downgraded position with one at the new rating, the opposite of the rule (“same pre-downgrade rating”). With that rule, credit quality would drift down as in Run 1. D would be correct if the stem described a model that kept the downgraded exposure on the books.

questions.question:
A quantitative analyst at a US bank is checking one tail scenario from the bank’s incremental risk charge simulation for a single A-rated bond position held in the trading book. The position has a three-month liquidity horizon and pays a 4.5% annual coupon. Each time the position is established or replaced, it is bought at a value of USD 100 million. The scenario shows the following at the end of each liquidity horizon:

| Horizon end | Event during the period | Value at end (USD million) |
|---|---|---|
| Month 3 | Downgraded from A to BBB | 96 |
| Month 6 | No rating change | 100 |
| Month 9 | Downgraded from A to BB | 91 |
| Month 12 | Default, recovery rate 40% | 40 |

Ignoring coupon income, the total credit loss that this scenario contributes to the one-year loss distribution is closest to:

options.text: USD 13 million
USD 60 million
USD 73 million
USD 113 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US bond, three-month liquidity horizon: total loss recorded in one IRC tail scenario.

**Concept and theory**

The IRC is the 99.9th percentile of a simulated one-year loss distribution for credit-sensitive trading positions. In each simulated year, a position is held for one liquidity horizon. At its end:

- if the position has been downgraded or has defaulted, it is sold, a loss is recorded on the sale, and it is replaced by a position with the original (pre-downgrade) rating;
- if nothing has happened, it is simply carried into the next horizon.

Both defaults and rating downgrades generate losses (the IRC widened the 2005 default-only scope to rating changes). Over a one-year scenario, the scenario’s loss is the sum of the losses recorded at each horizon end:

$L_{\text{scenario}}$ = $\sum_{k}$ ($V_{\text{start},k} - V_{\text{end},k}$) over horizons $k$ that end in a downgrade or default,

where $V_{\text{start},k}$ is the value at which the position was established or replaced (here 100) and $V_{\text{end},k}$ is its value at the sale. For a default, the end value reflects recovery: $V_{\text{end}}$ = recovery rate × 100.

**Applying it to this question**

Month 3 (A to BBB): $L_{1}$ = 100 − 96 = 4

Month 6 (no change): $L_{2}$ = 0 (no sale)

Month 9 (A to BB): $L_{3}$ = 100 − 91 = 9

Month 12 (default): $V_{\text{end}}$ = 0.40 × 100 = 40

$L_{4}$ = 100 − 40 = 60

$L_{\text{scenario}}$ = 4 + 0 + 9 + 60 = 73 (USD million)

The 4.5% coupon is irrelevant (the stem says to ignore coupon income). USD 73 million is one draw in the loss distribution; the IRC is the 99.9th percentile of many such draws, not this single number.

**Fragile fact.** Downgrades count and defaults count; a default loss is value lost net of recovery (100 − 40), not the full 100.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2, “Incremental Risk Charge” (99.9th percentile; downgrade losses added; replacement at pre-downgrade rating; “a loss is recorded from sale of the downgraded or defaulted position”). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b (liquidity horizon example, loss recorded on sale). Summing the recorded sale losses within one simulated year is an application of these statements; neither source sets out a worked numerical example.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (dropped term). USD 13 million = 4 + 9 counts only the downgrade losses and drops the default loss of 60. The IRC adds rating changes in addition to defaults. A would be correct if the month-12 event had been “no rating change”.

b.reason: (scope error). USD 60 million counts only the default, which is the default-only scope of the 2005 IDRC. Under the IRC, banks “were required to estimate losses associated with rating downgrades” as well. B would be correct if the stem asked for the loss under the original IDRC.

c.reason: USD 73 million captures both strands of loss the IRC covers: migration losses (4 and 9) recorded on sales of downgraded positions, and the default loss (60) net of recovery, with replacement at the original rating after each sale.

d.reason: (dropped term, recovery ignored). USD 113 million = 4 + 9 + 100 books the full position value as the default loss, ignoring the 40% recovery. The loss recorded on the sale of a defaulted position is the drop from 100 to its post-default value of 40. D would be correct if the recovery rate were zero.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at an Australian bank is reviewing how three positions should be treated under the Basel 2.5 trading-book rules. Position 1 is a re-securitization. Each position is already covered by VaR and stressed VaR where applicable; the question is which additional credit-related charge, if any, applies.

| Position | Description | Notional (AUD m) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Senior tranche of a CDO of ABS, correlation book | 120 |
| 2 | BB-rated corporate bonds held for trading | 85 |
| 3 | Exchange-traded currency futures held for trading | 300 |

Which mapping of the additional credit-related charge to each position is most accurate?

options.text: 1: IRC plus specific risk charge; 2: CR charge; 3: none beyond VaR and stressed VaR
1: CR charge; 2: IRC (default and migration); 3: none beyond VaR and stressed VaR
1: CR charge; 2: IRC (default and migration); 3: IRC (default and migration)
1: CR charge; 2: IRC (default only); 3: none beyond VaR and stressed VaR

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian risk committee: which additional credit-related charge applies to three trading positions.

**Concept and theory**

Basel 2.5 made three trading-book changes (GARP 22.2): (1) a stressed-VaR component; (2) capital for incremental risk, “roughly capturing the jump-to-default risk”; and (3) comprehensive risk capital for securitizations and related instruments.

| Charge | Positions covered | Losses captured |
|---|---|---|
| VaR and stressed VaR | All trading-book market risk posi- | Market price moves at 10 days, |
|  | tions | 99% |
| IRC | Credit-sensitive trading positions (outside the correlation book) | Default and rating migration, 99.9th percentile, one year |
| CR charge | Correlation book: securitizations, re-securitizations, related derivatives | Replaces IRC and specific risk charge for these |

GARP: “The Basel Committee addressed this issue by replacing the IRC and specific risk charge with a comprehensive risk (CR) charge for the correlation book.” Schweser: the IRC applies to “credit-sensitive instruments”, and banks “must consider ratings change sensitivities in addition to default sensitivity”.

**Applying it to this question**

- Position 1: a re-securitization in the correlation book. The CR charge replaces both the IRC and the specific risk charge. Charge: CR.
- Position 2: BB corporate bonds held for trading. Credit-sensitive, outside the correlation book. Charge: IRC, covering default and migration.
- Position 3: exchange-traded currency futures. No issuer default or rating migration exposure to capture; the incremental risk is a credit charge. Charge: none beyond VaR and stressed VaR.

Notionals are irrelevant to the mapping.

**Fragile fact.** For the correlation book, CR replaces both the IRC and the specific risk charge; the IRC itself covers default and migration on other credit-sensitive positions.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.2 Basel 2.5 (three changes; “Incremental Risk Charge”; “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure”). Schweser Reading 63, LO 63.b and LO 63.c. Boundary call: the CR charge is LO 63.c; it appears here only to mark where the IRC’s scope ends. That currency futures fall outside the IRC is an application of “credit-sensitive instruments” (Schweser) and “jump-to-default” (GARP); neither source lists FX instruments explicitly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 b, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (role misassignment). It swaps the two charges between positions 1 and 2: the re-securitization gets IRC plus specific risk, and the corporate bonds get CR. GARP says CR replaces the IRC and the specific risk charge for the correlation book. A would be correct only if position 1 were the corporate bonds and position 2 the CDO of ABS, with CR not yet introduced.

b.reason: Option B maps the correlation-book position to CR, the credit-sensitive bonds to the IRC with both default and migration, and leaves the currency futures to VaR and stressed VaR.

c.reason: (scope error). It extends the IRC to currency futures. The IRC covers credit-sensitive instruments, losses from default and rating changes; currency futures carry no such issuer risk. C would be correct if position 3 were, for example, a portfolio of corporate bonds denominated in a foreign currency.

d.reason: (sibling swap). It applies the 2005 IDRC scope (default only) to position 2. After the crisis the scope was “increased to include changes in ratings”. D would be correct if the stem asked about the original 2005 proposal.

questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a Japanese bank is presenting the Basel 2.5 changes to trading-book capital to a group of newly hired analysts. One slide introduces the comprehensive risk (CR) charge. Which of the following best describes the CR charge?

options.text: A charge for credit-sensitive trading-book positions at the 99.9th percentile over one year, assuming each position is rebalanced at the end of its liquidity horizon.
A charge computed from the most stressful 250-day window in the past seven years and added to the traditional VaR-based charge for all trading-book positions.
A single charge for positions in the correlation book that replaces both the incremental risk charge and the specific risk charge for those positions.
A single charge for positions in the correlation book that is added on top of both the incremental risk charge and the specific risk charge for those positions.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank, consultant presenting to new hires: which description of the CR charge is best?

**Concept and theory**

Basel 2.5 was the Basel Committee’s first response to the losses of 2007 to 2009 in banks’ trading books. GARP lists three changes to trading-book capital, all implemented by the end of 2011:

1. VaR calculations were expanded to include a stressed-VaR component (LO 63.a);
2. capital for incremental risk was added, roughly capturing jump-to-default risk (the incremental risk charge, IRC, LO 63.b);
3. comprehensive risk capital requirements were added for securitizations and related instruments (this LO).

The “related instruments” form what GARP and Schweser call the correlation book: securitizations, re-securitizations and derivatives written on securitizations. Their value depends on how the default risks of many underlying assets move together. GARP explains that, rather than stacking another charge on top, the Basel Committee addressed this issue “by replacing the IRC and specific risk charge with a comprehensive risk (CR) charge for the correlation book.” Schweser says the same: the CR charge is “a single capital charge for correlation-dependent instruments that replaces the specific risk charge (SRC) and the IRC.”

| Basel 2.5 element | What it covers | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| Stressed VaR | All market-risk positions | 250-day most stressful window in last seven years, added to normal VaR |
| IRC | Credit-sensitive trading-book positions | 99.9%, one year, defaults and downgrades, constant level of risk |
| CR charge | Correlation book only | Single charge replacing IRC and specific risk charge for those positions |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the best description of the CR charge. Three features decide it: (i) its scope is the correlation book, not all trading positions; (ii) it is one single charge; (iii) it replaces the IRC and the specific risk charge for those positions rather than adding to them. Only option C states all three correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Direction word: the CR charge REPLACES the IRC and the specific risk charge for the correlation book; it is not an add-on to them.

**Reference**

LO 63.c (ORR 22.c), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.” GARP Chapter 22 (Carey), Section 22.2 “Basel 2.5”, subsection “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure”, and Section 22.2 introduction (list of three changes). Schweser Module 63.1, “Comprehensive Risk Charge” (“a single capital charge . . . replaces the specific risk charge (SRC) and the IRC”). GARP and Schweser agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 c, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: (sibling swap). The 99.9th percentile, one-year horizon and rebalancing at the end of each liquidity horizon (the constant level of risk assumption) are the defining features of the incremental risk charge, LO 63.b. This option would be correct if the stem asked for the best description of the IRC.

b.reason: (sibling swap). A charge drawn from the most stressful 250-day window in the last seven years and added to the traditional VaR charge is stressed VaR, LO 63.a, which applies to market-risk positions generally. It would be correct if the stem asked about the stressed VaR component of Basel 2.5.

c.reason: Option C reproduces the GARP statement that the Committee replaced “the IRC and specific risk charge with a comprehensive risk (CR) charge for the correlation book” and the Schweser description of a “single capital charge for correlation-dependent instruments.”

d.reason: (polarity flip). The scope (correlation book) is right, but “added on top of” reverses “replaces.” The whole point of the CR charge is that correlation-dependent positions are captured by one comprehensive measure instead of by the IRC plus the specific risk charge. It would be correct only under a regime that layered a correlation surcharge over the existing charges, which is not what Basel 2.5 did.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing a model validation report on the bank’s EUR structured credit portfolio. The report must explain why the Basel II banking-book credit model was judged unsuitable for securitization tranches, leading to the comprehensive risk (CR) charge. Which of the following statements best explains this?

options.text: The Gordy model holds the correlation parameter constant across obligors and over time, yet correlations change over time and such changes move tranche values sharply.
The Gordy model holds the correlation parameter constant across types of assets, yet securitized pools combine asset types whose default correlations differ widely.
The Gordy model lets the correlation parameter vary over time, which overstated the risk of senior tranches and led banks to hold too much capital against them.
The Gordy model ignores default correlation entirely, so it is unsuitable for every portfolio of debt instruments, whether in the banking book or in the trading book.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German bank model validation: why the Basel II credit model was unsuitable for securitization tranches.

**Concept and theory**

Basel II banking-book credit capital (the IRB approach) is built on the Gordy (2003) one-factor model. In that model, every obligor’s default is driven partly by a common systematic factor and partly by its own idiosyncratic factor; the correlation parameter sets how much weight the common factor carries. GARP states the key simplifying assumption: the correlation parameter “is constant across obligors and over time (though not across types of assets).”

GARP then draws the boundary of where this assumption is acceptable:

- **Reasonable** for portfolios of debt instruments when determining banking-book capital.
- **Not reasonable** for instruments in the correlation book (securitizations, re-securitizations and derivatives written on securitizations).

Why the difference? A securitization places a pool of assets in a special-purpose vehicle and issues tranched liabilities of differing seniority, so each tranche has a different exposure to credit losses in the pool. The loss that reaches a given tranche depends heavily on whether the pool’s defaults are scattered (low correlation) or clustered (high correlation). GARP: “In reality, correlations change over time and such changes can have large effects on the value of tranches.” A model that freezes correlation therefore misses the main driver of tranche risk. The CR charge was designed for exactly these correlation-sensitive positions.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor needs the statement that names the right assumption (constant across obligors and over time) and the right consequence (correlation changes move tranche values). Option A does both. The other options misstate the dimension of constancy, the direction of the error, or the reach of the criticism.

**Fragile fact.** Constant across obligors AND over time, but NOT across asset types; acceptable for the banking book, not for the correlation book.

**Reference**

LO 63.c (ORR 22.c), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.” GARP Chapter 22 (Carey), Section 22.2 “Basel 2.5”, subsection “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure” (Gordy (2003) assumption and tranche paragraph). Schweser Module 63.1, “Comprehensive Risk Charge” says only that correlations “increase” in stress so even the highest-rated tranches become vulnerable; it does not discuss the Gordy assumption. Deciding fact from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 c, where it is Q2 of 10.

a.reason: Option A matches GARP word for word in substance: constant “across obligors and over time” and changes in correlation “can have large effects on the value of tranches.”

b.reason: (scope or condition error). GARP states explicitly that the correlation parameter is constant across obligors and over time “though not across types of assets”; Basel II does assign different correlations to different asset classes. The option moves the constancy onto the one dimension where it does not hold. It would be correct if the stem described a hypothetical model with a single correlation for all asset classes.

c.reason: (polarity flip). The Gordy model holds correlation fixed over time; it does not let it vary. And the problem in the crisis was understatement of risk for senior tranches (AAA tranches priced at near-zero default probability), not overstatement. Both directions are reversed. It would be correct only for a model with time-varying correlation that systematically overestimated senior-tranche risk.

d.reason: (absolute claim). The Gordy model does contain a correlation parameter, and GARP judges the constant-correlation assumption “reasonable for portfolios of debt instruments for purposes of determining banking-book capital.” Saying it is unsuitable for every debt portfolio overextends a criticism that applies only to the correlation book. It would be correct if the stem asked about a model with zero correlation applied to tranched instruments.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK bank is calculating the comprehensive risk (CR) charge for the bank’s correlation book under the standardized approach. The positions and the standardized schedule are shown below. The desk’s current 10-day 99% VaR on these positions is GBP 9.2 million.

| Position | Type | Rating | Exposure (GBP million) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Securitization | AA | 150 |
| 2 | Re-securitization | A | 40 |
| 3 | Securitization | BBB | 30 |
| 4 | Re-securitization | BB | 10 |
| 5 | Securitization | Unrated | 5 |

| Capital charge (%) | AAA, AA | A | BBB | BB | Below BB, unrated |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Securitizations | 1.6 | 4 | 8 | 28 | 100 |
| Re-securitizations | 3.2 | 8 | 18 | 52 | 100 |

What is the CR charge for these five positions?

options.text: GBP 1.46 million
GBP 14.20 million
GBP 18.20 million
GBP 27.40 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK bank: standardized CR charge for five correlation-book positions, with an irrelevant VaR figure.

**Concept and theory**

Under Basel 2.5 a bank may compute the CR charge with a standardized approach that, in GARP’s words, “depends only on the rating of the instrument,” with a separate, higher schedule for re-securitizations. GARP adds a vital reading note to Table 22.1: the “percentages are capital as a fraction of the exposure, not risk weights.” So each percentage is multiplied directly by the exposure to give capital; there is no further 8% step.

| Capital charge (%) | AAA, AA | A | BBB | BB | Below BB, unrated |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Securitizations | 1.6 | 4 | 8 | 28 | 100 |
| Re-securitizations | 3.2 | 8 | 18 | 52 | 100 |

Two features of the schedule matter here. Re-securitizations are charged roughly double the securitization rate in each bucket from AAA to BB, because they are more vulnerable to changes in correlations. And tranches rated below BB, or unrated, carry 100%: they must in effect be financed entirely with capital (“dollar-for-dollar” in Schweser).

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: for each position $i$ with exposure $E_{i}$ and schedule percentage $c_{i}$ (chosen by both rating and type),

CR charge = $\sum_{i} c_{i} \times E_{i}.$

Working, in GBP million:

Position 1 (securitization, AA) = 1.6% × 150 = 2.40

Position 2 (re-securitization, A) = 8% × 40 = 3.20

Position 3 (securitization, BBB) = 8% × 30 = 2.40

Position 4 (re-securitization, BB) = 52% × 10 = 5.20

Position 5 (securitization, unrated) = 100% × 5 = 5.00

CR charge = 2.40 + 3.20 + 2.40 + 5.20 + 5.00 = 18.20

The 10-day 99% VaR of GBP 9.2 million is excess data: it belongs to the market-risk VaR calculation, not to the CR charge. The result means the bank must hold GBP 18.20 million of capital against GBP 235 million of correlation-book exposure, with more than half of it driven by the BB re-securitization and the unrated tranche, which together are only GBP 15 million of exposure.

**Fragile fact.** Percentages in Table 22.1 are CAPITAL, not risk weights: multiply by exposure and stop; choose the row by TYPE and the column by RATING.

**Reference**

LO 63.c (ORR 22.c), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.” GARP Chapter 22 (Carey), Section 22.2 “Basel 2.5”, subsection “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure” and Table 22.1 “Comprehensive Risk Capital Charge Under the Standardized Approach.” Schweser Module 63.1, “Comprehensive Risk Charge” and Figure 63.1 (the figure’s values are not legible in the text extract, so the schedule is taken from GARP Table 22.1). Schweser’s Key Concepts describe the re-securitization figures as “higher risk weights”; GARP says the percentages are capital, not risk weights. GARP used. Schweser labels the last bucket “below BB−” and GARP “\<BB”; same bucket, notation only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 c, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: (unit slip (capital percentage treated as a risk weight)). 18.20 × 8% = 1.456 ≈ 1.46. This treats each percentage as a risk weight and then applies an 8% capital ratio, which GARP explicitly rules out. It would be correct only if the schedule had been a table of risk weights, as for Basel I style risk-weighted assets.

b.reason: (wrong input twin (securitization schedule used for re-securitizations)). Using the securitization row for positions 2 and 4 gives 2.40 + (4% × 40 = 1.60) + 2.40 + (28% × 10 = 2.80) + 5.00 = 14.20. It would be correct if positions 2 and 4 were ordinary securitizations.

c.reason: Option C applies GARP’s Table 22.1 exactly as instructed: the right row for each instrument type, the right column for each rating, percentages applied directly to exposure, and the 100% charge for the unrated tranche.

d.reason: (excess-data trap (irrelevant input added)). 18.20 + 9.2 = 27.40 adds the desk’s VaR to the CR charge. The VaR figure is not an input to the standardized CR calculation. It would be correct only for a stem asking for the sum of this VaR figure and the CR charge.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is reviewing how SGD and USD trading positions have been allocated for capital purposes. She asks which positions belong in the correlation book and are therefore subject to the comprehensive risk (CR) charge. Which of the following positions is least likely to fall within the correlation book?

options.text: A mezzanine tranche of a CDO whose collateral pool consists of tranches issued by other asset-backed securitization vehicles.
A senior unsecured bond issued by a single investment-grade industrial company and held in the trading book for resale.
A credit default swap written on a mezzanine tranche of a residential mortgage securitization and held in the trading book.
A AAA-rated senior tranche of an auto-loan securitization issued by a special-purpose vehicle and held in the trading book.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank CRO: which trading position is least likely to sit in the correlation book?

**Concept and theory**

The CR charge applies only to the correlation book. GARP identifies its contents as “securitizations, re-securitizations and derivatives written on securitizations”; Schweser names asset-backed securities (ABSs) and collateralized debt obligations (CDOs). What unites them is structure: such instruments “place a portfolio in a special-purpose vehicle and create tranched liabilities that differ in seniority, and thus in their exposure to credit losses in the portfolio.” Because a tranche’s loss depends on how defaults in the pool cluster, its value is driven by correlations between default risks, which is precisely the LO’s phrase.

| Instrument | Correlation book? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Securitization tranche (any rating) | Yes | Tranched claim on a pool in an SPV |
| Re-securitization (e.g., CDO of ABS) | Yes | Pool is itself made of tranches |
| Derivative written on a securitization | Yes | Value derived from a tranche |
| Single-name bond in trading book | No | No pool, no tranching; IRC territory |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each position against the GARP list. A is a CDO of ABS tranches: a re-securitization. C is a CDS written on a securitization tranche: a derivative written on a securitization. D is a securitization tranche held in an SPV, and its AAA rating does not remove it (rating affects the charge, not the scope). B is a single-name corporate bond: there is no pool and no tranching, so its value is not driven by correlations between default risks. Its default and downgrade risk is captured by the incremental risk charge (LO 63.b).

**Fragile fact.** Scope is decided by STRUCTURE (pooled and tranched, or a derivative on such a tranche), not by rating.

**Reference**

LO 63.c (ORR 22.c), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.” GARP Chapter 22 (Carey), Section 22.2 “Basel 2.5”, subsection “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure” (“securitizations, re-securitizations and derivatives written on securitizations”; SPV and tranched liabilities). Schweser Module 63.1, “Comprehensive Risk Charge” (ABSs and CDOs). Derivatives on securitizations are named by GARP; Schweser does not list them separately. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 c, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: (sibling swap (re-securitization mistaken for an outsider)). A CDO whose collateral is tranches of other securitizations is the textbook re-securitization (Schweser’s “CDOs of ABSs”). It is firmly in the correlation book, with higher charges than plain securitizations. It would be the answer only if the collateral were whole loans held directly by the bank rather than securitized.

b.reason: Option B is the only position outside GARP’s description of the correlation book (securitizations, re-securitizations, derivatives written on securitizations), so it is least likely to be subject to the CR charge.

c.reason: (scope or condition error (derivatives on securitizations overlooked)). GARP includes “derivatives written on securitizations” in the correlation book. Taking the scope as cash securitizations only drops this condition. It would be the answer if the CDS referenced a single corporate name rather than a securitization tranche.

d.reason: (absolute claim (high rating treated as no correlation risk)). A AAA tranche is still a tranched claim on a pool and is in scope; GARP stresses that AAA tranches priced as near-riskless before the crisis fell in value when correlations moved. It would be the answer only if the bank held the auto loans directly rather than a tranche issued by an SPV.

questions.question: A portfolio manager on the structured credit desk of a Canadian bank notices that, under the standardized approach to the comprehensive risk (CR) charge, a CAD 50 million BBB-rated re-securitization tranche attracts a capital charge of 18%, whereas a BBB-rated securitization tranche of the same size attracts 8%. Which of the following best explains the difference?

options.text: The underlying pool of a re-securitization consists of single-name corporate bonds, so the higher charge captures jump-to-default risk of individual obligors rather than correlation risk.
The percentages for re-securitizations are risk weights rather than capital charges, so the higher figure reflects a different scaling convention rather than any difference in risk.
The underlying pool of a re-securitization is always made up of subprime mortgages, so the higher charge reflects the quality of the collateral regardless of the tranche’s rating.
The underlying pool of a re-securitization consists of the tranched liabilities of securitization vehicles, so the tranche is more vulnerable to changes in correlations.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank: why a BBB re-securitization attracts 18% versus 8% for a BBB securitization.

**Concept and theory**

A securitization takes a pool of ordinary assets (mortgages, auto loans, credit card receivables), places it in a special-purpose vehicle and issues tranches. A re-securitization goes one step further: its underlying pool is made of tranches issued by other securitization vehicles. GARP defines re-securitizations as instruments “for which the underlying pool of assets are the tranched liabilities of securitization vehicles.”

Why does that make them riskier for a given rating? Each underlying tranche already has a payoff that is highly sensitive to how defaults cluster in its own pool. Stacking tranches of tranches compounds that sensitivity: a shift in correlation moves every underlying tranche at once, and the re-securitization tranche magnifies those moves again. GARP concludes that re-securitizations “are more vulnerable to changes in correlations,” so “capital requirements are much higher for them.” Schweser attributes the higher charges to “the experience of the financial crisis.”

| Rating | AAA, AA | A | BBB | BB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Securitization charge (%) | 1.6 | 4 | 8 | 28 |
| Re-securitization charge (%) | 3.2 | 8 | 18 | 52 |
| Ratio | 2.0 | 2.0 | 2.25 | 1.86 |

**Applying it to this question**

Both tranches in the stem have the same rating (BBB) and the same size, so rating cannot explain the gap; only the type differs. The deciding fact is the structural one in option D: the re-securitization’s pool is tranched liabilities of securitization vehicles, which makes it more vulnerable to changes in correlations.

**Fragile fact.** Same rating, higher charge: the reason is STRUCTURE (tranches of tranches, so more correlation-sensitive), not rating or collateral.

**Reference**

LO 63.c (ORR 22.c), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.” GARP Chapter 22 (Carey), Section 22.2 “Basel 2.5”, subsection “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure” and Table 22.1. Schweser Module 63.1, “Comprehensive Risk Charge” (“resecuritizations, such as CDOs of ABSs, have higher capital requirements than normal securitizations”). Schweser’s Key Concepts call these “higher risk weights”; GARP says the figures are capital, not risk weights. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 c, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: (sibling swap (IRC rationale)). Jump-to-default risk of individual obligors is the risk the incremental risk charge roughly captures (LO 63.b). A re-securitization’s pool is tranches, not single-name bonds, and its extra charge is about correlation sensitivity. This would be correct if the stem asked why the IRC was introduced for single-name credit positions.

b.reason: (sibling swap (risk-weight convention)). GARP states that the Table 22.1 percentages are “capital as a fraction of the exposure, not risk weights,” for both rows. Both rows use the same convention, so the gap is a real difference in required capital. This would be correct only if the two rows were expressed in different units, which they are not.

c.reason: (absolute claim (collateral always subprime, charge set by collateral)). The standardized approach depends only on the rating and on whether the instrument is a securitization or a re-securitization, not on the collateral type; and re-securitizations are not by definition backed by subprime mortgages. This would be correct only under a collateral-based schedule, which Basel 2.5 does not use.

d.reason: Option D restates GARP’s reason directly: re-securitizations, “for which the underlying pool of assets are the tranched liabilities of securitization vehicles,” are “more vulnerable to changes in correlations.”

questions.question:
A supervisor at the French banking regulator is reviewing a bank’s application to use an internal model for the comprehensive risk (CR) charge on its EUR correlation book. The bank’s model documentation contains the following statements:

I. The model may be used only with supervisory approval, and the model-based charge may not be less than a fraction of the charge under the standardized approach.

II. The model must capture multiple default and rating change events, together with volatility in correlations and in credit spreads.

III. Because correlations are hard to estimate, the model may hold correlations and recovery rates constant, provided it revalues the whole portfolio in each simulation.

IV. The model must capture basis risk, such as the difference between CDS and underlying index values, as well as the dynamics of hedges.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French supervisor reviewing a bank’s application: which statements about the CR internal model are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The standardized CR charge is simple but blunt: it looks only at ratings and instrument type, and so cannot see how well positions hedge one another. Basel 2.5 therefore lets banks “use an internal model to estimate the CR charge if approved to do so by supervisors.” GARP attaches two safeguards and a demanding modeling standard.

- **Approval and floor.** Supervisors must approve the model, and “the model-based charge may not be less than a fraction of the charge under the standardized approach.”
- **Completeness.** Because the instruments are complex and the main reason for a model is to capture hedges more fully, internal models “must be unusually complete, complicated and robust.” GARP lists what must be modeled: multiple default and rating change events; volatility in correlations and credit spreads; basis risk (e.g., the difference between CDS and underlying index values); the dynamics of hedges; and volatility in recovery rates, ideally with simulations that revalue the whole portfolio in each iteration.

Schweser’s list is similar: credit spread risk, multiple defaults, volatility of implied correlations, the relationship between implied correlations and credit spreads, the cost of rebalancing hedges and the volatility of recovery rates, plus a requirement to “routinely perform rigorous stress tests.”

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against GARP’s list.

- I: supervisory approval and a floor at a fraction of the standardized charge. True.
- II: multiple default and rating change events, volatility in correlations and credit spreads. True.
- III: holding correlations and recovery rates constant. False: volatility in both must be modeled. Full revaluation is desirable but does not excuse static inputs.
- IV: basis risk (CDS versus index) and dynamics of hedges. True.

Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** The CR internal model must make correlations, spreads and recovery rates MOVE (model their volatility); a static-correlation model fails the standard even with full revaluation.

**Reference**

LO 63.c (ORR 22.c), verbatim from Schweser: “Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.” GARP Chapter 22 (Carey), Section 22.2 “Basel 2.5”, subsection “Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure” (internal model paragraph). Schweser Module 63.1, “Comprehensive Risk Charge” (internal model factor list and stress-testing requirement). GARP includes the floor and basis risk; Schweser omits the floor and adds stress tests, the implied correlation and spread relationship and the cost of rebalancing hedges. Different emphasis, no conflict on these statements.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 c, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: Option A contains exactly the three statements GARP supports and excludes statement III, which contradicts GARP’s requirement to model volatility in correlations and recovery rates.

b.reason: (polarity flip in statement III, plus omission). This set accepts III, which reverses “volatility in correlations . . . and volatility in recovery rates must be modeled” into “may hold . . . constant,” and drops two true statements. It would be correct only if II and IV were false and III true.

c.reason: (polarity flip in statement III, plus role omission). This set accepts III and rejects I, missing that supervisory approval and a floor tied to the standardized charge are conditions of using a model. It would be correct only if banks could adopt models without supervisors and with no floor, and could freeze correlations.

d.reason: (absolute claim). “All four” requires III to be true. Holding correlations constant is the very Gordy-model simplification the CR regime was built to move beyond. It would be correct only if III instead said the model must capture volatility in correlations and recovery rates.
