questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the difference between the convertible bonds traditionally issued by non-financial companies and the contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) issued by banks. Which of the following statements best describes that difference?

options.text: Both instruments convert at the option of the holder, but a CoCo holder converts when the share price falls below a threshold, whereas a traditional holder converts when it rises above one.
A traditional convertible converts automatically when the issuer is in distress, whereas a CoCo converts at the option of the holder when the bank’s share price exceeds a threshold.
A traditional convertible converts at the option of the holder when the share price exceeds a threshold, whereas a CoCo increases the bank’s equity when distress occurs, through indenture triggers.

A traditional convertible converts at the option of the holder when the share price exceeds a threshold, whereas a CoCo converts at the option of the holder once the supervisor declares the bank nonviable.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK bank, induction session: what distinguishes a traditional convertible from a CoCo?

**Concept and theory**

A convertible bond is a debt instrument whose indenture (the bond contract) allows it to become shares of the issuer. The question for any convertible is: who decides that it converts, and in what state of the world does conversion happen?

GARP starts with the traditional instrument. Traditional convertibles were issued by non-financial firms that wanted to avoid the dilution of issuing equity before their performance improved. “At the option of the holder”, such bonds converted into equity when the firm’s share price exceeded thresholds specified in the indenture. So the holder decides, and conversion happens in good times, when the shares are worth more than the bond.

GARP then calls CoCos “the mirror image”: they cause a bank’s equity to increase when distress occurs, as reflected by triggers written into the indenture, and not at the option of the holder. Schweser says the same thing in other words: CoCos “convert to equity automatically when certain conditions are met”, typically when the bank is experiencing financial strain.

| Feature | Traditional convertible | CoCo |
|---|---|---|
| Typical issuer | Non-financial firm | Bank |
| Who decides | Holder (an option) | Indenture trigger (automatic) |
| When equity is created | Share price above threshold (good times) | Distress (capital ratio or regulator trigger) |
| Purpose | Defer dilution until performance improves | Add loss-absorbing equity when it is needed |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the difference. An accurate answer must get both halves right: the traditional bond’s holder option exercised when the share price is high, and the CoCo’s automatic, trigger-driven increase in equity in distress. Option C is the only one that states both halves correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: traditional convertible = holder decides, share price high; CoCo = indenture decides, bank in distress.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. Schweser Reading 63, Module 63.3 “Contingent Convertible Bonds” and Key Concepts LO 63.g. No content conflict; Schweser uses “automatically” where GARP says “not at the option of the holder”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (role misassignment plus polarity flip). A gives the CoCo holder a conversion option and then flips the share-price direction to “falls below”. Neither appears in the source: the CoCo decision belongs to the indenture trigger, not the holder. A would be correct only for a hypothetical instrument giving the holder a put-like right to convert into shares on a price fall, which is not a CoCo as described.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B swaps the two instruments’ mechanisms: it gives the traditional convertible the CoCo’s automatic distress conversion and gives the CoCo the traditional holder option on a high share price. B would be correct if the labels “traditional convertible” and “CoCo” were exchanged.

c.reason: C restates GARP’s two sentences: traditional convertibles convert “at the option of the holder” when “the firm’s share price exceeded thresholds specified in the indenture”, while CoCos “cause a bank’s equity to increase when distress occurs, as reflected by triggers written into the indenture, and not at the option of the holder”.

d.reason: (role misassignment). D correctly describes the traditional bond and correctly names a real CoCo trigger (the regulator declaring the bank nonviable), but it puts the conversion decision back with the holder. Under GARP, once the trigger occurs, equity increases “not at the option of the holder”. D would be correct if the stem asked which event can activate a CoCo, with the holder-option wording removed.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian bank is preparing a report on one of the bank’s outstanding CoCos. The bond carries a principal write-down feature rather than a conversion-into-shares feature. Selected data at the latest quarter end are shown below.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| CoCo principal outstanding (AUD million) | 500 |
| Trigger: Core Tier 1 capital to RWA (%) | 7.0 |
| Core Tier 1 capital to RWA at quarter end (%) | 6.6 |
| Liquidity coverage ratio (%) | 118 |

Which of the following statements is the analyst most accurate to include in the report?

options.text: The bond’s value is written down without any action by the holders, and the reduction in the liability increases the bank’s equity.
The holders may elect to accept the write-down or to keep the bond as debt, and the bank’s equity increases only if they accept it.
No loss absorption occurs, because a CoCo can increase the bank’s equity only by converting into shares, so the write-down is unenforceable.
The bond’s value is written down without any action by the holders, and the loss recognized on the write-down reduces the bank’s equity.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank: write-down CoCo, trigger 7.0%, ratio 6.6%; what happens to equity?

**Concept and theory**

A CoCo exists to add loss-absorbing equity to a bank at the moment the bank needs it. GARP describes two contractual ways in which that happens: “With CoCos, equity increases either because the bond converts to equity or because its value is written down.”

Why does a write-down increase equity? Use the balance-sheet identity

Equity = Assets $- \text{Liabilities}.$

The CoCo is a liability. If its principal is written down by an amount $W$ while assets are unchanged, liabilities fall by $W$ and equity rises by $W$ :

∆Equity = −∆Liabilities = +$W.$

Conversion does the same thing by a different route: the liability is cancelled and new shares are issued, so the amount moves from the debt side to the equity side. In both cases the holder is not asked: the change happens because a trigger in the indenture has been met.

| Route | What happens to the bond | Effect on the bank’s equity |
|---|---|---|
| Conversion | Debt cancelled, shares issued to holders | Rises; holders become shareholders |
| Write-down | Principal reduced; no shares issued | Rises; the liability shrinks |

**Applying it to this question**

Trigger level = 7.0%

Actual Core Tier 1 to RWA = 6.6% \< 7.0% ⇒ trigger met

Instrument feature = principal write-down

Result = liability reduced, equity increased, no holder decision

The liquidity coverage ratio of 118% is an irrelevant input: CoCo triggers in the reading are capital-ratio or regulator-based, not liquidity-based, and the LCR does not affect what the write-down does.

**Fragile fact.** Write-down direction: the bank’s liability falls, so the bank’s equity rises; the loss sits with the CoCo holder.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. GARP and Schweser differ: Schweser describes only conversion to equity; GARP adds the write-down route. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: A matches GARP exactly: the trigger is met, the bond’s value is written down without holder action, and equity increases because the value of the bond is written down.

b.reason: (role misassignment). B gives the holders a choice. GARP says the increase in equity occurs as reflected by triggers in the indenture and “not at the option of the holder”. B would describe a voluntary liability-management exercise (for example, an exchange offer), not a CoCo trigger.

c.reason: (scope error (absolute)). C narrows the mechanism to conversion only. That is how Schweser compresses the topic (it speaks only of conversion), but GARP explicitly adds the writedown route. C would be correct only if the question were restricted to a conversion-only CoCo and asked whether a conversion-only bond could be written down.

d.reason: (polarity flip). D gets the mechanism right but reverses the direction of the effect on equity. The write-down is a gain to the bank’s shareholders (a liability disappears), not a loss. D would be correct from the perspective of the holders: their asset is written down and they bear the loss.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Chinese bank is drafting a term sheet for a new CNY-denominated CoCo issue and has listed four candidate conditions under which the bond would convert into equity:

I. The bank’s Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio falls below a stated threshold.

II. The bank’s primary regulator declares the bank to be nonviable.

III. The bank’s share price rises above a stated conversion price and the holder elects to convert.

IV. The ratio of the bank’s market capitalization to its assets falls below a stated minimum.

Which of the listed conditions are consistent with the triggers described for CoCos?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank term sheet: which of four candidate conditions are recognized CoCo triggers?

**Concept and theory**

A trigger is the contractual event that turns a CoCo from debt into loss-absorbing equity. Because the whole point is to recapitalize a bank under strain, every trigger must be a signal of deterioration. The reading names three families:

| Trigger family | Condition | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Accounting capital ratio | Core Tier 1 (Tier 1 equity) to RWA falls below a threshold | GARP (“a common trigger”); Schweser (Credit Suisse 2011 example) |
| Regulatory judgment | Primary regulator declares the bank nonviable / supervisors judge it needs public aid | GARP; Schweser (Credit Suisse) |
| Market value | Market capitalization to assets falls below a minimum | Schweser only |

GARP notes that “triggers have varied somewhat across CoCos”, so its two named triggers are common examples, not an exhaustive list.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement for two things: is it a distress signal, and is the conversion automatic?

- I: capital ratio falls below threshold. Distress signal, automatic. Consistent.
- II: regulator declares nonviability. Distress signal, automatic. Consistent.
- III: share price rises and the holder elects to convert. Good-times signal and holder option. This is the traditional convertible. Not consistent.
- IV: market capitalization to assets falls below a minimum. Distress signal, automatic. Consistent (Schweser).

So I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of every trigger: ratios fall below a floor; a share price rising is the traditional convertible, never a CoCo trigger.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. Schweser Reading 63, Module 63.3 “Contingent Convertible Bonds” and Key Concepts LO 63.g. The market capitalization to assets trigger and the Credit Suisse 2011 example are Schweser only (content from Schweser, a condensed source); GARP names two common triggers and says triggers have varied.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). A keeps only the two triggers GARP lists and drops the market-value trigger. GARP’s list is not exhaustive (“triggers have varied”), and Schweser names the market capitalization to assets ratio as a potential trigger. A would be correct if the stem asked which triggers GARP specifically describes as common.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B includes III, which is the traditional convertible’s conversion condition (share price above a threshold, at the holder’s option), and omits II and IV. B would be correct only for a stem about a traditional convertible combined with a capital-ratio covenant, which is not what the reading describes.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C includes the traditional-convertible condition III and omits the most common CoCo trigger, I. C would be correct only if III were replaced by the capital-ratio trigger, that is, if the set were I, II and IV.

d.reason: D lists exactly the three trigger families named in the reading: the Tier 1 equity to RWA ratio, the supervisor’s or regulator’s judgment, and “a minimum ratio of a bank’s market capitalization to its assets” (Schweser).

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is validating the regulatory capital classification of four outstanding CoCo issues. Each bond’s trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio, as follows:

| Bond | Trigger ratio (%) | Principal (CAD million) | Coupon (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bond 1 | 7.000 | 750 | 6.25 |
| Bond 2 | 5.125 | 400 | 7.10 |
| Bond 3 | 5.000 | 600 | 7.40 |
| Bond 4 | 4.500 | 250 | 8.00 |

Which of the following classifications should the auditor accept as correct?

options.text: Bonds 1, 2, 3 and 4 in Additional Tier 1 capital, since each is debt with a trigger that causes conversion or a write-down
Bonds 1 and 2 in Additional Tier 1 capital, and Bonds 3 and 4 in Tier 2 capital
Bond 1 in Additional Tier 1 capital, and Bonds 2, 3 and 4 in Tier 2 capital
Bonds 1 and 2 in Core Tier 1 equity capital, and Bonds 3 and 4 in Additional Tier 1 capital

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank: classify four CoCos with triggers 7.000%, 5.125%, 5.000%, 4.500%.

**Concept and theory**

Basel III divides regulatory capital into Core Tier 1 (Tier 1 equity: common equity, retained earnings and similar), Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2. GARP lists among the components of Additional Tier 1 “debt with appropriate triggers that cause conversion to equity or write-downs”, which is exactly a CoCo.

Why does the trigger level matter? A higher trigger means the bond turns into equity earlier, while the bank is still a going concern, so it supports the bank before failure. A low trigger only bites when the bank is close to collapse, so its loss absorption is closer to that of Tier 2 capital, which GARP describes as designed to absorb losses after failure, protecting depositors and other creditors. (This intuition is an interpretation: GARP states the rule without giving the reason.) GARP gives the rule:

Additional Tier 1, trigger threshold ≥ 5.125%

CoCo classification = $\{$

Tier 2, trigger threshold \< 5.125%

A CoCo is never Core Tier 1 while it is outstanding, because it is a debt instrument until conversion.

**Applying it to this question**

Bond 1: 7.000% ≥ 5.125% ⇒ Additional Tier 1

Bond 2: 5.125% ≥ 5.125% ⇒ Additional Tier 1 (boundary is inclusive)

Bond 3: 5.000% \< 5.125% ⇒ Tier 2

Bond 4: 4.500% \< 5.125% ⇒ Tier 2

Principal and coupon are irrelevant inputs: classification depends only on the trigger threshold.

**Fragile fact.** The 5.125% boundary is inclusive (“or higher”); at or above it is AT1, below it is Tier 2; never Core Tier 1 before conversion.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. Also GARP Section 22.3 “Basel 3”, subsection “The Definition of Capital” (AT1 includes debt with triggers). The 5.125% rule is GARP only; Schweser does not state it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). A uses the true fact that AT1 includes debt with conversion or write-down triggers but drops the threshold condition. A would be correct if all four triggers were at or above 5.125%.

b.reason: B applies GARP’s rule (“Additional Tier 1 Capital if the threshold is 5.125 percent or higher, and Tier 2 capital otherwise”) to each bond, including the inclusive boundary for Bond 2.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). C reads “5.125 percent or higher” as “strictly above 5.125 percent”, pushing Bond 2 into Tier 2. C would be correct if Bond 2’s trigger were, say, 5.100%.

d.reason: (sibling swap). D promotes every bond one tier: high-trigger CoCos to Core Tier 1 and low-trigger CoCos to AT1. CoCos are debt when issued and do not appear in the equity account until converted, so they cannot be Core Tier 1. D would be correct only after conversion, when the new shares (not the bond) would count in Tier 1 equity.

questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-22 g Q5
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Singapore bank asks the treasurer why the bank should issue SGD-denominated CoCos, given what the 2007 to 2009 crisis revealed about how distressed banks were recapitalized. Which of the following best explains the motivation that operates in a stress period?

options.text: Conversion shifts the losses onto insured depositors, so the deposit insurer rather than the government recapitalizes the bank.
Conversion supplies cash to meet withdrawals, so the bank survives a funding run while its equity remains unchanged.
Conversion turns private bondholders’ funds into equity, a loss cushion that helps prevent insolvency without public money.
Conversion guarantees that the bank cannot become insolvent, so capital buffers above the regulatory minimums are no longer needed.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank board: what is the stress-period motivation for issuing CoCos?

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains what the crisis taught regulators: it was not enough for banks to remain solvent up to the point of maximum loss; they had to be able to operate as a going concern afterwards, which needed substantial capital after the losses. “In many cases, governments provided capital, but such provision was unpopular.” Buffers above the minimums were needed, “as were means of recapitalizing failed banks.”

A CoCo is one such means. Schweser states the motivation directly: in periods of financial stress “the bonds convert to equity, providing a cushion against loss, which helps prevent insolvency. The needed capital is provided by private sector bondholders rather than the government, allowing the bank to avoid a bailout.” The key point is that the money is already inside the bank: the bondholders paid it in when the bonds were issued. Conversion (or write-down) simply reclassifies that funding from debt to equity, so no new cash and no taxpayer is needed at the worst moment.

| Question | Government recapitalization | CoCo conversion |
|---|---|---|
| Who supplies capital | Taxpayers | Private bondholders |
| When the money arrives | In the crisis | At issue, years earlier |
| Political acceptability | Unpopular (GARP) | Avoids a bailout (Schweser) |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks specifically about the stress-period motivation and links it to how banks were recapitalized in the crisis. The deciding facts are: equity is created in stress, it absorbs loss and helps prevent insolvency, and it comes from private bondholders rather than government. Only C contains all three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: in a CoCo conversion the capital comes from private bondholders, not the government and not depositors; and it “helps prevent” insolvency, it does not guarantee solvency.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” Schweser Reading 63, Module 63.3 “Contingent Convertible Bonds” and Key Concepts LO 63.g. GARP Section 22.3 “Basel 3”, opening list of weaknesses the crisis revealed (“governments provided capital, but such provision was unpopular”). The explicit “avoid a bailout” wording is Schweser’s; GARP makes the point indirectly. Schweser’s Key Concepts says “preventing insolvency” while its body says “helps prevent”; the body wording is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: (role misassignment). A puts the loss on insured depositors and the cost on the deposit insurer. In the reading the loss-absorbers are the CoCo holders, and GARP describes subordinated capital such as Tier 2 as protecting depositors and other creditors, not drawing on them. A would be correct only if the question concerned a deposit-insurance payout after a bank failure.

b.reason: (sibling swap (liquidity for solvency)). B treats conversion as a cash event that fixes a funding run. Conversion changes the composition of the liability side (debt into equity); it does not bring in new cash, and its purpose is a loss cushion against insolvency. B would describe a liquidity facility or the LCR’s role, which belong to LO 63.f.

c.reason: C is the Schweser sentence in compressed form, and it fits GARP’s diagnosis that government provision of capital was unpopular and banks needed means of recapitalizing themselves.

d.reason: (absolute claim). D promises that insolvency becomes impossible and that buffers are unnecessary. Schweser’s own wording is that the cushion “helps prevent insolvency”; GARP stresses that buffers above minimums are still needed and that banks will fail in future despite the reforms. D would be correct only with “guarantees” replaced by “helps” and the claim about buffers removed.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a European asset manager is analyzing a bank that must raise EUR 300 million of new capital. The bank can issue either common equity or CoCos paying an 8% annual coupon. Ignore taxes, and assume the CoCos are not triggered during the year.

| Item | EUR million |
|---|---|
| Book equity before the raise | 1,200 |
| Net income before any coupon on the new capital (either plan) | 180 |
| New capital to be raised | 300 |
| Risk-weighted assets | 9,500 |
| CoCo trigger: Core Tier 1 capital to RWA (%) | 7 |

Which of the following correctly states the bank’s reported return on equity (ROE) for the year under the CoCo plan, and how it compares with the ROE under the common equity plan?

options.text: 13.0%, which is 1.0 percentage point higher than under the common equity plan
15.0%, which is 3.0 percentage points higher than under the common equity plan
10.4%, which is 1.6 percentage points lower than under the common equity plan
12.0%, which is the same as the ROE reported under the common equity plan

questions.solution:
Stem summary: European bank raising EUR 300m: ROE under CoCo plan versus common equity plan.

**Concept and theory**

Return on equity measures profit per unit of shareholders’ book equity:

ROE = $\frac{\text{Net income}}{\text{Book equity}}$

where net income is after all interest expense, and book equity is the equity account on the balance sheet.

GARP identifies the accounting advantage of CoCos: “because they do not appear in the equity account until converted, a bank can report a higher return on equity.” Schweser makes the same point: during normal periods the bonds are debt “and thus do not drag down return on equity”. Two effects work in opposite directions:

- The CoCo coupon is an interest expense, so it lowers net income (the numerator).
- The CoCo is not in the equity account, so it does not raise book equity (the denominator). If the denominator effect dominates, reported ROE is higher under the CoCo plan, even though (Q7) CoCos are economically expensive.

**Applying it to this question**

Equity plan:

Book equity = 1,200 + 300 = 1,500

Net income = 180 (no coupon on common equity)

$\text{ROE}_{\text{equity}}$ = $\frac{180}{1{,}500}$ = 12.0%

CoCo plan:

CoCo coupon = 8% × 300 = 24

Net income = 180 − 24 = 156

Book equity = 1,200 (CoCos are debt until converted)

$\text{ROE}_{\text{CoCo}}$ = $\frac{156}{1{,}200}$ = 13.0%

Difference = 13.0% − 12.0% = +1.0 percentage point

Risk-weighted assets and the 7% trigger are irrelevant inputs: the CoCos are not triggered, so they stay outside equity all year. The result means that the CoCo plan flatters reported ROE by 1.0 point, which is exactly the accounting motivation GARP describes.

**Fragile fact.** Numerator and denominator move separately: the coupon reduces net income, but the CoCo stays out of book equity until conversion.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. Schweser Reading 63, Module 63.3 “Contingent Convertible Bonds” and Key Concepts LO 63.g. The ROE formula itself is not stated in either source (a standard definition, outside-source); the deciding fact (CoCos outside the equity account until converted) is from both sources.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: A is the only option that both deducts the coupon from net income and keeps the CoCos out of the equity denominator, giving 13.0% against 12.0%.

b.reason: (dropped term). B omits the coupon: 180/1,200 = 15.0%, which is 15.0% − 12.0% = 3.0 points above the equity plan. B would be correct only if the new capital carried no servicing cost, which is not true of a coupon-paying bond.

c.reason: (sibling swap (CoCo treated as equity)). C deducts the coupon but adds the CoCos to book equity: 156/1,500 = 10.4%, which is 1.6 points below 12.0%. That treats the bonds as if they were already converted while still paying the coupon. C would be correct only if the CoCos sat in the equity account while outstanding, which GARP says they do not.

d.reason: (intermediate result). D reports 12.0%, which is the equity-plan ROE computed in the first step, not the CoCo-plan ROE. D would be correct if the stem asked for the ROE under the common equity plan.

questions.question: The chief risk officer at a US bank is reviewing a board paper that describes CoCos as “a cheap form of capital”. The CRO wants the paper to reflect the economic argument about how investors should price CoCos. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: CoCos should be cheaper than equity, because holders receive most of the upside when the bank does well, while losses at failure fall first on equity holders.
CoCos should be expensive to issue, because holders get little of the upside when the bank does well but bear losses similar to equity holders when it fails.
CoCos should be cheaper than equity, because holders can choose to convert into shares when the share price rises, which gives them a valuable option.
CoCos should be priced like senior debt, because they are debt instruments when issued, so their holders bear losses only if the bank is liquidated.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: US bank board paper calls CoCos “a cheap form of capital”; what is the pricing argument?

**Concept and theory**

The required return on any security depends on what its holder gets in good and bad states. GARP reasons as follows: “Economically, it is not obvious why the market would price CoCos to make the cost of capital for them less than the cost of equity. Because CoCos are debt instruments when issued, the holders receive little or none of the high returns received by equity holders when a bank does well, but holders bear losses not so different from those of equity holders when a bank fails. Thus, they should be expensive for a bank to issue.”

| State of the bank | Common equity holder | CoCo holder | Senior debt holder |
|---|---|---|---|
| Does well | High returns | Little or none of the upside | Fixed coupon |
| Fails | Large losses | Losses close to equity’s | Smaller losses |

A security with capped upside and equity-like downside should demand a high return. GARP then adds: “But they do have an accounting advantage”: not appearing in the equity account until converted, they let the bank report a higher ROE.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO wants the economic pricing argument. GARP’s answer is that CoCos should be expensive, for two linked reasons: limited upside in good times and equity-like losses at failure. Option B states that argument.

**Fragile fact.** Cost direction: CoCos should be expensive, not cheap; their attraction to the bank is accounting (higher reported ROE), not a low cost of capital.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. The pricing argument is GARP only; Schweser presents the motivation (no ROE drag, loss cushion) without discussing cost.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (polarity flip). A reverses both payoff claims: it gives CoCo holders “most of the upside” and shields them from failure losses. GARP says holders receive little or none of the upside and bear losses close to equity’s. A would be correct for a security with an equity-like upside and debt-like downside protection, such as a traditional convertible bond in a firm that is not near failure.

b.reason: B reproduces GARP’s reasoning almost clause by clause and reaches GARP’s conclusion that CoCos “should be expensive for a bank to issue”.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C attaches the traditional convertible’s holder option to the CoCo. CoCo conversion is not at the option of the holder, so CoCo holders have no valuable call on the upside. C would be correct for a traditional convertible bond, whose holder converts when the share price exceeds the indenture threshold.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). D takes the true fact that CoCos are debt when issued and over-extends it to their loss profile, ignoring the trigger. Conversion or write-down happens on distress, before any liquidation, so holders bear losses earlier and larger than senior creditors. D would be correct for ordinary senior unsecured debt with no trigger.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Japanese bank on the trigger design for a JPY-denominated CoCo. The bank is choosing between an accounting trigger based on the ratio of Tier 1 equity capital to risk-weighted assets and a market-value trigger based on the ratio of market capitalization to assets. Which of the following statements about this choice is most accurate?

options.text: A market-value trigger removes all scope for manipulation, because neither the bank nor investors can influence the bank’s share price.
A market-value trigger may increase balance sheet manipulation but would reduce the scope for manipulating the bank’s stock price.
An accounting trigger may reduce balance sheet manipulation but might instead introduce manipulation of the bank’s stock price.
A market-value trigger may reduce balance sheet manipulation but might instead introduce manipulation of the bank’s stock price.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank choosing between an accounting trigger and a market-value trigger.

**Concept and theory**

A trigger must be measurable, and whoever can move the measured number may be tempted to do so. Schweser compares the two objective trigger types:

- An accounting trigger uses the ratio of Tier 1 equity capital to risk-weighted assets. Both numerator and denominator come from the bank’s own balance sheet and risk models, so the bank may be tempted to manipulate them to stay above the threshold (“balance sheet manipulations”).
- A market-value trigger uses a minimum ratio of market capitalization to assets. The numerator is set by the stock market, not by the bank’s accounting choices, so the scope for balance-sheet manipulation shrinks; but anyone who gains from conversion (or from avoiding it) could try to push the share price, so it “might instead introduce stock price manipulation”.

| Trigger | Measured by | Manipulation concern |
|---|---|---|
| Accounting | Tier 1 equity / RWA | Balance-sheet manipulation |
| Market value | Market capitalization / assets | Reduces balance-sheet manipulation; may introduce stock-price manipulation |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks which statement about the choice is most accurate. The deciding fact is Schweser’s trade-off sentence: market value triggers “may reduce balance sheet manipulations . . . but might instead introduce stock price manipulation”. D says exactly that.

**Fragile fact.** Which trigger, which risk: accounting ratio → balance-sheet manipulation; market capitalization ratio → stock-price manipulation.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” Schweser Reading 63, Module 63.3 “Contingent Convertible Bonds” and Key Concepts LO 63.g. Content from Schweser, a condensed source: GARP names the capital-ratio and regulator triggers but does not discuss market-value triggers or the manipulation trade-off.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (absolute claim). A says a market trigger removes all manipulation because no one can influence the share price. The source says the opposite about the share price: it might be manipulated. A would be correct only if share prices were immune to trading pressure, which the source contradicts by warning that the share price might be manipulated.

b.reason: (polarity flip). B reverses both directions for the market-value trigger: it increases balance-sheet manipulation and reduces stock-price manipulation. B would be correct with “increase” and “reduce” exchanged.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C attributes the market-value trigger’s trade-off to the accounting trigger. The accounting trigger is the one exposed to balance-sheet manipulation, since it is built from the bank’s own reported numbers. C would be correct with “an accounting trigger” replaced by “a market-value trigger”.

d.reason: D attributes the right benefit (less balance-sheet manipulation) and the right cost (possible stock-price manipulation) to the right trigger (market value).

questions.question: A regulator at a national supervisory authority is training staff on the two routes by which a global systemically important bank could be recapitalized with its own investors’ funds: CoCos that become equity, and the bail-in of certain wholesale debt liabilities. Which of the following comparisons is most accurate?

options.text: CoCo terms are written into the bond indenture and often require conversion while the bank still appears solvent; bail-ins are governed by national law, with details chosen by authorities after they seize the bank.

CoCo terms are governed by national law, with details chosen by authorities after they seize the bank; bail-in terms are written into the debt indenture and often apply while the bank still appears solvent.

CoCo terms are written into the bond indenture but require conversion only after authorities have seized the bank; bail-ins are governed by national law, with details chosen by authorities after seizure.

CoCo terms are written into the bond indenture and often require conversion while the bank still appears solvent; bail-in terms are also fixed in the debt indenture at issue and apply automatically before any seizure.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Supervisory training: CoCo conversion versus bail-in as routes to self-recapitalization.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s resolution-planning section starts from the premise that banks will fail despite Basel I, II and III, so G-SIBs must be able to recapitalize themselves. It names two routes: “Recapitalization might be accomplished by causing convertible bonds to become equity or by bail-in, in which certain wholesale debt liabilities are either written down or converted to equity.” Both routes end in the same place (debt becomes equity or is written down), but they differ in where the rules come from and when they operate:

| Feature | CoCo conversion | Bail-in |
|---|---|---|
| Source of the terms | Written into the bond indenture | Governed by national law |
| Who sets the details | Agreed in the contract at issue | Chosen by authorities |
| Timing | Often while the bank still appears solvent | After authorities have seized control |

GARP: “The terms of conversion are written into the indentures of convertible bonds and often require conversion when a bank appears to be solvent, whereas bail-ins are governed by national law and details are generally chosen by authorities after they have seized control of a bank.”

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the comparison. The deciding facts are the source of the terms (contract versus law) and the timing (going concern versus after seizure). Only A gets all four cells right.

**Fragile fact.** Contract versus authority: CoCo = indenture, often while still apparently solvent; bail-in = national law, authorities, after seizure.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation” (paragraph on TLAC and recapitalization). GARP only; Schweser does not discuss bail-in. Boundary call: only the CoCo mechanics in this paragraph are tested; TLAC and the FSB key attributes are not.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: A restates GARP’s sentence on both routes without alteration.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B swaps the two routes’ features completely. B would be correct with the labels “CoCo” and “bail-in” exchanged.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). C keeps the indenture as the source of CoCo terms but moves the conversion to after seizure. GARP says the indenture terms “often require conversion when a bank appears to be solvent”, which is what lets a CoCo recapitalize a going concern. C would be correct only for a CoCo whose sole trigger is a resolution authority’s action after seizure, which the reading does not describe.

d.reason: (role misassignment). D is right on CoCos but hands the bail-in to the debt contract instead of to the authorities. GARP says bail-ins are governed by national law with details chosen by authorities after seizure. D would be correct if bail-in terms were purely contractual, which would make bail-in debt just another CoCo.

questions.question:
A credit analyst at a Brazilian investment firm covers both a BRL-funded manufacturing company that has issued traditional convertible bonds and a bank that has issued CoCos. The analyst drafts four statements for a sector note:

I. Traditional convertibles were issued by non-financial firms that wished to avoid the dilution of issuing equity before the firm’s performance improved.

II. Conversion of a traditional convertible adds equity when the issuer is doing well, whereas a CoCo adds equity to the bank when it is in distress.

III. A holder of a traditional convertible converts into equity when the issuer’s share price falls below a threshold specified in the indenture.

IV. CoCos, like traditional convertibles, are mainly issued by non-financial firms that wish to avoid diluting their shareholders before performance improves.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I and II only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian analyst sector note: four statements on traditional convertibles versus CoCos.

**Concept and theory**

To see why GARP calls CoCos the “mirror image” of traditional convertibles, start with the issuer’s problem in each case.

A non-financial firm whose shares are currently cheap does not want to issue equity now, because new shares sold at a low price dilute existing shareholders heavily. It issues a convertible bond instead. If the firm does well and its share price rises above the threshold in the indenture, the holder chooses to convert, and the equity is issued at a better time. GARP: traditional convertibles “were issued by non-financial firms who wished to avoid the dilution of issuing equity before the firm’s performance improved”.

A bank’s problem is the reverse: it needs equity exactly when things go badly. A CoCo therefore creates equity when distress occurs, through indenture triggers, regardless of what the holder wants.

|  | Traditional convertible | CoCo |
|---|---|---|
| Issuer | Non-financial firm | Bank |
| Equity created when | Issuer does well (share price up) | Bank is in distress |
| Decided by | Holder | Indenture trigger |

**Applying it to this question**

- I: true; it is GARP’s stated motivation for traditional convertibles.
- II: true; it is the “mirror image” contrast (good times versus distress).
- III: false; the holder converts when the share price exceeds the threshold.
- IV: false; CoCos are bank instruments, and their purpose is equity in distress, not deferring dilution.

Accurate statements: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Traditional convertible: share price above the threshold, holder converts; the motivation is avoiding dilution now.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. The dilution motivation for traditional convertibles is GARP only; Schweser describes their mechanics but not why they were issued.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error (incomplete set)). A accepts I but rejects II, which is a correct statement of the mirror-image idea. A would be correct if II had reversed the timing (for example, “a CoCo adds equity when the bank is doing well”).

b.reason: (polarity flip). B accepts III, which flips “exceeded” to “falls below”. A holder would not convert into shares worth less than the bond. B would be correct if III read “rises above a threshold”.

c.reason: C selects the two statements that match GARP’s description of traditional convertibles and of CoCos as their mirror image.

d.reason: (role misassignment). D accepts IV, which assigns the traditional convertible’s issuer and motivation to CoCos, and rejects the true statement I. D would be correct only if IV described banks issuing CoCos to obtain equity in distress and I were false.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee at a GBP-reporting bank is reviewing a draft memo on the bank’s planned CoCo program. The bank currently has no CoCos outstanding. Which of the following statements in the memo is least accurate?

options.text: Credit Suisse’s 2011 CoCos used both a Tier 1 equity capital to RWA trigger and a trigger based on supervisors judging that the bank needed public sector aid to avoid insolvency.
The accounting advantage of CoCos is that conversion adds them to the equity account, which is what lets the bank report a higher return on equity.
A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 6% may be included in the bank’s Additional Tier 1 capital.
When a CoCo trigger is hit, the bank’s equity increases either because the bond converts into equity or because its value is written down, and the holder cannot prevent this.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: GBP-reporting bank risk committee memo on a planned CoCo program: which statement is least accurate?

**Concept and theory**

This question pulls together four facts of the LO:

1. Triggers: Tier 1 (Core Tier 1) equity to RWA falling below a threshold, and supervisory or regulator judgment (Schweser’s Credit Suisse 2011 example uses both).
2. Capital treatment: AT1 if the trigger is 5.125% or higher, Tier 2 otherwise (GARP).
3. Mechanism: equity increases through conversion or write-down, not at the holder’s option (GARP).
4. Accounting motivation and its timing: CoCos “do not appear in the equity account until converted”, so the ROE advantage exists before conversion (GARP); Schweser: “during normal financial periods, the bonds are debt and thus do not drag down return on equity”.

The source of the accounting advantage is the denominator of ROE. While the CoCos are debt they are kept out of book equity, so a given net income is divided by a smaller equity base. Conversion is the event that moves them into the equity account, enlarging the denominator; it is the end of the advantage, not its source.

ROE = $\frac{\text{Net income}}{\text{Book equity}} ,$ CoCo outside equity ⇒ smaller denominator ⇒ higher reported ROE

**Applying it to this question**

Check each memo statement:

- A: matches Schweser’s Credit Suisse 2011 description (capital ratio trigger and supervisors’ public-aid judgment). Accurate.
- B: says the advantage comes from conversion adding the CoCos to the equity account. GARP says the advantage exists because they do not appear in the equity account until converted. Inaccurate.
- C: 6% ≥ 5.125%, so AT1 eligible. Accurate.
- D: GARP’s conversion or write-down mechanism, not at the holder’s option. Accurate.

**Fragile fact.** Source of the ROE advantage: CoCos sit outside the equity account until conversion; conversion brings them in and ends the advantage.

**Reference**

LO 63.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.” GARP Chapter 22, Section 22.4 “Resolution Planning and Preparation”, subsection “CoCos”. Schweser Reading 63, Module 63.3 “Contingent Convertible Bonds” and Key Concepts LO 63.g. Credit Suisse 2011 example is Schweser only (a condensed source); the 5.125% rule and the write-down route are GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-22 g, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (accurate statement (not the answer)). A is a correct summary of Schweser: Credit Suisse issued CoCos in 2011 that convert if Tier 1 equity to RWA falls below a threshold or if supervisors determine the bank needs public sector aid to avoid insolvency. A would be the answer only if it named a trigger the bonds did not have, such as a share-price rise.

b.reason: B is the least accurate statement. It is a polarity flip of GARP’s sentence: “because they do not appear in the equity account until converted, a bank can report a higher return on equity.” Adding the bonds to equity enlarges the ROE denominator, so it cannot be what produces the higher reported ROE.

c.reason: (accurate statement (not the answer)). C applies GARP’s threshold rule correctly (6% ≥ 5.125%). C would be the least accurate statement if the trigger were below 5.125%, for example 4.5%, which would make the bond Tier 2.

d.reason: (accurate statement (not the answer)). D is GARP’s mechanism. D would be the answer if it said that equity increases only through conversion, or that the holder chooses whether to convert.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 a Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a French universal bank is preparing a one-page briefing for a newly appointed board member who asks why the Basel Committee built the Basel III framework in the first place. Which of the following statements best describes the motivation for the Basel III framework as the Basel Committee sets it out?

options.text: It was designed mainly to lower the level of capital requirements so that banks could keep supporting the real economy through the economic cycle.
It addresses shortcomings in the pre-crisis regulatory framework and lays a foundation for a resilient banking system that helps avoid a build-up of systemic vulnerabilities.
It replaces the risk-weighted capital framework with a single leverage ratio, because risk weights had failed to prevent the systemic shocks of the crisis.
It concentrates on the solvency of each individual bank, leaving systemic risks from interlinkages across institutions to be handled by national authorities.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French bank briefing a new board member: why the Basel Committee built Basel III.

**Concept and theory**

Basel III is the Basel Committee’s response to the global financial crisis of 2007 to 2009. GARP opens Chapter 23 by stating that the framework “is a central element of the Basel Committee’s response to the global financial crisis” and that it “addresses a number of shortcomings in the pre-crisis regulatory framework and provides a foundation for a resilient banking system that will help avoid the build-up of systemic vulnerabilities.” It adds that the framework “will allow the banking system to support the real economy through the economic cycle.”

Schweser frames the same motivation from the failure side: the framework in place during the crisis “failed to prevent the systemic shocks that severely weakened the global banking system and the global economy”, and the Basel III revisions and the December 2017 reforms are designed to address those shortcomings.

Three ideas sit inside this motivation:

- **Shortcomings, not a blank sheet.** Basel III repairs a pre-crisis framework that existed but proved inadequate.
- **Resilience.** Banks must be able to absorb losses in stress. That is why the initial phase raised both the quality (CET1) and the level of capital.
- **Systemic focus.** The crisis showed that risk builds up across the system (interlinkages, procyclicality, systemically important banks), so Basel III added macroprudential elements on top of bank-by-bank rules.

Supporting the real economy through the cycle is the result of a resilient system, not a reason to cut capital.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the motivation as the Committee sets it out. Look for the option that combines (i) repairing pre-crisis shortcomings and (ii) building resilience against systemic vulnerabilities. Option B states both, almost word for word from the GARP introduction. Every other option contradicts one of the three ideas above.

**Fragile fact.** Basel III raised the quality and level of capital and added a systemic layer; “support the real economy” is an outcome of resilience, never a reason to lower capital.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms”, introduction (first section, before “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk”). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a, opening paragraph. No conflict: GARP states the resilience aim, Schweser states the crisis failure; both describe the same motivation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (polarity flip). The option borrows a true phrase (supporting the real economy through the cycle) but attaches it to lowering capital requirements. GARP lists “increasing the level of capital requirements to ensure that banks are sufficiently resilient to withstand losses in times of stress” as an initial-phase aim. Support for the real economy comes from resilience, not from lower capital. The option would be right only if the question asked about a deregulatory policy designed to boost lending at the cost of resilience, which Basel III is not.

b.reason: B matches GARP’s opening statement: Basel III “addresses a number of shortcomings in the pre-crisis regulatory framework and provides a foundation for a resilient banking system that will help avoid the build-up of systemic vulnerabilities.”

c.reason: (sibling swap). GARP describes the minimum leverage ratio as a requirement to “constrain excess leverage in the banking system and complement the risk-weighted capital requirements.” The option swaps “complement” for “replace” and so gives the leverage ratio a role it does not have. It would be right only if the stem described a hypothetical regime that abandoned risk weights altogether.

d.reason: (scope error). The option drops the systemic dimension. GARP’s initial phase added “macroprudential elements”, including a large exposures regime that “mitigates systemic risks arising from interlinkages across financial institutions” and a capital buffer for the externalities of systemically important banks. A bank-by-bank focus describes a purely microprudential regime, so this option would fit only a description of the pre-crisis framework’s weakness, not of Basel III’s aim.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 a Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore-based bank is reviewing a training slide headed “Initial phase of Basel III reforms (before the December 2017 finalisation)”. The slide lists the following measures:

I. Placing a greater focus on going-concern loss-absorbing capital in the form of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.

II. Introducing the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and the Net Stable Funding Ratio to mitigate excessive liquidity risk and maturity transformation.

III. Removing the use of internal model approaches for calculating operational risk capital requirements.

IV. Establishing a large exposures regime that mitigates systemic risks arising from interlinkages across financial institutions and concentrated exposures.

Which of the measures are correctly placed under the slide’s heading?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore auditor: which of four measures belong to the initial phase of Basel III.

**Concept and theory**

GARP separates Basel III into two layers.

**Initial phase** (the post-crisis package that came first). GARP lists six components:

1. improving the **quality** of capital, with a greater focus on going-concern loss-absorbing capital in the form of CET1;
2. increasing the **level** of capital requirements so banks can withstand losses in stress;
3. enhancing **risk capture** in areas that proved “acutely miscalibrated”: market risk, counterparty credit risk and securitisation;
4. adding **macroprudential** elements: (i) capital buffers built up in good times and drawn down in stress to limit procyclicality, (ii) a **large exposures regime** that mitigates systemic risks from interlinkages and concentrated exposures, (iii) a capital buffer for the externalities created by systemically important banks;
5. a **minimum leverage ratio** to constrain excess leverage and complement risk-weighted requirements;
6. an international **liquidity** framework: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR).

**December 2017 finalisation** (“the Committee’s now finalised Basel III reforms complement these improvements”). Its four aims are: enhancing the standardised approaches for credit, CVA and operational risk; constraining internal model approaches (input limits under the IRB approach, removal of internal models for CVA and operational risk); a leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs; and a revised output floor.

**Applying it to this question**

Sort each statement into one of the two layers:

- I: CET1 focus. Initial phase, item 1. Correctly placed.
- II: LCR and NSFR. Initial phase, item 6. Correctly placed.
- III: removing internal models for operational risk. This is in the 2017 list (“removing the use of the internal model approaches for CVA risk and for operational risk”). Wrongly placed.
- IV: large exposures regime. Initial phase, item 4(ii). Correctly placed.

Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Removal of internal models for operational and CVA risk is a 2017 measure; CET1 quality, LCR and NSFR, buffers and the large exposures regime are initial phase.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction: list beginning “The initial phase of Basel III reforms focused on strengthening. . . ” and list beginning “The revisions seek to restore credibility. . . ”. Schweser LO 64.a lists only the four 2017 goals and does not list the initial-phase measures; the initial-phase list is GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). “I and II only” leaves out IV, treating the large exposures regime as if it were not part of the initial phase. GARP lists it explicitly under the macroprudential elements. A would be right only if statement IV had described something outside the initial phase, for example a 2017 item such as the G-SIB leverage ratio buffer.

b.reason: (sibling swap). “I, III and IV only” accepts III, attributing a December 2017 measure (removing internal models for operational risk) to the initial phase, and drops the genuine initial-phase LCR and NSFR. B would be right if the slide’s heading had read “Measures aimed at capital” and statement III had been an initial-phase capital measure such as raising the level of capital requirements.

c.reason: (sibling swap). “II and III only” makes the same 2017-for-initial swap on III, and also rejects two genuine initial-phase measures (I and IV). C would be right only if statements I and IV had described December 2017 measures (for example the G-SIB leverage ratio buffer and the revised output floor) and statement III had described an initial-phase measure such as the minimum leverage ratio.

d.reason: D is the only option that keeps all three initial-phase items (I, II, IV) and excludes the 2017 item (III), exactly as the GARP introduction separates them.

questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a German Landesbank is drafting a gap analysis that separates the measures adopted in the initial phase of Basel III from those added by the reforms finalised in December 2017. Which of the following measures was introduced by the December 2017 reforms rather than in the initial phase?

options.text: A leverage ratio buffer designed to further limit the leverage of global systemically important banks.
A minimum leverage ratio requirement designed to constrain excess leverage across the banking system.
A capital buffer designed to address the externalities created by systemically important banks.
Capital buffers designed to be built up in good times and drawn down in times of stress.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German Landesbank gap analysis: which measure was added in December 2017 rather than the initial phase.

**Concept and theory**

Three measures in this area sound alike but belong to different layers and do different jobs:

| Measure | Layer | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum leverage ratio | Initial phase | Constrain excess leverage across the system; complement risk-weighted requirements |
| Risk-weighted capital buffer for systemically important banks | Initial phase | Address the externalities created by systemically important banks |
| Leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs | December 2017 | Further limit the leverage of G-SIBs |

The 2017 buffer builds on the two initial-phase measures. GARP explains that, “to maintain the relative incentives provided by both capital constraints”, the finalised reforms add a leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs, consistent with the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer. Countercyclical-style buffers (built up in good times, drawn down in stress) are a fourth, separate initial-phase macroprudential element.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks which measure arrived in December 2017. Check each against the GARP lists. Only the leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs appears in the 2017 list: “introducing a leverage ratio buffer to further limit the leverage of global systemically important banks (G-SIBs)”. The other three are in the initial-phase list.

**Fragile fact.** Minimum leverage ratio and the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer are initial phase; the leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs is the 2017 addition.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction (both lists) and “Leverage Ratio Framework: Buffer for Global Systemically Important Banks”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a, third goal. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: A is the third of the four 2017 aims in GARP’s introduction, and Schweser’s LO 64.a list includes “Introducing a leverage ratio buffer for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs).”

b.reason: (sibling swap). The minimum leverage ratio is the initial-phase twin of the 2017 buffer. GARP lists “specifying a minimum leverage ratio requirement to constrain excess leverage in the banking system” under the initial phase. B would be right if the question asked which measure was introduced in the initial phase to constrain system-wide leverage.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The capital buffer for the externalities of systemically important banks is the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer, an initial-phase macroprudential element (item (iii) in GARP’s list). It shares the “G-SIB” label with option A but is risk-weighted, not leverage-based. C would be right if the question asked which initial-phase measure targeted systemically important banks through risk-weighted capital.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Buffers built up in good times and drawn down in stress “to limit procyclicality” are initial-phase macroprudential item (i). D would be right if the question asked which initial-phase measure addressed procyclicality.

questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.

questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 a Q4
questions.question: The treasurer of an Australian regional bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the reforms that the Basel Committee finalised in December 2017. She wants one sentence that captures what the revisions, taken together, were seeking to achieve. Which of the following statements is the most accurate summary of that aim?

options.text: To raise the quality of regulatory capital by placing a greater focus on going-concern Common Equity Tier 1 capital.
To introduce an international framework that mitigates excessive liquidity risk and maturity transformation at banks.
To restore credibility in the calculation of risk-weighted assets and improve the comparability of banks’ capital ratios.
To widen the dispersion of risk-weighted assets across banks so that capital ratios reflect each bank’s own model choices.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian treasurer to new analysts: one-sentence aim of the December 2017 revisions.

**Concept and theory**

After the initial phase, the main remaining problem was trust in the denominator of the capital ratio. A capital ratio is

Capital ratio = $\frac{\text{Regulatory capital}}{\text{Risk-weighted assets (RWA)}} .$

If two banks with similar portfolios report very different RWAs, mainly because their internal models differ, then their ratios cannot be compared and the RWA figures lose credibility. GARP states the purpose of the finalised reforms directly: “The revisions seek to restore credibility in the calculation of risk-weighted assets (RWAs) and improve the comparability of banks’ capital ratios”. They do so through four aims: better standardised approaches, constrained internal models, a G-SIB leverage ratio buffer and a revised output floor.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the aim of the 2017 revisions taken together. Two options describe genuine Basel III aims but from the initial phase (A and B). One option reverses the 2017 aim (D). Only C states the purpose GARP gives for the finalisation.

**Fragile fact.** The 2017 package is about the RWA denominator: restore credibility and comparability. CET1 quality and LCR/NSFR are initial-phase answers.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction, sentence beginning “The revisions seek to restore credibility. . . ”. Schweser LO 64.a does not state this overarching purpose (it says the reforms “are designed to address those shortcomings”); the deciding fact is GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). Improving capital quality through a greater focus on going-concern CET1 is the first item in GARP’s initial-phase list. A would be right if the question asked for the aim of the initial phase’s capital-quality reforms.

b.reason: (sibling swap). The LCR and NSFR liquidity framework is also an initial-phase component. B would be right if the question asked which initial-phase measure targeted liquidity risk and maturity transformation.

c.reason: C reproduces GARP’s statement that the revisions “seek to restore credibility in the calculation of risk-weighted assets (RWAs) and improve the comparability of banks’ capital ratios.”

d.reason: (polarity flip). The 2017 reforms aim to reduce unwarranted RWA variability and improve comparability. Widening the dispersion of RWAs is the problem, not the aim. GARP’s IRB section speaks of measures “to further reduce unwarranted RWA variability”. D would describe the shortcoming that motivated the reforms if it were phrased as a problem rather than a goal.

questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian commercial bank that uses only standardised approaches is preparing a report for the bank’s risk committee on how the December 2017 Basel III reforms affect banks like hers. Which of the following statements should she include in the report?

options.text: The reforms enhanced the robustness and risk sensitivity of the standardised approaches for credit risk, market risk and counterparty credit risk.
The reforms enhanced the robustness and risk sensitivity of the standardised approaches for credit risk, credit valuation adjustment risk and operational risk.
The reforms left the standardised approaches unchanged and directed every revision at banks that calculate capital with internal model approaches.
The reforms require a bank that relies only on standardised approaches to adopt internal model approaches in order to remain compliant with the Basel framework.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian SA-only bank: statement on how the 2017 reforms affect standardised-approach banks.

**Concept and theory**

The first of the four 2017 aims is “enhancing the robustness and risk sensitivity of the standardised approaches for credit risk, credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk and operational risk” (GARP). Schweser phrases it as “Expanding the robustness and sensitivity of the standardized approach (SA) for measuring credit risk, credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk, and operational risk.”

Why it matters: GARP notes that credit risk “accounts for the bulk of most banks’ risk taking activities” and that the standardised approach “is used by the majority of banks around the world, including in non-Basel Committee jurisdictions.” The SAs also anchor the revised output floor, so a better SA improves the floor too.

What the aim does not include: market risk, counterparty credit risk and securitisation were the “acutely miscalibrated” areas revised in the initial phase (the revised market risk framework was published in January 2016).

A further impact for SA-only banks: GARP’s transitional section states that “a jurisdiction which does not implement some or all of the internal-modelled approaches but instead only implements the standardised approaches is compliant with the Basel framework.”

**Applying it to this question**

The bank uses only standardised approaches, so the relevant aim is the enhancement of the SAs. The deciding detail is the list of three risk areas: credit, CVA and operational risk. Option B states exactly those three. A swaps in two initial-phase areas, C denies that SAs changed, and D contradicts the compliance statement.

**Fragile fact.** The 2017 SA aim covers credit, CVA and operational risk; market risk, CCR and securitisation were the initial phase’s “acutely miscalibrated” areas.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction (both lists); “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk” (opening paragraph); “Transitional Arrangements” (compliance of SA-only jurisdictions). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a, first goal. No conflict on content; Schweser says “expanding”, GARP says “enhancing”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). Market risk and counterparty credit risk belong to the initial-phase list of areas “that proved to be acutely miscalibrated, including the global standards for market risk, counterparty credit risk and securitisation”. A would be right if the question asked which areas of the risk-weighted framework the initial phase revised to enhance risk capture.

b.reason: B matches the first 2017 aim in both GARP and Schweser: SA robustness and risk sensitivity for credit risk, CVA risk and operational risk.

c.reason: (polarity flip). The SAs were the first target of the 2017 reforms, not left unchanged; the revised SA for credit risk, for example, makes residential mortgage risk weights depend on the loan-to-value ratio. C would be right only if the December 2017 package had consisted of the internal-model constraints alone, with no aim directed at the standardised approaches.

d.reason: (absolute claim). GARP states the reverse: a jurisdiction that implements only the standardised approaches is compliant. Nothing in the reforms forces adoption of internal models. D would be right only in a hypothetical regime where internal models were mandatory for internationally active banks.

questions.question: The head of model validation at a UK bank is checking a summary table, prepared for the board, of how the December 2017 reforms constrain the use of internal model approaches in three risk areas. Which of the following summaries is most accurate?

options.text: Credit risk: limits placed on certain inputs to the IRB approach. CVA risk: internal model approach removed. Operational risk: internal model approach removed.
Credit risk: internal model approach removed. CVA risk: limits placed on certain inputs to the internal model. Operational risk: internal model approach removed.
Credit risk: limits placed on certain inputs to the IRB approach. CVA risk: internal model approach kept, subject to input floors. Operational risk: internal model approach removed.
Credit risk: limits placed on certain inputs to the IRB approach. CVA risk: internal model approach removed. Operational risk: internal model approach kept, subject to an income floor.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK model validation: how the 2017 reforms constrain internal models in credit, CVA and operational risk.

**Concept and theory**

The second 2017 aim is to constrain internal model approaches. GARP is precise about how, and the mechanism differs by risk area:

| Risk area | Mechanism (GARP) | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Credit risk | Limits on certain inputs to the IRB approach (IRB remains available) | IRB approaches too complex, not comparable, not robust for some asset classes |
| CVA risk | Internal model approach removed | CVA is too complex to be modelled robustly and prudently by banks |
| Operational risk | Internal model approach (AMA) removed; single standardised approach | Capital proved insufficient; losses from misconduct and weak controls were hard to model |

GARP’s wording: “constraining the use of the internal model approaches, by placing limits on certain inputs used to calculate capital requirements under the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach for credit risk and by removing the use of the internal model approaches for CVA risk and for operational risk.”

Schweser compresses this to “Restricting the use of internal model approaches for credit risk, CVA risk, and operational risk”, which hides the difference between limiting (credit) and removing (CVA, operational).

**Applying it to this question**

Check each row of each option against the table. Credit risk must say “limits on inputs” (not removal); CVA must say “removed”; operational risk must say “removed”. Only option A has all three rows right.

**Fragile fact.** Credit risk: limit (IRB inputs constrained, IRB survives). CVA and operational risk: remove the internal model.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction (second aim); “Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk”; “CVA Risk Framework”; “Operational Risk Framework”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a, second goal. Difference: Schweser says “restricting” for all three areas; GARP distinguishes input limits (credit) from removal (CVA, operational). GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: A reproduces GARP’s mechanism for each of the three areas.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B swaps the credit and CVA treatments: it removes internal models for credit risk and merely limits inputs for CVA. In fact IRB approaches remain available for credit risk (with input floors and a narrower A-IRB scope), while the CVA internal model is gone. B would be right only if the credit and CVA rows were relabelled the other way round.

c.reason: (scope error). C correctly handles credit and operational risk but keeps the CVA internal model “subject to input floors”, extending the credit-risk mechanism to CVA. GARP says the revised CVA framework “removes the use of an internally modelled approach” and consists of a standardised and a basic approach. C would be right if the CVA row had read “internal model approach removed”.

d.reason: (scope error). D keeps the operational risk internal model with an “income floor”. GARP states that the AMA and the three existing standardised approaches “are replaced with a single risk-sensitive standardised approach to be used by all banks”; income is an input to that standardised approach, not a floor on an internal model. D would be right if the operational risk row had read “internal model approach removed”.
