questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 a Q7
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Japanese megabank is explaining to the board risk committee why the Basel Committee decided to constrain the use of internal model approaches in the December 2017 reforms. Which of the following reasons is the Basel Committee **least likely** to have cited?

options.text: The IRB approaches for credit risk were excessively complex, and banks’ internally modelled capital requirements lacked comparability.
CVA risk is a complex risk that, in the Committee’s view, banks cannot model in a robust and prudent manner.
Operational risk losses from events such as misconduct and inadequate systems and controls showed how hard such risk is to model.
Internal models had systematically produced higher capital requirements than the standardised approaches, penalising sophisticated banks.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese megabank CCO: least likely reason the Committee constrained internal models.

**Concept and theory**

Why would a regulator restrict the very models it once encouraged? GARP gives a separate reason for each risk area.

- **Credit risk (IRB).** “The financial crisis highlighted a number of shortcomings related to the use of internally modelled approaches for regulatory capital, including the IRB approaches to credit risk. These shortcomings include the excessive complexity of the IRB approaches, the lack of comparability in banks’ internally modelled IRB capital requirements and the lack of robustness in modelling certain asset classes.”
- **CVA risk.** CVA risk was “a major source of losses for banks during the global financial crisis, exceeding losses arising from outright defaults in some instances”; it “is a complex risk”, and “the Committee is of the view that such a risk cannot be modelled by banks in a robust and prudent manner.”
- **Operational risk.** Capital “proved insufficient to cover operational risk losses incurred by some banks”, and the nature of the losses (“misconduct, and inadequate systems and controls”) “highlighted the difficulty associated with using internal models”.

The common thread is that internal models produced capital that was too low, too variable or not credible. That is also why the output floor exists: it “places a limit on the regulatory capital benefits that a bank using internal models can derive relative to the standardised approaches.” The direction is always that models produced lower capital than the SAs.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a least likely question, so three options are genuine reasons and one is not. A, B and C each paraphrase one of the three GARP passages above. D claims internal models produced higher capital and penalised sophisticated banks, the reverse of the concern behind both the constraints and the output floor.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: internal models produced lower (and more variable) capital than the SAs. The fix limits the model benefit; it never protects banks from “too high” model capital.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk” (opening), “CVA Risk Framework”, “Operational Risk Framework”, “Output Floor”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a (second goal) and LO 64.b (IRB and operational risk paragraphs). The per-area shortcomings are discussed in the LO 64.b sections of both sources; they are used here only as the motivation for the LO 64.a goal. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (true statement, not the exception). Excessive complexity and lack of comparability are two of the three IRB shortcomings GARP lists. A would be the answer only if it had claimed IRB models were simple and highly comparable.

b.reason: (true statement, not the exception). GARP gives exactly this as the reason for removing the internal CVA model. B would be the answer only if it had said CVA risk could be modelled robustly but was removed for simplicity.

c.reason: (true statement, not the exception). GARP’s second operational risk shortcoming is that misconduct and weak systems and controls losses showed the difficulty of internal models. C would be the answer only if it had attributed the operational risk change to excessive capital rather than insufficient capital.

d.reason: D is the reason the Committee would not cite. The reforms constrain models because they let banks lower capital relative to the standardised approaches, which is why GARP describes the output floor as a backstop limiting “the extent to which banks can lower their capital requirements relative to the standardised approaches.”

questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 a Q8
questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a Canadian domestic bank asks the chief risk officer whether the leverage ratio buffer introduced by the December 2017 Basel III reforms applies to the bank, and why the buffer exists. The CRO tables the following data.

| Item | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Leverage ratio exposure measure | 85.0 | CAD billion |
| Tier 1 leverage ratio | 4.6 | % |
| CET1 risk-weighted capital ratio | 12.1 | % |
| Designated as a global systemically important bank | No |  |

Which of the following responses by the CRO is most accurate?

options.text: The buffer applies to the bank, because the reforms impose it on all internationally active banks to limit excess leverage in the system.
The buffer does not apply to the bank; it was introduced to replace the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer with a simpler, non-risk-based measure.
The buffer does not apply to the bank; it targets G-SIBs, to further limit their leverage and keep the relative incentives of both capital constraints.
The buffer does not apply while the bank’s leverage ratio stays above 3%; below that level it is triggered to limit procyclicality in a downturn.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian non-G-SIB bank: does the 2017 leverage ratio buffer apply, and why does it exist?

**Concept and theory**

Two capital constraints run side by side under Basel III:

- a **risk-weighted** requirement (capital over RWA), which for G-SIBs includes an additional risk-weighted G-SIB (higher loss-absorbency) buffer; and
- a **leverage ratio** (Tier 1 capital over a non-risk-based exposure measure), which GARP says “complements the risk-weighted capital requirements by providing a safeguard against unsustainable levels of leverage and by mitigating gaming and model risk”.

If only the risk-weighted requirement were raised for G-SIBs, the leverage ratio would become relatively less binding for them, and the balance between the two constraints would shift. GARP: “To maintain the relative incentives provided by both capital constraints, the finalised Basel III reforms introduce a leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs. Such an approach is consistent with the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer, which seeks to mitigate the externalities created by G-SIBs.” The introduction states its aim as “to further limit the leverage of global systemically important banks”. Scope follows from the purpose: the buffer applies to **G-SIBs**, not to every bank.

**Applying it to this question**

The decisive row in the table is “Designated as a global systemically important bank: No”. The leverage exposure measure, the 4.6% Tier 1 leverage ratio and the 12.1% CET1 ratio are deliberately irrelevant to whether the buffer applies, because applicability depends on G-SIB status. So the buffer does not apply, and the correct reason is the G-SIB-specific rationale.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the leverage ratio buffer applies to G-SIBs only; the minimum leverage ratio applies to all banks.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction (third aim) and “Leverage Ratio Framework: Buffer for Global Systemically Important Banks”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a (third goal) and LO 64.b (“Leverage Ratio Framework”). No conflict. The buffer’s calibration (50% of the risk-weighted higher-loss absorbency requirement) belongs to LO 64.b and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). A extends a G-SIB-only buffer to “all internationally active banks”. The system-wide leverage constraint is the minimum leverage ratio from the initial phase. A would be right if the question asked about the minimum leverage ratio requirement.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B gets the applicability right but the purpose wrong: the leverage buffer is “consistent with” the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer; it does not replace it. Both apply to G-SIBs together. B would be right only if the reforms had abolished the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer, which they did not.

c.reason: C gives both parts right: the buffer is for G-SIBs, and it exists to further limit G-SIB leverage while keeping the relative incentives of the risk-weighted and leverage constraints, as GARP states.

d.reason: (condition error). D invents a ratio trigger and borrows the procyclicality rationale of the initial-phase buffers that are built up in good times and drawn down in stress. The G-SIB leverage buffer depends on G-SIB status, not on whether a bank’s leverage ratio falls below 3%. D would be right only if the question described a countercyclical-style buffer.

questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.

questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 a Q9
questions.question: A policy analyst at a European banking supervisor is drafting the background section of a consultation on the December 2017 Basel III reforms. One paragraph must explain why the Basel Committee replaced the output floor that had been introduced under Basel II. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: The Basel II floor had been implemented inconsistently across countries, partly because it was based on Basel I standards that many banks and jurisdictions no longer applied.
The Basel II floor had restricted the capital benefit of internal models too severely, so the revised floor removes any limit on that benefit relative to standardised approaches.
The Basel II floor had applied only to banks using standardised approaches, so the revised floor extends a comparable minimum to banks using internal models.
The Basel II floor had been based on Basel III standardised approaches that proved miscalibrated, so the revised floor returns to Basel I capital requirements.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: European supervisor’s consultation: why the Basel II output floor was replaced.

**Concept and theory**

An **output floor** stops a bank’s modelled capital from falling too far below a simpler benchmark. Under Basel II, GARP says, the floor was “based on Basel I capital requirements” and “calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I capital requirements.”

Why replace it? GARP gives two linked reasons: “Implementation of the Basel II floor has been inconsistent across countries, partly because of differing interpretations of the requirement and also because it is based on the Basel I standards, which many banks and jurisdictions no longer apply.” What replaced it: “The Basel III reforms replace the existing Basel II floor with a floor based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches.” Its impact:

- it “places a limit on the regulatory capital benefits that a bank using internal models can derive relative to the standardised approaches” (a risk-based backstop);
- it “helps to maintain a level playing field between banks using internal models and those on the standardised approaches”;
- it “supports the credibility of banks’ risk-weighted calculations, and improves comparability via the related disclosures.”

Schweser’s summary of the goal: “Creating an output floor that is more robust and risk-sensitive than the current Basel II floor.”

**Applying it to this question**

The paragraph must explain why the old floor was replaced. Option A gives GARP’s two reasons: inconsistent implementation, partly because the benchmark was Basel I, which many no longer used. The other options misstate the direction of the floor, the banks it binds, or its basis.

**Fragile fact.** Old floor: Basel II floor, based on Basel I. New floor: based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches. The floor always binds banks using internal models.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction (fourth aim) and “Output Floor” (opening paragraphs). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a, fourth goal. The revised floor’s 72.5% calibration and the approaches used to calculate it belong to LO 64.c and are not tested here. Note: GARP’s “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk” section calls the floor being replaced “the existing Basel I floor”, while the “Output Floor” section calls it the Basel II floor based on Basel I; both describe the same floor. Schweser says “Basel II floor”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: A restates GARP’s reasons for replacing the Basel II floor.

b.reason: (polarity flip). The revised floor still limits the benefit of internal models; it does not remove that limit. GARP says it is “consistent with the original floor” in placing such a limit, and makes it more robust. B would be right only if the reform had abolished output floors, which is the reverse of what happened.

c.reason: (role misassignment). An output floor constrains banks using internal models; a bank on standardised approaches is already at the standardised result. C assigns the floor to the wrong group of banks. It would be right only if a floor had been designed to cap the capital of SA banks, which is not the purpose of any output floor.

d.reason: (sibling swap). D reverses the two bases: the Basel II floor was based on Basel I, and the revised floor is based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches. D would be right with the bases swapped back, that is, describing the move from Basel I to Basel III benchmarks.

questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Chinese joint-stock bank is preparing a note for the asset-liability committee on the implementation and impact of the December 2017 Basel III reforms. Her draft contains the following statements:

I. The revised standardised approach for credit risk and the revised IRB, CVA and operational risk frameworks are implemented from 1 January 2022.

II. A jurisdiction that implements only the standardised approaches, and none of the internal-model approaches, is compliant with the Basel framework.

III. Because the Basel framework sets maximum standards, a jurisdiction may not impose requirements that are more conservative than the reforms.

IV. The leverage ratio buffer for global systemically important banks is implemented from 1 January 2022.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank ALCO note: four statements on implementation and impact of the 2017 reforms.

**Concept and theory**

The reforms were announced in December 2017 but took effect later, and they set a floor for national rules, not a ceiling. GARP’s Table 23.5 gives the implementation dates:

| Revision | Implementation date |
|---|---|
| Revised SA for credit risk; revised IRB; revised CVA; revised operational risk | 1 January 2022 |
| Revised market risk framework | 1 January 2022 |
| Leverage ratio: existing exposure definition | 1 January 2018 |
| Leverage ratio: revised exposure definition; G-SIB buffer | 1 January 2022 |
| Output floor | Phased in from 1 January 2022 |

Schweser agrees: the Basel III revisions “will be implemented beginning in 2022.”

Two further impacts in GARP’s “Transitional Arrangements”:

- “a jurisdiction which does not implement some or all of the internal-modelled approaches but instead only implements the standardised approaches is compliant with the Basel framework”;
- “jurisdictions may elect to implement more conservative requirements and/or accelerated transitional arrangements, as the Basel framework constitutes minimum standards only.”

**Applying it to this question**

- I: 1 January 2022 for the revised SA credit, IRB, CVA and operational risk frameworks. True (Table 23.5).
- II: SA-only jurisdictions are compliant. True (Transitional Arrangements).
- III: claims the framework sets maximum standards. False; GARP says minimum standards, and stricter national rules are allowed.
- IV: G-SIB leverage buffer from 1 January 2022. True (Table 23.5).

Accurate set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Basel standards are minimum standards: national rules may be stricter, and an SA-only jurisdiction is still compliant. Main implementation date: 1 January 2022.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, Table 23.5 “Implementation Dates of Basel III Post-Crisis Reforms and Transitional Arrangement for Phasing in the Aggregate Output Floor”; “Transitional Arrangements”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a, opening paragraph (“implemented beginning in 2022”). Statements II and III draw on GARP-only content. The output floor phase-in percentages belong to LO 64.c and are not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). “I and II only” rejects IV, typically by assuming the G-SIB leverage buffer took effect with the existing leverage exposure definition in 2018 or with the end of the output floor phase-in. Table 23.5 gives 1 January 2022. A would be right if statement IV had given 1 January 2018 as the buffer’s start date.

b.reason: B is the only option that contains all three true statements and excludes III.

c.reason: (polarity flip). “I, III and IV only” accepts III, turning “minimum standards” into “maximum standards”, and rejects the true statement II. C would be right if III had read “Because the Basel framework sets minimum standards, a jurisdiction may impose more conservative requirements” and II had claimed SA-only jurisdictions were non-compliant.

d.reason: (scope error). “II and IV only” rejects I, for example by assuming the revisions took effect immediately in 2018 or only at the end of the floor phase-in in 2027. D would be right if statement I had given a date other than 1 January 2022.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a US bank holding company prepares a table that links shortcomings exposed by the financial crisis to the four aims of the December 2017 Basel III reforms.

| Row | Shortcoming observed |
|---|---|
| 1 | Bank-estimated probabilities of default and loss given default in some portfolios showed too little conservatism. |
| 2 | Across whole balance sheets, banks using internal models obtained large capital savings relative to the standardised approaches, weakening the level playing field. |
| 3 | The largest, globally systemically important banks ran high leverage, and their distress created externalities for the system. |
| 4 | A single flat risk weight applied to all residential mortgages, regardless of the loan-to-value ratio. |

The four aims are: (P) constraining internal model approaches; (Q) introducing a revised output floor; (R) introducing a leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs; (S) enhancing the robustness and risk sensitivity of the standardised approaches. Which of the following mappings is most accurate?
questions.solution:
Stem summary: US consultant’s table: mapping four crisis shortcomings to the four 2017 reform aims.

**Concept and theory**

Each of the four 2017 aims answers a specific shortcoming. Think of capital as a measurement system with four weak points:

| Shortcoming | Reform aim that answers it (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Bank-estimated model parameters lack conservatism | (P) Constraining internal models: IRB “input” floors “to ensure a minimum level of conservativism in model parameters” |
| Internal-model banks gain large capital savings versus SA banks; | (Q) Output floor: “places a limit on the regulatory capital benefits that a bank using internal models can derive relative |
| uneven playing field | to the standardised approaches” and “helps to maintain a level playing field” |
| Excess leverage at G-SIBs; | (R) Leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs: “to further limit the |
| externalities | leverage of global systemically important banks” |
| Flat, risk-insensitive SA risk weights | (S) Enhanced SA: “the Basel II standardised approach assigns a flat risk weight to all residential mortgages. In the revised standardised approach mortgage risk weights depend on the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio” |

The pairing that is easiest to confuse is P and Q, because both target internal models. The difference is the level at which they act: P works inside the model on individual parameters (PD, LGD); Q works on the total output, comparing aggregate modelled RWA with the standardised result.

**Applying it to this question**

- Row 1 is about parameter conservatism (PD, LGD): P.
- Row 2 is about aggregate savings relative to standardised approaches and the level playing field: Q.
- Row 3 is about leverage at G-SIBs: R.
- Row 4 is about a flat SA mortgage risk weight ignoring LTV: S.

Mapping: 1 P, 2 Q, 3 R, 4 S, which is option C.

**Fragile fact.** Input floors act on parameters inside the model; the output floor acts on the total RWA relative to the SA. Do not swap the two.

**Reference**

LO: “Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.” GARP Chapter 23, introduction (four aims); “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk”; “Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk”; “Leverage Ratio Framework”; “Output Floor”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.a (four goals) and LO 64.b. Mechanics of each revision (input floor values, LTV bands, 72.5% calibration) belong to LO 64.b and 64.c and are not needed to answer. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 a, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). A swaps P and Q: it treats parameter conservatism as an output-floor issue and whole-balance-sheet savings as an input-floor issue. Both target internal models, but at different levels. A would be right if row 1 had described aggregate savings versus the SA and row 2 had described weak PD and LGD estimates.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B swaps R and S: it answers G-SIB leverage with better SA risk weights and the flat mortgage weight with a leverage buffer. A leverage ratio is deliberately non-risk-based, so it cannot fix a risk-insensitive risk weight. B would be right if row 3 had described flat SA risk weights and row 4 had described excess leverage at G-SIBs.

c.reason: C is the only option in which each shortcoming is matched to the aim GARP links it to.

d.reason: (sibling swap). D swaps P and S: it treats weak bank-estimated parameters as a standardised-approach problem and flat SA mortgage weights as an internal-model problem. Bank-estimated parameters exist only under internal models; flat risk weights exist only under the SA. D would be right if row 1 had described the flat mortgage weight and row 4 had described weak PD and LGD estimates.

questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 b Q1
questions.question:
A senior credit risk analyst at a Canadian regional bank is presenting the December 2017 revisions to the standardized approach (SA) for credit risk to a group of newly hired analysts. Her draft slide contains the following statements:

I. The single risk weight previously applied to all residential mortgages is replaced by risk weights that depend on the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of the mortgage.

II. Mechanical reliance on credit ratings is reduced by prohibiting the use of external credit ratings in every jurisdiction that adopts the revised SA.

III. Credit conversion factors for off-balance sheet items are made more risk sensitive, including positive conversion factors for unconditionally cancellable commitments.

IV. The risk-weight treatment of unrated exposures to banks is made less granular, with a single flat risk weight replacing the earlier treatment.

Which of the statements on the slide are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian regional bank: audit of four slide statements on the revised standardized approach for credit risk.

**Concept and theory**

Credit risk accounts for the bulk of most banks’ risk taking and therefore of their regulatory capital. The standardized approach (SA) is the method most banks around the world use, including banks outside Basel Committee jurisdictions. Under the SA the bank does not model anything: it multiplies each exposure by a risk weight set by the regulator, and RWA is the sum. The weakness of the Basel II SA was that its risk weights were coarse. A single flat weight covered all residential mortgages, a flat weight covered unrated bank exposures, and the scheme leaned mechanically on external ratings.

The December 2017 revisions had three aims for the SA (GARP, “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk”):

(i) Improve granularity and risk sensitivity. Mortgage weights now depend on LTV; unrated bank exposures get a graded treatment (the SCRA grades A, B and C) instead of a flat weight; corporates get a more granular look-up table with a specific SME weight; covered bonds, project, object and commodities finance get standalone treatments; real estate, retail, subordinated debt and equity get finer weights; and credit conversion factors (CCFs) become more risk sensitive, with positive CCFs for unconditionally cancellable commitments (UCCs).

(ii) Reduce mechanistic reliance on credit ratings, by requiring banks to do sufficient due diligence and by building a granular non-ratings-based approach for jurisdictions that cannot or do not wish to rely on external ratings.

(iii) As a result, provide the foundation for the revised output floor (the floor mechanics belong to LO 64.c).

| Item | Basel II SA | Revised SA (Dec 2017) |
|---|---|---|
| Residential mortgages | One flat weight | Weight varies with LTV |
| Unrated bank exposures | Flat weight | Graded (SCRA A, B, C) |
| External ratings | Mechanical reliance | Due diligence; non-ratings route |
| UCCs | No positive CCF | Positive CCF (10%) |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the GARP list. I matches the mortgage example exactly. II overreaches: the reform reduces mechanical reliance; ratings remain usable where a jurisdiction permits them (Table 23.1 is literally split into “jurisdictions where the ratings approach is permitted” and those where it is not). III matches the off-balance sheet item. IV reverses the direction: unrated bank exposures move away from a flat weight. Accurate set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the revised SA reduces mechanical reliance on ratings; it does not ban them, and unrated exposures get more granular, not less granular, treatment.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk” and Table 23.1 (Overview of Revised Standardised Approach to Credit Risk). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, “Standardized Approach (SA) for Credit Risk”. Schweser says only “reducing the reliance on external credit ratings”; GARP adds the words “mechanistic” and the due-diligence and non-ratings mechanism. No conflict, Schweser is condensed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: (absolute claim). It includes II, which turns “reduce mechanistic reliance” into a blanket prohibition on external ratings in every jurisdiction. GARP keeps a ratings-based table for jurisdictions where ratings are permitted and adds a non-ratings approach only for jurisdictions that cannot or will not use them. II would be correct only if the stem said “for jurisdictions that do not permit the use of external ratings, the revised SA provides a non-ratings-based approach”.

b.reason: (polarity flip). It accepts II (absolute claim, as above) and IV, which flips “more granular than the existing flat risk weight” into “less granular, with a single flat weight”. IV would be true as a description of the Basel II treatment that the reform replaced, not of the revised SA.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It correctly includes I and III but adds IV, the reversed statement on unrated bank exposures. It would be right only if the revision had collapsed the SCRA grades into one flat weight, which is the opposite of what GARP describes.

d.reason: GARP states that mortgage risk weights now depend on LTV (I) and that CCFs are made more risk sensitive, “including the introduction of positive CCFs for” UCCs (III). Both statements survive; II and IV do not. Option D is the only option containing exactly I and III.

questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at an Australian mortgage lender is recomputing risk-weighted assets (RWA) for three residential mortgage loans under the revised standardized approach (whole loan approach). An excerpt of the applicable risk weights and the loan data are shown below. Under the lender’s previous approach, every residential mortgage carried the same flat risk weight of 35%. Where the revised-SA criteria are not met, the applicable counterparty risk weight is 75%.

| Revised SA, general residential real estate (excerpt) | Risk weight |
|---|---|
| LTV below 50% | 20% |
| LTV 50% to 60% | 25% |
| Criteria not met (any LTV) | Risk weight of counterparty |

| Loan | Balance (AUD million) | LTV (%) | Revised-SA criteria met? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4.0 | 45 | Yes |
| 2 | 6.0 | 58 | Yes |
| 3 | 2.0 | 52 | No |

What is the total RWA of the three loans under the revised standardized approach?

options.text: AUD 2.3 million
AUD 2.8 million
AUD 3.8 million
AUD 4.2 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian mortgage lender: RWA of three residential mortgages under the revised SA whole loan approach.

**Concept and theory**

Under the Basel II SA, a mortgage at 45% LTV and a mortgage at 95% LTV attracted the same weight, even though the borrower with little equity is far riskier and the collateral cushion is far thinner. The December 2017 revision makes the risk weight a function of the LTV band, so RWA now tracks the collateral cushion. GARP Table 23.1 gives, for general residential real estate under the whole loan approach, 20% below 50% LTV and 25% for 50% to 60% LTV, with the weight rising across higher bands. Where the qualifying criteria are not met, the LTV table is not used at all: the risk weight of the counterparty applies to the whole exposure.

RW(LTV band of loan $i$) if criteria are met

RWA = $\sum_{i} \text{Exposure}_{i} \times\text{RW}_{i}, \text{RW}_{i}$ = $\{$

RW of counterparty if criteria are not met

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one loan per line:

Loan 1 (LTV 45%, criteria met): 4.0 × 20% = 0.80

Loan 2 (LTV 58%, criteria met): 6.0 × 25% = 1.50

Loan 3 (criteria not met): 2.0 × 75% = 1.50

Total RWA = 0.80 + 1.50 + 1.50 = AUD 3.80 million

The flat 35% weight belongs to the old approach and is irrelevant to the revised calculation. The total RWA of AUD 3.8 million against total balances of AUD 12.0 million is an average weight of about 32%, but it is now driven loan by loan: the two qualifying loans carry low weights because of their equity cushions, while the non-qualifying loan carries the full counterparty weight.

**Fragile fact.** Condition: the LTV table applies only when the criteria are met; otherwise the counterparty weight applies to the whole loan, whatever its LTV.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Standardised Approach for Credit Risk” (residential real estate bullet) and Table 23.1, residential real estate exposures, whole loan approach. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b (mortgage LTV example). The 35% legacy weight and the 75% counterparty weight are stem inputs, not source values. The OCR of the GARP Table 23.1 header is garbled for the higher LTV bands, so the question uses only the two unambiguous bands (below 50%: 20%; 50% to 60%: 25%).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: (dropped term). AUD 2.3 million is 0.80 + 1.50, the RWA of Loans 1 and 2 only; Loan 3 has been left out, as if a loan that fails the criteria carried no capital. It would be correct only if the stem asked for the RWA of the qualifying loans.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). AUD 2.8 million is 0.80 + 1.50 + 2.0 × 25% = 2.80: Loan 3 is weighted by its LTV band (52% falls in 50% to 60%) even though the criteria are not met. It would be correct if Loan 3 met the revised-SA criteria.

c.reason: GARP: residential real estate risk weights “vary based on the LTV ratio of the mortgage (instead of the existing single risk weight)”, and where the criteria are not met the counterparty risk weight applies. Applying the band weights to Loans 1 and 2 and the counterparty weight to Loan 3 gives AUD 3.8 million.

d.reason: (sibling swap (old regime)). AUD 4.2 million is 12.0 × 35% = 4.20: the Basel II single flat weight applied to all balances. It would be correct if the question asked for RWA under the previous approach, which is exactly what the revision removed.

questions.question:
The CRO of a German banking group with supervisory approval for both the foundation IRB (F-IRB) and advanced IRB (A-IRB) approaches is planning the transition to the revised IRB framework. The group has total assets of EUR 310 billion and currently uses an internal-model approach for each of the four portfolios below.

| Portfolio | Description |
|---|---|
| P1 | Loans to corporates with consolidated revenues of EUR 750 million |
| P2 | Listed and unlisted equity holdings |
| P3 | Project finance loans (specialized lending) |
| P4 | Interbank placements with other banks |

Which of the following correctly states the most advanced approach that remains available for each portfolio under the revised framework?

options.text: P1: F-IRB; P2: SA; P3: A-IRB; P4: F-IRB
P1: A-IRB; P2: SA; P3: A-IRB; P4: F-IRB
P1: F-IRB; P2: F-IRB; P3: A-IRB; P4: F-IRB
P1: F-IRB; P2: SA; P3: F-IRB; P4: F-IRB

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German banking group: most advanced IRB approach still available for four portfolios.

**Concept and theory**

Under the IRB approaches the bank’s own models feed the Basel risk-weight function. In the advanced IRB (A-IRB) approach the bank estimates PD, LGD, EAD and maturity; in the foundation IRB (F-IRB) approach the bank estimates PD while LGD and EAD take fixed supervisory values. The crisis exposed three shortcomings: excessive complexity, lack of comparability of IRB capital across banks, and lack of robustness in modeling certain asset classes. The Committee therefore removed the A-IRB option for asset classes that cannot be modeled in a robust and prudent manner and removed IRB entirely for equities (GARP Table 23.2).

| Portfolio | Basel II: available | Basel III: available |
|---|---|---|
| Large and mid-size corporates (revenues > EUR 500m) | A-IRB, F-IRB, SA | F-IRB, SA |
| Banks and other financial institutions | A-IRB, F-IRB, SA | F-IRB, SA |
| Equities | Various IRB | SA |
| Specialized lending | A-IRB, F-IRB, slotting, SA | A-IRB, F-IRB, slotting, SA |

**Applying it to this question**

P1: consolidated revenues of EUR 750 million exceed EUR 500 million, so P1 is a large or mid-size corporate exposure: F-IRB at most. P2: equities lose all IRB approaches: SA. P3: specialized lending keeps A-IRB (GARP footnote 3: banks may continue using the advanced and foundation IRB approaches). P4: banks and other financial institutions: F-IRB at most. The total assets figure of EUR 310 billion is irrelevant; the corporate test uses the borrower’s consolidated revenues.

**Fragile fact.** Equities lose all IRB approaches; large and mid-size corporates and banks lose only A-IRB; specialized lending keeps A-IRB.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk”, “Removing the Use of the Advanced IRB Approach for Certain Asset Classes”, Table 23.2 and footnote 3. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, “Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) Approaches for Credit Risk”. Schweser does not mention the equity removal, the specialized lending carve-out or the EUR 500 million revenue threshold; these are GARP-only details.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: Option A lists F-IRB, SA, A-IRB and F-IRB, which is the Basel III column of Table 23.2 applied to each portfolio.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It keeps A-IRB for P1, which is only possible if the corporate fell below the large and mid-size threshold. The threshold is consolidated revenues above EUR 500 million, and EUR 750 million exceeds it. B would be correct if P1’s borrowers had revenues of, say, EUR 300 million (other corporates, where A-IRB remains available).

c.reason: (sibling swap). It gives equities the corporate treatment (A-IRB removed, F-IRB kept). For equities GARP removes all IRB approaches, leaving only the SA. C would be correct if P2 were a portfolio of large corporate loans rather than equity holdings.

d.reason: (scope or condition error (overextension)). It extends the A-IRB removal to specialized lending. Specialized lending keeps both the advanced and foundation IRB approaches (the Committee will review the slotting approach in due course). D would be correct if P3 were a loan to a large corporate rather than project finance.

questions.question:
A model validation analyst at a Japanese bank is checking parameter estimates for three IRB portfolios against the input floors in the revised IRB framework. Corporate X uses the A-IRB approach and Corporate Y uses the F-IRB approach, under which LGD is a supervisory value. All corporate exposures shown are unsecured.

| Portfolio | Approach | Bank PD (bp) | Bank LGD (%) | PD floor (bp) | LGD floor (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corporate X | A-IRB | 3 | 20 | 5 | 25 |
| Corporate Y | F-IRB | 4 | n/a | 5 | 25 |
| Retail revolvers | A-IRB | 8 | 55 | 10 | 50 |

Which of the following sets of adjustments is required by the revised framework?

options.text: Raise X’s PD to 5 bp and its LGD to 25%, raise the revolvers’ PD to 10 bp, and leave Y’s PD at 4 bp, as floors bind only under A-IRB.
Raise X’s PD to 5 bp and its LGD to 25%, raise Y’s PD to 5 bp, and raise the revolvers’ PD to 10 bp.
Raise X’s PD to 5 bp and its LGD to 25%, raise Y’s PD to 5 bp, and lower the revolvers’ LGD to 50%.
Raise X’s PD and Y’s PD to 5 bp and the revolvers’ PD to 10 bp, and leave X’s LGD at 20%, as LGD floors apply only to secured exposures.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank: applying revised IRB input floors to three portfolios.

**Concept and theory**

An input floor is a minimum value for a bank-estimated parameter. If the bank’s estimate is below the floor, the floor value is used; if the estimate is above the floor, the bank’s estimate stands. Floors exist to ensure a minimum level of conservatism in model parameters for asset classes where IRB remains available, and so to reduce unwarranted RWA variability across banks.

Which floors apply depends on which parameters the bank estimates:

| Floor | F-IRB | A-IRB |
|---|---|---|
| PD floor (bank estimates PD in both) | Applies | Applies |
| LGD floor | N/a (supervisory LGD) | Applies |
| EAD floor | Not applicable (supervisory EAD) | Applies if EAD modeled |

GARP Table 23.3 gives, among others: corporate PD 5 bp and unsecured LGD 25%; retail revolvers PD 10 bp and LGD 50%. Secured LGD floors vary by collateral type (0% financial, 10% receivables, 10% real estate, 15% other physical); for partially secured exposures a weighted average is used.

**Applying it to this question**

X (A-IRB): PD = max(3, 5) = 5 bp; LGD = max(20%, 25%) = 25%

Y (F-IRB): PD = max(4, 5) = 5 bp; LGD: supervisory, no floor test

Revolvers (A-IRB): PD = max(8, 10) = 10 bp; LGD = max(55%, 50%) = 55%

Three PDs are raised and one LGD is raised; the revolvers’ LGD of 55% is already above its floor and stays.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and approach: PD floors bind under both IRB approaches; LGD and EAD floors bind under A-IRB only, and a floor never lowers an estimate.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Specification of Input Floors”, Table 23.3 (Minimum Parameter Values in the Revised IRB Framework) and footnote 4. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b: “required input floors for PD, LGD, and EAD”. Schweser does not say which approach each floor applies to; the A-IRB-only scope of the LGD and EAD floors is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It restricts all floors to A-IRB and so leaves Y’s PD at 4 bp. Only the LGD and EAD floors are A-IRB-only; the PD floor applies in F-IRB too, because the bank still estimates PD there. A would be correct if the question concerned an LGD floor for Y.

b.reason: GARP: the floors “include PD floors for both the F-IRB and A-IRB approaches, and LGD and EAD floors for the A-IRB approach”. Option B raises all three PDs to their floors and raises X’s unsecured LGD to 25%, and nothing else.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It treats the floor as a target and lowers the revolvers’ LGD from 55% to 50%. A floor only ever raises an estimate; an estimate above the floor is kept. C would be correct only for a cap (a maximum), which the framework does not impose.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). It claims LGD floors apply only to secured exposures and so leaves X’s unsecured LGD at 20%. Table 23.3 gives an unsecured LGD floor (25% for corporates) alongside the collateral-specific secured floors. D would be correct if X’s LGD were already at or above 25%.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing a project memo that summarizes the December 2017 revisions to the IRB approaches for credit risk. Which of the following statements in the memo is most accurate?

options.text: Under F-IRB, banks estimate LGD and EAD while PD takes a fixed supervisory value, which removes two important sources of RWA variability.
The 1.06 scaling factor applied to IRB RWAs is retained, because the new input floors alone cannot remove unwarranted RWA variability.
For unsecured exposures to non-financial corporates, the supervisory F-IRB LGD is raised from 40% to 45% to add conservatism.
Under F-IRB, banks estimate PD while LGD and EAD take fixed supervisory values, which removes two important sources of RWA variability.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank audit: which memo statement on F-IRB and additional IRB enhancements is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The IRB revisions tackle RWA variability from three directions: (i) remove A-IRB where modeling is not robust; (ii) introduce input floors; (iii) specify estimation practices more tightly. Moving a portfolio from A-IRB to F-IRB matters because of who sets which parameter:

| Parameter | A-IRB | F-IRB |
|---|---|---|
| PD | Bank | Bank |
| LGD | Bank | Supervisor (fixed value) |
| EAD | Bank | Supervisor (fixed value) |

GARP says F-IRB removes “the two important sources of RWA variability” because it applies fixed values to LGD and EAD. The Committee also adjusted the F-IRB supervisory parameters: for exposures secured by non-financial collateral, collateral haircuts were increased and LGD parameters reduced; for unsecured exposures to non-financial corporates, the LGD parameter was reduced from 45% to 40%. Finally, given the IRB enhancements and the new aggregate output floor, the 1.06 scaling factor applied to IRB RWAs was removed.

**Applying it to this question**

The memo statements differ on one fact each: who sets which parameter (A and D), whether the 1.06 factor survives (B), and the direction of the unsecured LGD change (C). Only D gets its single fact right.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the F-IRB unsecured corporate LGD goes down, 45% to 40%, while haircuts on nonfinancial collateral go up; and the 1.06 factor is removed.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk”, “Removing the Use of the Advanced IRB Approach for Certain Asset Classes” and “Additional Enhancements”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, IRB bullets. The 1.06 scaling factor and the 45% to 40% change are GARP-only; Schweser mentions only “more specific requirements for how banks estimate model parameters”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: (role misassignment). It swaps the actors: the bank is said to estimate LGD and EAD while the supervisor fixes PD. That describes neither IRB approach. It would be correct only if the stem described a hypothetical approach with a supervisory PD, which does not exist in the framework.

b.reason: (polarity flip). The 1.06 scaling factor is removed, not retained, and GARP gives the reason: the IRB enhancements together with the new aggregate output floor. B would be correct for the pre-2017 Basel II IRB framework, where the 1.06 factor applied.

c.reason: (polarity flip). The unsecured LGD for non-financial corporates is reduced from 45% to 40%, not raised from 40% to 45%. C would be correct if the stem asked how the parameter moved if you ran the change in reverse (from the revised to the old value).

d.reason: D matches GARP: banks keep estimating PD under F-IRB (the PD floor applies to F-IRB precisely because PD is bank-estimated), while LGD and EAD are fixed, removing two important sources of RWA variability. Schweser agrees: F-IRB “requires fixed values for LGD and EAD”.

questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a Brazilian bank is presenting to its risk committee the three objectives behind the revised credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk framework. Which of the following pairs an objective with the design feature that the Basel Committee uses to achieve it?

options.text: Consistency: like the market risk approaches, the standardized approach rests on fair value sensitivities to market risk factors.
Risk sensitivity: the internally modeled approach is removed, because CVA risk cannot be modeled in a robust and prudent manner.
Robustness: the framework now captures the exposure component of CVA, which moves with transaction prices, along with its hedges.
Consistency: CVA risk is treated as a form of default risk, so its approaches are calibrated to the IRB framework for credit risk.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank: pairing each CVA objective with the correct design feature.

**Concept and theory**

CVA risk is the risk of mark-to-market losses on derivatives caused by deterioration in a counterparty’s creditworthiness. GARP notes it was a major source of bank losses in the crisis, in some instances exceeding losses from outright defaults. The initial phase of Basel III introduced a CVA capital charge; the December 2017 revision reshaped it around three objectives:

| Objective | Design feature (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Enhance risk sensitivity | Capture the exposure component of CVA (which depends on the prices of the transactions and so on market risk factors) together with its associated hedges; the old framework omitted it. |
| Strengthen robustness | CVA is complex and cannot be modeled robustly and prudently, so the internally modeled approach is removed; the framework consists of a standardized approach (SA-CVA) and a basic approach (BA-CVA). |
| Improve consistency | CVA risk is a form of market risk, so SA-CVA and BA-CVA are designed and calibrated consistently with the revised market risk framework: SA-CVA rests on fair value sensitivities to market risk factors, and BA-CVA is benchmarked to SA-CVA. |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for a correctly matched objective and feature. Each option names an objective and a feature; the test is whether the feature belongs to that objective. A pairs consistency with the fair value sensitivity design, which is exactly how GARP explains the consistency objective.

**Fragile fact.** Attribution: exposure component and hedges → risk sensitivity; no internal model → robustness; fair value sensitivities and market-risk alignment → consistency.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “CVA Risk Framework”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, “Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Risk Framework”. Wording difference: Schweser says the reform removes “the option of using the IRB approach to CVA risk”; GARP says it removes “the use of an internally modelled approach”. Same substance; GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: GARP, under “improve its consistency”: the SA-CVA, “like the market risk approaches, is based on fair value sensitivities to market risk factors”. Option A states this pairing.

b.reason: (sibling swap). Removing the internal model belongs to the robustness objective, not risk sensitivity. B would be correct if it were labeled “Robustness”.

c.reason: (sibling swap). Capturing the exposure component and its hedges belongs to the risk sensitivity objective, not robustness. C would be correct if it were labeled “Risk sensitivity”.

d.reason: (sibling swap (wrong parent framework)). GARP describes CVA risk as a form of market risk, realized through changes in the mark-to-market value of derivatives, and aligns the CVA approaches with the revised market risk framework, not with the IRB credit risk framework. D would be correct only if the Committee had treated CVA as default risk, which it explicitly does not.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a mid-sized Dutch bank is preparing for the revised CVA risk framework. Until now the bank has used an internally modeled approach for CVA risk. Its derivatives book is summarized below.

| Item | EUR billion |
|---|---|
| Aggregate notional, non-centrally cleared derivatives | 85.0 |
| Aggregate notional, centrally cleared derivatives | 140.0 |
| Counterparty credit risk capital charge | 0.9 |

Which of the following best describes how the bank may calculate its CVA capital charge under the revised framework?

options.text: It must use the standardized approach, because its total derivatives notional of EUR 225 billion exceeds the EUR 100 billion threshold.
It may keep its internally modeled approach, because its non-centrally cleared notional is below the EUR 100 billion threshold.
It may use the standardized or the basic approach, or set the charge as a simple multiplier of its counterparty credit risk charge.
It must set the charge as a simple multiplier of its counterparty credit risk charge, because this method is mandatory below EUR 100 billion.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Dutch bank: which CVA capital methods are available under the revised framework.

**Concept and theory**

After the revision, no bank may use an internal model for CVA risk. The framework consists of two approaches: the standardized approach (SA-CVA), based on fair value sensitivities, and the basic approach (BA-CVA), benchmarked to SA-CVA. GARP adds a proportionality option for smaller derivatives users: a bank with an aggregate notional amount of non-centrally cleared derivatives less than or equal to EUR 100 billion may calculate its CVA capital charge as a simple multiplier of its counterparty credit risk (CCR) charge.

| Bank profile | Available CVA methods |
|---|---|
| Non-centrally cleared notional > EUR 100bn | SA-CVA or BA-CVA |
| Non-centrally cleared notional ≤ EUR 100bn | SA-CVA, BA-CVA, or multiple of CCR charge (optional) |
| Any bank | Internal model: not available |

**Applying it to this question**

The relevant test uses only the non-centrally cleared notional: EUR 85.0 billion ≤ EUR 100 billion, so the simple multiplier is available as an option. The centrally cleared notional (EUR 140 billion) does not enter the test. The CCR charge of EUR 0.9 billion is the base to which the multiplier would apply, but its size does not affect which methods are available. The bank’s existing internal model must be abandoned.

**Fragile fact.** The EUR 100 billion test counts non-centrally cleared notional only, and passing it gives an option, not an obligation.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “CVA Risk Framework” (robustness bullet). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b: SA or basic approach required, IRB option removed. The EUR 100 billion simple-multiplier option is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It adds centrally cleared notional to reach EUR 225 billion. The threshold applies to non-centrally cleared derivatives only. A would be correct if the bank’s non-centrally cleared notional alone exceeded EUR 100 billion, and even then it could still choose BA-CVA, so “must use the standardized approach” would remain too strong.

b.reason: (absolute claim reversed (scope error)). The internal model is removed for all banks; the threshold unlocks a simpler method, not a modeled one. B would be correct only for the pre-revision framework.

c.reason: GARP: the revised framework “removes the use of an internally modelled approach” and consists of a standardized and a basic approach, and a bank at or below EUR 100 billion of non-centrally cleared notional “may” use a simple multiplier of its CCR charge. C lists all three permitted routes.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). It converts a permission (“may”) into an obligation (“must”). A bank below the threshold can still use SA-CVA or BA-CVA. D would be correct if the stem asked which simplified method is additionally available below the threshold.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a UK bank is reviewing a briefing on why and how the operational risk capital framework was revised in December 2017. The briefing contains the following statements:

I. Operational risk capital requirements before the crisis proved insufficient to cover the operational risk losses incurred by some banks.

II. Losses from events such as misconduct and inadequate systems and controls highlighted the difficulty of estimating capital with internal models.

III. The new standardized approach assumes that operational risk increases with a bank’s income, but at a decreasing rate.

IV. The advanced measurement approaches are withdrawn, but the three existing standardized approaches remain available as alternatives for smaller banks.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK bank board briefing: audit of four statements on the revised operational risk framework.

**Concept and theory**

Before the reform, banks could use the advanced measurement approaches (AMA), based on internal models, or one of three standardized approaches. GARP identifies two shortcomings exposed by the crisis:

(i) Capital requirements for operational risk proved insufficient to cover the operational risk losses incurred by some banks.

(ii) The nature of the losses (events such as misconduct and inadequate systems and controls) highlighted how hard it is to estimate operational risk capital with internal models.

The response was to streamline: the AMA and the three existing standardized approaches are replaced by a single risk-sensitive standardized approach used by all banks. It sets capital from two components, a measure of income and a measure of historical losses, on two assumptions: operational risk increases at an increasing rate with income, and banks with greater historical losses are more likely to suffer losses in future.

**Applying it to this question**

I and II are GARP’s two shortcomings, stated almost word for word. III flips “increasing rate” to “decreasing rate”. IV keeps the three old standardized approaches, but GARP replaces them along with the AMA. Accurate set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: operational risk rises with income at an increasing rate; and the single SA replaces the AMA and all three old standardized approaches.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Operational Risk Framework”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, “Operational Risk Framework”. Schweser says income is “assumed to be positively correlated with future operational risk” and does not state the increasing rate; GARP’s “increasing rate” wording is used here. No conflict in direction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: Option A (I and II only) contains both shortcomings and neither of the corrupted statements.

b.reason: (polarity flip). It includes III. GARP says operational risk increases “at an increasing rate” with income, which is why the BI marginal coefficients rise from 12% to 15% to 18%. III would be correct only if the coefficients fell as the BI grew.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). It includes IV, which keeps the three legacy standardized approaches for smaller banks. A single standardized approach is used by all banks; proportionality comes from the low first-bucket coefficient (and the ILM discretion), not from a separate approach. C also drops the true statement I.

d.reason: (scope or condition error). It adds IV to the two true statements. It would be correct only if the reform had withdrawn the AMA alone, which is a common half-remembered version of the change.

questions.question:
A senior operational risk analyst at a euro area bank is computing the bank’s operational risk capital under the new standardized approach. The national supervisor has used its discretion to set the internal loss multiplier (ILM) equal to one for all banks in its jurisdiction. The analyst has gathered the data below.

| Business indicator (BI) component | EUR billion |
|---|---|
| Interest, leases and dividends component | 18.0 |
| Services component | 15.0 |
| Financial component | 7.0 |
| Average annual operational risk losses, preceding 10 years | 0.5 |

| BI bucket | BI range | Marginal coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | up to EUR 1 billion | 0.12 |
| 2 | above EUR 1 billion, up to EUR 30 billion | 0.15 |
| 3 | above EUR 30 billion | 0.18 |

The bank’s operational risk capital requirement is closest to:

options.text: EUR 4.47 billion
EUR 6.27 billion
EUR 6.62 billion
EUR 7.20 billion

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Euro area bank: operational risk capital from BI components with the ILM set to one.

**Concept and theory**

The new standardized approach computes

Operational risk capital = BIC $\times\text{ILM}.$

- BI (business indicator) is a proxy for income: the sum of the interest, leases and dividends component, the services component and the financial component.
- BIC (business indicator component) = $\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} \text{BI}_{i}$, where $\text{BI}_{i}$ is the part of the BI that falls in bucket $i$ and $\alpha_{i}$ is the marginal coefficient for that bucket: 0.12 up to EUR 1 billion, 0.15 above EUR 1 billion up to EUR 30 billion, 0.18 above EUR 30 billion. Marginal means each coefficient applies only to the slice of BI inside its bucket, like income tax brackets. Rising coefficients encode the assumption that operational risk rises with income at an increasing rate.
- ILM (internal loss multiplier) is a function of BIC and the loss component (LC = 15× average annual losses over the preceding 10 years): ILM = ln $[e^{1} -$ 1 + $\text{(LC/BIC)}^{0.8}]$. At national discretion the supervisor may set ILM = 1 for all banks, so capital depends on BIC alone.

**Applying it to this question**

BI = 18.0 + 15.0 + 7.0 = 40.0

Bucket 1 slice = 1.0, 0.12 × 1.0 = 0.12

Bucket 2 slice = 30.0 − 1.0 = 29.0, 0.15 × 29.0 = 4.35

Bucket 3 slice = 40.0 − 30.0 = 10.0, 0.18 × 10.0 = 1.80

BIC = 0.12 + 4.35 + 1.80 = 6.27

Capital = BIC × ILM = 6.27 × 1 = EUR 6.27 billion

The loss data are irrelevant because the supervisor has set ILM to one. The bank’s capital is about 15.7% of its BI, an effective rate between the marginal 15% and 18% because most of the BI sits in bucket 2.

**Fragile fact.** Convention: the coefficients are marginal (each applies only to its slice of BI), and when ILM is set to one the loss history drops out of capital.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Operational Risk Framework” (BIC, BI buckets, ILM and footnote 5). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, mentions only income and historical losses; the BIC, bucket coefficients, LC and ILM formula are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: (intermediate result). EUR 4.47 billion is 0.12 + 4.35, the BIC accumulated through bucket 2 only; the EUR 10 billion slice above EUR 30 billion has been dropped. It would be correct if the BI were exactly EUR 30 billion.

b.reason: GARP gives capital = BIC × ILM, with marginal coefficients by bucket, and states that where supervisors set ILM equal to one, capital requirements “would be determined solely by the BIC”. That gives EUR 6.27 billion.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). EUR 6.62 billion applies a computed ILM despite the national discretion: LC = 15 × 0.5 = 7.5, LC/BIC = 7.5/6.27 = 1.196, $\text{1.196}^{0.8}$ = 1.154, ILM = ln($e -$ 1 + 1.154) = ln(2.872) = 1.055, so 6.27 × 1.055 = 6.62. It would be correct in a jurisdiction where the supervisor had not set ILM equal to one.

d.reason: (wrong input (average versus marginal coefficient)). EUR 7.20 billion is 0.18 × 40.0: the top bucket’s coefficient applied to the whole BI, as though coefficients were average rates. It would be correct only if the coefficient were a flat rate chosen by the bucket in which the total BI falls, which is not how the BIC works.

questions.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 b Q10
questions.question: A policy analyst at a national banking regulator is briefing the regulator’s board on the internal loss multiplier (ILM) in the new standardized approach for operational risk, where capital equals the business indicator component (BIC) multiplied by the ILM. Which of the following statements in the briefing is most accurate?

options.text: The loss component equals 15 times the bank’s average annual operational risk losses over the preceding five years.
Where the supervisor sets the ILM equal to one, banks are no longer required to disclose their historical operational risk losses.
The ILM rises as the ratio of the loss component to the BIC rises, although it does so at a decreasing rate.
The ILM rises as the ratio of the loss component to the BIC rises, and it does so at an increasing rate.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Regulator board briefing: properties of the internal loss multiplier.

**Concept and theory**

The ILM converts a bank’s own loss history into a scaling of its income-based capital. Its inputs are:

- LC (loss component) = 15× the bank’s average historical operational risk losses over the preceding 10 years.
- BIC (business indicator component), the income-based measure.

ILM = ln$[e^{1} -$ 1 + $\left( \frac{\text{LC}}{\text{BIC}} \right)^{0.8}]$

When LC/BIC = 1, ILM = ln($e$) = 1. A bank whose losses are high relative to its BIC has LC$/\text{BIC} >$ 1 and ILM > 1; a bank with relatively low losses has ILM \< 1. GARP states that the ILM increases as LC/BIC increases, “although at a decreasing rate” (the 0.8 exponent and the logarithm both dampen the response). This encodes the assumption that banks with more past losses are more likely to suffer future losses, without letting one bad history explode capital.

At national discretion a supervisor can set ILM = 1 for all banks in its jurisdiction; capital is then determined solely by the BIC. However, to aid comparability, all banks must still disclose their historical operational risk losses.

| LC/BIC | 0.5 | 2.0 |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{(LC/BIC)}^{0.8}$ | 0.574 | 1.741 |
| ILM | 0.830 | 1.241 |

Illustration: quadrupling LC/BIC from 0.5 to 2.0 raises the ILM by less than half, consistent with a decreasing rate.

**Applying it to this question**

The four statements test the look-back period (A), the disclosure rule under the discretion (B), and the shape of the ILM curve (C and D). Only C matches GARP.

**Fragile fact.** Two different curvatures: BIC rises with income at an increasing rate; ILM rises with LC/BIC at a decreasing rate.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Operational Risk Framework” and footnote 5. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b: historical losses “assumed to be positively correlated with future operational risk”. ILM formula, LC definition, the national discretion and the disclosure rule are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: (wrong input (look-back period)). LC is 15 times average historical losses over the preceding 10 years, not five. A would be correct if the stem specified a five-year averaging window, which the framework does not.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). Setting ILM to one removes losses from the capital calculation, but GARP keeps the disclosure requirement “to aid comparability”. B would be correct only if disclosure were tied to the use of losses in capital, which it is not.

c.reason: GARP: “The ILM increases as the ratio of (LC/BIC) increases, although at a decreasing rate.” Option C states exactly this.

d.reason: (polarity flip). It flips “decreasing rate” to “increasing rate”. D would be correct for the BIC’s relationship with income (rising marginal coefficients), not for the ILM’s relationship with LC/BIC.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 b Q11
questions.question:
A capital planning analyst at a Japanese global systemically important bank (G-SIB) is checking the bank against its leverage ratio requirements under the revised framework. The bank’s data are shown below.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Risk-weighted G-SIB higher-loss absorbency requirement (%) | 1.5 |
| Leverage ratio exposure measure (JPY trillion) | 120.0 |
| Tier 1 capital (JPY trillion) | 4.2 |
| of which Common Equity Tier 1 (JPY trillion) | 3.6 |
| CET1 risk-weighted capital ratio (%) | 12.4 |

The additional Tier 1 capital the bank needs in order to meet its full Tier 1 leverage ratio requirement, including the G-SIB leverage ratio buffer, is closest to:

options.text: JPY 0.00 trillion
JPY 0.30 trillion
JPY 0.90 trillion
JPY 1.20 trillion

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese G-SIB: additional Tier 1 capital to meet the leverage ratio requirement with the G-SIB buffer.

**Concept and theory**

The leverage ratio is Tier 1 capital divided by a non-risk-based exposure measure. It complements risk-weighted requirements by guarding against unsustainable leverage and by mitigating gaming and model risk in both internal models and standardized approaches. G-SIBs already face a risk-weighted higher-loss absorbency (HLA) buffer. If only the risk-weighted side were raised, the leverage ratio would bind less often for G-SIBs; to keep the relative incentives of the two constraints, the reforms add a leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs:

Leverage buffer = 50% × risk-weighted HLA requirement

Tier 1 leverage requirement = 3% + leverage buffer

The buffer must be met with Tier 1 capital (not only CET1).

**Applying it to this question**

Leverage buffer = 0.5 × 1.5% = 0.75%

Total Tier 1 leverage requirement = 3.00% + 0.75% = 3.75%

Required Tier 1 = 3.75% × 120.0 = 4.50

Current leverage ratio = 4.2/120.0 = 3.50%

Shortfall = 4.50 − 4.20 = JPY 0.30 trillion

The CET1 risk-weighted ratio of 12.4% is irrelevant to the leverage test. The bank meets the 3% minimum but falls 0.25 percentage points short of its buffered requirement, so it needs about JPY 0.30 trillion more Tier 1 capital.

**Fragile fact.** Numbers and capital tier: buffer = 50% of the risk-weighted HLA, added to the 3% minimum, and met with Tier 1, not CET1.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Leverage Ratio Framework”, “Buffer for Global Systemically Important Banks”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b: buffer for G-SIBs “that must be met with Tier 1 capital”. The 50% calibration and the 3% minimum are GARP-only in this reading.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: (dropped term). JPY 0.00 trillion tests only the 3% minimum: 3% × 120.0 = 3.60 \< 4.20, a surplus of 0.60, so no capital appears to be needed. It drops the buffer. It would be correct for a non-G-SIB bank with no leverage buffer.

b.reason: GARP: the G-SIB leverage ratio buffer “must be met with Tier 1 capital and is set at 50% of a G-SIB’s risk-weighted higher-loss absorbency requirements”, and the Tier 1 leverage ratio requirement is the 3% minimum plus the buffer. The calculation gives JPY 0.30 trillion.

c.reason: (wrong input twin). JPY 0.90 trillion uses CET1 instead of Tier 1 as the numerator: 4.50 − 3.60 = 0.90. The buffer is met with Tier 1 capital. It would be correct if the requirement had to be met with CET1 only.

d.reason: (dropped scaling (unit slip)). JPY 1.20 trillion sets the buffer equal to the full HLA: (3% + 1.5%) × 120.0 = 5.40, 5.40 − 4.20 = 1.20. It omits the 50% factor. It would be correct if the leverage buffer were 100% of the risk-weighted HLA requirement.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 b Q12
questions.question:
A risk committee member at a G-SIB is reviewing the bank’s capital position. The bank is subject to a 1% risk-weighted G-SIB buffer and a 0.5% leverage ratio buffer. It currently reports a CET1 risk-weighted ratio of 6.80% and a Tier 1 leverage ratio of 3.20%. The applicable conservation standards are shown below.

| CET1 risk-weighted ratio | Tier 1 leverage ratio | Minimum capital conservation ratio (% of earnings) |
|---|---|---|
| 4.5% to 5.375% | 3% to 3.125% | 100% |
| above 5.375% to 6.25% | above 3.125% to 3.25% | 80% |
| above 6.25% to 7.125% | above 3.25% to 3.375% | 60% |
| above 7.125% to 8.0% | above 3.375% to 3.50% | 40% |
| above 8.0% | above 3.50% | 0% |

Which minimum capital conservation ratio applies to the bank?

options.text: 0% of earnings
60% of earnings
70% of earnings
80% of earnings

questions.solution:
Stem summary: G-SIB with CET1 ratio 6.80% and Tier 1 leverage ratio 3.20%: applicable conservation ratio.

**Concept and theory**

The leverage ratio buffer works like the risk-weighted buffers: it is divided into five ranges, and a G-SIB that falls into a range must retain a minimum percentage of earnings (capital distribution constraints). The constraints depend on two ratios:

- CET1 risk-weighted ratio, against 4.5% minimum + 2.5% conservation buffer + G-SIB HLA (here 1%): full requirement 8.0%.
- Tier 1 leverage ratio, against 3% minimum + G-SIB leverage buffer (here 0.5%): full requirement 3.5%.

GARP’s rule: a G-SIB meeting both is unconstrained; one that misses one requirement faces that requirement’s conservation ratio; one that misses both faces the higher of the two conservation ratios.

**Applying it to this question**

CET1 ratio 6.80% ∈ (6.25%, 7.125%\] ⇒ 60%

Tier 1 leverage ratio 3.20% ∈ (3.125%, 3.25%\] ⇒ 80%

Both requirements missed ⇒ max(60%, 80%) = 80%

The bank must conserve at least 80% of its earnings: the leverage side is the binding constraint here, even though the bank is further from its risk-weighted requirement in absolute terms.

**Fragile fact.** When both requirements are missed, the constraint is the higher (more restrictive) of the two conservation ratios.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Buffer for Global Systemically Important Banks” and Table 23.4 (Capital Conservation Ratios for a G-SIB Subject to a 1% Risk-Weighted Buffer and 0.5% Leverage Ratio Buffer). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b does not cover distribution constraints; this is GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: (dropped term). 0% treats the bank as unconstrained because 6.80% exceeds the 4.5% CET1 minimum and 3.20% exceeds the 3% leverage minimum, ignoring the buffers stacked on top. It would be correct if the bank’s ratios were above 8.0% and 3.5%.

b.reason: (polarity flip). 60% takes the lower of the two conservation ratios (equivalently, looks only at the CET1 side). It would be correct if the bank met its leverage requirement and missed only the CET1 requirement.

c.reason: (wrong aggregation rule). 70% averages the two ratios. GARP specifies the higher of the two, not a blend. It would be correct under a hypothetical averaging rule that the framework does not use.

d.reason: GARP: “A G-SIB that does not meet both requirements will be subject to the higher of the two associated conservation requirements.” The higher of 60% and 80% is 80%.
