questions.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 b Q13
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of an Australian bank is preparing a regulatory update on the refinements to the leverage ratio exposure measure agreed in December 2017. Which of the following statements should be included in the update?

options.text: In exceptional macroeconomic conditions, a jurisdiction may exempt central bank reserves temporarily, if it recalibrates the minimum and banks disclose the impact.
A jurisdiction may exempt central bank reserves from the exposure measure permanently and at its discretion, with no change to the minimum requirement.
The refinements change how derivatives enter the exposure measure, and the treatment of client-cleared derivatives is now regarded as settled.
The refinements align off-balance sheet exposures with their measurement under the IRB approaches, rather than the standardized approach.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank compliance update: refinements to the leverage ratio exposure measure.

**Concept and theory**

Besides the G-SIB buffer, the Committee refined the definition of the leverage ratio exposure measure (the denominator):

- Derivatives: the way derivatives are reflected in the exposure measure is modified.
- Off-balance sheet exposures: their treatment is updated to be consistent with their measurement in the standardized approach to credit risk (the revised CCFs).
- Central bank reserves: jurisdictions may exercise national discretion, in periods of exceptional macroeconomic circumstances, to exempt central bank reserves from the exposure measure on a temporary basis. Jurisdictions that do so must recalibrate the minimum leverage ratio requirement commensurately to offset the impact, and must require banks to disclose the impact of the exemption on their leverage ratios.
- Client-cleared derivatives: the Committee continues to monitor the treatment and will review its impact on banks’ provision of clearing services and on central counterparty resilience.

Schweser summarizes the purpose as refining the exposure measure “to better reflect the exposure from derivatives and off-balance sheet items”.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option tests one feature: the conditions on the central bank reserve exemption (A and B), the status of client-cleared derivatives (C), and the reference point for off-balance sheet items (D). Only A keeps all three conditions of the exemption: exceptional circumstances, temporary, with recalibration and disclosure.

**Fragile fact.** Conditions: central bank reserves exemption is discretionary, temporary, for exceptional conditions only, and comes with recalibration plus disclosure.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Leverage Ratio Framework”, “Refinements to the Leverage Ratio Exposure Measure”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b, “Leverage Ratio Framework” (derivatives and off-balance sheet bullet). The central bank reserve discretion and the client-cleared derivatives review are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: A restates GARP’s conditions: exceptional macroeconomic circumstances, temporary exemption, commensurate recalibration of the minimum and bank disclosure of the impact.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). It drops all three conditions: the exemption is temporary, available in exceptional circumstances, and requires a commensurate recalibration of the minimum. B would be correct only for a regime with an unconditional, permanent exclusion of central bank reserves.

c.reason: (absolute claim). The first half is true (derivatives treatment modified), but GARP says the Committee continues to monitor the treatment of client-cleared derivatives and will review its impact. C would be correct if it said the treatment remains under review.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Off-balance sheet exposures are aligned with the standardized approach to credit risk, not the IRB approaches. D would be correct with the two approaches reversed.

questions.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 b Q14
questions.question:
A junior analyst at an Indian bank is preparing a one-page summary of the December 2017 revisions. For which of the following areas did the revisions remove internally modeled approaches altogether, for all banks and all exposures, rather than restrict them?

I. The internal ratings-based approaches for credit risk

II. The CVA risk framework

III. The operational risk framework

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III
II and III only
III only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Indian bank summary: areas where internal models were removed outright rather than restricted.

**Concept and theory**

A recurring theme of the December 2017 revisions is constraining internal models. The degree of constraint differs across the five LO areas:

| Area | Internal models after reform | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| SA for credit risk | Not applicable | Standardized by design; made more granular |
| IRB for credit risk | Restricted | A-IRB removed for large and mid-size corporates and banks; F-IRB kept; IRB removed for equities; A-IRB kept for specialized lending; input floors added |
| CVA risk | Removed | SA-CVA or BA-CVA (or CCR multiplier at or below EUR 100bn) |
| Operational risk | Removed | AMA replaced by a single SA for all banks |
| Leverage ratio | Not applicable | Non-risk-based measure; G-SIB buffer added |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I fails the “altogether, for all banks and all exposures” test because F-IRB survives for corporates and banks and A-IRB survives for specialized lending. Statements II and III both pass: CVA’s internally modeled approach and operational risk’s AMA are removed for every bank.

**Fragile fact.** Removed outright: CVA and operational risk. Restricted only: IRB credit risk.

**Reference**

LO: “Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: the standardized approach to credit risk; the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk; the CVA risk framework; the operational risk framework; the leverage ratio framework.” GARP Chapter 23, “Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk”, “CVA Risk Framework” and “Operational Risk Framework”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.b key concepts: “restrict the use of the A-IRB approach”, “remove the option of using the IRB approach for CVA risk”, “allow only one SA for operational risk”. Wording note: Schweser calls the removed CVA method the “IRB approach”; GARP calls it “an internally modelled approach”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 b, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). It counts IRB as removed and omits operational risk. IRB is only restricted; the AMA is fully removed. A would be correct if the stem asked for areas where internal modeling was constrained and listed only those two.

b.reason: (scope or condition error (overextension)). It treats the partial IRB restriction as a full removal. B would be correct if the stem asked where internal models were constrained in any way.

c.reason: GARP: the CVA revision “removes the use of an internally modelled approach”, and for operational risk the AMA and the three old standardized approaches “are replaced with a single risk-sensitive standardised approach to be used by all banks”. For IRB, GARP describes removal of A-IRB only for certain asset classes. So II and III only.

d.reason: (sibling swap). It recognizes the operational risk removal but not the CVA removal, as if CVA kept an internal model the way IRB does. D would be correct under the pre-reform CVA regime, where an advanced, model-based method existed.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 c Q1
questions.question: The head of regulatory capital at a German universal bank with approval to use internal models is presenting the revised Basel III output floor to newly hired analysts. Which of the following statements best describes what the revised output floor does?

options.text: It places a minimum on Tier 1 capital relative to a non-risk-based exposure measure, acting as a backstop against excessive leverage at all banks.
It places a limit on the capital benefit that banks using internal models can derive relative to the standardised approaches, acting as a risk-based backstop.
It places a limit on the capital that banks using the standardised approaches must hold relative to internal models, acting as a ceiling on standardised RWAs.
It places a minimum on the bank-estimated PD, LGD and EAD values used as model inputs, acting as a floor on each modelled parameter.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German bank briefing: what the revised output floor does.

**Concept and theory**

Basel capital rules let a bank compute risk-weighted assets (RWAs) in two broad ways. The standardised approaches (SAs) apply regulator-set risk weights and formulas. Internal model approaches (for example IRB for credit risk) let a bank estimate risk parameters itself, subject to supervisory approval. Internal models usually produce lower RWAs than the SAs for the same exposures, and the financial crisis showed that such modelled requirements could be excessively complex, hard to compare across banks and not robust for some asset classes.

An output floor limits how far modelled RWAs can fall. GARP: “the revised floor places a limit on the regulatory capital benefits that a bank using internal models can derive relative to the standardised approaches. In effect, the output floor provides a risk-based backstop that limits the extent to which banks can lower their capital requirements relative to the standardised approaches.” It is called an output floor because it floors the result (total RWAs), not the inputs.

| Tool | What it constrains | Risk-based? |
|---|---|---|
| Output floor | Total RWAs relative to 72.5% of standardised RWAs | Yes |
| Leverage ratio | Tier 1 capital relative to an exposure measure | No |
| IRB input floors | Individual PD, LGD and EAD estimates | Parameter level |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks what the floor does. The deciding facts are the actor (banks using internal models), the reference point (the standardised approaches), the direction (a limit on the capital benefit, that is, on how low RWAs can go) and the label (a risk-based backstop). Option B contains all four.

**Fragile fact.** Output floor floors the result (total RWAs) against standardised RWAs; input floors floor the parameters. Same word, different level.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor”; contrast “Specification of Input Floors” (IRB) and “Leverage Ratio Framework”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c. Schweser frames the purpose as restricting large banks’ advantage; GARP speaks of any bank using internal models. Same substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). This describes the leverage ratio, a separate Basel III tool that sets Tier 1 capital against a non-risk-based exposure measure to constrain excess leverage. GARP describes the leverage ratio as complementing risk-weighted requirements by mitigating gaming and model risk, which is why it is easily confused with the floor. It would be correct if the stem asked what the leverage ratio requirement does.

b.reason: Option B restates GARP’s description of the revised floor almost word for word: a limit on the regulatory capital benefits that a bank using internal models can derive relative to the standardised approaches, providing a risk-based backstop. Schweser makes the same point: the floor restricts the ability of banks to gain an advantage by sharply reducing capital requirements through internal approaches instead of the SA.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It reverses the direction and the actor: the floor limits how low modelled RWAs can fall for banks using internal models; it does not cap how high standardised RWAs can be. No reform in the reading places a ceiling on standardised RWAs. It would be correct only if the stem described a hypothetical cap protecting standardised banks, which does not exist.

d.reason: (sibling swap). This describes the IRB input floors from LO 64.b: minimum values for bank-estimated PD (F-IRB and A-IRB) and LGD and EAD (A-IRB), which ensure a minimum level of conservatism in model parameters. The output floor works on the output (total RWAs), not on individual inputs. It would be correct if the stem asked about the revised IRB framework’s input floors.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 c Q2
questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Canadian bank is reviewing a briefing memo on the revised Basel III output floor. The memo contains the following statements:

I. The floor helps to maintain a level playing field between banks using internal models and banks on the standardised approaches.

II. The floor supports the credibility of banks’ risk-weighted calculations and improves comparability via the related disclosures.

III. Banks will be required to disclose their risk-weighted assets based on the revised standardised approaches.

IV. Once the floor is fully phased in, banks using internal models can no longer report total RWAs below their standardised-approach RWAs.

Which of the statements in the memo are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian board risk committee: audit of four statements on the purpose and disclosure of the output floor.

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives three reasons for the revised floor beyond the basic “backstop” idea:

- **Level playing field.** Without a floor, two banks holding identical portfolios could report very different capital ratios simply because one uses internal models. The floor “helps to maintain a level playing field between banks using internal models and those on the standardised approaches.”
- **Credibility.** The crisis damaged confidence in modelled RWAs. The floor “supports the credibility of banks’ risk-weighted calculations”.
- **Comparability via disclosure.** It “improves comparability via the related disclosures”: banks “will also be required to disclose their risk-weighted assets based on the revised standardised approaches”. Investors can then compare every bank on a common standardised yardstick.

The key quantitative feature: the floor is set at 72.5% of standardised-only RWAs, not 100%. A bank with internal models can still report RWAs as low as 72.5% of its standardised figure, so it keeps up to a 27.5% benefit.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: level playing field. True (GARP “Output Floor”).
- II: credibility and comparability via related disclosures. True (same paragraph).
- III: disclosure of RWAs based on the revised standardised approaches. True (GARP, end of the list of approaches).
- IV: claims fully phased-in models can no longer report RWAs below standardised RWAs. False: the floor is 72.5% of standardised RWAs, so modelled RWAs may sit anywhere between 72.5% and 100% (or above) of the standardised figure.

**Fragile fact.** The floor bites at 72.5% of standardised RWAs, not 100%: models keep up to a 27.5% benefit.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor” (purpose paragraph and disclosure sentence). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c covers the purpose and the 72.5% rule; the level playing field, credibility and disclosure points are GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). It rejects III, treating disclosure as outside the floor framework. GARP explicitly ties the floor to disclosure: banks must disclose RWAs based on the revised standardised approaches, and comparability is achieved “via the related disclosures”. “I and II only” would be right if III had claimed that banks must disclose their internal model parameters, which the reading does not say.

b.reason: (absolute claim). It accepts IV and drops I and III. IV promises a complete elimination of the model benefit; the true calibration of 72.5% leaves up to a 27.5% benefit. This set would be correct only if the floor were 100% of standardised RWAs and the floor had no level-playing-field or disclosure role, neither of which matches GARP.

c.reason: Option C (I, II and III only) is the only option that accepts the three statements GARP makes and rejects IV, which overstates the floor as if it were calibrated at 100%.

d.reason: (absolute claim). It accepts IV (the same 100% overstatement) and drops II, the credibility and comparability rationale that GARP states in the same sentence as the level playing field. “I, III and IV only” would be right if IV read “below 72.5% of their standardised-approach RWAs” and II were false.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 c Q3
questions.question: A policy analyst at the UK prudential regulator is drafting a history note on the capital floor that the December 2017 Basel III reforms replaced with the revised output floor. Which of the following statements most accurately describes the floor that was replaced?

options.text: It was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I requirements, and was implemented inconsistently partly because many banks no longer apply Basel I standards.
It was calibrated at 72.5% of the relevant Basel I requirements, and was implemented inconsistently partly because many banks no longer apply Basel I standards.
It was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I requirements, and was implemented uniformly because all jurisdictions shared one interpretation of the rule.
It was calibrated at 80% of the revised Basel III standardised requirements, and was implemented inconsistently partly because of differing interpretations.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK regulator history note: the floor replaced by the revised output floor.

**Concept and theory**

Floors are not new. GARP: “The Basel II framework introduced an output floor based on Basel I capital requirements. That floor was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I capital requirements.” Its purpose was the same as today’s: stop banks moving to Basel II internal models from cutting capital too far below the older, simpler rules.

Why replace it? GARP: “Implementation of the Basel II floor has been inconsistent across countries, partly because of differing interpretations of the requirement and also because it is based on the Basel I standards, which many banks and jurisdictions no longer apply.” A floor measured against rules that banks no longer run is hard to compute consistently. The reforms therefore “replace the existing Basel II floor with a floor based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches”, calibrated at 72.5%.

|  | Old (Basel II) floor | Revised (Basel III) floor |
|---|---|---|
| Benchmark | Basel I capital requirements | Revised Basel III SAs |
| Calibration | 80% | 72.5% (after phase-in) |
| Implementation | Inconsistent across countries | Common benchmark, with disclosure |

**Applying it to this question**

The note concerns the replaced floor. Three facts decide: the benchmark (Basel I), the calibration (80%) and the implementation record (inconsistent, for two reasons). Only option A gets all three right.

**Fragile fact.** Basel II floor, Basel I benchmark, 80%. Revised floor, Basel III SA benchmark, 72.5%. Keep the framework that introduced the old floor (Basel II) separate from the one it was measured against (Basel I).

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor” (opening paragraph); the introduction says the reforms replace “the existing Basel II output floor”, while the standardised credit risk section says the revised floor replaces “the existing Basel I floor”: both refer to the same Basel II-era floor based on Basel I. Schweser LO 64.a key concepts mention a “more robust and risk-sensitive” floor than the Basel II floor but give no calibration; the 80% and the implementation record are GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: Option A matches GARP: 80% of Basel I requirements, implemented inconsistently partly because the Basel I standards are no longer applied by many banks and jurisdictions.

b.reason: (sibling swap). It attaches the new floor’s calibration (72.5%) to the old floor’s benchmark (Basel I). The 72.5% figure belongs to the revised Basel III floor. Option B would be correct if the stem asked for the calibration of the revised floor and the benchmark were the Basel III standardised approaches.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It turns “inconsistent” into “uniform” and invents a single shared interpretation, whereas GARP cites differing interpretations as one cause of inconsistency. It would be correct only if the stem asked what the reforms were trying to achieve with a common benchmark.

d.reason: (sibling swap). It gives the old floor the new floor’s benchmark (revised Basel III standardised requirements). The Basel II floor was based on Basel I. It would be correct if “80%” were replaced by “72.5%” and the stem asked about the revised floor’s design.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is estimating the bank’s total risk-weighted assets (RWAs) under the revised output floor, assuming the floor is fully phased in. The bank has supervisory approval for internal models for credit risk and market risk only. Her data are shown below; the approved column uses IRB for credit risk and internal models for market risk, while CVA risk (BA-CVA) and operational risk (standardised approach) are the same in both columns.

| Risk category | Approved approaches (JPY trillion) | Standardised approaches only (JPY trillion) |
|---|---|---|
| Credit risk | 30.0 | 46.0 |
| Market risk | 4.0 | 5.0 |
| CVA risk | 2.0 | 2.0 |
| Operational risk | 6.0 | 6.0 |
| Leverage ratio exposure measure |  | 150.0 |

The bank’s total RWAs after applying the output floor are closest to:

options.text: JPY 42.00 trillion
JPY 42.78 trillion
JPY 45.35 trillion
JPY 47.20 trillion

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank: total RWAs after the fully phased-in output floor from a four-category table.

**Concept and theory**

The revised floor compares two totals. GARP: “banks’ risk-weighted assets must be calculated as the higher of: (i) total risk-weighted assets calculated using the approaches that the bank has supervisory approval to use in accordance with the Basel capital framework (including both standardised and internal model-based approaches); and (ii) 72.5% of the total risk-weighted assets calculated using only the standardised approaches.”

$\text{RWA}_{\text{floored}}$ = max$\left(\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}}, f \times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}\right)$

where $\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}}$ is total RWAs across all risk types using whatever mix of internal and standardised approaches the bank is approved for; $\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$ is total RWAs recomputed as if the bank used only the standardised approaches for every risk type; and $f$ is the floor percentage (72.5% when fully phased in). GARP calls it the aggregate output floor: the comparison is made once, on totals, not risk type by risk type.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\text{RWA}_{\text{floored}}$ = $\text{max(RWA}_{\text{approved}},$ 0.725 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$).

$\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}}$ = 30.0 + 4.0 + 2.0 + 6.0 = 42.0 trillion

$\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$ = 46.0 + 5.0 + 2.0 + 6.0 = 59.0 trillion

Floor amount = 0.725 × 59.0 = 42.775 trillion

$\text{RWA}_{\text{floored}}$ = max(42.0, 42.775) = 42.775 ≈ 42.78 trillion

The leverage ratio exposure measure (JPY 150 trillion) is irrelevant: it belongs to the leverage ratio, not the RWA floor. Meaning: the bank’s models cut RWAs by 1 − 42.0/59.0 = 28.8%, more than the 27.5% the floor allows, so the floor binds and adds JPY 0.775 trillion of RWAs.

**Fragile fact.** The floor is applied once, to total RWAs, at 72.5% of total standardised-only RWAs; never per risk category, and never at 80%.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor” (higher-of rule) and Table 23.5 (“Aggregate Output Floor”). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c, which states the same higher-of rule with “regulatory approval”. No conflict. Table data are illustrative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (dropped term). JPY 42.00 trillion is $\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}}$, the first leg alone, ignoring the floor leg. It would be correct if the bank’s approved RWAs were at or above 72.5% of standardised-only RWAs (for example, if standardised-only RWAs were JPY 57.9 trillion or less).

b.reason: Option B is the higher of the two totals, with the 72.5% applied to the total standardised-only RWAs, exactly as GARP and Schweser state.

c.reason:
(scope error). JPY 45.35 trillion applies the floor risk category by risk category and sums the results:

max(30.0, 33.35)+max(4.0, 3.625)+max(2.0, 1.45)+max(6.0, 4.35) = 33.35+4.0+2.0+6.0 = 45.35. Flooring each category separately removes the offset that the aggregate floor allows: in the aggregate test, categories whose approved RWAs sit above 72.5% of their standardised RWAs (market, CVA and operational risk here) cushion the credit risk shortfall. The reading defines one comparison on totals (an aggregate floor), so this is wrong. It would be correct only under a hypothetical rule that floored each risk category separately.

d.reason: (wrong percentile). JPY 47.20 trillion uses 80%, the calibration of the old Basel II floor: max(42.0, 0.80 × 59.0) = 47.2. It would be correct if the stem asked about the replaced Basel II-style floor applied to these figures.

questions.question: The treasurer of a Singapore bank that uses internal models for most of its credit portfolio asks the bank’s risk consultant: “Once the revised output floor is fully phased in, how far can our approved approaches lower total RWAs relative to the standardised approaches before the floor starts to bind?” Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: By up to 27.5%: the floor binds when approved-approach RWAs fall below 72.5% of total standardised-only RWAs.
By up to 20%: the floor binds when approved-approach RWAs fall below 80% of total standardised-only RWAs.
By up to 72.5%: the floor binds when approved-approach RWAs fall below 27.5% of total standardised-only RWAs.
By up to 27.5%: the floor binds when total standardised-only RWAs fall below 72.5% of approved-approach RWAs.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank: how far approved approaches can lower RWAs before the floor binds.

**Concept and theory**

The higher-of rule (Q4) can be read as a ratio test. Write

$r$ = $\frac{\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}}}{\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}} .$

The floor leg is 0.725 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$. The floor binds whenever $\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}} <$ 0.725 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$, that is, whenever $r <$ 0.725. Equivalently, the maximum reduction internal models can deliver relative to the standardised approaches is 1 − 0.725 = 27.5%. This is the quantitative meaning of GARP’s phrase “limits the extent to which banks can lower their capital requirements relative to the standardised approaches.”

**Applying it to this question**

The treasurer asks two things: the maximum reduction and the binding condition. From the rule:

Floor binds if $\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}} <$ 0.725 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$

Maximum reduction = 1 − 0.725 = 0.275 = 27.5%

Only option A pairs 27.5% with the correct binding condition (approved-approach RWAs compared with 72.5% of standardised-only RWAs).

**Fragile fact.** 72.5% is the floor level; 27.5% is the most models can save. The benchmark is always standardised-only RWAs.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor”. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c. The 27.5% figure is arithmetic from the 72.5% rule, not stated in either source. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: Option A follows directly from GARP and Schweser: RWAs are the higher of approved-approach RWAs and 72.5% of total standardised-only RWAs, so models can lower RWAs by at most 27.5% before the floor takes over.

b.reason: (wrong percentile). It uses the old Basel II floor’s 80% calibration, giving a 20% maximum reduction. It would be correct if the stem asked about the replaced floor calibrated at 80% of Basel I requirements.

c.reason: (polarity flip (complement swap)). It swaps the floor percentage with its complement: 72.5% is the retained share of standardised RWAs, not the permitted reduction, and 27.5% is the permitted reduction, not the floor level. It would be correct only if the floor were calibrated at 27.5% of standardised RWAs.

d.reason: (role misassignment). It reverses which total is floored against which: it compares standardised-only RWAs with 72.5% of approved-approach RWAs. The floor applies to the bank’s RWAs, using the standardised total as the benchmark. It would be correct only if the rule were written with the two legs exchanged, which neither source does.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a French bank is reviewing the methodology the bank uses to compute the “standardised approaches only” leg of its output floor. The methodology document specifies the following treatments:

I. Derivatives counterparty credit risk: exposure measured with SA-CCR, then multiplied by the counterparty’s risk weight under the standardised approach for credit risk.

II. CVA risk: 100% of the bank’s counterparty credit risk capital requirement, this being the CVA treatment the bank is eligible for and uses.

III. Securitisation exposures: the internal ratings-based securitisation approach that the bank’s supervisor has approved for its main RWA calculation.

IV. Operational risk: the standardised approach for operational risk.

Which of the treatments are consistent with the Basel III requirements for calculating the output floor?

options.text: I and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French bank internal audit: which methodology treatments fit the output floor rules.

**Concept and theory**

The floor’s second leg recomputes every risk type with a standardised (non-internal-model) method. GARP lists the approaches to be used:

| Risk type | Approach used for the floor |
|---|---|
| Credit risk | SA for credit risk; carrying value for credit risk mitigation (simple, or comprehensive with standard supervisory haircuts); includes failed trades and non-DvP transactions |
| Counterparty credit risk | SA-CCR for derivative exposure, then multiplied by the borrower risk weight under the SA for credit risk |
| CVA risk | SA-CVA, BA-CVA or 100% of CCR capital requirement, depending on which the bank is eligible for and uses |
| Securitisation | SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or a 1250% risk weight |
| Market risk | Standardised (or simplified standardised) approach of the revised market risk framework |
| Operational risk | Standardised approach for operational risk |

The logic: the floor’s benchmark must be free of internal modelling, otherwise it would not be an independent backstop.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: SA-CCR exposure times SA credit risk weight. Consistent.
- II: 100% of CCR capital for CVA, where that is the treatment the bank is eligible for and uses. Consistent.
- III: an internal ratings-based securitisation approach. Not consistent: the only securitisation options are SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or 1250%.
- IV: standardised approach for operational risk. Consistent.

**Fragile fact.** Every input to the floor leg is standardised: securitisation is SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or 1250%, never an internal approach.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor” (list of standardised approaches to be used). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c (same list in condensed form; quiz Q6 tests the CVA options). No conflict on these items.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). It rejects II, treating the floor’s CVA treatment as limited to SA-CVA or BA-CVA. GARP (and Schweser) list a third option, 100% of the bank’s counterparty credit risk capital requirement, depending on which approach the bank is eligible for and uses. “I and IV only” would be correct if II had said the bank used an internal CVA model.

b.reason: (sibling swap). It accepts III, carrying the bank’s approved internal securitisation approach into the standardised-only leg, and rejects I. Using the bank’s main-calculation approach belongs to the first leg (approved approaches), not the floor leg. “II, III and IV only” would be correct only if III named SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or 1250% and I had used the internal exposure model.

c.reason: Option C (I, II and IV only) accepts exactly the three treatments GARP lists and rejects the internal securitisation approach.

d.reason: (absolute claim). It treats every listed treatment as acceptable, including the internal securitisation approach. That would be right only if III were replaced by one of the three permitted securitisation methods.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Swiss bank is building the output floor calculation for one netting set of over-the-counter interest rate derivatives with an unrated corporate counterparty. The bank has supervisory approval to model counterparty exposure internally and to use the IRB approach for this counterparty. The inputs are:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Gross notional amount (EUR million) | 900.0 |
| Exposure under the bank’s internal exposure model (EUR million) | 36.0 |
| Exposure under SA-CCR (EUR million) | 50.0 |
| IRB risk weight for the counterparty (%) | 55.0 |
| Risk weight for the counterparty under the SA for credit risk (%) | 100.0 |

The amount this netting set contributes to the bank’s total RWAs calculated using only the standardised approaches is closest to:

options.text: EUR 27.50 million
EUR 36.00 million
EUR 36.25 million
EUR 50.00 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Swiss bank: one derivatives netting set’s contribution to standardised-only RWAs.

**Concept and theory**

For derivatives, the floor leg needs two things, each standardised. GARP: “to calculate the exposure for derivatives, banks must use the standardised approach for measuring counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR). The exposure amounts must then be multiplied by the relevant borrower risk weight using the standardised approach for credit risk to calculate RWA under the standardised approach for credit risk.”

$\text{RWA}^{\text{SA}}_{\text{CCR}}$ = $\text{EAD}_{\text{SA-CCR}} \times\text{RW}_{\text{SA}}$

where $\text{EAD}_{\text{SA-CCR}}$ is the exposure measured with SA-CCR and $\text{RW}_{\text{SA}}$ is the counterparty’s risk weight under the standardised approach for credit risk. The bank’s internal exposure model and IRB risk weight belong to the approved-approaches leg, not to the floor leg. The 72.5% factor is applied later, once, to the bank’s total standardised-only RWAs.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\text{RWA}^{\text{SA}}_{\text{CCR}}$ = $\text{EAD}_{\text{SA-CCR}} \times\text{RW}_{\text{SA}}$.

$\text{EAD}_{\text{SA-CCR}}$ = 50.0 million

$\text{RW}_{\text{SA}}$ = 100%

$\text{RWA}^{\text{SA}}_{\text{CCR}}$ = 50.0 × 1.00 = 50.0 million

The gross notional (EUR 900 million) is irrelevant: SA-CCR has already converted the netting set into an exposure amount. Meaning: this netting set adds EUR 50 million to total standardised-only RWAs, which will later be multiplied by 72.5% as part of the aggregate comparison.

**Fragile fact.** Floor leg for derivatives: SA-CCR exposure and SA credit risk weight; the 72.5% comes later, on the total.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor”, counterparty credit risk bullet. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c (“The SA for credit risk is then applied to the counterparty”). No conflict. Exposure and risk-weight figures are illustrative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (wrong input twin). EUR 27.50 million = 50.0 × 55%: correct SA-CCR exposure but the IRB risk weight. It would be correct if the stem asked for a hybrid that the rules do not allow; no source treatment pairs SA-CCR with an IRB weight for the floor leg.

b.reason: (wrong input twin). EUR 36.00 million = 36.0 × 100%: the internal model exposure with the SA risk weight. It would be correct if the floor allowed internally modelled exposures, which GARP rules out (“banks must use . . . SA-CCR”).

c.reason: (scope error). EUR 36.25 million = 0.725 × 50.0: applies the 72.5% factor at the netting-set level. The 72.5% is applied once to total standardised-only RWAs; it would be correct only if the stem asked for this netting set’s pro rata share of the floor amount.

d.reason: Option D uses the SA-CCR exposure and the SA borrower risk weight, the two inputs GARP prescribes.

questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-23 c Q8
questions.question: A risk consultant is validating the output floor methodology of a Chinese commercial bank and is checking the bank’s summary of the standardised approaches it uses for the floor calculation. Which of the following statements in the summary is NOT correct?

options.text: For the default risk charge on securitisations held in the trading book, the bank may use the internal models approach of the revised market risk framework.
For credit risk mitigation, the bank must use the carrying value when applying the simple approach or the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts.
For market risk, the bank uses the standardised approach, or the simplified standardised approach, of the revised market risk framework.
For CVA risk, the choice among SA-CVA, BA-CVA and 100% of the counterparty credit risk capital requirement depends on the bank’s eligibility and use.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank validation: which statement on floor approaches is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

Several floor approaches carry details that GARP states and Schweser compresses:

- **Credit risk mitigation.** “When calculating the degree of credit risk mitigation, banks must use the carrying value when applying the simple approach or the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts.” Bank-estimated haircuts are therefore excluded.
- **Market risk.** “The standardised (or simplified standardised) approach of the revised market risk framework.”
- **Trading-book securitisations.** “The SEC-ERBA, the SEC-SA or a 1250% risk weight must also be used when determining the default risk charge component for securitisations held in the trading book.”
- **CVA risk.** SA-CVA, BA-CVA or 100% of the CCR capital requirement, “depending on which approach the bank is eligible for and uses for CVA risk”.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT correct. B, C and D restate GARP. A allows the internal models approach for the trading-book securitisation default risk charge, which contradicts the requirement that SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or 1250% “must” be used. A is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** “Standardised only” reaches inside the market risk charge: trading-book securitisation default risk still uses SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or 1250%.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor” (credit risk, market risk and CVA bullets). Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c says only that the SA is permitted for market risk and lists the CVA options without the eligibility condition; the carrying-value rule and the trading-book securitisation rule are GARP only. No contradiction, only compression.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: Option A is NOT correct because the floor leg never uses an internal model; for the default risk charge on trading-book securitisations GARP mandates the same three securitisation methods as in the banking book.

b.reason: (correct statement, not the exception). This is GARP’s credit risk mitigation rule verbatim in substance. It would be the answer if it said “own-estimate haircuts” or “fair value adjusted by internal haircuts”.

c.reason: (correct statement, not the exception). GARP permits the standardised or the simplified standardised approach of the revised market risk framework. It would be the answer if it said “the internal models approach” or omitted the simplified option as forbidden.

d.reason: (correct statement, not the exception). GARP lists the three CVA treatments and ties the choice to eligibility and use. It would be the answer if it added an internal CVA model as a fourth choice.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank is computing total RWAs for reporting during calendar year 2026, using the output floor percentage that the Basel Committee’s transitional schedule sets from 1 January 2026. The supervisor has not exercised any discretion to cap the effect of the floor. The bank’s figures are:

| Item | BRL billion |
|---|---|
| Total RWAs under approved approaches (standardised and internal) | 500.0 |
| Total RWAs using only the standardised approaches | 900.0 |
| CET1 capital | 62.0 |

The bank’s total RWAs for 2026 after applying the output floor are closest to:

options.text: BRL 500.0 billion
BRL 585.0 billion
BRL 630.0 billion
BRL 652.5 billion

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank: floored RWAs for 2026 under the transitional schedule.

**Concept and theory**

The 72.5% calibration is the end point of a phase-in. GARP Table 23.5 (“Transitional Arrangement for Phasing in the Aggregate Output Floor”):

| From | Floor percentage (%) |
|---|---|
| 1 January 2022 | 50.0 |
| 1 January 2023 | 55.0 |
| 1 January 2024 | 60.0 |
| 1 January 2025 | 65.0 |
| 1 January 2026 | 70.0 |
| 1 January 2027 | 72.5 |

The percentage rises by 5 points a year, then by 2.5 points in the final step. Phasing in gives banks for which the floor binds time to adjust capital.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\text{RWA}_{\text{floored}}$ = $\text{max(RWA}_{\text{approved}}, f_{2026} \times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$).

$f_{2026}$ = 70%

Floor amount = 0.70 × 900.0 = 630.0 billion

$\text{RWA}_{\text{floored}}$ = max(500.0, 630.0) = 630.0 billion

CET1 capital (BRL 62 billion) is irrelevant to RWAs; it would matter only for a capital ratio. Meaning: the floor raises RWAs by BRL 130 billion in 2026, and will raise them further to 652.5 billion from 2027.

**Fragile fact.** 70% in 2026, 72.5% only from 1 January 2027; each year’s percentage starts on 1 January.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, section “Output Floor” and Table 23.5. Schweser Reading 64, LO 64.c gives only the 72.5% end point; the phase-in schedule is GARP only. Figures are illustrative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: (polarity flip). BRL 500.0 billion takes the lower of the two legs: min(500.0, 630.0). It would be correct only if the bank’s approved RWAs were at or above the floor amount (for example, standardised-only RWAs of BRL 714 billion or less in 2026).

b.reason: (wrong percentile). BRL 585.0 billion = 0.65×900.0 uses the 2025 percentage, a one-year slip in the schedule. It would be correct if the stem asked for reporting during 2025.

c.reason: Option C applies the 2026 percentage (70%) to total standardised-only RWAs and takes the higher of the two totals.

d.reason: (wrong percentile). BRL 652.5 billion = 0.725×900.0 uses the fully phased-in calibration. It would be correct for reporting from 1 January 2027.

questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian bank is reconstructing the bank’s total RWAs for 2025 for a back-testing review. The bank’s supervisor has exercised the national discretion available during the phase-in period to cap the increase in total RWAs that results from applying the output floor. The bank’s figures are:

| Item | AUD billion |
|---|---|
| Total RWAs under approved approaches, before the floor | 200.0 |
| Total RWAs using only the standardised approaches | 400.0 |

Using the output floor percentage applicable from 1 January 2025, the bank’s total RWAs for 2025 are closest to:

options.text: AUD 200.0 billion
AUD 215.0 billion
AUD 240.0 billion
AUD 250.0 billion

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank: 2025 RWAs with the transitional cap exercised.

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “at national discretion, supervisors may cap the increase in a bank’s total RWAs that results from the application of the output floor during its phase-in period. The transitional cap on the increase in RWAs will be set at 25% of a bank’s RWAs before the application of the floor. Put differently, if the supervisor uses this discretion, the bank’s RWAs will effectively be capped at 1.25 times the internally calculated RWAs during that time.”

$\text{RWA}_{t}$ = min$( \text{max} \left(\text{RWA}_{\text{pre}}, f_{t} \times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}\right),$ 1.25 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{pre}})$

where $\text{RWA}_{\text{pre}}$ is total RWAs under approved approaches before the floor, $f_{t}$ is the phase-in percentage and 1.25 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{pre}}$ is the cap.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\text{RWA}_{2025}$ = min $($ $\text{max(RWA}_{\text{pre}}, f_{2025} \times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$), 1.25 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{pre}})$.

$f_{2025}$ = 65%

Floor amount = 0.65 × 400.0 = 260.0 billion

Uncapped floored RWAs = max(200.0, 260.0) = 260.0 billion

Increase due to floor = 260.0 − 200.0 = 60.0 billion

Maximum increase = 0.25 × 200.0 = 50.0 billion

$\text{RWA}_{2025}$ = min(260.0, 1.25 × 200.0) = 250.0 billion

Meaning: the floor would add AUD 60 billion, but the cap limits the increase to AUD 50 billion during the phase-in.

**Fragile fact.** The cap’s base is pre-floor RWAs (cap at 1.25 times), and it applies only during the phase-in.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, “Transitional Arrangements” and Table 23.5. Schweser Reading 64 does not cover the phase-in or the cap; content is GARP only. Figures are illustrative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (dropped term). AUD 200.0 billion ignores the floor entirely (pre-floor RWAs). It would be correct only if the floor amount were at or below AUD 200 billion, for example a floor percentage of 50% or less on these figures.

b.reason: (wrong base). AUD 215.0 billion = 200.0 + 0.25 × 60.0: takes 25% of the floor-driven increase instead of 25% of pre-floor RWAs. It would be correct only if the cap were defined as a quarter of the increase, which GARP does not say.

c.reason: (wrong percentile). AUD 240.0 billion = max(200.0, 0.60 × 400.0) uses the 2024 percentage; the increase of 40 is below the cap, so the cap does not bind. It would be correct for 2024.

d.reason: Option D applies the 2025 percentage, then caps the increase at 25% of pre-floor RWAs, as GARP describes.

questions.question:
A supervisor at a national banking authority is preparing guidance on the transitional arrangements for the revised output floor. A draft lists the following statements:

I. Supervisors may, at national discretion, cap the increase in a bank’s total RWAs that results from applying the floor during its phase-in period.

II. Where the cap is used, it is set at 25% of the bank’s RWAs after the application of the floor.

III. The cap would be removed on 1 January 2027, when the floor reaches 72.5%.

IV. A jurisdiction may implement accelerated transitional arrangements, because the Basel framework constitutes minimum standards only.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Stem summary: National supervisor guidance: transitional arrangements for the output floor.

**Concept and theory**

The transitional arrangements around the floor have four features in GARP:

- **Discretion.** Supervisors may, at national discretion, cap the increase in total RWAs caused by the floor during its phase-in period. It is optional, not mandatory.
- **Base.** The cap is “25% of a bank’s RWAs before the application of the floor”, so RWAs are capped at 1.25 times internally calculated RWAs.
- **Duration.** “The cap would apply for the duration of the phase-in period of the output floor (i.e., the cap would be removed on 1 January 2027).”
- **Minimum standards.** “Jurisdictions may elect to implement more conservative requirements and/or accelerated transitional arrangements, as the Basel framework constitutes minimum standards only.”

**Applying it to this question**

- I: national discretion to cap during phase-in. True.
- II: base is RWAs after the floor. False: GARP says before.
- III: removed on 1 January 2027, when the floor reaches 72.5%. True (Table 23.5 and the cap sentence).
- IV: acceleration permitted because Basel sets minimum standards. True.

**Fragile fact.** Cap: optional (national discretion), base is pre-floor RWAs, gone from 1 January 2027.

**Reference**

LO: “Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.” GARP Chapter 23, “Transitional Arrangements” and Table 23.5. Schweser Reading 64 does not cover these arrangements; content is GARP only. Boundary call: the minimum-standards sentence is general, but it governs the floor’s phase-in, so it is treated as part of this LO.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-23 c, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). It rejects IV, treating the Basel phase-in schedule as a ceiling on how fast jurisdictions may move. GARP says jurisdictions may elect accelerated transitional arrangements because the framework sets minimum standards. “I and III only” would be correct if IV had said jurisdictions may slow the phase-in.

b.reason: Option B (I, III and IV only) accepts the three statements GARP makes and rejects II, which misstates the base of the cap.

c.reason: (polarity flip). It accepts II (“after” instead of “before” the floor) and rejects I. A cap measured on post-floor RWAs would be circular. It would be correct only if II said “before” and I had described the cap as mandatory.

d.reason: (absolute claim). It treats every statement as accurate, including II. It would be correct only if II were reworded to “RWAs before the application of the floor”.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German savings bank group is preparing a briefing for newly hired analysts on how the Basel III standardized approach (SA) for operational risk relates to the approaches that preceded it. The analyst drafts the following statements:

I. The AMA was introduced under Basel II as one of three approaches to operational risk capital, alongside the basic indicator approach (BIA) and the standardized approach of Basel II (TSA).

II. The SA replaces only the AMA, so the BIA and TSA remain available to banks that are not internationally active.

III. The SA applies to internationally active banks on a consolidated basis, and supervisors have discretion to apply it to banks that are not internationally active.

IV. Like the SA, the BIA was intended for use by internationally active banks and banks with significant operational risk exposures.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German savings bank briefing; four statements on the origin and scope of the SA and the earlier approaches.

**Concept and theory**

Basel II was the first accord to set a capital requirement for operational risk. It offered three approaches of rising sophistication. The basic indicator approach (BIA) set capital at 15% (the alpha factor) of average annual gross income over three years. The standardized approach (TSA) split gross income by business line and applied a beta of 12%, 15% or 18% to each line. The advanced measurement approaches (AMA) let a bank model its own capital with internal models, subject to supervisory validation. GARP (Chapter 2) notes the BIA “was not intended to be used by internationally active banks or banks with significant operational risk exposures.”

The December 2017 finalization of Basel III discontinued this three-tier regime. GARP Chapter 24 states that the new standardized approach “replaces all existing approaches in the Basel II framework” (paragraphs 644 to 683), and GARP Chapter 23 adds that the AMA and the existing standardized approaches are replaced “with a single risk-sensitive standardised approach to be used by all banks.” First published as the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA), it was later renamed the Standardized Approach (SA).

| Feature | Basel II regime | Basel III SA |
|---|---|---|
| Number of approaches | Three (BIA, TSA, AMA), bank chooses | One, for all banks |
| Scope | BIA aimed at simpler banks | Internationally active banks, consolidated; supervisors may extend |

**Applying it to this question**

I: true. The AMA was the most advanced of the three Basel II approaches. II: false. The SA replaces all existing approaches, not only the AMA, and the BIA was scheduled to be phased out on 31 December 2022. III: true. This is the scope of application stated in GARP 24.1. IV: false. The BIA was explicitly not intended for internationally active banks or banks with significant operational risk exposures. So only I and III are correct.

**Fragile fact.** The SA replaces all three Basel II approaches, not just the AMA; the BIA was never meant for internationally active banks.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.1 “Introduction”; GARP Chapter 23 “Operational Risk Framework”; GARP Chapter 2, “Pillar 1 Capital for Operational Risk” (BIA, TSA, AMA and SMA renamed SA); GARP Chapter 21 “Capital for Operational Risk”. Note: GARP Chapter 23 describes the old regime as the AMA plus “three standardised approaches”, while Chapter 2 counts the three approaches as BIA, TSA and AMA; the question avoids counting.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). Including II narrows the SA’s replacement to the AMA alone. The source says it replaces all existing Basel II approaches. A would be right only if the stem described the Basel II era, when banks chose among the three approaches, and asked which approaches coexisted.

b.reason: (scope error and sibling swap). Both II and IV are false: II wrongly keeps the BIA and TSA alive, and IV transfers the SA’s internationally active scope to the BIA. B would be right only if the question asked which statements are incorrect.

c.reason: Option C (I and III only) matches GARP 24.1: the SA “applies to internationally active banks on a consolidated basis” and “supervisors retain the discretion to apply” it to non-internationally active banks, while I matches the Basel II structure in GARP Chapters 2 and 21.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Statement IV attributes the SA’s intended population (internationally active banks) to the BIA, which was designed for simpler banks. D would be right if IV read “Unlike the SA, the BIA was not intended for internationally active banks.”

questions.question: The treasurer of a large Canadian bank (business indicator equivalent to EUR 45 billion) is reviewing the work of the operational risk modeling team. Under the AMA, the team estimated Pillar 1 capital with a loss distribution approach: a Poisson frequency, a lognormal severity, Monte Carlo simulation and the 99.9th percentile of one-year losses. Which of the following best describes what replaces this process for Pillar 1 capital under the SA?

options.text: A prescribed calculation in which the BIC, built from the business indicator and regulatory marginal coefficients, is scaled by an ILM derived from the loss component relative to the BIC.
The bank keeps its loss distribution model for Pillar 1, but the 99.9th percentile output may not fall below the BIC derived from the business indicator and marginal coefficients.
The 99.9th percentile output of the bank’s loss distribution model becomes the loss component, which is then compared with the BIC to derive the internal loss multiplier.
Only the BIC remains, because the SA is non-model-based and internal loss history no longer affects Pillar 1 operational risk capital for any bank, whatever its size.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank’s AMA loss distribution approach; what replaces it for Pillar 1 under the SA.

**Concept and theory**

Under the AMA, a bank built its own statistical model of operational losses. The common loss distribution approach fits a frequency distribution (for example Poisson) and a severity distribution (for example lognormal or Weibull), simulates many years of losses by Monte Carlo, and reads capital at the 99.9th percentile of one-year losses. The modeling choices were the bank’s own, subject to supervisory validation.

The SA removes these choices. Schweser describes it as “a single, nonmodel-based method” that “combines financial statement information with the internal loss experience of the specific bank.” GARP 24.2 gives its components:

ORC = BIC × ILM

BIC = $\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} \times$ (slice of BI in bucket $i$)$, \alpha_{1}$ = 12%$, \alpha_{2}$ = 15%$, \alpha_{3}$ = 18%

ILM = ln$[$exp(1) − 1 + $\left( \frac{\text{LC}}{\text{BIC}} \right)^{0.8}]$

LC = 15 × average annual operational losses over 10 years

where BI is the business indicator (a financial-statement proxy), $\alpha_{i}$ are the regulatory marginal coefficients, LC is the loss component and ILM is the internal loss multiplier. Every element is prescribed; no distribution is fitted and no quantile is estimated.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s BI of EUR 45 billion places it in bucket 3, so internal losses enter through the ILM. The question is what replaces the AMA model: the answer is a prescribed formula with no model choice, in which the bank’s own losses enter only as a ten-year average multiplied by 15.

**Fragile fact.** “Non-model-based” does not mean “loss-insensitive”: the SA still uses internal losses, through a prescribed LC, for banks above EUR 1 billion BI.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 “The Standardised Approach” (Business Indicator Component, Internal Loss Multiplier, Operational Risk Capital Requirement); GARP Chapter 4, “Capital Modeling for Operational Risk”; GARP Chapter 21, “Some Details of the AMA Approach”. The ILM formula is an image in the GARP Chapter 24 text; its wording is taken from GARP Chapter 23 footnote 5 and Chapter 2.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: A describes exactly the GARP 24.2 structure: BIC from BI and marginal coefficients, scaled by an ILM that depends on LC relative to BIC. This is the “single, nonmodel-based method” of Schweser 65.b.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B keeps the internal model and turns the BIC into a floor, which resembles the output floor that limits internally modeled credit and market risk capital. Under the SA there is no internal model for Pillar 1 operational risk capital at all; GARP Chapter 4 notes there are “no formal requirements” to model operational risk capital any more. B would be right for an approach that kept internal models subject to a standardized floor.

c.reason: (role misassignment). C gives the model output the role of the loss component. The LC is a prescribed quantity, 15 times the average annual losses of the previous ten years, not a simulated 99.9th percentile. C would describe a hypothetical hybrid in which a modeled quantile fed the multiplier.

d.reason: (scope error). D overextends a condition. Internal losses do not affect capital only for bucket 1 banks (BI up to EUR 1 billion) or where a supervisor sets the ILM to one for all banks. This bank is in bucket 3, so its losses do enter through the ILM. D would be right for a bucket 1 bank, or in a jurisdiction that sets ILM equal to one.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a French universal bank is validating a training note that compares the AMA with the SA. The note contains the following statements:

I. Under the AMA, capital was set to cover operational losses up to a 99.9% confidence level over a one-year horizon; under the SA, capital comes from prescribed coefficients applied to a financial-statement proxy, scaled by a loss-based multiplier.

II. A qualifying AMA framework had to draw on internal loss data, external loss data, scenario data and business environment and internal control factors; the SA loss component draws on the bank’s internal loss data.

III. Under the SA, as under the AMA, a bank may directly offset up to 20% of its operational risk capital requirement with insurance that meets stringent requirements.

IV. AMA methodologies varied widely across banks, often combining parametric Monte Carlo simulation with scenario analysis, whereas SA capital follows one formula for all banks.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French bank training note; four statements contrasting AMA mechanics with the SA.

**Concept and theory**

The AMA aimed to make regulatory capital reflect each bank’s risk profile “as closely as possible” (GARP Chapter 4). Its key features were:

- a one-year, 99.9% VaR-like loss measure (capital to cover losses in 999 out of 1,000 years);
- four required inputs: internal loss data (ILD), external loss data (ELD), scenario data (SD) and business environment and internal control factors (BEICF); GARP Chapter 21 adds that each need not enter the calculation directly but the overall process must include all four;
- wide methodological freedom: popular methods were a parametric Monte Carlo approach and scenario analysis, often combined;
- recognition of risk mitigants: a bank could offset at most 20% of the operational risk capital charge with insurance that met stringent requirements.

The SA instead computes ORC = BIC × ILM for all banks. Insurance has no separate capital offset in this formula. Insurance recoveries matter only in the loss data set: losses are recorded net of recoveries, and only once payment is received (GARP 24.6).

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (AMA 99.9% one-year; SA prescribed coefficients on BI times ILM). II: true (four AMA inputs; the SA loss component uses internal losses). III: false. The 20% insurance offset was an AMA feature; the SA formula has no such term. IV: true (AMA methods varied widely; SA is one formula). So I, II and IV are correct.

**Fragile fact.** The 20% insurance offset belongs to the AMA; under the SA insurance works only through recoveries, net of the loss, once received.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 4, “Operational Risk Regulatory Capital”; GARP Chapter 21, “Capital for Operational Risk” and “Some Details of the AMA Approach”; GARP Chapter 24, Sections 24.2 and 24.6 (“Gross Loss, Net Loss, and Recovery Definitions”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error (incomplete)). A omits IV, which is true: GARP Chapter 21 states that “AMA methodologies vary widely across different banks.” A would be right if IV claimed that AMA banks all used the same method.

b.reason: (scope error (incomplete)). B omits I, which is true. B would be right if I had a wrong confidence level or horizon, for example 99% over ten days.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C accepts III, which carries the AMA’s insurance offset over to the SA, and drops II. C would be right if III said “Under the AMA, but not under the SA, a bank could offset up to 20%. . . ” and II were false.

d.reason: D is the only option that includes all three true statements and excludes III. Each true statement is a direct contrast drawn from GARP Chapters 4, 21 and 24.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Brazilian bank is explaining to the board risk committee why the Basel Committee replaced the AMA with the SA. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Best practices emerged as AMA flexibility declined, but the calculations remained too complex, so the SA was designed mainly to simplify the work of banks that already produced comparable results.
The hope that best practices would emerge as AMA flexibility declined was never realized, so the wide range of modeling practices kept results hard to compare and calculations overly complex.
AMA models converged on comparable results, but they ignored each bank’s own loss experience, so the SA was designed mainly to bring bank-specific internal loss data into capital for the first time.
The AMA’s prescriptive rules left banks too little room to reflect their own risk profiles, so the SA was designed mainly to give banks more freedom to choose how they model operational risk.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian CRO explaining to the board why the SA replaced the AMA.

**Concept and theory**

The AMA, introduced with Basel II, was a principles-based framework. Rather than a formula, it set principles and let banks estimate capital with a range of internal modeling practices. The Basel Committee hoped that, over time, flexibility would narrow and best practices would emerge. Schweser states that “this never happened”: the variety of modeling practices left capital results hard to compare across banks, and the calculations stayed overly complex.

The Committee therefore set a goal of greater comparability and less complexity. The SA was the result: a single, non-model-based measure that still includes bank-specific loss data. GARP Chapter 23 places this within the wider Basel III aim to “restore credibility in the calculation of risk-weighted assets and improve the comparability of banks’ capital ratios”, partly by constraining internal model approaches.

|  | AMA | SA |
|---|---|---|
| Design | Principles-based, flexible | Single prescribed formula |
| Comparability | Poor (many modeling practices) | Higher (same formula) |
| Complexity | High | Lower |
| Internal losses | Used (one of four inputs) | Used (via LC and ILM) |

**Applying it to this question**

The board wants the reason. The deciding fact is that convergence never occurred, so comparability and complexity problems persisted. Any option that says convergence happened, or that the AMA ignored internal losses, or that the AMA was rigid, contradicts the source.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: flexibility belonged to the AMA, and best practices never emerged; the SA reduces flexibility.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” Schweser Reading 65, “Standardized Approach vs. Earlier Approaches”. The “best practices never emerged” account is from Schweser, a condensed source; GARP Chapter 24 does not discuss the rationale. GARP Chapter 23 (introduction) supports the comparability aim in general terms.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (polarity flip). A says best practices did emerge. The source says they did not. A would be right only in a counterfactual where AMA results had converged and complexity were the sole problem.

b.reason: B restates Schweser 65.b: the hoped-for best practices never emerged, the range of modeling practices impaired comparability, and calculations remained overly complex.

c.reason: (sibling swap). C claims the AMA ignored internal losses, which describes the BIA and TSA, not the AMA. Internal loss data were a required AMA input. C would be right if “AMA” were replaced by “BIA and TSA” and the claim about comparable results removed.

d.reason: (polarity flip). D reverses which framework was flexible. The AMA was the flexible, principles-based one; the SA removes modeling discretion. D would be right if it described the move from the BIA to the AMA under Basel II.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing a memo prepared for the board of a Singapore bank on the shortcomings of the earlier operational risk framework, which included the AMA, and on the assumptions of the SA that replaced it. Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT consistent with the Basel Committee’s reasoning?

options.text: The SA assumes that banks with larger historical operational losses are less likely to suffer future losses, because large past losses usually prompt remediation of controls.
The financial crisis showed that operational risk capital under the earlier framework proved insufficient to cover the operational losses incurred by some banks.
Losses from events such as misconduct and inadequate systems and controls highlighted how difficult it is to estimate operational risk capital with internal models.
The SA assumes that operational risk increases at an increasing rate with a bank’s income, which the rising marginal coefficients across the BI buckets reflect.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank board memo; which statement on the earlier framework’s shortcomings and the SA’s assumptions is NOT consistent.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Chapter 23 (“Operational Risk Framework”) gives two shortcomings of the pre-reform framework that the financial crisis exposed:

1. capital requirements for operational risk proved insufficient to cover the operational losses incurred by some banks;
2. the nature of those losses, such as misconduct and inadequate systems and controls, highlighted the difficulty of using internal models to estimate operational risk capital.

The replacement SA rests on two stated assumptions: (i) operational risk increases at an increasing rate with a bank’s income, captured by the BIC’s rising marginal coefficients (12%, 15%, 18%); and (ii) banks that have experienced greater operational losses historically are more likely to experience operational losses in the future, captured by the ILM rising with LC/BIC. Schweser 64.b describes both measures as “positively correlated with future operational risk.”

**Applying it to this question**

B and C restate the two shortcomings. D restates assumption (i). A reverses assumption (ii): it says higher past losses mean lower future losses. So A is the statement that is not consistent.

**Fragile fact.** Past losses are assumed to raise, not lower, future operational risk; LC above BIC means ILM above one.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 23, “Operational Risk Framework”; GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 “The Internal Loss Multiplier”; Schweser Reading 64, “Operational Risk Framework”. Boundary note: GARP Chapter 21 gives a different angle, that AMA capital at some banks became a material fraction of total capital because internal loss data included large penalties; the question relies on the Basel Committee’s account in Chapter 23.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: A is a polarity flip of the SA’s loss assumption. If the Committee believed past losses signaled lower future risk, the ILM would fall as losses rise. In fact GARP 24.2 states that a bank with high losses relative to its BIC “is required to hold higher capital.”

b.reason: (true statement (not the exception)). B matches GARP Chapter 23’s first shortcoming. It would be the answer only if the stem claimed capital had been excessive, which is not the Committee’s account.

c.reason: (true statement (not the exception)). C matches the second shortcoming. It would be the answer if it claimed internal models had captured misconduct losses well.

d.reason: (true statement (not the exception)). D matches assumption (i). It would be the answer if it said risk increased at a decreasing rate with income, which would imply falling marginal coefficients.
