questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is preparing a JPY-denominated report for the risk committee on how internal operational loss data enter regulatory capital under different approaches. Which of the following statements should the analyst include?

options.text: Internal loss data enter the capital calculation for the first time under the SA, since the BIA, the TSA and the AMA all relied only on income-based exposure indicators.
Under both the AMA and the SA, internal loss data are combined with external loss data, scenario data and control factors in a single model that determines capital.
The AMA used internal loss data as one of four required inputs to the bank’s own model, while the SA uses them in a prescribed loss component equal to 15 times average annual losses over ten years.
The AMA used internal loss data as one of four required inputs to the bank’s own model, while the SA uses them in a prescribed loss component equal to 15 times average annual losses over three years.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank report on how internal loss data enter capital under the AMA and the SA.

**Concept and theory**

A common misconception is that the SA introduced internal loss data into capital. It did not. Under Basel II:

- BIA and TSA: capital depends only on gross income; internal losses play no role.
- AMA: internal loss data are one of four required inputs (with external loss data, scenario data and BEICF) to the bank’s own model. GARP Chapter 21 notes at least five years of internal data were required.

Under the SA, internal losses enter through a prescribed loss component:

LC = 15 × average annual operational losses over the previous 10 years,

which drives the ILM. The ten-year window differs from the BI’s three-year averaging window. External data, scenarios and control factors do not enter the SA formula.

**Applying it to this question**

The report needs a statement that correctly describes both approaches. The test points are: did the AMA use internal loss data (yes); does the SA combine all four inputs (no, only internal losses); and is the LC window ten years (yes).

**Fragile fact.** Windows: BI is a three-year average; LC uses ten years of losses (five allowed during transition for non-AMA banks).

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 “The Internal Loss Multiplier”; GARP Chapter 4, “Operational Risk Regulatory Capital”; GARP Chapter 21, “Some Details of the AMA Approach”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). A puts the AMA together with the income-based BIA and TSA. The AMA did use internal loss data. A would be right if it said internal loss data entered capital for the first time under the AMA, compared with the BIA and TSA.

b.reason: (sibling swap). B carries the AMA’s four-input design over to the SA. The SA uses internal losses only. B would describe the AMA alone.

c.reason: C is consistent with GARP Chapter 4 (four AMA inputs) and GARP 24.2 (LC equals 15 times average annual losses over the previous ten years).

d.reason: (wrong input twin). D replaces the ten-year loss window with the three-year window used to average the BI. D would be right for the BI, not the loss component.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a small Australian mutual bank that used the TSA under Basel II and has now moved to the SA. The bank has ten years of high-quality loss data, including several large fraud losses, and its supervisor has not exercised national discretion to include internal loss data for banks in the first BI bucket. The bank’s figures, converted to EUR, are shown below.

| Item (EUR-equivalent) | Amount (EUR million) |
|---|---|
| Business indicator, three-year average | 750 |
| Gross income, three-year average | 680 |
| Average annual operational losses, past ten years | 30 |

The bank’s minimum operational risk capital under the SA is closest to:

options.text: EUR 90.0 million
EUR 102.0 million
EUR 112.5 million
EUR 150.8 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Small Australian bank, BI EUR 750 million, large loss history; SA capital.

**Concept and theory**

The SA applies the ILM only to banks above the first bucket. GARP 24.2: “For banks in bucket 1 (ie with BI ≤ EUR 1 billion), internal loss data does not affect the capital calculation. That is, the ILM is equal to 1, so that operational risk capital is equal to the BIC (= 12% · BI).” National supervisors may choose to include loss data for bucket 1 banks, but only if they exercise that discretion.

This creates an interesting comparison. For small banks, the SA behaves like the old indicator approaches (BIA, TSA): capital depends only on a financial-statement proxy, not on loss history. The differences are the proxy (BI rather than gross income) and the coefficient (12% rather than the BIA’s 15% alpha). For larger banks, the SA adds loss sensitivity through the ILM.

**Applying it to this question**

Bucket: BI = 750 ≤ 1,000 ⇒ bucket 1

BIC = 12% × 750 = 90.0 (EUR million)

ILM = 1 (bucket 1, no national discretion exercised)

ORC = 90.0 × 1 = EUR 90.0 million

The large fraud losses do not change capital under the SA, just as they did not under the TSA. Gross income and the loss average are irrelevant for this bank’s SA figure.

**Fragile fact.** Bucket 1 (BI up to EUR 1 billion): ILM equals one, so loss history does not affect capital unless the supervisor chooses otherwise.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 “The Standardised Approach Operational Risk Capital Requirement” and Table 24.1; GARP Chapter 21 (BIA at 15% of gross income). Boundary note: the bucket mechanics belong to LO 65.a; here they serve the comparison with the indicator approaches.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: A applies the bucket 1 rule: capital equals the BIC, 12%× BI.

b.reason: (sibling swap). EUR 102.0 million is the BIA charge: 15% × 680 = 102.0. It assumes small banks stay on the BIA, but the SA replaces all earlier approaches. B would be right under Basel II’s BIA.

c.reason: (wrong input twin). EUR 112.5 million is 15% × 750: the BIA alpha (or the bucket 2 coefficient) applied to the whole BI. C would be right only if the coefficient for BI up to EUR 1 billion were 15%.

d.reason:
(scope error). EUR 150.8 million applies the ILM despite the bucket 1 condition:

LC = 15 × 30 = 450$, \text{LC}/$BIC = 450/90 = 5

ILM = ln $[e -$ 1 + $\text{5}^{0.8}]$ = ln(1.7183 + 3.6239) = ln 5.3422 = 1.6756

ORC = 90 × 1.6756 = 150.8

D would be right if the supervisor had used its national discretion to include loss data for bucket 1 banks, or if BI exceeded EUR 1 billion.

questions.question: A junior analyst at a UK bank notes that the percentages 12%, 15% and 18% appear both in the Basel II standardized approach (TSA) and in the Basel III SA, and asks a senior analyst whether the two approaches use them in the same way. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Both the TSA and the SA set 12%, 15% and 18% by the perceived riskiness of each business line; the SA only swaps gross income for the business indicator as the exposure proxy.
The TSA set 12%, 15% and 18% by business line, whereas the SA sets them by BI size, with the coefficient of a bank’s bucket applied to its whole BI once the bank enters that bucket.
The TSA set 12%, 15% and 18% by the size of a bank’s gross income, whereas the SA sets them by business line, using the business indicator rather than gross income as the exposure proxy.
The TSA set 12%, 15% and 18% by business line, whereas the SA applies them as marginal coefficients to successive slices of the BI, so that capital grows more than proportionally with size.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK analyst asks whether 12%, 15% and 18% mean the same in the TSA and the SA.

**Concept and theory**

The same three percentages appear in both regimes, which makes them a classic trap.

**TSA (Basel II).** Gross income was split into eight business lines. Each line’s income was multiplied by a beta of 12%, 15% or 18% “depending on the perceived riskiness of the underlying business line” (GARP Chapter 2). For example, retail banking was weighted 12% and trading and sales 18%.

**SA (Basel III).** The exposure proxy is the business indicator, which “replaces the ‘gross income’ used in the former TSA approach.” The percentages are now marginal coefficients by size: 12% on BI up to EUR 1 billion, 15% on BI from EUR 1 billion to 30 billion, and 18% on BI above EUR 30 billion. Each coefficient applies only to the slice of BI in its bucket. Because the coefficients rise with size, capital grows more than proportionally with the bank’s size; GARP Chapter 2 says regulators have “recognized that the level of operational risk increases more than proportionally with size.” GARP also notes the SA “departed from this view” of business-line weights, because operational losses across business lines over the past 20 years “did not match expectations.”

|  | TSA | SA |
|---|---|---|
| Proxy | Gross income | Business indicator |
| 12/15/18% set by | Business line riskiness | Size slices of BI |
| How applied | Each line’s income × its beta | Marginal, slice by slice |

**Applying it to this question**

The senior analyst should say that the percentages coincide but their basis differs: business line in the TSA, size slice in the SA, applied marginally.

**Fragile fact.** TSA: by business line. SA: by size slice, marginal. Same numbers, different basis.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 2, “Pillar 1 Capital for Operational Risk” (From January 2023: Standardized Approach; Until January 2023: BIA, TSA, AMA); GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 “The Business Indicator Component” and Table 24.1; GARP Chapter 21, Example 21.4.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (sibling swap). A carries the TSA’s business-line logic into the SA. The SA explicitly moved away from business-line weights. A would be right as a description of the TSA alone.

b.reason: (scope error). B gets the basis right but applies the bucket coefficient to the whole BI. GARP’s example shows marginal slicing: for BI of EUR 35 billion, BIC = 1 × 12% + 29 × 15% + 5 × 18% = 5.37 billion, not 35 × 18% = 6.30 billion. B would be right for a step-function design rather than marginal coefficients.

c.reason: (role misassignment). C swaps the bases of the two approaches: size for the TSA and business line for the SA. C would be right if “TSA” and “SA” were exchanged and the SA’s marginal design described.

d.reason: D states both halves correctly: TSA betas by business line, SA marginal coefficients on successive BI slices, producing more-than-proportional growth.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a eurozone universal bank is estimating how the bank’s minimum operational risk capital would have changed had it moved directly from the BIA to the SA. The bank’s supervisor has confirmed an internal loss multiplier of 0.92.

| (EUR billion) | Year $t -$ 2 | Year $t -$ 1 | Year $t$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gross income | 27.4 | −1.2 | 30.6 |
| Net income | 3.2 | −4.9 | 4.1 |
| Business indicator, three-year average |  | 38.0 |  |

The change in minimum operational risk capital (SA capital minus BIA capital) is closest to:

options.text: +EUR 894 million
+EUR 1,087 million
+EUR 1,560 million
+EUR 2,537 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Eurozone bank, BIA versus SA capital, BI EUR 38 billion, ILM 0.92.

**Concept and theory**

**BIA.** Capital is 15% (alpha) of average annual gross income over the past three years. Years with negative or zero gross income are excluded from both numerator and denominator (GARP Chapters 2 and 21; Chapter 21’s example divides by two after dropping a negative year):

$K_{\text{BIA}}$ = 15% $\times\frac{\sum_{\text{years with} GI>0} GI_{t}}{n_{\text{positive years}}}$

**SA.** ORC = BIC × ILM, with marginal coefficients 12%, 15% and 18% on successive slices of BI. Net income plays no role in either approach; it is an irrelevant input here.

**Applying it to this question**

Positive gross income years: 27.4 and 30.6 (year $t -$ 1 of − 1.2 excluded)

Average gross income = (27.4 + 30.6)/2 = 29.0

$K_{\text{BIA}}$ = 15% × 29.0 = 4.350 EUR billion

BIC = 12% × 1 + 15% × (30 − 1) + 18% × (38 − 30)

= 0.12 + 4.35 + 1.44 = 5.910 EUR billion

$\text{ORC}_{\text{SA}}$ = 5.910 × 0.92 = 5.4372 EUR billion

∆ = 5.4372 − 4.350 = 1.0872 EUR billion ≈ +EUR 1,087 million

Interpretation: even with a favorable loss history (ILM below one), the switch raises capital by about a quarter, mainly because the marginal coefficients reach 18% above EUR 30 billion of BI.

**Fragile fact.** BIA: drop negative-income years from both the sum and the count. SA: coefficients are marginal, then multiply by the ILM.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 21, “Capital for Operational Risk” and Example 21.4; GARP Chapter 2 (BIA, alpha 15%, negative or zero years excluded); GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 and Table 24.1. Boundary note: the BIA and SA calculations themselves are LOs 62.g and 65.a; here they quantify the comparison.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: (wrong input twin). +894 million comes from applying a flat 15% to the whole BI: 15% × 38 × 0.92 = 5.244; 5.244 − 4.350 = 0.894. This uses the BIA alpha in place of the SA’s marginal coefficients. A would be right if the SA used a single 15% coefficient.

b.reason: B is the result of applying each approach’s own rules: BIA with the negative year excluded, SA with marginal coefficients and the ILM.

c.reason: (dropped term). +1,560 million omits the ILM: 5.910 − 4.350 = 1.560. C would be right for a bank in a jurisdiction where the ILM is set to one.

d.reason: (wrong denominator). +2,537 million divides the positive gross income by three instead of two: 15% × 58.0/3 = 2.900; 5.4372 − 2.900 = 2.537. Excluded negative years must also leave the denominator. D would be right only if all three years had been positive with the same total.

questions.question: A regulator at a national supervisory authority is comparing the supervisory work required under the AMA with that required under the SA. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Under the AMA, the supervisor prescribed one loss distribution model for all banks; under the SA, the supervisor must validate each bank’s own internal capital model before it can be used.
Under the AMA, approval typically took about three years and needed independent validation; under the SA, a bank that fails the loss data standards may return to its approved AMA model.
Under the AMA, the supervisor validated each bank’s own model, which took about three years to prepare; under the SA, a bank that fails the loss data standards holds at least 100% of the BIC.
Under the AMA, approval typically took about three years and needed independent validation; under the SA, if the supervisor sets the ILM to one, banks need not disclose historical losses.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Regulator comparing supervisory work under the AMA and the SA.

**Concept and theory**

**AMA.** Banks were “free to assess their own capital needs, provided that the regulatory authority of each country . . . validates its model and framework” (GARP Chapter 2). GARP Chapter 4 adds that obtaining AMA approval “took on average three years to prepare and required internal and external validation by independent parties and the fulfilment of around 30 criteria, both qualitative and quantitative.”

**SA.** There is no model to approve. The supervisory focus moves to loss data. GARP 24.4: banks with BI above EUR 1 billion must use loss data as a direct input; national supervisors “should review the quality of banks’ loss data periodically”; banks that do not meet the loss data standards must hold capital “at a minimum equal to 100% of the BIC”, and supervisors may require an ILM greater than one. GARP 24.2: at national discretion, supervisors may set the ILM equal to one for all banks, but banks “would still be subject to the full set of disclosure requirements.”

**Applying it to this question**

The correct statement must describe AMA model validation and the SA consequence of failing loss data standards. Any statement that keeps the AMA as a fallback, or that removes disclosure, contradicts the source.

**Fragile fact.** Failing SA loss data standards leads to at least 100% of the BIC (possibly ILM above one), never back to the AMA; ILM set to one does not remove disclosure.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 4, “Operational Risk Regulatory Capital”; GARP Chapter 2, AMA description; GARP Chapter 24, Sections 24.2, 24.4 “Minimum Standards for the Use of Loss Data Under the Standardised Approach” and 24.10 “Disclosure”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (role misassignment). A reverses the roles: under the AMA the bank built its own model and the supervisor validated it; under the SA there is no internal model to validate. A would be right if the regimes were swapped and the SA described as prescribing one method.

b.reason: (scope error). B lets a bank fall back on the AMA. The SA replaced all earlier approaches; the fallback for failed loss data standards is at least 100% of the BIC, possibly with an ILM above one. B would be right only under Basel II, when a bank could move between approaches.

c.reason: C pairs the AMA’s bank-by-bank model validation (about three years to prepare) with the SA’s 100% BIC minimum for banks that fail the loss data standards.

d.reason: (scope error). D drops a condition: when the ILM is set to one, disclosure obligations remain in full. GARP 24.10 requires such banks to disclose annual loss data for each of the ten years in the ILM window. D would be right if it said disclosure still applied.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a bank that used the AMA until the SA took effect is advising the head of operational risk. The bank has six years of high-quality internal loss data in a format the SA accepts, and a large team of experienced loss distribution modelers. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Like any bank with fewer than ten years of data, it is expected to use the five-year transitional treatment, and it may keep its AMA model for Pillar 1 capital until ten years of data exist.
The five-year transitional treatment is not expected to apply to banks that used the AMA, and the modeling team’s expertise can be redeployed to Pillar 2 capital assessment and stress testing.
Because it has fewer than ten years of high-quality data, it must calculate its capital requirement based solely on the BIC, and the modeling team’s expertise is no longer of any regulatory use.
The five-year transitional treatment is mandatory for banks that used the AMA, and the output of the bank’s former AMA model acts as a floor on its SA operational risk capital requirement.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Former AMA bank with six years of loss data and a large modeling team.

**Concept and theory**

**Data window and transition.** The LC must be based on ten years of high-quality annual loss data. As part of the transition, banks without ten years “may use a minimum of five years”; banks without five years must calculate capital solely on the BIC (GARP 24.2). Footnote 4 adds that “this treatment is not expected to apply to banks that currently use the advanced measurement approaches.” The reasoning: AMA banks already had to collect internal loss data, so they are expected to have the full history.

**Legacy of AMA modeling.** With the SA, “there are no formal requirements for financial institutions to model their operational risk capital anymore” (GARP Chapter 4). However, the knowledge built under the AMA is being transferred to Pillar 2 and ICAAP capital assessment, stress testing and operational resilience; “the logic of the approach has not changed with the decommissioning of AMA.”

**Applying it to this question**

The bank was an AMA user, so the five-year transitional relief is not expected to apply to it. Its modelers cannot be used for Pillar 1, but their skills transfer to Pillar 2 and stress testing.

**Fragile fact.** The five-year transitional minimum is aimed at banks that were not on the AMA; fewer than five years means BIC only.

**Reference**

LO 65.b (ORR 24.b), verbatim from Schweser: “Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).” GARP Chapter 24, Section 24.2 “The Internal Loss Multiplier” and footnote 4; GARP Chapter 4, “Capital Modeling for Operational Risk”. Schweser 65.a mentions the five-year transition but not the AMA exception; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 b, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (scope error). A applies the five-year relief to every bank, ignoring the AMA exception, and keeps the AMA for Pillar 1, which the SA replaced. A would be right for a former BIA or TSA bank, minus the AMA clause.

b.reason: B states both points from the source: footnote 4 on the transition and GARP Chapter 4 on redeploying AMA expertise.

c.reason: (scope error and absolute claim). C applies the BIC-only rule, which is for banks with fewer than five years of high-quality data, and says modeling has no regulatory use, contradicting its role in Pillar 2 and stress testing. C would be right for a bank with fewer than five years of data, without the second clause.

d.reason: (polarity flip and role misassignment). D makes the transition mandatory for AMA banks (the source says it is not expected to apply) and gives the old model output a floor role that no source describes. D would be right if it said the transition was not expected to apply and dropped the floor.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the general criteria for internally generated loss data used in the loss component of the Basel III standardised approach for operational risk. The bank is about to move to the standardised approach for the first time. Which of the following statements about the observation period should she present as most accurate?

options.text: A five-year observation period is the standard requirement, and it is extended to ten years once the bank has built up ten years of high-quality loss data.
A ten-year observation period is required; five years is accepted exceptionally on first adoption if good-quality data are unavailable beyond five years.
A ten-year observation period is required, but any bank may move to five years at any time if its supervisor judges its older loss data to be of poor quality.
A three-year observation period is required, consistent with the three-year averaging window that the standardised approach applies to the business indicator.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst presenting the loss data observation period to new hires, bank about to adopt the standardised approach.

**Concept and theory**

Under the Basel III standardised approach, a bank’s own loss history enters capital through the loss component (LC), which is built from average annual operational risk losses. An average is only meaningful if it covers enough years to capture the rare, severe events that dominate operational risk: a short window can easily contain no large loss at all, or one freak year, and either way it would misstate the bank’s exposure. That is why the Basel Committee fixes the length of the window as the first general criterion for loss data.

GARP 24.5(a) sets the rule in two layers:

| Layer | Rule |
|---|---|
| Standard | Internally generated loss data used for regulatory capital must be based on a **10-year** observation period. |
| Exception | When the bank **first moves** to the standardised approach, a **five-year** period is acceptable **on an exceptional basis** when good-quality data are unavailable for more than five years. |

The exception is transitional: it exists because many banks did not have a decade of clean, consistently collected data when the framework was introduced. It is not a permanent alternative, and it is triggered by the combination of first adoption and a lack of good-quality data beyond five years. (What happens when a bank has fewer than five years, namely capital based on the BI component alone, belongs to LO 65.a.)

**Applying it to this question**

The stem places the bank at the point of first adopting the standardised approach and asks for the most accurate description of the observation period. The deciding facts are the default length (ten years) and the narrow conditions for the five-year exception (first move, and good-quality data unavailable for more than five years). Option B states both.

**Fragile fact.** Ten years is the rule, five is the exception, and the exception needs both first adoption and a lack of good-quality data beyond five years; three years belongs to the BI, not to losses.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.5 “General Criteria on Loss Data Identification, Collection and Treatment”, item (a); see also 24.2 “The Internal Loss Multiplier”. Schweser Reading 65, Module 65.1, LO 65.c general criteria. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (polarity flip). The option makes five years the norm and ten years the extension, reversing which period is standard and which is the exception. The source makes ten years the requirement and five years the exceptional, transitional allowance. It would be correct only if the stem described a hypothetical regime in which a short window is the default and longer histories are an optional refinement.

b.reason: GARP 24.5(a): internally generated loss data calculations “must be based on a 10-year observation period. When the bank first moves to the standardised approach, a five-year observation period is acceptable on an exceptional basis when good-quality data are unavailable for more than five years.” Schweser repeats the same two layers. Option B is a faithful restatement.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). The option keeps ten years as the standard but widens the exception to “any bank” at “any time” on a supervisory finding about old data. The source confines the exception to a bank that first moves to the standardised approach and lacks good-quality data beyond five years. It would be correct if it read “a bank first moving to the standardised approach may use five years when good-quality data are unavailable for more than five years”.

d.reason: (sibling swap). Three years is the averaging window of the business indicator (the BI terms are averaged over years $t$, $t -$ 1 and $t -$ 2), not the loss data window. The option transfers the BI’s property to the loss component. It would be correct if the stem asked over how many years each BI component is averaged.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing the bank’s JPY operational loss data framework against the Basel Committee’s general criteria for the use of the loss component. She drafts the following statements for her report:

I. Because internal loss data are most relevant when clearly linked to current business activities, technological processes and risk management procedures, the bank must have documented procedures and processes for identifying, collecting and treating them.

II. The procedures and processes need to be validated only after the loss data have been used in at least one capital calculation, and then reviewed annually by the first line of defence.

III. A supervisor may request the bank to map its historical internal loss data into the Level 1 supervisory categories of Annex 9 of Basel II, and the bank must document its criteria for allocating losses to event types.

IV. The bank must have processes to independently review the comprehensiveness and accuracy of its loss data.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Japanese trust bank auditor checking four statements on loss data procedures, validation, independent review and Level 1 mapping.

**Concept and theory**

Loss data drive capital directly for banks with a BI above €1 billion, so the Basel Committee does not only specify what must be collected; it also specifies the governance around collection. GARP 24.5 lists these general criteria:

- **Relevance and documentation (b).** Internal loss data are most relevant when clearly linked to the bank’s current business activities, technological processes and risk management procedures. Therefore the bank must have documented procedures and processes for the identification, collection and treatment of internal loss data.
- **Validation and audit (b).** Those procedures and processes must be validated before the loss data are used in the capital measurement methodology, and be subject to regular independent reviews by internal and/or external audit functions.
- **Mapping and allocation (c).** For risk management purposes and to assist supervisory validation or review, a supervisor may request the bank to map its historical internal loss data into the Level 1 supervisory categories of Annex 9 of Basel II and provide the data. The bank must document criteria for allocating losses to the event types.
- **Independent review (h).** Banks must have processes to independently review the comprehensiveness and accuracy of loss data.

The logic is simple: a number that sets capital must be produced by a documented, validated process and checked by someone independent of the people who produce it.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the source:

- I restates 24.5(b): relevance rationale, then documented procedures. True.
- II reverses the timing (validation after use instead of before) and swaps the reviewer (first line of defence instead of independent internal and/or external audit). False.
- III restates 24.5(c): the supervisor may request the Level 1 mapping, the bank documents allocation criteria. True.
- IV restates 24.5(h). True.

The correct set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Validation comes before the loss data are used in capital; reviews are by independent internal and/or external audit; the supervisor may request the Level 1 mapping, the bank documents allocation criteria.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.5 “General Criteria on Loss Data Identification, Collection and Treatment”, items (b), (c) and (h). Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c general criteria. Schweser compresses (c) into “a bank must be able to categorize historical internal loss data into the appropriate Level 1 supervisory categories . . . and be prepared to provide this to supervisors when requested”; GARP frames it as a supervisory request. Same substance; GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (polarity flip, accepting corrupted statement II). Choosing “I and II only” accepts the timing reversal in II (validation after use rather than before) and also rejects two true statements. II would be correct only if it said “validated before the loss data are used, and subject to regular independent reviews by internal and/or external audit”.

b.reason: (role misassignment, accepting statement II). This set accepts II, whose reviewer is the first line of defence, the business itself, whereas the source requires independent review by internal and/or external audit. It also drops I, which is true. It would be correct only if II were rewritten with the right timing and reviewer and I were false.

c.reason:
(absolute claim). “I, II, III and IV” assumes every statement is a fair paraphrase.

Statement II fails on two counts (timing and actor). It would be correct only if II were restated faithfully.

d.reason: GARP 24.5(b): procedures and processes “must be subject to validation before the use of the loss data within the operational risk capital requirement measurement methodology, and to regular independent reviews by internal and/or external audit functions.” Statements I, III and IV are near-verbatim restatements of (b), (c) and (h). Only II is corrupted, so D is correct.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Brazilian banking group is briefing the board risk committee on loss collection thresholds under the Basel III standardised approach. The group’s business indicator is equivalent to about €14 billion. A committee member asks how the threshold for including loss events works. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The minimum threshold is €20,000; at national discretion, supervisors may raise it to €100,000 for average annual losses, for banks with a BI above €1 billion.
The minimum threshold is €20,000; the bank itself may raise it to €100,000 after its first year on the standardised approach, with no supervisory role.
The minimum threshold is €20,000; at national discretion, supervisors may raise it to €100,000 for every bank, bucket 1 banks using loss data included.
The minimum threshold is €100,000; at national discretion, supervisors may lower it to €20,000 for average annual losses, for banks with a BI above €1 billion.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian group CRO (BI about EUR 14 billion) explaining the loss collection threshold to the board risk committee.

**Concept and theory**

A loss data set must be comprehensive: GARP 24.5(d) requires internal loss data to capture all material activities and exposures from all appropriate subsystems and geographic locations. Comprehensiveness, however, does not mean recording every trivial error. A minimum threshold separates events that must be captured from immaterial noise and keeps the average annual loss comparable across banks.

GARP sets the threshold in two parts:

| Element | Rule (GARP 24.5(d)) |
|---|---|
| Default | Minimum threshold for including a loss event in data collection and in the calculation of average annual losses: **€20,000**. |
| Who can change it | **Supervisors**, at **national discretion**. |
| To what | Up to **€100,000**. |
| For what purpose | The calculation of **average annual losses**. |
| For whom | Banks in **buckets 2 and 3** only (BI greater than €1 billion). |

The higher threshold is a supervisory concession for larger banks, whose capital is driven by large losses; small events matter little to their average.

**Applying it to this question**

The question tests the five elements of the table: default value, direction of the change, actor, purpose and eligible banks. The group’s BI (about €14 billion) puts it in bucket 2, so it is eligible for the higher threshold if its supervisor exercises the discretion. Option A gets all five elements right.

**Fragile fact.** Default €20,000; supervisors, not banks, may raise it to €100,000, for average annual losses, for buckets 2 and 3 only.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.5, item (d). Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c general criteria. **Conflict:** Schweser says that when a bank first moves to the standardised approach a €20,000 gross loss threshold is acceptable and that “afterward” it may be increased to €100,000 for buckets 2 and 3, without naming the actor; GARP makes €20,000 the minimum threshold and gives the power to raise it to supervisors at national discretion, for the calculation of average annual losses. GARP used; the difference looks like Schweser compression rather than a version change.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 24.5(d): “The minimum threshold for including a loss event in the data collection and calculation of average annual losses is set at €20,000. At national discretion, for the purpose of the calculation of average annual losses, supervisors may increase the threshold to €100,000 for banks in buckets 2 and 3 (ie where the BI is greater than €1bn).” Option A states this exactly.

b.reason: (role misassignment). The option moves the discretion from the supervisor to the bank and adds a timing trigger. GARP gives the power to supervisors “at national discretion”. It would be correct if it read “the bank’s national supervisor may raise it to €100,000” (Schweser’s compressed wording, “afterward, this threshold may be increased”, is the likely source of this trap; see Reference).

c.reason: (scope or condition error). The option extends the higher threshold to every bank, including bucket 1 banks that use loss data. GARP limits it to buckets 2 and 3, where the BI exceeds €1 billion. It would be correct if “every bank” were replaced by “banks in buckets 2 and 3”.

d.reason: (polarity flip). The option swaps the two figures: it makes €100,000 the default and lets supervisors lower it to €20,000. The source has €20,000 as the default and €100,000 as the permitted increase. It would be correct only in a regime where the larger figure were the baseline.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a UK building society is drafting the GBP loss event recording standard that will support the society’s standardised approach loss data set, and is checking it against the Basel Committee’s general criteria on the information to be collected for each loss event. Which of the following statements is NOT accurate?

options.text: Descriptive information on the drivers or causes of each loss event must be collected, with a level of detail commensurate with the size of the gross loss.
The date of discovery is when the bank became aware of the event, and the date of accounting is when a loss, reserve or provision is recognised in the P&L.
The date of occurrence must be recorded for every loss event, and an event for which it cannot be determined must be left out of the loss data set.
Information on recoveries of gross loss amounts must be collected for each event, alongside the gross loss amount and the reference dates of the event.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK building society analyst checking which statement about per-event information requirements is NOT accurate.

**Concept and theory**

A loss figure without context is of little use: supervisors and the bank need to know when the event happened, when it was found, when it hit the accounts, what was recovered and why it happened. GARP 24.5(e) therefore requires, aside from the gross loss amount:

| Item | Definition and condition |
|---|---|
| Date of occurrence | When the event happened or first began, **where available**. |
| Date of discovery | When the bank became aware of the event. |
| Date of accounting | The date (or dates) when the event results in a loss, reserve or provision being recognised in the P&L. |
| Recoveries | Information on recoveries of gross loss amounts. |
| Drivers or causes | Descriptive information, in detail commensurate with the size of the gross loss. |

The phrase “where available” matters. The beginning of a long-running fraud or mis-selling may be impossible to pin down; the Committee accepts that, while the date of accounting, which drives the loss data set, is always available because it comes from the bank’s own books.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the statement that is NOT accurate. A, B and D are faithful paraphrases. C turns “where available” into an absolute requirement and adds an exclusion that the source does not contain. C is therefore the inaccurate statement.

**Fragile fact.** Date of occurrence is collected where available; discovery is awareness; accounting is P&L recognition; descriptive detail scales with the size of the loss.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.5, item (e). Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c general criteria (Schweser lists the same dates and drivers but omits “where available” and the “commensurate with size” qualifier). No conflict of substance; GARP qualifiers used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (true statement: no corruption). GARP: the bank must collect “descriptive information about the drivers or causes of the loss event. The level of detail of any descriptive information should be commensurate with the size of the gross loss amount.” A is accurate, so it cannot be the NOT-accurate statement. It would be the answer if it said the same detail is required for every event regardless of size.

b.reason: (true statement: no corruption). The definitions of date of discovery (“the date on which the bank became aware of the event”) and date of accounting (when the event results in a loss, reserve or provision being recognised in the P&L) match GARP. It would be the answer if the two definitions were swapped, a common sibling swap.

c.reason: GARP 24.5(e) requires information on “the date when the event happened or first began (‘date of occurrence’), where available”. The qualifier makes the date of occurrence a best-efforts item. Nothing in the criteria removes an event from the data set because that date is missing; indeed the data set is built on the date of accounting (GARP 24.6). C is false, so C is the answer.

d.reason: (true statement: no corruption). GARP: “the bank must collect information on recoveries of gross loss amounts”, alongside gross loss and the reference dates. D is accurate. It would be the answer if it said only net amounts need to be recorded.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German bank (BI above €1 billion) is preparing the bank’s EUR loss data set under the standardised approach. Its supervisor has not raised the collection threshold. She is reviewing four operational risk events from the past year.

| Event | Description | Loss (EUR 000) |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | Forged collateral documents on a mortgage; the loss is accounted for in credit risk RWAs as a defaulted exposure | 1,850 |
| E2 | Failure to register a security interest on a corporate loan; the loss is not accounted for in credit risk RWAs | 640 |
| E3 | A trader keys a bond order with an extra zero; the loss arises from closing out the unintended market position | 2,300 |
| E4 | An erroneous duplicate supplier payment that could not be recovered | 14 |

Which events should be included in the loss data set?

options.text: E2 and E3 only
E1, E2 and E3 only
E3 only
E2, E3 and E4 only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: German bank analyst sorting four events (credit-related, market-related, small) for the loss data set.

**Concept and theory**

Operational risk losses often sit on the border with other risk types. A forged mortgage document produces a credit default; a keying error produces a market loss. The Basel Committee needs a rule to stop the same loss being capitalised twice and to stop it slipping through the gaps. GARP 24.5 gives that rule:

| Boundary | Condition | Loss data set |
|---|---|---|
| Credit risk Credit risk | Related to credit risk and accounted for in credit risk RWAs Related to credit risk but **not** accounted for in credit risk RWAs | Excluded Included |
| Market risk | Operational risk losses related to market risk | Included |

The credit test is about double counting: if credit RWAs already capitalise the loss, it stays out. The market test is the opposite: market-related operational losses are treated as operational risk and are subject to the standardised approach. Separately, the minimum threshold (24.5(d)) is €20,000 unless a supervisor has raised it.

**Applying it to this question**

- E1: credit-related and accounted for in credit RWAs, so excluded.
- E2: credit-related but not accounted for in credit RWAs, so included (EUR 640,000 is above the threshold).
- E3: operational error producing a market loss, so treated as operational risk and included.
- E4: EUR 14,000 is below the €20,000 minimum threshold, so it is not included.

The set is E2 and E3.

**Fragile fact.** Credit-related: the test is “accounted for in credit RWAs?” (yes = out, no = in). Market-related operational losses are in.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.5, items (d), (f) and (g). Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c general criteria. Schweser states only that losses tied to credit RWAs are excluded and those tied to market risk included; GARP adds that credit-related events not in credit RWAs are included. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 24.5(f): “Operational loss events related to credit risk and that are accounted for in credit risk RWAs should not be included in the loss data set. Operational loss events that relate to credit risk, but are not accounted for in credit risk RWAs should be included.” GARP 24.5(g): operational risk losses related to market risk “are treated as operational risk . . . and will therefore be subject to the standardised approach”. Together with the €20,000 threshold this gives E2 and E3 only.

b.reason: (scope or condition error). Including E1 drops the RWA condition and treats every credit-related operational event as in scope. E1 is already capitalised in credit RWAs, so including it would double count. B would be correct if E1’s loss were not accounted for in credit risk RWAs.

c.reason: (scope or condition error: overextension). Excluding E2 applies the exclusion to all credit-related events, which is how Schweser’s compressed version reads (it mentions only the exclusion). GARP explicitly includes credit-related events that are not in credit RWAs. C would be correct if E2’s loss were reflected in credit risk RWAs.

d.reason: (dropped condition: threshold ignored). Adding E4 ignores the €20,000 minimum threshold for including a loss event in data collection. D would be correct if E4’s loss were €20,000 or more.

questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q6
questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Singapore bank on how recoveries should be treated when it builds its SGD loss data set under the Basel III standardised approach. The bank’s draft policy contains four candidate statements. Which of the following statements should the consultant endorse as most accurate?

options.text: Reductions in corporate income tax liability caused by an operational loss count as recoveries and may be used to reduce the loss in the data set.
Only non-insurance recoveries may reduce a loss; insurance recoveries stay in the loss so that the data show losses before any risk transfer.
Once an insurer confirms a claim in writing, the receivable counts as a recovery and may reduce the loss before any payment is received.
A recovery is a related but independent occurrence, separate in time, with funds received from a third party; it reduces a loss only once paid.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Consultant advising a Singapore bank on which policy statement about recoveries is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 24.6 defines three amounts that every loss event must support:

- **Gross loss**: the loss before recoveries of any type.
- **Net loss**: the loss after taking into account the impact of recoveries.
- **Recovery**: an independent occurrence, related to the original loss event, separate in time, in which funds or inflows of economic benefits are received from a third party. Examples: payments from insurers, repayments from perpetrators of fraud, recoveries of misdirected transfers.

Banks must be able to identify gross loss, non-insurance recoveries and insurance recoveries for every event, and they use losses net of recoveries (including insurance recoveries) in the loss data set. Two guard rails stop optimistic netting:

- Recoveries reduce losses only after the bank **receives payment**; receivables do not count. Verification of payments received must be provided to supervisors on request.
- Tax effects (for example lower corporate income tax because of the loss) are **not** recoveries (GARP footnote 6).

The cash-received rule exists because a promised recovery can be disputed, delayed or never paid; netting it early would understate the loss history and therefore capital.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks which policy statement is most accurate. The deciding facts are the definition of a recovery and the payment-received condition. Option D states both; each other option breaks one rule.

**Fragile fact.** Insurance recoveries are netted, but only once cash is received; receivables and tax effects are never recoveries.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.6 “Specific Criteria on Loss Data Identification, Collection and Treatment”, subsection “Gross Loss, Net Loss, and Recovery Definitions”, footnotes 6 and 7. Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c specific criteria (Schweser says data should be “net of insurance recoveries” and does not mention the receivables or tax rules; GARP nets all recoveries including insurance). GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error). The option widens “recovery” to include tax effects. GARP footnote 6: tax effects such as reductions in corporate income tax liability due to operational losses “are not recoveries”. A would be correct only if it concerned a payment from a third party such as an insurer or the perpetrator of a fraud.

b.reason: (polarity flip). The option bars insurance recoveries from netting. GARP requires losses “net of recoveries (including insurance recoveries)”. B would be correct only under a rule that netted non-insurance recoveries but kept losses gross of insurance; the Basel criteria net both kinds once payment is received.

c.reason: (scope or condition error). The option treats a written confirmation as enough. GARP is explicit: recoveries reduce losses only after payment is received, and receivables do not count. C would be correct if the insurer had already paid the claim.

d.reason: GARP 24.6: “The recovery is an independent occurrence, related to the original loss event, separate in time, in which funds or inflows of economic benefits are received from a third party” and “recoveries can be used to reduce losses only after the bank receives payment. Receivables do not count as recoveries.” Option D is a compressed but faithful statement of these two sentences.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q7
questions.question:
An operational risk analyst at an Australian bank is calculating the amount to enter in the standardised approach loss data set for a single cyber incident. The finance team has itemised the following amounts, all recognised during the current year.

| Item | Amount (AUD 000) |
|---|---|
| Settlement paid to affected clients, charged to the P&L | 2,400 |
| External legal fees directly linked to the incident | 310 |
| Cost of replacing damaged servers to restore the pre-incident position | 450 |
| Upgrade of the monitoring system after the incident | 600 |
| Annual premium on the bank’s cyber insurance policy | 85 |
| Insurance recovery received in cash | 900 |
| Further insurance claim approved by the insurer, not yet paid | 500 |
| Reduction in corporate income tax due to the loss | 320 |

What amount should the bank enter in the loss data set for this event?
questions.solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank analyst computing the loss data set amount for a cyber incident from an itemised list.

**Concept and theory**

The loss data set records each event at its net loss: gross loss less recoveries actually received. Building the number therefore takes two filters.

**Filter 1: what goes into gross loss** (GARP 24.6).

| Must be included | Must be excluded |
|---|---|
| Direct charges to the P&L (impairments, settlements) and write-downs due to the event | Costs of general maintenance contracts on property, plant or equipment |
| External expenses with a direct link to the event (legal, advisor, supplier fees) and repair or replacement costs to restore the pre-event position | Internal or external expenditure to enhance the business after the loss: upgrades, improvements, risk assessment initiatives and enhancements |
| Provisions or reserves in the P&L against the potential loss | Insurance premiums |
| Material pending losses; material timing losses (with conditions) |  |

**Filter 2: what counts as a recovery.** Only funds actually received from a third party, such as insurers. Receivables do not count and tax effects are not recoveries.

The intuition: gross loss captures the cost of the event and of putting the bank back where it was; it does not capture investment to make the bank better than before, routine costs that would have arisen anyway, or the price of insurance cover.

**Applying it to this question**

Net loss = Gross loss − Recoveries received

$$\text{Gross loss} = \underbrace{2{,}400}_{\text{settlement}} + \underbrace{310}_{\text{legal fees}} + \underbrace{450}_{\text{restore servers}} = 3{,}160 \text{ (AUD 000)}$$

Excluded : upgrade 600, premium 85

Recoveries received = 900 (approved claim 500 is a receivable; tax effect 320 is not a recovery)

Net loss = 3,160 − 900 = 2,260 (AUD 000)

The bank enters AUD 2,260,000: the cost of the incident and of restoring the pre-incident position, less the cash the insurer has actually paid.

**Fragile fact.** Restore = in, enhance = out; insurance cash received is netted, an approved but unpaid claim is not; premiums and tax effects never enter.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.6, “Gross Loss, Net Loss, and Recovery Definitions” and the inclusion and exclusion lists, footnote 6. Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c specific criteria. Schweser says “net of insurance recoveries”; GARP nets all recoveries (including insurance) once received. Here only an insurance recovery is received, so both give the same number.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error: receivable netted). AUD 1,760,000 = 3,160 − 900 − 500. It deducts the approved but unpaid insurance claim, although receivables do not count as recoveries. A would be correct if the insurer had already paid the further AUD 500,000.

b.reason: Every included item matches GARP’s inclusion list (settlement as a direct P&L charge; legal fees as external expenses with a direct link; server replacement as a cost of repair or replacement to restore the prior position). Upgrades and insurance premiums are on the exclusion list. GARP requires losses net of recoveries including insurance, but only after payment is received; receivables and tax effects do not count. B follows all these rules.

c.reason: (sibling swap: enhancement treated as restoration). AUD 2,860,000 = 2,260 + 600. It adds the post-incident monitoring upgrade, confusing an excluded enhancement with an included repair or replacement cost. C would be correct only if the AUD 600,000 had been spent to restore the system to its pre-incident state rather than to improve it.

d.reason: (intermediate result). AUD 3,160,000 is the gross loss before recoveries. The loss data set uses losses net of recoveries, including insurance recoveries already received. D would be correct if the question asked for the gross loss amount the bank must be able to identify.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q8
questions.question:
A model validation manager at a Hong Kong bank is testing whether the bank’s HKD gross loss computation follows the Basel Committee’s specific criteria. After a fire at a branch, the following costs were recorded:

I. Fees paid to external advisors and loss adjusters with a direct link to the fire.

II. The cost of installing a new fire suppression system that exceeds the branch’s pre-fire capability.

III. The cost of repairing the branch to restore the position that prevailed before the fire.

IV. The cost of the bank’s general maintenance contract on the branch’s equipment.

Which of the costs must be included in the gross loss computation?

options.text: I only
I, II and III only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Hong Kong bank validator classifying four costs after a branch fire as inside or outside gross loss.

**Concept and theory**

Gross loss is designed to measure what the operational risk event cost the bank, not what the bank chose to spend afterwards. GARP 24.6 sets out:

- **Included:** direct P&L charges and write-downs; costs incurred as a consequence of the event, including external expenses with a direct link to the event (for example fees paid to advisors, attorneys or suppliers) and costs of repair or replacement incurred to restore the position that was prevailing before the event; provisions or reserves against the potential loss; material pending losses; material timing losses that meet the conditions.
- **Excluded:** costs of general maintenance contracts on property, plant or equipment; internal or external expenditures to enhance the business after the loss (upgrades, improvements, risk assessment initiatives and enhancements); insurance premiums.

The line between repair and upgrade is the most heavily tested: spending that brings the bank back to where it was is a cost of the event; spending that takes it beyond where it was is an investment.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: external advisors and loss adjusters with a direct link to the fire. Included.
- II: a suppression system that exceeds pre-fire capability is an enhancement after the loss. Excluded.
- III: repairs that restore the pre-fire position. Included.
- IV: a general maintenance contract on equipment. Excluded.

The required set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Restore to the pre-event position = in; enhance beyond it = out; routine maintenance contracts = out.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.6, lists of items included in and excluded from the gross loss computation. Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c specific criteria. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error: repair cost dropped). “I only” omits the repair cost, treating all post-event spending as excluded. GARP includes repair or replacement costs that restore the pre-event position. A would be correct if item III described an upgrade beyond the pre-fire position.

b.reason: (sibling swap: enhancement treated as restoration). Adding II treats an upgrade beyond pre-fire capability as if it were a repair. GARP excludes upgrades, improvements and enhancements after the loss. B would be correct if II described replacing the old suppression system like for like.

c.reason: GARP 24.6 includes “external expenses with a direct link to the operational risk event (eg legal expenses directly related to the event and fees paid to advisors, attorneys or suppliers) and costs of repair or replacement, incurred to restore the position that was prevailing before the operational risk event”. Items I and III match; II and IV are on the exclusion list. C is correct.

d.reason: (sibling swap: maintenance treated as event cost). Adding IV treats a general maintenance contract as an event cost. GARP excludes the costs of general maintenance contracts on property, plant or equipment, since they arise regardless of the event. D would be correct if IV were an external supplier’s fee for emergency repairs directly linked to the fire.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is reviewing two CNY items for the bank’s standardised approach loss data set.

- A material failed payment of CNY 12 million has a definitive financial impact, but it is still booked in a suspense account and is not yet reflected in the P&L.
- A material booking error overstated revenue across two prior financial accounting periods and was corrected this year with a negative adjustment of CNY 30 million. The error has given rise to no legal risk.

Which of the following best describes how the Basel Committee’s specific criteria treat these items?

options.text: Both are required: the failed payment because its impact is definitive, and the booking error because it is material and spans more than one period.
Neither is required: the failed payment because it is not yet in the P&L, and the booking error because its net impact over time is zero.
Only the booking error is required, as it has been booked in the P&L, while the failed payment enters only once it leaves the suspense account.
Only the failed payment is required, within a period commensurate with its size and age; the booking error is not, as it creates no legal risk.

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank analyst classifying a suspense-account failed payment and a prior-period booking error with no legal risk.

**Concept and theory**

Two of GARP’s gross loss inclusions deal with losses whose accounting is out of step with the economics.

**Pending losses.** Losses from operational risk events with a definitive financial impact that are temporarily booked in transitory or suspense accounts and are not yet reflected in the P&L. GARP footnote 8 explains why: in some countries the impact of events (for example legal events or physical damage) can be known before a reserve is established, and reserve practice varies across banks. Rule: material pending losses should be included in the loss data set within a time period commensurate with the size and age of the pending item.

**Timing losses.** Negative economic impacts booked in a financial accounting period because of operational risk events that affected the cash flows or financial statements of previous periods (for example revenue overstatement, accounting errors, mark-to-market errors). Footnote 9: these events have no true net impact over time, but if the error continues over more than one period it may materially misrepresent the financial statements. Rule: material timing losses should be included when they are due to operational risk events that **span more than one financial accounting** **period and give rise to legal risk**.

| Item | Inclusion condition |
|---|---|
| Pending loss | Material; include within a time period commensurate with its size and |
| Timing loss | age Material; spans more than one accounting period; **and** gives rise to legal risk |

**Applying it to this question**

The failed payment has a definitive impact, is material and sits in a suspense account: it is a pending loss and must be included within a period commensurate with its size and age. The booking error is a material timing loss spanning two periods, but the stem says it gives rise to no legal risk, so it fails the third condition and is not required. Option D gives exactly this split.

**Fragile fact.** Pending losses: material, include within a period commensurate with size and age. Timing losses: material and multi-period and legal risk.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.6, gross loss inclusions (d) and (e), footnotes 8 and 9. Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c specific criteria (Schweser: “materiality will dictate” inclusion of pending losses, and timing losses that are material and due to events that give rise to legal risk and cross more than one accounting period). No conflict; GARP’s “commensurate with size and age” detail is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error: legal risk condition dropped). The option requires the booking error on materiality and multi-period grounds alone, dropping the legal risk condition. A would be correct if the booking error had given rise to legal risk.

b.reason: (polarity flip). The option excludes the pending loss because it is not yet in the P&L, which is precisely the situation the pending loss rule is designed to capture. Its reason for excluding the timing loss (zero net impact) is GARP’s description of why timing losses are often not true losses, not the deciding condition. B would be correct if the failed payment’s financial impact were not yet definitive (or the item were immaterial); even then, the correct reason for leaving out the booking error is the absence of legal risk, not a zero net impact.

c.reason: (sibling swap). The option swaps the two rules: it requires the timing loss because it reached the P&L and defers the pending loss until it leaves suspense. GARP requires the material pending loss now (within a commensurate period) and makes the timing loss depend on legal risk. C would be correct only if the timing loss gave rise to legal risk and the pending item were immaterial.

d.reason: GARP 24.6(d): “Material pending losses should be included in the loss data set within a time period commensurate with the size and age of the pending item.” GARP 24.6(e): “Material ‘timing losses’ should be included in the loss data set when they are due to operational risk events that span more than one financial accounting period and give rise to legal risk.” D applies both.

questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q10
questions.question:
A compliance officer at a UK bank is recording a GBP mis-selling case in the bank’s loss database. The timeline of the case is shown below.

| Step | Date |
|---|---|
| Overcharging of customers begins | 14 February 2021 |
| Internal audit identifies the overcharging | 9 November 2022 |
| Customers file a legal claim against the bank | 14 March 2023 |
| Legal reserve for the probable estimated loss established in the P&L | 30 June 2024 |
| Settlement paid to customers | 12 May 2025 |

Under the Basel Committee’s specific criteria, what is the latest reference date the bank may use to include this legal loss in its loss data set?

options.text: 30 June 2024
14 March 2023
9 November 2022

questions.solution:
Stem summary: UK bank compliance officer choosing the latest reference date for a legal mis-selling loss from a five-step timeline.

**Concept and theory**

A loss event has several dates (occurrence, discovery, accounting), and the loss data set must pick one to decide which year a loss falls into. GARP 24.6 sets the rules:

- Banks must use the **date of accounting** for building the loss data set.
- For legal events, the bank must use a date **no later than the date of accounting**.
- For legal loss events, the date of accounting is the date when a **legal reserve is established** **for the probable estimated loss in the P&L**.

Why the date of accounting? It is objective, auditable and always available (it comes from the bank’s books), unlike the date of occurrence, which may be unknown. The “no later than” rule for legal events stops a bank from postponing a legal loss until a settlement is paid: once the loss is probable and estimable and reserved, it must be in the data set.

**Applying it to this question**

Map each step to its role:

- 14 February 2021: date of occurrence.
- 9 November 2022: date of discovery.
- 14 March 2023: claim filed (a step in the legal process, not one of the reference dates).
- 30 June 2024: legal reserve for the probable estimated loss established in the P&L, so the date of accounting.
- 12 May 2025: settlement paid (after the date of accounting).

The latest date the bank may use is the date of accounting, 30 June 2024.

**Fragile fact.** For legal events the ceiling is the reserve date (the date of accounting), not the settlement or payment date.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.6, reference date paragraph; definitions of the dates in 24.5(e). Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c specific criteria. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: (wrong input twin: cash settlement for accounting date). 12 May 2025 is when the settlement was paid. It falls after the date of accounting, which the rule forbids for legal events. A would be correct only if no reserve had been established earlier and the settlement payment were the first P&L recognition of the loss.

b.reason: GARP 24.6: “The bank must use a date no later than the date of accounting for including losses related to legal events in the loss data set. For legal loss events, the date of accounting is the date when a legal reserve is established for the probable estimated loss in the P&L.” Schweser: the date of accounting is “the latest date that can be used”. B is correct.

c.reason: (sibling swap: legal trigger for accounting date). 14 March 2023 is when the claim was filed. A claim makes legal risk visible, but it is not the reserve date and it is earlier than the date of accounting. C would be correct if the bank had established the legal reserve on the day the claim was filed.

d.reason: (sibling swap: date of discovery). 9 November 2022 is the date of discovery. It is earlier than the date of accounting, so it is not the latest permitted date. D would be correct if the question asked for the date on which the bank became aware of the event.

questions.question:
A risk committee member at a Canadian bank is reviewing how a single operational risk event, an investment product mis-selling that began in 2021, has been entered in the bank’s CAD loss database. The amounts below were posted to the bank’s accounts over three years.

| Year | Accounting entry | Amount (CAD million) |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | Initial provision charged to the P&L | 4.0 |
| 2024 | Additional provision charged to the P&L | 2.5 |
| 2025 | External legal fees directly linked to the event | 1.0 |

Which of the following best describes how these losses should be allocated in the loss database?

options.text: CAD 7.5 million in 2023, the year the first amount was posted to the accounts
CAD 7.5 million in 2021, the year the mis-selling first began
CAD 4.0 million in 2023, CAD 2.5 million in 2024 and CAD 1.0 million in 2025
CAD 7.5 million in 2025, the year the final amount was posted to the accounts

questions.solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank risk committee member checking how a mis-selling event posted over three years is allocated in the loss database.

**Concept and theory**

Many operational risk events, especially conduct and legal cases, generate losses that reach the accounts in instalments: an initial provision, a top-up, then legal fees. GARP calls these grouped losses: losses caused by a common operational risk event, or by related events over time, but posted to the accounts over several years.

GARP 24.6 rule: such losses “should be allocated to the corresponding years of the loss database, in line with their accounting treatment”. This is consistent with the reference date rule: the loss data set is built on the date of accounting, so each amount sits in the year in which it was recognised in the accounts.

Why this matters: the loss component averages annual losses over ten years. Allocating everything to one year would make that year’s figure spike and would move losses into or out of the ten-year window depending on an arbitrary choice of date.

**Applying it to this question**

The three amounts were posted in 2023, 2024 and 2025. In line with their accounting treatment, each is allocated to the year in which it was posted: CAD 4.0 million in 2023, CAD 2.5 million in 2024, CAD 1.0 million in 2025. The year the mis-selling began (2021) is the date of occurrence and does not drive allocation.

**Fragile fact.** Grouped losses follow their accounting years, amount by amount; not the occurrence year, the first year or the last year.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.6, grouped losses paragraph (and the reference date rule). Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c specific criteria. **Conflict in wording:** Schweser says losses from a single event or related events recorded in different years “should be attributed to the year in which the loss actually occurred”; GARP says “allocated to the corresponding years of the loss database, in line with their accounting treatment”. GARP used; Schweser’s phrase is best read as the year each loss was recognised, not the year the event began.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (scope or condition error: first-posting year). Putting the whole CAD 7.5 million in 2023 treats the first posting as the date for all later amounts, overriding the accounting treatment of the 2024 and 2025 entries. A would be correct only if all three amounts had been recognised in 2023.

b.reason: (sibling swap: date of occurrence for date of accounting). Allocating to 2021 uses the date of occurrence. The loss data set is built on the date of accounting, and grouped losses follow their accounting treatment. B would be correct if the question asked when the event first began.

c.reason: GARP 24.6: “Losses caused by a common operational risk event or by related operational risk events over time, but posted to the accounts over several years, should be allocated to the corresponding years of the loss database, in line with their accounting treatment.” Option C is that allocation.

d.reason: (scope or condition error: final-posting year). Putting everything in 2025 waits for the last posting, deferring amounts recognised in 2023 and 2024. D would be correct only if all three amounts had been recognised in 2025.

questions.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
