questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-24 c Q12
questions.question:
A treasurer at a French bank is checking the average annual loss figure that feeds the bank’s loss component. The bank is in BI bucket 2, with a BI of €12 billion and a business indicator component of €1.77 billion. It has ten years of high-quality loss data, and its national supervisor has exercised its discretion to raise the loss threshold for average annual losses to €100,000. Qualifying losses for the previous nine years, measured on the same basis, total €54.0 million. The current year’s loss events are listed below.

| Event | Loss (EUR 000) | Event | Loss (EUR 000) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,250 | 7 | 95 |
| 2 | 2,600 | 8 | 60 |
| 3 | 3,300 | 9 | 90 |
| 4 | 150 | 10 | 70 |
| 5 | 45 | 11 | 15 |
| 6 | 80 |  |  |

What is the bank’s average annual loss for use in the loss component?

options.text: EUR 6.13 million
EUR 6.17 million
EUR 6.81 million
EUR 7.30 million

questions.solution:
Stem summary: French bucket 2 bank treasurer computing average annual losses with a EUR 100,000 supervisory threshold and ten years of data.

**Concept and theory**

The loss component (LC) of the standardised approach is built on average annual operational risk losses (LO 65.a uses them; here we only build the average). Two general criteria shape the average:

- **Observation period** (24.5(a)): ten years of data; five years only as a first-adoption exception when good-quality data are unavailable for more than five years.
- **Threshold** (24.5(d)): €20,000 by default; at national discretion supervisors may raise it to €100,000 for the calculation of average annual losses for banks in buckets 2 and 3.

So, for a bucket 2 bank whose supervisor has raised the threshold, only events of at least €100,000 count in the average, and the average is taken over ten years:

$$\overline{L} = \frac{1}{10} \sum_{y=1}^{10} L_{y}, \qquad L_{y} = \sum_{\text{events in year } y \text{ with loss} \,\ge\, \text{threshold}} \text{loss}$$

where $\overline{L}$ is average annual loss and $L_{y}$ the qualifying losses in year $y$.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: $\overline{L}$ = (previous nine years + current year qualifying losses)/10.

Threshold in force = €100,000 (bucket 2, supervisory discretion exercised)

Qualifying current-year events = 1,250 + 2,600 + 3,300 + 150 = 7,300 (EUR 000)

Below threshold, excluded = 45 + 80 + 95 + 60 + 90 + 70 + 15 = 455 (EUR 000)

Ten-year total = 54,000 + 7,300 = 61,300 (EUR 000)

$\overline{L}$ = 61,300/10 = 6,130 (EUR 000) = EUR 6.13 million

The BIC of €1.77 billion is irrelevant here: it is needed only later, when the LC (15 times $\overline{L}$) is compared with it to form the ILM. The average of EUR 6.13 million is the input that the loss component scales.

**Fragile fact.** The €100,000 threshold applies only if the supervisor raises it and only for buckets 2 and 3; the average is over the full ten-year window including the current year.

**Reference**

LO 65.c: “Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.” GARP Chapter 24, section 24.5, items (a) and (d); section 24.2 “The Internal Loss Multiplier” for the use of average annual losses. Schweser Reading 65, LO 65.c general criteria. Threshold actor conflict as noted under Q3; GARP used. Whether the threshold is tested on gross or net loss is not specified in GARP (Schweser says gross); the stem gives one amount per event so the point does not arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-24 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: The bank is in bucket 2, its supervisor has raised the threshold to €100,000 for average annual losses, and it has ten years of high-quality data, so the ten-year observation period applies. Only events 1 to 4 qualify, giving EUR 6.13 million.

b.reason: (wrong input twin: default threshold instead of the raised one). EUR 6.17 million = (54,000 + 7,300 + 440)/10 = 6,174. It applies the €20,000 default, so events 5 to 10 (total 440) are added; only event 11 (15) is dropped. B would be correct if the supervisor had not exercised its discretion and the previous nine years had been measured on the same €20,000 basis.

c.reason: (unit or period slip: wrong observation period). EUR 6.81 million = 61,300/9 = 6,811. It divides by the nine previous years instead of the ten-year observation period that includes the current year. C would be correct only if the window covered nine years, which the source does not allow.

d.reason: (intermediate result). EUR 7.30 million is the current year’s qualifying total (7,300), before it is added to the previous nine years and averaged. D would be correct if the question asked for this year’s qualifying losses.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the seven Basel II event risk categories and identify examples of operational risk events in each category.
questions.reading: ORR-1: Introduction to Operational Risk and Resilience
questions.topic: Introduction to Operational Risk and Resilience
questions.source: 2024 PE2 Q9 (also in 2023 PE2 Q9)
questions.question: A senior risk consultant is discussing different types of operational risk with a group of managers at Bank JKY. During the discussion, the consultant describes the seven Basel event categories for the classification of operational losses and provides examples of losses in each of the categories. Which of the following describes an operational loss that Bank JKY should classify in the Execution, Delivery, and Process Management loss category?

options.text: A client files a lawsuit against Bank JKY for a breach of fiduciary responsibility in the client’s investment account, and Bank JKY pays a monetary settlement to the client.
The data capture system of Bank JKY fails to capture correct market prices, causing OTC derivative trades to occur at incorrect prices and resulting in significant losses.
A rogue trader makes a series of unauthorized derivative trades, which are liquidated by Bank JKY for a sizable loss after the trades are discovered.
A corporate client of Bank JKY suffers a major financial loss from a cyber-attack and is therefore unable to make payments on its debt to Bank JKY, which triggers a default.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

The seven Basel event types: internal fraud; external fraud; employment practices and workplace safety; clients, products and business practices; damage to physical assets; business disruption and system failures; execution, delivery and process management. An event is classified by its cause, and a loss that reaches the bank as a borrower’s default is credit risk, whatever caused the default.

**Exam trap.** Boundary case in option D: an operational event at a client that leads to its default is a credit loss for the bank. Transaction capture errors are execution, delivery and process management, not fraud.

**Learning objectives tested:** ORR-1b, ORR-3c.

**Source:** 2024 PE2 Q9 (also in 2023 PE2 Q9) (All past year questions, Question 136).

a.reason: This is an operational risk in the Clients, Products and Business Practices classification related to disputes over performance of advisory activities.

b.reason: This loss was caused by an error in transaction capture, which is classified as an operational loss in the Execution, Delivery and Process Management category.

c.reason: This is a loss in the Internal Fraud category.

d.reason: This is an example of a credit risk loss for Bank JKY, even though it resulted from an operational risk event at the counterparty. Also, monetary loss due to a cyber-attack should be classified by the client in the External Fraud category.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain the Basel regulatory expectations for the governance of an operational risk management framework.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.question: The board of directors of a midsize bank has recommended that the bank improve its processes for managing operational risk. The CEO asks an enterprise risk manager to review the bank’s tools and processes for managing operational risk and to suggest improvements that are consistent with Basel II and Basel III guidelines for operational risk governance. The bank also plans to adopt the new Basel III standardized approach (SA) to determine its regulatory capital for operational risk. Which of the following actions should the manager recommend that the bank take?

options.text: Use third-party outsourcing agreements to replace most internal controls performed by senior managers and business line managers.
Develop an internal approach to model the distribution of operational risk losses and use it to determine the bank’s regulatory capital.
Require an independent review of the bank’s operational risk management framework.
Designate the risk management function as the primary owner of risk exposures within each business line.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Basel governance principles: the board approves and oversees the operational risk management framework and makes sure it is independently reviewed. Senior management implements it. Business lines own the risks. The independent risk function sets policy and challenges.

**Exam trap.** Role-sensitive. The business line, not the risk function, is the primary risk owner. Outsourcing and insurance complement internal controls; they never replace them.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q4 (All past year questions, Question 138).

a.reason: Banks should view risk transfer tools, such as outsourcing and insurance, as complementary to a process of thorough internal operational risk controls. Outsourcing should not be viewed as a replacement for internal controls or to relieve management of the responsibility to manage operational risk. In addition, outsourcing can actually introduce operational risk to the bank.

b.reason: The standardized approach does not require the use of an internal model, and in fact, the new Basel recommendation of the standardized approach for all banks phased out the earlier Advanced Measurement Approaches, in which some large banks developed internal models to determine their regulatory capital.

c.reason: The board of directors of a bank should ensure that the bank’s framework is subject to independent review by audit or other appropriately trained parties.

d.reason: Risk owners are those responsible for the consequences of the risks they generate or supervise and, as such, their assessment and mitigation. This refers to the business lines, which should serve as the primary owners of the risk taken within their business lines, and not the risk management function. Instead, the risk management function should develop and maintain policies to manage operational risk, review the business lines’ risk management activity and have the power to challenge the relevance and consistency of the business unit’s implementation of risk management controls. These responsibilities do not make the risk management function the primary owner of the risk, however.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the “three lines of defense” model for operational risk governance and compare roles and responsibilities for each line of defense.
questions.reading: ORR-2: Risk Governance
questions.topic: Risk Governance
questions.question: A community bank uses the three lines of defense approach to manage its operational risk exposures. The bank is in the process of implementing an enterprise risk management (ERM) framework, and the CRO decides to extend the three lines of defense approach to its implementation of ERM. The CRO also wants to ensure that the ERM framework appropriately reflects the bank’s risk appetite and risk culture. Which of the following actions should the CRO recommend for the bank to take?

options.text: The third line of defense should continuously monitor the bank’s implementation of its ERM framework to ensure its effectiveness.
Business line managers, as part of the first line of defense, should have the authority to take on risk exposures within the bank’s risk appetite limits.
The bank should implement a set of risk culture indicators as part of its ERM framework in order to accurately quantify the losses that could occur due to failures of risk culture.
As part of the second line of defense, the executive committee should perform an independent review of the bank’s risk management framework.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Three lines of defence. First: business line management, which owns the risk and takes it within the risk appetite. Second: the independent risk management function, which sets the framework, monitors and challenges. Third: internal (or external) audit, which independently reviews the framework.

**Exam trap.** Options A and D each give one line’s job to another. Independent review is always the third line. Risk culture indicators track culture; they cannot accurately quantify the losses from culture failures.

**Learning objectives tested:** ORR-2c, ORR-7a.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q39 (All past year questions, Question 139).

a.reason: The risk management function, which is part of the second line of defense, should have this responsibility. The third line of defense is an independent review of the firm’s risk management framework by internal or external auditors.

b.reason: Business line managers are part of the first line of defense. As the primary risk owners, they should have the authority to expose the bank to risks within its risk appetite limits.

c.reason: (See Foundations of Risk Management, chapter 8). As discussed in the Foundations section, risk culture indicators are effective metrics to include as part of an ERM program to track the current state of and trends in risk culture. However, they cannot accurately quantify losses due to culture failings.

d.reason: The third line of defense, not the second line of defense, is responsible for performing an independent review of the design and effectiveness of the firm’s risk management framework. This review should be performed by internal or external auditors who are independent of the risk management function or the firm’s senior management.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in extreme risk identification for operational risk.
questions.reading: ORR-3: Risk Identification
questions.topic: Risk Identification
questions.question: A large global bank recently held an internal workshop to develop a set of scenarios involving extreme operational risk events. An internal auditor at the bank reviews the process used to develop scenarios at the workshop as well as some conclusions drawn by the workshop participants. Which of the following would the auditor find to be most reasonable and aligned with best practices?

options.text: Participants began the workshop by reviewing a set of scenarios provided by an external industry source and used these as a guide to generate the scenarios discussed in the workshop.
Participants assigned a high probability to the occurrence of a severe new pandemic in the future given that one had occurred in the previous year.
Participants consolidated two scenarios in which different external events caused the same impact on the bank’s infrastructure into a single scenario.
Participants emphasized scenarios arising from external causes, such as geopolitical crises and cyber-attacks, as losses from internal causes were considered to be unlikely.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Scenario analysis for extreme operational risk: generate scenarios internally first, then compare with external and industry scenarios; consolidate scenarios that have the same impact on the firm; and guard against behavioural biases such as myopia (overweighting recent events) and anchoring.

**Exam trap.** Consolidating by impact is good practice even when the causes differ. Starting from vendor scenarios biases the exercise, and internal causes must not be dismissed.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q9 (All past year questions, Question 140).

a.reason: (p. 42.) The use of industry scenarios procured externally is only an appropriate practice after the bank has generated its scenarios internally. Introducing external scenarios first can bias the scenario generation process.

b.reason: (p. 41.) This introduces a bias known as myopia – the overestimation of the probability of severe events that have happened recently.

c.reason: (p. 41.) The consolidation of scenarios involving the same internal impact but different external causes is described as a reasonable practice in the scenario selection phase, as the scenarios have the same effect on the firm and can be assessed as a single operational loss scenario. This helps make the number of scenarios more manageable.

d.reason: (p. 41). A significant proportion of losses experienced by financial firms are due to internal events, and while firms often emphasize external events, these internal causes should be evaluated as well.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply the Level 1, 2, and 3 categories in the Basel operational risk taxonomy.
questions.reading: ORR-3: Risk Identification
questions.topic: Risk Identification
questions.question:
An operational risk analyst at a large bank is preparing a year-end report of the bank’s operational loss events. The analyst uses the Basel operational risk taxonomy to classify different events into Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3. As part of this process, the analyst considers the following four events that occurred during the year:

- A sales representative in the lending department forged a senior manager’s signature to approve an application for a large commercial loan that defaulted.
- The bank failed to deliver sufficient collateral to support a swap position, which was later terminated at a loss.
- Several managers in the bank’s wealth management group were found to have misused confidential customer information by sharing this information with other employees and a third-party vendor representative.
- Some personal customer information was stolen in a cyber-attack in which an external hacker broke into a database stored in the cloud.

In classifying the four events and considering the Basel taxonomy in general, which of the following actions would be most appropriate for the analyst to take?

options.text: The analyst should classify the forged signature under the Level 1 category of Clients, Products, and Business Practices.
The analyst should classify the failure to deliver sufficient collateral under the Level 3 category of Improper Business or Market Practices.
The analyst should classify the misuse of confidential information under the Level 2 category of Suitability, Disclosure, and Fiduciary.
The analyst should classify both the forged signature and the cyber-attack under the same Level 1 event-type category.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

The Basel taxonomy has three levels. Level 1: the seven event types. Level 2: categories within each event type (for example “suitability, disclosure and fiduciary” within clients, products and business practices). Level 3: examples of individual activities.

**Exam trap.** Level 3 items are examples of activities, not categories. A forged signature by an employee is internal fraud and a cyber-attack from outside is external fraud: different Level 1 types.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q17 (All past year questions, Question 141).

a.reason: This event should be classified under Level 1 as Internal Fraud

b.reason: Level 3 categories are used to describe individual activities, not categories of activities. The proper classification would be level 1: Execution, Delivery and Process Management and level 2: Transaction, Capture, Execution and Maintenance.

c.reason: This is the correct Level 2 classification of this event.

d.reason: The forged signature is classified under the Level 1 Internal Fraud category, while the cyberattack is classified under the Level 1 External Fraud category.
